Country of Publication: United States The Fifteenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination)

I bow to the one adorned with serpent-hoods, who, by means of the goad of instruction in the practice of worshiping the Supreme Lord, has brought the elephant of worldly existence under control, even though it was not inherently powerful, yet now possesses great strength.
Now, in order to define the sacrifice consisting of the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and so forth, he makes a formal promise with the second half [of the verse]:
"Next, for the sake of its application, the sacrifice is first defined."

"For the sake of its application" means for the purpose of applying—that is, for the sake of accomplishing—this aforementioned commencement of initiation (*dīkṣā*). For in initiation, the sacrifice consisting of the eternal [deities] and so forth is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) because it serves as the preliminary application; this is because its accomplishment follows immediately after that.
As it has been said:
"When the daily rite (nityāhnika) is completed, the wise person should perform the occasional rite (naimittika)."

Now, one might object: "What indeed is the purpose of initiation (dīkṣā), such that even for its commencement and application, sacrifice (yajana) is said to be a subsidiary part? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, initiation alone serves as the means for both worldly enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (mukti). (15.1)
Or, that limb [of initiation] is demonstrated as being either "by itself" or "through connection with refinement" (*saṃskāra*).

"By itself" means directly, without dependence on anything else—this is the meaning. "Through connection with refinement" refers to the process of bringing about eligibility for knowledge and so forth. Among these, *dīkṣā* pertains to one who follows the worldly path (*lokadharmin*).
For the *sādhaka*, there is the means for enjoyment (*bhoga*), and for the seedless (*nirbīja*) *putraka*, the means for liberation (*mokṣa*);

for the one following the Śiva-dharma (*śivadharmin*), there is the means for enjoyment, and for the seeded (*sabīja*) *putraka*, the means for liberation through the application of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra-yoga*). For in these two cases, once the purificatory rite has been performed by means of initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the respective goal is attained].

By means of which eligibility for yoga, knowledge, and so forth arises, through which both worldly enjoyment and liberation may be attained; "that" refers to this very [state], because it is the means for both enjoyment and liberation.
He shows this very point along with a corroborative statement:
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in whatever [place], he is appointed to that very [place]. (15.2)
"The Lord [declared] in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: 'One partakes of success through the power of mantra.
According to one's fitness, wherever a person's latent impression (*vāsanā*) lies, there he [attains it]. (15.3)
"One who is joined [to the path] does not fall from it"—thus, speaking in the *Śrīmālinīmata*, our Guru declares that initiation is a means for the attainment of enjoyment and other goals. (15.4)

The Guru, stating "in the venerable Sūkṣma-svāyambhuva and other [scriptures]," has told us that initiation is a means for enjoyment and so forth; this is the connection. This is introduced with the words "in the venerable Mālinīmata. What was said there:
"Whichever latent impression (vāsanā) has arisen for someone through the power of their inherent aptitude,
that person should be assigned to that very [practice] at the time of initiation by those who are discerning."
"Whoever is joined to a particular reality does not turn back from it.
Having thus stated that initiation itself is the means for [attaining] enjoyments, he says the same regarding liberation as well:
"And there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation;
nor does this [initiation] result in eligibility for Yoga alone. (15.5)

"Even the authority over mantras and liberation [are attained] through Śiva-initiation"—in this statement from the Mālinīvijaya, initiation is explicitly established as the means to liberation. (15.6)

The fact that initiation (dīkṣā) is the means for liberation and enjoyment has been stated by the preceding text; it is now stated again [here] through the lineage and its purificatory refinement. (15.7)

Now, one might object: "In this very context, by the subsequent passage 'And liberation [is attained] through Śiva-initiation,' it was stated that initiation is the direct means to liberation; whereas by the preceding passage, it was stated that [initiation grants] eligibility for yoga and so forth.
How then can this be stated here without such distinction? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The preceding," and so on.
"Successively" means that through initiation (*dīkṣā*) there is purification (*saṃskāra*); from that, one gains the qualification for yoga and so forth;

and from that, liberation through the perfection of yoga and enjoyment through the perfection of mantra—thus it is said to be the means for both liberation and enjoyment. Therefore, for some, initiation functions by way of purification.
It would thus be stated that it is the cause for both liberation and enjoyment. ||7||
This has not been stated only here, but also in other scriptures—as he says:
"For those who possess the resolve [to attain knowledge] but lack the capacity for the [standard] Vidyā, this method from the Guru is declared as an easy means. (15.8)
Thus, in the venerable *Mataṅga*, the means to liberation has indeed been stated.

For those who, due to ignorance and incapacity, lack the firm conviction or certainty regarding the means to liberation— that is, regarding *vidyā*, which is by nature perfect knowledge— this [instruction] is provided by the Guru.

The injunction is declared to have action as its primary element and to be an easy means; thus, their liberation would occur without effort. This has also been stated in the venerable Mataṅga-śāstra and other texts.
Now, in this context, ignorance is the effect of the impurity consisting of the soul-substance (dravyātman) which acts as an obscuration to knowledge and action;

and that [ignorance] does not cease so long as its cause remains unremoved, just as blindness does not cease for the blind so long as cataracts and the like are not removed. Upon the removal of that [cause], however, it is indeed action alone [that effects the cessation].

[The eye] is capable [of seeing], but knowledge is not [capable] of removing that [obstruction], because no efficacy [for such removal] is observed. For indeed, without the intervention of a physician, this cataract would not be removed by the mere knowledge that "this is a cataract. Action alone is the direct means for the removal of an obstruction.
Anticipating the question, "In what sense is this called 'knowledge' (jñāna)? he says:
"For Vidyā, whose very nature is perfect knowledge, is the direct liberator. (15.9)

In this context, that which is called "impurity" (*mala*) is not some kind of substance; rather, it is ignorance, and it has been established many times previously that this ignorance ceases only through the arising of knowledge. Therefore, it is rightly stated that perfect knowledge alone, by dispelling its own opposite—ignorance—is the direct cause of liberation for persons.
"For those unskilled regarding the knowledge that brings about direct liberation, ritual action is the easy means.
And this has not been explained by us as our own invention; thus he says:
"It was stated in that very [text] according to the causal relationship of the principles (tattvas)."
It is clear that the section concerning what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted is called the Vidyāpāda. || 15-10 ||

In that regard, in the venerable *Mataṅgaśāstra*, specifically in the *Vidyāpāda*, while discussing the nature of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted based on the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) of the principles (*tattva*), it is said: "Knowledge that is not intent upon the [true] process... (*sva.* 11.199).

By the reasoning stated in such passages as "thus," all of this has been clearly explained—unfaded because it is free from doubt and error; what is the use of further prolixity? It should be understood from that very source—this is the meaning. As it was said there:
"Discrimination (viveka) is that wherein the principles (tattvas), according to the distinction between cause and effect,
are described as they truly are, and that which is to be abandoned is likewise explained."
Having introduced [the topic] with: "That is to be known as the Vidyāpāda... (2.9), [it continues]:
"The bound, the binder, and the bonds—this triad is thus established."
Just as that [relationship] becomes manifest through the statement of the state of being the probandum and the probans.
"In that manner, one must speak correctly; first, let this knowledge be mastered"—thus [it is taught] in many ways through the medium of questions and answers. (6.3) || 10 ||

Now, one might object: "If knowledge alone is the direct means of liberation, then what is the purpose of initiation and the other practices comprised within the three remaining feet [of the system], such as ritual action? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But for those who are incapable in that regard, there are initiation, ritual conduct, and meditative absorption."

"But surely, in this way, the state of Śadāśiva is attained through yoga, or through conduct, or else through initiation; or liberation is attained through the differentiation of the mind, or else the fourfold [attainment]? (Mataṅga 26.63)
Based on such statements, liberation would occur without distinction from all four—knowledge and the rest;
so how can knowledge, or even the Guru who possesses it, be considered supreme in every respect?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
Since they are preceded by knowledge, therefore the knower is the highest of the high.
"Preceded by knowledge"—the sense is that practice must indeed occur after one has gained understanding. ||11||

Now, one might object: "According to the reasoning just stated, there could be no eligibility for yoga, knowledge, and so forth without initiation; therefore, it must be said that knowledge is preceded by initiation.
On the contrary, how is this stated otherwise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

And since that knowledge is derived from scripture, and scripture must not be heard by one who has not been initiated, therefore initiation serves for him merely as a purificatory rite (saṃskāra). || 15.12 ||
"One who is not initiated should not be made to hear [the teaching]," and "it is for the purpose of mere purification. As it has been said:
"One should not utter the Śiva-paddhati in the presence of those who are uninitiated";
for only one who is a Śaiva and thus purified becomes fit for its recitation.
Likewise, in listening, studying, performing oblations, worship, and so forth.
"One whose self is purified through conduct and meditation attains the state of the Lord. (Svacchandatantra 4.79).
Thus [it is said]. ||12||

Now, one might object: "Since this [initiation] would serve merely for purification (*saṃskāra*), why was it said that by the power of this *yojanikā*, one may attain and reach various specific levels? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Wherever he may be joined by the Guru, the knower attains a fruit that is appropriate to his own realization; indeed, it was said of old that "he is a knower. (15.13)

The phrase "appropriate for one's own consciousness" means that even a *samayin* who has not yet been joined to the reality (*tattva*) of Śiva may attain identity with That by practicing knowledge in such and such a manner; this is the intended meaning. The word "previously" refers to the beginning of the fourth chapter and so forth. (13)
For one who has been purified by an intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*), there is no further need for the application of those purificatory rites; thus he says:
"But for him whose divine fitness has arisen through the grace of the Lord, there is no utility whatsoever for initiation, whether for the Guru or for the disciple. (15.14)

Now, one might object: "If initiation has no utility for such a teacher and disciple, then how could they possibly have the qualification for the acquisition of knowledge and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that case, knowledge itself is the initiation, according to the teaching of the venerable *Traiśika*."
"Knowledge" here refers, by implication, to innate knowledge (*sāṃsiddhika*). As it is said there:
"For one who knows thus according to reality, initiation leading to liberation occurs without doubt, even without the offering of sesame seeds and clarified butter. (Parātrīśikā 25)
Having begun thus, [it says]:
"That yogi shall eternally possess accomplishment; he is truly initiated.
Thus.
And it is said that only one who possesses that [realization] is the supreme and most qualified candidate in all the scriptures—thus he says:
"The state of knowing the meaning of all scriptures arises for him spontaneously. (15.15)

Thus, according to the venerable *Mālinī-nīti*, he who possesses innate consciousness is the one of supreme qualification; for such a person, being possessed of knowledge, is considered a Guru. (15–16)
"Of innate consciousness" (sāṃsiddhika-saṃvidi) means one whose correct reasoning (sattarka) functions spontaneously. As was stated previously:
"He who possesses this correct reasoning spontaneously is qualified for everything."
He has been consecrated and initiated by the goddesses of his own self-awareness.
"He alone is proclaimed as the foremost among all teachers. (4.43) ||16||
And that knowledge of his is said in the scriptures to have all things as its object—thus he says:
"Whether for oneself or for others, one who desires their welfare should cause this to be known.
By this statement, all of that has been made manifest in the Mālinīśāstra (verses 15–17).
Regarding the phrase "having spoken thus": as it was stated there— "All this must be fully understood by the yogin who desires his own welfare or that of others; otherwise, it cannot be attained."

The word "that" refers to innate knowledge (*sāṃsiddhika-jñāna*). "All" means having as its object the entirety of the fourfold system beginning with the sciences (*vidyā*)—this is the meaning. It has already been stated that for this [innate knowledge], only knowledge regarding one's own self is required; however, those [knowledges] pertaining to others are manifold.

With reference to the distinction of that [disciple's] disposition, one must take into account all [factors] such as ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth, by which his favor may be accomplished. It is with this very intention that it is said: "One who is skilled in the meaning of the *Vidyāpāda* and maintains the sequence of the *Kriyāpāda*..."
One who has practiced the yoga of the foundational steps (yogapāda) and follows the path of conduct (caryāpāda).
"The Guru should perform the initiation...
and so forth; this has been stated elsewhere [in other texts]. ||17||
An objection is raised: "What is the proof for the statement that others are diverse? Anticipating this, he says:
"Some are fit for knowledge, and likewise others are fit for conduct;
some are fit for initiation, and others are fit for yoga—thus it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa* ritual manual. (15–18)
As it is said there:
"O Tārkṣya, the Lord bestows grace exactly upon those who exist in whatever state they may be;
and among them, some are fit for ritual action, and their liberation is likewise of that same nature."
"Likewise, some are fit for knowledge, while others are fit for conduct;
thus, for each person, liberation is attained precisely through that which has been prescribed for them. (18)
Thus, this much has been established; so he says:

"In that regard, one who possesses the characteristics described, who is proficient in action, yoga, and knowledge, and who is superior by virtue of the progressively higher stages, is declared to be the Guru. (19)
As it has been said:
"The yogin is superior to the performer of ritual action; and he is even more so than the one possessed of knowledge.
And he alone is authorized for the rite of initiation; thus it is said:
"Having examined or questioned the disciple who has been purified by one of the aforementioned descents of power (śaktipāta), he should perform the rite of initiation. (15–20)

Or, in the case of an alternative: since his state of desiring worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣutā*) or desiring liberation (*mumukṣutā*) has not been directly perceived through examination, the Guru should perform the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*) with reference to the question: "Are you one who desires enjoyment, or one who desires liberation? (20)
In this context,
according to the perspective expressed in [the passage], "Initiation (dīkṣā) is taught in the Svacchanda," it is primarily in the Śrī Svacchandaśāstra itself that initiation is [discussed].

The definition has been stated; however, we too shall express it here as being adorned on all sides by that very purpose. To indicate this, he corroborates it right at the outset: "And it is said in the *Svacchanda-śāstra* that the Guru himself should question the disciple:"
Whatever kind of fruit you desire, I shall undertake the corresponding means.

The attainment of the goal, impelled by mantra, occurs according to the difference in latent impressions (*vāsanā*); that is, whether the form is one of enjoyment (*bhukti*) or liberation (*mukti*). The means is the procedure of initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*). The latent impression of the disciples is "I am one who desires enjoyment" or "I am one who desires liberation," and that of the Guru is likewise of such a kind.
"I shall perform initiation for him"—this is a specific mental synthesis; the goal to be accomplished is either worldly enjoyment or liberation.

One might object: "Could there not also be a distinction [in the ritual] due to the differences in mantras and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the homa, the status of mantras, mudrās, paths, and substances is common [to all]. (15.22)
The fruit for disciples and for the Guru differs according to the distinction of their latent impressions (vāsanā).
For there is no superiority whatsoever in the mantras and so forth regarding either worldly enjoyment (bhukti) or liberation (mukti)—this is the intended meaning.
And for this very reason, there is a distinction among disciples; thus he says:
"The practitioner is of two kinds: one who follows the Śaiva dharma and one whose state is abandoned by the world. (15.23)

One who conforms to worldly dharmas, one who desires fruits, one established in the auspicious and abandoned by the inauspicious, one desiring liberation in two ways, the seedless, and one devoid of the pledges and so forth. || 15-24 ||

One who is a child, an infant, an elderly person, a woman, one addicted to enjoyments, or afflicted by disease and so forth—another type is the "with-seed" (sabīja) initiation, for whom such [a rite] is taught in the teaching of Śiva. (15–25)
But for those learned ones who can endure the pairs of opposites, there is the initiation with seed (*sabījā*) consisting of the *samaya*;
it is a grace-bestowing initiation that must be observed, as indeed are the specific *samayas* by them. (15–26)

In this context, the seeker who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) is the practitioner (*sādhaka*). He is of two kinds: one who follows the way of Śiva (*śivadharmī*) and one who follows the worldly way (*lokadharmī*).

The seeker who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) is the spiritual son (*putraka*). He is also of two kinds: the "seedless" (*nirbīja*) and the "with-seed" (*sabīja*). Only the "with-seed" type, having received initiation, is the teacher (*ācārya*)—such is the distinction. [This concludes the section on] the state of being a *samayin*.
Furthermore, because he is a vessel worthy of attaining this very state, he is not mentioned here separately. As it has been said:
"The [initiate] consisting of the rule (samayin) is like a prince. He is "devoid of the rules and so forth" because children and others lack the capacity to observe them.

It is "of the nature of the pledge" (*samayātmikā*) because the learned ones and others possess the capacity to maintain it; for this very reason, it has been stated by them that the specific pledges (*viśeṣasamaya*) must be observed. As it is said therein:
"In that regard, there are two kinds of practitioners (*sādhaka*); among them, one is established in the Śiva-dharma."
The path purified by the Śiva-mantra is joined with the mantra of the object to be accomplished.
One who possesses knowledge, has been consecrated, and is devoted to the propitiation of mantras—
he, the practitioner of Śiva, is indeed worthy here for the threefold accomplishment.
The second stands on the worldly path, devoted to the performance of sacrifices and charitable works;
performing rituals while desiring their fruits, he is established solely in the auspicious and abandoned by the inauspicious.
"His duty is always the destruction of inauspicious portions by means of mantras" (4.86);
and:
"The seeker of liberation is said to be of two kinds: the seedless and the one with seed."
For children, the ignorant, the elderly, women, those addicted to sensual pleasures, and those afflicted by disease.

For them, O Dear One, initiation is seedless (nirbījikā), devoid of the rules of conduct (samaya) and so forth; however, for those who are learned and capable of enduring the pairs of opposites, it is proclaimed to be seeded (sabījā).
For them, initiation is the bestower of grace, conjoined with the conduct of the rules (samayācāra),
as well as the specific rules of conduct proclaimed in the section known as Mantra.

"These [two] must be protected here with effort by one who desires the attainment of liberation; however, that [initiation] which resides in the *putraka* and the *ācārya* should be known as 'with seed' (*sabījā*). (Svacchanda Tantra 4.90). Thus [it is said]. ||26||
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of initiation for these [beings], and of what kind is it, and for whom?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One should thoroughly contemplate the non-existence of those actions that occurred previously."
For one who desires liberation and is indifferent to worldly concerns, only *prārabdha* karma remains; it cannot be purified.
For the sake of the practitioner’s prosperity, one should purify [the elements] in this very manner;
this initiation, which conforms to the nature of Śiva, removes the worldly dharmas. (15.28)

This initiation, which belongs to the worldly way (*lokadharminī*), is for those whose nature is unrighteous; it is not a purification for those who are virtuous, as it is devoid of the propitiation of mantras. (15.29)
"Of those belonging to the past" means those acquired here in previous births prior to initiation; "those belonging to the future" means those to be performed here after initiation.
"Of the independent one" means...

Because, unlike the practitioner (sādhaka), there is no orientation toward enjoyment [in the case of the soul already liberated]. Anticipating the objection—"What then is the destiny of that which is currently oriented toward bestowing the fruit?"—he says: "One should not purify that which has begun; it is purified only through experience."
Because of its excessive flow. As it has been said:
"That by which this [world] exists is indeed through experience.
And for the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the purification of karma occurs in this very manner; however, that is for the sake of prosperity, for him.

For indeed, because of the inclination toward enjoyment (*bhoga*), the mind is permeated precisely by those latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it is for this very reason that the point previously asserted—that there is a difference in results due to the difference in latent impressions—has been established here. As it has been said:
"But for the sake of the practitioner's prosperity, one should thus purify prior karma."
"And having meditated upon that which moves according to prior karma and is situated as one, one should initiate [the disciple]. (4.142).

And here, the author of the *Uddyota*, setting aside the reading "in this manner" (*ittham*) and reading instead "one" (*ekam*), explains that from among the auspicious and inauspicious karmas that initiate the body, one should purify even that single inauspicious [karma] of this [disciple].
That [explanation] is to be disregarded, because it has already been demonstrated that it is impossible to sever the karma that has begun its effects and that initiates the body,
and because such a thing is not recorded anywhere in the scriptures. For this very reason,
it is stated even in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
In this very way, through the yoga of action, even the elemental [nature] becomes both supreme and non-supreme;
however, the *prārabdha* karma of the embodied soul remains for the purpose of not separating from the body.
"One should join with and protect that which is to be accomplished through Śaiva practice;
one should burn away anything else along with its consequences.
Thus it was stated by the author of the treatise. And because of its appropriateness, this reading has been adopted here by us.
He is protected. By him, "in this manner" means in the way that will be described, and that [manner] is stated in the second half [of the verse].
"That which removes worldly dharmas" is because of being intent upon the propitiation of mantras and so forth.
"Of those whose nature is unrighteousness" refers to both past and future [beings], but not to those who have already begun a physical body.
Because the statement "one should not purify *prārabdha* alone" has universal applicability; as it has been said:
"It causes the destruction of both past and future unrighteousness (*adharma*).
And in the case of [the initiation] that bestows immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadā*), although there are indeed karmas that initiate the body...
Although its purificatory nature will be explained [later], nevertheless, this [purification] is intended only for one whose death is imminent;

thus, there is no purification here for those who have already begun their work, but rather for those who have completed their task and whose [karmic] residue is nearly exhausted. Therefore, even in that case, this [teaching] does not become devoid of scope. || 29 ||
Anticipating the question, "What would happen to him because of this?", he says:
"But upon the dissolution of the body that was commenced [in this life], he enjoys the powers such as aṇimā and so forth;
having enjoyed them, he goes upward to where he is joined with the Sakala or the Akala [state]. (15.30)

In this context, wherever it may be— according to the principle stated in such passages as, "Whoever should desire enjoyments in whatever place..."— in any intended world-sphere (*bhuvaneśvara*) or the like, whether it be the *sakala* [state] or otherwise; and furthermore...
At the conclusion of the enjoyment of the fruits of auspicious karma, the seeker of liberation, having been joined with the partless Śiva, shall go to that very state.
As it has been said:
"Having established the one who follows worldly dharma in the Lord of the universe, who is the object of [one's] devotion..."
"One should effect the attainment of those qualities, or the desire for liberation in Śiva.
Thus [ends verse] 30.

Having thus determined the initiation for enjoyment (*bhogadīkṣā*), he now determines the initiation for liberation (*mokṣadīkṣā*): "In the seedless initiation (*nirbījā*), one should purify the bond of conventional conduct (*samayācāra*).
Through initiation alone, liberation occurs, provided there is constant devotion toward the God and the Guru. (15.31)
This very [initiation] is called "seedless" (nirbījā) because it bestows immediate liberation;
it is that which severs the three bonds (pāśatraya) consisting of the past, the future, and those already undertaken.

"By initiation alone," and not by the performance of daily rites (*nitya*) and so forth, because children and others lack the capacity for that; for this very reason it was stated previously: "devoid of the rules (*samaya*) and so on.
In this [initiation], the only necessary rule is devotion to the deity and the guru; thus it is said: "by devotion to the deity..."

Regarding the word "gurau" (in the teacher): this *nirbīja-dīkṣā* not only bestows immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇa*), but furthermore, by severing the three bonds (*pāśatraya*)—those of the past, the future, and those already begun—it is called "bestowing immediate liberation"; such is the connection [of the text].
Anticipating the question, "What would happen even by this twofold method?",
he says: "At the conclusion of initiation, for one who is purified, there is the supreme state upon the abandonment of the body—
whether that purified person remains for some time or not."
Anticipating the objection that there may be a distinction even when one who possesses the seed (sabījā) abandons the body, he says:
"Upon the abandonment of the body, [the practitioner] perishes due to the absence of karma in the case of the 'with-seed' [practice]. (15.33)
One who has been initiated must always observe the bond of the conduct of the *samaya*.

In this initiation which possesses a seed (*sabījā*) and consists of the observance of the *samaya*, if there is an absence of— that is, a failure to perform— the rite known as the observance of the *samaya* even at the time of casting off the body, one perishes.
For some time,

by the principle stated in such passages as, "O Goddess, due to the transgression of my command, you shall become a flesh-eater for a hundred years," he fell away from his own Śiva-nature and attained the state of a carnivore.

One who has been initiated by means of initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣā*) should, like one initiated by means of seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*), maintain the bond of the rules of conduct (*samayācārapāśa*) even if it has not yet been purified; he should be solely intent upon its performance, so that he may always be animated by the attainment of the state of Śiva.

Having thus explained the reality of initiation and the initiate according to the system of the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra*, he introduces the actual performance of the rite of initiation that was previously commenced:
"Having asked thus, having fully understood, and having deliberated himself, the Guru... (15.34).
Desiring to bring about that appropriate [state], one should resort to such a latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Thus, the Guru himself should ask the disciple,
"Are you a seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*)," and [he should adopt] whichever of those two states has been expressed by him.

Having fully understood that [state] and having examined it according to its intense, mild, or other forms, one who desires to properly perform the appropriate initiation— whether it be for a seeker of worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or another type—
should resort to a corresponding latent impression (*vāsanā*) such that, for these two [types of seekers], only that which is suitable for them [is realized].
There would be the attainment of each respective fruit.
One might ask: "What would happen to this person through such an effort directed toward another? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For one upon whom the descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred, the teacher [has no choice] regarding initiation. (15.35)
"Śambhu has declared the injunction that one should not show contempt [at the time of ritual action] for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra.
As it is said:
'And no contempt should be shown at the time of action regarding the deliverance from saṃsāra.'"
"One who obstructs a disciple during the instruction on mantras, initiation, or vows shall become a denizen of hell.
Thus it is said.
In this matter, it is not only that he must act in accordance with [the disciple's] lack of suitability, but also in accordance with his suitability;
thus he says:
"The Guru himself should perform the initiation of a poor person using his own wealth. (15.36)
Or even if a child begs for initiation with mere *dūrvā* grass and water;
as it is said:
"Initiation must be performed even by one who lives like a dog, even for a child whose wealth has been exhausted."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: "If even the Guru were to be without wealth, what would be the recourse for these two? To this it is replied: "Even with dūrvā grass and water. It is with this very intention that it is stated here and there: "...one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth."
Thus it has been stated. Or, one who possesses the intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*) may, even after begging, take wealth for the sake of initiation; thus he says, "Or else," and so forth.
One might object: "How indeed can wealth that is tainted by the fault of being acquired without harming others be fit for sacrifice and other such rites? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The disciple [should offer] wealth—whether obtained through begging or his own—to the Guru first. (15.37)
One should give that by which it becomes purified and attains fitness for sacrifice;
"one's own" refers to that which has come down through the lineage of one's ancestors.

Having thus examined the suitability (*aucitya*) of the disciples— characterized by their respective capacities according to their various distinctions— he prepares this introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*) in order to expound the different types of ritual bathing and so forth:
"In that regard, first [is] that very immersion into the sovereignty of attaining the state of Śiva" (15.38).
For he alone should be made the Guru, since he is capable of performing initiation;
nor is this impossible to accomplish—as he says: "And his immersion into the state of Śiva has been shown to have many means. (15.39)

The sequential external form, however, has been demonstrated through bathing, ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth; by implication, this refers to the non-sequential form, while the sequential form is now being shown—this is the remainder of the sense.

Now, one might object: "If the penetration into the state of Śiva (*śivatāveśa*) can be achieved through even a single act such as ritual bathing, then what is the purpose of teaching so many of these? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In those various and numerous rites, [one should realize] Śiva-nature within the heart. (15.40)
Maintaining this firmly, one of serene intellect attains the state of Śiva;
having become Śiva, whatever he may desire, that he strives to accomplish. (15.41)
The external means consisting of the conceit of being Śiva is not the giver of liberation;
therefore, it is his firm internal conviction of the penetration of Śiva-nature alone that bestows the attainment of the desired goal—
thus he says:
"This is Śiva; I am indeed Śiva"—thus [should be the realization] of both teacher and disciple. (15.42)
For the conviction of firmness through the relationship of cause and its possessor is indeed what liberates the individual soul (aṇu).
And this is established not only by logic, but also from scripture—as he says: "There is no external without the internal, nor is there an internal devoid of the external. (15.43)
"That [reality] is accomplished through knowledge and action; it shines forth as the second.
Thus the Lord described it in the *Śrībrahmayāmala*. (15.44)
"That which is second" is the definition of the internal. ||44||

Now, one might object: "Granted that this be so, nevertheless, bathing is the antidote to impurity; yet that [impurity] cannot possibly exist for one who possesses the identification with Śiva—so what is the use of it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And in the venerable Ānandaśāstra, there is no impurity for the wise man."
However, bathing and wearing fine garments will produce contentment. || 15-45 ||
"Thus the Lord described"—this connects with what precedes.
*Tuṣṭi* (contentment) is the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) of supreme bliss through the orientation toward one's own true nature.

For this very reason, for those who bathe [in the sacred waters], there occurs an effortless immersion into supreme consciousness through the subordination of the subjectivity of the body and so forth, according to their respective capacities; thus he says:
"There, by means of the sequence of purification of the well-known subjects such as the body..."
Then, for those who bathe therein, there shall be internal purity effortlessly, from within and without.
"Tataḥ" means after the bath. ||46||
Now, one might object: "Bathing indeed consists of sprinkling with water and other external substances; how could it be so by means of that alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the bathing of the God of gods is that which is called his eightfold form."
In that very state, when the internal impurities have been burnt by the blazing of the mantra, there is immersion. (15.47)
"In the burning of impurity" means for that purpose. Here, the reason is "because of the blazing of the mantra";

otherwise, even cowherds would perform entering and exiting within the dust of cows, and even fish would dwell within the water—thus, bathing would be accomplished by everyone spontaneously, without distinction. || 47 ||
He explains this very point through the sequence beginning with earth:

"There, having placed the heart of the chosen mantra [within himself], and having gone three steps into the dust of the cows' tracks and returned, one should perform the earthly bath which bestows steadfastness. (15.48)
Then, having shaken off impurities with clay consecrated by the Astra-mantra, one should gradually wash from the head down to the feet with water consecrated by the five-limbed mantras.
One should immerse oneself while reciting the mantra called *sāṅgamūla*, until one becomes absorbed in it;
then, having risen, one should contemplate the sky as containing within it the entire radiant light of the deity.
One should satisfy the Sun, the satisfier of the universe, with water using the *mālinī* [mantra];
"with the desired [mantra]" means being intent on the application of whichever mantra is preferred.
"Consecrated" means seven times. "Shaken of impurity" means, by implication, according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). "Five" refers to the *astra* [mantra].
Because it is prescribed for ritual bathing (malasnāna). As it has been said:
"Even in the case of bathing with water, one should take earth over which the Weapon-mantra (astra) has been recited seven times."
For the sake of impure bathing, one should smear the body according to the sequence of withdrawal;
thereafter, one should cover it from the head downwards with the five limbs of the Vidyā.
"One should perform the consecration with the root mantra itself, accompanied by the six limbs. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.6).

And regarding this, the teachers maintain that "the root" here refers to the *parā* [mantra]. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "from the head down to the feet," the mouth, heart, and secret place are included; as he will state:
"...in the mouth, heart, secret place, and feet... (54).

The meaning is that one should satisfy the Sun with water—that is, one should perform the rite of *upasthāna* by casting a handful [of water] toward him. The reason for this is that [the Sun] contains within himself all the deities of the pure light (*sajjyotis*).
And [it is called] "the one who satisfies all."
He elaborates on the very fact that [the offering] satisfies all:
"The gods, the ancestors, the sages, the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, and other elemental beings. (15.51)
The vital breath (prāṇa), whose essence is vigor, satisfies everything, and it is that very breath which is the Sun;
therefore, one should recite the supreme, singular mantra according to the previously described method of pronunciation. || 15.52 ||
This is considered the water-bath until the realization of identity with That [the Self] occurs;
it is the ash arising from fire, consecrated with the weapon-mantra, which removes impurity. (15.53)
Then, having consecrated the ashes with the five limbs [of the mantra] at the mouth, heart, secret place, feet, and head,
one should thereafter throw a handful of ashes— over which the root mantra has been recited along with its limbs— upon the head.
Having washed the hands and feet with water alone, one performs the sipping of water (ācamana) and so forth;
the libation (tarpaṇa) and recitation (japa)—this indeed is the fiery bath of ashes (bhasmasnāna).
When the wind is neither excessive nor deficient, and is pleasant, one should perform the Vāyavya bath while reciting mantras during the practice of going out and returning. || 15.56 ||
When one sits with the gaze fixed one-pointedly upon the pervasive sky while recollecting the mantra, what greater purity could there be than that? (15.57)
Or, while engaged in the recitation of mantras, if one should touch the body with water falling from a cloudless sky— such is the "celestial bath" (nābhasa-snāna).
Thus, by contemplating the splendors of the moon and the sun with the nature of Śiva, one becomes immersed [in them];
having washed away all impurity, where indeed would such a person not become fit? (15.59)
The Self alone is the Supreme Lord, the great lake devoid of ritual conduct;
having submerged the universe therein, He remains as both the pure and the purifier. (15.60)
For he, as the sun itself, would satisfy the entire multitude of living beings, beginning with the gods; by him being satisfied, everything becomes satisfied—this is the meaning.
Since no distinction is specified, this life-force (*prāṇa*), whose essence is vigor, [satisfies] all of this.

The meaning is that this entire universe is indeed enlivened by [the breath]. The word "ca" (and) indicates a reason. "Tataḥ" (then) means immediately after the worship of the Sun. "Ekām" (one) refers to the single-syllabled [mantra].
And this should be performed preceded by the general rites of sipping water (ācamana), the Aghamarṣaṇa, sprinkling (mārjana), and ritual placement (nyāsa). As it has been said:
"Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the purification (mārjana) with the *bhūrivarṇā* vidyā;
having performed the general ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* with the second [vidyā];
and one should perform the worship (upasthāna) with the *mālinī*, while reciting the supreme single-syllable [mantra]. (Mālinīvijaya Tantra 8.8)

"O Agni," [refers to] the auspicious fire; "having recited" means seven times. "Consecrated" (mantritam) means having performed the consecration. "Possessing the dust of cows" (gorajovatī) is the clear reading. "Mantra" refers to the Astra-mantra and Parāparā.
As it has been said:
One should perform the Vāyavya bath with dust raised by cows;
while reciting the Mahāstra mantra, one should walk seven steps while absorbed in meditation.
"That very [state] may return again by recollecting the higher and the lower.
By the word "purity," its utility here is stated. "In this way"—by means of the practice of going and coming and so forth.
"Worthy"—meaning one who possesses the qualification (*adhikārī*). "Great lake"—this is said because of the suitability for bathing. It is the purifier.
Thus—the vision of the supreme sight belongs to another as well. ||60||
He concludes this very point by adding further details: "Thus, these eight ablutions are progressively more excellent for the sake of purification.
In every case, one should subsequently bring forth that mantra as a unified whole. (15.61)
"Everywhere"—that is, even in the eightfold ritual bathing (*snānāṣṭaka*). "Him"—referring to that which was previously deposited in the sun and so forth.
"Becoming one"—with one's own self. As it has been said:
"Having taken up the mantra from the sun and so forth, one should go while recollecting the weapon-mantra (*astra*)."
Thus [ends section] 61.
Anticipating the question, "What would come of this [practitioner's] eightfold bath? he says:
"The sage devoted to the eightfold bath attains, in due order, stability, nourishment, the burning away of impurities, vigor, pervasion, purity, maintenance, and non-duality. (15.62)
Now, one might object: "Since earth and the other elements are insentient, how could they bestow such fruit? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For these eight forms are of the nature of Śiva and consist of grace;
by meditating upon them both in their own essential nature and as the form of Śiva, they grant their respective fruits. (15.63)
The meaning is that if they were of the singular nature of Śiva, their very state as a group of eight would not exist—this is the point.
Not only would this result from bathing and so forth, but it would also follow from their worship; thus he says:
"By this procedure, during worship, one should perform the conjunction of the kandādhāra and the other [centers]."
By performing [the ritual] through both detailed and concise methods, one shall enjoy the fruit thereof, beginning with the earth.

By this method— consisting of meditation and so forth upon both the essential nature (svarūpa) and the form of Śiva— one effects the placement of the elements beginning with earth, both concisely and in detail, within the support of the bulb (kandādhāra) and other locations for the purpose of worship;
thereby, one partakes in the fruits such as stability (dhṛti) and others associated with those forms of the elements beginning with earth.
The meaning is: "he obtains. ||64||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not been stated that in all cases worship cannot occur without mantras? And since mantras consist of the supreme light of 'I-consciousness' (ahaṃprakāśa), what indeed is this specific difference in their fruit?
He pacifies this doubt by demonstrating the meaning of the scriptures:
For thus, in the movement of yoga, the mantras on earth are of the nature of the earth; those in water are of the nature of water, and so on, until in Śiva they consist of the nature of Śiva. (15.65)
The intention is that these [entities] existing in the midst of the time-periods (adhvan) possess their own specific fruits.
Regarding this point as well, he says that it has been stated in another manner:
"In the venerable *Nirmaryāda-śāstra* also, that has been well-determined in this way."
And there is a specific distinction regarding the earth that is approved by heroic practitioners.
The dust of battle, the water of heroes, the ashes of heroes, the great wind, the cremation ground, the forest, the sky, and the moon and sun situated therein; 15.67.

The Self, firmly established by having shaken off all afflictions of conceptual construction without exception—this is the eightfold form to be worshipped by heroes during bathing, ritual offerings, and other such acts. (15.68)
"In this manner" means by the method that is about to be described, and that has been stated in the passage beginning with "the earth and so forth.
"Hero-water" is the water of Śiva; "hero-ash" is that which arises from the cremation fire. "Great wind" is the whirlwind carrying the dust of the cremation ground. (68)
Not only has this octad of baths for heroes been taught, but elsewhere even a ninth—the bath of liquor—is mentioned; thus he says:
"In the venerable *Triśiras*, it is declared [to be performed] with liquor, rum, wine, and so forth."
[Water] that is delicious, clear, light, and very fragrant. || 15-69 ||
Having performed the fivefold consecration internally and externally upon the *kandala* and other vessels, one should perform inspection, sprinkling, striking, nourishing, and veiling. (15.70)
In the center of that wheel of mantras, one should perform worship and the sprinkling of drops;
by means of that, there is self-consecration and the ritual empowerment with the vase-mudrā.

The propitiation of the deities, which relies upon both the path of the body and the path of the vital breath, enjoys the fruit of all sacred fords, austerities, sacrifices, gifts, and so forth. (15.72)
Through bathing in wine, the supreme practitioner who seeks liberation becomes solitary (kevalī).

Regarding the phrase "with wine, *śīdhu*, *surā*, and so forth": *madya* refers to various kinds of intoxicants produced from grapes and other sources, designated by terms such as *madya*; *śīdhu* is that made from sugarcane; *surā* is that prepared from *vibhītaka* and other ingredients.
By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of its varieties, such as *vāruṇī* and others.
As those who know Āyurveda say:
"Mārdvīka is to be known as honey... [and so forth].
Thus:
"....................śīdhu [is made] from sugarcane juice.
Thus.
"Light and wholesome is the *vaibhītaka* liquor that is not excessively intoxicating.
And:
"The *vāruṇī* is known as *prasannā*, and likewise the *parisrut* wine."
"Kādambarī is thick wine; below that, jagala is prescribed. And:
"With the subtle"—meaning with the light. "Internally and externally"—the meaning is "having that form.
By this, the inspection is internal in form, while the sprinkling is external in form. Thus it has been stated there:
Beholding with the vision of the mantra and sprinkling with the water of the arghya offering.
There was striking with the king of weapons, as well as nourishing with the eye.
"Enveloping even with the armor [mudrā]...
and so forth. Regarding the "vase mudrā" (*kalaśamudrā*), its characteristics are as follows:
the two hands have their fingers joined together, with the backs of the hands placed within the interior of a half-moon.
"With the thumbs closely joined at the base, this is proclaimed as the Kumbha-mudrā.
Elsewhere, its definition is stated:
"Having bound that Kālaśī-mudrā, one should sprinkle the form with it."
"Having performed the consecration according to the rule, one should satisfy the deities of the mantra.
Thus it is said.
Anticipating the objection—"Why is the drinking of wine itself the cause for the state of isolation (kevalībhāva)?"—he says:
"Because wine consists of Śiva, and all mantras originate from Śiva. (15.73)
There is no difference between Śiva and Śakti; the rays [of consciousness] arise from Śakti. Therefore, wine—which generates bliss for those rays—is identical with Śiva. (15.74)
When consciousness is awakened into its full form, one becomes a vessel for authority;
"a vessel for authority" means that by virtue of having the nature of awakened and full consciousness, one becomes a *kevalin* (an isolated soul)—
this is the meaning.

Now, it may be argued that others hold this view: that because of the scriptural declaration of results—"In the beginning, one should perform the bath which destroys all sins"—the bath is not an ancillary part of the sacrifice; as they say:
Is it not improper [to claim] that "that which lacks a fruit in the proximity of something possessing a fruit is an ancillary part (aṅga) of it"? To this he says:
"But that bathing which [is performed] through the distinctions of mantra, meditation, and meditative absorption—that is not [the same]. (15.75)
Bathing is appropriate because it brings about fitness for rites such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*);
this eightfold bathing possesses a twofold nature, being both external and internal. (15.76)

Furthermore, as for the claim that bathing is not a constituent part of the sacrifice because it is distinct from mantra, meditation, and so forth—which rely on distinctions—that is not tenable; for it is said: "One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors."

Thus, by means of this vision, one brings about the fitness characterized by qualification for the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth; through the instillation of that [fitness], it indeed becomes an aid to the sacrifice—this is the meaning. Nor is there a rule that a subsidiary (*aṅga*) must be fruitless in its entirety, as in the case of the subsidiary [vessel] mentioned in the injunction: "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a *godohana* vessel."
Because the hearing of a result is observed [in some cases], even though no result is seen in the primary sacrifice itself, such as the Viśvajit and others.
Having described this as being external there, he now designates it as internal as well:
"That which is internal is, for example, the overflowing nectar of the stream from the upward moon;
for [the channels] remain pervading one and a half finger-breadths, ascending through the apertures. (15.77)
All eight forms are said to extend individually up to the *dvādaśānta*.
Regarding the phrase "the upward moon": this refers to the moon of Śiva situated at the *dvādaśānta*. Here, the reason is stated with the words "since," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "Should these eight ablutions be performed simultaneously, or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
One should perform one of these ablutions, or even two, three, or more.
"One or another" means according to the place, time, and other such factors. ||78||
Having concluded this, he introduces another [topic]:
"Thus has the procedure for bathing been proclaimed by Bhairava for the sake of purification;
now this which is to be performed after the bath is taught. (15.79)
He says that very thing:
"Having observed that one's state of being is serene, one should then proceed to the sacrificial hall.
Anticipating the doubt—"But where indeed should the sacrificial hall itself be constructed?"—he includes it within his statement.
He introduces the object of knowledge called "the arrangement of locations" (sthānakalpanā), which was indicated in the subsequent summary:
"That which is called a mountain peak, a riverbank, a solitary linga, and so forth. (15.80)
In this context, that which is external is for the sake of attaining specific supernatural powers (siddhis), not for liberation;
whereas the internal [practice] consists of the union of the vital breath within the body, beginning from the tips of the trees and so forth.
This may serve as a means for practitioners toward accomplishment (*siddhi*), but not toward liberation (*mukti*).
It is stated in the scriptures that a sacred seat (*pīṭhasthāna*) is always fit for sacrifice (*yāga*). (15.82)
And that [is] very clear externally and within the body, from the external and internal form;
where [the text says] "yadi" (if), the clear reading is "iha" (here). Now, one might ask: "Are these only three locations, or are there others?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "pīṭha," etc.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", he says: "Because the Supreme Lord has described it in the *Śrīnaiśasañcāra*. (15.83)

He states that very same point by way of its meaning: "His will is the sacred seat (pīṭha), the support upon which the moving and the unmoving abide; that foremost [seat] is Kāmarūpa, from which arise the two, bindu and nāda. (15.84)
The seat of Nāda is Pūrṇagiri; to the south and again to the left is the seat of Uḍḍiyāna, which is the Bindu. These indeed are the three principal seats. (15.85)
Beyond that, the object of knowledge (jñeya) is the half-pīṭha in the form of conceptualization (saṅkalpanā).
Then there is the śākta [pīṭha], Kuṇḍalinī, and the triple upapīṭha consisting of the Vedas and the Kalās. (15.86)
Devīkoṭṭa and Ujjayinī are the two [sites], as well as Kulagiri, which is the next;
Lālana, Baindava, and Vyāpti constitute the triad of *saṃdohakas*.
Puṇḍravardhana, Vārendra, and likewise this Ekāmra outside;
that seat (pīṭha) is said to be ninefold according to the internal and external sequence.

For those who know the sacred fields, the eight fields are the eight petals of the heart-lotus: Prayāga, Varaṇā, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantikā; [the others being] Kāśmīra, Ekāmra, Kailāsa, and Pūrṇagiri. (15.89)
Vārāṇasī, Kāliṅga, Kulūtā, and likewise Lāhulā—
these they call the eight secondary fields (upakṣetra), corresponding to the eight petals at the tip of the heart-lotus.
Viraja, Uḍikā, Hālā, Elāpūra, Kṣīrikā, and the city of Māyā, as well as the Maru region, exist both externally and internally. (15.91)
The joints of the petals of the heart-lotus reach their ultimate state at the secondary junctions:
Jālandhara, Naipāla, Kaśmīra, Gargikā, and Hara. (15.92)
The Mleccha direction is the gateway-vihara, as is Kurukṣetra and Kheṭaka;
a place where two roads meet is so called from the conjunction of two, and a place where three roads meet from the meeting of three. (15.93)
They consider this to be the crossroads resulting from the dissolution of the possessor of power;
it is situated within the body, extending from the end of the nose to the cavity of the palate.
That which is designated as the middle [path] is said to be between the eyebrows, the throat, and the heart;
that triad of the Kaulas is the abode of great bliss at the bulb (kanda) of the navel.
A mountain peak, a riverbank, or even a solitary linga—what need is there for so many words? All of these are contained within consciousness, which is then centered in the vital breath.
Therefore, because it resides within the body, it becomes that which has the body as its abode.
And it has been stated that "its seat" (*pīṭha*) is a mere designation; it is called the "support" (*ādhāra*), and it is that wherein the moving and the unmoving abide. As it is said therein:
That will of His which is known as Śakti has attained the state of being the Pīṭha;
the Pīṭha is the foundational support, and within it resides all that is moving and unmoving.
"Therefore, the designation 'Pīṭha' is traditionally held to be based on the [divine] power (śakti) as a secondary cause.
Here, "agrya" means primary; for this very reason, it is said to be the form of *kāma*, that is, of desire (*icchā*). "From that" means from the primary *Kāmarūpa*. As it has been stated there:
"Then, O beloved, two seats arise consisting of Bindu and Nāda;
Bindu is designated as being on the left, and Nāda is said to be on the right."
But the foremost seat, O Supreme Goddess, is that which was previously described as pertaining to Śakti;
thus the triad of seats has arisen, beginning with Kāmarūpa, as it is remembered.
"The foremost is that Kāmarūpa; Pūrṇagiri is said to be on the right;
and the third, named Uḍḍiyāna, is in the north.
And: "Beyond this, the Half-Pīṭha consists of the nature of the conceptualization of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Thus, it is "half."

"The seat (pīṭha) is said to be ninefold according to the internal and external sequence"—this contradicts the conclusion [of the text], is not based on scripture (anāgamika), and because it is not of human authorship (anārṣatva), it should be disregarded.
"The Veda-part" (vedakala) consists of four beats (catuṣkala); "the three secondary seats" (tryupapīṭhaka) refers to the three secondary seats (upapīṭhas).
This is the collective summary. As it is stated there:
"The Śākta Great Seat (mahāpīṭha) arises from Power (śakti) and resides in the middle of the state of Kuṇḍalinī;
the Baindava Seat arises from the Bindu and consists of the four parts of the seminal sphere (golaka)."
O Dear One, that which is born of sound (nādaja) should be known as being below the pervasion (vyāpti), while that which goes upward from the two apertures is above;
these are indeed the three secondary seats (upapīṭha). Now hear their names according to the external [tradition].
"Devīkoṭṭa is known as Śākta; Bindu is known as Ujjayinī; Giri is known as Kaula; in the center, there is the downward movement of pervasion by Vyāpinī.
Thus, "pervasion" (vyāpti) is Śakti, the locus of expansion. Regarding the term "saṃdohaka":
Because they are essentially the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *upapīṭhas*. As it is said there:
"Furthermore, O fair-faced one, these three are known as the *saṃdohas*:
the *lalanā*, the *gartaka*, and the *śākta*, located in the middle of the *puṭa* of the *baindava*."
That which is born of sound (nādaja) is situated in the middle of the pervasion; these three, in brief, are designated as Puṇḍravardhana within the lalanā.

"Vārendra is to be known as baindhava, and Ekāmra is designated as vyāpti. Thus, there are nine [sites], because the three categories of *pīṭha*, *upapīṭha*, and *saṃdoha* each have three types. "City" (*purī*) refers to Rājapurī;
"called Māyā" refers to Māyāpurī. This has been stated therein:
O fair-faced one, the eight fields are the petals of the heart-lotus;
the secondary fields are the tips of the petals, and the gathering places are the joints between the petals.
"Thus there would be twenty-four... Beginning thus, [the text] mentions them by name: "Kheṭaka, Kurukṣetra, the Saṃdohas, and the Vīranāyakas."

Thus far. "Two" refers to the characteristics of the left and right channels (*nāḍī*). "Three" means together with the central power (*madhya-śakti*). "Of the possessor of power" refers to the Self (*ātman*). "To the end of the nose" means the end of the power of the nose, which is the place of expansion designated by terms such as "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). "Of the aperture" refers to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

The "tip of the crest" (*antaścūlikāgra*) refers to the middle, which is the *āṇava* [means]; the "kaulikam" refers to the *śākta*, by implication the first, which is the *śāmbhava*. "That very same" refers to all three types, beginning with the end of the nose.
As it is said there:
The flow through both the left and right channels is considered the supreme *dvipatha* (two-path);
that same [flow] through the *parā* [channel] is called *tripatha* (three-path), and it is indeed superior.
That which was previously described as the supreme mass below the pervasion—
therein is one crossroads, and the second is from the middle of the palate.
"One should know that triad at the tip of the crest-lock (cūlikā) as the third;
the supreme is said to be between the eyebrows, and beyond that is the crossroads (catuṣpatha)," and so forth in many ways. Now, is this not also found in other scriptures?
Prayāga is situated at the navel, while Varaṇā is in the region of the heart;
Kulādri is located in the throat, and Bhīmanāda is in the palate.
In the place of the *bindu* is that called Jayantī, while in the place of *nāda* is Caritraka;
Ekāmra is within the *śakti*, and this should be known by those who have realized the Self.

"It is said that [the planet] Jupiter is retrograde for ten million years, and likewise for the eighth [year]," and so forth—it has been stated otherwise. So, what would be the use of such an instruction?
Let some essential meaning (tātparya) be stated here. "Certainly," he says, beginning with "What else... and so on. From that...

"It moves through the vital breath" (prāṇaga) because consciousness first undergoes transformation into the vital breath. "Therefore"—because the sacred seats (pīṭha) and so forth reside within the body itself—for that reason.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then one should practice only that which resides within the abode of one's own body; what is the purpose of mentioning external sites (pīṭhas) and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But externally, there are those who are experts in the path of yoga situated in such [internal] ways. (15.97)
The goddesses arise from their own nature; that is said to be the external *pīṭha*.
For the goddesses indeed arise externally by their very nature, through the aforementioned pervasion and due to their expertise in internal knowledge, yoga, and so forth.
The meaning is that because they attain manifestation for the sake of external favor, it is appropriate to call them the "external seat" (bāhyapīṭha). Thus it should be stated.
Now, one might object: "If the goddesses are thus [internal], on what basis can there be the status of an external *pīṭha*?
He pacifies this doubt by showing an analogy:
"Just as by their very nature the Mlecchas abide on the path of unrighteousness. (15.98)
In that regard, knowledge and yoga are established in some places by necessity in this manner;

just as, due to their inherent devotion to unrighteousness, among the Mlecchas, unrighteousness alone exists necessarily in that very land by way of its own nature and extends to all people, so too [is it with knowledge and yoga].

Because the goddesses possess the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), their manifestation occurs only in certain places such as sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and the like, but not everywhere; thus it is rightly said that "that sacred seat is called [the locus] of knowledge and the other [yogas]."
Now, one might raise the objection: "If such knowledge-yoga and so forth are established there, what would that effect for others?
To allay this doubt, he provides an illustration:
"And just as even one who is not of their nature incurs sin through association with them" (15.99).

Likewise, even one who occupies a sacred seat (pīṭha) may become a fit vessel for knowledge, yoga, and so forth; yet he remains alienated from them, free from sin, and excluded from knowledge, yoga, and the like— by those [who are] sinful and by those who occupy the seats.

Now, one might object: "If knowledge, yoga, and so forth can be accomplished simply by wandering externally to sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and the like, then what is the use of internal contemplation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For one who perceives [the goal] primarily within the body, in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and in consciousness... (15.100)
What is the use of other grand displays of wandering to external shrines when this entire universe [is the goal]?

Furthermore, the "internal" nature of the body and so forth is intended according to their respective contexts. And this distinction regarding the seats (pīṭhas) and so on is a matter solely for those who seek enjoyment (bubhukṣu); thus he says:
Thus, for those who seek the fruits of the various wheels (cakras) both internally and externally, [this is the case]. || 15.101 ||
The distinction of locations is manifold and, according to the scripture, it is beyond numbering.
The word division here is "sthānabheda" (distinction of locations). "Sa" (it) refers to that distinction of locations. "In the scripture" means in the Śaiva [scripture].
He demonstrates that very point:
"In the Śrīvīrāvalihṛdaya, there are seven locations: the [three] powers and the pair of lotuses. (15.102)

The cremation ground known as the "crossroads of the path of the gods," as well as the solitary tree in a desolate place—these, according to the perspective of etymological derivation, the qualities of their state, and metaphorical usage, are said to be nothing other than pure consciousness itself. (15.103)
And when the wheel is presided over by that [power], the sacrifice may take place within the body or externally.

"Śakti" refers to the locus of its arising, the support of birth. "Path of the gods" (surapatha) means the triple path (tripatha), because of the triad of the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. "Śūnya" (the void)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]
It is a single tree because of the absence of anything else. As it has been said:
"Śiva is declared to be the single tree...
[and so forth]. Regarding the etymological explanation (*nirvacana*): because awakening itself is the untying (*varaṇāt*) of the bonds (*pāśa*) for those who are to be graced.

And it is called a "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) because of its destruction [of impurities]. Regarding the phrase "abiding in qualities": because of its distinctness from others, it is as if it were a single point (*ekānta*). As for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*):
"Nevertheless, its supreme abode is the casket of the heart-lotus."
By this statement, because of the identity of the location [with that which occupies it], the heart-lotus is meant—just as in the expression, "the beds cry out.
This should be understood in other instances as well. In the phrase "presided over by that," the word "that" (tat) refers back to awakening (*vibodha*).
Therefore, since there is no distinction in consciousness everywhere, in liberation—which consists in attaining identity with that [consciousness]—[there is no difference].
There is no conceptualization of different locations at all—thus he says:
"Therefore, for the sake of liberation, no distinction of location is prescribed for the sacrifice. (15.104)
That [attainment] does not arise from external means, for it comes from the clarity of one's inner being (*bhāva-prasāda*).
Nor is this a matter that relies solely on logic; thus he says:
"And it is said in the *Śrīniśācāra* regarding those who desire the accomplishment of supernatural powers (*siddhi-sādhana*): (15.105)
A seeker of liberation should abandon this very place like a snake sheds its skin;
for when [the truth] has reached the path of one's hearing, liberation is not produced by staying in that place. (15.106)
The reality of the Guru is liberation; however, worship is for the sake of its firm consolidation.
Regarding the phrase "this [place]": it refers to a fixed location consisting of a sacred seat (*pīṭha*) and so forth. As it has been stated therein:
"O fair-faced one, that which was previously told by me to you..."
For this ritual procedure is the means for accomplishing the siddhis for those who desire success.
One who seeks liberation should discard all this like a snake sheds its skin;
one becomes liberated at that very moment when [the truth] has entered the path of the ears.
"The knowledge that has issued from the mouth of the Guru is supremely difficult to obtain;
having once realized self-awareness through it, what else would one wish to conquer?
Thus [it is said].

One might object: "Since a sacrifice cannot exist without a locus, even one seeking liberation must necessarily resort to a distinction of locations; so how can it be said that for the sake of liberation there is no distinction of location for the sacrifice? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Wherever the lotus of the heart attains expansion, || 15-107 ||
In that very abode, the splendor of the outer and inner sacrifice is firmly established.
Now, one might ask: "Would there not be greater ease even there by going to the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
There is no liberation through going elsewhere; it comes from cutting the knot of ignorance.
And that [is achieved] through the expansion of consciousness, according to the venerable *Vīrāvalī* tradition.
"That" refers to the cutting of the knot of ignorance. Nor is this merely my own invention; thus it is said:
"according to the venerable *Vīrāvalī* tradition. Furthermore, the intention of the Gurus is as follows regarding both cases:
"Purity of being alone is the cause"—thus he says:
"But for the gurus, it is either in liberation or in perfection that the intellect is stainless. (15.109)

The word "cause" (*hetu*) applies to both cases as well. That which is pleasing to the mind is the abode of sacrifice (*yāgauka*); that which is pleasing to the mind is the abode of sacrifice—this is the injunction. For this very reason, it is stated in various places without distinction:
"First, there, in an auspicious field, the abode of sacrifice, which is pleasing to the mind."
Thus, likewise:
"In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place... and so forth; likewise, [the following].
It has been said: "...or wherever the mind finds delight."

Now, an objection might be raised: "Has it not been stated everywhere that each specific accomplishment (siddhi) emerges by virtue of the totality of conditions (sāmagrī), such as particular place, time, and so forth? Therefore, how could the mere purity of the entity (bhāvavaimalya) alone serve as the cause in that case?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Although [the result] arises from the causal complex due to the connection with the power of necessity, || 15.110 ||
"Even though the supernatural powers (siddhis) and the purity of existence are likewise entirely supreme, [one might ask]:
'Since all the requisite means (upakaraṇa-jāta), such as place and so forth, exist, why is this alone the most excellent?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:"
For that which has a purified heart may reflect [the truth] therein. || 15-111 ||
That object to be accomplished (sādhya) becomes conducive to success through its firmness;
"therein" means in the heart that has become purified; "that" refers to the object to be accomplished.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", he says:
"And it is stated in the venerable Sāraśāstra that one who is free from conceptual construction indeed attains success. (15.112)
But those possessed of conceptual construction suffer even when what is taught in the Kalpas has been performed;
for even by great people it is said, "This has been accepted"—thus he says: "The mantras, having seized that power... and "This alone is the manifest arising. (15.113)
This very point has been established by such statements from the *Spanda* as follows:
"Having seized that power, the mantras, endowed with the power of the Omniscient One..."
They proceed for the sake of their respective functions, like the organs of embodied beings.

"In that very [state] they are completely dissolved, tranquil in form and stainless; together with the mind of the worshipper, these possess the nature of Śiva. (2.1–2) Having begun thus, [it continues]: "This indeed is the emergence of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator."
It is the attainment of identity with that [reality] for the practitioner who so desires.
"This alone is the attainment of the nectar; this alone is the grasping of the Self; and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva. (2.6–7) Thus [it is said].
He summarizes this very point:
"Therefore, for the sake of accomplishment or liberation, [one should apply oneself] to worship, recitation, and meditative absorption. (15.114)
That is the place where the heart becomes beautiful through rest.
Having thus described the conceptualization of the locations, he outlines the varieties of the general placement (nyāsa):
"Having reached the abode of sacrifice, the pure-souled one remains established even outside. (15.115)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in a general manner for the successful accomplishment of the external sacrifice.
Regarding that very point, he says:
"Either the Mātṛkā, or the Mālinī, or both, in sequence or out of sequence. (15.116)

One should perform each [of these] individually, in groups, or in pairs, through the two processes of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and reabsorption (*apyaya*), either sequentially or non-sequentially—meaning first *mātṛkā*, then *mālinī*, or their reverse. Reabsorption is dissolution (*saṃhāra*). "Each individually" means by way of any one of the forms beginning with emanation. "In groups" means—
By way of the threefold nature beginning with emanation; "in pairs"—by virtue of being contained within the Mātṛkā and Mālinī systems.
He analyzes this very point:
[The piercing] occurs in the forehead, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the cheeks, the teeth, and the lips. (15.117)
In each of the two [shoulders] and in the crest and tongue, there are sixteen [syllables] ending with the visarga;
on the right and left shoulders, arms, hands, fingers, and nails, are the [letters] ka and ca.
One should assign the *ṭa*-group and *ta*-group respectively to the hips, the thighs, and so forth;
the *pa*-group to the two sides, the back, the belly, and the heart—thus nine [locations]. (15.119)
Beginning with skin, blood, flesh, sinews, bone, fat, and semen—this is the Mātṛkānyāsa; now the Mālinīnyāsa is described.

"In pairs, in pairs" means in the form of right and left, starting from the eyes and so forth. "But in the case of the teeth and so forth," it is according to the sequence of downward and upward. "In succession" means in the form of the right and left shanks. "Starting from the thighs and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," the toes and nails of the feet are included. "Of the two sides" means of the right and left.
The *sūtras* are the sinews. As it has been said:
"One should assign the second vowel (*ā*) to the forehead and (*va*) to the mouth;
having placed *i* and *ī* on the two eyes, one should assign *u* and *ū* to the two ears."
Likewise, one should place *ṛ* and *ṝ* in the two nostrils, *ḷ* and *ḹ* on the two cheeks;
*e* and *ai* on the lower and upper teeth, and *o* and *au* on the two lips.
One should fashion the tongue with the syllable *Aṃ* at the crest (*śikhā*) and the visarga;
likewise, one should assign them to the right shoulder, the arm-staff, the hand, the fingers, and the nails.
One should place the *ka*-group on the left in the same manner, starting from the beginning in sequence;
likewise, one should place the *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups, as before, on the hips, thighs, and so forth.
One should assign the *pādya* (water for washing the feet) to both sides, the back, the abdomen, and the heart in sequence;
one should then assign the *ya*-group [of consonants] to the skin, blood, flesh, and sinews.
"The fivefold [group] consists of skin, blood, flesh, bone, fat, semen, and the sheaths of the vital breaths.
These fifty Rudras who are the denotations of these [letters] will be explained in the "Chapter on Unification" (Ekīkārāhnika); therefore, they should be understood from that very source.
He now defines the Mālinī-nyāsa itself:

*na* is the tuft (*śikhā*); *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* are the garland of the head (*śiromālā*); then the forehead (*mastaka*); the eyes are *u* and *ū* (the latter being above and the former below); *ī* is the nose; *ṇu* and *ṇū* are the two ears. (15.121)
The letters *ba*, *ka*, *va*, *ga*, *i*, and *ā* are for the curved tooth and the tongue respectively;
*va*, *bha*, and *ya* are for the throat and the right and left shoulders; and *ḍa* and *ḍha* are for the two arms. (15.122)

Ṭha is in the two hands; jha and ña are the fingers; jra and ṭa are the trident and skull-bowl; pa is the heart; cha and la are the breasts; mā is the milk; and sa, joined with the visarga, is the life-force.
The letter *pra* is said to be *prāṇa*; *ṣa* and *kṣa* are located in the belly and the navel;
*ma* through *śa* reside in the hips, the private parts, and the pair of thighs; likewise, [the letters] are in the knees. (15.124)
The two *e* vowels are located in the thighs; *da* and *pha* are on the feet.

The garland of heads begins with the skull (*kapāla*). "The head" refers to the center of that [skull]. "Above" means on the forehead. "The others" means on the right and left. The meaning is that *ṇu* and *ṇū* are the two ears and the two gestures (*mudrā*).
The sequence is as follows: by that [sequence], the letter *ṇa* represents the two ears, and their ornament is the letters *u* and *ū*. As stated in the Śrīsiddhātantra:
"The seventh letter of the *jha*-group stands for the two ears; their ornaments are the letters *ī* and *parau*."

Thus: *ā* is the form of the vowel *a* in the plural. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the left shoulder is indicated; thus, *bha* is on the right shoulder and *ya* on the left.
