On the two arms, i.e., the right and left. *Śākhā* refers to the fingers of the right and left hands. *Jra* refers to the trident together with its staff; by that, [the placement] of the trident [is indicated].

The letter *ra* is on the staff (*daṇḍa*), and the letter *ja* is on the crests (*śikhā*). Moreover, that [letter *ja*] should be placed face upwards (*uttāna*), by which there is the direct manifestation of the trident (*śūla*). As it is said in the *Śrīsiddhātantra*:
"On the right hand, the trident is to be known; on the staff is the seventh vowel (*e*)."
But the seventh [letter] of the letter *kha* should be given in an upright position.
"O Dear One, it should indeed be a manifest trident, joined with three prongs.

Regarding the term "jīva": this refers to both the Self (ātman) and the universal vital breath (prāṇa). Because there is no distinction between these two, they are designated as one; thus, the letter *sa* pertains to the Self directly, whereas the visarga pertains to the nature of the vital breath.
"Prāṇa" means distinguished. "Ma-śāntāḥ" refers to the letters *ma*, *śa*, *na*, *ta*, and *ka*.

"Jānvādi" means in the sequence starting from the right [knee] and so forth. The two vowels following those are *o* and *au*. And the fifty powers (*śaktis*) denoted by these—beginning with Nādinī and ending with Phetkārikā—are taught in various places.
And so it is stated in the venerable *Triśirobhairava*:
"Nādinī resides at the tip of the crest-lock, designated by the syllable 'na'.
The vowels ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ, beginning with Nivṛtti, constitute the garland situated upon the head."
The syllable *tha* is the goddess Satī at the head; *dha* is the beautiful-eyed one at the eyes;
*ri* is the power of the secret organ; and *vyāptā* resides at the nose, pervading from the middle of the eyes.
Having pervaded [the universe], the Goddess remains; the third eye, Cāmuṇḍā, the Supreme Sovereign, shines resplendent situated upon the forehead.
The letter *ba* is her face; Vajriṇī is her imperishable spear. The *ka*-group is her sharp teeth; Kaṅkaṭā is Kālikā, the auspicious one.
Ghoraghoṣā and Śivirā are proclaimed to be in the ka-group;
Māyādevī is the tongue (jihvā), while a is considered Vāgīśvarī, the Mistress of Speech.
Nārāyaṇī is not in the ears, but their ornament is Ū;
likewise, Mohanī and Prajñā are at the throat, while Śikhivāhanī is at the crest.
The goddess Lāmā Vināyikī holds the two arms of the Lord firmly;
Pūrṇimā, stationed at the region of the hand, is considered by the Lord to be named Ṭha.
Jhaṅkārī, Kundaṇā, and Jhañāvaṅgulī follow in sequence;
Kāpālinī is on the left hand, and Parameśvarī is the letter Ṭa.
The illuminating spear-staff is correctly proclaimed as the letter *ra*;
O Maheśvarī, the spear of the Goddess of gods becomes the syllable *ja*, which is Jayantī.
Bhīṣaṇī and Vāyuvegā are on both shoulders;
Pāvanī is fixed at the heart, while Ṣaṣ and Lambikā are in the belly.
O Bhairavī, this letter *kṣa* is the deity Saṃhārikā at the navel;
Chagalī and Pūtanā are proclaimed as the two breasts, *cha* and *la*.
The letter *ā* is proclaimed as the milk contained therein;
this letter *sa* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), while *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and *ambikā* is the power (*śakti*).
The power of will, known as emission, remains pervading within the self of the vital breath;
Mahākālī occupies the hips, and Kusumāyudhā the secret place.
The goddess Śukrā is the syllable *śukra*, while Anusvāra is Bhairavī;
Tārā is the letter *ta* situated on the thighs, and both *e* and *ai* are Knowledge and Action.
O Goddess, the two knees of the high-souled Bhairava are established [therein];
Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī are proclaimed as the two shanks, O Au.
"Dahanī is located on the right foot, and Phetkārikā on the left, [at the letters] da and pha.

This has also been stated in the *Śrīmata-bhaṭṭāraka* and other texts, divided in both ways according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); therefore, one should understand this for oneself from those sources as well.
However, for fear of excessive prolixity, it has not been corroborated word-for-word.
He explains her essential nature, which contains the essence of the withdrawal [of the universe]:
"Thus, this Goddess Mālinī is that from which the Possessor of Power is agitated. (15.125)
"Because of the penetration by the *kṛtyā*, that body is essentially of the nature of Śakti.
Thus has this Blessed Lady been described; for it is said [by the Lord] in relation to the possessor of power (*śaktimant*): "In this context, Śiva is the seed... (*Mālinīvijayottara-tantra* 3.12).
By this statement, because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, she is agitated by the letter-group (avarga),

brought into a state of instability, and made to face toward herself; then, through immersion in the action of the ritual gesture (kṛti), that body of power (śāktī tanuḥ) becomes, in the ultimate sense, one whose own nature has emerged due to the union with the desire to manifest externally.
This is the meaning.
For this very reason, because she is oriented toward the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*), she possesses supreme capacity for bestowing all accomplishments (*siddhi*) and so forth—thus he says:
"From the mutual agitation of the seeds and matrices, there arises the state of emission. (15.126)
What accomplishment would it not bestow, or what deficiency would it not fulfill?
As it has been said:
"Now I shall further proclaim the supreme ritual application of Mālinī."
Subjugation, inciting enmity, eradication, praise, paralyzing, and killing.
"O Goddess, O lady of good vows, for one who practices yoga, [success] arises from meditation alone"; likewise:
"In all expiations, one should recite the unbroken garland."
Whether it be divided or undivided, according to the relative strength or weakness of the transgression.
"O Dear One, beginning from a single recitation up until three hundred thousand," (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 13.18).

Now, one might object: "In the scriptures, many kinds of *kṣobha* (vibration/agitation) are taught regarding seeds (*bīja*) and matrices (*yoni*); so how can it be said that this [particular] one alone possesses such power? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Although the intermingling of the letters of the matrices and the seeds exists in many ways," (15.127)
Nevertheless, this sequence from *na* to *pha* is proclaimed as the primary one.
He demonstrates its very primacy:
"By the pronunciation beginning with *pha* and ending with *na*, the circle of the paths [is traversed]. (15.128)
How can that full consciousness, once withdrawn, be described by words?
Therefore, in the scriptures, it is described in many ways through metaphors such as the "family doll" (kulaputtalikā) and so forth.
This *Mālinī*, beginning with *na* and ending with *pha*, is indeed the primary [form] of the *Gītā* through its various divisions.

Here, the Supreme Goddess, who is Consciousness (*saṃvit*), first manifests the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogyabhāva*), thereby attaining a state of exclusive function as the Supreme Sound (*paranāda*).

Desiring to illuminate the entire universe, she enlivens the whole multitude of existents by way of weaving together the four seeds of the *sañjīvanī*; yet, because her essence is pure reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), she rests within the *nāda* alone, and then, through the manner of re-unfolding, [she manifests the world].
Preceded by the non-manifestation of the gross and the subtle, and through the sequential pronunciation of the phonemes of sound,
she withdraws this entire circle of the paths (*adhvamaṇḍala*) into the void-self, whose sole nature is the reflective awareness of negation, thereby resting in her own self alone.
Resting in fullness through independence from anything else, and being unable to tolerate being designated by terms such as "existent" or "non-existent," she cannot be conceptualized; thus,
although she is celebrated in other scriptures under various names such as *kulaputtalikā* and so forth, she remains one.

The meaning is that Mālinī, whose essential nature consists of the letters from *na* to *pha*, is primary because she is distinct from the internal agitation inherent in the various types of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and matrices (*yoni*).
One might object: "Granted that this may be so, what is the cause for the application of these terms to the *Mātṛkā* and *Mālinī*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which exists within the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) of Bhairava, by virtue of its non-expansion... (15.130)
Because she will become [the mother], she is called Mātṛkā;
she is Mālinī because she is garlanded by the Rudras, and the Sustainer (Dhārikā) of both supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mokṣa). || 15.131 ||
Blossoming upon the fruits, she is to be worshipped as the six-legged bee of the sound of withdrawal;
for she is endowed with the powers of withdrawal, bestowing, and taking, since *ra* and *la* are interchangeable.
"Śambhunātha has explained that they remember [it] as one;

for that power which belongs to the Blessed One, the mass of sounds whose nature is full light, having attained identity with the internal subject due to the absence of outward orientation, is indeed [that one]."

The meaning is as follows: because it does not swell (*anucchūnatā*) due to the manifestation of those various distinctions, it exists as something yet to be; thus, by the rule of the suffix *kan* in the sense of "like" (*iva*), it is called *mātṛkā*, which means it is designated by that term because it is "like a mother" (*mātṛ-tulyā*).
It is garlanded (*mālyate*), that is, held and accepted as one's own self by the Rudras; and it maintains (*malate*) the nature of both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

The term *mālā* is used here in both the passive and active senses of the root *dhṛ* (as in *mala malla dhāraṇe*, "to wear" or "to hold"). It refers to that which has arisen for the sake of attaining specific results such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth;
for although the word *mālā* is conventionally established in the sense of a "flower garland," it is applied here to a part [of the ritual] by metaphorical extension from the whole.

The meaning is that she is "puṣpiṇī" because she possesses flowers (having performed the act of offering flowers). By this very etymology, she is "pūjyā" (the one to be worshipped), as she possesses a garland (*mālā*) which serves as the instrument of worship; she is the "alinī" (bee) who reflects upon *saṃhāra* (withdrawal), which is signified by the syllable *mā*.

She is so called because she gives (*rāti*) or takes (*lāti*) the dissolution denoted by the word *mā*; this is derived from the two roots *rā* in the sense of "giving" and *lā* in the sense of "taking."
Now, one might object: "Since there is no difference between these fifty phonemes, what indeed is this so-called distinction?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Assembly of Sounds (Śabdarāśi) and Mālinī—this [system] consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti. (15.133)
Because each one is complete in itself, it possesses the nature of Śiva and Śakti. [The word] *tu* is used here in the sense of *hi* (for/indeed). Now, if this is so, then how is it said:
"Every power of Śambhu is praised as being a denoter"? (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.12)
Having raised the objection, "Is this not what was stated [in the previous passage]? he says, "In each one also," and so forth.
However, in the *Mālinī*, there is an intensification of the Śākta nature, by which it is said: "In the ultimate sense, that is the Śākta body."
"And what accomplishment would it not bestow, or what deficiency would it not fulfill?
Thus it is said.
For this very reason, the kindling of even other mantras is performed by means of that which has the nature of the fire-drill (*araṇi*) for all mantras—thus he says:
"Therefore, when the ritual procedure, the potency, or the essential form has fallen away, [it is restored] by this supreme [mantra]. (15.134)

Mantras that have been deposited [on the body] are fulfilled again through re-deposition and bestow their fruit; for that reason— namely, by virtue of being of the nature of Śakti— even when there is a lapse in the Vidyā established in one's own specific Tantra,
mantras belonging to another Tantra, when deposited, serve as an illuminator of the entire splendor of the Mantra.
The meaning is that by the further deposition (nyāsa) of the venerable Mālinī, those [mantras] which bestow their respective fruits become supremely fulfilled;
they are rendered ready to grant the fruits prescribed in their own traditional lineages (svāmnāya).
And this is not our own invention; thus he says:
"It is stated in the venerable *Pūrvatantra* regarding [a rite] devoid of specific injunctions. (15.135)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Mālinī, whose phonemes have distinct origins, for the sake of the body of Śakti;
this is a qualification [of the action], and the causal sense of the reason has been explained. (15.136)
And for the sake of accomplishing desired fruits, he spoke this very point there:
as it was said in that [text]:
"For the complete accomplishment of desired fruits for those who follow the mantras and tantras..."
In those rites of ritual placement (nyāsa) that lack specific injunctions, the knower of mantras [should proceed as follows].
"One should deposit Mālinī of distinct origin for the sake of the Śākta body" (3.15).

"This" refers to the characteristic of being devoid of specific injunctions. It has been "described" by the passage beginning with "when the rule has fallen away," and so forth. Not only this, but something else is also stated here—as he says:
"Yathā" and so forth; "this" refers to that which is about to be explained.
He says that very thing:
"Even those mantras such as the Gāruḍa and others which possess seed-syllables (sāñjana) are not supreme. (15.137)
Filled with the Mālinī for the sake of accomplishment, yet by its very power it leads to liberation;
therefore, even one desiring fruit should install another mantra here [only] after having installed the Mālinī.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) and, having recited [the mantra], one should recite it again effortlessly for the sake of liberation;
thus, they are fulfilled through the placement once more.
Having thus established, as an incidental discussion, the excellence of Mālinī’s potency, he states the actual subject at hand:
"In this manner, one should install either the Mātṛkā or the Mālinī, or both, in their proper sequence. (15.139)
Alternatively, according to the sequence of accomplishment and liberation, one may place the vowels simultaneously in both [the left and right hands].
*Akṣahrīṃ* and *naphahrīṃ*: these two are the *piṇḍa* mantras for the assembly and the abandonment [of afflictions], respectively. (15.140)

The two designators are the *nyāsa*; when this *nyāsa* has been performed by these two, or even by one alone—either conjoined with the limbs (*aṅga*), the body (*tanu*), and Brahmā, or the reverse thereof. (15.141)
In the collective arrangement, one should place these two *piṇḍas* separately in sequence, or alternatively, place them without sequence, or even join them as one. (15.142)

"According to the sequence of accomplishment and liberation" means by way of the order of emanation and reabsorption (*sṛṣṭi-saṃhāra*). "Simultaneously" means in the form of *anakṣapha* and so forth. "In the aggregate" means because all phonemes are internalized through the technique of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). "When the deposition has been performed" means by means of other mantras.

"Single" (ekaka) means because of the avoidance of the placement of other mantras. "This" refers to the placement of Mālinī and the others. "Body" (tanuḥ) means the form (mūrtiḥ), and here the limbs (aṅga) and so forth are as described in the Śrīsiddhātantra and other texts. "Or its reverse" means due to the absence of the application of the limbs and so forth. "Collective" means through the fusion of Mātṛkā and Mālinī.
"Separately"—that is, not by means of mixing them together like colors. ||142||
Now, one might object: "What is the use of such a display of ritual action? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"He who desires success through ritual action should perform that action extensively;
even for him who does not desire it, that [action] leads to an abundance of his own fruit. (15.143)

But he who desires supernatural powers (siddhi) through the practice of meditation and recitation may perform further ritual action at his own will for the sake of purification, according to the previously mentioned method. || 15.144 ||
Alternatively, one who desires liberation may perform [the rites] for him according to his own preference;
for the attainment of Śiva-nature is indeed the sole purpose of these acts, such as the ritual depositing (nyāsa).

Here, the second half [of the verse] provides the reason. "Not desiring" (anīpsuḥ) means because he has no longing for mere results. "To him" (tasmai) means for the sake of a greater result. Furthermore, he who desires to attain perfection through meditation and other means may, by virtue of his state of knowledge, perform the rite either briefly or extensively according to his own will.

Or rather, one should perform [the rites] for the sake of supreme refinement (*saṃskṛti*), that is, for the purpose of bestowing fitness; or else, according to the manner just described, one should perform even more extensive ritual action so that there may be supreme refinement itself.
The word "atha" (then/now) serves to aggregate alternative positions; by it, even one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) [is included] for the sake of refinement.

One may perform the ritual action according to one's own will; or, since even the refined (saṃskṛta) practice culminates in liberation, one should perform it for that very liberation as desired, either in brief or in detail,
because for those who act in such a manner, the attainment of the state of Śiva is the result of rites such as nyāsa.
The meaning is that "artha" refers to the ultimate fruit—this is the sense. ||145||
Having thus concluded this, he explains the procedure for the *arghapātra* (the vessel of honor):

"Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, one should carry out the procedure for the *arghapātra*. Thereafter, according to the stated method, one should worship it with the mantras that have been placed. (15.146)
He says that very thing:
"Because all entities are non-different from Śiva—who consists of accomplishment (siddhi) and is full—there is here, through worship, the non-distinctness of the causal factors. (15.147)
The terms "consisting of accomplishment" (siddhimaya) and "from the full" (pūrṇāt) are stated with reference to those who desire enjoyment and those who desire liberation, respectively. ||147||

Now, one might object: "What is the purpose of meditating on the sacrificers and others as non-different from Śiva at that very moment, since in all subsequent times they appear only as distinct from Him?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The entire multitude of causal factors has been shown to be non-different from Śiva;
thus, in the example of worship, everything—even such acts as going and so forth—is fully encompassed.
For in the description of worship, the entire multitude of causal factors has been shown to be non-different from Śiva;
therefore, one should extend that [realization] even to all worldly activities such as walking, pervading them as well by means of their non-difference from Śiva—this is the meaning. ||148||

One might object: "If the non-separation from Śiva is thus practiced by the factors of action (*kāraka*) within the act of sacrifice (*yajikriyā*), how could it also apply to worldly actions such as walking and so forth?
To pacify this doubt, he speaks by means of providing an illustration:
For just as a horse that has attained mastery over the movements of the rider's circle does not deviate from its training even when mounted in battle, so too [is the yogi]. (15.149)
Anticipating the objection, "But what would happen if it were so?", he says:

"Thus, one whose causal factors (kārakas) have been transformed into Śiva through the practice of the rite of worship abandons the duality of the causal factors even while walking or standing. (15.150)

Likewise, for one established in the practice of [realizing] oneness, this entire universe will, through the force of [that realization], suddenly begin to throb as if dancing with the unshakeable state of perfect Śiva-hood. (15.151)
As even the Gurus have said—thus he spoke: "In the *Pūjanastotra*, our supreme Guru indeed said:
'Oh, what an indescribable festival consisting of the worship of Śiva, possessing such a delicious flavor! (15.152)
In that [state] where the agitation of even the thirty-six principles fully radiates—
this "agitation" is characterized by complete fullness.

And therefore, for those who cultivate [this practice] in this way, there is no fruit other than the immersion into auspiciousness (śivatāveśa); thus he says: "Therefore, for the sake of such an immersion into the full Śiva and the universe, [there is] worship... (15.153).
They indeed perform auspicious acts toward those who are complete; what further fruit could there be?
Anticipating the objection—"How can it be so from mere action alone?"—he says:
"Even without knowledge and yoga, action such as ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship (arcana)... (15.154).
Thus, by bestowing the attainment of oneness, she grants the supreme fruit.
"Thus" means: by the sequence of meditative cultivation leading to the attainment of the state of Śiva.
This [mantra] bestows the desired fruit not only for one who seeks liberation (mumukṣu), but even for one who seeks worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu)—as he says:
"It also grants success to the practitioner (sādhaka) once he has attained oneness with that mantra. (15.155)
The universe, proceeding without obstruction, would swiftly bring about its own perfection;
for "proceeding without obstruction" means that everything has the single nature of consciousness.
For one who has ascended to this state, not even the slightest means (sādhana) is to be adopted; thus he says that this is the traditional teaching:
"And it has been said by the Supreme Lord: 'There is no injunction, nor any sequence of worship. (15.156)
"In the Matas and so forth" means in the Śrīsiddhāmata and other such traditions, it is held that the desired accomplishment is attained through mere remembrance.
He concludes the very subject at hand: "Therefore, since the act of worship bestows the state of identification with That... (15.157).
Therefore, its supreme form is the identity with all the factors of action (kārakas).
"By that" means by virtue of bestowing the state of becoming one with that [reality].
Then he analyzes that very identity:
"The identity of the sacrificer and the support [arises] through the sequence of the ritual for the purification of the locus. (15.158)
The sacrificer, the sacrificial offering, its substratum, the instrument, the taking, and the recipient—
through the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), these rest in identity with the state of Śiva.
The purification of the place is accomplished by means of the expulsion of obstructing spirits and other such rites. ||159||

Now, the sacrificer (*yaṣṭṛ*) is indeed designated as the agent (*kartṛ*), and the object of sacrifice (*yājya*)— namely, the substance such as flowers— is the object (*karman*), because it is said that "sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity," and thus it is that which is sacrificed to the deity. Furthermore, the sacrificial hall (*yāgaveśma*) is the locus (*ādhāra*) of both that agent and that object.

And [it includes] the manifest and unmanifest, as well as the *saṃpradāna* (the recipient), according to the principle that "sacrifice (*yāga*) is the giving (*pradāna*) to the deities (*devatā*)" and so forth. Anticipating the question, "Furthermore, what is meant by *ādāna* (taking) or *karaṇa* (instrument)? he says:
The *arghapātra* is the point of departure (*apādāna*), from which [the water] is taken;
and that water and so forth contained within it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for purification and worship. (15–160)
Regarding the phrase "water and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes wine and other substances; by this, the author has begun to define the suitability of various materials. || 160 ||
One might ask: "How can purification be achieved by water and so forth that reside within [the vessel] itself? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Indeed, everything touched by droplets of water from the arghya-vessel is purified.
What other purification could there be than that which comes from contact with the rays of the sun that is Śiva? (15–161)
And this is not established by logic alone; thus he says:
"The All-pervasive Lord spoke in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* regarding the rule for the vessel of oblation (*arghapātra*).
He states that very point: "One should not prepare any object whatsoever that has not been purified. (15–162)
By that [means], everything is pure; even that which is impure is pure.

Now, it has been stated many times previously that purity and impurity are not some property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*), because they lack the capacity to produce a modification in manifestation (*pratibhāsa*)—just like blue and other such qualities. Therefore, what is this so-called "impurity"?
Anticipating the objection, "Could purity be achieved even by means of removal?", he says:
"And impurity is to be understood as arising from the intent of the teachings of the bound souls (paśu). (15–163)
Now, one might object: "How can another person possess such a nature based on the intention of someone else? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Either because of his own prior state as it was, or even from that which has been imagined."

For, in the case of entities, whether from an impure state imagined as a drop of water from a half-filled vessel or from a pure state, the self remains exactly as it was; in both cases, there is indeed no difference—
this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "If indeed the nature of entities is exactly the same whether they are pure or impure, then how is their distinction determined? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Therefore, whatever is near here [becomes manifest] through the grace of consciousness.
To even a small degree, that [mind] is extremely fit for this sacrifice, just like the living being itself. "To a small degree" means from a slight amount.
In this way, consciousness (*saṃvit*) is also far from pure—thus he says: "By this application of the method, [the distinction between] proximity and distance... (15–165).
One should then determine the suitability or unsuitability therein through direct perception;
and thus,
the substance residing within one's own body is the most auspicious and excellent elixir.

By such statements as these, because it is in close proximity to consciousness (*saṃvit*), the nectar (*amṛta*)—designated by terms such as "essence" (*sāra*) and so forth—is intended by the Gurus as being fit for sacrifice; thus he says:
"Therefore, here for the heroes (*vīras*), the nectar is mutually their own reflection. (15–166)
That which is prescribed by the gurus of purified soul in each respective sacrificial rite—
"mutually the nectar of one's own image"— means that, through mutual conjunction with one another,
it pertains to one's own image in the form of the six-spoked mudrā.

The meaning is that *amṛta* is a specific substance known as *kuṇḍagolaka*, which arises from the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of both [the male and female principles]. Furthermore, by the phrases "of the heroes" (*vīrāṇām*) and "by those whose selves are purified" (*bhāvitātmabhiḥ*), it is stated that this concerns a specific class of qualified practitioners.
Thus, only that object which causes consciousness to overflow is fit for worship—so he says:
"That which thoroughly causes submerged consciousness to emerge is [the best]. (15–167)
Bliss is what is fit for worship, because it is the emergence of consciousness;
therefore, this is established—thus he says:
"Therefore, that which causes the submergence of the predominance of the insentient body and so forth... (15.168).
That which generates bliss, is worthy of worship, and captivates the heart— precisely with this intention [it was said]:
"Whatever consciousness is noble, and whatever state is beautiful with bliss..."
"Whatever possesses a wondrous form in this world, that is all a manifestation of Your form, O Goddess"—
thus and more has been said by others.
For this very reason, the supreme majesty of wine and similar substances—which produce an excess of bliss—is proclaimed in all the scriptures; thus he says:
"Therefore, in the Kula tradition, the Transcendent (Uttīrṇa), the Trika, the Sāra, the Mata, and so forth... (15-169).
The supreme majesty belongs to substances such as wine (*madya*), *kādambarī*, and *śīdhu*;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), meat, sexual union, and so forth are included. As it has been said:
"There are no rivers flowing with honey, nor is there meat like a mountain."
"The entire world is not composed of women; how then can there be accomplishment (siddhi) in the Kula tradition? Thus it is said.
[Objection: "But if this is so, then how is it that the impurity of wine and other such substances is declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, and other texts?
To this he says:
"In order to establish worldly convention, [the impurity] of wine and other such things was taught in the scripture for bound souls (paśuśāsana). (15–170)
For impurity has indeed been proclaimed in that very context, yet its purity exists somewhere within that same context.

One might ask: "Why is it said that the impurity of wine and such things is mentioned here merely to establish worldly convention and not in an ultimate sense? Anticipating this doubt, it is stated: "For its purity exists somewhere within that very same [context]."
"Somewhere"—that is, in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.

It is not only that purification is taught even for impure things such as liquor which are established in worldly convention, but there are many other such things as well—as he says: "The purity of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the purity of the moon and the vessel for grinding. (15–171)
The ritual procedure includes the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha-snāna) and holding a black antelope horn in the hand;
there is no sacrifice without a wife, and [the sacrificer] attains equality with all the deities.
In the *brahmasattra* sacrifice, there is an oblation of wine (*surā*), and an oblation of the omentum, intestines, and heart.
"Grinding" refers to the pressing [of the soma]. Regarding the term "one possessing a black antelope horn" (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇin*):
it means one who possesses a horn (*viṣāṇa*) of a black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*) employed for scratching and other such purposes. "Equality with all deities" [is the meaning].
For the deity of those who maintain the Vedas is verbal; no distinction is heard there in the scripture, as it says:
"One scratches with the black antelope horn."
"The wife and the sacrificer should both place the fuel;
they offer the cups of *surā*; one should immolate a Brahman for the Brahman; they proceed with the morning libation using the omentum; and one cuts off the portion from the heart first."

Now, one might object: "How can this be so in the case of the Pāśava scriptures, which are established within the realm of Māyā, since they are not suited to the non-dual (advaya) system? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even in the Pāśava scriptures, that [non-duality] was shown by the Great Lord. (15–173)
"Like a sudden flash of light in the midst of a terrible, pitch-black winter night;

surely, in the Pāśava teaching, a distinction between purity and impurity is stated, whereas here there is no such distinction—so which of these two systems is logical? Having raised this doubt, he says:
"Is the swan edible? Is it not edible?"—in such conflicting views. || 15-174 ||
"He alone triumphs over the Smārta traditions who is purified by non-difference from Śiva.
Regarding the term "to be consumed," the Śruti says:
"The swan, the wolf, and the cat—these are the Indras."

Regarding "not to be eaten"—as the Smṛti states in the section on forbidden foods: "The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, and the village cock... Regarding "in conflicting views"—this refers to the Śruti.
He states the cause for that victory:
"For these—ignorance, lack of vision of the Vedas, passion, hatred, and so forth—" (15.175).
Anticipating the objection—
"Indeed, what kind of ignorance or similar defect could these [sages] possess that would even enable them to undermine the authority of their own words?"— he says:
Even in the Veda, that which is inedible is taught as being edible. || 15-176 ||

For even in the Veda, according to the perspective already demonstrated, swans and other such creatures—which are prohibited by the Smṛtis and other texts—are heard of as being fit for consumption; thus, their lack of vision regarding the Veda, their ignorance thereof, and the passion and so forth that are inseparable from that ignorance mean that their word is simply not a means of valid knowledge. ||176||
One might object: "Even so, would there not still be both conjunction and optionality regarding what is edible and what is inedible?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"There is no single locus for the two dharmas known as injunction and prohibition."

Now, if it is argued that [the meat] is edible only in specific cases such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice when consumed by a Kṣatriya or others, but otherwise inedible, then there is no fault in the distinction between purity and impurity established according to the difference in context; thus he says:
Then, if that [food] was not available there to be eaten, he [acted] accordingly, in that manner, and from that [source].
Thus, due to the difference in subject matter, the Śruti does not sublate the teaching of Śiva.
"Therein" means elsewhere than the Aśvamedha sacrifice. "In that manner" means as food. "From that" means from the Śruti.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the Veda does not sublate the word of Śiva when their subject matters differ; but when the subject matter is the same, what contradiction or sublation could there be? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If, in some cases, there is a relationship of the sublated and the sublator due to the identity of the subject matter... (15.178)
That this very scripture (śruti) is what is sublated has already been established;
"already" refers to the fourth chapter (āhnika). As it was stated there:
"If this [Smṛti] were sublated by the Vedic [scripture], why would the reverse not occur?"
If you correctly consider that there is sublation because [the subsequent cognition] has a more distinguished object.
One should not apply an exception when a general rule has been established;
for purity and impurity, O Knower of Reality, are established by general rules.
"Only when that [person] is sublated is it so; and thus it has been described here.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body and the vessel for the offering (arghapātra), we shall now speak of the subject at hand.
Having sprinkled all the sacrificial implements with droplets from the general arghapātra water,
one should thereafter perform the external sacrifice.

"Prakṛtam" means that which has been introduced, namely the external sacrifice (bāhyayāga) and so forth. "Sāmānyam" (general) is said because the specific [rite] will be described later. "Bāhyayāgam" refers to what was indicated in the subsequent enumeration as "external worship" (bahirarcā).
He states that very thing:
In a circle of light, in the sky, or on well-smeared ground,
one should worship the trident, the sun, the bull, the Mothers stationed in the directions, and the guardian of the field (kṣetrapa).
And the Yoginīs [should be worshipped] with separate mantras joined with "Oṃ namo" and their respective names, or else by a single utterance designated as the "outer retinue. (182)
The mantra for worship consists of the name [of the deity] ending in the dative case, followed by "namaḥ.

Regarding "in the circle of light" (prabhāmaṇḍale)—this refers to the temple and so forth. Regarding "in the sky" (khe)—this refers to one's own body and so forth. Regarding "on the earth" (bhuvīti)—this refers to the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and so forth. Regarding "with a single utterance" (ekoccāreṇa)—this refers to abbreviated initiation (saṃkṣiptadīkṣā) and similar rites.
Concluding the external ritual, he states another door [of entry] mentioned immediately thereafter:
"Having thus worshipped externally, one should sprinkle the door and worship it thoroughly. (15.183)
And that procedure seen in the Triśiraḥśāsana and other texts is now described:
Gaṇeśa and Lakṣmī are above the door, on the right and left respectively; and then again, [the others]. (15–184)
In the center is Vāgīśvarī, and likewise the pair Diṇḍi and Mahodara, situated respectively on her own right and left; and in this same sequence.
One should properly worship each of them individually: Nandin and Kāla, the triple-pathed Gaṅgā, Kālindī, and those with the faces of a goat and a ram, on the two doorposts to one's right.
One should worship the lower threshold, Ananteśa, and the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti);
in the middle of the door, one should worship Sarasvatī and the Great Weapon (Mahāstra).
All [the deities] situated upon the lotus-base have arisen as destroyers of obstacles;
for the worship, the mantra is prepared as before with two lamps. (15.188)
One should perform worship here with offerings of water (argha), flowers, garlands, incense, food (naivedya), and prostrations;
and the argha should be prepared with the finest substances.
Or one may perform the worship of the deities stationed at the gateway with a single utterance;
if one performs the secret worship, that constitutes the external retinue.
One should worship the door-keepers before the inner deity according to the sequence of visualization;
by casting a flower consecrated with the Astra-mantra into the blazing chamber, one destroys all obstacles.
Having entered, one should look upon the dwelling with a gaze kindled by the rays of Śiva;
one should bind the directions with the Weapon-mantra and cover them all with the Armor-mantra.
There, one desiring liberation, or one who is like him, should enter facing the northern direction;
for in that way, the fire Aghora consumes the binding fetters.
"That procedure" refers to the characteristic worship of the door; he explains that very thing with the words "Gaṇeśa," and so forth. As it is stated there:
"Having worshipped Śambhu above the door, likewise Gaṇeśa on the right."
"One should meditate upon Śrī and Vāgīśī on the left and worship them in the center.
Regarding the word "one's own" (sva): it is according to the intention of the practitioner. Regarding the word "by this" (etena): by means of the right and left [hands] themselves.
Furthermore, regarding the intention of the gates, there is a reversal here. As it is stated therein:
"Then, at the base, to the north, [one installs] Nandirudra and Jāhnavī;
and to the south, Mahākāla with Daṃṣṭra and Yamunā."
Thus: "below" means on the lower *uḍambara* (threshold). "In the middle of the door" means on the upper *uḍambara*.

"Joined with the supreme substance" means not, however, with the eight limbs (*aṅga*). "With a single utterance" means: *Oṃ sarvadvārapālebhyaḥ namaḥ*. "By way of the sequence of visualization" means not, however—
"Directly," as in the ritual procedure of the Tantras. "Having cast"—this means, by implication, with the *nārāca-mudrā*.

"The state of having eyes kindled by the rays of Śiva" arises from relying upon the supreme mode (*paravṛtti*). "One should gaze"—for the purpose of bestowing qualities; furthermore, it is said that one should "bind the directions" and "cover them" in order to prevent re-entry.

"To such a one"—that is, to one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) at the time of initiation; it is established by implication that for one desiring enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), however, this is otherwise. As it has been said:
"Facing the east or with a gentle face... (*Mālinīvijayottara* 8.18).
Thus [ends the verse]. ||193||

Now, one might object: "In this doctrine of non-dual consciousness (*saṃvidadvayavāda*), what indeed is this thing called 'direction' (diś), for which there could even be a division such as east, west, and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even though there exists no such thing as direction—neither 'east' nor 'west' and the like—"
For there could be no cognition of that single, unconditioned [entity]. (15.194)

And by this immediate sequence of entry, the nature of the directions (*dik*) has been introduced. Now, it has indeed already been stated by the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas): "Space (*dik*) exists as that which is to be inferred from cognitions of 'east' and so forth, which are distinct from mere cognitions of trees and the like."

Thus [it is said]. And that [consciousness] is one everywhere, because there is no distinction in its cognition thereof. Now, if this is so, how could there be a distinction such as "prior" and "subsequent" for that single [consciousness], which does not possess an imposed form?
To this he says: "Prior," etc. (verse 194).
Now, if it is argued that there must be some such limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) alone which is the object of the conventional usage of "east" and so forth,

then it would be that other entity designated as the adjunct that functions in such a way, and not that which is called "direction" (*diś*) that would experience the status of being the locus for the cognitions of east and so forth— thus he says:
If it is argued that "priority and so forth are designated by means of an adjunct (upādhi)," then that has already been refuted by the [previous] discussion on direction.
If it is further argued, "Even so, let this [adjunct] be accepted, since it establishes the conventional usage of 'east' and so forth which we desire," [the author] says: "No."
But how could mere limiting adjuncts (upādhi) alone bring about such variety? || 15-195 ||
"So be it"—that is, by way of the spatial orientation of priority and posteriority and so forth. ||195||
"In that case, has victory not been achieved by the Buddhists themselves, who deny space and time as being anything more than the intrinsic nature of entities?
To this he replies:
"Therefore, this light of consciousness, through its aspect of appearing as form..."
He is intoxicated by the vivid delineation of the manifold variety known as the divisions of the directions, such as the east and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point by dividing it according to the descending order:
"In that regard, whatever is capable of being always assimilated by the Light is 'above' in nature as Light; however, that which is unfit for contact is 'below'. (15.197)
Slight luminosity is the center; from that, indeed, the emergence of the directions occurs.
That which is slightly capable of being illuminated extends forward, facing [the observer]. (15.198)
But that which is turned away from it is "behind"; thus two directions have been reached.
Light, having grasped an object facing it, possesses intensified rays. (15.199)
Where one stands facing the south, that is the direction of light;
situated to the east of the south is designated as the left (vāma). (15.200)
For that very [consciousness] is indeed made gentle by the touch of the moon of the object revealed by it; indeed,
here, even for the Supreme Lord, whose body is supreme light,
there exists a state of absorption in the experience of mere bliss of consciousness.
"In accordance with the principle stated in [Śivasūtra 1.3], 'Her will is of such extent, her knowledge is of such extent,

and her action is indeed of such extent,' for one who has entered into the states of the supreme, the non-supreme, and both, there is 'uprightness' (*ūrdhvatva*) because, in the supreme aspect, the universe consists solely of light; and in the non-supreme aspect..."

It is "below" because of its unfitness for contact with light and touch; it is "middle" by virtue of being an intermediate state due to its partial contact with both light and non-light, from which the emergence of the directions arises. In that regard, it possesses the fitness for an orientation toward some slight manifestation.
That which faces forward, toward the world that is manifesting before it, is called "prācī" (the east);
however, because of contact with some degree of non-manifestation, that very same [direction] faces away as if turned back, and is thus called "paścāt" (the west).
Thus, these two directions are indeed undeniable. He...

Thus, that which is slightly luminous, having perceived the universe in contact with itself, abides within that Self consisting of self-luminosity, which is characterized by fullness; that very [direction] is the southern direction because it conforms to luminosity. On the other hand, that which is slightly non-luminous...
In some way, when it is intensified— due to its being a balanced aggregate with such a portion of light— it is as if commanded by that [light];

because it vomits forth a hostility toward light due to the predominance of the object of cognition and being nourished by contact with the lunar light, it becomes a vessel for the name "Vāmā" (the Left).

One might object: "In this way, due to the connection of verticality and the division of the center within the state of Paraśiva, and by virtue of that propriety, would there not likewise be only six directions even in the higher states? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, in this quartet of directions, by virtue of resting in the center... (15.201).
There is another tetrad, by which the eight directions are presided over.
Regarding the phrase "another tetrad": it is characterized by the east, south, southwest, west, northwest, north, northeast, and [the zenith].
"Presided over by this or that" means they are presided over by this or that aspect—
whether facing forward or turned away, intensified or not intensified, manifest or unmanifest— and are thus touched within their own self as having repose as their essence; such is the meaning.
He demonstrates, by way of conclusion, that the detailed expansion (*prapañca*) of this very division of directions is well-known in both the scriptures and the world:
"Thus, in this supreme Śiva, the granter of boons, who consists of pure light alone... (15.202).
The division of directions is established in the world and is likewise described in the scriptures.

Thus, this division of directions exists within the Supreme Lord— who is of the singular nature of light and intent upon bestowing grace upon others— as the manifestation of the multitude of objects residing within the Self of the Master.

The meaning is this: by the reasoning stated in such passages as, "Desire and reflective awareness proceed only because [the Self] exists and not without it" (Rigvidhānaprakāśa 1.5.10), [the subject], abiding as identical with his own Self, is described in that way in both scripture and the world;
that is to say, he manifests as being worthy of being designated by terms such as "above" and so forth.
In this regard, he states the scriptural division of the directions:
"Because the Lord Sadāśiva, whose body consists of the five mantras, [proceeds] in sequence... (15.203).

Following the state of Śiva and Śakti, the Lord Sadāśivanātha, whose body consists of the five mantras, comes into being through the division of the directions according to Īśāna, Aghora, Vāma, Sadyojāta, and Agha (Adhaḥ).
For it is from the differentiation of the faces beginning with Īśāna that the sixfold directions manifest.
The meaning of the sentence.
He analyzes this very point:
"The Lord (Īśa) is above because of his luminosity; that which is extended forward is the face. (15.204)
The male [direction] is the south, fierce; the female is the north, gentle.
By virtue of being turned away, the west is immediately designated as such. (15.205)

Because its lower face, the mouth of the netherworld (*pātāla*), remains unmanifest, the Lord is said to be the upward direction due to His nature as pure light; Tatpuruṣa is the east because He flows forth toward that light, and Aghora—

The South is so called because it is favorable to the intensification of diffused light; Vāmadeva is [the North] because it is contrary to that; the North is Vāmā because it primarily consists of contact with the moon of the object of knowledge; Sadyojāta is the West because of its aversion to light; and Picuvaktra is the Lower because of its unfitness for contact with light. In this context, the division of the faces has been traditionally taught through the pervasion of the elements; anticipating the question, "What then is this sixfold division of them?", he says:
"For its faces are indeed ether, air, fire, water, earth, and the void. (15.206)
Primarily, space alone is said to be luminous above;
for it is clearly that very same [space] which is primarily non-luminous below. (15.207)
The intention is that space is indeed the substratum for both darkness and light.

Now, one might object: "Since the negation of one of two contradictory states—such as manifestation and non-manifestation—necessarily implies the affirmation of the other, what room is there for the four directions?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But that which is the light in the center is neither an object of illumination nor anything else;
because it is the very nature of light, the four directions are indicated within it.
Furthermore, in the center there is neither manifestation nor its absence;

rather, it is the object of manifestation that has been made the object of some degree of manifestation, and which, precisely because of the diversity of limiting conditions such as its forward movement toward the face, is perceived as differentiated. Thus it stands.
Thus, here is the division of the directions, beginning with the east. || 208 ||
He concludes the very subject at hand: "The Lord, whose body consists of the five mantras, is thus the sovereign of all directions.
The word "thus" refers both to the pervasion of the faces [of the deity] as previously described and to his fitness for resting in the center.
He extends this very principle to other causes: "Beyond that, Īśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā likewise abide. (15.209)
"So be it"—by means of the sequence beginning with Sadāśiva. ||209||
Now, does "likewise" imply that this is an extension [of the rule] to all [faces]? No—so he says:

"Because Viṣṇu and the Creator (Dhātṛ) are incapable of manifesting the upward [face], they do not have a fifth face, since those two are the lords of emission and maintenance, which consist of duality. (15.210)
The intention is that [they are] characterized by a predominance of duality and a lack of skill in the non-dual reflective awareness of supreme consciousness. || 210 ||
One might object: "In that case, if there is no connection with the five faces, would not the division of the directions rooted in them also cease to exist? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But the division of the directions arises from that [fivefold nature] through the four faces."
Even in the absence of an upward-facing face, since that which arises from it— consisting of the upper and lower faces—
is inseparable from the set of four faces, the distinction of directions exists; thus, the extended application (*atideśa*) is indeed logical.

Now, one might object: could not the division of directions also be established in relation to the four faces? Since each subsequent face resides in the position of each preceding one, and since Rudra and others are associated with upward-facing orientations, it is possible for Brahmā and Viṣṇu to exist there as well; so why is this division necessarily dependent upon those four faces?
Having raised the doubt—“Is this a division of the directions, or is it the upward-turning of the fifth face?”—he says:
“If the fifth [face] is joined, those two have abandoned their own inherent natures. (15.211)
"Having abandoned their own selves" means that they have dissolved into that [one]. ||211||
Having thus described the scriptural division of the directions, he now describes the worldly one as well:

"Then, even within the center of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the all-pervasive Sun, whose nature is the density of light, being the power of knowledge, effects the division of the directions. (15.212)

He demonstrates that very point: "For instance, during the equinoxal conjunction (viṣuvad-yoga), that direction in which [the sun] is first seen is the east; and where its shadow falls is declared to be the west. (15.213)
For him who desires to go toward that [city], his left side becomes the right;
and there he shines as if blazing intensely with fierce splendors.
That which stands before it on the left is slightly permeated by its light;
for that very reason, it is gentle, yet it is not without luminosity. (15.215)
The established rule is that where he sets is the western direction;
yet it is precisely in that west that for some there is the first perception of light. (15.216)

"That very [direction] which was previously described for them according to the path is seen here"—that is, the sun. "In that"—meaning, in the western direction which is the object of the desire to go. Furthermore, for one going there, that which is to the left becomes the right because it is favorable for the attainment of light.
The meaning is that it is designated by that word [“tejas”]. For this very reason, it is said there:
“This shines as if blazing intensely, through each successive stage, due to the excellence of the intensity of its radiance. For this same reason, even in the state of Paraśiva...

It has been stated [in the text]: "Where light abides with its rays intensified" (Śloka 15.119), and so forth. "Standing in front of that" means standing directly before that southern [light] at an equal level—this is the meaning. "From that" means by its slight radiance.

Because it is inlaid [with that description]. "In that very place" means at the location of the sun's setting. "Of whom" refers to those dwelling in other continents. For this very reason, the observation of a reversal is accepted, such as when what is the eastern direction for others becomes the western for the people of Surāṣṭra, and what is the southern for the Mālavas.
"On the path" means on the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*). As it is said there:
"Meru is to the north of all [the worlds], while Lokāloka is to the south. (8.110)
But if this were so, then the western direction would become the eastern, and the eastern would also become the western. [Yet it is said:
"One who eats facing east gains longevity; one facing south gains fame;
one facing west attains prosperity; and one facing north eats according to truth."
Having raised the doubt, "By such statements as these, how can their capacity to bestow specific fruits be logically consistent?", he says:
"Sā sā dik ca tathā tasya phaladāpi viparyaye" (15.217). [That very direction likewise bestows its fruit for him even in the reverse case.]
Since the attainment of various fruits depends upon light,

so too, even though there is a variety of reversals consisting of west, east, and so forth, that very direction— whether characterized as east, west, or otherwise— is [determined] for the people residing in their respective continents accordingly.

Since [the powers] bestow their fruits by virtue of being specifically determined, the attainment of the fruit depends solely upon the Light (*prakāśa*), and the direction (*diś*) has that expansion as its essence. Now, it was stated that the Supreme Light alone is capable of delineating the divisions of the directions; how then [is this so]?
Anticipating the objection, "Would the sun also act in that same way? he says:
"In this manner, the direction would be dependent upon the sun; though it is manifold, it remains of such a nature. (15.218)
Presided over by Maheśvara, who assumes various forms,
the direction that has the sun as its support is likewise conceived in this manner;
for, because it lacks a fixed, singular form, it is variegated even while having the sun as its support.

The meaning is that they are presided over by Maheśvara, who assumes the manifold form of those directions as their subtle, intermediate, and gross natures, and are thus fixed upon the very wall of supreme light.

The directions are not divided solely with reference to the Sun, which is the form of the pervasive Lord’s power of knowledge; rather, they are divided even with reference to the practitioner, whose nature is contracted. Thus he says:
"Or rather, why say more? From the point directly facing that sacrificer... (15.219).
Even the directions—east, south, north, and west—are differentiated;
here too, the Supreme Lord alone is the presiding authority—as it is said: "And Sadāśiva [establishes] that division of directions created according to his own [will]. (15.220)
Because he presides over it like the sun with his manifold form;
it is not only the Supreme Lord who presides over this, but even the group of world-protectors such as Śakra and others, who are forms consisting of portions of His power— thus he says:
For the directions, though arisen from themselves, are presided over by their respective lords, Śakra and the others.
For they are portions of the power of light and conform to that light;
not only are they [the directions] produced from themselves, but even those belonging to the sun are so—this is what is indicated by the word "even" (api).
He demonstrates that these [directions] are indeed portions of the power of light:
That which is the sovereignty of light is Indra, and that which is its majesty is Mahas.

That fire is Yama in its capacity as a controller and in its dreadfulness; it is Rakṣas in its deficiency. Varuṇa is that which is to be manifested, and it is called Vāyu because of its mobility. || 15-223 ||
Through the accumulation of existence he is the Lord of Wealth (Vitteśa); upon its dissolution, he is the All-pervading One (Vibhu).
With an invisible form, he is Ananta; above Brahmā, he is the all-pervading Expander (Bṛṃhaka).

The guardians of the world (lokapās) are proclaimed to be portions of the power of Light itself. [The word] *indra* is derived from the root *idi*, meaning "supreme sovereignty. *Yama* is so called by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "one who restrains," from the root *yam*, meaning "to restrain. "Its deficiency" (*tadūnimā*) refers to the deficiency of that Light due to the overflow of its own radiance.

The meaning is "subordination. For this very reason it was said: "Varuṇa is that which is to be manifested. "That" refers to the object to be manifested. "Upon its dissolution" means upon the dissolution of that accumulation of states—i.e., when the essential nature [of consciousness] becomes predominant. "Whose form is unseen" is because of its downward position.
And precisely because they are portions of the power of illumination (prakāśa-śakti), they possess the capacity to bestow supreme grace; thus he says, "the guardians of the world," and so forth.

Now, it has been stated that direction is of an indeterminate form because it depends upon various substrates in the sequence beginning from Paramaśiva down to Sadāśiva and so forth; therefore, we do not know which of those we should rely upon— anticipating this doubt, he says:
In this way, although its form is self-dependent, the solar direction is nevertheless taught.
In that regard, indeed, everyone attains a state of unshakable luminosity.

In the manner thus described, because there is an absence of fixed determination, even though direction is independent in nature, it is taught as being solar alone— it is spoken of as an object of perception— since this entire world remains unshakably established therein.
The meaning is that he attains luminosity and becomes firmly possessed of realization.

Now, an objection may be raised: "It has been stated that Indra and others are the presiding deities of the directions, and they possess the essential nature of the powers of Indra and the other directions belonging to the Supreme Lord. Since those powers are all-pervasive, how can they exercise sovereignty over specific directions and bestow fruits appropriate to them?"—this is the doubt.
He pacifies [the doubt] by showing an illustration: "Just as the wind, though all-pervading, is fanned by a fan... (15.226).
Once awakened, one should perform one's own activities, such as the removal of sweat and so forth;
in the same way, all pervasive powers (śaktis) clearly manifest as the various functions of the senses. (15.227)
"Awakened by the practitioner’s assurance, they bestow their respective desired fruits.

Regarding the phrase "awakened by the practitioner’s assurance": the meaning is that they are awakened—that is, manifested with certainty—by means of the practitioner’s assurance in the form of [the realization] that "this indeed is the eastern direction," and so forth.

Not only is this direction, which relies upon the sun, presided over and bestows its fruits by the supreme powers of the Lord such as Indrī and the others, but it is also [presided over] by the fivefold group of causes—
as he says:
In this way, the solar direction [is presided over] by Īśāna, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Sauśiva.
Presided over [by Him], [the mantra] bestows its respective fruits through the firmness of consolation;
Īśāna is Rudra; Īśa is Īśvara.
But has it not been stated that the direction facing the sacrificer is the eastern direction? In that case, he would never face the north,
[contradicting the injunction] "he should enter facing the northern quarter" (verse 193).
Anticipating the question, "How was this stated?", he says:
"Whatever field, mandala, or dwelling the practitioner may resort to... (15.229).
In accordance with that [devotee's] inclination, Śaṅkara becomes the mediator.
For whatever field (*kṣetra*) or other object the sacrificer (*yaṣṭṛ*) resorts to, there Śaṅkara, whose essence is supreme light,
abides and becomes the mediator by assuming the intention of the practitioner and by performing that specific function.
The meaning is that it attains the state of being the "middle. For the light of consciousness alone is called the "middle," since from it alone proceeds the differentiation of all other things.
For this very reason, he said: "For he is the presiding lord over all by way of neutrality; such is his [nature]. (15.230)
The solar light is situated first; thus is the arrangement of the directions.

"All"—meaning the east, west, and so forth. For just as one's own shadow, even though one desires to step over it, remains ever in front, so too does the Supreme Lord remain [in front], even though He is conceived as being in the east and so on.
The intended meaning is that it attains a state of centrality. "Of him" refers to Śaṅkara, the presiding lord of all. "Solar" means having the nature of the rising of the sun.
And for this reason, it is rightly said: "Facing east or with a gentle countenance... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.18)—thus he says:
In order to seize the southern splendor of the Lord situated in their midst.
One should face north to receive [the breath] from behind, and face east to receive it from the front.
This has been shown immediately following as pertaining to those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) and those seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*). Thus it is said:
"When situated in the eastern direction, [the breath] bestows enjoyment; however, when facing west, it is directed toward the front."
"In her gentle face, however, is the Bhairava-like [aspect], terrifying for its incineration of saṃsāra.
Thus it is said.
One might ask: "Having sat down in this manner, what should one do? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having sat down in his own place, he should perform the purification of the body. (15.232)
"His own"—that is, appropriate for one who desires liberation and so forth. ||232||
And by this, the purification of the body, vital breath, and so forth—which was immediately mentioned after the nature of the directions—is commenced.
He states that very thing:
"Rising from the tip of the big toe, brilliant with the flames of the fire of time..."
Having meditated upon the weapon-mantra, one should burn the body internally and externally with its flames.
Now, one might ask: "What is meant here by 'burning' (dāha)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Burning is said to be destruction itself; that which destroys is known as mantra.
It is a fire permeated by the essence of its own mental construction, which is called 'intentional discourse'. (15.234)

"It is indeed destruction"—but not a reduction to ashes like wood. And what is the nature of the energy known as mantra? To this he says: "In that way"—that is, the essence (*rasa*) of the conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), which consists of one's own freedom as the subject and is designated by those expressions or sounds composed of successive phonemes.
The meaning is: it is woven together—that is, composed as a single whole—by that investigation which constitutes its very essence by virtue of being the life-force itself. || 234 ||

"Now, destruction (dhvaṃsa) is indeed non-existence (abhāva), and that is not perceived in the visible body. Therefore, how can it be said that 'one should burn the body,' since this contradicts direct perception?"—anticipating this objection, he says:
"By that fire of mantra, there is burning in the body as well as in the *puryaṣṭaka*."
It arises precisely from the destruction of the egoity [associated with] the body and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka). || 15-235 ||
"By him"—that is, by one of such a kind. ||235||

One might object: "Even if the destruction of the sense of 'I' (ahantā) has occurred, we do not perceive the burning of the body, because its existence is established by direct perception? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This body does not [become the Self] by its mere existence, like any other body;
for corporeality consists in the sense of "I," and when that is destroyed, it certainly burns that [body]. (15.236)

And here is the formal argument (*prayoga*) in this case: this body of the practitioner, which is the subject of dispute, is not a "body," because it is not the locus of the sense of "I" (*ahantā*). Whatever is not the locus of someone's sense of "I" is not that person's body, because it is not the locus of their sense of "I. Whatever is not the locus of someone's sense of "I," that...

His body is not like any other body. Whatever is someone’s body is the locus of that person’s ego-identity (*ahaṃtā*), just as the body of a commoner is. And this body is not the locus of his ego-identity;
therefore, it is not [his] body. ||236||

Thus, having discarded even the permeation of that [notion of self] within the body and so forth, which are by nature non-self, how might one rest in the true nature of the conscious Self (cidātman), which consists of the supreme awareness of "I"? To this he says: "Then, that mass of residual impressions (saṃskāra) belonging to the body, which remains in the form of ashes..."
Having shaken that off with the wind of the armor-mantra, one should abide in the pure self of consciousness.
Anticipating the question, "What would result from his resting therein?", he says:
"Having attained absorption in that stable, waveless state, because consciousness possesses the nature of emanation, it enters its primordial state of being wavy. (15.238)
That very [power] is known as Mūrti (Form), whose nature consists of the *tāra* (the syllable Om), the *sad* (the six vowels), and the *bindu* (the nasal point).
"That very" refers to the primordial one who has become wavy [with creative vibration]. "Mūrti" refers to the limited subject consisting of the body, vital breath, and so forth.

Upon the arising of the creation of the pure body (*śuddha-śarīra*), there is the attainment of *samucchraya*— which, according to the reading "mūrchā mohasamucchrayayoḥ," consists of the state of being immeasurable (*aparimitīkaraṇa*).
As it has been said:

"Endless is the height of Bhairava; this is considered the supreme form, by the mere placement of which the state of being a limited individual (aṇutva) dissolves. Here, *tāra* is the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), and "consisting of the eternal bindu" means having the form of *haṃ*. Thus it has been said:
"Then one should apply to him the Aparājita power, [reciting] 'so'ham'.
Thus [it is said].
Now, in order to describe the variety of the specific placement (viśeṣanyāsa), he says:
"Then, by means of the deity Navātman, the placement consists of the emergence of the principles (tattva). (15.239)
One should assign its limbs and faces to their respective places;
then, as before, by means of the Mātṛkā, it consists of the manifestation of each respective principle (tattva).
When the three-fold placement of the principles (tritattvanyāsa) has been performed upon his back, reaching the three girdles,
then follows the placement of the eight Aghoras, whose head consists of their feet.
Even beyond that, the deposition of the true being of Śiva (śivasadbhāvanyāsa) is conjoined with one’s own limbs.
When this pentad has been performed in this manner, that which is its primary essence arises.
One should employ that which is to be worshipped and adored, along with its ancillaries, in the sixth placement (nyāsa);
by this means, the Blessed Lord Ratiśekhara is suitable for placement here.

The placement [of the letters] should be upward for that which is called the "Nine" (navākhya), since in its primacy there is a mutual state of being the locus [of one another]. "Consisting of the emergence of the principles" (tattvodayātmaka) states the fruit of the placement. "The three principles" refers to the characteristic of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman; otherwise, indeed, in this system, [the fruit would belong to] the venerable Ratiśekharabhairava.

There would be no exclusion from the procedure of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). "On its back" means above the *mātṛkā*-placement. "Having reached the three enclosures" means having reached the three enclosures characterized by the crest, the heart, and the feet—this is the meaning.

And in this context, regarding the statement, "joined with the form and the limbs" (verse 247)— *mūrti* means existence (*sattā*), that is, being (*sadbhāva*). *Ūrdhve* refers to the fivefold deposition (*nyāsa*).
Now, an objection may be raised: "It was stated that whichever deity is primarily to be worshipped is the one to be employed in the sixth deposition;

so how is it now said here that Ratiśekhara is to be deposited there? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the one called Nava," and so forth—therefore, Ratiśekhara [is to be placed] in the location of the first deposition.
It should be applied; however, in the sixth [chapter], it is the "ninefold self" (navātman).
Thus, this same principle applies elsewhere as well; so he says: "In this way, if [the disciple] is primarily established in the true being of Bhairava... (15.244).
Ratiśekhara is to be installed first in each respective location as the object of worship.
Nor is this merely our own invention; thus he says:
"In this way, [my teacher] described my tradition to me in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra. (15.245)
For Śambhunātha is indeed a deity in the ritual of nyāsa; otherwise, why would he be excluded from this nyāsa? For he possesses limbs as well. (15.246)
Regarding the phrase "by Śambhunātha": the intention is that, according to the system of the venerable Lakṣmaṇagupta, the procedure for ritual placement (nyāsavidhi) is indeed otherwise.

Anticipating the question, "What is the intended meaning behind the venerable Śambhunātha’s formulation of the ritual placement in this manner?", he says: "The Lord," and so forth. The Lord is Ratiśekhara.
Anticipating the objection, "How can it be avoided? It is not right to avoid it," he says:
"For its limbs also exist," the intention being that this is because [the Śrīpūrvaśāstra] shares the same logical principle as other Bhairava scriptures, such as the *Śrībhairavasadbhāva*.
Śrī Lakṣmaṇagupta, however, explained this differently, saying:

"Form, emission, and the three principles—these eight, together with the limbs of form and Śiva along with his limbs, are to be known as the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) as it has been proclaimed. (15.247)

Then, upon this, one should perform the sixfold Śākta nyāsa. Above that [is] Mūrti with her limbs (aṅgas) and faces, and Navātmā; in the Śākta nyāsa, above that is Parāparā with her limbs and faces. Above that is Sṛṣṭi, then Mātṛkā, and above that Mālinī. [Then] the three principles (tritattva).
The form of the ninefold self (navātmarūpa) is the crest-jewel of the delight in the true being of Bhairava; above that is the triad beginning with Parā.
Above that are the eight [deities] beginning with Aghora, and above those is the group of eight beginning with Aghorī. Regarding "the limbs of the form" (mūrtyaṅga):
these are the limbs of the ninefold form, and above those is the pentad of the limbs of Vidyā. Śiva.
The true essence of Bhairava possesses limbs and faces, and above that, the true essence of the Mothers likewise possesses limbs and faces.
He concludes this in both ways by stating: "The deposition (nyāsa) is proclaimed to be sixfold.
The word *nyāsa* should be applied according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). "Of this" refers to the Śāmbhava deposition.
He says that very thing: "Then [one should worship] Parāparā with her faces as before; then Mālinī as before. (15.248)

Afterwards, the triad beginning with *parā* is placed respectively on the crest, the heart, and the feet; then [the remaining mantras] are placed on the head, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, the secret place, and the thighs. (15–249)
On the knees and feet, one should likewise [place] Aghorī and the others, followed by the five limbs of the Vidyā;
thereafter, one should invoke the Śakti whose nature is the true essence (sadbhāva) of the Mothers.
When, however, this very [deity]— the supreme, perfect Yogeśvarī, Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, the eternal—
is desired to be realized in accordance with the scriptures, then this is the distinction; thus he says:
Exceeding by twelve the number of limbs, faces, retinues, and powers.

The Guru should contemplate [the deity] at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the distinction of the practice to be accomplished. Now, one might object: "In this system, the triad alone is the ultimate reality; what is the purpose of teaching this fourth form? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
She who stands as the indivisible one in the midst of the triad of goddesses is Para herself.
This [state] is proclaimed as the existence of pure consciousness (cinmātra) without limitation;
therefore, it is celebrated by the Goddess in both the Sāraśāstra and the Yāmala. || 15.253 ||
The form with its faces, the Śakti, the triad of Śaktis, then the group of eight, the five limbs, and the Supreme Śakti—this sixfold deposition (nyāsa) belongs to the Śākta tradition. (15.254)
"This great nyāsa of the Yāmala bestows the fruits of both supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mukti).
Thus it was proclaimed—namely, by the Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha—to the Goddess, who stood as the questioner. It was precisely with this intention that [it was stated] previously:
"That is the essence, that is the heart, and that is the supreme emission, the Lord;
in the *Yāmala* scripture of the Goddess, she is called Kālakarṣiṇī."
"In the Mahāḍāmara sacrifice, she resides at the summit of Śrīparā;
in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, she is described as the true essence of the Mothers.
Thus it has been stated (3.71), and so forth. For this very reason, the *nyāsa* belonging to the Śākta [tradition] is also sixfold—as he says with the words "by that," and so on.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: for that very reason—that the Supreme Goddess herself is taught separately by virtue of her being the nature of uninterrupted pure consciousness—the Śākta nyāsa is also proclaimed to be sixfold. Regarding the term "form" (mūrti):
it refers to the Mālinī, who is the Parāparā Śakti, because she resides therein (tātsthya).
Now, one might ask: why are these Śaiva or Śākta nyāsas performed simultaneously?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Furthermore, one who seeks liberation as their sole goal should first perform the Śākta nyāsa. (15.255)
As it has been said:
"This left-hand rule (vāmavidhi) should be practiced by those who rely upon the path of liberation. ||255||

Regarding this very point, there is also another interpretation; thus he says: "But the Gurus have declared that as for the two types of nyāsa which have been illustrated, they should be performed by one seeking liberation (mumukṣu) starting from the feet and so forth, according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhṛti). (15.256)
And this sequence does not apply here alone; thus he says:
"However many divisions have been proclaimed as denoting Śambhu, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu), even among all those mantras, the sixfold deposition (nyāsa) is proclaimed. (15.257)
However, whichever mantra is to be invoked, it should be accompanied by its limbs;
thus, in all cases, this [mantra] is declared to be sixfold. (15.258)
In this context, there are indeed certain mantras belonging to other tantras, divided into categories such as the Śāmbhava and so forth;
for these as well, this very deposition (nyāsa) must be performed according to the stated sequence by way of their vital potency (vīrya).
However, whichever mantra is to be invoked as the object of worship in a particular [deity], that very mantra should be applied in the sixth position.

By this [method], it is stated that this very sixfold nyāsa (sixfold ritual deposition) bestows the respective desired fruits everywhere in the scripture; with reference to which it is said immediately thereafter: "Therefore, when the rite, its potency, or its essential nature has been lost, [it is restored] by means of this supreme [method]."
"It has been said: 'The mantras that have been deposited [once] are fulfilled by being deposited again; they bestow their fruit' (verse 135). ||258||
But surely, in this way, the state of Bhairava would be established within one's own self; for the mudrās must necessarily be displayed as the cause for the presence of Bhairava, as it is said:
"O Great Goddess, one should display these mudrās to Bhairava."

Having raised the doubt— since it has been stated [in the scriptures], "At the invocation, at the end of the worship, and likewise at the dismissal," should that visualization be performed here during the invocation and so forth, or not?— he says:
The display of mudrās follows through body, mind, and speech.
Regarding "with the mind," [it is said]:
"The powers of Śiva are designated as mudrās."
The meaning is: consisting of such contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*). As it has been said:
