"The mudrā is known to be threefold: born of the mind, residing in the mouth of the Guru, and arising from speech; born of mantra, arising from the body through the gestures of the limbs."
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that here one has merely begun to effect the purification of the locus (*deśaśuddhi*), and since that could be accomplished by even a single placement (*nyāsa*), what is the intention behind its being sixfold? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The five states beginning with waking, and the sixth named the Absolute (*anuttara*). (15.259)
Because it possesses six causes and six natures, there is the application of the thirty-six principles;
thus, when this great sixfold deposition has been performed, this entire universe is forcibly [united].
Having attained identity with the body, one should manifest the pure creation;

that is to say, even so, by means of the presiding influence of the six causes upon each of the six states, through their sixfold nature, and by means of the contemplative connection with the thirty-six principles.

As has been stated by this very [author] elsewhere: "In that regard, there are five states beginning with waking, and a sixth called the 'Supreme' (anuttara), which is the state of one's own nature (svabhāvadaśā) to be realized; thus, the deposition (nyāsa) becomes sixfold. Therein, of the causes..."

Because of the installation (*nyāsa*) of the entire collection of thirty-six principles— including those that transcend worldly principles— which function non-differently from the venerable Lord Bhairava through their respective presiding over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and the Unconditioned (*anāśrita*), there is fullness.
"The state of Bhairavī. Thus [it is said].
Anticipating the objection, "What indeed is its purity?", he says:
"That emanation which has spread forth here, beginning from the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa)... (15.261).
Having brought about non-differentiation, she is rendered pure through the sequence of the power of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*);
here,
"having attained absorption in that stable, waveless [state]."
Because consciousness possesses the nature of creation, it attains its primordial state of being wavy.
Beginning with the passage, "That very [deity] is known as the *mūrti*...

(*Tantrāloka* 23.8), the emanation of the practitioner’s body that has proceeded from the installation of the *mūrtis* (*mūrtinyāsa*) onwards is here rendered pure by being brought to a state of non-difference through the sequence of the power of the installation (*nyāsabala*).
The meaning is: whose essential nature consists in the firm stabilization of the state of Bhairavī.

And for this reason, those who raise the objection— "Since the sacrificer has ascended to Śiva, the pure conscious self, immediately after the cremation of the body, what need is there for the creation of a pure body again?"— are cast far away. Thus he says:
Therefore, those fools who raised objections regarding the shaking off [of bondage] through the burning of the fetters—‖ 15.262 ‖

"Once one has ascended to the state that is accomplished, peaceful, and auspicious, why would one descend again?"—those who ask such things have been cast far away from the supreme reality of Śiva. (15.263)
Devoid of the essence of the radiance of self-awareness, they do not know [this].
He establishes the very realization of the supreme reality of Śambhu:
"Indeed, this Śiva, known as 'the Peaceful,' is not some [entity] possessed of differentiation. (15.264)
"Excluded from all other times, it exists somewhere like a jar.
Anticipating the objection, "If Śiva is not of such a nature, then who is? he says:
"For this consciousness, whose nature is great light, unfolds [in this way]. (15.265)
"That Śiva is Śiva-ness itself" means that his manifestation as the universal form unfolds;
the meaning is that he shines forth in every form. For this alone is the Śiva-nature of Śiva: that he manifests in various such forms, as it has been said.
His state of Śiva-hood is indeed manifested through manifold forms.
And because its very nature is such, it has no dependence on another in this regard—as he says: "Therefore, the union with such a manifestation unfolds by its own inherent force. (15.266)

Now, one might object: "If this [reality] appears only as differentiated in this way, then there would always be saṃsāra, and never at any time would there be liberation (kaivalya). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this context, that which is being manifested is both non-difference from one's own self and indeed difference."
"Here"—that is, in such a manifestation that occurs spontaneously.
And it is precisely in this [state] that the distinction between bondage and liberation occurs—as he says:
"When duality has unfolded, Māyā unfolds for the sufferer of Māyā. (15.267)
"The nature of Śiva unfolds as non-difference within this very subject of Māyā.

Now, one might raise the objection: "How can there be non-difference for him while he is a subject of Māyā, such that his being the self of Śiva would be inseparable from it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The illusory subject [attains this] through proficiency in the repeated practice of conceptualizations of that very form. (15.268)
Śiva alone is proclaimed as the fruit of that practice, such as the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then what is the use of these depositions and the rest? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The fruit of its practice. This means that the practice itself is the fruit—the purpose—of this [teaching].

Anticipating the objection, "But how can Śiva-hood arise from mere practice alone?", he provides an illustration while internalizing this doubt: "For just as it is for one who contemplates, 'I am a doer of evil deeds'... (15.269).
Likewise, for one who contemplates, "I am Śiva, I am none other," just as for one who contemplates,
"I perform evil action," the state of being an evildoer would arise and not the state of being a doer of good deeds; so it is with [the thought], "I am Śiva, I am non-dual," and so forth.
The meaning is that for one who meditates in such a manner, there is indeed the state of Śiva itself.
Now, one might object: "Was it not previously stated that non-conceptuality arises from the proficiency gained through the practice of conceptualization?
How, then, can it be said here that this constitutes the state of Śiva? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This very thing is called firmness when it has reached the heart of reflective awareness. (15.270)
The state of non-conceptuality is the gateway to the flood of conceptualizations regarding identity with Śiva;
it is that which has come to rest at the culmination of the cultivation whose nature is the repeated practice of conceptualizations such as "I am Śiva."

The meaning is that "the state of Śiva" (śivatva) is everywhere said to consist solely in the reality of non-conceptual reflective awareness (nirvikalpatā-vimarśa), and it is likewise designated as firmness (dārḍhya).
He demonstrates this very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"Otherwise, for that pure [consciousness] which subsists with reflective awareness as its vital breath... (15.271).
How indeed could the nature of that which has the property of manifesting remain unexamined?
For if this state of Śiva— which consists of the reflective awareness of a non-conceptual self— were not attainable through contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
then [how could it be realized] as the self-luminous one whose essence is innate reflective awareness, free from the stain of conceptualization?
How indeed could its form be unexamined? It must be constantly examined—this is the meaning.
For if this were not so, how could even the subjects consisting of the body and so forth fail to manifest as the self of Śiva? Thus he says:
"Therefore, by the power of His independent will, which accomplishes the most difficult tasks... (15.272).
Even though this subject— the body and so forth— appears as the self, one should not conceptualize it as such through the intellect of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other faculties.
For that reason, because the state of Śiva is attainable through contemplation (*bhāvanā*), and because its appearance otherwise would be impossible,
this subject, though appearing [as the body], exists as the nature of Śiva.

The meaning is that, by the power of the will of the Supreme Lord who performs such various difficult feats, one should not conceptualize oneself as being other than the nature of Śiva; rather, one should contemplate it as such. The word *ghaṭanā* (the act of joining/performing) is derived from the root *ghaṭ*, with the suffix *aṅ* applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *bhid*.
"Surely, let there not be such a reflective awareness (parāmarśa) for this [subject]; on the contrary, there exists a connection with a contrary reflective awareness.
To this he says:
"On the contrary, [it perceives] its own nature as being contrary to the extremely independent Self. (15.273)
Having ascertained that the nature of what is subject to destruction consists in its lack of dependence on a master, one sinks [into despair];
for dependence means being subject to another's will.

Thus, he concludes that it is precisely the attainment of Śiva-hood through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that is logical: "Therefore, [one should practice] that which destroys the certainty belonging to the realm of transmigratory existence... (15.274).
One should resort to a state free of conceptual construction by means of the ascertainment of [the Self as] eternal and so forth.

"In that manner" means by way of its contrary nature; for this very reason it was said, "by means of the ascertainment of [the Self as] eternal and so forth," where the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes [qualities such as] lordship and independence.
Now, has it not been stated by all [the authorities] that "There is no need for any means whatsoever, nor even for meditative cultivation" (Śivadr̥ṣṭi 7.6)?
So why is this practice beginning with āsana, which culminates in meditative cultivation, mentioned here?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"But those who enjoy the purity resulting from the power intensified by the highest degree [of intensity]... (15.275).
It has been described that they do not perform the *anunyāsa* following the *dīkṣā*.
Regarding the phrase "it has been described"—this was stated in the second chapter (*dvitīyāhnika*).
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"In this way, being the body of the universe, he has clearly attained the state of being the self of the universe. (15.276)
By the mere act of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship the body, which has thus become [divine], with flowers and other offerings;
either elaborately with separate mantras or concisely with the root mantra.
"By means of incense, food offerings, satisfaction, and so forth, both extensively and concisely.
"Separately" means according to the distinctions of the limbs, faces, and so on.
Now, one might object: "All these acts, such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), are actions to be performed by the hand; by which hand, then, are they performed?
We do not know. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But because it is the practice of the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*) regarding transmigratory existence, everything is done with the left hand. (15.278)
And the Guru should perform the rite of libation with that [wine] which is free from impurity;
for the "left-hand" (vāma) practice—which is contrary to worldly norms, excluded by society, and conducive to liberation—is the secret conduct.
For this very reason, the scripture also speaks thus—stating that "the secret is expressed by the word *vāma* even in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other [texts]. (15.279)
As it has been stated there, beginning with: "In that regard, through secret speech, the left [path] is remembered as the Lord's energy consisting of action" (Mataṅgapārameśvara 1.4.25).
"Therefore, that Blessed One is proclaimed as Vāmaguhya" (Maṭaṅga 1.4.28).
By the word "etcetera," [texts such as] the *Śrīnandiśikhā* and others are included. As it is said therein:
"The Left (Vāma) is declared to be the Secret (Guhya), the Nectar beloved by the Khecarīs."
"The secret of all beings is proclaimed by the word 'Vāma'. || 279 ||
The word "vāma" does not only denote a secret meaning in this context, but elsewhere as well—
as he says: "The practitioner of mantra, devoted to the 'left-hand' practice (vāmācāra), should perform the sacrifice," clearly.
Likewise, in the illustrious Bhargaśikhāśāstra and in the venerable Gamaśāsana.
As it has been said therein:
"The practitioner of mantra, devoted to the Vāmācāra, should then perform the sacrifice.
Now, let this be granted; however, as for the libation (tarpaṇa), it is performed with the ring finger of the left hand.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the proof for this being an effect?", he says: "In that way," and so forth. ||280||

He recites that very [verse]: "O Dear One, whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by the libation offered with the ring finger (anāmā). (15.281)

*Anāmā* means [the ring finger] joined with the thumb. As it is said in that very same place: "In the union of Tumburu and the one reciting on the left hand, a mere drop [of nectar] should be offered, arranged higher and higher."

Thus, in the *Śrīsaṅkarṣaṇīyāmala*: "O auspicious lady, one should worship this supreme bliss, the great all-encompassing unsurpassed [mantra], the beloved of the Yoginīs, within the vessel for the offering (*arghapātra*)."

"Therefore, it is traditionally taught that at all times, the satiation [of the deities] should be performed with only a single drop [of water], using the left hand by joining the ring finger and the thumb. Thus it is stated; and also in the *Navanityāvidhāna*:
"One should satisfy the supreme goddesses with the thumb and the ring finger.
Elsewhere, however, satisfaction is also said to be performed by joining the middle finger with the thumb. Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmadānandeśvara* in twelve thousand verses:
O Bhairavī, one should offer divine splendor enriched with fragrance to the circle of Mothers using the left hand, by joining the middle finger and the thumb.
"Then one shall quickly attain the success (siddhi) spoken of in the Tantra; there is no doubt in this.
Also, regarding the agitation of the elements (bhūtakṣobha):
"The practitioner, having bound the Kāpālinī mudrā with his right hand..."
The vessel should be placed upon that by joining the middle finger and the thumb.
"Having cast a single drop into the mouth, one should satisfy the host of deities.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīpañcāmṛta*:
"The index finger is prescribed for victory over enemies; the middle finger is remembered for libation (*tarpaṇa*)."
The ring finger (anāmā) is to be employed for drying, and the little finger (kanīyā) for lowly tasks.
Therefore, with every effort, by means of the union of the middle finger and the thumb,
one should satisfy the Lord of the God of Gods, especially the circle of Mothers;
for the middle finger is praised because of its efficacy in all ritual actions.
Thus it is said:
"The thumb is Bhairava himself, and the middle finger shall be Cāmuṇḍā;
for this union of the two is the supreme bestower of all accomplishments."

Thus, in this way, whatever scripture the practitioner has undertaken for which the consecration of wine (*madyasaṃskāra*) is intended, he must perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) in accordance with that very same scripture—
such is the division of the subject matter. ||281||
Now, one might object: "If it is thus established that the word *vāma* denotes a secret meaning, what then is the proof for its being the left hand? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And in the venerable *Nandiśikhā* and the venerable *Ānandaśāsana*..."
As it has been said: "The *sruk* ladle is used for the *pūrṇāhuti*, and the *sruva* ladle is used for the oblation of clarified butter. (15.282)

The remaining acts, such as worship, fire-oblation (homa), and recitation (japa), are to be performed with the left hand alone. Here, in the final oblation of clarified butter (pūrṇāhuti), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are to be held with both hands by implication,
as it has been said:
"Now I shall describe for you the procedure for the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Standing with the body straight, the neck straight, and the feet level,"

At the position of the navel, the base of the *sruk* ladle should be placed with its tip facing upward and its mouth level; O Goddess, having placed the *sruva* spoon upon the *sruk*, it should likewise be turned face downward.
Having offered the flower at the tip of the *sruc* ladle, with both hands joined together by a blade of *darbha* grass,
one should grasp them firmly with a fist.
"O beloved, having grasped the right hand in front and the left hand behind with both fists, using the method of upturned hands.
Furthermore, all other remaining rites such as worship and so forth should be performed with the left hand alone.
"It would be"—this is the meaning of the sentence.
Now, one might ask: "What would be gained by sacrificing the body in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this manner, [the body] becomes completely filled with bliss and devoid of all outward orientation. (15.283)
Having produced the body through sacrifice, one should contemplate it as being of the nature of Śiva.
Now, one might ask: "How can this body and so forth, which are of the nature of the non-self, be contemplated as being of the nature of Śiva?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
When the orientation toward sense objects and limitation have been dissolved, || 15-284 ||
What would remain in the body apart from the essence of the bliss of Śiva?
Therefore, the practitioner who is thus endowed with practice becomes Śiva himself—so it is said:
"Filled with the essence of the bliss of Śiva, overflowing with the thirty-six principles. (15.285)
"Beholding and worshipping the body day and night, one should become identical with Śiva.

Now, if the practitioner's identity with Śiva were to arise through such means as the contemplation of the body alone, then what would be the use for him of external symbols (liṅga) and so forth? "Quite so," he says:
Satisfied by resting within the body that is the self of the universe, he is established in its *liṅga*.
One does not desire external signs, vows, sacred sites, or ritual conduct.
However, for one who lacks such repose [within], these external things are prescribed; thus it is said:
"Ritual actions are taught for consciousness that has not yet found repose through those means alone. (15.287)

The subsequent [stages] end with the external sacrifice; however, what is to be accomplished here is the state of being Śiva. Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of explaining even these external ritual actions? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "But what is to be accomplished here is the state of being Śiva. The particle *tu* (but/however) indicates the reason.
Now, in order to describe the special argha-vessel (viśeṣārghapātra), which was mentioned immediately after the various types of special placements (viśeṣanyāsa), he says:
"Then the supreme argha-vessel, consisting of non-difference from Śiva, should be prepared. (15.288)

Filled with the essence of bliss and satisfying all the deities of the universe, it is indeed exactly like [the ritual] from the cremation and so forth up to the end of worship within the body. (15.289)
The offering of *argha* should also be performed through the application of both concise and detailed methods;
the essence of bliss takes the form of wine and other such substances.
One might raise the objection: "Why have the various substances required for the worship of one's own self or the *arghapātra* not been mentioned here? Having presented this doubt, he refutes it:
"What are the substances for the sacrifice, and what indeed is the *argha*? This has not been stated. (15.290)
For one who desires accomplishment, the means of practice alone is the cause for that accomplishment;
for one who desires liberation, nothing is prohibited and nothing is enjoined.
Whatever is pleasing to the heart is suitable for the non-differentiation from the consciousness of Śiva;
having prepared the vessel of honor (arghapātra), one should sprinkle flowers and other offerings with its droplets.
And having performed [this], one should worship oneself as the supreme Śiva.
Indeed, no specific material substance has been prescribed here for the purpose of worship and so forth;
for, for one who desires accomplishment (*siddhi*), that accomplishment—which consists of pacification (*śānti*) and the like—is already determined within that [practice].

The very accomplishment [of a specific aim] is the cause for the employment of a particular substance: when a practitioner begins a rite for pacification (*śānti*), he must employ only white substances and not red ones; likewise, in rites for subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth, only red substances are used and not white ones. However, for one who desires liberation (*mukti*), nothing at all is prescribed or prohibited.

Or rather, regarding him, which substance among these do we designate as that very thing which captivates his heart, and which serves as the means for liberation— liberation consisting in the attainment of identity with the consciousness of Śiva? Thus it is said.

Now, it might be objected that other [authorities], beginning with the words "having prepared the vessel for the guest-offering" (*kṛtvārghapātram*) and so forth, and stating "having worshipped oneself with those flowers" (*tasthaiḥ kusumaiḥ svamabhyarcya cātmānam*), have declared that the worship of one's own self and so on must be performed using only the flowers produced from the *argha* vessel; how then can it be done here with [flowers] merely sprinkled with droplets from that [vessel]?
Anticipating the objection—"Is it not denoted by something else, such as a flower?"—he says:
"For fear of being mixed with the flowers offered during the worship of the argha vessel. (15.293)
One should not place flowers in the *argha* vessel for the purpose of worshipping the deity;
rather, it is only the water, having become nectar (*amṛta*), that is worshipped within the *argha* vessel. (15.294)
Solely for the satisfaction of the mantras and for the purification of the sacrificial substances,
having thus worshipped the body, [one worships] the forms consisting of vital breath, intellect, and the void.
One should worship those who have become mutually absorbed in such a state of Śiva.
Regarding the word "that": it refers to the water in the arghya vessel, because flowers are not to be used for the purpose of worshipping the deities and so forth. As it has been said:
"The substance is declared to be water, which conforms to the various divisions such as Kula and Ucchuṣma."
Thus: "mutually become one with each other" means because they are inseparable from one another.
And how should the worship of these three forms—the vital breaths and so forth—be performed? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, when the placement (nyāsa) based on the vital breaths has been mentally constructed... (15.296).
Through the empowerment of emptiness (*śūnyādhiṣṭhāna*), everything is worshipped with a single effort.

For here, the contracted self, by means of resorting to the subjectivity of emptiness, should preside over the intellect and perform the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) upon the vital breath; thus it is for all three as well.
The meaning of the sentence is that worship is accomplished without a separate effort.

Since worship here must be preceded by the deposition of the paths (*adhvan*), he begins with the mental sacrifice (*manoyāga*) and first sets forth the position regarding the seat (*āsana*); he then defines the very process of deposition (*nyāsa*) upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by delineating the division of each respective category (*tattva*).
One should install the Ādhāraśakti four finger-breadths below the navel.
It is the form of a ship for the earth, the waters, and the fire, established as the limit of the measurable;
it is the nature of the root of the winds, because it threads together the universe.
One should place four finger-breadths each for the space-womb (vyomagarbha);
this pure āmalasāraka [mandala] is slightly [elevated] all around. (15.299)
Then one should conceive the staff known as Ananta, extending up to the uvula (lambikā).
From the level of the subtle elements (tanmātra) up to the level of Kalā, above that is the knot (granthi) consisting of Night (niśā). || 15-300 ||
In that knot composed of Māyā, there is the group of eight beginning with dharma and adharma, starting from the southeast (Agni) and proceeding eastward;
for Māyā is their source, while the intellect (dhī) is their manifestation. (15.301)
One should meditate upon a four-legged throne consisting of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), situated above the knot of Māyā and below the trident, and joined with two coverings.
And that reality is to be meditated upon as abiding between the uvula (*lambikā*) and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

The Supreme Lord’s sustaining power (*dhārikā śaktiḥ*), whose nature is will (*icchātmā*), resides at the limit [of the body] as the foundational energy (*ādhāraśakti*); within it, the entire universe, beginning with the earth, is supported. As it has been said:
For this [universe], beginning with the earth and so forth, which is characterized by a sequential relationship of support,
is ultimately established within the power of Śiva, whose nature is sustenance.
"She is established in the first portion in the proximity of all reality;

she is called the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) residing at the ultimate limit in the scriptures. Because it consists of the act of crossing over, it is appropriate for the boat to be established on the further shore, as is the case with light.

It has been stated that [the vital breath] acts as an auxiliary cause in the determination of the entire object of knowledge—this is expressed by the phrase "because it is established at the furthest limit of the object of knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "from the weaving of the universe": the intention is that the vital breath (*marut*) indeed first weaves out the universe according to the principle, "First, consciousness transforms into the vital breath. The term "containing space within its womb" (*vyomagarbhaka*) means:
Because space is all-pervasive, it exists within the interior of everything;

this [universe], beginning with the earth, is interwoven with the wall of the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*). Although it is slightly [different] from reality because its nature is that of the manifest (*prakāśya*), it is pure on all sides by virtue of having the nature of the Supreme Lord’s power.
Because it possesses the capacity to sustain everything and because it is the essence, it is called *sāraka*; thus, it is termed *āmalasāraka*. As it has been said:
"First, one should [visualize] the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) four finger-breadths below the navel."
The fourfold [classification] consists of the earth, the ocean, the boat, and the bulbous root.
"Each finger-breadth of this trident shall consist of *amalasaraka*. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.55).

Regarding the term "named Ananta"—this is because it is presided over by that Rudra. "Up to the tip of the uvula" means up to the cavity of the palate. "Fire, east, and so forth" refers to what has been stated:
One should sequentially assign Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya,
which are white, red, yellow, and black in color, situated in the directions starting from the southeast (Āgneyī) up to the northeast (Īśānī).
"Their feet are in the form of lions; they have three eyes and possess terrifying prowess. (Svacchanda Tantra 2.62).
"Adharma, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty [are located] in the eastern direction."
"And the limbs [of the seat] should be established at the northern limit, white in color" (Svacchanda Tantra 2.64).

Now, one might object: "But dharma and the other seven are the eight qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*); so how can they be said here to be in *māyā*? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "For *māyā* is their source; its manifestation (*vibhava*), however..."
Regarding the word *dhī*: "the fourfold" (*catuṣkikā*) refers to that which has the form of a cushion (*asūraka*), consisting primarily of a square pedestal (*pīṭhikā*).
Regarding "the two covers": the lower cover is of the nature of *māyā* which conceals one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), while the upper [cover] is that which conceals *māyā*.
The form of Vidyā. As it has been said:
"Māyā is indeed the lower covering, while Vidyā is certainly the upper one.
Regarding the phrase "between the lambikā and the brahmarandhra"—that is to say, in the middle. As it has been stated:
"One should contemplate that specific principle between the *kaka* and the *lambikā*," thus [it is said in] Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.61.
Now, one might ask: "Is this established solely on the basis of scripture, or is there also a sign of it elsewhere? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the connection with light is thus [evident] here in the sight, hearing, taste, and so forth. (15.303)
One should deposit two groups of nine Śaktis, rotating from Dakṣā and Anyā;
although this has already been mentioned regarding the Vidyā-lotus here, it is shown once again.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikarika, Balavikarika, Balapramathinī, Bhūtamathinī, Manonmanikā, and Śāntā—these should be here, radiant as the bow of Indra. (15.305)

Vibhvī, Jñapti, Kṛti, Icchā, Vāgīśī, Jvālinī, as well as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—these [deities] are located starting from the eastern petal, all of them like the fire of time (kāladahana). || 15-306 ||
One should meditate upon the triad of the sun, moon, and fire within the filaments and the pericarp of the lotus, presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara according to their respective positions.

For it has been stated more than once that non-conceptual knowledge, which consists of mere observation, is indeed the unfolding of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā); therefore, the followers of Suśruta maintain that for this reason, the diversity of injuries to the sense organs in people arises from the diversity of blows [to the vital points].
"Dakṣānyāvartata" means that one should install the nine [deities] beginning with Vāmā by turning to the right—that is, the group of nine starting with Vibhvi.
Here, by the word "vidyā," Īśvara, who presides over that [tenth] state, is meant. "Here" (atra)— [End of excerpt]
Below the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). As it has been said:

"Then one should meditate upon the Īśvara-tattva, which is of the nature of the element of space (kha), shaped like a lotus, provided with a pericarp and filaments, possessing its seed-syllable, and blossoming white."
Starting from the first leaf on the right and proceeding to the left, one should place the group of nine beginning with Vāmā:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and likewise the others.
Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī,
and likewise Balapramathanī, as well as Sarvabhūtadamanī.
One should place Manonmanī in the center by way of the solar path;
one should then arrange another group of nine, beginning with Vibhu, in reverse order.
"Vibhu, Jñānī, Kriyā, Icchā, Vāgīśī, and likewise Jvālinī;
as well as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—all [these] possess the radiance of the fire of time. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.66).
The phrase "previously" refers to the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*). The phrase "is shown again" is for the sake of strengthening conviction.
Regarding the phrase "Indra’s bow"—as it was stated, beginning with:
"One should place Vāmā on the eastern petal... (Svacchandatantra 2.68).
"O Goddess, the maṇḍala of Śakti, resembling Indra’s bow, is to be meditated upon. (Svacchanda Tantra 2.71).
Regarding the phrase "from the eastern petal"—the word "above" is to be understood as the ellipsis. ||307||
One might object: "Since Brahmā and the others reside within Māyā, how can they possess the state of presiding over its [Māyā's] condition?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For that form of Brahmā and the others which was previously described as transcending Māyā..."
But this very seat should be used, and not one smeared with the ointment of illusion.
"Pure" refers to the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan). ||308||

Furthermore, since Īśvara and Sadāśiva possess an eternal form that transcends Māyā, their placement here is made without distinction; thus he says: "Above Rudra is the god Īśvara, and above him is Sadāśiva."
And he is called "the great corpse" (mahāpeta) in the scriptures. || 15-309 ||
Due to the metaphorical identification of the presiding agent and the object presided over, the word *rudra* here denotes *māyā*.
"He" refers to Sadāśiva. (309)
Anticipating the question, "What is the cause of its greatness and its state as a *preta* (ghost)? he says:

"Because it pervades all the *tattvas*, it is a 'Great Ghost' (*mahāpreta*) due to its awakening; and because it has reached the highest excellence, being absorbed [in that state], it does not descend to a lower level. (15.310)

All the principles (*tattvas*) ending with Śakti are thirty-five; therefore, Sadāśiva here is called the Lord Anāśrita-bhaṭṭāraka. For it is proclaimed everywhere that he is indeed his supreme form. "From awakening" means: he goes forth pre-eminently, he awakens.

Regarding the phrase "due to reaching the excellence": because he goes to the preeminent, highest station, once he has attained this, he would not go to a lower state, but rather takes refuge in the supreme Śiva—this is the meaning. ||310||

Now, an objection is raised: "Has it not been stated everywhere that one who abides in the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) does not descend to a lower level? So how is it that this very person is a 'preta' (hungry ghost)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
All the lords of knowledge and ignorance have indeed attained higher and higher states;
having become Sadāśiva, they have thereafter taken refuge in the Supreme Śiva.
For indeed, all the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and so forth,
having attained a progressively higher state according to such views as "Anantanātha attains liberation, while Sūkṣmarudra enters that abode," reach the state of Sadāśiva.
"Immediately thereafter, they have resorted to the supreme Śiva"—between these [two stages], there is contact with the progressively lower levels. ||311||
But this is not so; thus he says:
"Therefore, Sadāśiva is eternally characterized by an upward gaze and a luminous nature;
he is 'emaciated' due to the weakness of being an object of cognition, and a 'corpse' because of his loud laughter and other such [attributes]. (15.312)

Therefore, because he has descended to the lower plane, this Sadāśiva is eternally upward-looking due to his orientation toward supreme illumination; for that very reason, being of the sole nature of light, he is radiant in essence; and for that same reason, due to the dissolution even of the latent impressions of the object of knowledge (*meyasaṃskāra*), he is emaciated. Thus...
The meaning is that he is like a *preta* (hungry ghost) because of his laughing form, characterized by the awareness of the inner sound (*nāda*).
The intention is that, through the power of his loud laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*), he would always appear in the world as if he were one who has produced a roar.
As it has been said:
"And [he saw] the great preta Īśvara, conscious and laughing, with a body like ten million fires of cosmic destruction... (Mā.vi. 8.68). ||312||
Thus, by this much, the seat established in the other Tantras consisting of the left, right, and both has been described;
now, however,
in order to state the sequence of the seat which indicates the meaning of the Trika that transcends those [dualistic categories] and whose pervasion is beyond them, he says:

One should contemplate that [light] which has arisen from his navel and emerged through the three apertures of the head, consisting of the end of sound (nādānta), radiant with Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.
Three spokes ending in twelve [petals], and there too three [spokes] of the Unmanas;
this white lotus-seat consists of thirty-seven [principles].

From the navel— that ground which serves as the locus of birth for that Great Lord whose self is Sadāśiva— there has arisen [the energy] which, characterized by the void-nature of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā, has emerged through the three apertures of the head; it is for this very reason that it consists of three coils.
One should contemplate the triad of vowels ending with *nāda* up to the end of the twelve [fingers];

the meaning is that one should meditate on it as having reached the limit of the *dvādaśānta*. By the phrase "arisen from the navel," it is revealed that this is eternally manifest for everyone by its very nature. Regarding the term *aunmanasa*:
For here, even though duality has dissolved, it persists in some way by means of mere latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
It is "white" because it is devoid of the coloring of objects to be sought after and so forth. Therefore, it has been said:
"Beyond the *unmanā* state, that which shines forth is the supreme reality, the inexpressible (*anākhyam*). Thus,
"having thirty-seven as its essence" means that the thirty-seven principles (*tattvas*), or the thirty-seventh principle which consists of the thirty-seven principles, is the self (*ātman*).
That whose ultimate nature has the knower as its foundational substratum is described as such.
For, up to this point, all principles (tattvas),
being animated by duality and consisting of the nature of the object of knowledge (prameya), find their rest in the supreme knower (paramātṛ).
This is the state of being. As it has been said:
"One should contemplate the trident of power (*śakti-śūla*) arising from his navel, its three prongs having emerged through the three voids (*kha*) and reaching as far as the *dvādaśānta*."
"Then, one should contemplate upon its peaks three lotuses belonging to Śakti;
white and presiding over all—this is the supreme seat. (Mālinīvijaya Tantra 8.70). ||314||

Now, it was indeed stated previously that the worshiper must first be made to consist of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) through the sequence of the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*); and it will likewise be said for the object of worship. Thus, even for that which stands as the "foot beneath," this very same nature is being described.
"How indeed can they possibly come together?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this regard, all the principles (tattvas) have differentiation as their very life-force; therefore..."
For the object of consciousness is traditionally held to be distinct from it by virtue of being its locus. || 15-315 ||
These very principles (tattvas), however, were dissolved into Supreme Bhairava;
then they were emitted through identity for the purpose of applying differentiation and denotability. (15.316)

But these very same principles, when endowed with the sovereignty gained through the attainment of identity with the glorious consciousness of Bhairava, fully attain the state of being worshippers. (15.317)

"By way of being seats"—this is stated by implication. "Of consciousness"—referring to that which was previously described as having thirty-seven aspects. "Object"—meaning the focal point, the support, or the substratum. "Created as if distinct"—as it has been said:

"By his own sovereignty, the Lord, having fashioned himself—who is liberated through sovereignty and whose nature is non-dual—into forms such as Īśa and others through his volitions, carries out worldly activity. (Rijuvimarsini 1.47).
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of being worthy of worship"—the meaning is: for the sake of establishing his status as an object of veneration.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the oneness of awakening" (*bodhaikyalābha*): the sense here is that, preceded by the burning away of the impure body and so forth, there occurs a gradual progression (*taratamabhāva*) precisely in the intent toward the production of a pure body.
He concludes this very point with an additional insertion:
The worshiper is the self of the supreme reality (paratattva), while the object of worship is the reality that is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara).
Because it has been emanated, the network of non-supreme realities serves as the locus for the seat.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If other networks of principles (tattvajāla) have been described as seats (āsana), how is it that this alone is called the 'Supreme Seat' (paramāsana), such that its supremacy among seats is asserted here?"— incorporating this doubt within itself,
[the author] demonstrates the superiority of this [system] over other groups of scriptures:
In the Siddhānta, [the levels] end with Vidyā and Kalā; in the scriptures of the Left and Right, they end with Sadāśiva; and in the Mata-yāmala, they extend as far as Samanā. (15.319)
This supreme seat is said here to extend to the end of Unmanā;
having worshipped the seat, the lineage of gurus should be honored as previously described.
"As will be stated later"—namely:

"Gaṇapati, Guru, Parama, Parameṣṭhin, Pūrvasiddha, Vāk, and Kṣetrapati—this group of seven has been declared by our teachers as that which is to be worshipped in the ritual of the lineage of gurus. (18.10)
Thus [ends the section]. ||320||

Regarding the worship of the seat (*āsana*), he speaks in order to state some remaining points from another Tantra: "In that regard, one should first project the two-fold [mantra] consisting of one and a half syllables, which has become the form [of the deity], onto the seat as its pervader; thus it is stated in the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*. (15.321)

There, when this had been said, [he placed] the Aparā-Bhaṭṭārikā— who consists of two and a half syllables and who, though embodied, is to be worshipped— upon the three lotuses of the *unmanas* state at the foremost point of the seat,
by means of her nature which internalizes the totality of all the paths (*adhvan*) below.
"One should assign by way of pervasion"—the meaning is that one should apply [the mantra] by virtue of its denoting that [reality]. ||321||

He recites the very text from that [source] by way of its meaning: "One should worship Sadāśiva as the Great Corpse (Mahāperta) in his form consisting of one and a half syllables; and above him, as the Supreme, one should worship Parā with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. (15.322)
Then, one should imagine a second form, called the Self (Ātman), which is the embodiment of knowledge (vidyāmūrti).
As it is stated therein:
"And above [this] there should be a lotus, with petals and coverings belonging to the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara)."
One should worship Īśvara, known as Sādākhya, who has the form of a ghost, at the base of the pericarp.
One should cause the single form consisting of two and a half syllables to be bestowed,
accompanied by the six limbs, according to the path of reciting one's own mantra.
Above that, one should cause another to be offered as the supreme;
then, with perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense, and sacred threads.
"One who knows the ritual procedure should worship with devotion using garments, jewels, and so forth.
And here, having read "sārdhākṣarām," [one should understand] the two mother-sequences (mātṛkās), namely Mālinī and [the other].

One should not say "one should deposit [the seed-syllables]," for in that case, the expression here would denote the three lotuses of the *unmanasa* state. Furthermore, in the passage "then one should conceive the second called the Self," there would have to be a reading of "the third" or "the fourth," and so too in the *Siddhātantra*.
Furthermore, since this would result in redundancy with the text to be stated later beginning with the words "saikārṇa" and so forth,
enough of this conversation with those who are devoid of the traditional lineage of the Guru’s oral transmission. Now, regarding everything indeed...
In order to describe the worship of the mantra-wheel, he says:
"In the center is Bhairavasadbhāva; on the right is Ratiśekhara. (15.323)
To the left is the Navātman, and likewise the triad of Bhairavas along with their goddesses;
in the center is Parā, resembling the full moon, and again on the right— || 15.324 ||
On the right horn is Parāparā, red in color, slightly fierce but not terrifying;
on the left horn is Aparā, terrifying, blackish-brown in color. (15.325)
As before, the sixteenfold placement (nyāsa) is here twofold, performed upon the body just as it was done;
thereafter, one should contemplate their bodies as being appropriately formed through volition (sāṅkalpika).
According to the specific ritual requirements, [the deity may have] two, four, six, or more arms,
holding such items as a skull-cup, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a water-pot, and so forth.
One should conceive [the arrangement] according to the variegated placement on the left and right;

"as before" means by the sequence beginning with the ninefold Self (navātman) and the Supreme (parā). "Conceptual" (sāṅkalpika) refers to *saṅkalpa*, which is a particular intention belonging to the practitioner; for this very reason it is said: "in accordance with the distinction of the task."
Regarding "left and right"— by this, it refers to the variety of arrangements, such as the skull-cup on the left and the trident on the right.
Now, one might ask: "Why was it said that one should thus conceive of them according to the distinction of their functions?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In reality, those goddesses are of the nature of universal form, because they consist of pure consciousness. (15.328)
Those whose essence is nothing but uninterrupted pure consciousness (cinmātra) shall attain liberation;
from that [consciousness] proceeds everything, beginning with the limbs and faces and ending with the world-protectors and their weapons.
The one named the Goddess (Devī) is to be worshipped in the center; thus, the triad becomes worshipped.
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (thereafter)—it means immediately after the contemplation of the body and so forth. Now, one might ask: why is this [Goddess] to be worshipped specifically in the center?
Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "the triad becomes worshipped. For it is here that the worship is performed.
The intention is that this should apply everywhere. Thus it has been said:
"In this manner, one should always perform worship in the center of the trident-lotus."
He demonstrates that these are indeed non-different from the Goddess:
"Then, from that mass of consciousness situated in the center, which is eternally divine... (15.330).
The [mantras] such as the limbs (aṅga), which have issued forth separately in the form of sparks, are to be worshipped;
"therefore" means that they are to be worshipped because they are non-different from the Goddess.
Now, one might ask: "Why is it stated that this very Goddess who resides in the center is to be worshipped as non-different [from the others]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Goddess who indeed resides in the center is she alone whose nature is the True Being (sadbhāva). (15.331)
Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī is terrible, peaceful, and mixed in every respect;
in the Siddhātantra, she is celebrated as the Supreme Goddess (Parā Devī) consisting of a single syllable.
Seti—the Goddess situated in the middle. ||332||
The supreme Goddess is not only situated in the center as the single vowel *e*, but she is also called *Mātṛkā* and *Mālinī*; thus he says:
"The supreme Goddess is Mātṛkā, while Mālinī is said to be situated in the center."
In this very context, by way of the meaning, he recites the passage from the Śrīsiddhātantra:
"One should place in the center the Supreme [Consciousness], which possesses the luster of the sun and consists of all letters. (15.333)
Regarding her, it is said therein: "One should place the auspicious Ekā, who consists of all letters, upon the tip of her crest; and [one should likewise place] her limbs and so forth. Furthermore:
"In the center, one should place Ekā, who is composed of all syllables and is auspicious."
Resplendent like ten thousand shimmering suns, she illuminates this entire world.
One should place upon the tip of its crest the supreme, auspicious, single-syllabled [mantra],
which resembles the finest crystal and flows with nectar on all sides.
"Having placed the supreme *Āpyāyanakarī* [mudrā], which bestows the highest accomplishment (*siddhi*),
upon the tip of its crest, one should then arrange the limbs (*aṅga*).
Thus it is said.
Now, one might ask: "Is it established by scripture alone that this [central point] is to be worshipped, or is there also some reasoning for it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From that, the universe has emerged; it is worshipped in the south and the north. (15.334)
It would indeed be worshipped by him; one should worship it once in the center.
Then, because this universe—which consists of those respective mantras and so forth—has emerged from the very center, it is effectively worshipped there;
and by virtue of being the self that is merely its expansion, it is worshipped in both the north and the south as well.
The meaning of the sentence is that one should worship [the Goddess] only once in the center, thinking "it must indeed be so.
Not only is this nature of the Goddess, who resides in the center and whose form is pure existence (*sadbhāva*), described in the *Śrīsiddhātantra*, but it is stated elsewhere as well; thus he says:
And it is stated in the Śrīdevyāyāmala, in the sacrifice known as the Ḍāmara: [15.335]
He recites that very [verse]: "Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, who always resides at the tip of the nose, constantly draws in the threefold time;
situated in the mouth, she draws [time] into the heart by means of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. (15.336)
Through inhalations and breath-retentions she sustains [time], but through exhalation she devours it;
rising up in an instant by means of exhalation, she devours all of time.
The supreme power of will (icchāśakti), known by the name Parā, awakens the triad of powers; she is to be worshipped, for she draws forth everything that shatters the support of time.
Indeed, here the Blessed Lady Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, residing in the mouth, always—

by means of the unification of the inhalation and exhalation of her own breath through the two lateral channels— [withdraws] the threefold time characterized by prāṇa, apāna, and udāna into the heart, the central abode, at the tip of the power of the nose.

She draws [the breath] with that form and causes it to circulate; for by means of exhalation (*recaka*) she withdraws, by inhalation (*pūraka*) she grants entry, and by retention (*kumbhaka*) she holds [it]; and by upward exhalation (*ūrdhvarecaka*), having arisen through the sequence of transcending each respective causal state, she remains at all times.
In an instant, she withdraws [all things] by means of the process of reducing them to their own essential nature (*svarūpatā*) without interruption.
As it is said: "The first *tuṭi* belongs to Will (*icchā*)," this supreme power of Will is [the source] of the triad of powers whose nature begins with Will.

The "place of origin" (*utpattibhūḥ*)—by the name *Kāsaṅkarṣiṇī* (the Attractor of Kāla) according to what has been introduced—is that which is to be sacrificed to; the meaning is that it attracts the wind (*prabhañjana*), which is the support of time consisting of the entire pentad beginning with breath, and causes it to manifest as both internal and external. As it is said therein:
In these two paths, time moves grossly for yogis;
it flows through the left, the right, and the middle, adorned by the three powers.
"She, as Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, shall likewise swallow the threefold time," and,
"By the name Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, she [swallows] the time situated within the cavity of her mouth."
The regulation of his inhalation and exhalation is the Saṅkarṣaṇa [mantra] within the heart.
"One should hold [the breath] all around with inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka); the goddess, arisen by means of exhalation (recaka), devours time in an instant.
Thus it is said.
"And: 'The supreme power of will, known by name as Śaktitritayabodhinī, when worshipped, draws forth everything that shatters the support of time. (338)
Now, by way of summarizing the previously mentioned circle of the worshipable deities, he explains the essential nature—beginning from the seat—as it accords with his own philosophical system:
"In this [system], it is indeed said that Śiva consists of vision, action, and will; however, these [powers] exist when the object of knowledge has been dismantled."
In the gross and the subtle [states], there arise respectively the Sakala and the Pralayākala.
But those who, while pure, have fallen into a state of unconsciousness (jñānākala), upon awakening, are called Mantras; they are knowers of a limited number of distinct objects of knowledge. (15.340)
But when all that is to be known has been differentiated, there are the Mantreśas and the Maheśas;
when it is both differentiated and non-differentiated, this path (adhvan) extending up to Suśiva is said to belong to them. (15.341)
These very [energies], as the expansion of duality gradually dissolves, attain their full development;
yet they remain unmixed with one another until the three states have dissolved their sense of difference. (15.342)
This triad of lotuses, along with the state beyond mind (*unmanasī*), should serve as the seat;

this is stated primarily. Regarding the phrase "in the subtle" (*sūkṣme*): it refers to the *pralayākala*, because for him, the portion consisting of the objects of knowledge remains only as residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the phrase "pure" (*śuddhā*): [it refers to those who are free from such objects].

"By some means" means through the removal of the turbidity of the object of knowledge (*vedya*). "Asleep" means unawakened. "Consisting of a few" means not the whole; for if it were so, they would possess the status of Mantreśvaras.
"Distinct and non-distinct" means because the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*) has come to rest within the sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*). "To this extent" means—by implication.

It is characterized by differentiation (*bhedapradhāna*). It says "it flows" (*galati*)—and not "it has flowed" (*galite*), for if that were the case, these [channels] would not possess the state of being three lotuses (*padmatrayatva*). They "attain expansion" because the trident (*śūla*) has an open form.
For this very reason it is said: "mutually unmixed" (*anyonyāsaṅkīrṇā*).
Now, one might object: "In this way, it would only be stated that will, knowledge, and action possess the status of a support (*āsana*) by virtue of being the substratum;
but what of the supported—is it to be understood as something distinct from those, worthy of worship, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
These very [powers], through their desire not to abandon the delimitation of the distinctions consisting of their mutual identity... || 15-343 ||
It is said that these [powers], through their divisions such as power (śakti) and its possessor (tadvat), have attained the status of being worthy of worship;
for they themselves are vision, action, and will, desiring to avoid contact with the distinctions of mutually exclusive forms.
The meaning of the sentence is that [the powers] rest upon the state of the object of worship by means of the triad beginning with Śakti.
Now, one might object: "Even though these [energies] possess the nature of the Self, their suchness was not perceived as manifest in the *sakala* and other states;
what is the reason that it is perceived so clearly here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because, starting from the very first stage of the dissolution of duality, each [energy] manifests its own respective form. (15.344)

These [powers], however, maintain a state of threefoldness; this is clearly perceived among them due to their association with the impurity of the knowable (vedya) and their mutual intermingling. || 15-345 ||

Previously, it did not arrive at a clearly manifest state of threefold being, but here it is not so; this is because of the dissolution of differentiation from the very first moment—namely, that which consists of the three spokes (of the wheel). Regarding the phrase "due to their mutual intermingling":
for, by virtue of the turbidity of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), there would otherwise be no distinct otherness among them.
The state [of being]. "Previously" means in the subject (pramātṛ) such as the Sakala and others.
Thus, even by means of the extreme differentiation and emaciation of these [powers], their triad-nature would not exist; so he says:
"Because it devours the calculation that delimits the mutual differentiation of its own nature, consciousness—whose essence is pure sovereignty—is called Kālakarṣiṇī. (15.346)

These [energies], by virtue of being mutually identical, possess the essence of absolute freedom (svātantrya) because they have internalized their own intermediate natures— such as will and the rest— due to their inherent tendency to swallow even the subtlest trace of the perception of duality.

The meaning is that consciousness, whose nature is the supreme subject, is called Kālakarṣiṇī; she is designated as such everywhere. Therefore, when these [energies] are mutually unmixed yet their differentiation is dissolving, they possess the state of the three nights (arātrayatva); when their differentiation has completely dissolved, they possess the state of the three lotuses (padmatrayatva).

When there is mutual identity and the state of difference is dissolving, there is the triad of power and so forth; but when difference has completely dissolved, there is this very nature [of oneness]. ||346||

This [power] has not only been described as such because of its devouring nature with respect to time—which consists of differentiation and limitation—but also because of its external extraction; thus he says:
"And that same [power], moreover, extracts time from itself and projects it here externally."
She is called Saṅkarṣiṇī; her true presence resides within these Mothers.
But surely, it was stated here immediately prior: "The goddess who indeed resides in the center is she whose nature is true being;
she is Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī... (332).
Having stated this and so forth, one might ask: "What is the ground for applying the term *mātṛsadbhāva* here as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Reality (*tattva*) is existence (*sattā*), [and] attainment; by means of this [term], the object of knowledge is present within the subjects."
For within the powers that give birth to the universe, the ultimate reality is indeed nothing but absolute sovereignty.

And this very [consciousness] is the *sattā*—the reality (*tattva*) consisting in existence (*bhavana*)—in these seven Mothers just mentioned, beginning with Sakala; it is the state of being existent (*sato bhāvaḥ*), that is, existence (*sattā*), and it is the attainment (*prāpti*) through the recovery of one's own essential nature as the subject (*pramātṛtātmatva*). Thus, by means of this...

Even an insentient object, as a cognizable entity, comes to rest within the subjects through a consciousness whose essence is mere reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Likewise, because it has been stated that this very [consciousness] rests solely in their power of autonomy (*svātantrya-śakti*),
[it rests] within the subjects— the powers of will (*icchā*) and so forth— which are the causes of the manifestation of the universe.
The ultimate reality is of the nature of mere independence. || 348 ||
Now, one might object: "Since this too consists of will and so forth, just like the seat [of the deity], how indeed could it be worthy of worship?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This is worthy of worship because, while consisting of desire, knowledge, and action, it is unconditioned."
In which all directions, even those that are limited, are entirely subsumed. || 15-349 ||
"Unconditioned" (anavacchinnam) means having the nature of light consisting of pure reflective awareness (vimarśa).
"In which" refers to that unconditioned form whose essence consists of the acts of willing, knowing, and acting. "Completely subsumed" means rendered incapable of any effect. ||349||
One might object: "Let mere luminosity alone be worthy of worship; what is the use of its being of the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For here, that which is devoid of conceptualization (avikalpa) does not attain the status of being worthy of worship..."
"It does not attain the state of being worthy of worship" means that because a light devoid of self-reflective awareness (vimarśa) is essentially insentient.
One might object: "Granted that there may be a state of consisting of reflective awareness (vimarśamayatva) here, but what is the use of purity in that [other] case?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And conceptual construction does not exist in a single [entity]; there are many dharmas. Therefore, whatever dharma [is perceived], it consists of that many dharmas. (15.350)

Established therein, it projects [the universe] as the most excellent, while others remain below it. For it is *vimarśa* itself, when, due to its state of congealment, it rests upon impurity because its life-force is differentiation,
that is called *vikalpa*.
And when that [consciousness] has the nature of reflecting upon whatever appears, there is no other appearance beyond it:

"Because of the mere exclusion of what is not that, by those who partake in the manifestation of 'that' and 'not-that,' this conceptual construction 'this is a jar' is said to be the ascertainment of that. (Ri-pra. 1.6.3)
According to this principle, [the Absolute] is not touched at all.

How, then, can that nature—which is the undivided essence of all attributes such as will, knowledge, and action—be grasped by a conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) that apprehends each attribute individually? It cannot.

It is logical that the state of being worthy of worship belongs to that condition of Light which has entered into a state of pure self-reflection (*vimarśa*) that is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, it is precisely this power (*śakti*), characterized by the autonomy (*svātantrya*) consisting of pure self-reflection, which exists by projecting forth the infinite varieties of powers such as will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).

The supreme Light, resting in that very state, is to be worshipped as being most excellent; other lights, however, which possess various limitations, are inferior and thus remain in lower states— this is the meaning.

And this has been stated by us according to the tradition of the Guru and the scriptures—thus he says: "This is the reality of the supreme worship of Bhairava in the great sacrifice (mahāyāga) of the venerable Ḍāmara. (15.351)

The illustrious Śambhu, being himself perfectly gracious, instructed me as follows: "Granted that it may be so; even then, in the sacrifice of the mind (manoyāga), should the limbs and other parts be worshipped only in the center, or everywhere? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In the external sacrifice, however, one should worship [the deities] within all three lotuses.
"The flood of attendants ends with the weapons; such is the tradition of our teachers.
Anticipating the question, "How is this so?", he says:
"The five limbs of Vidyā are in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and the End (Nirṛti). (15.353)
One should likewise assign the Śakti-limbs and the Śiva-limbs here; furthermore, in these two, one should assign the Astra-mantra in the four directions and that named Locana in the center.
On the eight petals are the two groups of eight [mantras] beginning with Aghora, each joined with its own consort;
likewise, the group of twelve, the group of six, and the group of four are mixed in pairs. (15.355)
In this manner, one should worship all [the deities] twice as many times by way of enclosures;
thereafter, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons in their respective ten directions in due order.
Thus, by abiding in the state of identity with the Goddess who extends as far as the trident, and offering the entire universe here, one should satisfy the host of deities. (15.357)
Then one should perform the recitation (*japa*) for each mantra twice or five times.
The end is the end-maker; its direction is the south. As it has been said:
"Thereafter, one should place the five limbs of the Vidyā in the southeast and the other directions."
"...of Agni, Śara, Rakṣas, and Vāyu, and on the south, respectively. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.76).
Likewise, it follows the sequence beginning with Āgneyī (the southeast). Here, "in the pair" refers to that characterized by the limbs of Śakti and Śiva.
"In the four directions"—this implies a distinction from the previous case where [the deity] was located specifically in the southern direction.

"In the middle, that which is named Locana"—this applies as a remainder to all [the preceding cases]. "Mixed" means by way of being in the form of a *yāmala* (pair). "Twice" means two times; thus, when the group of twelve is doubled, there are twenty-four, and so forth.

The sequence: "In every way" (*sarvaśaḥ*) means that whatever is to be worshipped—in whatever manner, such as the group of eight (*aṣṭaka*) and so forth—that very thing exists in a twofold form; this is the meaning. And this has already been corroborated previously.
"With weapons" (*sāstrān*) means those who have weapons in their hands, as it has been said:
"The world-protectors (lokapālas) are likewise proclaimed as having short weapons;
they, held in [their] hands, are to be worshipped...
Thus, she is the Goddess whose limit is the trident—because she is the place of rest, she is the true nature of the Mothers (mātṛsadbhāva).
"Dvipañcadhā" means tenfold.
He connects this very point also by way of pervasion (vyāpti):
"Because each one consists of a triad, and because there is no difference whatsoever. (15.358)

In each individual mantra, there is a triad, and within each [of those], there is another triad contained therein; thus, because of the universal self-nature (sārvātmya) in every mantra, there is a state of ninefoldness, and because of the indivisible nature of abiding in one's own essential form (svarūpa), there is oneness—thus, the state of tenfoldness. || 358 ||
Visualizing the wheel of mantras at the navel, heart, throat, palate, and the upper cavity like a blazing fire, one should perform the oblation by burning the entire universe therein.
When the rite of initiation (dīkṣā) is to be performed, the Guru, desiring to carry out the initiation by whichever path (adhvan), should first primarily apply that very [path] to the body. (15.360)
"Like a flame" means with extreme brilliance. As it has been said:
"...one should subsequently begin the recitation (japa).
Having become absorbed in that essential nature (svarūpa), one should contemplate each [syllable] ten times."

"Having meditated upon [the deity] resembling a blazing fire, the practitioner of mantra should utter [the mantra] ending in *svāhā* once for each [oblation], for the successful accomplishment of the rite of *homa*. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.78).

Regarding the phrase "in the rite of initiation"—it does not refer to the mere daily (*nitya*) ritual alone. Regarding the phrase "by means of which"—by means of any one of the *tattvas* and so forth.
The word "that" (tam) refers to the path (adhvan) intended as the object to be purified. ||360||
One might ask: "What would happen if this were done? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Recalling this trident from its base up to the limit of the twelve (dvādaśānta), with its tip reaching the wheel of the Goddess, one who has abandoned sequential order attains the state of moving through the sky (khecaratā). (15.361)
This Khecarī consists of filling the space at the tip of the void, extending from the Mūlādhāra to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths];
she is so called because of her movement and abiding in the void, and because of her consumption of the nectar of the void. (15.362)

Meditating upon this trident whose true nature has been thus described— extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *dvādaśānta*, with the wheel of goddesses situated at its exceedingly sharp tip and edge— one attains the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratā*) by resting in the unconditioned plane (*nirāvaraṇapada*) and abandoning all sequential progression.
The meaning is that one should proceed as a traveler through the sky of supreme awakening (parabodha).

This very [channel] extends correctly in the form of a staff from the *mūlādhāra* up to the spaces (*kha*) characterized by the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Due to its upward movement and because it abides right there in the form of cessation, it has attained identity with that [state] which consists of the filling of the voids— namely, those abiding at the *dvādaśānta* through the pervasion of four finger-breadths each, and which consist of the powers of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā; for this very reason, it is the [source] of the nectar of the sky (*khāmṛta*).
The meaning is that because she moves for the purpose of consuming the movement of the bliss of supreme awakening, she is called *khecarī*;
she is the *mahāmudrā*. As it has been said:
"Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the yogin should place the lord of the eyes (the gaze) upon the navel."
One should lead that [wind] in the shape of a staff as far as the three voids.
"Having restrained [the breath] there, one should quickly fill that [space] with the three voids (*kha-traya*).
Having bound this, the great hero attains movement in the sky. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 7.15).
Therefore, for one who does not understand the pervasion of the trident (*triśūla*) in this manner, even in the binding of the Khecarī Mudrā—
The intended meaning here is that there would be no attainment of the nature of the other at all. As it has been said:
"O fair-faced one, without knowing this, even if one binds the Khecarī Mudrā, one does not fly up from the surface of the earth due to the Śakti-śūla. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.81)
Thus [ends the section]. ||362||

Right here, he demonstrates the pervasion even by way of the predominance of the three goddesses: "One should shorten this trident of Śambhu by four finger-breadths; from that [point], it extends to the Śākta, and from there to the Āṇava; thus that triad of tridents is situated. (15.363)

"From that" means from that which resides at the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths) by virtue of the predominance of Parā; "in the Śākta" means in that which extends four finger-breadths below the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā) and is characterized by the predominance of Parāparā; "from that too, in the Āṇava, one should decrease it by four finger-breadths"—this is the connection. Therefore, above the *brahmarandhra*,...
The *śūla* of the *āṇava* [level], which is secondary to the other, has a distance of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*).

As it has been said: "Thus, this is declared to be the *śāmbhava*; that which ends at eight [finger-breadths] is held to be the *śākta*; one should know that which ends at four [finger-breadths] to be the *āṇava*. This is considered the triad of *śūlas*. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.82)
Thus [ends the section]. ||363||
Anticipating the question, "Even so, what would happen to him? he says:

"Having offered his very self to the wheel of goddesses situated one above the other on the three tridents, what is there that he does not become, or what is there that he does not know, or what is there that he does not do? (15.364)
"What is it that is not born?"—the meaning is that he becomes the very soul of the universe. ||364||

In this very context, he states another distinction regarding the separate sacrifice: "Or else, one should worship each [deity] individually, or the single mantra residing in the lotus, according to the various conceptual options concerning the existence or non-existence of the union of the couple, the limbs, the faces, and so forth. (15.365)

"Mantra" refers to any one of [the mantras] beginning with Navātman. And here, that lotus—its petals pervading the sides and its two spokes—should be contemplated as the seat. Furthermore, the sacrifice here is performed either according to the *yāmala* (coupled) method, or as a single hero (*ekavīra*), either through the conjunction of limbs, faces, and so forth, or without such conjunction.
The meaning is "conceptual construction. ||365||
Thus,

according to the perspective expressed in such passages as "Having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva," one should contemplate the state of being Śiva within the self— beginning with the vital breath— and then perform the external sacrifice.
One should act—thus he says:
"In this way, having made one's own consciousness, from the vital breath up to the plane of space, into Śiva through the yoga of worship, one should thereafter perform the external ritual. (15.366)
"Thus"—by means of the sequence of the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). "Space"—the void (*śūnya*). ||366||
Now, one might object: "If the sacrifice has been performed internally, then what is the use of an external one? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"If the external sacrifice is considered primary for the sake of attaining supernatural powers (siddhi) and so forth, then the internal sacrifice serves for the purpose of purification; otherwise, the worshipper is a mere beast. (15.367)

But he who is averse to supernatural powers and the like worships the Lord externally for the sake of attaining internal absorption in the Great Sacrifice; by that alone, he achieves his purpose. (15.368)
"The reason for its primacy is that it is conceived as the accomplishment [of the goal] and so forth"—that is, "for the sake of purification," namely, of the vital breath and the rest.
"Otherwise" refers to what was stated:
"He who, without performing the mental sacrifice, should undertake another sacrifice..."
"But that [state] should be known as inauspicious; it is not prescribed for liberation" (Svacchanda Tantra 3.32).

Regarding the phrase "by that very [means]"—it refers to the internal firm establishment of the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*). For while the state of being Śiva has been accomplished for the body through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other such rites, what remains for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the void (*śūnya*) except through the internal sacrifice?
That which is to be accomplished by means of external sacrifice. ||368||
Since for those desiring to ascend [the path], the internal practice arises through the external sequence,
he speaks of the external sacrifice— beginning with the seizing of the site and so forth— saying:
"Having performed the internal sacrifice and having taken grains and other materials consecrated with the Astra-mantra..."
One should cast [the offerings] in the directions to dispel obstacles, and having withdrawn them, one should lead them to the northeastern direction.
Inspection, sprinkling, striking, and nourishing, as well as veiling—these are the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) common to all, according to the Triśiromata. (15.370)

One should consecrate the cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk, and clarified butter with the [five] faces and the six limbs ending with the upward-pointing one; then, one should sprinkle the area with this water mixed with *kuśa* grass.
One should set aside the remaining ground for the sake of the disciples and prepare the *pañcagavya*;
that in which the five products of the cow are present along with water and *kuśa* grass is called *pañcagavya*. (15.372)
In the scripture, the water of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the destroyer of external impurity;
for when worldly impurity has been wiped away, then internal impurity is likewise cleansed.
One should employ that which is non-worldly, such as mantras and the like, in order to burn away impurity.
And in this regard:
"Sesame seeds, parched grain, barley, dūrvā grass, and auspicious white mustard seeds..."
And there were many white flowers, fragrant and abundant.

"This auspicious scattering [of grain] is mixed with the paste of red sandalwood. Thus, the scattering of grain and so forth is to be understood. Regarding the phrase "consecrated"—it means seven times. As it has been said:
"One should consecrate the scattered offerings with the water of Śiva joined with the weapon-mantra (astra)."
Having stood seven times in the eastern direction in the center with the mantra of the weapon (astra-mantra), one should remain there.
One should scatter grains upwards and downwards and contemplate them as having become the weapon-mantra;
one should then collect them with a beautiful white chowrie while reciting the weapon-mantra.
"Facing exactly toward the northeast, up to the northwest and ending at the northeast.
Regarding the phrase "with their bases"—this applies to all ritual acts (*sarvakarmasu*). This has been corroborated in the section on bathing (*snānaprakaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "one should consecrate with mantras"—this means [consecrating] each [substance] separately as it resides in its own vessel. Regarding the phrase "up to the top"—by that...

Cow’s urine with *sadyojāta*, up to clarified butter (*ājya*) with *īśāna*—this is the sequence. By the word "by this"—meaning by that which is combined with cow dung and the other ingredients—the worship of the Earth, Gaṇeśa, and the weapons is commenced immediately after the *pañcagavya*. [Regarding] the term *pañcagavya*:

He explains [the passage] beginning with "the five products of the cow" (*pañcagavya*) and so forth: that in which the five products of the cow—those things beneficial to cows (*gavya*)—are collected together within the *kuśa* water, that is described as such. "It should be accepted" means it should be contemplated (*anusandhātavya*).
For this very reason, he said:
"One should meditate on the single [vowel] from *pha* to *na*, which extends from earth up to Śiva. (15.374)
For it is appropriate to burn away the internal impurity of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*); thus it has been said.
(374) One should scatter a handful of flowers in the center, as well as incense, perfumes, wine, and so forth;
likewise, one should offer these in the middle of the sacrificial chamber, whereby the form [of the deity] quickly [manifests]. (15.375)
The entire circle of deities is conceived as presiding over the lotus that has infinite stalks, petals such as Dharma and the rest, and a pericarp consisting of the true physician.
One should worship Gaṇeśa, situated in the northeast, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings on a sixfold pedestal;
