having worshipped him who has arisen for the sake of destroying obstacles, one should then dismiss him.
Then, he filled a jar with highly fragrant liquid substances.

Having worshipped and anointed it with the root mantra, one should consecrate it a hundred times with the sword, provided that the preliminary weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) has not already been performed. (15.379)
One should worship that pitcher in the northeast, accompanied by the water-pots situated on its left;
then, starting from the direction of the Sun (the east), one should worship the world-protectors along with their weapons.
Having performed the ritual with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, preceded by mantras, the disciple then, holding a sword and a water-pot in his hands, lets fall a stream [of water].
The preceptor Kumbhahasta, following behind and speaking thus, said:
"O Śakra, for the pacification of obstacles in your own quarter..."
By the command of Śiva, one must perform the ritual action with full attention;
in a three-syllable name that is predominantly *nirṛti*, the word "bhoḥ" should be used once.
Since this mantra has been declared to be bound by a meter (chandas),
one should remove [the obstacles] and place that water-pot upon the scattered offerings (vikiro) in that eastern direction.
Now, the vessel for weapons (*astravārdhānī*) should be placed to the right of the jar;
the word "dadyāt" (one should give) is the point of division here. By "tena" (by that)—meaning by the cause consisting of the scattering of handfuls of flowers and so forth—it has been said:
Then one should perform the Vāstuyāga by means of the recitation of the Mālinī mantra;
filling the joined palms with flowers while pronouncing the syllables beginning with 'pha'.
"Having meditated upon the path ending with Śakti, one should cast it into the end of the letter Na. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.89).

Regarding the phrase "in the pericarp of the true physician": the meaning is that it is in the form of the lotus of Vidyā, wherein the true physician is indeed Śuddhavidyā itself, which serves as the pericarp. Regarding the phrase "in the Ṣaḍuttha": as it has been said—

"Having bestowed infinite Dharma, as well as Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, together with Karṇikā—this is the seat consisting of six [petals]. (8.93). Thus, "eśagam"— [The commentary continues: Regarding "eśagam": "e" refers to the *mūlādhāra*; "śa" refers to the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; "ga" refers to the *maṇipūra*. It is called "gam" because it goes (*gacchati*) there. "A" refers to the *anāhata*; "i" refers to the *viśuddhi*; "ka" refers to the *ājñā*. It is called "kam" because it is the peak (*kāṣṭhā*). "Eśagam" means that which has gone to these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the goal (*gantavya*). "Eśagam" means that which has reached these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme state (*gati*). "Eśagam" means that which has attained these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme abode (*gṛha*). "Eśagam" means that which has entered these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme reality (*tattva*). "Eśagam" means that which has realized these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme truth (*satya*). "Eśagam" means that which has known these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme light (*prakāśa*). "Eśagam" means that which has shone forth in these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme bliss (*ānanda*). "Eśagam" means that which has experienced these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme power (*śakti*). "Eśagam" means that which has manifested these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme consciousness (*cit*). "Eśagam" means that which has awakened in these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme liberation (*mokṣa*). "Eśagam" means that which has attained these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme state of Śiva. "Eśagam" means that which has become one with these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme essence (*sāra*). "Eśagam" means that which has extracted the essence from these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). "Eśagam" means that which has realized the reality of the Self in these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme state of the Guru. "Eśagam" means that which has been taught by the Guru in these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "ga" is the *maṇipūra*, "a" is the *anāhata*, "i" is the *viśuddhi*, and "ka" is the *ājñā*. It is called "gam" because it is the supreme state of the disciple. "Eśagam" means that which has been initiated into these [six centers]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "e" is the *mūlādhāra*, "śa" is the

"...one should lead [it] toward this direction" (369), because the ritual action was already introduced in that very place. "Arisen"—because it is intent upon warding off the multitude of obstacles. As it has been said:
With the syllable *gau* (or *gām*), one should worship Vighneśa with perfumes, incense, and other offerings;
its limbs [are worshipped] with the letter *ga*, through the application of the six long and short vowels.
"Having meditated upon the three-eyed one, who has arisen as the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa] in a dwarf form. (8.92).
Regarding the phrase "for one desiring success"—this does not refer to one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). As it is said:
"But one who desires success should worship the Great Weapon (*mahāstra*) in due order. (8.92).
Thus. Regarding the word *āśā*—the meaning is that it is surrounded or joined with the eight measures (*mātrā*) by means of the sword (*sāstra*).
As it has been said:
"Having meditated upon [him] above this, one should place [the deity] who bears a sword and a shield."
Terrible with great fangs, most fierce, with a face knit in a frown.
Endowed with its six limbs in their own syllables, surrounded by the Mothers of the Directions,
and likewise its six limbs in their own syllables, it is illuminated by the syllable *phaṭ*.
Having visualized that very form, one should then place the eight Mothers;
one should simultaneously remember Indrāṇī, holding a thunderbolt, upon the eastern petal.
Then the wise one [should visualize] the goddess of the southeast with a spear in her hand, that of the south with a staff in her hand, as well as those of the southwest, the west, and the northwest.
"O Dear One, one should contemplate [the goddesses] simultaneously as being equipped with a sword, a noose, and a banner;
Kauberī holding a mallet in her hand, and Īśānī joined with a trident. (8.98).
"Afterwards"—that is, following the sacrifice of the weapons (*astrayāga*). The fire-oblation (*homa*) here is also of that same number.
This is implied by the sense. As it has been said:
"First, one should prepare a jar empowered with a thousand [mantras] and so forth;
there, one should perform a thousand oblations, and then, having recited [the mantra], one should dismiss [the deity]."
"One hundred and eight [recitations] completed... (8.100).
"From that" means immediately after the worship of the Astra-kalaśa and so forth. By the term "Parāmodī," [the author indicates] its primacy.

The aforementioned has been stated. Regarding the word "discussed"—it refers to [the ritual] with mango sprouts and so forth. The connection is: "one should consecrate a hundred water-jars (*karkarī*) with the sword. As it has been said:
"In that regard, first taking a jar made of gold or other materials, free from flaws..."
Containing all kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs, and filled with fragrant water.
With a face adorned by mango sprouts, his neck encircled by a string of garlands,
marked with a protective *tilaka* that wards off demons, and draped in a pair of white garments;
"Consecrated by reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times, and likewise honored with the *vārdhānī* [water-pot], yet that [other vessel] is honored with the *astra-mantra*. (8.103).
"If it has not been done"—this refers to the case of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). For in that context, that very [vessel] serves as the *karkarī*.

The sense is that [the vessel] should become worthy of worship. Regarding the phrase "the jar situated on the left": this refers to what was stated beginning with, "On the left side of the jar... (Svacchanda Tantra 3.77), and so forth, up to the point where it says, "and having sprinkled the *vārdhānī* with the auspicious waters of Śiva..."
"...endowed with auspiciousness. Having smeared it like a water-pot, one should place it upon the seat. (Svacchandatantra 3.78).
Thus it ends. Regarding the phrase "causing a stream to fall": this refers to following the sequence starting from the east and so on, by resorting to the directions of the sun.

"This" refers to what is about to be stated. "In the region of Nirṛti"—by this it is meant that in the southwest (nairṛta), one should recite "Bhoḥ" and so forth. "Bound by meter"—the implication is that if the meter were broken, this would no longer be a mantra. "To the south"—referring to the jar. As it has been said:
"Having brought it there, one should first place the jar, which has become the embodiment [of the deity], upon that seat;
to its southern side, one should set down the water-vessel. (8.107) Thus it is said.
Now, one might ask: "What would be the result of worshipping the jar in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The multitude of mantras is empowered by its identification with the water residing within the jar. (15.385)
Meditated upon as having the nature of pure light, it nourishes the entire ritual procedure;
therefore, the Guru should worship the entire assembly of mantras within the water-pot (kumbha).
According to the previously mentioned rite, one should worship the weapon-mantra (astra) in a water-pot (karkarī) that dispels obstacles;
then, in the middle of the house, the Guru should perform worship upon a mandala of fragrant paste.
The triad [of deities] may be worshipped individually through their union as couples or as a single mantra-deity;
"the entire ritual" refers to that which will be described hereafter. "Therefore" means because it effects the nourishment of all rituals.
"By the preceding ritual" refers to the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) and so forth. "In the middle of the house" means within the interior of the house.
"In the place of Brahmā"—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Having prepared a mandala of fragrant paste in the place of Brahmā, the wise one should worship there either the group of six, the group of three, or even just one. (8.109)
Thus [it is said].
Now he begins to describe the ritual of the fire-offering (agnikārya):
"Then, for the performance of the fire-ritual, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). (15.388)
[The fire-rite] arises from the conceptualization and verbal discourse of pure mantras and so forth, and is unprecedented. Thus,

immediately following the worship of the mandala, in order to perform the fire-rite (*agnikarma*), [one proceeds] with that which is pure by virtue of being of the nature of non-duality, and for that very reason, consists of mantras and the like.
"Kriyā is Kuṇḍalinī, the sacrificial pit...

and so forth; [the practitioner] should conceive of the extraordinary (apūrva) sacrificial pit, which has arisen from the volition (saṅkalpa) consisting of the sprouting of such internal discourse (sañjalpa) directed toward the Self.
Therefore, because it is supramundane, one should fashion the sacrificial pit externally in this manner, reflecting as follows:
This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "In every case, it has been stated that the external construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is accomplished through a series of purificatory rites consisting of scraping, sprinkling, pounding, and so forth;
why then is it described here in this manner? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because of the contemplation that the sacrificial pit is the power of action (kriyāśakti) of Śiva. || 15.389 ||
Indeed, this supreme rite is [effective] even without other sequences of action.
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well:
"In this manner, whether in the body, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), or in the liṅga, the vessel, the water, or the fire" (15.390).

Anticipating the objection—"What is the authority for this primary consecration (*saṃskāra*) performed upon flowers and the like, or upon a child who is such as Śiva?"—he says: "It has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrīyogasañcāra* as follows. (15.391)

He recites that very point: "In the fourteen kinds of beings, in flowers, incense, and offerings, in lamps, in recitation, and likewise in fire-oblations—in all these cases here, it is Caṇḍikā. (15.392)
She offers oblations, mutters prayers, performs worship, laughs, and goes about;
in eating and in sexual union, she alone, residing within the body, is the performer of action. (15.393)
"Preddhe" means "it shines. Thus, the essential point here is that one must everywhere understand that it is supreme consciousness itself that manifests in those various forms. ||393||
However, for those in whom such an awakening of consciousness (*saṃvitpraroha*) does not exist, this external sequence of ritual action is intended; thus he says:
"But those who do not rest upon such an established consciousness..."
In order to achieve that through non-sequential means, a sequential method is taught. || 15-394 ||
And so that their accomplishment may occur, he says:

"I am Śiva, consisting of mantra; my volitions are of that same nature; and that which arises from them—the sacrificial pit, the fire, and so forth—I should clearly remember as being of the nature of Śiva. (15.395)

For this very reason, even in that case, because one observes whether there is firmness or lack of firmness, the refinement— whether it be small or great— is performed either while [the rite] is being done or when it has already been completed.
"In that case too"—meaning, in the sequential ritual—[it is] "not very much," as was stated previously:
"He who desires success through action should perform extensive action," and so forth in many ways. ||396||
He makes this very point clear by means of an illustration:
"Just as someone who is poor in innate intuition grasps a sentence through the proficiency of practice, so too should it be understood here at the outset. (15.397)

In that regard, he first states the purificatory rites for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa): "Scratching, sprinkling, pounding, smearing, the four paths, the enclosure of the axle, the arrangement of the cover, the surrounding fence, the seats, and the placement—these are the ten purificatory rites pertaining to the pit, performed with the weapons. (15)
Ullekha is digging; seka is moistening; kuṭṭana is making firm;
lepa is leveling. A seat made of darbha grass with a knot in the middle is called a viṣṭara. ||398||
The rest he explains by himself due to its complexity:
"The taking of the center, the covering of the walls with two *darbha* blades, three lines facing east, upward lines, and the surrounding cover of *kuśa* grass on the outside. (15.399)
The preparation of the sacrificial ground, the square altar, the ritual for the worship-seats of the ten world-protectors,
the placement of the residence, and the protection of the sacrificial pit by means of the splendor of the weapon-mantra and fire.
The purposes [of the ground] are the holding of the auspicious fire, power, and the removal of obstacles;
thereafter, when the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been worshipped, it is clearly manifest as the power of action (kriyāśakti). || 15-401 ||
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of either the Mātṛkā or the Mālinī, which consists of the form of one's intention (saṅkalpa).
With two blades of darbha grass, facing east and north, one should arrange them in the shape of a crossroads (catuṣpatha) to form four paths.
Above the walls of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should surround it with kuśa grass blades pointing upwards.

The enclosure is the pit-fence (*akṣavāṭa*). The "vajrification" (*vajrīkaraṇa*) consists of drawing lines extending north-south through the middle of three lines extending east-west using the tips of *kuśa* grass. The "spreading" (*stara*) is the covering of the exterior of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with *kuśa* grass consisting of masses of light. [This applies] to those to be worshipped in the directions starting from the east.

The four enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are auspicious branches, one cubit in length, complete with their bark, originating from the sacrificial tree; they represent the foundational powers (*ādhāra-śakti*) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, and Śivā.
Among them, two face the east and two face the north. By means of these...

A square arrangement arises outside the *kuṇḍa*. He states their respective purposes with the words beginning "ten" (*daśa*), etc. The term "Lord of the World" (*lokeśa*) is an elliptical designation; by it, [the inclusion] of Brahmā and the others is also implied, as has been stated.
"...Brahmā on the eastern seat" (Svacchanda Tantra 2.220).
Regarding the phrase "the settling of the abode": for the sake of concealment, a house is fashioned for Vāgīśī primarily by means of a surrounding enclosure (*akṣavāṭa*); this is what is meant here.

The purpose is as follows: "Protection" refers to the *astra-mantra*. "Power for the maintenance of the Śiva-fire" refers to the four [rites] beginning with tracing (*ullekha*) and the act of making [the site] adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*). "Removal of obstacles" refers to the [rites of] strewing [the sacrificial grass]. By the word "ten," [the rites] beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) are indicated.

It is hinted that the five *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites) are not enumerated here; for it has been stated that they are common to all ritual actions (*sarvakarmasu*). "When worshipped"—by means of the formula: "Oṃ, salutation to the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), whose essence is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). "Consisting of resolve (*saṅkalpa*)"—means: [The text continues: ...that which consists of the form of resolve. This is because the fire-pit is the very nature of the ritual action (*karman*) itself, and the ritual action is of the nature of resolve. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the ritual action, and by worshipping the ritual action, one worships the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the worship of the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is said to be the body of the deity, and the deity is said to reside within the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the fruit of the ritual action. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the fruit of the ritual action. Moreover, the fire-pit is the seat of the deity, and the deity is the presiding lord of the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of union (*sāyujya*) with the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of union with the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the womb of the deity, and the deity is born from the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being born from the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being born from the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the abode of the deity, and the deity resides in the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of residing in the same abode as the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of residing in the same abode as the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the support of the deity, and the deity is supported by the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being supported by the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being supported by the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the manifestation of the deity, and the deity is manifested through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being manifested by the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being manifested by the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the power of the deity, and the deity possesses the power of the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of possessing the power of the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of possessing the power of the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the essence of the deity, and the deity is the essence of the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being identical in essence to the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being identical in essence to the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the door to the deity, and the deity is entered through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of entering the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of entering the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the path to the deity, and the deity is reached via the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of reaching the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of reaching the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the vehicle of the deity, and the deity is conveyed by the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being conveyed by the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being conveyed by the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the messenger of the deity, and the deity is summoned by the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being summoned by the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being summoned by the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the servant of the deity, and the deity is served by the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of serving the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of serving the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the ornament of the deity, and the deity is adorned by the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being adorned by the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being adorned by the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the glory of the deity, and the deity is glorious through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being glorious like the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being glorious like the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the light of the deity, and the deity is illuminated by the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being illuminated by the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being illuminated by the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the radiance of the deity, and the deity shines forth through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of shining forth like the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of shining forth like the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the splendor of the deity, and the deity is splendid through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being splendid like the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being splendid like the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the majesty of the deity, and the deity is majestic through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being majestic like the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being majestic like the deity. Moreover, the fire-pit is the sovereignty of the deity, and the deity is sovereign through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being sovereign like the deity. Thus, the worship of the fire-pit is established as being for the sake of the attainment of the state of being sovereign like the deity. Furthermore, the fire-pit is the authority of the deity, and the deity is authoritative through the fire-pit. Therefore, by worshipping the fire-pit, one worships the deity. And by worshipping the deity, one attains the state of being authoritative like the deity
In the form of Vāgīśvarī.
For this very reason, he said:
"The triangular abode of emanation belonging to the Goddess Saṅkalpa is of the nature of action. (15.402)
Having agitated it three times there, one should deposit a drop of the seminal essence of gnosis (*jñāna-śukra*).
And she [is], by implication, one who has reached her menses. As it has been said:
"She who has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus and possesses beautiful eyes during her menses..."
Having meditated in this manner, one should establish the goddess in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Regarding her installation, [one should recite]: "Oṃ hrīṃ, O Blessed Mālinī, preside over this place;
obeisance! and "Oṃ, O Blessed Śabdarāśi, preside over this place; obeisance!"

And the projection [of the lines]. It is said to be triangular because it is the abode of emanation (*sṛṣṭidhāman*), in accordance with the generation of fire. "Having agitated three times"—this is for the purpose of agitating the *yoni* outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). As it has been said:
"...one should place the Vidyā, namely *oṃ hrīṃ*."
Having assigned "Śiva" and "Om," one should again worship the pair.
"One should bring the Jātavedas [fire] into a copper vessel or a clay bowl;
having meditated upon it as the semen of Śiva, one should cast it into the womb of the Vidyā. (8.113).
Likewise:
"With the *dhruva* [mantra], one should cause it to descend by circling three times outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Thus [it is said].
He elaborates on this very point by incorporating the concept of pervasion:
"Knowledge, stirred by will, [resides] in the state of action whose essence is reflective awareness. (15.403)
Having known [the Self] as firmly established and clearly manifest through the five limbs beginning with "knowing" (jña),
knowledge— aroused by an intense longing consisting of the wonder of the outburst of supreme bliss— blazes forth intensely here. Being thus agitated,
it enters into the activity characterized by absolute freedom, whose essence is solely self-reflection.
"The All-Knowing One, the Maker of all, the Pervasive Supreme Lord who is at rest—
he alone am I; through such firm conviction that 'I am of the Śiva-dharma,' one becomes Śiva."
Thus, by this methodological approach, because infinite power is accepted as being independent through [attributes] such as omniscience and so forth,
[the Lord] shines intensely and clearly with five qualities precisely as the supreme subject of all.
The meaning is that it throbs. Furthermore,

through the mutual connection of their mutual attachment, the form of *vīrya* (vital potency) arises from desire within the creative activity of Vāgīśvarī, who is of the nature of volition (*saṅkalpa*).

The meaning is: when the reality (*sat*) has fully attained its growth within the locus of emanation (*sṛṣṭidhāman*), and is touched by way of being refined through the five limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) consisting of omniscience and so forth, it blazes intensely; through the sequence beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending with the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), it attains external perfection.
For this very reason, he said:
"With those five limbs alone, one should offer oblations once each. (15.404)
By that much, the fire becomes purified through all the sacraments beginning with birth (*janmādi*).

Regarding the term "beginning with birth" (*janmādi*): it is a *ekaśeṣa* compound meaning "birth and so forth," where "so forth" refers to the entire series of sacraments beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and including naming (*nāmakaraṇa*) and the rest; thus, [it includes] conception, the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).
And by this, the accomplishment of the five sacraments known as *jātakarman* and *nāmakaraṇa* is achieved.
As it has been said:
"Then one should offer five oblations with the very limbs of the Vidyā."
"From that [arise] birth and so forth; thus, when this is done, every action is truly performed. (8.114) |||
One might ask: "How can it be so by this much alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The five limbs themselves, consisting of earth and the other elements, are [characterized by] hardness and the rest. (15.405)
"Endowed with the powers residing in the fire, one should perform the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbha).
Now, one might object: 'Are not other specific consecrations (saṃskāra), such as the facing [of the fire] and the sprinkling (abhighāra), also remaining?
Why are they not mentioned here? Anticipating this doubt, he speaks in order to achieve their full completion:"
Then [one should worship] Parāparā, who contains within her the wheels of goddesses belonging to all the paths.
By means of the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation), while recollecting [the deity], one should complete the consecrations of the fire;
the reason for this completion is that [the fire] contains within it the Goddess who is the reality of all paths.
Thus, in order to bring about the state of Śiva within the conditioned fire, he says: "Likewise, blazing with the splendor of true resolve joined with the Lord of Mantras... (15.407).
The fire, through its identity with that resolve of Śiva, is of the nature of Śiva.

Likewise, the teacher—who, by the method previously described, is joined with the mantras and the Lord (Īśvara) and has attained oneness with Him—becomes truly Śiva himself through the fulfillment of his intended purpose; such is his nature.
The meaning is as follows: *saṅkalpaḥ* (volition); by its *mahaḥ*, that is, its majesty, *jvalan*—shining through the attainment of excellence in accordance with its nature;
*vahninā*—by that fire; through identity (*tādātmya*) with Śiva who is being willed by it, one becomes *śivātmakaḥ* (of the nature of Śiva), possessing His very attributes. This is the sense.
And this has been stated by us as it was handed down through the lineage of gurus; thus it is worthy of discernment—so he says:
"This very reality of purification (saṃskriyātattva) Śrī Śambhu explained to me. (15.408)
"O you of pure intellect, let it be discerned by me as well;

for this very reason, those who are mistaken in this matter have been cast far away. Thus he says: "Therefore, regarding this, those who raise the objection that [this is] like the purification of a child... (15.409).
If fire were to be ignited by another fire, and that by yet another, there would be an infinite regress regarding the consecration;
therefore, in this system of the Guru’s vision, they are frustrated by the impossibility of such an arising.

"Elsewhere" means in another fire. "Infinite regress" [is as follows]: for is that other fire unrefined or refined? Here, if it were unrefined, it would be unfit for the *homa* offering. As for its refinement, would it occur in itself or in another? If in itself, then it must have been so from the very beginning.

Let it be; what is the use of depending on another fire? However, if one were to consider this further, there would be no end to such reflection. "Stymied by the lack of emergence"—the sense is that in this system, there is no dependence whatsoever on another fire, nor is any such dependence even logical. ||410||

Now he states what must be done immediately thereafter: "Once the Śiva-fire has been produced and consecrated, having worshipped the two parents—the Assembly of Sounds (Śabdarāśi) and Mālinī—one should dismiss one's own pure abode. (15.411)
Having taken a portion of the pure fire, one should set it aside separately for the purpose of the sacrificial pap (caru).
Even so, with regard to those who have been purified by firm conviction and are thus independent of external rites,
he states another method for consecrating the fire:
Alternatively, having taken the flame of the fire with the left breath, one should join it with that residing in the heart.
"Having brought [the fire] into unity with the fire of consciousness (cidagni), one should cast it out through the right [nostril] once it has been consecrated.
Regarding "the crest-lock" (śikhā)—this refers, by implication, to that which has not yet been consecrated. "Having taken"—by means of the technique of inhalation (pūraka).
"One should cast"—by means of the method of exhalation (recaka). "Consecrated"—because it has attained a state of aesthetic identity (sāmarasya) with the fire of consciousness residing in the heart.
As it has been said:
"Or else, having drawn in with the left [nostril] the flame of a blazing fire,
one should compress it in the heart and then expel it again through the right."
"And one should offer the full oblation as before; this is another rule regarding the fire of Śiva. (8.117) Thus it is said.
Now, what is the intention behind stating this?—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For [true] vision occurs through a firm sense of identification as Śiva. (15.413)
The reality of everything is its purification; that [reality] is stainless for him because of this.
Right here, he also states the position of another scripture:
"Then one should offer nine oblations, together with the ninefold self. (15.414)
The consecration (saṃskriyā) should be performed with the mantra "Śivāgnaye" preceded by the syllable Om (Tāra) and ending with Svāhā;
thereafter, [it is performed] in the fire whose nature is the space of universal Śiva-consciousness.
As before, one should join the support (ādhāra), the supported (ādheya), and the circle of goddesses (devīcakra).
*Tāra* is the *praṇava*. "Then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after such a consecration (*saṃskāra*).
[Objection: Surely the consecratory oblation (saṃskārahoma) must be performed in the fire with the *sruva* and other implements; why then was their consecration not performed first? To this he says:
"The Guru should look at the *sruva* and the *sruk* [ladle] one after another with their openings facing downwards. (15.416)

"They are to be worshipped as Śiva and Śakti; thus one should perceive this process of their consecration"—that is, from the perspective of the Supreme (paradṛṣṭyā). And this is an elliptical indication for all four [rites], beginning with sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), for it has been stated that these are common to all ritual acts. "With faces turned downwards" (adhomukhau)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends here.]

This is with the intention of being oriented toward emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). "In this manner" means by way of the sequence beginning with the visualization [of the deities] with faces turned downward. As it has been said:
"...one should place them with faces turned downward" (*Svacchanda Tantra* 2.231).
Thus:
"...the power of the *sruk* is the *sruva*, which is Śiva."

Now, one might object: "In other places, many varieties of the collection of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have been described for these two [initiates], yet in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra), even their names are not mentioned, such that here it is said that mere inspection and worship alone are the cause of those purificatory rites. What does this mean?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
Apart from the manifestation of reality, there is no other life for the formative forces.
Thus, the Lord did not prescribe the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruva* ladle and other implements in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra).

For in that [tantra], the various sets of consecrations are taught here and there only to impart the fitness for *homa* to the *sruc*, *sruva*, and so forth. And since that [fitness] is already established by this much alone, what is the purpose of this [consecration]? For in our own system:

The attainment of the state of Śiva is itself the supreme consecration (*saṃskāra*). And that is accomplished simply by means of the sprinkling of drops from the *argha* vessel and so forth, as has been stated many times previously.
As the scripture also says:
"One who possesses the purification of one thing must also perform it for any other object here by this very method, provided he is discerning. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.51).
This should be understood to apply to clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth as well. Therefore, there is no [need to refer] to other scriptures in this matter.

There is nothing whatsoever to be expected, because the purification is accomplished merely through the sprinkling of drops from the vessel of honor (*arghapātra*) and so forth; thus, there is no need for such expectation. Otherwise, everything would indeed have to be expected, and the ritual performance would never reach its conclusion. As they say:
And it is proper to compose [a work] in another treatise what has been heard in another treatise;
for that [work], being produced by human intellect, does not depend on other treatises.

"Even when there is dependence, dependence itself is the authority; as long as one depends [on something], the effect must come from that alone, and not from anything else, because otherwise there would be an infinite regress.
Having thus explained the abiding within the fire, he speaks of the libation (tarpaṇa):
Then, by means of sesame seeds, the Guru [should perform the rite] for the female deer through the control of the middle and thumb fingers. (15.418)
Having performed the root [mantra], one should satisfy it with a hundred oblations of clarified butter using the *sruva* ladle;
likewise, the limbs and faces with a sixth part, and the remaining [deities] with a tenth part.
Even a homa of a thousand [oblations] or more is for the sake of satisfaction, according to one's means.
Having performed [the visualization] as a deer, as it has been said:
"O Maheśvarī, when the middle and ring fingers are joined at the tips of the thumbs..."
The index finger and the little finger are raised and made sparse.
"The Great Seal (mahāmudrā) named Mṛgī...

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, he states that the rule for the fire sacrifice (*homa*) is not limited to one hundred [offerings] by saying "one thousand," and so forth. For this very reason, in that [context]:
In that regard,
it is said: "One should not practice stinginess regarding one's wealth."

Now, one might object: "If satisfaction is accomplished by a hundred oblations alone, then what is the use of a thousand or more, which causes the depletion of wealth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even when wealth exists, one who is seized by greed and the like [pursues] the primacy of external [means]. (15.420)
One who manifests [the external] through the subordination of consciousness does not attain the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
This is because he manifests the primacy of the external, due to his attachment to external objects such as wealth and the like. As it has been said:
"He who, despite possessing wealth, does not perform the elaborate ritual out of greed..."
"He never attains the fruit, O Supreme Goddess.
Now, one might ask: what is the proof that he does not experience the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by this much alone?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
It is stated in the Svacchandatantra that even one who has been initiated into that [system] does not partake in liberation. (15.421)

In this regard, there is no dispute that what has been performed does not become unperformed. However, one might raise the following objection: "What would be the fruit of an action performed during initiation for one who possesses greed and other such afflictions?"—thus he anticipates the doubt.
Now, one might ask: "What is the fruit of that ritual action performed during his initiation?
To this very question, he provides the answer:
"In that regard, those who know the scriptures of the Left (Vāma) say that [the fruits] then consist of the power of Vāmā. (15.422)
The mantras bind him properly within the great prison-house of existence;
that is to say, when external predominance exists and consciousness has become subordinate.
Now, one might object: "If their *vāmā* power alone bestows such results, then would the *jyeṣṭhā* power, though arisen [along with it], not be entirely useless? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But that *anugrāhikā* (gracious) power of theirs is ignited by the Guru. (15.423)
One should purify the act of transgressing the desireless [rules] established in one's own scripture.

Furthermore, that power which is the grace-bestowing capacity for those who have received initiation into the conduct (*vṛtta*), being stimulated by the Guru through ritual action (*karma*), yoga, and knowledge, [becomes manifest] within oneself.

One should purify the transgression of the *samaya*— consisting of injunctions and prohibitions— which pertains to one who abides in the scripture after it has been made one's own through the performance of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other rites; this transgression is committed unintentionally and without desire for personal gain, even though such [transgression] exists.
"Therefore, because his obstruction has been removed, after remaining for some time as the supreme king of the Piśācas,
he becomes pure in essence and attains equality with the Supreme Lord.
According to this view, [the process] culminates in the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), with the external being primary.

Because of the subordination of consciousness (*cit*), however, when one is presided over by the *vāmā* power, the essential nature is concealed from the very root; thus, it is rightly said that one would not accomplish anything at all:
"One who is seized by greed and the like does not find the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*)" (4.21).
Thus it has been said before:
"Indeed, even when the knowledge of Śiva is heard, that which resides solely in duality does not abandon it;
firmly established in the Vāmā [power], he is the best among the bound souls (paśus)."
"Having been concealed by Śiva himself and established by the force of necessity, how could one who is dependent [upon it] proceed to the state of the Lord? (13.316).
Thus, at the conclusion of the *homa*, a *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) must be offered for the sake of attaining its fullness.
He states its application:
"Then, through the placement above and below, it is beautiful due to their mutual orientation toward one another. (15.424)

Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, which are of the nature of Śiva and Śakti and filled with the nectar of clarified butter, one should do so through the yoga of the method of identity, wherein the mind, vital breath, and body are equalized. || 15.425 ||
Having placed the left hand on the handle of the *sruc* and the right hand with its supporting ring below the neck, one should exert effort, pressing firmly.
One should lower the *sruk* ladle while directing the vital breath higher and higher, until it reaches the moon-wheel within the fire of awakening at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths]. (15.427)

As the supreme, most delightful, and excellent nectar falls from the tip of the sacrificial ladle, one should cast the oblation ending in *vauṣaṭ* into the fire, which is the mouth of the mantra. (15.428)

"By placing [them] above and below" and "consisting of Śiva and Śakti" are to be understood according to their respective application; thus, the *sruk* is above and the *sruva* is below. As it has been said:
"The base of the *sruk* is located at the navel, with its tip and mouth facing upward and level."
"O Goddess, having placed the *sruva* over the *sruc* with its face turned downwards.

For this very reason, because these two consist of the nature of Śakti and Śiva, their mutual orientation toward one another is appropriate, by which the attainment of the desired fruit occurs. Therefore, through this mutual orientation...

Because their respective natures have mutually entered into one another, it is said without distinction that [the vessel] is "filled with the nectar of clarified butter," even though it resides solely in the *sruva* ladle. Having thus taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* in this manner,
the Teacher— through the contemplation of supreme non-duality— has attained the state of oneness such that his body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth are unified.

Having placed the left hand palm-upward like a *sruc* ladle, and the right hand— with the *upayāma* ring— downward-facing like a *sruva* spoon, with its base at the root of the handle; and having made the front part of the base, which is below the neck of the *sruva*, shaped like a pedestal and joined to its edge.
Firmly pressing with hands arranged in this manner,

being diligent and attentive, one should direct the vital breath (prāṇa) starting from the heart, moving progressively upward through the sequence of correctly transcending each respective station, while maintaining the continuous flow of the clarified butter like a stream of ghee, [holding] the sacrificial ladle (sruk).

One should gradually lower [the breath] until it reaches the fire of awakening (bodhāgni) situated at the dvādaśānta, which consumes the universe; for one who abides in the supreme limit of the sacrificial ladle (sruk) characterized by consciousness—
which, in its wheel-like form, is supremely blissful— therefore...
The supreme nectar should fall— that is, it should flow forth by way of awakening the fire of consciousness— and until that occurs, through the contemplation of the oneness of all mantras,
one should effect the swallowing of each respective substance into the mouth and into the external fire, thereby providing satisfaction.

The meaning is that one should cast the oblation ending with *vauṣaṭ* and offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. The *upayāma* is a cord made of *darbha* grass, shaped like a braid, which is recognized as the upward-pointing knot (*ūrdhvagranthi*) and serves as the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*). As they say:
"A sword made of thirty-six palm-lengths of darbha grass,
consecrated seven times with the Śivāstra mantra, is the supreme sword of awakening.
Thus [ends verse 428].
One might ask: "If this is the underlying intention, what exactly is the purpose? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is indeed consciousness in the upper [realm] is reflected in the *kuṇḍa*;
the fire is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are [the senses], and the oil is the essence of consciousness consisting of volition. (15.429)
Having understood this from the beginning, one should firmly restrain the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva), the clarified butter (ājya),
and the mantras within the fire of awakening at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), and then cast the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having reflected that the awakening which indeed abides above is, by implication, the fire reflected below in the vessel,

that such a vital breath (*prāṇa*) constitutes the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and that the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*), whose nature consists of the awareness of duality, is the oil— having thus contemplated this first:

Having firmly restrained the *kuṇḍa* and the other [elements] within the fire of awakening at the *dvādaśānta*, and having brought them to a state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) in each respective location— there being predominantly the reflected image (*bimba*)— one should cast the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) by means of the ascending sequence,
so that these external things, which are predominantly reflections, may come to abide lower and lower.

Anticipating the objection, "If the original object (bimba) is situated higher and higher, would not its reflection (pratibimba) be situated lower and lower? What kind of logic is this?"— the author provides an illustration while internalizing this doubt.
For just as the reflection of a swan sinks into the water as it flies up into the sky, so too is this the rule here. (15.431)
"Bimba" means that which has the nature of a reflection. ||431||
In this manner of investigation, he states another classification:
"The natural, the stable, the liquid, the radiant, the mobile, and space; likewise Māyā, the Bindu, the Ātman, the Nāda, the Śakti, and Śiva. (15.432)

Thus, having distinguished the internal interior by way of the pervaded and the pervader, [one should likewise distinguish] those elements situated below it, from Earth up to Mūla, as well as the Person (puruṣa). || 15-433 ||

Ignorance (avidyā), attachment (rāga), necessity (niyati), time (kāla), illusion (māyā), and limited agency (kalā); likewise the individual soul (aṇu), knowledge (vidyā), its two lords (tadīśeśau), the state called Sadāśiva (sādākhya), power (śakti), and the coiled energy (kuṇḍalī).

One should join Vyāpinī with Samanā and Unmanā, and then [join them] into the Nameless (Anāmaka); established in exhalation, one should effect the union at the junction of the central channel—this is what is meant by "the Guru. (15.435)
It is stated in the *Traiśirasa-tantra* during the description of the supreme application (*parayojana*):

"In this context, the power of the Supreme Lord known as Māyā, which takes the form of concealing one's own nature, because of its all-pervasiveness [conceals] His innate nature consisting of knowledge, agency, and so forth."

"Pervading" means that it remains having covered [everything]; thus, the contracted Self—the Sakala and others—remains pervaded in this manner, according to the sequence to be described, by the stable earthly form because of its pervasiveness.
Furthermore, the *bindu* is the liquid watery element because of its moistening nature, and the *nāda* is the radiant fiery element.
Power is characterized primarily by touch and is mobile, being of the nature of air; and Śiva is of the nature of space because he is unobstructed. This is so.

According to the perspective expressed in such passages as, "Earth, water, fire, air, and space— these five are the principles (tattvas) by which the entire world is pervaded," [the system] encompasses the thirty-five principles beginning with earth and ending with Śakti.
The Guru, who knows the vital points (*marmajña*) because he is situated at the junction of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), and who likewise abides in the upward *recaka*,
[acts] by means of transcending each respective stage according to the method: "Through the abandonment of six, there is dissolution in the seventh" (Svacchanda-tantra 4.267).

Having pierced through each successive inner layer from the innermost inward, one should, by means of the method just described, unite [the soul] with the Supreme Śiva, who resides at the *dvādaśānta*— in the state beyond naming (*anāmaka*), beyond description (*anākhya*). Thus it is stated in the section on Union (*yojanikā-prakaraṇa*) in the venerable *Triśirobhairava*.
Having thus explained this as a digression, he speaks in order to describe the preparation of the *caru*:
"Then, by means of the fire previously established and consecrated with the assigned mantra... (15.436).
The *caru* is to be prepared either by the disciples or simultaneously with the *homa*;
and for the *caru*, one may use heroic substances (*vīradravya*) or worldly substances according to one's preference. (15.437)
In the accomplishment of the *caru*, all ritual actions are performed through the application of the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).
Then, having taken up the *caru* filled with clarified butter (*ājya*), the Guru—
Having fashioned either the *sruk* or the *sruva* ladle according to one's pursuit of enjoyment or liberation,
one should prepare three each for the deities, the *śaktis*, and the *yantras*.
Reciting the seventh, the *mātṛsadbhāva*, one by one in sequence,
he should offer the remainder of the clarified butter into the fire with the syllable *svā* as the nectar-syllable.
One should offer the sacrificial pap (*caru*) repeatedly in the form of the fire of the weapon (*hetirūpa-agni*).
The word "then" (*tataḥ*) means after the libation (*tarpaṇa*). As for what was stated regarding the other mantra:
"The waters, the sacrificial pap, and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) [are offered] into that which has been consecrated by the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*)."
"In a fire where Śiva has not been invoked, the oblation is [ineffective]; however, when Śiva has been invoked, the oblation is auspicious.
For this reason, it is stated there that [the fire] must be "pure. Regarding the term "sādhya" (to be accomplished)—it refers to the preceptor himself.
Regarding the phrase "simultaneous with the oblation"—it is because the disciples are not distracted during the oblation and other rites.
Heroic substances (*vīradravyāṇi*) are those consisting of *sāra* (essence) and so forth; worldly substances (*laukikāni*) are those consisting of milk, rice, and so forth.

"According to one's desire" means whether by heroes (*vīra*) or non-heroes (*avīra*). "All the ritual actions" refers to the taking up of the cooking pot and other vessels, their consecration with mantras, the stirring with the ladle, and so on.

"By means of the nectar-colored [syllable]"—because it causes the nourishment of both [the self and the deity]. "In the form of fire"—because the letter *ha* denotes Śiva and thus possesses the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*). "Again and again"—the meaning is that the ritual application should be performed in this manner at every oblation (*āhuti*). For in this way, [one says] *svāhā* in the fire.
The portion of Soma is placed within the oblation (caru) which has Soma as its essence, and with the utterance "Hā," the portion of Agni is also deposited,
by means of which both together become of the nature of Agni and Soma; as the Śruti says:
"Indeed, for whoever offers that oblation to Agni and Soma, this [body] of his becomes immortal.
Thus [it is said].
For this very reason, he said:
"Thus, through the single unifying thread of the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the fire of consciousness... (15.441).
Through the reflective awareness of "svāhā," there arises the supreme non-duality accompanied by mantra;
it is called "supreme non-duality" because of the attainment of the single essence of Agni and Soma.
Now, one might object: "In this way, would it not be said that there is simply equality between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer? What does this mean?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This is the consecration by contact; for the eater of the sacrificial oblation (caru) is indeed presided over [by it]. || 15-442 ||

The supreme essence of the object of enjoyment is that which causes the object of enjoyment to dance with effort; it is called the "supreme essence" because the object of enjoyment comes to rest within the enjoyer, and for this very reason it is said to "dance," meaning it vibrates in the form of agitation.
He demonstrates the etymological significance of the term *saṃpāta*:
"Because of the simultaneous falling together (*pāta*) of the enjoyer and the enjoyed through a single unifying awareness. (15.443)
And it is spoken of in this way because of mutual falling together and meeting;
here, the meaning of "simultaneous time" is the meaning of the individual parts (*avayavārtha*), while the meaning of "meeting" is the meaning of the whole (*samudāyārtha*).

Having thus prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru), he divides it into six parts: he should offer one portion each upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the water-pot (kumbha), and the small jar (karkarī). || 15.444 ||
Through a portion [of the offering], there is satisfaction of the mantra in the fire; and for both the disciple and the self, there is [satisfaction].
Having thus performed the prescribed duties and having informed the Lord, he is impelled by Him.
In order to purify the disciples through the sequence of the descent of power (śaktipāta), he should go outside;
there, for them, there shall be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the cleaning of the teeth.

Its fall is auspicious when directed toward the east, north, northeast, or upward; it is inauspicious elsewhere. In that case, there should also be one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra.
With their eyes bound by excellent cloths consecrated with the Netra-mantra, they were rendered motionless; thus, through forceful restraint, their hearts became focused on nothing else.
Having caused them to enter with their joined palms filled with pearls, gems, flowers, and so forth, the Guru, kneeling on his knees, seated them before the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should cause that handful [of flowers] to be cast by those disciples whose minds are purified;
then, having again filled their hands with a handful, one should quickly [reveal] the cloth to them.
He too should restrain his gaze, for the disciple perceives instantly;
and it is said:
"The success of the sacrificial oblation comes from the heart, [accomplished] by the performers of sacrifice with milk and rice."
Then, having divided the total sum by seven mantras, it is further divided into six parts.
"The water-pot (*vārdhānī*) and the jar (*kumbha*) of Śiva, Agni, the Guru, and the disciple are equal. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra).
Having thus informed [him]:
"O Supreme Lord, I have been commanded by you yourself in your capacity as my Guru..."
"You must favor these disciples who have been impelled by the power of Śiva."
"Therefore, these people of such a kind have arrived; show them favor by entering my body, so that I may become equal to you.
Thus it was said—"Do this"—meaning "speak thus. There—"outside," [the sense is] "one should give."
The remainder [of the verse]. Regarding the word *tasya*—it refers to the cleaning of the teeth. Regarding the word *tatra*—it refers to an inauspicious [result]. As it has been said:
"When [the tooth-stick] stands with its tip facing upward, one shall obtain a kingdom or liberation;
but when it is face-downward, death occurs; one should then offer a hundred oblations into the heart."
One should predict the perfection of yoga in the east, disease in the southeast,
death in the south, and strife in the southwest.
"In the western direction (Vāruṇī) there is the increase of wealth; in the northwestern (Vāyavya), there shall be eradication (uccāṭana);
in the northern (Saumyā), one attains success (siddhi); and in the northeastern region (Īśāna), liberation (mokṣa).
By this, the consecration of the teeth is described. "By them"—that is, by those [teeth] thus inserted.
"By the instigating agents. "For the sake of brevity"—the sense is: so that his vision of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) may occur instantaneously.
Anticipating the question, "What would happen for him in this case? he says:
"When a place is suddenly perceived, illuminated by the power of mantra... (15.451).
By the power of that immersion, the disciple attains identity with it.
He makes this very point clear by means of an illustration: "For just as one whose heart is filled with passion [perceives] those various qualities of his beloved for himself... (15.452).
One purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta) perceives the presence of the mantra in this way;
that is, "by oneself," and not by depending on other means, for if that were the case, he would not have such a vision instantaneously.
Now, one might object: "Granted that qualities such as beauty (lāvaṇya) are visible, so those whose hearts are attached to them may indeed behold them;
but since mantras are invisible, even though they are present, how could they come within the range of the eyes and other senses of those with limited vision?"
Anticipating this objection, he says: "For, when such a cooperative cause for the sense organs, such as the eye, [is present]... (15.453).
Indeed, even if something has never been seen before, the capacity [for its cognition] would arise;

for when the auxiliary condition characterized by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) exists, there occurs the conceptual knowledge (*vikalpa-jñāna*)— despite the absence of prior impressions from experience— even with respect to that which was previously entirely unseen, such as in the case of the visual and other sense organs.
The meaning is that it should be conceived as possible that even in the case of mantras and so forth, which are not [direct] objects, a capacity for performing the act of seeing might arise.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the proof for this?", he says:
"For those of perfected wisdom [perceive] the body, water, and land as being infused with mantra. (15.454)

Those who perceive [the deity] in images and the like recognize the presence and absence [of the deity]; likewise, he says this even to those who deny self-awareness (svasaṃvedana): "Sealed by the Bhūtas and others, they are rendered auspicious by the rays of the deposited mantras. (15.455)
"‘As if trembling’ means by those various conscious faculties and their auxiliary factors.

For in the world, beings who are sealed by spirits and the like are seen as if they were trembling before a teacher or similar person whose splendor and good fortune have been manifested through the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*). Thus, by that [process] such as the descent of power (*śaktipāta*),"

The meaning is that, through the various sense organs acting in concert, depending on the proximity or non-proximity of this or that [object], the insentient [body] becomes as if sentient. By this much, the final consecration, characterized by the penetration of the mantra (*mantrāveśa*), has been described.
Now he describes the ritual of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta):
"Then, [the teacher places] that blazing [power], filled with all the paths, upon the right hand. (15.456)
One should worship the mantra-wheel with the left hand, which burns away the bonds;
that [hand] should be placed upon the head of the disciple, whose continuum of the paths has been deposited within his body. (15.457)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on all the limbs in due order and touch him with that very [mantra].
Now, one might ask: "Since this was not stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* relevant to the present context, from where has it been brought?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And this has been stated in the Dīkṣottara [Tantra] by means of that which is beautified by the falling of flames: || 15-458 ||
By means of the *śivahasta* bestowed by [the Guru], he is ordained as a *samayin*;
while still living, he possesses the fitness for study regarding the principle (*tattva*) of the Lord (*īśvara*), which is the state of union (*sāyujya*). (15.459)
Regarding the phrase "with the descent of flames": this is due to the presence of the splendor of the mantra. As it has been said:

"Having meditated on the All-pervasive Lord in the Hand of Śiva, [one sees] the collection of mantras blazing intensely" (Svacchanda Tantra 3.142). The term "in Īśvara" refers to that which exists above the Vidyā-tattva, and not to that which resides below the Earth-tattva.

In the *Kālāgnirudra*, such [a reading] is not seen in the scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, since Uddyotakara alone has exerted effort regarding this matter, what is the use of stating it here? It should be understood from his work itself. "Adhīti" means study (*adhyayana*). As it has been said:
"For one who is thus purified by the *śamaya* [initiation], there arises the fitness for its recitation."
Likewise, in listening, studying, performing oblations, and in worship and so forth;
"One whose self is purified through conduct and meditation attains the state of the Lord. (Svacchandatantra 4.79) ||459||
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well; thus he says:

"In the Śrīdevyāyāmala, however, it is said regarding the wheel with eight spokes and a trident at its center, which has Bhairava as its navel and consists of the eight [deities] beginning with Aghora. (15.460)
The outer and inner [circles] are the lower and upper [rims], with the middle being the spear, both supreme and non-supreme;
it is filled with flames, ruddy, and terrifying with the rotating Mother-syllables (Praṇavas). || 15-461 ||
When the external hand is visualized upon being contemplated, one becomes a possessor of the pledge (samayin).
As for the paralysis of the bonds and so forth, that which is about to ascend immediately belongs to him.
Having worshipped it outside, one should place that [initiation], which severs [the soul] from the vital breaths, upon the head;
by this "Hand of Śiva," one clearly becomes a *samayin*. (15.463)
Here, for one whose wheel is presided over by the eight [deities] beginning with Aghora, who wanders everywhere through every spoke, who is formidable with the sound of *pheṃ*,
whose navel is adorned by the three Bhairavas, and who reflects the two locations characterized by the outer rim and the spokes—

When the trident— situated within the middle prong of the eight-spoked wheel of the Goddess Parāparā, which is vermilion-red and for that very reason filled with flames— is visualized, and when such a hand, both externally and internally, is properly perceived as being primarily characterized by the supreme good;
The meaning is that by the paralysis of the *pāśa* (the fetter), one becomes a *samayin*; by that alone, his initiation into the *samaya* (observance) is accomplished.

It is not only the initiation into the *samaya* that occurs through this, but even the initiation into *nirvāṇa*—as he says in the passage beginning with "But he who... He who, moreover, desires to depart [from the body]...

Having worshipped that very Hand of Śiva— which effects the separation from the vital breaths— in a field or other location outside [the body] that is suitable for the breath, one should cast it upon the head; by the mere touch of it,
the initiation of immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*) occurs for him— this is the meaning.
As it has been said there:
"Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel, complete with hub and rim,
marked above by tridents and [divided] by spokes and intervals."
Thus it begins, and then says: "...one should place Bhairava residing in the navel."
"The group of eight beginning with Aghora is to be worshipped...";
"Those [energies] residing upon the eight spokes..."
Thus,

the goddess who is both supreme and non-supreme (Parāparā) stands upon the trident, resembling vermilion in her ruddy hue; while the goddess who is non-supreme (Aparā) and supreme (Parā) rests upon the outer rim.
Thus:
"The whirling [light], red in radiance, situated in the center of the Bhairava-cakra.
Thus.
Having meditated upon the great wheel, filled with garlands of flames,
in his hand, he should place his left foot there upon the staff of the trident on all sides, joined with his right knee across all the spokes.
Thus it is said:
"From seeing, one attains stobha; from touching, one certainly dies. ||463||
One might ask: "What would be the result of this for him by virtue of being a *samayin*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"For that very person, when there is the loosening of the bonds of the *tattvas* according to the procedure for the future [initiate], the status of a *putraka* arises; and he should be joined to the supreme *tattva* by the teachers. (15.464)
He alone, who knows the classes of mantras and understands the reality of recitation, fire-oblations, and so forth,
[should first perform the rite] with the Nirvāṇa-vase, and thereafter with that known as the Īśvara-vase.
The initiate (sādhaka) who has been consecrated shall, at the end of his enjoyment, attain absorption into the Supreme;
this is what is meant by "will happen," as stated in the sixteenth chapter and elsewhere. "He" refers to the spiritual son (putraka). "He himself" refers to the initiate bound by the rules (samayī).
This should also be connected here with the phrase: "when the severance of the bonds of the principles (tattva-pāśa) has been performed according to the procedure for those yet to come."
The same applies to what follows. Regarding "jāti"—this refers to *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and so forth. Regarding "nirvāṇa"—here, Śiva is said to be the bestower of liberation.
For even when the initiation (*yojanikā*) into Śiva has been performed for the practitioner, he may still remain in the state of Sadāśiva for the sake of enjoyment; therefore, he says:
"At the end of his enjoyment, there is dissolution into the Supreme."
Endowed with these qualities, he is initiated into the teaching of Śiva.
One who is proficient in the four-footed *saṃhitās*, devoted to the eighteen *tantras*, and who knows the ten *tantras* and the supreme path— he is designated as an *ācārya*.
Starting from the earth and ending with Nirvāṇa, the supreme Guru should perform the measurement of this [mandala] for the consecration rite of the Ācārya. (15.468)

"By these"—meaning by such qualities as being a knower of mantra and tantra. "Ending in nirvāṇa"—meaning in the state of Paramaśiva—for the sake of authority (adhikāra). Furthermore, his abiding is in Śiva, who is the lower Śiva (aparaśiva). As it has been said: "For the sake of authority, the teacher's station is in the state that is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara)."
One should know that for practitioners seeking the state of Śiva, initiation is performed in Sadāśiva.
"In the supreme reality of the Son (putraka), and likewise in the Samayin and Īśvara [stages]. ||468 ||

Now, one might ask: "If this has been stated in such a way, what would have been said regarding the initiate (samayin)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By these statements, this has also been declared: the initiate (samayin) is like a prince;
he is qualified for all three stages, beginning with that of the spiritual son (putraka). (15.469)
For just as a prince is authorized over the kingdom and so forth, so too is this initiate (samayin) authorized over his son and so forth;
indeed, all initiations are said to be preceded by the initiation of the initiate (samayidīkṣā). || 469 ||

Although there is no difference between the *putraka* and the *ācārya* regarding their union with the supreme reality (*paratattva*), the following statement expresses a certain distinction: "But when the *putraka* becomes a teacher (*daiśika*), he becomes one whose union is equal [to that of the *ācārya*].
He is an authority (*adhikārī*) therein, yet not so in the practice (*sādhana*) where the union is different. (15.470)

"He" refers to the spiritual son (*putraka*). "In the performance of rites" (*sādhane*) refers to initiation, consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and so forth—for the sake of which the teacher's abiding in the "higher-lower" state (*parāparapada*) has been described. Thus he says: "in the application of the differentiated" (*bhinnayojane*). ||470||
One might object: "Is it not possible for even a *samayin* to undergo the initiation involving the removal of the sectarian mark (*liṅgoddhāra*) at an earlier stage?
Why, then, is it stated here that 'the *samayin* is like a prince'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this Tantra, one who has obtained the subsequent rites through the sequence beginning with the *samayin*..."
The preceptor, moreover, must never be a Buddhist, a Vaiṣṇava, or any other such [adherent of a different sect].
Thus, having resolved this incidental point, the subject at hand is now described:
having performed the rite of Śiva’s Hand, by which the bonds are incinerated; (15.472)

Having established the disciple through the yoga of meditation until the point of ultimate rest, he [should then place] that disciple into the water-pot, the weapon-vessel, the fire, and his own self.
Afterward, one should cause [the disciple] to perform prostration and cast the offering (bali) to the spirits and the Mothers.
The term "preceptor" (ācārya) is used as an illustration; by it, the practitioner (sādhaka) is also included, as he will say:
"For those who previously bore sectarian marks, the initiation for liberation is devoid of authority."
"Those who have been reborn are not fit for the path of the *sādhaka* or the *ācārya*. (22.29).
For this very reason, it was stated immediately thereafter:
"...initiated in the teaching of Śiva. (467)
Thus. "By him" means by the hand of Śiva.
Now, he speaks regarding the preparation of the bed:
"Then, having worshipped Śaṅkara, [one should prepare] the bed consecrated with the Astra-mantra. (15.474)
Having performed this and having placed the disciple upon it, and having applied the mantra,
one should cause the disciple’s heart-cakra to rest and proceed to his dvādaśānta.
He may become one whose web of digits is exhausted through the arising of the twelve notes;
thereafter, he shines with the sixteen digits accumulated through the process of entry.
The full moon of one’s own self-consciousness should rest within the heart of the disciple;
then, until the time of natural emergence, it should proceed to the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta).

Furthermore, one should enter the heart-cakra; such is the sequence for the procedure of sleep. "The twelve vowels" refers to the form of the solar *kalās*. "In this manner" means by the aforementioned method characterized by the entry and exit of the breath (*prāṇa*) of both the disciple and the self—this is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection, "If this were so, what would happen?", he says:
"This disciple has attained sleep; [he is like] the stainless moon and sun. (15.478)
In the heart-cakra, one forcibly unites those [energies] consisting of fullness and thinness.
Anticipating the question, "What indeed would follow from this? he says:
"By means of the light of the moon and sun rendered pure through forceful practice, one perceives the truth. (15.479)

Anticipating the objection, "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this [dream], which is skilled in making manifest the difference between future auspiciousness and its opposite?", he says: "And it has been said:
'Having meditated upon the Full and the Waned in the sphere of the twelve... (15.480).
Having entered [the heart], one should meditate; sleeping, one shall attain freedom. And when sleep has come upon the child, the Guru, having worshipped Śaṅkara, [should proceed].
He should eat the sacrificial oblation (caru) with his companions, and thereafter consume the tooth-cleansing stick;
he should then sleep with his mind fixed upon the heart-center ignited by the rays of the mantra.
In the morning, the Guru, having performed all his daily obligatory rites and worshipped Śaṅkara,
discerns the two objects seen in the dreams of both himself and the disciple according to their relative strength.
