What has been perceived by oneself is more powerful than anything else, due to the intensity of one's awakening; moreover, when there is equality in awakening, there would be equality between teacher and disciple, like that of a dream. (15.484)
The gods, fire, and gurus; the causes for their worship and ritual implements;
a charming woman; the drinking of liquor; and the eating of raw meat. (15.485)
Drinking blood, decapitation, being smeared with blood, feces, and urine, and mounting mountains, horses, elephants, or vehicles that are pleasant to the heart. (15.486)
Whatever generally leads to delight is declared to be auspicious;
one should proclaim that for the increase of satisfaction, for joy is indeed the supreme fruit.
Therefore, for any other inauspicious [sign], one should perform eight hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra.
The Guru should tell the disciples: "Inauspicious is not inauspicious. (15.488)
Indeed, a great effort is required to sever a doubt that has become deeply rooted;
however, for those whose doubt has dissolved, [the experience] arises as if by the power of a dream. (15.489)
"Nothing, whether auspicious or inauspicious, would exist...

so it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*. And in that [text], the reading is "both the stout and the emaciated. Regarding the word *carum*: it refers to that which was previously set aside for one's own sake. Regarding the word *vitte*: [it means] in wealth.
"Reflects upon"—this is the meaning. By this, the investigation of the dream state is commenced.

"The other"—that which is seen by the disciple. "Similarity to a dream"—and not a matter of relative strength or weakness (*balābala*). "Generally"—the sense is that there is no capacity to produce pleasure from such things as the decapitation of one's own head. "That"—[refers to the aforementioned].
An auspicious dream. "From this" means from the aforementioned dream. "The other" refers to its opposite, such as eating cooked meat and so forth. As it has been said:
"This very same [dream], when it occurs otherwise, is proclaimed as a bad dream."

"...eating cooked meat, anointing with oil, falling into pits and so forth. The phrase "from the weapon" means by means of the *astra* [mantra]. The second half of the verse is the reason for not describing the inauspicious.

Regarding the word "of them"—that is, of those whose doubts have dissolved; for indeed, in one who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), there is no distinction between auspicious and inauspicious at all.
The intention is that it would be so.
And because they consist of the three *guṇas*, these [beings] possess variety even in the dream state—thus he says:

"...the one whose nature is *sattva* clearly perceives [objects] in this way by virtue of their diversity; the one whose nature is *rajas* [perceives them] merely through the subtle body (*liṅga*). (15.490)

For him, there is nothing consisting of *tamas*, nor [anything consisting of] pleasure or pain, or the auspicious or inauspicious. One might object: "In this world, one who is characterized by *tamas* would not perceive even the slightest thing; so how could he have a determination regarding what is auspicious or inauspicious? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "For him..."
From pleasure and pain come the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Now, having raised the objection—"But how can there even be eligibility for a person of tamasic nature in this rite of initiation?"—the author refutes it:
"But how could one called 'tamasic' here be fit for the ritual procedure? (15.491).
"Let there be no dispute; indeed, the quality of anyone belongs to someone else at some time.

The word *vai* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), and it should be connected everywhere [in the verse]. Regarding the word "quality" (*guṇa*)—by implication, it means that which is preeminent (*udrikta*).
He demonstrates this very point:
"Even if one's conduct is entirely characterized by *sattva*, if one is *tāmasa* regarding food... (15.492).
Is he therefore base, or is he superior because of the opposite?

"Therefore" means: because of being *tāmasa* (dark/ignorant) regarding food alone. "The opposite of that" means: being *tāmasa* in all respects, while being *sāttvika* (pure/good) regarding food alone.
He applies this very point to the subject at hand:
"Even one who has received the descent of power (śaktipāta) and even one who is initiated [is not liberated] as long as he remains within the state of the qualities (guṇa). (15.493)
The self indeed becomes manifold, yet it remains concentrated on the primary object;
this is because of the persistence of the qualities—that is, because the natural body persists for some time. "On the primary object" means on that characterized by initiation (dīkṣā).
Now, in order to explain the ritual action pertaining to the occasion (sāmaya-karma), he says: "Then the Guru [performs] the worship of the deity for the disciple, preceded by the mantra. (15.494)
The Guru, being composed, should then instruct him, perform that [rite], and consecrate him;
he should do so for the six [deities] beginning with Brahmā, who reside in the six wheels starting from the heart. || 15-495 ||

Purified by the touch of consciousness, one should perform each of the eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the child, beginning from the heart and ending with the pair of feet, by means of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti). || 15.496 ||
The word "tataḥ" (then) means immediately after the instruction on the worship of the deity and so forth. He explains that very point with the words beginning with "hṛdādi" (the heart and so forth):
the cakras beginning with the heart are six, characterized by the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
"Each one"—the meaning is that by thus multiplying the eight [factors] by six, there are forty-eight refinements (*saṃskāra*). "Purified by the touch of awakening"—[as it is said:
"...through the renunciation of the six, there is absorption into the seventh" (4.267).

The meaning is: "purified" by the touch—not by direct absorption—of that consciousness which, in the form of the supreme subject, resides at the *dvādaśānta*, such that it becomes permeated by it. As he will say:
For one who has attained the state of a twice-born through unification with his own nature at the *dvādaśānta*,
by resting upon mere touch and descending instantly [to the lower centers], [the result is achieved].
"By which the initiate becomes consecrated through the attainment of the state of Rudra. (Tantrāloka 15.521). ||496||
And by this much alone, his accomplishment of the other purificatory rites (saṃskāra) is established; thus he says:

"By the destruction of the defects such as the state of [needing] food and seed, one becomes a twice-born (dvija); thus, being filled with the purificatory rites known as the eight and the four Vedas, one stands as a twice-born. (15.497)
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), place (*deśa*) is intended. As it has been said:
"One becomes a twice-born (*dvija*) through the consumption of seed (*bījāhāra*) as well as the purity of state and place" (*Svacchanda-tantra* 4.68).
In that regard, the defect of food (*āhāradoṣa*) arises from the failure to carry out [the practice] according to the procedure prescribed in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
"The defect of the seed [is such that] Brahminhood would arise through purity of seed, and that [purity] resides in women;
yet their minds are fickle and run even toward Caṇḍālas."
Thus [it is said].

Because the purity of the seed (*bījaśuddhi*) is impossible for one who dwells in [wrong] views; because there is a defect of disposition (*bhāvadoṣa*) due to association with untruth, lack of sincerity, and so forth; and because there is a defect of place (*deśadoṣa*) due to contact with barbarians (*mleccha*) and the like.
By means of the forty-eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), [namely] the eight *vasus* and the four *vedas*.
The meaning is "conditioned. ||497||

He states those very [rites]: conception, the rite for a male child, parting the hair, the birth-ceremony, naming, the first outing, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and likewise the eighth [rite]. (15.498)
The *iṣṭi* rites for the binding of the vows consist of the Mauñjī and Bhautika ceremonies, followed by the Saumika;
these, along with the Godāna, constitute the purificatory rites (*saṃskriyā*) pertaining to the Vedas and the moon, beginning from the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
The Pratyudvāha is the fifteenth; after that come the seven Pākayajñas, the Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, and the two sacrifices of Śrāvaṇī and Āgrāyaṇī.
Following the Caitrī and Āśvayujī sacrifices, there are exactly seven oblation-sacrifices (havirmakha):
the establishment of the sacred fires (ādheya), the agnihotra, and the full-moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsa) together with the new-moon sacrifice (darśa). || 15.501 ||
The Cāturmāsya, the Paśubandha, and the Sautrāmaṇī; these, along with the Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, and the Vājapeya. (15.502)
The Āptoryāma and the Atirātra—these seven are the forms of the Soma sacrifice;
the Hiraṇyapāda and other sacrifices are encompassed by a thousand [of these].
The thirty-eighth is the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha); by this much, the stage of the householder (gārhasthya) is completed.
The stages of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the wandering mendicant (pārivrājya) are considered to consist of these forty [years].
Compassion, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, gratitude, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of craving—this is remembered as the eightfold set of personal qualities. (15.505)

The departure [from the womb], the beholding of the sun, the binding of the vow (*vratabandha*), and the initiation (*upanayana*); the fourfold set of observances (*vrata*) to be performed during the period of Vedic study beginning with the *iṣṭi*s;
and at the conclusion of the Vedic study, the shaving of one's hair and so forth, characterized by the gift of a pair of cattle to the teacher.

The gift of a cow (*godāna*). "The Vedas are four, and Indra is one; therefore, O beloved, the gift of a cow consists of fourteen [units]" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.396). "After this"—that is, immediately following the marriage. *Śrāddha* refers to the rite concerning deceased ancestors and others.
The two *āgrayaṇī* offerings consist of the sacrifice of new grain (*navānna-yāga*) during the autumn and spring. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*atipūrva*):

it refers to the *atyagniṣṭoma*. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) indicates a type; thus, the meaning is that there is the *hiraṇyapāda* and the tenfold *caityayajña*. Regarding the phrase "with a thousand": [it refers to] each one.
Because it is surrounded by a hundred [levels]. As it has been said:
"Hiraṇyapāda is the first, and likewise Guhyahiraṇyadhṛt;
Hiraṇyameḍhra, Hiraṇyanābhi, and Hiraṇyagarbha as well."
Hiraṇyaśrotra, Hiraṇyatvak, and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa,
Hiraṇyajihva, and Hiraṇyaśṛṅga— these are proclaimed as the ten sacrifices (Yajñas).
"But here, each one is understood to be surrounded by a hundred. (Sva. 10.406).

"Vānasthyam" means the state of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Compassion (*dayā*) is sympathy for others. Patience (*kṣānti*) is the absence of retaliation toward those who do harm, even when one has the power to do so. Respectful treatment (*satkṛti*)...

"Excellence of performance" arises from carrying out [the practice] without effort. "Auspiciousness" is the cultivation of praiseworthy things. Regarding the word "self" (ātman)—it refers to the group of internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) which are proximate to the self, but not the self directly.
Of the self, because it consists solely of consciousness. ||505||
Right here, he shows the inclusion of other purificatory rites (saṃskāra) as well:
"The girdle, the staff, the deerskin, the triple longevity, the worship of fire, the twilight devotions, and alms-seeking—these are the seven purificatory rites and the seven vows. (15.506)
Bhauteśa and Pāśupatya, Gāṇeśa and Gāṇapatyaka, Unmattaka, Asidhārā, and Ghṛteśāna—these are the fourteen. (15.507)

These, however, are recorded as the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) belonging to the primary rite of the initiation into vows (vratabandha). For the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya), the final rite (antyeṣṭi) occurs within the womb; thus is one consecrated. (15.508)
Then he becomes a twice-born one fit for the attainment of the portion of Rudra;
the Guru should apply these purificatory rites (saṃskāras) precisely according to the sequence of the vital breaths.

Alternatively, by means of oblations of sesame seeds and other substances preceded by mantras, one should apply the *tryāyuṣa* mark with sacred ash (*bhasmapuṇḍraka*). Regarding the statement "of the initiation (*vratabandha*), which is the principal [rite]," it has been said:
"The ninth is the initiation (*vratabandha*), and that is proclaimed to be the principal. (Svacchandatantra 10.388)
Thus; "these"—that is, forty-eight.
He clarifies the statement "preceded by mantras" [as follows]:
"The Praṇava, the Heart, the Name, 'I purify,' and the Beloved of Agni. (15.510)

In this manner, by means of the limbs beginning with the head (mūrdhan) and so forth, this [mantra] is repeated again and again. "The heart" refers to that which is connected to the limbs of the Vidyā. Therefore, he says—with reference to each refinement—that the fivefold group of Vidyā-limbs must be applied through such an inference (ūha); thus it has been stated.
This, moreover, [is stated] repeatedly.
Having raised the objection, "But why was it said that this [person] would be fit for attaining the status of Rudra through the attainment of the state of being twice-born (dvijatva)? he says:
"Because this very nature of consciousness (cid-dharma), consisting of tranquility and so forth, is what constitutes 'twice-bornness'. (15.511)
Through that very process, consciousness arises in the form of Rudra, by which it attains what is called "twice-born-ness," as in:
"He is peaceful, self-controlled, and has conquered anger..."

Through such a perspective, since consciousness (*cit*) arises as being of the nature of tranquility (*śānti*) and so forth, its very characteristic is that of accumulation; by virtue of that specific accumulation, consciousness itself is born as Rudra through the manifestation of its attainment of the state of the twice-born (*dvijatva*).
The intention is that he would become fit for attaining a portion of that [state].
He makes this very point clear through an illustration: "Just as, in the smelting of metals such as gold, [the purity] occurs by way of successive stages... (15.512).
Likewise, in the purification of consciousness within another state of being, such as that of the twice-born:

for just as when specific substances that are the causes for the production of gold and so forth undergo smelting, they come to exist in that [refined] state through a process of attaining the nature of silver and so on, exactly so it is with consciousness.

The meaning is that while [the soul] is being refined within the state of the twice-born, there occurs the attainment of the status of a portion of Rudra by way of prioritizing the acquisition of that [refinement].
Now, one might object: "Is it not said that a twice-born (dvija) is one born from an undegenerated Brahmin father into an undegenerated Brahmin mother?
How then can this [other definition] be stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that case, the womb is not the cause; one whose self is tranquil is called twice-born. (15.513)
Anticipating the objection, "By whom was this said?", he says:
"This has been analyzed by the Sage in the Mokṣadharma and other works;
for it was stated by him:"
The gods know him as Brahmā, by whom all this is known— both nature and its transformation— and who understands the destinies of all beings.
"He who grants fearlessness to all beings and from whom all beings receive fearlessness—
he who has become the self of all beings, the gods know him as a Brahmin.
Thus it is said.
Even a Śūdra who is endowed with virtuous conduct and possessed of good qualities may become a Brāhmaṇa,
provided that even he has crossed the terrible ocean of the five senses.
"To him, O Yudhiṣṭhira, immeasurable gifts should be given. O King, birth is not what is seen; it is virtues that bring about well-being.
Thus [it is said].
And this has not been stated by him alone; thus he says:
"It has also been set forth by the Lord in the Mukuṭa and other scriptures. (15.514)
As it is said there:
"One who follows the Śiva-dharma, is full of faith, and whose very self is Śiva;
one who is devoted to Śiva, to knowledge, and to the guru, and who is affectionate toward his fellow students."
Free from envy, having perceived the truth, and refined in the sacrificial rite of Śiva—
even if born of the lowest caste or lacking a limb— such a practitioner partakes in liberation.
One whose soul is devoid of these qualities does not partake in liberation even if he be a Brahmin;
a twice-born man who is deceitful should be rejected, whereas a Mleccha who is free from deceit should indeed be accepted.
He was beloved by Maheśa, learned in the four Vedas, and free from hypocrisy;
yet he was a hater of Śiva, a doer of evil deeds, and a reviler of the Śiva-dharma and other such teachings.
"A sin committed by a Brāhmaṇa, or a meritorious deed performed by a Śūdra—what is the reason for that? Is birth praised as the basis for dharma and adharma? Thus, and in many other ways. (514)
Now, one might object: "How can this be consistent, given its contradiction with other scriptures such as the *Smṛti*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because of the merging of consciousness with the body, and because of the arising of the similar from the similar..."
By intention regarding the [mother's] status, a twice-born man is considered a son of two twice-borns according to the Smṛti.

For consciousness arises from a similar and unimpaired [cause] by depending on the union of bodies; because of this reason, according to the intention of the majority in the Smṛti scriptures, the son of two twice-born [parents] is traditionally known as "twice-born" (dvijanman). ||515||
Now, one might ask: "From where has this been stated so extensively? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Since they have obtained birth from mothers who are of the lowest caste and are the progenitors of those with the intellects of dogs and such, how could the sages, whose minds are thus elevated, be worthy recipients [of grace] through their devotion to Brahman? (15.516)
"Dhīve" means "fisherwoman" (dhīvarī). "Ṛṣayaḥ" refers to Vyāsa and others. ||516||
With this very intention, he says that in our doctrine there is no acceptance of caste and so forth:
"For this very reason, in this secret scripture which teaches the true reality of the object, the practice of caste and so forth is not prescribed in the Śāmbhava [tradition]. (5.17)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, why has it not been stated in the same way regarding memory and the other [mental faculties] as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But the scriptures pertaining to bound souls (pāśava) consist entirely of the power of Vāmā."
Śambhu’s doubt regarding the accomplishment of creation and so forth, and the formulation of its result.
The worldly convention consists of creation and so forth. "Doubt" refers to what has been stated in such passages as: "doubt regarding genus, doubt regarding substance...
and so on. Its fruit is heaven, hell, and the like.
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"For one who has attained the state of being twice-born [a brahmin] through unification with his own [Self] at the *dvādaśānta*,
and who descends immediately without resting upon mere tactile sensation," (15.519)

"By which the initiate (samayin) becomes consecrated through the attainment of the state of Rudra. "He does not rest"—the sense is that in this way, union with Paramaśiva itself has been accomplished. Now, one might ask: "What would happen to him once he is thus consecrated? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
One should always be devoted to study, listening [to the teachings], worship, and service to the guru.
One who has been authorized as a *samayin* may worship the Lord elsewhere, with the exception of [the daily rites];
"elsewhere" means on occasional occasions (*naimittika*) and so forth. As it has been said:
"The Guru and the practitioner (*sādhaka*) alone should perform the triad beginning with the daily (*nitya*) rites."
"In this manner, by the command of Śiva, one should always maintain these two others for as long as life lasts.
Thus [it is said].

Anticipating the doubt, "What indeed must he hear or study?", the teacher begins to explain the rules of conduct (*samaya*), internalizing that very doubt: "The Guru should cause him, whose portion of Rudra has been brought forth, to hear the rules of conduct. (15.521)
These eightfold groups of eight, as described in the *Yāmala* and other scriptures of the Goddess, consist of:
speaking no falsehood, non-performance [of forbidden acts], concealment [of one's spiritual status], worship, libation, and contemplative realization. (15.522)
Slaying and deluding—thus the eightfold observances (samaya) are eightfold;
it is the natural state of mantras and tantras, the union of the conduct of the observances. (15.523)
One should not speak idle chatter, harsh words, or falsehoods in their eight forms;
nor should one engage in fruitless exertion, violence, or the violation of another's wife. (15.524)
One should not practice pride, hypocrisy, or the treatises on spirits, poisons, and diseases;
nor [should one display] one's own mantra, rosary, or the knowledge that is the very nature of wisdom.
One should conceal one's conduct, virtues, afflictions, and signs of spiritual accomplishment;
likewise, one should conceal the guru, the scriptures, the deity, the fire, those advanced in knowledge, women, and one's religious vows.
One should worship this group of eight according to one's ability:
the assembly of gurus, the poor, the afflicted, the ancestors, the guardians of the field, and the hosts of living beings and birds.
One should satisfy the host of spirits dwelling in the cremation ground, the deities of the body,
Śiva, Śakti, as well as oneself, the mudrā, and that which is the very nature of the mantra.
One should contemplate the enjoyments and liberations of saṃsāra from the mouth of the guru;
likewise, passion, hatred, envy, contraction, jealousy, and pride. (15.529)
One should cause those who break the samaya, as well as those who act improperly—to be slain;
likewise the cruel, the hateful, the slanderous, and the dull-witted who abide on the path of the sacrificial animal.
One should delude the king’s wicked followers and those who create obstacles;
the Śākinīs are also to be worshipped, and they are described in this manner in the Śrī-gama.
For those women whose violence is twofold, whose passion is fourfold, and whose greed is eightfold—it is sufficient to suspect them as *śākinīs*. (15.532)
"In the Śrīmādhava Kula, it is said: 'One must not dwell together with those beasts who, though established in the family tradition, remain outside the heroic substances. (15.533)
One should always worship the circle of deities, the guru, the fire, and the scripture with equanimity;
one should not consume anything whatsoever that has not been offered to these.
One should not take away this substance; rather, one should honor the group of gurus.
And that [relationship] would generally be one formed through knowledge, such as with his brother’s wife or daughter-in-law. (15.535)
That worldly [bond] created by the connection of birth is merely like that of a beast;
however, it serves as a ground for attachment for the sake of accomplishing the propitiation of the Guru. (15.536)

One should not worship them by virtue of their own greatness, but rather as a group like that of the Guru; one should not engage in the censure of the Guru, nor should one act as a cause for such censure. (15.537)
One should not listen to her, nor provoke him to anger, nor do anything before him without his permission, except for that which is required by service to him. (15.538)
Worldly and supramundane tasks, wrath, play, austerity, and recitation;
whatever has been enjoyed by the guru, such as the bed, clothing, seat, and so forth—(15.539).

One should not consume that, nor touch it with one's feet, but rather pay homage to it. By the words beginning with "avāda," he demonstrates that these very [observances] consist of eight groups of eight. *Samaya* is the form of those various secret sacrifices; *ācāra* is the action appropriate to them. "One should not practice" [refers to improper conduct].
One should not do so—this is the meaning. "Knowledge" refers to scholarship and the like, pursued for the sake of one's own superiority.
"The nature of knowledge" is the thorough understanding of reality (*tattva*). "One's own vow" refers to mudrās and other such observances.
"Multitudes of living beings" refers to cows and the like. "Nothing whatsoever is this" is the contemplation of *saṃsāra*.

Hatred is characterized by a burning nature. Envy is the attribution of faults to those who possess virtues. Jealousy is the inability to endure the excellence of others. The term "twofold" refers to the intention directed toward another woman. "He" refers to the group of elders. "Tuk" means a son; as the *Nighaṇṭu* states: [it denotes a son].
Regarding the phrase "a son is one's own self" (2.2): "he" refers to one related by birth. Being the ground for attachment to him is the reason for [the gravity of] worshiping him.
"To her" means for the sake of censuring the guru. "That" refers to the censure of the guru. "Him" refers to the guru; for his service is indeed [the remedy].
The sense is: "It would come about even without his command."
Now, one might ask: "Why is such emphasis placed on the propitiation of the Guru? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It is also stated in the venerable *Traiśirasa* [Tantra] that [the merit gained] by means of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances... (15.540).

Even if one stands in the forest like a piece of wood, even if one observes the vow of the sword’s edge, and even if one is established in restraints and observances, one does not attain that supreme state. (15.541)
But one who is intent on the propitiation of the guru through mind, action, and speech, attains from the satisfied guru the full and most wonderful supreme good. (15.542)
Just as the earth is covered on all sides by falling snow,
it remains forever like stone through its union with the binding power of the wind.
Just as when the breath is first made steady, a single state is grasped, so too from a Guru who has been properly propitiated, the fullness of expanding gnosis is attained. (15.544)
One whose discourse concerns that consciousness which is omnipresent and resides within the object of knowledge leads [the disciple] upward immediately; therefore, one should propitiate the Guru.
Even by conversing with him, sin is destroyed in an instant according to the *Śrīsāra*.
Therefore, having examined him with effort through the words of the scriptures and the characteristics of knowledge... (15.546)
One should act according to the conduct prescribed by the scriptures and likewise cultivate association with them;
one may speak of knowledge out of affection, for such a person is not led astray by greed. (15.547)
When he is satisfied, the gods and the ancestors themselves are satisfied;
having crossed over from hell, they immediately go to the great city of Śiva.
"Wherever one eats or stays in a house, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
Knowing this, one should always worship one's own guru during the ancestral śrāddha ceremony. (15.549)
The Guru himself should eat, or he should instruct others to do so for his sake;
however, one who has been initiated [for that specific rite] should perform the ritual independently during the Śrāddha and other such ceremonies. (15.550)
All of that becomes fruitless for him, and he transgresses the samaya;
one should avoid substances offered by followers of the Siddhānta that are fit for Caṇḍī.
One should never utter a word that denotes a *śākinī*;
women are to be honored even if they are deformed, elderly, or subsist by their craft. (15.552)
And courtesans with limbs that are pliant and who act according to their own will [are to be honored];
likewise, it is stated in the Śrī-gama that they should be worshipped with great effort. (15.553)
Devoid of proper conduct, eating all things, and abandoned by both dharma and adharma, they roam at will, gluttonous and lecherous like deities. || 15-554 ||
Prostitutes are to be honored, and their house is like Prayāga; here one should perform the sequence of worship.
Toward women, one should not do anything by which one might feel contempt for them. (15.555)
Therefore, one should not look at them naked, nor with their breasts exposed;
nor should one feel disgust toward the seal (mudrā) of an old woman or one who is deceased.
In that regard, one should not reveal one's transformation, beauty, or secret meeting;
one should worship the form of the deity as the void-body at the triple-path and other such sites.
On all festival days, both general and specific, and especially on the occasion of a gathering with the Guru, there shall be worship, cessation of study, and the avoidance of greed. (15.558)
One should never feel disgust toward intoxicants and other substances of the heroes; rather, one should not disparage them, but should always honor those who partake of them.
There is no fault in giving instruction provided the heart does not harbor resentment;
one should also strive to eliminate the fragments of heterogeneous conceptual constructions. (15.560)

Since the names of the Guru, the scripture, and the goddesses appear within the mantra, they should not be uttered elsewhere than during worship; once invoked, one should then satisfy them with libations.
"If one does not perform the *tarpaṇa* for a mantra that has arrived, it takes away half of one's body; thus the Blessed One has declared. (15.562)

In the venerable Ūrmi[-tantra], one should certainly not publicize the conduct of the goddesses and the heroes, nor should one feel disgust toward it; one should speak [of it] only when one's hands are not empty of the ritual substances (adravya).
The name [of the deity] should be spoken preceded by "Śrī," and likewise that of the Guru with the word "dravyakara.
One must not step over the shadow of the Guru and others, nor should one associate with those who follow non-Vedic paths (tīrthikas).
While engaged in discourse, one should speak of the meaning of one's own scriptures and not merely hint at them;
furthermore, one should perform the special worship that is constant during the occasional ritual.
Even during the middle of that year, and even during the Pavitraka festival,
one whose mantra has not been consecrated should not exist, nor should another scripture be practiced.
For consciousness that has not yet fully developed may waver due to the cultivation of other things, such as houses, utensils, weapons, and the practice of deity-yoga and sacrifice. (15.567)
Thinking them worthy of honor, one should certainly not touch them with one's feet, nor should one step over them;
when the group of preceptors has arrived at the house, one should perform some special act of hospitality.
One should not engage in criticism or the like toward those who have been initiated out of a spirit of malice;
there is no fault in providing instruction, for that is not preceded by malice. (15.569)

One should not associate at all with those who hold lower views, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others; one should not share meals, beds, and so forth with them, nor should one reveal one's own spiritual status to them. (15.570)
It is stated in the Śrīmādhavakula that one should always avoid the Vedic declarations and the Vaiṣṇava declarations of those who abide by other [heterodox] doctrines.

"Being one in essence"—the meaning is that he is motionless because of his focused attention on that very [reality]. The reason for the expanding nature of knowledge is his consciousness (*cit-tva*), which resides everywhere and is situated within the object of knowledge.
This state may arise not only from such instruction, but even from merely conversing with him.
Thus he says: "the story of that," referring to one who has passed away, i.e., is dead. "Therein" means in the seal (*mudrikā*).

"Those devoted to that" refers to those who delight in the substances of the heroes (*vīra-dravya*). "For the sake of instruction" refers to such [teachings] as, "Where is wine, and where is devotion to Śiva? For in this case, the only fruit is the mere satisfaction of the disciple's disposition.
"Within the year" means that whenever the necessary conditions (*sāmagrī*) may arise—this is the intended sense.
"Another scripture" refers to one that contradicts one's own scripture. "Household utensils" refers to things such as stoves and the like.
"By them" means by those [teachings] situated in the Vedas and so forth. The reason for this is as follows:
From association with those of no noble lineage, there is the fear of falling from one's own family;
therefore, one should avoid them in the tradition of the single vessel. (15.572)
If a friendship has been formed through negligence, one should worship the Cakra in a social gathering;
this is stated in the venerable Ūrmi for one who serves other Āgamas. (15.573)
One should never associate with a fool who is devoted to other gurus, who subsists on the property of the deity, who harms those possessed of power, or who is wicked. (15.574)

One should not go to a temple or similar place for initiation and so forth out of mere conceptualization; nor should one perform such acts as a cause for relaxing the established commitments that have been taught. (15.575)
One should not look upon those established in the teaching according to their former caste, nor should one address them as such;
rather, one should interact with all of them solely by means of their non-difference from Śiva. (15.576)
One should sit together with those possessing the six sciences and strive for the illumination of knowledge;
one should not approach an unrefined person, nor should one allow that [knowledge] to become fruitless.
The practice at midnight in a cremation ground should indeed be free from people;
for he who smells the scent of burning flesh and the like is not beloved by the Goddess. (15.578)
Fulfilling the command of the guru, one should renounce everything and become composed of mantra;
[this includes] the study of scriptures, worship, recitation, meditation, discernment, and the services rendered therein. (15.579)
One should never perform any of the three types of action fruitlessly;
one should not engage in debate regarding mantras and tantras, nor should one consume poison.

And in the event of a transgression of the commitments (samaya), one should consult the Guru; if he is absent, one should consult his circle or one's own lineage; and if he too is absent, another. (15.581)

One should diligently practice what has been taught by him without conceptualization, because one’s mind has been made identical with that through the awakening provided by the scriptures and other means. (15.582)
The Guru is indeed Śiva; no untruth shall ever issue from his speech.
Furthermore, one should bow before the Guru for the sake of purifying one's own self as that of Śiva. (15.583)
For the sake of both [the teacher and the disciple], the satisfaction of the teacher bestows fruit upon the child-disciple;
for even the initiate (samayin) possesses awakening, since his sole accomplishment depends entirely upon the guru.
One should recognize the teacher as most venerable through the high esteem for that awakening;
therefore, having attained higher knowledge, he who treats the teacher with outward contempt [is lost].
He does not trust in consciousness, nor is he one who has fallen away from untruth;
his mind is not confident in cognitions, for he is disciplined by the scriptures through mere words. (15.586)
One should never honor with one's heart a devotee who corrupts true knowledge;
such a person should not be made a guru, and even if he has been made one, he should be abandoned. (15.587)
One should not regard as the primary teacher those who belong to the Vaiṣṇava and other such lineages;
likewise, a specific qualification regarding the teacher is stated in the venerable work titled the Ūrmi.
Even when one's life is at stake, the command of the Guru must not be neglected nor questioned;
for the Kaula initiation, the Kaula scripture, and the knowledge of reality have been revealed. (15.589)
By virtue of this, he is called a Guru; indeed, others are merely bearers of the name.
And in the venerable Ānandaśāstra, that same qualification is stated: || 15-590 ||
He from whom one receives initiation, the mantra scriptures, and the knowledge of reality—he indeed is the Guru.
He should remain with unmanifest signs and should never wear any sectarian mark.
One should not engage in social or ritual association with any who merely bear external marks;
those who wear such marks should simply be protected, for they are not to be loathed despite their deformed appearance.
And it is stated in the illustrious Rātrikula that liberation arises from the removal of doubt;
for one whose latent impressions (vāsanā) are impure, even this talk of liberation is difficult to attain. (15.593)
One should not write down the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) proclaimed in the Śrīmanmālā;
rather, one should extract the mantra from its constituent parts, but one should not cause it to be written on a leaf.
One should not, out of partiality, form an attachment to what is unreal—namely, those things arising from birth, learning, family, conduct, body, country, qualities, or wealth. (15.595)
One should quickly abandon the eight *grahas*, as shown in the *Gahvara*, and likewise those indicated as things to be discarded in the *Śrīniśicāra* and other [texts]. (15.596)
"I am a Brahmin; how could I perform anything other than what is prescribed by the Vedas and Shastras?
This obsession with caste is a hindrance to others. (15.597)
In this manner, other [objections] may also be cited by way of the path of the *kulagahvara*.

Regarding the phrase "those"—it refers to those situated in the Vedas and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by means of doubt"—it means through uncertainty. The intention is that one whose mind is free from doubt should indeed proceed according to the method to be described hereafter.
The connection is as follows: one should perceive the previously mentioned castes, characterized by being Brahmins and so forth, as non-different from Śiva, and so on. As it has been said:
"O Goddess, prior to the utterance of caste, a man would be subject to penance."
For three days it belongs to Rudra, and for five days to Keśava.
"He is indeed cooked in hell for one *pakṣa* of the Grandfather [Brahmā]," (Svacchanda Tantra 4.545),
and:
"O Goddess praised by heroes, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras..."

"And those who are appointed to the office of teacher are all remembered as Śivas" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.414). "He should go to" means he should associate with one who is unrefined and has not received initiation. "Born from that" refers to the *kuṇḍa*, *golaka*, and so forth. "He should abandon everything" means so that his command may be observed.

The state [of being]. "He should ask"—[this refers to] expiation (*prāyaścitta*). "Another"—another guru. "Of him"—of his own lineage. "By him"—by another. For in the case of a salutation to Śiva, there is no distinction regarding Śiva himself, but rather regarding the self of the one who salutes; however, in the case of the guru, it is otherwise.
It has been stated that even in the case of one's own refinement (*saṃskāra*), there will certainly be that same joy; thus, it is for the sake of both purposes.
Regarding the phrase "even having done"—it means through negligence. Regarding the phrase "is not conceptualized"—it means [one does not doubt] whether it should be performed or not.
Anticipating the objection, "Why has the description of [the senses] as 'graspers' (grahas) been made with respect to genus (jāti) and so forth?", he says:
"He who, even though not subject to it, displays the nature of that which is not his own essence... (15.598).
That which obscures its own nature is here called a "grasping" (graha), arising like a seizing demon;
he elaborates on this very point:
"In the essential nature of consciousness, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever, such as genus and the like. (15.599)
Any conceptual construction whatsoever regarding the reality of consciousness, which is of an undivided nature, completely obscures that very form by means of a form that is not its own. (15.600)
Everyone who causes contraction should abandon that [state];
this was declared by the Supreme Lord in the Śrīmadānandaśāstra. (15.601)
The Lord Vāma is independent; purity is not the cause therein.
In the sacrifice, the satisfaction of the Goddess comes from blood and flesh, not from the application of ritual purity.
Even rays of light should not be discussed as equal to the twice-born and the outcastes;
for one who causes no transformation [of the mind], hell arises from such conceptual constructions.
It is clearly established that the body within all living beings consists of all the gods;
this has been well-demonstrated by the illustrious Nakuleśa and others as well. (15.604)
The body alone is the sanctuary; one should not go to any other sanctuary.
One should remember a single mantra as the sacred ford and avoid all other sacred fords. (15.605)
Having easily understood this method, one should abandon the web of ritual rules;
for samādhi is not attained by any other means than through resolute determination.
Thinking thus, one who knows the ritual rules should completely abandon delusion;
for apart from the heart of the mantra, there is nothing else supreme anywhere. (15.607)
Thinking thus, one who knows the ritual procedure should abandon the web of mantras;
he should cause the food offering to be consumed by a river and cast its remains into the water.
"There is no fault in eating those aquatic creatures that have been previously initiated.

Now, raising the doubt—"What is the cause for the application of the word *samaya* (observance) here?"—he says: "Because they must necessarily be observed and because of their union with the Supreme Reality. (15.609)
Because they are the means for attaining gnosis, they are proclaimed as the *samayas*.
Having thus caused [the disciple] to hear the *samayas* and having fully worshipped the deity, the instructor—
One should dismiss [the deity] into the tranquil space of one's own consciousness by dissolving its form,
provided that the initiation of a "spiritual son" (putraka) is not to be performed immediately thereafter.
Then one should consecrate that disciple with the Weapon-mantra using the Śiva-vessel, and likewise oneself, because Maheśvara is the embodiment of water. (15.612)

One who is joined with mantra and nourishes all things should perform that consecration (*abhiṣecana*). Its nature consists in being necessarily to be observed, which is established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); and by etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), it is so called because "by means of this, they come together and unite with the supreme reality" (*samayanti saṅgacchante paraṃ tattvam anena*), and because "from this, correct movement [toward the goal], that is, knowledge, arises."

The word *samaya* has been employed—this is the meaning. "It should not be performed" means that there would be no further consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for one who has already completed the task; this is the intended sense.
He concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with the first half-verse:
"Thus has this initiation into the rule been revealed both in detail and in brief. (15.613)
"Extensively"—that is, in terms of meaning. "Concisely"—that is, in terms of the text. May there be auspiciousness! || 613 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation into the Rule" (*samayadīkṣāprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 15.

Having mastered the fivefold expansion of the manifold web of ritual acts consisting of many types such as the permanent (nitya) and occasional (naimittika), he who is known by the name Jayaratha has extensively explained this fifteenth chapter.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Initiation into the Rule" (*samayadīkṣāprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by Śrī Jayaratha. 15.
The Sixteenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
I bow to Balabhadra, who possesses the power to pierce through and sever the entire flow of bonds.
Balabhadra possesses strength filled with skill in the movement of the vital breaths and horses.

Now, immediately following the initiation into the pledges (*samayadīkṣā*), he makes a promise with the second half [of the verse] to describe the forthcoming initiation of the spiritual son (*putrakadīkṣā*): "Next, for the sake of achieving the status of a spiritual son, the procedure prescribed by Śiva is described here. He states that very procedure:
But when the instructor desires to appoint one who abides by the observance to the status of a spiritual son, or to the status of a teacher, or to the status of a practitioner; (16.1)
Having performed the consecration (adhivāsa) on that day, one should draw the mandala on the second day;
this applies both to the communal sacrifice (sāmudāyika-yāga) and elsewhere, as previously described.
He defines the collective sacrifice itself:
"In the scripture known as the Śrīpūrva, a pentad of wheels is taught, numbering six, eight, twice that [sixteen], and twenty-four. (16.3)
In the venerable *Traiśirasa* doctrine, that [number] is doubled to thirty-two;
however, in the *Śrīsiddhā* and other scriptures, the connection with innumerable wheels (*cakra*) has been described. (16.4)
And in both these cases, it is appropriate that the mandala be precisely a trident-lotus; thus he says:

"Therefore, in whatever manner the sacrifice is performed, as long as it is commensurate with the wheel (cakra), one should worship with that [mandala], and herein one should draw three tridents. (16.5)

On the three tridents, the triad of goddesses is worshipped through their successive manifestations; by means of the distinction between the middle, the right, and the other [left], they become fully worshipped. (16.6)
The procedure for the mandala will be taught briefly hereafter:
having drawn the mandala, its cleansing is performed with a fragrant cloth. (16.7)
Having bathed, the Guru, as before, should worship the deities located outside at the front of the maṇḍala,
and the deities of the gateway at the entrance.
In the front part of the mandala, one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others, ending with Kṣetrapāla, in sequence starting from the northeast (īśāna) direction and proceeding to the southeast (āgneyī).
Gaṇapati, Guru, Parama, Parameṣṭhin, Pūrvasiddha, Vāk, and Kṣetrapati—this group of seven is declared by our gurus to be worshipped in the ritual of the lineage of gurus (gurupaṅkti). || 16-10 ||
Then, having received the command, one should thoroughly worship [the deity] with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
beginning from the base of the trident up to the foundational power (ādhāraśakti).

"At the end of Śiva" means at the end of the white lotus, upon the three tridents in succession; "by way of rotation" means in order. "In the front" refers to the thirty-first chapter. "The external deities" refers to the outer retinue. "Previously established" refers to the one who introduced this system of philosophy.
The former has a severed lineage, whereas the latter— the specific, contemporary lineage of gurus established in the particular scriptures—
is not to be worshiped in external worship; this is what is indicated by this [statement].
Alternatively, when the specific lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*) is being worshipped, one should worship this [deity] and others as well. "Speech" (*vāk*) refers to Vāgīśvarī.
In this very context, in order to show the abiding of the triad of goddesses together with Bhairava through the relationship of subordinate and principal, he says:
"In the central spike, Sadbhāva, situated in the center, should be with Parā. (16.12)
On the left, together with Aparā, is Navātmā; on the right is Para. On the trident, Ratiśekhara resides at the middle prong.
In the right [hand], Bhairava is together with Parāparā;
in the left, the Trident; and the Navātman stands in the middle together with Aparā. (16.14)
Bhairava may be with the Supreme (Parā) on the right spoke, and he may also be on the left spoke.

"Vāma" (left) is relative to the center. "Param" (the supreme) refers to the remaining [aspect], characterized as both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara), namely Ratiśekhara. "Dakṣiṇa" (right) is relative to the practitioner (sādhaka). "Dakṣa" (dexterous/skillful)...

Thus—in that very same [text], specifically in the remaining spoke on the left (*vāmāra*). "On the left" (*vāma*) is said with reference to the practitioner (*sādhaka*). "The supreme" (*para*) refers to Bhairava, who resides in the other remaining spoke on the left.

The word "iti" means "and Sadbhāvabhairava. The particle "ca" (and) is used with reference to what precedes it. Furthermore, for those [mantras] where there is "śya," followed by "para" together with "parā," and "saṃ" on the left spoke, [there is] Bhairava.
There is no "half-iti" (ityardha); one should apply [the formula] to them as "Bhairava is before and Satpara is to the right.

As for [the statement], "Ratiśekhara is on the left spoke together with Parāparā," this should indeed be disregarded because its meaning has already been established. Thus, regarding Parā in the central trident:
Primacy belongs to Parāparā on the right and Aparā on the left; as for the other two goddesses, they exist everywhere on both sides as subordinate members (aṅga).
Even so, Parā alone has a direct presence within all three tridents, whereas the other two—
Because it is not [present] in such a way through a state of being conjoined— as distinguished from other things— it is by virtue of its primacy that she alone possesses omnipresence.
For this very reason, he says:
"Thus, while the all-pervasiveness of the venerable Goddess Parā is established... (16.15).
The sacrifice becomes perfectly complete through that alone being presided over;
therefore, even in a sacrifice with a single trident, one should contemplate it as being presided over by that.
"One who does not know the rule is [yet] one who knows the rule"—thus it is stated in the *Triśika*.
Therefore, [it applies] everywhere: in the center, as well as on the right, the left, and the peak. (16–17)
One should worship [the deities] from the World-Guardians (lokapālas) up to the Weapons (astras) as a single essence,
and one should worship all the deities as being supreme.
Then, by means of the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga), [one worships] the glorious Mātṛsadbhāva-bhaṭṭāraka, who is free from ailment, as well as the eight Bhairavas who are limbs of the Vidyā.
One should worship the Yāmala and the goddesses of the wheels in their respective places on the outside,
as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons, using perfumes, flowers, wine, and other offerings.
One should worship with supreme devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth;
then [one worships] the pitcher, the weapon-pitcher, the mandala, the locus, and the self. (16–21)
One should effect the connection of the five through the meditation on non-duality;
however, those who do not find that non-dual pervasion which is of the nature of Śiva— || 16-22 ||
"By means of the application of the mantra-nāḍī, they enter the non-dual path.
"Well-filled" (susaṃpūrṇa)—because this [nāḍī] has filling as its primary characteristic. "Therefore"—because the sacrifice attains completion merely through that presiding presence.
And the *Triśikā-brāhmaṇa* has been explained many times before.

"In its own place" means in the form of Agni, Īśa, and so forth. "From that" means immediately after the worship of the maṇḍala. "From the contemplation of non-duality" means from the realization in the form:
"I alone am situated everywhere. "They do not find" means—
Thus, because there is no arising of the reflective awareness of non-duality.
He describes that very application of the mantra-channel:
"Having emerged from one's own right side, [it enters] from the left of the one situated in the mandala. (16.23)
Having entered by one [door] and exited by another, [the breath moves] into the pitcher (kumbha), into the small jar (karkarī),
and into the fire (vahni) in this sequence, until it reaches its own [position] from its own left.

When the thread of the vital breath is woven together through the power of tracing back to the root, the light of pervasive consciousness shines forth as the self-manifestation of this oneness. (16.25)
Then one should perform a special worship characterized by non-duality.
"By another" means by the right hand. "In this manner" means by the method already described, characterized by exiting and entering through the right and left [nostrils]. "To one's own left" means—

That is to say, one should enter [the state] when the threads of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) have been joined—meaning, when there is a merging of the vital breaths of one's own mandala and others with one another. For otherwise, how could this practice, whose essence is the flashing forth of unity, be accomplished? This is the meaning.

Now, one might ask: "In this case as well, what is the meaning of 'being non-dual'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For that which is sprinkled with the nectar of the non-duality of Śiva is indeed supreme. (16.26)

Therefore, that vision of non-duality with Śiva which arises regarding the water for the guest-offering (argha), flowers, perfumes, and so forth, as well as the wine and the sacrificial animal—that is purification; it is the act of making [the object] supreme. || 16-27 ||
Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be such a transformation into the Supreme (paramīkṛti) because the water for honor (argha), flowers, and so forth are employed in worship;

but what is the purpose of this for the bound souls (paśus)?"—incorporating this doubt, [the author] proceeds immediately after the contemplation of identity with the mandala to describe the offering of the bound souls.

To explain the extent [of the offering], he says: "One should present before the Lord living beings and the elements derived from them—whether perfected, unperfected, or mixed—or whatever else exists among the moving and the immobile. (16.28)

"Jīvas" means living beings, namely animals. "Siddhān" means cooked [offerings]. It is not only the animal and such that are to be offered here as the "moving" (cara), but even the "non-moving" (acara) as well; thus he says: "or whatever moving and non-moving. By the plural number in "jīvān," he expresses the multiplicity of animals implied by the term "living beings."

The sacrificial animal (paśu) is of eight types: the seen, the sprinkled, the one watched over, the seized, the appropriated, the joined, the offered, and the hero; each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
One should never give [this] to those who are unworthy, as it becomes progressively more sublime; for not everyone is fit to consume the sacrificial offering dedicated to Śiva.
"Successively superior" (uttarattottama) means that it is increasingly more excellent as one proceeds further. ||30||
Now, one might object: "What is the greatness of this sacrificial offering (havis) such that it was said that no one at all is permitted to consume it?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But he who, even though devoid of initiation, is impelled by the ordinance of Śiva’s will..."
He who eats with devotion becomes complete; such a person is a well-cultivated initiate (samayin). || 16-31 ||
"The cause for eating with devotion is being impelled by the injunction of Śiva’s will. As it has been said:
"It is only through His grace that devotion arises in men. Therefore, the implication is that if one eats out of greed or similar motives, there would be a transgression. || 31 ||
This very group of eight sacrificial animals (paśvaṣṭaka) is defined according to their respective designations:

"The *dṛṣṭa* (seen) and the *avalokita* (beheld) [are so called] because of the casting of a gaze kindled by rays; the *prokṣita* (sprinkled) is indeed merely sprinkled with droplets from the vessel of honorific water (*arghapātra*). (16.32)

One who has beheld [the deity], who has been shown the entire mandala and performed the proper worship, who has received the initiations and been consecrated by the three aforementioned [rites]—he too should shake [the vessel]. (16.33)
It may tremble, flow, become rigid, or dissolve, each succeeding state being more severe than the last;
thus it is seized when the sacrifice is imminent and pacified by the winds of the ritual instruments.

He is joined [to the supreme state] through the process of abandoning causal factors by means of union with Śiva; he is extinguished [of worldly existence] through the offering of his life-force and mind to the Guru, having performed the necessary practice.
"By means of the right [hand] through the dissolution of the network of the lunar digits into the fire.

"Kevalam" (alone) means by way of avoiding the gaze. "Refined by the aforementioned triad" means refined by the aforementioned triad characterized by gazing, sprinkling, and the vision of the maṇḍala.

The meaning is "one who has undergone the purificatory rites" (*kṛtasaṃskāraḥ*). Regarding the observation "in ascending order": there is shaking during sprinkling (*dhūnana*), trembling during the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and flowing during the visualization of the mandala (*maṇḍaladarśana*). Alternatively, the meaning is that one should become motionless, with all functions of the senses dissolved through the degrees of intensity (*taratamabhāva*). In the phrase "by the winds of the weapons" (*śastramārutaiḥ*): [the rest of the commentary follows].

The examination by means of the vital air (*māruta*) is for the purpose of demonstrating its forceful movement. And by relying on the dissolution of the network of parts belonging to the animal-like *apāna* aspect of the self— which is lunar and consists of the fire of breath— the teacher, having practiced the conquest of the vital breath and mind through the right [nostril], [proceeds].

The meaning is as follows: because of the offering of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*), through the state of unification with the animal-like breath and so forth, the "animal" (*paśu*) that was previously presented is said to be "extinguished" (*nirvāpita*) by means of making it seedless (*nirbījīkaraṇa*).
He elaborates on this very point:
"For in this way, at the outset, one should take recourse in the supreme form through the state of unification. (16.36)
Therefore, one should enter the garland of flames by means of the movement of fire;
with the left [hand] of the sacrificial animal, one should melt the mass of moonbeams with heat.
Then one should rest in the navel-cakra along with the multitude of the rays of the vital breath;
having become supreme by means of one's own power, one should envelop the individual soul (jīva) here with the life-force (jīva).
Having heated it with the sun of one's own consciousness, one should melt away each and every part (kalā);
then, having brought that melted web of parts to a state of unity within the Self.
One should, with fervor, uproot from the very depths this [individual] who is bound by karma, even though he is filled with all the principles (tattvas) and performs the rite of nourishment.
Then, by means of the yoga of uprooting and unwinding, moving around to the left,
one should employ one's own vital breath, filled with the nectar of Kuṇḍalinī.
Having assumed the form of the filaments of nectar within the heart-lotus through the process of counter-clockwise rotation, [the breath],
by attaining ascent upon the pericarp of the heart, liquefies the element of vitality (ojodhātu).

Having taken the essence consisting of pure moonlight, slightly reddish-yellow in color, into the body of the vital breath which resembles the tip of an elephant's trunk, [one should place it] within the form of the life-force. (16.43)
Having emerged, one should instantly enter by way of the left channel of one's own self,
nourishing [the breath] within the heart-lotus of the lunar wheel known as apāna.
One should satisfy that circle of deities situated there with that essence.
Here, first of all, having resorted to the form of the other [the victim]— since the capacity for restraint and so forth within one's own self would otherwise be inexplicable—
one emerges from one's own right side emitting flames of fire, enters through the left side of the victim, and...

Having melted that mass of digits (kalājāla) connected with the lunar apāna by the heat of one’s own prāṇa-fire, and remaining established in one's own support within that very navel-center by encompassing all the vital breaths,
one envelops that individual soul (jīva) with one's own life-force through the heat of the fire of one's own consciousness by means of one's own majesty.
Having dissolved that web of time (tat-kalājāla) by bringing it to a state of unity within oneself through its power of nourishing one’s own perfectly full form,
and having uprooted it with earnest zeal by means of the process of unwinding from the bondage of karma, he revolves counter-clockwise.

The teacher, having reached the region of the nectar-filled pericarp of the heart-lotus, and thus having his own vital breath-bellows filled with the nectar of the *kanda-kundalinī*, abides in a state of sprouting right within the pericarp of the heart; it is slightly reddish-yellow, and for that very reason, it consists of pure *soma*.

Having drawn up the essence characterized by the *ojas* constituent, which had been liquefied by the fire of one's own vital breath (*prāṇa*), by means of that *prāṇa* resembling the tip of an elephant’s trunk— crooked and curled— and having quickly exited through the right [nostril] and entered through one's own left;

Thus, nourishing one's own self with that essence thus gathered, one should satisfy the circle of deities residing in the heart-lotus; the meaning is that one should bring them into a state of singular, equal flavor (ekasamarasa).
He does not merely extract the element of vitality (ojodhātu) in this way, but also others; thus he says:
"By this method, likewise all [elements], such as the essence (rasa), blood (rakta), and so forth. (16.45)
One should collect the relics either individually according to the order of the Saṅgha, or else [collect] only those situated in the midst of the conjunction of fire, moon, and sun. (16.46)
Then one should extract the living soul (*jīva*), which is of the nature of light and is called the power of *prāṇa*,
as being situated in the midst of the union of fire,
moon, and sun— that is, seated in the center of the heart-lotus, which consists of the union of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *udāna*.
This is the meaning.
One might ask: "What indeed should one do with these [elements] thus gathered? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One should bring the individual soul (jīva) to a state of equal flavor (samarasīkuryāt) with the wheel of goddesses through meditative contemplation. (16.47)
That alone is the primary libation; it is indeed the identity of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
Now, one might ask: "Should this be performed with mantras or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Great One consists of the fire-enclosed blossoming syllable, the triangle, and Time. (16.48)
The *piṇḍa* (syllabic cluster) is used for the movement, attraction, and so forth of the stream of the essence of blood and other fluids.
*Agni* is the letter *ra*; *phullārṇa* is the letter *pha*; *tryaśra* is the letter *e*; and *kāla* is the letter *ma*.
Thus, [the syllable] is *phreṃ*. As it has been said:
"Krodha (the letter K), situated within the fire-enclosure (the letter R) and differentiated by the triangle (the vowel I) and time (the bindu),
is considered this 'knife' (kṣurikā) for the extraction of the mass of blood and other fluids.
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might ask: "In what length of time or by how much recitation will this be accomplished? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this manner, through the yoga of repose, when half a ghaṭikā has elapsed... (16.49).
Through the application of a hundred repetitions, the immolation of the animal occurs. And in this matter, practice at the preliminary stage (prākkoṭi) is to be undertaken; thus he says:
"Having practiced there for some time with undistracted mind... (16.50).
Just as it is stated regarding the *cintāmaṇi*, the knower of yoga, free from doubt, attains accomplishment in that very form; this must clearly be kept secret like one's own life. (16.51)

"In the *Cintāmaṇi*" means in the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*. "By him" means by one who has performed the practice. "Fearless" refers to what was said: "One attains perfection when fearless; therefore, one should avoid doubt in this matter."
"For one who possesses a mind of false compassion is indeed not a hero and perishes.
As for the phrase "it is to be concealed"—it is because it is contrary to worldly norms. ||51||
He extends this very rule to the initiation of one who is absent:
"Even in the case of an animal [representing an absent person], this procedure should apply toward its unification [with the deity].
Once it has been brought into the sacrificial ground, killed right there, and consecrated... (52).
And one who is favored by the Wheel (cakra) in that very place is called a "heroic sacrificial animal" (vīrapaśu).
"In that very place" means on the sacrificial ground (yāgabhuvi); "favored" (juṣṭaḥ) means enjoyed (upabhuktaḥ).

Now, one might object: "Even if an animal is killed in battle, on the marketplace, or elsewhere, it may still be offered in sacrifices and the like; so how is it that only eight types [of victims] have been mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But that which is slain elsewhere, either in its entirety or even in part... (16.53)
He who would offer [the victim] to the God is indeed considered an external animal (paśu).
In this very context, he indicates the fruit [of the practice] in sequence: sovereignty, gain, then stability therein, devotion to Śiva, and finally identity with Him. (16.54)

The knowledge of Śiva, the attainment of the world of mantras, membership in its retinue, and union with it [are attained] by the bound soul (paśu) through similarity to the external and other [levels] of the hero's dharma. (16.55)
Even flowers and other such offerings partake in that gain through the worship of Śiva.

"Gain" refers to [the attainment of] the earth and so forth. "Being in its retinue" means proximity to it. Thus, for the external animal (paśu), there is sovereignty; for the beloved one, there is gain; and up to the heroic animal (vīrapaśu), there is union with the mantra.

Now, one might object: "In that case, why should even non-moving and moving beings, such as animals, flowers, and so forth, partake in the attainment of that [liberation] through the worship of Śiva? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By a single means, the Lord of Gods, whose nature is the universal bestowal of grace... (16.56)
There is nothing, whether moving or unmoving, that is not favored by sacrifice;
therefore, it should not be imagined that acts such as the slaughter of animals and bloodshed are violent. Thus he says:
"Therefore, even one who is not a hero, even one possessed of doubt and the like, and even one who is compassionate... (16.57).
One should never entertain a mind of violence regarding the ritual involving animals.

For that reason— by virtue of the inclusion of animals and so forth— an Ācārya who is either a non-hero (avīra), one possessed of conceptual thought (savikalpa), or even one who is compassionate, should never at any time engage in the ritual involving animals during a sacrifice or similar rite, due to the presence of doubt and other such factors.
One should not entertain the notion that this is violence; one should not conceive of it in such a way—this is the meaning.
For indeed, because it is prescribed by injunction, this cannot be considered violence. As they say:
"The violence toward the animal in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is not truly violence."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, outside of sacrifice, this is indeed violence because it is prohibited. As the scripture states:
"One who knows the ritual injunctions, O fortunate one, should never kill an animal by force, nor when there is no state of affliction, nor with a specific motive prior to a sacrifice."
Thus:
"O Great Goddess, one should never kill an animal for the sake of marriage, nor ever for one's own sake; [only] at the time of sacrifice, O Great Goddess, or upon meeting with beloved kinsmen."
O fair-faced one, one should not kill an animal for the sake of sport except during a sacrifice;
for he who offers it at the time of sacrifice does so for the gratification of the Mothers.
But when each one is given once according to the previously mentioned procedure,
it is equal to ten million times a thousand recitations and ten thousand times a hundred worship offerings.
"One would obtain that fruit immediately once the animal sacrifice has been performed. And also from the Smṛti:
"As many hairs as there are on the animal's body, so many times does one undergo death."
"One who slaughters animals in vain attains [this state] after death, birth after birth. (Manu 4.38) Thus it is said.

Now, one might object: "Granted that this is so, nevertheless, is this initial 'slaying' of the bound soul (paśu) not a great misfortune? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This is a great benefit for the bound soul; though it may seem unpleasant at the time, [it is for his ultimate good]. (16.58)

The illustration here is the application of medicine for the removal of disease through austerity; even though it is unpleasant for the victim at that moment, this great act of assistance, characterized by compassion, consists of such things as killing, wherein the removal of disease and so forth serve as the illustration. Medicine—

Alkaline substances and the like, as well as ascetic practices such as the *kṛcchra* penance. As the scripture states: "O fair-faced one, for the sake of favoring those bound souls (*paśu*), they indeed liberate them from sins and sever those floods of fetters."
"For those animals that have been utilized, there shall always be an upward movement" (Neṭa. 20.9).
The Śruti also says:
"The animal, indeed, while being led away, beheld death; he did not desire the gods in this manner..."
The gods said to him, "Come; we shall cause you to go to the heavenly world."
Now, one might raise the objection: "If liberation occurs simply through killing, then what is the purpose of initiation (dīkṣā) and the like?
To pacify this doubt, he corroborates [the view] with scripture:
"In the venerable *Mṛtyuñjaya*, it is stated that once the fetters of the bound soul (paśu) have been severed... (16.59).
Through the separation from the three impurities, the body does not grow;
indeed, through the severance of the flood of merit and demerit, the body falls away.
Therefore, this is not called "killing"; rather, this initiation is of a manifold nature.
For that which is the separation from the vital breaths of one whose fetters have taken root is indeed what constitutes "killing."
But this very application [of the sacrifice] serves for the propitiation of the deity by means of the sacrificial animal;
[it is performed] with the flood of dharma and adharma belonging to that which constitutes the body. As it is said there:
"By cutting the root, they indeed seek to destroy the three impurities (malas) of the bound soul (paśu)."
For one who is free from the three impurities, the body does not sprout again.
For that bound soul (paśu), there is no slaughter at all, as in the case of initiation;
rather, [he is liberated] by means of the pervasive essential nature and the power of his own inherent energy.
They sever the fetters of the beast by which the body perishes;
when the body is destroyed, there is liberation, not death.
"The wise know that death is the separation from the body of a person who has been bound by a firmly rooted noose. (Netratantra 20).
He concludes this very point as follows:
Therefore, relying on the word of the Lord, one should offer many animals. ||62||
Thus,
relying on the statement of the Lord beginning with, "...and one should sprinkle many sacrificial animals (paśu)," one should offer many sacrificial animals of nine kinds.
One should offer it—thus it is established. || 62 ||

Now, one might object: based on such statements as, "He may arise as one-born, two-born, or seven-born," it follows that even through differences in birth, animals possess superior and other forms; this being so, [what is the point here]?
Anticipating the question, "Why was this not stated [before]? he says:
"He who has been offered [as a victim], and having regained his body, is offered again—thus six times; such an animal is here considered the best of the six-fold birth. (16.63)

"Offered" (nivedita) means that, by means of the consecration of the respective mantra, one has attained identity with the supreme reality—this is the meaning. "Having regained a body" is said because [otherwise] a physical form could not possibly be produced in any way whatsoever. ||63||
He confirms its very supremacy by means of an illustrative example: "Just as gold is purified through the process of smelting, so too is he [the practitioner] proclaimed to be;
what accomplishment would he not bestow, or how could he himself not be liberated? (6.64)
For this very reason, it possesses the supreme quality of benefiting both oneself and others—as he says: "What accomplishment... and so forth (verse 64).
He corroborates this very point with scripture:
"It is stated in the *Ānandaśāstra* that one who possesses the purification of mantra (*mantrasaṃskāra*) should abandon [worldly life]..."
One should not disparage the pledges or the goddesses, nor should one give mantras without following the proper method.
Having received initiation, mantras, and so forth, one deluded by attachment to sons and other worldly ties may abandon them;
then, having attained human birth once more, one acts in this very same way again. (16.66)
In this way, having undergone one to seven births, this animal— of two kinds and either biped or quadruped— is born for the sake of the Goddess’s sacrificial offering (caruka).
Offered by the giver, he goes through that medium to Śiva in a state of union (sāyujya).
"In this way" means [by avoiding] the abandonment of the rules (samaya) and so forth. "Through that medium" means by the channel of offering to the giver—this is the meaning.
Thus, since his very origin is for the sake of the Goddess’s sacrificial pap (caru), he must not be employed elsewhere.
Thus he said:
"Having thus considered that wondrous activity of bound souls (paśu). (16.68)
"One should not perform that which is intended to be enjoyed [by others], except for that sacrificial animal.
Regarding the phrase "intended to be enjoyed": it means that which is desired to be consumed by the goddesses at the beginning of a sacrifice.
"Except for that" means except for the sacrifice itself.

Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so regarding an animal fit for sacrifice; however, an unfit animal, even if brought forward, should be removed from there and employed elsewhere according to one's own will.
Therefore, this rule—that one should not divert an animal intended for consumption to another purpose—does not apply. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Nor should one dismiss him after realizing that he is not fit [for the teaching]. || 16-69 ||
One should offer that animal; however, if there is a desire for a specific one, then that particular one should be presented.
Here, one should not give a neuter animal, nor indeed one with emaciated limbs.
"O Bhairavī, [one should not sacrifice] one who is too old, nor one who is too young, nor a woman, nor a beast"—

having understood that a beast of such a nature as described in these and other passages is unfit for sacrifice, one should nevertheless not remove that beast from the sacrifice already commenced; on the contrary, [one should proceed].

"If there is a desire for specific details regarding what has been stated— namely, 'A horned animal, young, with complete limbs, of a single color, and with a beautiful face; likewise, a buffalo, goat, or sheep— these three types [are required] for the success of the sacrifice'— then one should offer that particular animal endowed with those qualities."

By this, the fulfillment of one's desire would be achieved; thus it would have been said that as many animals as have been offered in the sacrifice must be given away, and not only those that are suitable.
Therefore he says:
"One should offer that many such sacrificial animals (paśu); thus it has been stated by the Great Lord. (16.70)
"Up to that extent"—meaning, until the fulfillment of the desire for specific details.
Having thus described the specific characteristics of the sacrificial animal (paśu) in their entirety, he now describes them even in part:

"When the omentum (vapā) and the fat (medas) of the animal have been melted in the midst of the fire, one should offer them to the Wheel of Power (śakticakra); this is considered the supreme libation. (16.71)
One should offer as the primary oblation the heart, intestines, head, shoulders, and liver;
or alternatively, the pericardium, the spinal cord, the marrow, and the ribs as the most excellent offering.
Then the instructor should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) into the fire for the circle of mantras;
having offered that to the deity, he should then address a petition to the Lord.
One should offer the liver as the primary black meat. The *karṇikā* is the *liṅgikā*;
the *kuṇḍalī* is the supreme *maṇḍalikā*. The marrow is the fat of the bones; the *parśavaḥ* are the channels of the ribs.
"Satisfying" (*tarpaṇa*) is as explained previously. (73)
"What should he request?"—to this he says:
"O Supreme Lord, I have been recognized by You Yourself as Your Guru, whether through direct instruction, dreams, and so forth, through recitations, or through the mouth of a teacher. (16.74)
"Disciples impelled by the power of Śiva are to be favored by you;
therefore, these who are of such a nature have arrived, and you should bestow grace upon them. (16.75)
"Absorb me with the rays of your own self, so that I may become Śiva.
