Then one should welcome the word of Śiva with the response, "So be it. (16.76)
Then, one should meditate upon the Self as non-different from Śiva, performing the fivefold cosmic acts;
and, out of a desire to bestow grace, one should contemplate the mantras as the instruments of one's own self and as His very form. (16.77)
Then, having bound the white turban, one should worship the two hands in sequence for the purpose of burning away the mutual bonds and for the release of the pure principles (tattvas).
One should worship the mantras in the form of radiant energy within the hand of Śiva,
excluding those belonging to the inner enclosure, the limbs, the retinue, and the seats.
Thereafter, one should contemplate oneself as solitary, like the moon reflected in water;
though appearing divided into sixfold due to the influence of functional adjuncts, it is in reality undivided.

The word *atha* means "immediately after obtaining that command. By this, he has also begun the illumination of his own nature (*svabhāva*), which was indicated immediately after the satisfaction of the fire (*agnitṛpti*). [He does so] by means of the mantras, both in their gross and subtle forms.

The connection is that one should meditate upon the form whose nature is both supreme and non-supreme. "With a white turban" means it has been consecrated seven times by the *navātman* mantra. "Mutually" means the right [hand] with the left, and the left with the right—this is the meaning.
It is stated "in the form of light" in order to reinforce its very capacity to burn away the fetters (*pāśa*).
Regarding the phrase "those situated in the womb-enclosure"—the meaning is those whose forms consist of the root mantra and its [five] faces. As it has been said:
"The auspicious Śivahasta (Hand of Śiva), conjoined with the five Brahmans and presided over by Śiva, severs the bonds and bestows security; thus it is proclaimed."

Thus: "single" (ekaka) means "without companion," because it does not depend on anything else. "Like the moon in water"—just as in reality there is only one moon, yet it appears as many due to the diversity of limiting conditions (upādhi) such as various receptacles of water, so too is this [Self]—this is the meaning. ||80||
In order to demonstrate that this [reality] is indeed divided sixfold, he explains the scriptural text that establishes it according to its essential purport:
"I myself am he who resides in the mandala and am the witness of all actions."
For the pure state of being the Seer has been conceived by me within the maṇḍala of Śambhu.
I abide in the fire as the locus of the oblation,
so that the mantras, ignited by my own nature, may be fully capable of burning away the fetters.

That it is indeed pure witnesshood has been determined by the passage beginning with "pure" (*śuddhā*). "Pure" means not mixed with agency (*kartṛtva*). "When [the mind] is ignited" means that its radiance has burst forth by virtue of the immersion (*āveśa*) into the Supreme Lord, who has assumed the form of fire. ||82||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is their power to burn away the fetters? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"The Lords of the Worlds, summoned from within the form of the universal light, and having been gratified and informed [of the disciple's state], do not exercise authority over the individual soul (aṇu). (16.83)
Until the end of the sacrifice, I remain stationed within the jar for the pacification of obstacles,
so that my state of generality may bring about the nourishment of the particular.
And within the body of the disciple, for the purpose of establishing the loosening of those bonds, he indeed exists as if shaking off the bonds by the power of his own will. (16.85)
Dwelling directly within my own body, I am the agent of acts of grace;
because of my sovereignty over knowledge and action, I am skilled in the rite of initiation.

"Having the form of a common light" means that they have attained identity with the mantra, whose nature is the splendor of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara) and which internalizes the three abodes (dhāman).
"And [the rites] such as invocation" refers to what will be explained later. "Authority" refers to [one's power] over one's own world and so forth.

The connection [is as follows]: "the jar"—meaning also the water-jar (*karkarī*), for otherwise its sixfold division would not exist. For it has been stated here that, by abiding as the very nature of the pacification of obstacles, it protects all specific ritual actions; this is its state as a universal form (*sāmānyarūpatā*).

"Causing the nourishment of excellence. Regarding "by the power of his own will": it has been stated many times previously that he does not depend on anything such as the ripening of impurity (*mala*). "Peśala" means capable.
Now, one might object: "How can this be so even when there is limitation due to the connection with a body and so forth?"—anticipating this doubt:
He provides an illustration:
"Just as I am clearly one who possesses the synthesis of the multitude of effects, forms, and the circle of senses, so too am I manifestly sixfold in nature, such as fire and the rest. (16.87)
Having reflected thus, he should worship that path along which he intends to perform the initiation;
for the sake of mental unification, he should sacrifice in the five [elements], with the exception of the disciple. (16.88)

For just as I am indeed one, yet [perform] various activities and possess various specific forms— according to the statement, "The senses, with the mind as the sixth... (Bhagavad Gītā 15.7)— I who am the very same one that sees among the group of six senses, I am that very same one.

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: by virtue of possessing the continuity of thought "I hear," I exist in six ways as the witness and so forth, witnessed by all people; this applies likewise to the mandala, the fire, and other such [elements].
"By which" means by any one of the categories beginning with the *tattvas* and *kalās*. (88)
One might ask: "What would be gained by this synthesis? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"And at the conclusion of the power of synthesis, one should make [the practice] thoroughly mastered—whether by way of concise or detailed exposition—and filled with the internal inclusion of the other. (16.89)

"From that [state] as well, one should further investigate through reflection the nature of Śiva, until it is absolute. The intention is that in this way, action will indeed be accomplished without fail.
"One should investigate"—this implies, by implication, within oneself alone. While explaining this very scriptural text:
He elaborates:
"I alone am the supreme reality, and that [reality] is not like a jar, existing anywhere [as a separate object]. (16.90)
Therefore, this entire universe exists within me as a great light;
yet that [light] is not deposited by anything else, like an external reflection.
"I am the agent of this [world]; it is not dependent on another, and it is presided over by me.
Thus purified by the realization of such a great pervasiveness, [one attains liberation]. (16.92)

A living being who has attained equality with Me is said to be liberated. "That" [refers to liberation] because, unlike a jar, there is an absence of any fixed, limited form. "By that"—the sense is that in a state of fullness, which is the nature of the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), the existence of everything indeed becomes manifest. "That" [refers to this state].
Because it is not projected by any external object, for this very reason it is not dependent on anything else;
since it is presided over by me, it rests in me alone—this is the meaning. As the scripture says:
"I am established as the presider and the agent of everything."
Thus, the reason for attaining equality with Me is as follows: it is with this very intention that [it is said]— "Liberation, indeed, is nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature;
and the true nature of the Self is consciousness, and nothing else... (Tantrāloka 1.156).
This and more has been stated previously. Now, one might ask: "What would come of such repeated contemplation?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Through the succession of heating, rubbing, sprinkling, and so forth, [the gold] attains the state of fire. (16.93)
Just as an iron ball attains the nature of fire, so too does the Guru attain the state of Śiva;
thereafter, [he may be seen] either standing before one or with a form manifested before one's eyes.
Alternatively, when initiation is performed in the absence [of the disciple], or when the disciple has died and is represented by darbha grass and other materials,
one should visualize and worship him with flowers and so forth, and then project that path of his [onto the disciple].
"By whichever path the teacher primarily desires initiation"—[the phrase] "standing before him" means in direct vision; "out of sight" means by virtue of being in another location;
"dead" means when death has occurred—this is the meaning. He demonstrates this very primacy:
Having deposited that [mantra] in the body, the established rule is that anything else should be internalized therein.
And by this, the procedure for the ritual placement of the paths (adhvanyāsa) within the body of the disciple has been described. || 96 ||

Now, however, he describes the variety of the objects to be purified (*śodhya*) and the purifiers (*śodhaka*): "When the path to be purified has been projected, one should project the purifier right there—namely, the mantra as desired—in accordance with the suitability of that which is to be purified. (16.97)

In some cases, even without performing the placement of the object to be purified (śodhya), the object to be purified becomes pure by itself through the mere placement of the purifier (śodhaka), by the power of the purifier. || 16.98 ||

"According to one's desire" means according to the wish of either the teacher or the disciple. "In accordance with the suitability of what is to be purified" means following the fitness of the object to be purified, as stated in such passages as: "One should join the group of eight beginning with Pibanī above Īśvara" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.73). "By its power" means—
As it has been said:
"The power of mantra is indeed inconceivable, having issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.151). ||98||

In that regard, in order to describe first the variety of that which is to be purified, he says: "By the will [of the practitioner], one resorts to the lower, the intermediate, and the higher ritual procedure; according to the application of those, the deposition (nyāsa) of the six paths is performed. (16.99)
Regarding the phrase "tadyojanā" (the application of that): by the word "that" (tat), there is a reference to the procedure beginning with the "lower" (aparā) level. ||99||
And how is the casting off of this body? He says:

"To the end of the forehead, at the Vedas (4) and Vasus (8); to the end of the apertures, at the Rasas (6) and apertures (9); and to the Dvādaśānta, at the Vasus (8), Indu (1), and [the end of the twelve]. This is the threefold procedure. (16.100)
It is described in sequence as it is seen in the scripture known as the *Śrīpūrva*:
"vedavasau" means eighty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); "rasarandhrake" means ninety-six;
and "vasukendau" means one hundred and eight.
He states that very commencement of the principles (tattvas):
"In that regard, among the principles, the placement [of the feet] is four finger-breadths at the end of the ankles. (16.101)

From the earth element up to the root of the water element, each is two finger-breadths (aṅgula) in sequence; from the navel upwards, it is six finger-breadths, consisting of six and four finger-breadths respectively. Thus, [the total is] six finger-breadths. (16.102)
For a male, one should project six principles up to the end of the *kalā*, each occupying three finger-breadths;
thus, it extends for eighteen finger-breadths, ending at the hollow of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*).
The fourfold group beginning with Māyā and ending with Sadāśiva occupies four finger-breadths each; thus, from the region of the Ālikātattva, they number forty-eight.
After that, one should contemplate the Śiva-principle, which is of the nature of radiant energy and undisturbed,
pervading all things both externally and internally.
From the water up to the end of the root, which measures two and a half cubits plus three finger-breadths, there is an excess of twelve finger-breadths; this is the procedure known as *parāpara*.
If the water reaches up to three finger-breadths, it is the *dhyanta*; if it reaches four, it is the *avyakta*.
By adding twenty-four [to each], there is also the rule for the *para* at eight hundred [finger-breadths].

Regarding the phrase "the channels of taste" (*rasaśrutī*): since the twenty-three principles from water up to the root (mūla) measure two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each, they total forty-six finger-breadths—this is the meaning. "Six finger-breadths above the navel" means up to that point. "In this manner" means because each of the six [channels] measures three finger-breadths.

"Each [is] four finger-breadths" means that because there are four [of them], each being four finger-breadths, they total sixteen finger-breadths. "Abdhivasu" means eighty-four. From the region of the *alika*.

Thus—"up to the region of the forehead" is the meaning. Right here, from the element water up to the intellect (*buddhi*), for each of the twenty-two principles, there is an increase of half a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) for the *sakala* (with parts) and two finger-breadths for the *parāpara* and *para* rites; thus there are twelve and twenty-four finger-breadths respectively.
They increase so that there are ninety-six or one hundred and eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*s), as it is said, "up to the end of the water. As it has been stated:
"This other procedure has been proclaimed; now hear the view of the Parāpara."
As before, the earth element should be known to be four finger-breadths in extent.
One should mark the measurements up to the *dhiṣaṇa* as two and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The *pradhāna* should be known as three finger-breadths; the remainder should be indicated as before.

"The others, as before, are the earth [element] measuring three finger-breadths; the principal [element] consists of four joints, and one should rely on the remainder as before. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 6.27) ||107||
Now, one might ask: "In this case, what is the authority for these three types of measurement? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The threefold measurement is clearly established from the earth and the directions by the decrease of the sun;
it has been stated likewise in the Mayatantra according to the desire for their respective fruits. (16.108)
"From the eight directions"—that is, from one hundred and eight [digits]. "Due to the sun's decrease"—this must be repeated.
By that, the meaning is: "due to the decrease of twelve digits each. ||108||
Having thus described the placement of the principles (tattvas) in their totality, he speaks of them also individually:

"One should perform the placement by means of one's own intellect through the placement of nine, five, four, three, or one principle, by contemplating the inclusion of the other principles within them. (16.109)
By this very [method], the placement of the five digits (kalā) and the four eggs (aṇḍa) is characterized.

In that regard, regarding the placement of the nine principles (tattva): *prakṛti* occupies fifty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), *puruṣa* three, *niyati* nine, *kāla* six, and *māyā*, *vidyā*, *īśvara*, and *sadāśiva* each occupy four.

"But Śiva is all-pervasive. Regarding the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the five principles (*pañcatattva*), however, there is this other method: earth occupies four finger-breadths, water forty-six, fire twenty-two, wind twelve, and space is all-pervasive. As it has been said:
Now, the five principles (tattvas) are described according to their presence in the body:
from the navel upwards, there are six joints in successive order.
The earth element pervades up to the ankles; the remainder here is pervaded by water.
Above that, the twenty-two joints are enveloped by fire.
"Therefore, the pervasion of Vāyu through the twelve joints has been described;

one should meditate upon the supreme, tranquil state ending in Ākāśa as the pervader of all. (In another part of the Mālinīvijaya, however, in two other injunctions, these twelve [joints] are located within the water-tattva itself.)
It should be considered that [the measurement] increases by twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

This same procedure applies even when performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the four principles (*tattva*) characterized as Earth, Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), Illusion (*māyā*), and Power (*śakti*).
However, in the ritual placement of the three principles, the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*) occupies seventy-two finger-breadths, and the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*)...
In the twelve [worlds], however, the Śiva-tattva exists as all-pervasive. As it has been said:
"In the Trikhaṇḍa, the Ātma-tattva is declared to extend up to the throat; above that is the Vidyā-tattva, while the Śiva-tattva is as before. (Mālinīvijaya Tantra 6.10)
"Of that many"—meaning of those remaining. "By this"—meaning by the very placement of the five or four principles (*tattvas*).

Now, one might object: "Let it be so that there are three kinds of measurement; however, how is it established that its threefold stationing extends from the forehead to the end? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And it is said in the *Triśirastantra*: "As it exists, situated within its own support... (16.110).
The upward extension from the body is twelve finger-breadths, equal and extending beyond the body;
that which resides within the body, up to the end of the head, measures seventy-two plus ten and two [eighty-four] finger-breadths.
O lady of beautiful hips, beginning from the feet up to the station of the Unstruck Sound (anāhata)—
that is, here, starting from the feet to the end of the head, reaching as far as the forehead and the limit of the Sound (nāda)—
the measurement of the body is seventy-two, ten, and two, which is eighty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas). This is the other measurement residing within the body.

This is the meaning. Thus, relying on another measurement as it stands, the upward extension from one's own support in the "shaven sky" (muṇḍavyoman) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is twelve finger-breadths;
this is the "para-apara" (intermediate supreme) measurement, totaling ninety-six finger-breadths. Beyond that, it transcends the body.
The elevation should be equal up to the *dvādaśānta*, measuring exactly twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), so that the ultimate measurement would be one hundred and eight finger-breadths.
Now, one might object: "If the measurement of the body alone has been undertaken to be discussed, how can that [measurement] be spoken of with respect to what transcends the body?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though it transcends the body, by virtue of the consciousness resting [therein], through the power of imagination. (16.112)
Therefore, the emergence [of the breath] extending twelve finger-breadths constitutes its state as the body;
it is for the sake of determining this that the one hundred and eight [verses] have been stated here. (16.113)
For since the supreme consciousness rests even beyond the body,
it possesses a conceptual nature of being the body; therefore, even the emergence of twelve finger-breadths from the *brahmarandhra* would constitute the body itself.
To determine this, it has been stated here in the venerable *Triśirobhairava* as consisting of one hundred and eight [verses];
such is the meaning. || 113 ||
Having thus described the deposition of the principles (*tāttvanyāsa*), he now speaks of the deposition of the worlds (*bhauvananyāsa*):
"Now, the deposition of the cities extends to the ankles; here there are sixteen cities.
From that point, each [city] occupies one finger-breadth, starting from Lakula. (16.114)
Up to the end of Dviraṇḍa, it is three finger-breadths; then Chagalāṇḍa is in the oceans (four).
Indeed, in the two groups of eight [worlds] beginning with Deva and Yoga, each is increased by a quarter-finger-breadth.
Thus, up to the level of Pradhāna, there are forty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
In this manner, there are fifty-six worlds (purāṇi) above; however, within the Earth (dharā), there are sixteen.
Beyond that, by an extension of half a finger-breadth, there are six cities in three fingers;
four in two [fingers]; and one city in one finger.
In this manner, within six finger-breadths, there are fifty-one cities of the Lord of Passion;
in one [finger-breadth] is the city of the Lord of Wrath, and in two, the Egg and this Vitality (vit).

In this manner, for Saṃvarta and Jyotis, as well as for Kalā and Tattva, there is a sequential pairing—one and two—respectively within the cities of Śūra and Pañcānta, and likewise in Niyati. (16.119)
"Sixteen"—this refers to the pervasion of each of the four finger-breadths by a quarter-finger-breadth.
"Up to Dviraṇḍa" means up to the nineteenth [tattva]. "Chagalāṇḍa" refers to the twentieth [tattva].
"In the oceans"—that is, in the four finger-breadths. This is their division here.
"By each finger-breadth of the foot" means sixteen; by implication, the cities are also four finger-breadths.

"Six cities" refers to those situated within the principle of the Person (puṃstattva). "Four" refers to those associated with Pracaṇḍā and the others. "In a pair" means in two finger-breadths. "One" means—
"Connected with Ekaśiva" means related to the Lord (Īśvara). "Numbered as eleven" refers to the eleven [rudras].

"In one" means in one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). "In two" means in two finger-breadths. "Caṇḍa" means related to Caṇḍa. "Vid" means knowledge (*vidyā*). "Thus" means the city of Saṃvarta is one finger-breadth.
Jyotiṣpura is two finger-breadths [in width]. Regarding "one pair": Śūrapura is one finger-breadth, and Pañcāntakapura is two finger-breadths. || 119 ||
To show that even the traditional scripture (āgama) supports this very interpretation regarding the triad beginning with Vidyā, he says:
"And that has been stated by the Supreme Lord Śambhu in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
'In the triad beginning with Vidyā, there is a division of two and one respectively, according to the sequence starting from the last. (16.120)
For within each of the three principles (tattva) beginning with Vidyā, there are two cities; therein, the upper city extends for two finger-breadths (aṅgula) and the lower one for one finger-breadth.
Thus, for each principle there are three finger-breadths, and across these three [principles], there are nine. || 120 ||
Now, one might ask: "How is it that these are taught here in reverse order? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because the sequence lacks essential substance, Niyati is at the beginning and Kalā is after it;
or else, the two principles may be designated by each other's names. (16.121)
Ekavīra, Śikheśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha are the three [deities] in each of the three times;
the prior arrangement of Kāla is here designated as Niyati.
Alternatively, indeed, designation by means of mutual designations is observed;
and in order to further corroborate this very point, it is stated again: "of time," and so forth.
He summarizes this very point:
"In this way, the group of six principles beginning with Puruṣa is [placed] within eighteen finger-breadths. (16.123)
Beyond that, the group of eight situated within the Māyātattva, extending down to the size of a thumb,
shall each occupy half a finger-breadth within the space of four finger-breadths.
Thus, in the two eyes during the night, there are twenty-eight ancient persons;
in the three cities within the two [eyes], they are three-fifths less than a finger-breadth, respectively.
Two [lines] for each of the two [sides], five cities in the medical [section], and four finger-breadths;
from there, eight cities of Īśa in a sequence of half-finger-breadths across four [sections].
Then, three in two, and two in each of the other two; thus, in the group of four, there is the fivefold Sādāśiva. Thus, in the eight [tattvas] there is one [tattva] for each sun (twelve).
The word *ittham* means "in the manner of unifying the eighteen and the four. Regarding the phrase *dvyakṣṇi*, this refers to twenty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
For it has been stated that when two finger-breadths are divided sixteenfold, the measure for each city (*pura*) is two parts.

"By three parts less than a finger, in sequence" means: "three" refers to the cities (*purāṇi*); "two" refers to two fingers. And that should be understood as being by the measure of a finger reduced by one-third.
"One for each of the Vasus" means eighteen cities; "in the sun" means in twelve fingers. (127)
This very point is summarized in both ways:
"The groups of cities are sixteen, fifty-six, twenty-eight, and eighteen;
there, the fingers are four, six, four, two, two, and twelve respectively. (16.128)
"Sixty-five" (rasaviśikha) means fifty-six. "Twenty-eight" (vasudvika) means twenty-eight.
"Eighteen" (vasuśaśī) means eighteen. "Four" (vedāḥ) means four. "Forty-six" (rasābdhi) means forty-six. "Twenty-two" (yugmākṣi) means twenty-two. "Twelve" (ravayaḥ) means twelve. ||128||
And thus this is established—so he says:
"In this body, which measures eighty-four [finger-breadths], one hundred and eighteen cities are deposited;
in that manner, however, Śiva-tattva is pervasive in what remains. (16.129)
Thus, another procedure, known as the "Supreme-Non-Supreme" (parāpara), has been described for the place of the hearing of the *rasa* [mantra].
In the subsequent procedure, the numerical count is eight arrows (five) and sky (zero) and sages (seven), which should be understood as 570.
"In the station of the hearing of flavors" means within the forty-six-fold self.
"Eight arrows" means fifty-eight—due to the addition of twelve. "Sky and sages" means due to the addition of twenty-four. ||130||
Now, one might ask: "How is there an excess of twelve or twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) here?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Of the multitude of worlds here, beginning with Lakula and ending with the group of eight yogas..."
One should increase the portion by means of calculation, sequentially for each of the two procedures. || 16-131 ||

"Of the multitude of worlds" means of that which consists of fifty-six [worlds]. "A portion" refers to a measure characterized by slightly more than five parts in the case of the Parāpara method; however, in the case of the Para [method], it is characterized by slightly less than half a finger-breadth (aṅgula). ||131||

Having thus described the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), he now speaks of the path of words (*padādhvan*): "Then follows the deposition of the path of words according to the threefold rule beginning with the Aparā [mantra]. When the previously mentioned *daśapadī* (ten-word sequence) is deposited as independent (*svatantrā*)," (16.132).
If initiation (dīkṣā) is to be performed by that very [method], then this arrangement of ritual depositions (nyāsa) is required;
for in initiation, the sequence of words [is used] due to the connection with the primacy of the principles (tattva) and so forth. (16.133)
In that case, it is included accordingly according to the respective principles (tattva) and so forth;
however, when the state of being primary belongs to initiation itself, [it follows] the sequence of the stages (pada).
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence, [visualizing the deity] as not looking toward the faces beginning with *tattva*.
"Previously" means in the eleventh chapter and so forth. "Independent" means primary.
"Therein" means in the *tattvas* and so forth. "In that manner" means by way of tenfold division. This is the application of its own primacy.
Thus it is reinforced by the statement: "not looking at the face of Tattvādī."
He says that very thing:
"In four, in eight, in eight, then in ten, and then in ten. (16.135)
Then, in ten, fifteen, and nineteen [syllables],
one should place the nine-worded Mātṛkā, which has entered into the Mālinī, along with the word for Earth (dharā).
One should apply the tenth step, known as Śiva, which is all-pervasive; this is done by excluding the five steps beginning with the step of Earth (Dharā).

There would be two procedures: having set aside twelve [units] each, there are four Vedas and fifteen Śarendavas (five and ten). Therein, in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), there is one [unit] for the single-syllable [mantra], two for the four-syllable, three for the five-syllable, and one.
The division of the nine verses consists of two syllables and three syllables. As it has been said:
"The first [verse] is four finger-breadths, while the other two are each eight finger-breadths."
"Ten finger-breadths from this [is one], three [are] fifteen finger-breadths; another is increased by four, and the ninth is the great pervasive one. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 6.20).
And here, "another" refers to the eighth, two-syllable word, which is increased by four finger-breadths.
With the fifteen remaining fingers that are left over, the ninth [word] consists of three syllables;
and the tenth, which is "Great" (mahat), consists of sixteen syllables and is all-pervasive (vyāpaka). This is stated for the sake of explanation:
"In the Vedas, arrows, and moons," [referring to] the tenth word designated as Śiva, which is pervasive.
Furthermore, as for what was explained by him in the *Pañcikā*— that the eighth step [is reached] through the extension of four [units] plus three, resulting in seven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
and the ninth through the extension of twelve finger-breadths by way of elimination— that...

This is the opinion of certain [authors] who are intent on establishing an identity of sequence between the levels of reality (*tattva*). For it is not possible to establish this by means of a universal rule; so what is the point of being obsessed with an impossible objective?
To illustrate: even though the *Chagalāṇḍa* world-sphere is two finger-breadths in extent within the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the worlds (*bhuvana*), [it is not necessarily so elsewhere].
How can the statement that [the worlds] have a thickness of three finger-breadths be reconciled? For the worlds are pervaded by the *tattvas*, but they do not consist of them.
Nor can it be said that these [worlds] exist within other *tattvas*, since they abide as being restricted to specific *tattvas*.
This is logical; enough with further elaboration. "Five" refers to those [fingers] occupying forty-six finger-breadths (aṅgula).
"Having placed" means, by implication, within those very five positions.
He extends this very same rule to other cases as well:
"This same procedure applies to the placement and application of the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) as well. (16.138)
For it was already stated previously that only the pervasion (vyāpti) would differ;
"previously" refers to the eleventh chapter and so forth.
Now, in order to describe the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), he says:
"Next, the arrangement of the path of phonemes is explained here according to the three procedures. (16.139)
One [syllable] should be placed in the four [fingers], and one in each of the two fingers respectively;
there should be twenty-three syllables [in total], with six syllables in each of the three [groups].
Then, four for each of the four [syllables] in reverse order—these are the letters of the Mālinī and Mātṛkā alphabets; they are the pervaders of the Śaiva [system], numbering sixty-six (rasendu).
Excluding the first letter, it should be like the Tattvas for every twelve [letters].
Within those twenty-three letters, there should also be another two-fold rule.

"One" refers to what he will say later regarding "in reverse order. "One by one" refers to "in the three"—by which, through a sixfold calculation in the three, there are eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*s). Likewise, in the case of the four as well, through a fourfold calculation, there would be sixteen finger-breadths; thus it is said—"each in the four."
"Four" means that "rasenduta" consists of sixteen syllables; this is the meaning.
The syntactical connection is that there would be another two methods. "Like the principles" (tattvavat) refers to what was stated immediately before.
"From *jala* up to *adhyanta*, two and a half [units]...
and so forth. (106) ||142 ||

For this very reason, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, this [threefold procedure] was taught at the beginning in relation to the *tattvas*, and subsequently it was extended to the words (*pada*) and so forth; thus he says: "Therefore, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, the threefold rule was stated first in relation to the *tattvas*."
But that which is extended by analogy is equal in both cases where the phonemes are either different or non-different from it. || 16.143 ||

He recites the very rule of extension (atideśavākya) found therein: "Indeed, the sixfold division of the phonemes (varṇas), though twofold, is said to be understood in its ultimate sense through the prescription of the path of the principles (tattvas). (16.144)

That which was stated regarding the words and so forth through both direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), has been further extended specifically therein, in this scripture that is the Lord of our heart. (16.145)

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: the twofold division of the phonemes (varṇas) residing within the Mātṛkā and Mālinī, which is further said to be sixfold through the individual pervasion of phonemes, words, and mantras, is to be understood in reality according to the previously mentioned sequence and the method of the path of the principles (tattvamārga).
By the phrase "the Lord of our heart," the fact that this very place is the locus of rest is indicated; he states that very point:
"Of the planes, mantras, kalās, and so forth, according to the preceding sūtra..."
One should effect the state of the triad by means of the path described for the letters of the principles (tattvas).
That has been stated regarding the mantras of the *pada*s; now it is described with respect to the *kalā*s.
Regarding the *pada*s and so forth, [it is said]: "Below the *pada*s are the five elements... (*Mālinīvijayottara* 6.2).

Following such sūtras as these, one should establish the state of being divided into three types—namely, the supreme, the non-supreme, and the supreme-non-supreme—by means of the path of reality (tattva) and so forth; this is the meaning. This has been stated immediately after [the previous passage].
He says that very thing:
"In four, sixty-four, twenty-two, and then twelve. (16.147)
There should be four [kalās] beginning with Nivṛtti; Śāntyatītā is the pervading one.
In the second kalā, however, there are twelve [fingers] each of twelve aṅgulas.

Having sequentially set aside the duality of ritual procedures— consisting of the higher, the lower, and that which is both— one understands by the word "etcetera" (ādi) here the procedure for the four cosmic eggs (caturaṇḍavidhi).
In accordance with the fourfold division of *kalās*, the three injunctions (*vidhi*) are to be stated therein;
"in the second" means in that which extends over forty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those contained in the venerable preceding statement are meant.
Thus, concluding the variety of that which is to be purified, he speaks in order to state the variety of the purifier:
"In this way, having first [purified] the sixfold path within the body of the disciple who is to be purified... (16.150).

Having deposited [the mantra] as the primary among the one or the other, one should deposit that which is considered the purifier (*śodhaka*). "That which is considered the purifier" means a specific mantra intended as the agent of purification—this is the meaning.
He says that very thing:
"In the path, the flood of mantras for the seat is indeed one purifier from the beginning. (16.151)
The mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) and Mālinī are twofold, according to whether they are taken collectively or individually;
or else, [they form] a group of six through the union of pairs, by virtue of being single heroes.

The five-faced [goddess] is sixfold due to the division between the power (śakti) and its possessor (śaktimān); furthermore, being twofold as solitary and as stainless, she thus consists of twelve aspects.
The six-limbed [mantra] is twofold due to its being either with or without parts; furthermore, when multiplied by twelve as it pertains to the faces, it becomes twenty-fourfold.
There are two groups of eight beginning with Aghora, and the third arises from the Yāmala;
and the Mātṛsadbhāva mantra is solitary, residing in the wheel of the Vedas.
Divided into one, two, three, and four, it consists of thirteen aspects;
yet as a single hero, it exists in fourteen ways.

In that regard, concerning the multitude of mantras for the seat (*āsana*): first, there is one purifier (*śodhaka*) because [the purification] would otherwise be impossible on the path; then there is the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), which is of two kinds—both distributed and collective—and likewise Mālinī.
Thus, there are four divisions. "As a single hero" (*ekavīratayā*) means as a single entity.

Because it consists of resting solely in its own essential nature. Regarding "by means of the union of pairs" (*yāmalayogataḥ*): due to the varying degrees of wonder arising from mutual orientation, there are twelve [faces] based on the agitated and unagitated states of the six;
and of these same six, there are twelve by taking them as faces either individually or in pairs.
These very limbs, being twelvefold, become twenty-four through their differentiated (*sakala*) and undifferentiated (*niṣkala*) aspects.
The "third" refers to the group of eight; thus, there are three groups of eight here. "Kevala" (alone) means because it is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*);
for this very reason, it is described everywhere as being "inexpressible" (*anākhyatayā*). "Śruti" refers to the four [states] beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*).
The wheels; thus, by way of being the unmanifested creation and so forth, they are of four kinds. ||156||

And this is not merely a difference of this magnitude—thus he says: The fourfold wheel of emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, and stability is augmented by its own deities through the true being of those Mothers. (16.157)
Thus, this group of purifiers consists of seventy mantras;
they are taught in the Trika scriptures (Ṣaḍardhaśāstra) and in the venerable Sāraśāstra. (16.158)
Here, the wise one should perform purification by means of the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghora,
or else by means of single-syllable mantras, or else according to the sequence of the Mātṛkā.
Or else, O Great Goddess, with the heart-mantra of Bhairavī, or with the heart-mantra of Khecarī, or with the [mantra] of Bhairava, or with the five [mantras] of the faces and limbs. (16.160)
"By whichever mantra the emergence [of the disciple] has been effected in this tantra, by that very one the mantrin should initiate him—such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (16.161)
Thus, seventy varieties [of initiation] have been proclaimed according to the distinctions of the purifiers (śodhaka).
When initiation is performed by means of these mantras without the placement of the objects to be purified (śodhya), [it is as follows]: || 16.162 ||
Then it should be known as seventyfold, devoid of birth and so forth.
By the plural "by mantras," the meaning is: by the three [mantras] associated with Parā and the others.
"By the heart of Bhairavī" means by the Mātṛsadbhāva mantra. "By the heart of Khecarī" means—

"By Piṇḍanātha"—that is, by Bhairava; "by whichever [form]" means by any one of the Navātman and others; "by whomsoever [the manifestation] was performed" means by whichever one is desired—this is the meaning.
Having thus described the variety of the objects to be purified (*śodhya*) and the purifiers (*śodhaka*), he speaks in order to explain the initiation (*dīkṣā*) brought about by their greatness:
"Now the differentiation of the objects to be purified must be stated; that too is told in brief. (16.163)
He states the very divisions of that which is to be purified:
"The division according to the principles (tattvas) is fourfold—consisting of one, three, five, and thirty-six;
likewise, the paths (adhvan) consist of five and one divisions, as does the quartet of cosmic eggs (aṇḍa). (16.164)
Thus, the tenfold object of purification becomes thirtyfold through its three methods;
by means of the distinction between the purified and the purifier, there are twenty-one hundred [divisions]. (16–165)
In this case as well, by means of the application of the ritual placement (nyāsa), when the path to be purified has been treated accordingly,
it becomes free from birth and the other [stages], consisting of twenty-one hundred divisions.

Thus, in the *Śatadṛśī*, the scripture [the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*] consists of one hundred and seventy verses concerning birth and so forth; that too is divided according to the distinctions of substance and cognition. (16.167)
"Of two kinds" means it would be eight thousand five hundred and ten;
it is proclaimed as being of two kinds because of its connection with worldly enjoyment and liberation. (16.168)

Through the complete purification of the impure and the subsequent purification of the pure, experience is twofold; in the case of the pure, purification occurs within that which is divided by the three times. (16.169)

Through the combination of one, two, or all together, enjoyment is sevenfold; it is eightfold when including the lineage from teacher to disciple. That too is further divided into two types. || 16-170 ||

Because in a direct initiation, the fruit of such initiation is complete when there is a single unifying intent between the two [the teacher and the disciple], whereas in the case of a discrepancy, there is ruin. || 16-171 ||
In cases such as initiation for one who has died out of sight, the Guru alone,
possessing the power of realization through the greatness of his ritual action and knowledge, shall lead that disciple to the desired abode.
When ritual action and knowledge are undivided, as well as the purification of karma, for you they are likewise [unified];
yet the connection is again divided, because karma is of that very nature.

And in the illustrious Svacchanda Śāstra, it is stated that even when the ritual actions and so forth are identical, the fruit for the disciples and the teacher differs according to their respective latent impressions (vāsanā). (16–174)

There is a variety [of experience] due to the variety of the purifier of enjoyment, the object to be purified, and the corresponding reflective awareness (anusandhi), since differentiation has variety as its very life-force. || 16-175 ||

"Five" refers to those remaining in the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*). "By way of the distinction between the object of purification and the purifier" means here by way of the distinction between the thirty objects to be purified and the seventy purifiers. "Seventy" refers to the previously mentioned number associated with the purifiers. Thus, there are four thousand two hundred and seventy [varieties].

Regarding the word *dravya*: by this, action (*kriyā*) is indicated. *Kha* is zero; *abdhi* refers to four. Thus, there are five thousand eight hundred and forty [units]. "Of the inauspicious alone" refers to one who follows worldly dharma (*lokadharmin*). "Of the auspicious as well" refers to one who follows the dharma of Śiva (*śivadharmin*). "Sevenfold" refers to the auspicious, for...
There are three single-fold divisions based on the distinctions of pure (*śuddha*), past, present, and future;
there are also three two-fold divisions based on the states of past-present, past-past, and present-future;
and there is one collective division. Thus, it is "eightfold"—meaning [the eightfold division] of the impure (*aśubha*) together with the pure (*śuddhi*). "That too" refers to—

The Guru says: "It is divided in this way"—according to the sequence that will be explained. "Dissension" means consisting of two distinct forms of mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*). "Only the Guru" [is the authority] because the disciple is located in another direction or is deceased. "In the same way" means in the undivided state. "Consisting of that" means animated by that synthesis.

In this regard, he demonstrates the very variety of the purifier: "For instance, when the path belonging to someone has been purified by certain [faces] of [the mantra], and he is joined by those very same [faces] to some desired principle (tattva) in order to experience it, he becomes an enjoyer endowed with its power. (16–176)
In this world, when auspicious karmas exist, there is a variety of enjoyments;
yet, when there is purity of karma, that very variety becomes something entirely different.

And enjoyment [occurs] either immediately upon departure, while still joined with the body, or at that very moment through practice, or else at the end of the body; thus there are four [possibilities]. (16–178)
Through the combination with the eightfold division mentioned previously, it is said that there are thirty-two divisions;
even though liberation is one, such is the case for the seed known as the *samaya*.

Whether it be a child or someone else known to be subject to imminent death and devoid of power, or an elder who is capable—[the rite] is of two kinds, depending on whether purification has been performed or not. (16–180)
"Regarding the threefold immediate departure [of the soul] for a Guru who is about to die, it must be performed;
this is the command of Maheśa as declared in the venerable Gahvara. (16–181)
Having seen the disciple seized by old age and afflicted by disease,
one should then cause him to ascend and unite him with the supreme reality.
These thirty-five varieties [of transgression] pertain to the Guru alone or to both the Guru and the disciple; through the aforementioned twofold calculation, they are proclaimed to be seventy.

Having eliminated those previously mentioned divisions pertaining to initiation by means of these [present] divisions, the Guru should state the calculation for the sake of achieving mastery in well-practiced knowledge.
The variety of purifications for auspicious [deeds] and so forth has been revealed by the passage beginning with "the variety of what is to be purified.
"At that very time" means immediately following initiation (*dīkṣā*). "Through practice" means through the sequence of mantra-worship.
"The thirty-two-fold division" results from multiplying the four [categories] by eight. "Capable" means...

The form beginning with the "learned one" (vidvad-ādi). "That" refers to immediate departure (sadya-utkrānti). It is said to be "spoken of"—by such passages as: "That too is divided into two kinds according to the sequence of teacher and disciple," and so forth.
He shows this very point by analyzing it:
"The one hundred and eighty-four [initiations] increased by forty that have been described—one should oneself determine the varieties of initiation by dividing that [total] by seventy. (16–185)
In this *Mālinītantra*, the classification of initiations (*dīkṣā*) consists of five hundred and ninety-seven thousand eight hundred [divisions]. (16–186)
"Having pierced" means having multiplied. || 186 ||
Having thus enumerated the primary divisions, he says that there are also other subdivisions here:
"The group of purifiers is sevenfold; the object of purification consists of thirty [principles] beginning with the single principle (ekatattva);
likewise, it includes the cosmic egg (sāṇḍa), the form of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvarūpa), and the fourfold procedure (itikartavyatā). (16–187)
That [power] consists of substance and knowledge; it is devoid of birth and so forth, yet it is endowed with them.
Furthermore, this [power] is thirty-five-fold due to the conjunction of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Since enjoyment is thirty-two-fold through the divisions of auspiciousness, purity, impurity, and time;
liberation is threefold; and [the powers] are doubled—thus there are seventy varieties of the objects of action.
"Twofold" refers to the distinction in the continuity of awareness existing between the teacher and the disciple.
He demonstrates the existence of other divisions:

"This initiation is divided in many ways due to the distinction between the purifier and the object of purification, as well as due to the distinction in the ritual procedures; however, when devoid of the object of purification, it is seventy-fold. (16–190)

This is due to the synthesis of the various divisions of mantras—such as those with all their limbs (*sakala*), those with some limbs (*itarasāṅga*), and those without limbs (*niraṅga*)—and the enumeration of the fifteen and other aforementioned divisions of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth that are to be purified. || 16–191 ||
It is impossible to enumerate all the varieties; thus, these varieties are unmixed.
However, there are other mixed varieties which, being numerous, occur in many ways. (16–192)
Because of the existence of various divisions, such as the purifier and the object to be purified, numbering two, three, and so forth;

"the other" refers to the partless (niṣkala). "As stated"—in the tenth chapter. "Unmixed divisions"—this is stated by implication. "Two, three, and so forth"—referring to [mantras] consisting of two goddesses, three, and so on.
Anticipating the objection, "But what would be the point of stating these distinctions in this way?", he says:
"When enjoyment is to be accomplished, the wise man should resort to whatever means are most effective. (16.193)
It is indeed not surprising that an abundance of causes leads to an abundance of results;
however, there is no such distinction regarding liberation, for in this regard, it depends upon the firmness of one's latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Alternatively, even a very slight action may be resorted to, or [the practice may be performed] in mere consciousness alone.
However, our teachers do not agree with this; thus [Abhinavagupta’s teacher] says:
"But Abhinavagupta’s teacher has said that when wealth, place, time, and so forth are present... (16.195).
For even in the state of liberation (apavarga), a comprehensive integration of extensive karma and cognition must be maintained.
He demonstrates this very point:
"Because of the variety of the fluctuations of consciousness, even though there is instability, [integration occurs] through gradual unification. (16–196)
In each and every object, established rootedness necessarily becomes of the nature of Śiva.
"This is the reality; it is of this nature; from this, the disciple has been raised up by me. (16–197)

In this way, even one who is deluded becomes identical with Śiva through the gradual realization [of consciousness], provided he beholds the Guru, who is graced by such a gradual descent of the grace of Śiva-nature. (16–198)

Even a child attains the state of Śiva through the power of devotion and by perceiving non-difference from Him; although even for one whose mental activity is still characterized by conceptual construction, liberation occurs at the end of the body solely through initiation.
The Lord has declared this in the scripture (*śāstra*), namely in the *Śrī Niśāṭana* and other works; nevertheless, a firm latent impression (*vāsanā*) is required.
Regarding "in the scripture"—it refers to the *Śrī Niśāṭana* and so forth—and that has been stated extensively in the first chapter (*āhnika*) and elsewhere.

And here he states another opinion of others: "Even in liberation there is a distinction arising from the smallness or abundance of ritual action, such as [residing] in the same world [as the deity] and so forth. (16.200)
Thus some [say], but that is incorrect, for he would have been described as nothing other than variegated experience (*bhoga*).
Now, if this is not tenable, which position should be adopted?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
During the life that continues as a remainder of past conditioning, there occurs for him the violation of commitments and so forth. (16.201)

For one who desires liberation and has been purified by initiation with seed (sabījadīkṣā), no web of obstacles arises from the abundance of ritual actions, nor do transgressions of the rules (samayalopa) and the like affect him. (16–202)
"Even after enjoying worldly pleasures, there is no liberation at all in the case of seedless initiation (nirbījadīkṣā).
Thus some believe; and that which is recorded in the scripture is also logical. (16–203)
The reason for this very point is that which is recorded in the scripture. ||203||
He says that very thing: "O Goddess, from the transgression of the rule (samaya), one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years. (16.204)
He concludes this very point:

Therefore, even with respect to liberation, the sequential ritual acts such as the extraction of the principles (*tattvoddharaṇa*), which are capable of bestowing the firm establishment of the state of Śiva within the minds of both teacher and disciple, are appropriately and extensively applied. (16–205)
For a Guru whose knowledge is well-practiced, there is no such restriction whatsoever in the presence [of the disciple]; thus he says:
"But that Guru who possesses well-practiced knowledge through constant contemplation may, for the sake of the disciple's liberation, employ whatever means he desires. (16.206)
Having thus explained this as a digression, he speaks of the subject at hand:

"In this way, having projected the path to be purified upon the body of the disciple as desired, one should project the purifying mantra above it, in accordance with the [corresponding] principles (tattva). (16.207)
"According to the reality"—this indicates the path to be purified (*śodhyādhvan*). By this, the supreme deposition (*nyāsa*), which consists of those respective mantras, is indicated. (207)
He says that very thing:

"The sequence of phonemes for the two Mātṛkās was previously taught according to the state of the principles (tattva); one should install it in that same way for the purification of each respective principle. (16.208)
"Of the two" refers to the Śabdarāśi and Mālinī [varṇas]. ||208||

Now, since it has been stated that "the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is likewise a cause of bondage," and thus the path of phonemes is equally a binder without distinction, how is it that [it is treated differently] here?
Anticipating the objection, "Even though it is that which is to be purified (*śodhya*), why is it called the purifier (*śodhaka*)?", he says:
"Although the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) is said to be that which is to be purified, for it consists of bonds (*pāśa*);
the purifier, however, is another—the nature of Śiva, consisting of supreme speech (*paravāṅmaya*). (16.209)

Now, one might ask: "What is the proof that a single entity can be both the object of purification and the purifier? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Sadyojyotis stated in his commentary on the *Svāyambhuva*:
'Truly, one is indeed of the nature of bondage (the fetter), while the other is of the nature of Śiva. (16.210)
Therefore, it is logical that the state of being the purifier and the purified belongs to that very same category. Our own tradition also teaches this; thus he says:
"And it is stated in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra: 'They are embraced by those [energies]' (16–211)."

Having performed the placement six times for the faces beginning with Sadyojāta and the five limbs beginning with the heart, one should perform the thirty-six-fold placement starting from the earth element (dhara).
By reversing the sequence of Parāparā, there should be three steps on Earth (Dharā);
then, from Water up to Ego (Ahaṅkāra), there are five [steps] based on the group of eight.
There are five steps: three in the triad known as the root of wisdom, the person, and passion;
one in the two [periods of] impure knowledge and time; and one in the regulator.
In this system, one state is said to belong to Kalā, Māyā, and the non-dual (Śiva) respectively;
there are five states among Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva. (16–215)
This supreme sequence of words consists of nineteen items;
as it is said therein:
"Being fully awakened by that [power], he agitates the womb with his powers."
The Lord created phonemes having the same sound as those [vowels], with the same number as them.
"Being embraced by them, they bestow the fruits of all desires. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.28).

Thus, the intended meaning here is that the single phoneme (*varṇa*), when meditated upon as being of the nature of Śiva, is the purifier; otherwise, it is the object to be purified. "Six times"—referring to the powers (*śakti*) and the possessors of power (*śaktimant*).

The meaning is: "having combined those [elements] related to each respective principle. Regarding the phrase "due to the reverse order": for in initiation (*dīkṣā*), the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) alone is appropriate;

therefore, even though they are described in the scripture according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) must be performed in this very [reverse] way—this is the intended sense.

"Three words" means *phaṭ*, *haḥ*, and *huṃ*, each consisting of one and a half syllables. "Five" refers to *phaṭ*, *ra-ra*, *ru-ru*, *he*, and *piba*, which consist of two and a half, two, two, one, and two syllables respectively. "In the principle of passion (rāga) together with the Person (puṃs)" means in the *rāga-tattva* accompanied by the *puruṣa*. "Three" refers to *vama*, *bhīṣaṇe*, and *bhīme*.

Two, three, and two syllables. "One" refers to *ghoramukhī*, which consists of four syllables. "One" refers to *haḥ*, which is a single syllable. "One" refers to *ghorarūpe*, which consists of four syllables. "In sequence" means:
thus, *rūpe* is in the *kalā* [tattva], and *ghora* is in the *māyā* [tattva]. "Five words and one" refers to *huṃ paramaghore*.

*Hrīḥ*, *aghore*, and *om*—this consists of one, five, one, three, and one [syllables] respectively. Regarding their distribution within the Vidyā: there is one pada in the Vidyā, one in Īśvara, two in Sadāśiva, and one in Śakti and Śiva.
In this very context, he states the division of the phonemes:
One and a half, one and one, two and a half, two, the moon (one), the eye (two), then a pair (two);
three, the eye (two) and the ocean (four), the moon (one), the ear (four), the moon (one), five, the moon (one) and the sun (twelve), and the moon (one):
this is the number of syllables in the verses of the Goddess up to the nineteenth [verse]. (16.216–217)
The number of its own phonemes is calculated as two Hal-dvayas, Vasu, Citragu, and Pari;
the portion ending with Mūla consists of one and a half phonemes, while the portion ending with Māyā consists of a single phoneme.
The rule for the placement of the *aparā* [kalā] is declared to consist of one [syllable] ending with *śakti*;
then the consonants end with *māyā*, and the vowel is said to be at the end of *śakti*. (16–219)
In the partless Śiva-principle, indeed, the supreme deposition (nyāsa) is declared to be supreme;
for the words "Parā" and "Aparā" belong to the two groups of eight beginning with Aghora.

In accordance with those [rules], one should cast these two [syllables] into the principles (tattvas) according to the distinction in the number of phonemes of all the syllables of the piṇḍas. (16–221)
Having assigned [the letters] up to the Unmanifest (avyakta) within the vowels, one should apply the remainder to the remaining [consonants].
One should conceive of the seed-syllables as pervading all the principles (tattvas).
Others, however, maintain that the piṇḍas should be assigned like seeds;
or else, even if the assignment for the object to be purified has not been performed, [the purification occurs] because of the inherent power of the thing itself. (16.223)
By the mere placement of the purifier (*śodhaka*), everything to be purified (*śodhya*) becomes completely pure.

"The Great One" (*mahaḥ*) refers to the three [energies] characterized as Moon, Sun, and Fire. "Endowed with two *hal* letters" means that it is augmented by two *hal* letters—that is, by the two vowelless forms of the letter *ṭa*. "Vasu-citra" refers to...
Thirty-eight. As it has been said:
"In the Niṣkala [state], there is the single-syllable *pada* and the pair consisting of the three-syllable and the one-syllable;
but in the Sakala [state], the two pairs of five-syllables and one-syllables are to be fully understood."
Two [mantras] of four and one syllable each are considered for the triad beginning with Māyā;
and one of four syllables is considered for the pair beginning with Kāla.
In the *rañjaka* [mantra], two syllables are indicated; in the *pradhāna*, three syllables are desired.
In the *buddhi* [mantra], due to the pervasion of the eight deities, there are words (*pada*) consisting of two, one, two, and two syllables respectively.
There are four *vidyā* words, and the fifth consists of one and a half syllables.
"In the earthly principle, however, there are three [syllables] consisting of one and a half letters each" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.23).
"Ending with the Root" means extending up to Prakṛti, pervading the two maṇḍalas—this is the meaning.
"One letter" means that which has four kalās. "One" refers to the seed-syllable of Māyā. "Ha-l" refers to...
From the context, this refers to the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*). Likewise, the vowel is the letter *au*. "The supreme" (*para*) refers to the visarga.
As it has been said:
"The two eggs (*aṇḍa*) are pervaded by [the letters] one by one, and each pair separately."
This pervasion of Aparā has been declared in reverse order.
"The three eggs are pervaded by Sārṇa, the fourth by Triśūla, and that which transcends all is pervaded by Visarga; this is held to be the pervasion of Parā. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.25).
"In accordance with that" refers to the very words of Parāparā mentioned immediately above.

The meaning is: "by following the pervasion of each respective reality. As it has been said: "The eight Yoginīs of great power, born from the limbs of the Parāparā, consist of five, six, five, four, two, three, and two syllables respectively."
"It should be known that [the mantras] consist of seven, eleven, and two syllables, joined with one and a half syllables" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.60).

Regarding "of the piṇḍa-syllables"—this refers to the Navātman and others. "Number"—nine and so forth. "Vowel"—in the letter *u*. "The remainder"—Puruṣa and the rest. "In the remaining"—in the letters beginning with *ya*. "Seeds"—this refers to the seed-mantras.

The *piṇḍapada* syllables, such as the single-syllable [mantras] and others, are like seeds; the meaning is that the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *piṇḍas* must also be performed for each *tattva* by way of pervasion.
Anticipating the objection—"What is the authority for the claim that even that which is to be purified (śodhya) becomes pure by the mere deposition of the purifier (śodhaka) alone?"—he says:
"And it has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Mṛtyuñjaya and other [scriptures]. (16-224)
He says that very thing:
"Now, by mere nyāsa, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is produced.
But one might ask: "Since this was previously stated here for the purpose of purifying the body, how does it cohere in this context?"
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even for the sake of purifying the body, this is in reality equal to that. (16.225)
If something stated in one context is appropriate for another context, whether by way of being an indicator (*jñāpaka*) or directly, why should it not be accepted elsewhere? (16.226)

The placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of the Mālinī-mātṛkā which was previously described in the ritual of worship is indeed the same as that for the placement of the mantras used solely for purification.
There should be three feet for each of the two [groups], and then eight syllabic feet; in the calculation of ten, one, one, six, twelve, five, five, two, two, one, and one. (16–28)
In the case of the Goddess measured in finger-breadths (aṅgula), there are eighteen [units] by way of manifestation;
this other measurement would be for the placement of the mantra that effects purification alone.
From the fourth state (turyapada) to the sixth state, there are two measures known as Parāpara and Parā;
each consists of twelve [units], and the rest above the principles (tattva) is as before.
"In reality" (vastutaḥ) means because of the equality of the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*) consisting of the purified and the purifier.

"Directly" (sākṣāt) means by way of being the prescriber. "Why is it not accepted elsewhere?"—the meaning is that, on the contrary, it is indeed accepted. "Of the limb" (aṅgasya) means of its essential nature. "Mere" (kevala)—meaning alone.

Excluding the purification (śodhya-parihāreṇa), however, when there is a merging with that which is to be purified (śodhya-saṃmīlanāyām), the placement (nyāsa) is exactly as previously stated according to the sequence of the phonemes and so forth. "That very same" means the placement and its sequence.
"The three-footed" refers to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra-krameṇa). "Of each pair" refers to the fingers; by that...

"Six fingers. Regarding "in eight": this refers to eight fingers. Regarding "śruti": four; thus, [the total] is thirty-two. Regarding "directions": ten. "Moon": one. "Taste": six. "Sun": twelve. "Arrows": five. "Eye": two. "Eighteen": these are the words [of the verse].
"By its majesty" means by its pervasiveness, as it has been said:
"There is another pervasive state... (6.24).
"Alone" means without excluding that which is to be purified. Starting from the fourth state (*turyapada*), there is the group of six states (*padaṣaṭka*).
Thus—where there are four [units] of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), one of ten finger-breadths, and one of one finger-breadth.
"Above"—the meaning is that by this, two finger-breadths are added for every step (*pratipada*) here. ||230||
Now, one might object: "Has not the placement of the words (*pada-nyāsa*) according to the sequence of the principles (*tattva-krama*) been taught immediately following this?
So how is it now stated here in a different manner? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Mahādeva [spoke thus] with the intention of teaching the placement of the purely purificatory mantras (*kevala-śodhaka-mantra*)."
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa) as taught in the sequence of the Tattvas, and also that which is contrary to it.

For Mahādeva, having first taught the sequential placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) to be purified— preceded by their respective assignments— now speaks of the placement of nineteen words, which, though seemingly contrary to that, is intended for the placement of the purifying mantras (*śodhakamantra*).
The meaning is that he also spoke of it as being otherwise. ||231||
He recites that very [verse]:

"In the Niṣkala [state] there is one syllable, up to three in the Pārthiva," and so forth; by this, the method of placement (nyāsa) according to the sequence of the principles (tattvas) has been declared. (16–232)
Furthermore, in the Mālinītantra,
having stated that the words are twofold according to the distinction between the Varga and the Vidyā, the All-pervasive Lord taught a different kind of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Regarding the word *udīrita* ("stated"): this was stated in the fourth chapter and has been corroborated immediately following that. Regarding the word *uktvā* ("having said"):
this refers to the sixth chapter. As it is stated there: "In this context, words are of two kinds, distinguished by the categories of *varga* and *vidyā*."

"Listen now to how their pervasion by those mantras occurs, just as it is at present. (Tantrāloka 6.19). "Of a different kind" means contrary to the sequence of the arrangement of the *tattvas*. ||233||
He states that very point:
"In that regard, each of the first three steps should be known as two finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
the next four are eight finger-breadths, and beyond that, ten finger-breadths. (16.234)
Two [parts] are two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula), and another two are six finger-breadths;
another is twelve finger-breadths, and the other two are each five finger-breadths.
Two feet have four joints, and likewise two others have two joints each.

Three feet are each two finger-breadths (aṅgula) long, thus [these] are six finger-breadths. In the phrase "eight finger-breadths," the word "each" (ekaika) is also to be connected here. Regarding "two feet are two finger-breadths"—each one [is so].

"One *pada* is one finger"—this is the meaning. "Separately" means each is five fingers; otherwise, each would be two and a half fingers. "Two *padas* consist of four joints"—because each consists of two joints. "Two [joints] with two parvas each"—[is the meaning].
The meaning is that each [finger] has a single joint.
He concludes this very point:
"In this way, the independent deposition (nyāsa) of the goddess Parāparā is declared. (16.236)

"Independent" (*svatantra*) means that it does not depend on the deposition of the *tattvas* and so forth. For previously, this [deposition] was dependent upon those [elements], such as the *tattvas* to be purified, by first depositing them; here, however, its deposition occurs independently, having set aside that [dependence].
This is the portion concerning the subject matter. It is with this very intention that—

It has been stated [in the scripture]: "Furthermore, this other *māna* (measure) would be solely for the purpose of purification in the *anunyāsa*. Therefore, because this *nyāsa*, which is described as being twofold due to its dependence on that which is to be purified (*śodhya*) and its own autonomy (*svātantrya*), is recited as "one or two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each," [the rule] of the former...
The three steps [measure] four finger-breadths; each of the two steps [measures] two finger-breadths;
and the other [step] measures exactly six finger-breadths. Together with the preceding one, however, they amount to twelve finger-breadths.
Even though the two steps [total] ten finger-breadths, one [step] is three finger-breadths and the other is seven finger-breadths.

Having stated that each of the two types of foot-measures is either four finger-breadths or two finger-breadths, and having then provided an interpretation by combining both sides through the transposition of finger-breadths in accordance with what precedes and follows, there is an abandonment of the archaic (ārṣa) reading.
Furthermore, the faults [of this interpretation] are: the conceptualization of hardship, the lack of utility for the statement, and the transgression of the venerable Guru’s explanation. ||236||

One might ask: "In that case, why was the placement (*nyāsa*) of the two goddesses not also mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "To show that one should apply the two Vidyās to the body of the disciple solely as its pervader (*vyāptṛ*), he did not describe a separate placement for them. (16-237)

Now, one might ask: "What would be the purpose of the twofold deposition (nyāsa) of the purifier? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that although there is no difference in the result, there is merely a variety in the procedure:
"Thus, by the deposition of the purifying mantra, through its connection with its rays..."
That net of snares shall dissolve through the power of meditation upon the Guru.
When all the wombs within the reality to be purified have been simultaneously exhausted through birth and experience, liberation occurs upon the destruction of karma. (16.239)
"Net of nooses" means consisting of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), and that is, by implication, cast away. "In the reality" (tattve) is an elliptical expression;
therefore, it applies to the six paths as well. And the ritual deposition (nyāsa) is established by implication. ||239||

Now, one might object: "Even if this atomic soul (aṇu) is simultaneously the enjoyer residing in multiple bodies, does there occur a mutual recollection between them, or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It is clearly a marvel that for this atomic enjoyer, even with so many bodies..."
The mental connection is not like the conjunction and disjunction of the atoms of the universe. (16-240)

In this world, for this contracted individual soul, there is clearly no distinct mental synthesis— even though it is the experiencer— of many bodies that exist simultaneously through the power of mantras and are initiated by the variety of various karmas; [such that one could think], "I am the very same one in another body."

The meaning is that the cognition "I am that very same person who ate [in the past], even here [now]" would not arise for him. An illustration for this very point is given: "like the conjunctions and disjunctions with the universe. For just as, because the Self is all-pervasive, [it remains present] throughout the conjunctions and disjunctions with the multitude of entities (bhāva) constituting the universe;
The meaning is that just as there is no such mental connection as "I am joined with this" or "I am separated from this," so it is here as well. ||240||
Now, one might object: "Is this example not unestablished? Since it is all-pervasive, should not such a mental process (anusandhi) occur there as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By necessity, the activity of the mind is restricted to the body alone; beyond that [it does not extend]."
For it is not a continuous sequence, since it is constructed by the senses joined with a single internal mind.

For, due to the constraint of the mind's power of determination (*niyati-śakti*), its function— which consists of synthetic awareness— occurs only within the body and not elsewhere; because that function of the mind does not give rise to simultaneous cognitions through any single sense organ, such as the eye or others.
According to the principle stated in [Nyāyasūtrabhāṣya 1.1.4], "The self is conjoined with the mind; the mind with the sense organ;
the sense organ with the object," the meaning is that [the object] is imagined by the sense organ joined with one's own internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and is therefore dependent upon it.

And since knowledge has a restricted function regarding the sense organs, how could the mind, by transgressing that very restriction, continue its connection with another body and so forth? Therefore, he says:
"The knowledge of the self functions only in specific locations; it is thus in each respective case."
The knowledge of what is to be experienced does not admit of continuity across other bodies.
"Knowledge of the object of experience" (bhogyajñāna) means the cognition whose objects are blue, pleasure, and so forth. ||242||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then why does the knowledge of yogis regarding objects beyond the senses arise from their intuitive cognition (*prātibhajñāna*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But when, for that mind which functions within the body, [there is] certainly..."
Then, for one who knows that [reality], there shall be the purification of yoga, mantras, ritual actions, and so forth. || 16-243 ||

Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): even for one whose mental activity is dependent on the external senses; "tadvidā"—the meaning is "by the knowledge of that," namely, the knowledge of that object which transcends the senses. ||243||

He applies this to the present subject as well: "Just as a pure mind perceives even that which is situated at a distance instantly, so too in the initiation by conviction (pratyayadīkṣā) there is the vision of each respective world. (16.244)
But when one desires to perform initiation for one who is free from birth and so forth, then the appropriate mental construction is: "I am rescuing this person [from that state]. (16.245)
When there is no object to be purified (*śodhya*), even if the placement of the purifier (*śoddhṛnyāsa*) is performed there by means of mantra,
one should carry out the sequence beginning with *janana* while remaining free from the fusion of the *tattvas*.

In the case of the solitary extraction-deposition (*ekākiśoddhṛnyāsa*) and when avoiding [the mention of] birth and so forth, one should conceive of that as the "encasement by the extractor" (*tacchoddhṛsaṃpuṭa*) alone. (16.247)

"Vision of those respective worlds"—the meaning is that for someone who possesses an intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*), there may even be a continuous mental connection (*anusandhāna*) with multiple bodies within various worlds.
"It is logical"—because [the Lord] has no desire to perform [acts such as] birth and so forth. "He would act"—[refers to this].
Because its specific qualities are not delineated by implication, it has been said: "devoid of connection with reality.
Having thus fashioned the name of the disciple conjoined with the desired purifier, what should one do?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In the initiation involving material substances, one should offer sesame seeds, clarified butter, unbroken grains,
and rice with their respective mantras during the conjunctions and separations of births.
"By means of that respective mantra" means by means of one characterized by the name of the disciple encapsulated within the purifier (*śoddhṛ*).
"In the case of birth, conjunction, and disjunction"—the meaning is that, in reality, these are caused by that [mantra]. ||248||
Furthermore, regarding the initiation of consciousness (*vijñānadīkṣā*), there is nothing else that must be done; thus he says:

"When one performs the initiation of consciousness for a disciple, then, by the power of the internal discourse of that mantra, one should perceive [the disciple] intensely until [the state] free of conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*) is reached. (16.249)

"Of that mantra" (tanmantra) means "of the mantra intended to be purified"—this is the meaning. The particle *ca* is displaced in order; it functions as a causal conjunction, thus [meaning] "and then by that. "Until the non-conceptual" (ā avikalpāt) means up to the point of resting in the non-conceptual state which is of the nature of direct realization—this is the meaning. ||249||
Now, one might object: "How can discursive thought (*sañjalpa*), which is of the nature of sound, find rest in the non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Discursive thought (*vikalpa*) is indeed composed of discursive speech (*sañjalpamaya*), because it is reflective (*vimarśaka*).
This reflection is of the nature of mantra, and that reflection is pure, being free from the nature of bondage. (16.250)

And [this] eternal [consciousness], fashioned as non-different from Śiva, the beginningless bestower of boons, through union with that, even the conceptual construction of the teacher shall attain the state of Śiva. (16.251)
