For the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is indeed discursive speech (*sañjalpa*), since it has the character of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) because its essence consists of the sovereignty of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). And this very discursive speech is the essence of mantra, and that which is inseparable from it is reflective awareness.
Because it possesses a single form that is free from conceptual construction, it is pure;
for this very reason—
this divine state belongs even to the bound soul (paśu).
By this method, [the Self] is of the nature of being free from bonds (*apāśava*), and for that very reason, it is eternal.
According to the principle stated in [Rauravāgama-pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya 1.5.11], "The nature of manifestation is...
and so forth, its essential nature is inseparable from that—this is the meaning. Now, [an objection]:

"How can such a capacity for deliberation belong to a gross conceptualization whose nature is discursive speech?"—anticipating this doubt, it is said: "It is fashioned through non-difference from Śiva, the primordial Bestower of Boons.
For it is precisely by entering into the essential nature of the mind of the one who recites the mantra that even conceptual thought attains the state of Śiva.
One should proceed and rest in a state entirely free from conceptual construction—this is the meaning. ||251||
And this is not established by reasoning alone; thus he says:
"This very thing was spoken by the Supreme Lord in the Śrīsāraśāstra. He recites that very [passage]:
The apprehension of an object which consists of the form of the grasped and the grasper.
That very power of mantra, which is indeed spread throughout the continuum of mantras,
consists essentially in the contemplation of meaning; it takes the form of the grasped and the grasper,
consists of that reflective awareness (āmarśa) which is like the pointing of a finger-tip toward its own head, and is primary, being non-conceptual by nature.

Practice (*pratipatti*) is precisely that power (*śakti*)— the meaning being that it is existence (*sattā*)— which, as the uninterrupted essence of all mantras, manifests in a state of internal concealment within the single nature of the subject.
Thus, he says that this would have been stated by him [in the following way]: "In this manner, the power of mantra is declared to have the nature of reflective awareness (parāmarśa). (16.253)
Reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is twofold due to its purity or impurity, and it differentiates the mantras.
It differentiates the mantras in two ways according to its pure and impure nature—
as he says in the passage beginning with "reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*).
And he analyzes this very point by means of scriptural citation:
"It is stated in the Śrīpauṣkara that others, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth, are contained within the cosmic egg. (16-254)

Those followers of Pradhāna are possessed of *añjana* (impurity) and consist of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; through their impure discernment, the Guru has been permeated by them. (16.255)
Those belonging to the Vaiṣṇava and other such traditions are declared to be "bound souls" (paśus) and are not fit for the teaching of the Lord (pati).
Those mantras situated on the pure path, such as those of Śivabhaṭṭāraka and others, [are fit]. (16-256)
According to the view of the venerable Mataṅga and other scriptures, the Guru is indeed Śiva, for he is "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*).
"Consisting of that" means having attained identity with the Lord Śiva Bhaṭṭāraka and the mantras, whose nature is pure self-reflection.
This is the meaning.

Now, let it be granted that conceptual thought possesses the quality of reflective awareness (vimarśakatva) due to its connection with the discursive speech (sañjalpa) delineated by the autonomy of the Knower (kṣetrajña); yet, this very connection [is what constitutes its nature].
Furthermore, from what does this [consciousness] primarily arise? To this he says:
"Surely, let there be the state of being reflective (vimarśitā) due to its connection with independent linguistic expression (sañjalpa). (16.257)
If it is asked from where that [initial state] arose prior to reflection, then from where did that [reflection] arise when it is investigated?
Likewise, the first [state] would have to be provided by a teacher who is free from conceptual construction. (16.258)
Whatever internal discourse (*abhijalpa*) may have been transferred, that too must have come from another instructor.

If it is argued that this [discourse] arises from reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), then from where does that [awareness] itself come? He says: "If from reflective awareness, then from where does that [awareness] also come?
For in this way, reflective awareness arises for conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) through its connection with internal discourse, and from that [awareness], [the discourse arises].
The meaning is that there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) between the act of verbalizing and the yoga itself.
This very point must be understood here; thus he says "in the case of definition" (*nirūpaṇe*), and so forth.
For in the case of a definition, [the knowledge] originates from some primary, foundational teacher characterized as being superior and mature.

Reflection (*vimarśa*) would assume the very nature of the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) just described; for it is that which, having been transmitted to the disciple, attains the state of being discursive speech (*sañjalpa*), and through connection with which even conceptualization possesses the capacity for reflective awareness (*parāmṛṣṭṛtva*). But if this is so, from where does this [reflection] originate even for the teacher?
Anticipating this objection, it was said: "For him too, there is another instructor."
Fearing that this infinite regress might thus lead to the destruction of the very root [of the tradition], he says:
"In this way, from the sequence of each preceding [teacher], it was exactly as it was from the primordial Guru in the beginning. (16.259)
For that conversation which was transmitted indeed still exists today; let it be understood thus:

by following the sequence of instruction in its proper order, from the presence of the Primordial Guru, the Supreme Lord whose nature is innate awareness, that very first conversation which occurred on all sides—
Having transferred itself into all subsequent teachings in successive order, it continues to persist even today by means of its transferred activity,
extending down to the level of the illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛ); let this be understood, for there is no infinite regress whatsoever.
This is the meaning.

And thus, whatever conceptual transaction arises brought about by its majesty, that too is certainly of its very nature—so he says: "Whatever independent [activity] there may be, by the power of such discourse... (16.260).
Even that conceptualization which is imagined is itself certain to be of the nature of that [consciousness] alone.
Thus, proceeding from the Primordial Guru onwards until this present time, it continues as a single entity through the transference of its functions,
manifesting in the form of various internal verbalizations.
Success!

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then in a case where there is a difference in reflective awareness (*parāmarśabheda*) when learning another word from a given word—such as *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*—what should be understood there? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Or if a distinction is defined in this way, such as 'jar' and 'pot'... (16.261)
That [position] too, because it involves the conceptualization of something else, must be diligently disregarded;
for it is clearly appropriate to apply the conceptual distinctions of "he bargains" and "he acts" [to the agent]. (16.262)

How indeed could those two, the verbal designations "hand" (kara) and "palm" (pāṇi), be confused? If indeed a distinction of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is described in such a manner— as when the reflective awareness of a "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is different from the reflective awareness of a "pot" (*kumbha*)— then that [distinction]...

Because it involves abandoning one's own appropriate prior reflection and adopting a different conceptualization, this [error] must be avoided even with great effort. Indeed, it is not at all appropriate to clearly conceive that the words *kara* and *pāṇi* mean "hand" simply because *kara* means "he does" (*karoti*) and *pāṇi* means "he deals" (*paṇāyate*) through gambling and the like.
"At some point they may even become conflated, as they partake in the nature of a single reflective awareness and verbal expression"—this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how can the acquisition of proficiency from one word to another—which is indeed possible—be denied? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Therefore, the acquisition of proficiency [in meaning] occurs from one word to another through an intermediary.
However, through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), that [consciousness] directly reflects upon various designations; therefore,

by means of the non-confusion of verbal discourse (*sañjalpa*) and through the mediation of bringing to presence its own appropriate prior reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), [it functions] from one word to another word.
Just as there is an understanding of the term "kumbha" (jar) from the term "ghaṭa," so too,
through the linguistic usage of elders, that proficiency arises directly and without mediation for everyone by virtue of the composition of words in their various forms— this is the meaning.

Thus, the true reality of the matter here is concluded—as he says: "The arising of the reflective awareness of that [object] should flash forth as consisting of one's own primordial self-reflection. (16.264)
To the extent that a child's cognition consists of unartificial reflective awareness (*vimarśana*),

therefore, the emergence of the reflective awareness of a jar or other objects arises as being composed solely of the reflective awareness of one's own self, transmitted through the lineage of the elders.

The meaning is this: since even for a child who has not yet acquired proficiency in the relationship between words and their referents, there occurs a vibration within the innate self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*)—which cannot be joined with verbal expression—what need is there to mention such proficiency in those who possess it? *Note: The term *vimarśana* refers here to the reflective awareness of one's own consciousness, which is non-artificial and transcends linguistic mediation.*
And for this very reason, there is this distinction of the mantras by which the Supreme Lord shows them favor; thus he says:
"Therefore, the conceptualization arising from the specific word-meanings of those mantras... (16.265).
The mantra is honored by one who perceives it as distinct from that which arises from other words;
and furthermore, that which was previously described as the nature of consciousness regarding seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and so forth. (16.266)

How could that [consciousness] belong to anyone other than Him? Why, then, should there be the conceptualization of another? For this reason—namely, because other words manifest as being composed of their respective primordial self-reflection—they [do not arise] from the conceptualizations produced by those other words.

The Lord has honored the mantra by directly perceiving— that is, by realizing through direct experience— the conceptualization that arises from the specific words and meanings of mantras, which consist of innate and uninterrupted self-reflection (*vimarśa*), as being distinct and characterized by difference.

The meaning is that it has been taught as being supremely worthy of adoption. Although other words denoting "that" (the Absolute) consist of supreme awareness (*paravimarśa*), they arise— according to the tradition of the usage of the elders— in their respective ways through a gradual process of descent (*avarohakrama*) in the form of gross discursive speech (*sañjalpa*).

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, the fact that mantras consist of an uninterrupted, innate awareness (*sahaja-parāmarśa*) from the beginningless Guru down to the present day remains entirely unchanged. For this very reason, as was previously stated:
By such passages as, “Everything consisting of seed-syllables and clusters [of phonemes], by effecting the state of vibration within consciousness...,” the nature of seed-syllables, clusters,
and so forth as being of the form of awareness has been stated; however, that belongs to that [consciousness] alone and not...
This is because it has already been stated that other words would likewise result in a gross form according to their respective natures.

Therefore, why should one postulate another act of reflective awareness (*vimarśāntara*)—which has descended through a lineage of successive teachers—regarding the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*), whose nature is uninterrupted consciousness? There is no such need here.
The meaning is: the state of being on an equal footing with internal discourse.
With this very intention, it is stated throughout the entire scripture that the primary characteristic of a guru is precisely his mastery of mantra and tantra—thus he says:
"For this purpose, the characteristics of the guru have been described with effort in various places therein. (16.267)

Thus has the characteristic been described: he who is proficient in mantra and tantra. Therefore, a teacher must in every way be one who is devoted to the thorough cultivation of the meaning of mantra—so it is said.
Therefore, for the sake of awakening to the meaning of the mantra, one should respectfully study the *Mantravārtika*.

Or the Guru should in every way employ the process of reasoning and refutation (ūhāpoha). Now, one might ask: "If such a Guru does not exist, then what should be done? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But in the absence of one who knows the meaning of the mantra, [one should practice] in every way that which is identical with the mantra. (16.269)
"One should make the guru...
identical with the mantra"—the meaning is that he has attained oneness with the mantra.
Therefore he says: "...
for through the practice of that, this [consciousness] consists of its volition.
Now, one might object: "Is there not also another kind of discursive thought (abhijalpa) belonging even to a Guru who possesses a firm and deeply rooted cultivation of the meaning of mantras?"

[Objection: "The majesty [of the mantra] is indeed equal to that of the Mantra itself; so how can it be said that there is no equality of status between mantras and other forms of internal discourse? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When there is an internal discourse identical to that [mantra], through the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra... (16.270)
"In that case, if there were total identity [between the mantra and other speech], tell me, what difference could there be?"—
anticipating the objection, "But total identity is unproven, for the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) of speech other than the mantra is indeed different," he says:
Moreover, if there were even a partial disparity, that causal efficiency would not arise from it. (16.271)
"In dissimilarity" (vaiṣamye) means: in the difference from the mantra due to its sequential order and so forth. "From that" (tataḥ) means: from the internal discourse (abhisañjalpa).
"That" (sā) refers to: the effect of the mantra. || 271 ||

But he who, even though there is a difference [between the causes], perceives a single purposeful action—as a worm [arising] from both a worm and cow dung, or as a single effect from both a worm and the recitation of a mantra—he is indeed Śiva; thus it is said:
"When, according to the principle that 'the worm comes from cow dung and from the worm,' [one perceives the unity of the effect]."
Even from within another verbal discourse, one perceives that very same purposeful action.
Therefore, he whose internal discourse is truth is said to be Śiva himself.
He demonstrates this very quality of having truthful internal discourse:
"Whatever he speaks, that indeed becomes a mantra bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (16.273)
With this very intention, the Blessed One has aphorized: "Speech is recitation" (Śivasūtra 3.27). ||273||
"But this is not our position," he says:
"This is not the position of Abhinavagupta, whose self is offered to the Mantra, who asserts that even two such similar insects possess distinct causal efficacy. (16.274)

Furthermore, this is not the view of the illustrious Abhinavagupta, who is intent upon contemplating the experience of the true nature of those respective mantras; for he describes a distinct causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) even for two insects produced from a worm and cow dung, because he admitted a difference in their effects (*kāryabheda*).
This is the meaning. ||274||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how can it be denied that even without a mantra, for those who possess a certain degree of contemplation on the meaning of the mantra, its accomplishment arises from mere verbalization alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One whose mind is offered to the mantra may, by saying something else, remove poison."
The meaning is that his mind is offered to the mantra; thus, he has established a continuous connection with the very potency (*vīrya*) of the mantra.
"Something" refers to verses, songs, and so forth, as was stated previously:
"Since whatever there may be, such as *śloka*s, *gāthā*s, and so forth, is joined with a beginning and an end,
therefore one who knows it sees all of that precisely as mantra. (Tattvāloka 3.225).

[Objection: "If the neutralization of poison and so forth could indeed be accomplished simply by fixing the mind upon a mantra, then what would be the point of uttering any word whatsoever, which would be irrelevant to that effect? [Reply: Certainly!—to this he says:
"That very mantra is the word; it is merely [the word] in that context, like a jar or other such objects. (16.275)

He makes this very point even more heart-felt by means of an illustration: "A lover, always beautiful through his conversations regarding union with his beloved, even while performing other tasks, remains satisfied within himself because he is permeated by those [conversations]. (16.276)

Likewise, one who has been cultivated by the internal discourse of that mantra will certainly produce the same effect, even when speaking something else and even without desiring it, because they have become of that very nature. (16.277)

"It is satisfied" means that, by virtue of the essence of the wonder of its enjoyment, it comes to rest within itself. "Speaking something else as well" means that even one who is unwilling, through the very act of speaking another thing, takes on that same nature insofar as it consists of the internal dialogue of mantra.

The meaning is that, by virtue of constant practice, he becomes composed solely of mantra; for this very reason, it is said that he performs his functions in accordance with the mantra alone. || 277 ||
One might object: "Even in the absence of the desire for verbalizing with mantras, how can there be the manifestation of this [reality] through its very identity?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For even while conceptualizing one object, one perceives another as well."
The meaning is that for a cognizer who conceptualizes a mountain, there would indeed be the perception of a jar.
He supports this by means of a scriptural citation: "It is stated in the Śrīpūrvaśāsana that [it is like] mantras and so forth that remove poison. (16.278)
And so it is said there:
"One whose mind is unwavering in reality, even while enjoying sense objects,
is not touched by their defects, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water."
"Even while consuming poison, one who is equipped with mantras and the like that remove poison is not deluded by it; likewise is the yogin of great intelligence. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 18.81).
Here, the meaning is as follows: just as a snake-charmer, even while consuming poison...

The great-minded yogi, even while experiencing sense objects, perceives the Self as abiding in its own essential nature alone; because his mind is unwavering, he regards them as the Supreme Reality itself. || 278 ||

As for what was said— that when one who is intent on the meaning of a mantra speaks in this very way and thereby removes poison, that is the manifestation of the mantra alone, and not of the word which is invariably concomitant with it— the author states another position regarding that very point:

Alternatively, even regarding the destruction of poison, there will be variety due to the difference in causes, arising from the infinite diversity of effects such as the replenishment of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and so forth. || 16-279 ||

"Due to the difference in cause" means [the difference] between that which consists of mantra, sound, and so forth. For, just like a mantra, even mere verbal discourse can produce any one of the effects such as the destruction of poison, the nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), or restoration. ||279||

Having thus stated the existence of mantras, he also states their purpose: "In this way, through the practice of the conceptualization of mantra-discourse, the manifestation of the object to be meditated upon occurs by means of the gradual diminution of that discourse. (16.280)
Thus, by the sequence described above, through the progressive intensity of the practice of the two— mantra and reflective awareness (vimarśa)—

the discursive nature and other qualities become subordinate, and there occurs the manifestation and direct realization of the reality that is the mantra-deity, which is meditated upon as non-different from oneself.
This is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection, "How can one who practices this mental discourse of mantras achieve the direct perception of the object to be realized?", he says:
"He meditates upon the object itself, and not upon this mental discourse again."
One employs the means of manifestation; but once it has manifested, what is the use of that [means] therein?
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then what is the purpose of its recourse to discursive thought (sañjalpa)? Anticipating this doubt, he says "this" and so forth.
To the question "What follows from that?", the intention is as follows: "Once the goal (upeya) has been attained, what further use is there for the means (upāya)?
He demonstrates this very point through the manner of a concluding summary:
Thus, when discursive thought has been diminished, the non-conceptual reality—consisting of innate self-reflection and characterized by supreme clarity—shines forth. (16.282)
But surely, even in the case of non-conceptual [cognition], it is said: "Those afflicted by lust, grief, fear, madness, thieves, dreams, and so forth,
perceive even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them."

Having raised the objection— “If, according to such statements, even that which exists does not appear, why then is it said that in this case too, only the real object (*vastu*) itself shines forth?”— he says: “And that non-conceptual consciousness perceives clearly just as it is.”
For that [object] exists externally as well, because it possesses that very nature of reality (tathātmatva). || 16-283 ||
For even in the case of external objects, their existence is entirely dependent upon that [consciousness]—this is the meaning. ||283||
But for the Guru, who possesses non-difference from Śiva, there is especially the state of having true intentions; thus he says:
"Especially for one who possesses non-difference from the Śiva-nature that transcends Māyā, verbal expression is the means to liberation; indeed, bondage and liberation proceed from that. (16.284)
The meaning is that [this] is the means for the disciple’s liberation. But surely,
by the statement "every conceptual construction (vikalpa) is saṃsāra," intentionality (saṅkalpa) would instead be a cause of bondage?

Anticipating the question, "Why is it stated here that this [Guru] is the means for liberation?", he says: "Bondage and liberation arise from him, so it is said. Here, bondage and liberation would indeed occur solely through the volition (*saṅkalpa*) of the Guru, who possesses non-illusory identity with Śiva; however, there is this much distinction: in the state of duality...
Otherwise, however, there is liberation. ||284||
Now, one might object: "Even so, this [liberation] is logically possible only from that which has reached the ultimate limit of non-conceptuality (*avikalpaka*), and not otherwise;
therefore, how can liberation arise from mere discursive speech (*sañjalpa*) alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even in the case of conceptual thought, [liberation occurs] through the Guru who fully partakes in non-differentiated Śiva-nature."
Waiting for the ultimate limit of non-conceptuality is not necessary. || 16-285 ||
In this context, the reason why [the guru] is not employed [as a separate entity] is that the guru consists of non-difference from Śiva. ||285||
And this is not established by reasoning alone; thus he says:

"For that deity of the mantra, who is to be expressed, has the nature of its own reflective awareness (vimarśa); she is said to be closely proximate to the Great Consciousness (mahāsaṃvid) in the venerable Gama scripture. (16.286)
The meaning is that the mantra is, by its very nature, of the essence of non-conceptual consciousness. ||286||

Thus, because they are in close proximity to the consciousness of another, mantras and the like are dependent upon it and are able to accomplish spiritual attainment (*siddhi*); in order to state this by first presenting an illustration, he says:
Just as those standing near kings can effectively accomplish for others the success associated with royalty,
so too do mantras and the like quickly bring about the supreme attainment.
"The supreme accomplishment" (parāṃ siddhim) refers to that characterized by liberation (mokṣa). As it has been said:
"The inferior accomplishment bestows subjugation; the middling accomplishment bestows the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva);
the superior accomplishment grants the severance of the fear of saṃsāra."
Thus [ends the section]. ||287 ||
And this has also been stated in our own scripture; thus he says:
"That which was stated in the Śrī Mālinīmata contains the aforementioned intention.
He states that very point:
When it was asked by the sages, "For what reason is this the definition of mantras? [it was replied: 16-288.
Why is this?—the sense is: since the question concerns the subject of yoga, why has the definition of mantra been stated?
As it has been said: "When asked by the Goddess concerning the procedure for the path of yoga, the Supreme Lord [responded]..."
"Even by one who holds that thesis, it has been asked: 'For what purpose is the definition of mantra? (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.2). ||288||
Desiring thus to resolve the Sage’s question, Kārttikeya spoke as follows to state that this has been taught precisely as a limb of yoga:
"They desire yoga to be the oneness of one entity with another entity."
That object is said to be "knowable" for the sake of establishing its status as something to be abandoned and so forth.
For the sake of its accomplishment, Śiva has taught the knowledge that has been described here,
as well as the characteristics of mantra, which are sufficient for the perfect attainment of yoga with seed (sabījayoga).
And there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śaṅkara without initiation;
and that [initiation] is said to be twofold, according to the distinction between action and knowledge. (16.291)
That [initiation] is to be performed in two ways, and for that reason this has been illustrated;
moreover, eligibility for yoga does not arise through this alone.
Furthermore, eligibility for the practice of mantra and liberation are attained through Śiva-initiation;
since this has already been established by the previous explanation, it is not analyzed and explained again here.
However, according to the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the author himself says this in order to explain it:
"By this, it is also stated that the yogi [acts] for the sake of achieving oneness with reality. (16.293)
With reverence, one should rely on the mantra as the root until reaching the state beyond conceptual construction (nirvikalpa),
while accomplishing either worldly enjoyment or liberation through the practice of mantra.

Therein, for the sake of attaining eligibility, one should receive initiation from a teacher (*daiśika*). By the word "respectfully" (*ādṛtaḥ*), his single-minded devotion to that [teacher] is expressed. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the recourse to mantras and so forth.
Therefore, through the greatness of this [practice], including the mantras and so forth, everything—including both worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti)—is accomplished; thus he says:
"By the power of that mantra, knowledge, and yoga, whatever one may strive to accomplish... (16.295)
That [realization] would belong to this disciple who is joined with the Guru, even though he possesses other principles;
"joined" (yukta) means "united" (yojita). By this, the distinction from the "uniter" (yojikā) and others is also indicated.

One might object: "If he has been joined to another reality (tattva) by the Guru, how then could his experience or liberation occur otherwise, solely through his own power? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For initiation is indeed useful for his purification; once purified, he [attains it]. (16.296)
The wise man attains either worldly enjoyment or liberation through his own power alone;
for this very reason, even if the rules of the *samayin* and other stages were established during initiation, they would not be necessary—thus he says:
"Therefore, one who is strong through the power of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*), yoga, and so forth, having previously been a *samayin*... (16.297).
A spiritual son (putraka) may not even be that much; rather, he is one who conforms to his own strength.
"That much" refers to either a regular initiate (samayin) or a spiritual son.
Now, one might ask: what is the situation for one who is weak in the yoga of knowledge and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But he who is barren of the yoga of higher knowledge and the like is like a blind man on a path. (16.298)
"Dependent upon the teacher alone would it be in every respect, both for enjoyment and for liberation.
Anticipating the objection—"But what can even a teacher do for one who is barren of knowledge, yoga, and so forth?"—he says:
"And initiation alone [bestows] one's own internal [realization], even without knowledge. (16.299)

It was previously stated, both through reasoning and scripture, that [the subject] is indeed the *mocikā* (the liberator). "Previously" refers to the beginning of the fifteenth chapter (*āhnika*) and so forth.
Anticipating the objection, "What would happen if one were to practice knowledge, yoga, and so forth, which are appropriate only for those who have been initiated? he says:
"But as for the disciple who, having relied solely on the union [with the deity] effected by initiation... (16.300)
Having resorted to the yoga of knowledge appropriate for that [attainment] in order to bring it to manifestation, he too attains identity with that very object with which he is joined. (16.301)
"In that very [state] he is disciplined" means by the Guru. ||301||
Therefore, this [attainment] depends solely upon the Guru; thus he says:
"Consequently, his entire state of being is dependent upon the Guru, initiation, mantra, and scripture.
Having thus explained this with respect to the *putraka* and others, he now explains it with respect to the *sādhaka*:
Of all those who are wicked—whether past, present, or future.

One who desires worldly enjoyment—such as a kingdom, heaven, and so forth—is like a child; for such a person, the purification of actions should not be performed through auspicious means alone. (16.303)

"Desiring to abandon supramundane enjoyment"—this refers to the practitioner who follows worldly dharma (*lokadharmī*) and seeks [mundane] objects. "Even in the auspicious"—the connection with the preceding [text] is that purification must be performed even in those [auspicious acts]. Here too, [it applies] to both action and knowledge.
Regarding its predominance, he says this specific distinction:
"In that regard, while performing initiation consisting of material substances (dravyamayi-dīkṣā) with clarified butter, sesame seeds, and so forth... (16.304).
The supreme teacher should offer oblations with the thought, "I shall purify his karma.
However, in the initiation consisting of knowledge, that [karma] is purified through the union [of the disciple's soul with the Supreme]. || 16.305 ||
Through the power of the Guru, who is firmly established in his own self-awareness, there occurs the destruction of that [karma];
when one's inauspicious karmas have been purified, then [only] the auspicious remains. (16.306)

"Because it relies on its own gradations, it bestows birth in the midst of the paths"—that is, *karman*. "Connected" means through continuous contemplation (*anusandhāna*). "Of this one" refers to the follower of worldly dharma (*lokadharmī*).

But regarding the enjoyment of the results of auspicious karma, one reaches the very station of conjunction; thus he says: "From the completion of the enjoyment of the fruits obtained through the sequence of the ripening of the auspicious. (16.307)

"Wherever this [individual] has been joined, remaining there once the destruction of future karma has been accomplished"— by implication, "remaining there" means that [destruction occurs] only through experience; for the purification of auspicious karma is not prescribed for one who follows the ways of the world— this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, as long as his future auspicious karma is not exhausted, he continues to experience [the results] here and there—thus it is said:
"And of those future [bodies], which are distinguished by being located in the first body or in other bodies... (16.308).
Upon the purification of the impure portions, there would be no exhaustion of experience itself—
referring to those [experiences] occurring from this day until the body [falls away], that is, during the time following initiation.
For this very reason, there shall be no experience of suffering for him anywhere; thus he says: "While he is constantly enjoying enjoyments until the end of the dissolution of māyā... (16.309).
"Nothing within the body and so forth, even in the midst of the path, yields the fruit of suffering—up to the end of the dissolution of Māyā. This means: as far as the end of the dissolution of Māyā.
Anticipating the question, "Once the dissolution into Māyā has occurred, what would happen to him? he says:
"Then, upon the dissolution into Māyā, having experienced all enjoyments of pleasure... (16.310).
"By the power of the *yojanikā* [union], one attains dissolution either in the partless (*niṣkala*) or the with-parts (*sakala*).
He concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with the first half of the verse:
'Thus has the object of knowledge been declared, as it pertains to the Guru at the time of initiation. (16.311)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Objects of Knowledge," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 16.

Thus, this object of knowledge has been explained here: in what manner and by what means the initiation of the Guru should be performed at the time of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). May there be auspiciousness! (311)
Having contemplated both the purifier and the object of purification as manifested through the greatness of the illustrious Guru,
the one known by the name Jayaratha has here explained this sixteenth chapter.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Objects of Knowledge," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. 16.
The Seventeenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
[I bow to] that which possesses the power of mastery in the skillful movement through the manifold expansion of karma produced by its own inherent powers.
I bow to the Bestower of Strength, who brings about the power to cross over worldly existence.
Now, with the second half of this very [verse], he promises to explain the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) which serves a great purpose:
"Next, I shall describe the method that bestows identity with Bhairava."
He states that very point: "Thus, in the five—the mandala, the jar, the fire, the disciple, and one's own self. (17.1)

Having grasped the pervasion through identity, one should project the path residing within the disciple onto his arms and likewise onto his throat— the three impurities of karma, māyā, and the individual soul (aṇu).
And the instructor should cast [the thread] upon the crest by means of a knot in the thread;
for here, by the word "pitcher" (kumbha), the small water-jar (karkarī) is also included by implication, since it was stated "in five.
"By means of a knot in the thread" means by way of its identity with that [deity]. As it has been said:
"Having first bound the cage of fetters— both adventitious and innate, pertaining to power—
with a triple-stranded thread of three qualities upon the arms, the neck, and the tips of the topknots.
Thus [it is said].
Anticipating the question, "What is the intention behind including these as knots (granthi)? he says:
"The appearance of that [Self] as having a nature other than its own is impurity (mala); it is proclaimed as the knot. (17.3)
The external knot is postulated for the sake of strengthening this conviction:

that which appears as something other than that Supreme Brahman— which is the nature of full light— and which manifests as a contracted self, is itself called *mala* (impurity) because it conceals one's true nature.
And because it acts as an obstruction, it is called a "knot" (granthi). To confirm this very point, knots are fashioned in this manner within the external *pāśasūtra* and other such items.
Anticipating the question, "Even so, why was this stated specifically regarding the arms and so forth? he says:
"The arms are the locus of action; Viṣṇu, whose nature is *māyā*, is situated in the throat. (17.4)
The crest-lock (śikhā) flows downwards and possesses the nature of an atom; therefore, this conceptualization has been made.
"Māyātman" [is said] because of its authority within that [māyā]. "Flowing downwards" means that the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti) extends from there as far as the heart.
One might ask: "Even so, what is the purpose of tripling the thread three times? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The manifold diversity of the triad known as Nara, Śakti, and Śiva. (17.5)
One should fashion a thread three times threefold (ninefold) for the purpose of tying it;
for this entire [universe] consists of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva—this is the intended meaning.
In this very context, in order to demonstrate pervasion even according to the system of other treatises, he says:
"This triad of fire, water, and food is each also threefold. (17.6)
Therefore, some [teachers] at the end of the Vedas (śrutyante) have accepted [the sequence] as white, black, and red.

Regarding "at the end of the Vedas": as it is stated in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* during the instruction to Śvetaketu—"From the one Supreme Brahman, fire (tejas) was born; from that, water (āpaḥ); from those, food (anna). Each one of these..."
"It became threefold; therein, fire came to have red, white, and black forms: that which was red is fire (*tejas*), that which was white is water (*āpas*), and that which was black is food (*anna*).
From this—because the triad of fire, water, and food is of such a nature—in this [context], within the direct locus of experience.
Since burning, drying, and other such effects might be expected when the severing of bonds (*pāśaccheda*) and so forth are performed upon the body, this process—

designated by the term *sūtra* because it suggests the infinite bonds and other factors residing in the primary body through its likeness to a substitute, and because it protects by serving as the means for their eradication— is here [described] as the severing of bonds and so forth.
"The task"—this is the meaning of the *pāśasūtra*. As the scripture states:
"The second is the body of the thread (*sūtradeha*), wherein these fetters (*pāśa*) reside; they are to be bound, severed, and likewise burnt while situated in the thread, not in the physical form."
Thus [it is said].
Having thus described the arrangement of the ritual manual, he speaks of the purification of reality:
"Then, in the fire, which is nothing but the space of consciousness, all mantras are offered as libations. (17.7)
One should perform the purification of the principles (tattvas) sequentially in their universal form;
for in our system, purification is indeed nothing other than the realization of them as being solely the universal space of consciousness (cidvyoma)— this is the intended meaning.
He says that very thing: "There, one should first invoke the Earth by means of the yoga of one's own mantra. (17.8)
Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, one should then satisfy [the deity] with clarified butter, sesame seeds, and so forth;
thereafter, one should worship the presiding deity of the Māyā-tattva, who pervades that very principle.
Having invoked the power of Māyā with her own mantra and worshipped her, one should satisfy her.

"Of that principle" (tattattva) refers to that principle called Earth (dharā). "The power of Māyā" (māyāśakti) refers to her in the form of Vāgīśvarī. "With her own mantra" (svamantreṇa) means with "Oṃ Hrīṃ."
Now, one might object: "Previously, it was stated that the collection of phonemes belonging to both the Mātṛkā and Mālinī [systems] constitutes the group of principles (tattva) beginning with Earth;
therefore, which of these is intended here as the mantra? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the invocation, the phoneme of the Mātṛkā; and in the worship, the phoneme of the Mālinī. (17.10)
The Guru said that one should perform [this] because of the two-fold nourishment of oneself;

"in worship"—that is to say, by implication, also in libation (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth. For since Mātṛkā is the mother of the universe, it is appropriate that she possesses a distinct nature from her own form; and as for Mālinī, [she is so] because the universe [is contained] within her own self.
It has been stated that [the mantras] possess the quality of sustaining and nourishing—due to the two functions of [maintaining] their own nature and providing nourishment.
This very point is shown here as a dyad:
the syllable *tāra*, then the word for the perfective case ending (*saṃbuddhi*), and thereafter the word *tvām*. (17.11)
Then follows the word for the action joined with the singular supreme [suffix], which serves as the illuminator;
thereafter, your name in the dative case (caturthī), which is likewise appropriately illuminated. (17.12)
Thus, one should perform each respective rite by means of the application of the *ūha-mantra*.

*Tāra* is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). A *varṇa* is a letter of the *mātṛkā*, such as *kṣaḥ* for the Earth (*dharā*). "In the vocative" refers to [the ending] *dhare* and so forth. "The supreme" refers to [the word] *āvāhayāmi* (I invoke). The "illuminator" is *namaḥ*.
"Name" refers to [the names] of the earth element and so forth. "Appropriate" means: *namaḥ* (salutation) in worship and the like; *svāhā* and so forth in the fire-oblation (*homa*).

Now, one might ask: "Why is worship and so forth prescribed here at the very beginning of the invocation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is taught that all ritual action follows immediately after the invocation. (17.13)
Now, one might object: "What indeed is meant by 'invocation' (āvāhana), since worship and other rites could be performed even immediately [without it]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And invocation is the awakening [of the deity] from its abiding in its own essential nature."
The state of being absorbed into identity with the self that consists of "I" (aham) is the nature of existence. || 17-14 ||

For "invocation" (āvāhana) is indeed the awakening of an entity already established in its own nature; they know that invocation is merely the bringing about of the presence of that which is already established.
According to this principle, [it occurs] within one's own self, whose nature is the reflective awareness of the perfect "I" (pūrṇāhaṃparāmarśa).

The state of being made to enter as a single identity is merely the act of becoming present before one, not the actual entry itself; for if it were the latter, it would be the Śiva-state (śaivī daśā) and not the Śakti-state—this is the intended meaning. ||14||
For this very reason, he says:
"And that very stage is called the Śākta, in which there is primary worshipability.
Now, why is it that worshipability exists primarily only on the Śākta level?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because it is unmanifest and because there is no difference, for that [consciousness] does not belong to the two natures of man and Śiva. (17.15)

"Because of its non-manifestation"—this means because of its insentience (*jāḍya*). "Because of non-differentiation"—this means because the distinction between the worshipped and the worshipper has dissolved. It is with this very intention that it was stated: "One should not employ mantras in the individual soul (*pums*), nor in the Supreme Reality (*para-tattva*), nor in the Power (*śakti*)," and so forth. (15)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, how can worship and the like be appropriate for insentient things such as the earth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, for the sake of establishing consciousness within the principles (tattvas) that appear as insentient, the Guru [proceeds]."
Having first performed the invocation using the case endings up to the fourth case ending.
One should conceive of full existence through the application of ending with the *namaskāra* (salutation).
He demonstrates this very point:
"Therefore, there is the state of having a full nature due to the union with the abundance of that form. (17–17)
For the object of meditation (dhyeya) becomes predominant by virtue of the meditator's (dhyātṛ) state of submissiveness;
for in an act of salutation, through the subordination of the one who salutes, the one being saluted alone attains primacy— this is the intended meaning.

Our teachers maintain that other scriptures should also be explained in exactly this same way; thus he says: "Having invoked, worshipped, and gratified [the deities]," as it is set forth in the *Śrīsvacchanda*. (17–18)
"Our teachers have declared that it must be led along this very path.

Now, one might object: "The Śākta state is both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā) because it consists of both difference and non-difference; however, the Śaiva state is supreme because it consists solely of non-difference. Therefore, how can it be said here that there is no worship?"
Anticipating this objection, he says: "But that which is to be worshipped as the Supreme is of the nature of autonomous consciousness. (17–19)
Because its luminosity is undivided, it is not an object of illumination anywhere.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then why is it said that the Self 'is to be known, is to be reflected upon, and is to be meditated upon'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For it is this [consciousness] that manifests as its being worthy of worship, its being the object of meditation, and so forth.
Its very sovereignty consists in its capacity to accomplish that which is otherwise most difficult to achieve.

For this very reason, since [qualities] such as being worthy of worship are not primary, there is no utility for summoning and so forth here; thus he says: "In that [reality], whose nature is pure consciousness, how could there be an invocation? (17–21).
Indeed, in the act of illumination, there would be no such thing as the luminosity of light.

Therefore, since [the state of being] worshipful and so forth is merely the unfolding of His sovereignty, how could there be an act of addressing Śiva, who is the very self that performs the act of addressing?

It is not logical for it to be something being awakened; for when illumination is produced by another, the light itself would not possess the nature of being luminous, but rather the state of being illuminated—
this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then when an invocation such as 'I invoke the deity' is performed, what should be understood [as the underlying reality]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even without the vocative case-ending, [the deity is present] by virtue of its capacity as the object (karman) and other grammatical relations. (17–22)
To demonstrate that [power] through its autonomy, one should perform this here, thinking, "I invoke the deity"; thereafter, the lamp for the deity. (17–23)
By the previously mentioned reasoning, the [mantras] beginning with *namaḥ* and *svāhā* bestow fullness;
thus, since modification (*ūha*) is possible here as well, the application of the "illuminator" (*dīpaka*) should be performed according to what is appropriate—
so he says, starting with "tataḥ" and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "Does every illuminating factor, such as salutation and the like, bestow fullness, or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Praise is fullness; it is the supreme nourishment arising from the union of fire and moon. (17.24)
One should kindle the nourishing *procchāla* with *vauṣaṭ* and so forth.
Regarding what was previously stated as "the conjunction of fire and moon"—
[it is] by means of the syllable of nectar, *śvā*.
Thus:
"............ by means of the form of fire............," so it is said.
"Paraṃ svāhā. "Proccālam"—the meaning is that by this [mantra], it brings about nourishment even more abundantly. As the scripture states: "Vauṣaṭ is prescribed for nourishing... and so forth.
Thus [ends the section]. || 24 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, since there is no distinction anywhere, should modification (ūha) be performed or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, even in the external [rite], the ritual action is enjoined as being established through identity [with the internal]. (17–25)
If the teacher should at any time not infer that word of action [through its own form],
then it is "renowned in the world" by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or similarity of form (*tādrūpya*)— this is the meaning. "It is enjoined" means "it is prescribed"— this is the meaning.
He demonstrates this very point:
"It is employed for the manifestation of that object which has not yet been manifested. (17.26)
What use would a mantra be there where that which is clearly manifest is already present?
Therefore, in rites such as sprinkling, consecration, and recitation, [the mantra] is certainly [required]. (17–27)
One should perform that *abhyūhana* (supplementation) of the ritual action; otherwise, it would result in an obstruction.

"Mantra" refers to the form of supplementing the words of the ritual action. "That" refers to the action to be supplemented. "By that" means by the reason that the action manifests itself externally on its own. For [actions such as] sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth—

The intended meaning is that [the object] clearly manifests externally precisely as suchness; therefore, one should not engage in excessive mental projection (atyabhyūhana) by means of such expressions as "I am performing the sprinkling" and so forth.
Furthermore, when such selfhood does not manifest externally, this is the result—thus he says:
"In the absence of such selfhood externally, the result is the extraction of the state of karma. (17.28)

In cases such as "I perform the satiation" (*tarpaṇam karomi*) or "I perform the worship" (*arcām karomi*), which involve satisfaction, the offering of oblations (*āhuti*), the burning of the noose (*pāśa-ploṣa*), and the severing [of bonds], one must apply the appropriate modification. For satisfaction and the like do not appear externally in their own form, in the same way that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites do— this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "hutabhukpāśaploṣe": the meaning is "at the burning of the bonds by the consumer of oblations (fire)," and so forth.
And one should not infer [the existence of] an action even when there is no manifestation of such a nature externally with respect to the intended whole; thus he says:
"Where, after a rule has been stated, [it is subsequently understood] through its endless constituent actions... (17.29).
There, [the goal] is to be accomplished through parts; there is no [need for] inference, as in the case of the rites of initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*) and so forth.

"That" refers to the object characterized by the prescribed rite. "By infinite parts consisting of action" refers to [rites] such as *garbhādhāna* (conception) and so forth. "As in the case of the rites of initiation and so forth"—for one does not say, "I am performing initiation."
The meaning is that this must be a single *ūha* (modification), namely: "I perform the consecration."
Having thus spoken in connection with this incidental topic, he states the subject at hand:
"Then, the striking of the disciple with the Astra-mantra at the location of each respective principle (tattva). (17.30)
Then, having performed [the rite] with the hand of Śiva, one should touch the heart;
thereafter, having reached the heart of the disciple indeed by way of one's own channel (nāḍī).
Having attained oneness with the self of the disciple and having taken him into one's own heart,
one should place him there, enveloped within the form of the *haṃsa*, by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
One should cause [the deity] residing in one's own heart to illuminate the body of the disciple with its splendors, without being separated from even a single ray of light. (17.33)

"Tataḥ" (then) means immediately after the libation to Vāgīśī. "Tattva" (the respective principle) refers to the striking with the Astra-mantra at the location of the invoked earth-principle and so forth, starting from the ankles. "Sva" (one's own) means on the right side for the Guru and on the left for the disciple. "Gatvā" (having gone) implies specifically to the heart. "Hṛd" (heart) refers to the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Regarding the *saṃhāramudrā*, it is said:
"Having slowly extended the right hand, starting from the little finger in sequence,
one should draw it back and form a fist, then press down with the thumb."
"The mudrā is declared to be the withdrawing one...
Thus it is said. The phrase "situated in one's own heart" should be applied according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (which serves both purposes simultaneously);
therefore, although situated in one's own heart, [it is characterized] by splendors that are never separated from the mere rays of light.
One should contemplate that which illumines the body of the disciple, so that the light of consciousness may never be separated from it.
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of bringing [the deity] from one's own heart to the disciple's self?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
By moving from its own place of bondage, by attaining its own independent state, and because it is not dependent on its own karma, it is capable of arising everywhere. (17.34)
Having first brought the person (pudgala) from his own heart by means of that [mantra],
he should then project its bodies— the principles of earth and so forth— into the illusion (māyā).
"In Māyā" means in the form of Vāgīśī. ||35||
And how does his creation occur? To this he says:

"In that regard, one should perform for him a single purificatory rite (saṃskriyā), beginning with the conception (garbhādhāna) along with the 'male-making' ceremony (puṃsavana) and so forth, up to the emergence from the womb. (17.36)
Birth and the state of being an enjoyer of experiences, when combined, constitute a single purification;
therefore, one should effect the dissolution of the self into identity with those very experiences. (17.37)

Then, one should perform the severance of the bonds of those respective principles (tattvas) within this group of four purificatory rites (saṃskāras), [employing] both the Aparā and the Parāparā [mantras].
One should apply the fifteen mantras or the supreme [mantra] in sequence;

by means of the first [mantra], the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) and so forth are included. Thus, by encompassing these intermediate sacraments (*saṃskāra*), the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) alone is the primary sacrament. Regarding this "tetrad":

[The stages] characterized by conception, enjoyment, being the enjoyer, dissolution therein, and the severing of the bonds; the word "vā" [in the original verse] is used in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya).
He divides the very fifteen mantras as follows: the group of eight beginning with Pibanī, the group of six beginning with Śastra, and likewise Parā. (17.39)
Thus, these fifteen [syllables] should be used in sequence for the consecration of dissolution (*līnatva*).
Right here, he shows the *homa* mantras: having first uttered the *aparā* mantra, and then [the mantra] beginning with "prāg" and "amukātmanaḥ. (17–40)
Saying, "I perform the *garbhādhāna*," the Guru, uttering that same mantra again ending with *svāhā*, should offer three oblations.
Then, [one recites] "of such-and-such a person," followed by the Parāparā mantra;
then one performs the Parāparā [mantra] for the purpose of granting the state of being an enjoyer of experiences to one who has been born.
Having first uttered "svāhā," he should offer three oblations;
then, having uttered the drinking mantra, [he says] "of such-and-such a self."

Thinking, "I shall cause [the deity] to dissolve into the enjoyments," one should again offer three oblations of clarified butter, sesame seeds, and other materials, ending with the word *svāhā*, using that same mantra.
This very same procedure applies from the *vamana* [rite] up to the end of the fifteenth;
first, the mantra consisting of the Supreme Self (*parātmaka*), and then "of such-and-such a person" (*amukātmanaḥ*).
Then, reciting the supreme mantra "I perform the severing of the bonds," followed by "huṃ svāhā phaṭ," one should offer three oblations.

Regarding these four groups of ritual actions that I have described, one should utter the word for the element Earth (dharātattva) prior to the words for the ritual action within those [mantras]. || 17-47 ||
Then, having addressed, worshipped, and gratified the image of the Lord of the Earth-principle (dharātattva),
the Guru, emboldened by the conceit of being Śiva, should command as follows:
O Lord of the Tattvas, by the command of Śiva, you must not place any obstacle in the way of this son of mine as he proceeds to the state free from suffering. (17.49)

Then, if the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should desire to purify separately the fivefold path beginning with the worlds, which resides within the interval between the earth-tattva and the [higher] principles, [he should proceed as follows].
Then, with a serene mind, one should offer three oblations each, as before, using the mantra *aparāmantra* joined with the modification "I purify the city" (*puraṃ śodhayāmi*). (17.51)

"Tameva" refers to the Aparā-mantra. "From the word 'karma'" means from that which has the characteristic of being "conception" (*garbhādhāna*) and so forth; therefore, the modification (*ūha*) consists of the Aparā-mantra in such forms as: "O Aparā-mantra, I perform the rite of conception for the soul named [so-and-so] in the earth-principle (*dharātattva*);
O Aparā-mantra, *svāhā*," and so on. "From that" refers to—

Immediately after the fourfold ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the word "having addressed" (*āmantrya*): because no other mantra is mentioned, it refers to the *aparā* mantra. As he will state: "In the purification up to the level of Māyā, all rites should always be performed with the *aparā* [mantra]. (Śloka 139)

Thus, in such an instruction, the cause is the state of being intensely absorbed in the conceit of Śiva. "From that" means immediately after the purification of the *tattvas*. "By means of the *aparā* mantra" means by relying upon the *aparā* mantra. By the phrase "as before," everything is implied, including other modifications (*ūha*). ||51||
He extends this very rule to other cases as well:
"In the same way, the wise one should offer three oblations each for the *kalās*, mantras, words, and phonemes, either separately or collectively. (17.52)
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the supreme mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
one should extract the disciple by means of the other mantra and lead him to the heart of one's own self.

"Separately" means one by one. "In their totality" means [thinking] "I shall purify the other five paths. "Having extracted" means from the purified principle. "The heart of the Self" refers to that of the Guru. (53)
Right here, he shows another opinion:
"But when, by means of one pure [principle], one considers its inclusion within that, one should not purify separately after hearing from the Lord of the Tattvas. (17.54)
Then, having offered the full oblation, one should lift up the individual soul (aṇu) and unite it with oneself;
for the sake of the yoga of abiding in that [Self] and abiding in the Self, one should offer further oblations with that same [mantra].
Some, however, maintain that one should give [the offering] accompanied by a verb;
others, the teachers, have declared that such [an offering] consists of creative contemplation (bhāvanā). 17.56
In this case, no separate external oblation should be offered to the teacher;
however, if one should offer it, there is no fault, for that is a means for meditative cultivation.
In this manner, the Guru should apply [the principles] to the former state of abiding in the body and abiding in the self;
thereafter, that Self should be led from that entire path into the heart of the disciple. (17.58)
And for the sake of achieving firmness in that purity, there should again be a full oblation with the *parā* [mantra].
First, the *mahāpāśupata* [rite] is for the purification of the reverse order. (17.59)
One should offer again with the Astra mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ" and cast it;
then, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should worship Māyā and subsequently dismiss her.
One should contemplate the earth-element as purified by water of pure form;
when mixed with that water, it then becomes fit for purification.

"By one"—that is, by any one of the paths beginning with the *tattva*. "One should not purify"—this implies the other fivefold path. "By that very same"—referring to the one previously introduced. "Offerings"—meaning three.
"Accompanied by the word for the object"—as in: "I make such-and-such a soul abide in the Self. "In this regard"—

Regarding the [terms] *tātsthyāt* and *mātmasthatva*: “of the spatial [teacher]” (*daiśikasya*) means of the agent (*kartuḥ*). “That” (*saḥ*) refers to the method characterized by external oblation (*bāhyāhutilakṣaṇaḥ*). “The previous” (*prāktana*) refers to [the passage]: “Then, by way of one’s own channel... ” (verse 17.31).

Thus it is stated in the passage beginning with "ityādi. Regarding the word "tataḥ" (from that): it means immediately after [the deity] has been led from the heart of the self to the heart. "The heart of the disciple is to be led"—the meaning is that [the deity] residing there should be made to act. Regarding the word "tāvataḥ" (of that much): it refers to the earth-nature (dharātman). Regarding "taddārḍhya" (for its firmness):
by the word "tat," there is a reference to the pure [state]. As it has been said:
Having lifted the disciple and established him within oneself, one should cause him to abide within that [disciple's] body;
then the wise one, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), should offer three oblations.

"By means of the Great Pāśupata weapon for the purification of the reverse order and so forth" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.68). "By water" means by the water-principle (*jalatattva*). "From that" means from the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the mixing of the earth-principle with the water-principle. || 61 ||
Extending that same principle by way of generalization, he distinguishes between purity and impurity:

"In the same manner, through the successive intermingling of the various principles (tattvas) of the city [of the body], the entire series of principles becomes Śiva-natured; otherwise, it remains pure only separately. (17.62)

"Thus" means in the manner described. "Otherwise" means impure. "Separately" implies that any entity distinct from Śiva is indeed a bond (*pāśa*); this is the intended meaning. As it was stated previously:
"That which is other than the supreme Śiva of the aforementioned nature is called a bond. (8.292)
Thus [ends the section]. ||62||
For this very reason, he says:
"And when that impurity called Māyā exists as a state of separation, there can be no liberation even upon the exhaustion of karma, as is the case with the Vidyeśvaras and others. (17.63)
Regarding "māyā"—as it has been said:
"The manifestation of differentiated objects of knowledge right here is that which is called māyā... (Rijuvimarsinī-prakaraṇa 63).

And he extends all that which was previously stated by analogy to the other principles: "From that [earth] as well, for the water-principle, [the ritual] from invocation and so forth up to its complete merging into fire, space, and the conscious self (cidātman) [is to be performed]. (6.64)

Thus, when the *kalā*-tattva has been purified in due order, one should sever the bond residing in the arms; for that *kalā* consists in the manifestation of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*). (17.65)
One should burn that knot, which consists of the manifestation of the impurity known as karma and is situated at the tip of the sacrificial ladle,
together with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the splendor of the fire-mantra.

"Thus"—that is, by the very sequence previously described. Now, one might ask: "What is the intended meaning of cutting the bond (pāśa) residing in the arms immediately after the purification of the *kalā*-tattva? Anticipating this doubt, he says "kalā," etc., and "him"—meaning that which resides in the thread of the bond attached to the arms. ||66||
Now, one might object: "Since the power of mantra is all-pervading, why resort to fire alone as its locus?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the mantra, being universal in form, appears as such by virtue of the support upon which it rests."
Then, manifesting in a visible form within the fire, he brings about the burning away of the fetters.

"So be it"—meaning, by way of fire. For the burning away of the fetters (*pāśa*) is its corresponding function; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "What indeed can be meant by the 'burning' of that which is formless? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The fetter is burnt, its nature dissolved with respect to him, just as [the world is burnt] for Śambhu."
He attains the state of being nothing more than the residual majesty of the Supreme Lord.

Right here he demonstrates the modification (*ūha*): "When the bond of karma is to be offered here by means of the *pūrṇāhuti*, one's entire [karma]—whether auspicious or inauspicious, whether past, present, or future—is [offered]. (69)
One should cast the full oblation with the mantra "dahāmi phaṭ trayaṃ vauṣaṭ.
Thus, when purification up to the end of Māyā is complete, one should offer the throat-noose into the fire.

The Guru should cast the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), saying: "I burn that [impurity] of the Full One, which is called Māyā and consists of the manifestation of the differentiation of bonds; PHAṬ PHAṬ PHAṬ VAUṢAṬ. (71)
If, however, the rite is to be performed without seeds (nirbīja), then one should cast another full oblation right here,
accompanied by the words for the burning of the seed known as the bond of the observance (samaya-pāśa).

"Impure" (aśubham) means: as the object of worldly phenomena (*lokadharmin*). "In this very [rite]" means: in the *kaṇṭhapāśahoma*. "The other" (aparām) means: the second [syllable]. "The *samaya*" means: "I burn the seed-syllable called the *samayapāśa*. Now, one might ask: in the case of initiation without seed (*nirbījadīkṣā*), why is the burning of the *samayapāśa* stated here without distinction?
But what of the case where devotion toward the Guru, the deity, and so forth is also prescribed as a *samaya* (observance)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Devotion toward the Guru, the deity, and likewise the scripture must be practiced by him;
for this is not a separate *samaya*, but rather the very nature of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). (7.73)

For one who has been initiated through the seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*), devotion toward the Guru and others arises as something that must be practiced; however, this is not a mere conventional rule (*samaya*), as it is said:
"But by His grace alone, devotion arises in men" (Mahābhārata).
According to this principle, this is the very nature of the descent of power (śaktipāta) itself; it is not something separate or distinct from that—it is nothing at all—such is the meaning. ||73||
Indeed, in order to demonstrate the distinction regarding the purification of the pure path (śuddhādhvan), he says:
"When purification has been attained at the end of Māyā, that Vāgīśī who existed previously—she, consisting of the power of Māyā, assumes the state of the power of Vidyā. (7.74)
Having summoned that Śuddhavidyā, one should employ the power of knowledge (vidyāśakti).
In this manner, when [the self] has been thoroughly purified even up to the level of Sadāśiva, it is complete.
Having cut the tuft together with its knot, one should burn the impurity of the novice (māṇavaka).
As it has been said:
"Then, one should bring the pervasive source (vyāpinī-yoni) of those sources which are to be purified."
"The wise one [should contemplate] that very Vidyā on the path at the end of Māyā, within the Pure [world]. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.57).
"Endowed with knots" means not merely having knots as before.

Now, one might ask: why was it stated here that "one should burn away only the *āṇava* impurity," when the *māyīya* impurity, which consists of the manifestation of duality, is certainly possible here as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because there are two bonds known as *adhikāra* (office/authority) and *bhoga* (enjoyment) in the state of Sadāśiva. (7.76)
By this statement, the *āṇava* bond [ends] here, while the *māyīya* bond lasts until nightfall;
the disciple should bathe as is appropriate, and the teacher himself should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
"When the impurity known as *āṇava* has been utterly consumed by the downward-flowing flame," as stated in the *Mataṅga* and other scriptures. "As is appropriate" means:
"For householders, [purification] is by water alone; for those committed to lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika*), however, it is by ashes."

Thus, "the downward-flowing crest" (adhovāhiśikhā) means that which has that as its primary [function]; for this very reason, it was stated previously: "The downward-flowing crest [attains] the state of the individual soul... (Śloka 17.5), and so forth.
Having thus explained the burning of the fetters (pāśadāha), he speaks of the unification (yojanikā):
"Then, reflecting upon all the objects of knowledge previously mentioned... (17.78).
Having joined the body, life-force, and so forth of the disciple with one's own body, life-force, and so forth,
one should contemplate the entire universe as being within one's own body, life-force, and so forth.

And by means of this very process described above, one whose intellect is firm and whose mind is focused on nothing else [perceives] the pair of space, time, and the path as residing in the vital breath (prāṇa), and the vital breath as residing in power (śakti).

And that pure consciousness residing within [his own] consciousness, which is of the nature of Śiva, non-different from the consciousness of the disciple, and non-different from the mantra, the fire, and so forth. || 17.81 ||

Meditating upon Śiva— whether as possessing parts (*sakala*), as partless (*niṣkala*), or as both— as before in the ritual application, one should cast the *pūrṇāhuti* with a completely tranquil instrument of action.

"Residing in power" (śaktigam) means "situated within the power of time. "Dual-natured" (dvyātmakam) means "having the nature of both the differentiated (sakala) and the undifferentiated (niṣkala). By the phrases "as previously stated" (prāgukta), "by the aforementioned method" (uktaprakriyayā), and "as before" (prāgvat), it is indicated that this has been explained in detail in the sixteenth and fifteenth chapters and elsewhere.
This has been recalled; for this very reason, we too have not elaborated upon it here for fear of making the book too voluminous, nor is this our own invention—thus he says:
"It has been stated in the Traiśirasa Tantra that [the reality] consists of the fulfillment of all things."
By the upward movement from the root, however, it is completely flooded by the moon of Śiva.
That nectar of knowledge which has arisen from the root-stream within the hollow of the end of birth, when stirred by the intense rays of the sun that is Śiva; || 17-84 ||
With that, one should properly satisfy [the deity] by means of the tranquilized senses;
for those locations— the birth-place, the support, the dvādaśānta, and the heart— are indeed hollow cavities resembling inner chambers, because they are the primary seats of abiding.
From this very root-stream, which consists of the initial vibration of primordial power (*ādyā-śakti*), [the breath] has arisen;
and because it moves upward from the *mūlādhāra*, it becomes agitated by the sharp digits of the sun-like vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose nature is Śiva, and thus turns its face outward.

It is completely flooded by the moon of Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta*, thereby brought to the state of being identical with one's own Self; for this very reason, it consists of the filling of all things, as [stated]:
"First, consciousness is transformed into breath."
According to this principle, knowledge itself—which consists of the unfolding of supreme consciousness and so forth—is the nectar;
with a mind that is perfectly tranquil, one should satisfy the wheel of mantras (mantracakra)—that is, the wheel whose nature has been described—by means of that [nectar].
The meaning is: one should establish it in its own essential nature by means of the offering of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Now, one might ask: "What is meant by the 'quiescence' of the instrument? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Resplendent with rays of light situated in the center of the lotus of the abode of the void. (17.85)
The embrace of the scripture of consciousness, which is free from the vibration of the relationship between the contained and the container;
it is the friction that shatters the single *sphoṭa* of the manifold of births, which is the contained. || 17.86 ||
Starting from the root-place and extending as far as the limit of Someśa,
as long as it remains like the sky, so long is it said to be "utterly tranquil" (praśānta).

In this context, the Teacher [states] regarding the lotus located in the *mūlādhāra*, the abode of emptiness— "in the lotus whose petals are the mandala that is eternally oriented upward and rests within the three corners"— according to the principle that will be explained [in verse 29.150]; [he speaks] of the power (*śakti*) which is light situated in the center of that lotus.

Radiant with rays, he is inflamed by the touch of those very rays; therefore, having embraced through the scripture and its stated reasoning the consciousness that has been awakened by the power [of grace]— which, though existing in a single form, is motionless within both the substratum such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the locus of birth— the [teacher] acts.
Therefore,

by the union of one *sphoṭa*— which consists of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*)— with the two bases and the based, characterized as birth and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the manner previously described, [the manifestation of] the phenomenal world occurs.
The meaning is that "grasping" (grāsa) is the friction through their state of equilibrium;
thus, having risen slowly from the *mūlādhāra*, one brings the moon of the *apāna*— which has been swallowed by the sun of the *prāṇa*—
to the *dvādaśānta*, remaining there as if it were the all-pervading sky (*kha*).
It is called "utterly tranquil" because of the dissolution of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper;
the meaning is that it has attained the state of *unmanī*.
And this has also been stated in our own scripture; thus he says:

"It is stated in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra: 'Having filled the sacrificial ladle with clarified butter, and having likewise established the disciple within oneself while recollecting the root mantra... (17.88)
Unifying Śiva, Śakti, the self, the disciple, the clarified butter, and likewise the fire, one should proceed slowly to the *dvādaśānta* with undistracted mind. (17.89)

There, having established the breath-retention (kumbhaka) and meditating upon the one who is both with parts and without parts, he should remain undisturbed until the exhaustion of the clarified butter.
"Root-mantra" means that which is intended to be given. "Having established the *kumbhaka* (retention)" means within the nature of the Great Void (*mahāvyoma*);

therein, having brought all else—consisting of the individual soul (*nara*)—to a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with Śiva and Śakti; such is the meaning, according to the propriety of the connection as "the manifest-and-unmanifest" (*sakalaniṣkala*). "Unperturbed" means...
The meaning is: resting solely within one's own self, which is the nature of perfect consciousness. || 90 ||
If this were so, what would happen? To this he says:
"Thus joined to the supreme reality by the Guru, who is the very form of Śiva, one whose bond of Māyā has been burnt no longer undergoes the state of a bound soul (paśu). (17.91)
Furthermore, regarding the initiation for enjoyment (bhogadīkṣā), there is this specific distinction—as he says:

"If, upon the fall of the body, one should again desire enjoyments within any of the principles (tattvas), whether in their entirety or individually, then [one attains] the supreme state at the end. (17.92)
Then, on that plane of reality, with a mind focused on nothing else, one should perform the re-unification (yojanikā) by means of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) within that specific number.
That initiation which is proclaimed as bestowing liberation, or bestowing both enjoyment and liberation, is twofold: by way of being "with seed" (sabīja) or "seedless" (nirbīja).
