When death is certain for a child, or when one is incapacitated by old age and the like,
the seedless initiation (nirbījikā-dīkṣā) should be performed upon the arising of the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta).
In the seedless initiation (nirbījā), one should also purify the bonds (pāśas) pertaining to the conventional rules (sāmaya).
One who has received the seedless initiation should be devoted to the deity, the fire, and the guru. (17.96)
"By this much alone, one may attain Śiva immediately, either after enjoying worldly enjoyments or not.
Regarding the word "samasta" (entirety): for in the state of *sāyujya* (union), there is the totality of enjoyments, whereas in *sālokya* and the other [lower states], they are partial.
Regarding the phrase "in its enumeration": the meaning is "when that [enumeration] is properly proclaimed and desired."
The word "immediately" (sadyas) means after initiation; "having enjoyed the fruits of experience" (bhogān vibhujya) means upon the fall of the body.
One might ask: "Is the process of unification (*yojanikākrama*) already stated in the passage 'he shall go to Śiva,' or is there something else as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And it is stated in the venerable *Dīkṣottara* regarding the movement within thirty-six finger-breadths. (17.97)
One should gradually abandon the principles (tattvas) and the worlds from the soles of the feet to the top of the head;
that which is merely a moment (tuṭi) is partless (niṣkala), bodiless, and that supreme "I" (aham).
Meditating, "By my power I shall cast him into that," he should initiate [the disciple].
"That" means the nature of the Supreme Brahman; for this very reason, it is said to be "partless" (*niṣkala*) and "bodiless" (*adeha*).
"I am supreme" means its essential nature is the self-reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*).
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"But in the initiation with seed (sabījā-dīkṣā), one should not purify the observances (samayas). (17.99)

However, this is the distinction regarding her: as long as the child lives, the Guru should perform the emanation of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) with a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the sake of the child's remaining livelihood.
Anticipating the question, "And how should one effect the emission of the pure reality (*śuddhatattva*) here?", he says:
"From the undivided ocean of Śiva’s awakening, which flashes forth simultaneously, one should meditate on the emitted mass of light-forms as it casts out the full web of principles. (17.101)
The connection is as follows: "One should meditate on the web of principles (tattva-jāla) flowing from the ocean of the awakening of Śiva.

(101) In this very context, he points out other opinions: "Or one may perform the emanation of the pure principles (viśuddha-tattva-sṛṣṭi) through the consecration of the water-pot (kumbhābhiṣecana)."
Likewise, it is attained either through the power of meditation alone, or else by means of full consecrations.
Because of the plural form in the word "abhiṣecanaiḥ," the power of meditative concentration (dhyānabala) is also included; thus, this position holds in its entirety. || 102 ||
He demonstrates their very purity:
"The earth, whose nature is solidity, when contemplated as the form of Śiva, makes that very contemplation firm; thus it becomes pure. (17.103)
Water nourishes it; fire brings about its luminosity;
wind provides the touch of bliss; and space bestows extension. (17.104)
In this way, even the group of subtle elements (tanmātra) is held to consist of the nature of Śiva;
it is the great pervasion of supreme bliss and the falling away of all impurities. (17.105)
In Śiva, there is the state of being the goer, the taking up [of the path], and the praise of Śiva as that which is to be attained;
furthermore, there is the smelling, tasting, seeing, and touching of the abundance of Śiva’s fragrance. (17.106)
The hearing of that [sound] is thus the purity of the senses;
[the stages are] conceptualization, determination, illumination, attachment, and stability. (17.107)
That which is this purity of the mind and other faculties by virtue of their being of the nature of Śiva;
[and] restraint, coloring, and the state of being an agent along with the act of conceptualization (kalana). (17.108)
Feeling (vedanā) is like being asleep regarding objects that ought to be abandoned;
thus, for one who has ascended to oneness with Śiva, even this group of six coverings (kañcukas) [is dissolved]. (17.109)
The person, being already pure, becomes purified upon attaining the state of Śiva;
among the principles (tattvas) such as those of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), there is no impurity whatsoever.
Thus, through the emanation of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*), the disciple also becomes identical with them; for this has been indicated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*: (17.111)

"Is purified" means "becomes pure. "This" refers to the contemplation [of the self] as having the nature of Śiva. "One should bring about" implies [the result] from that contemplation. "In this way" means precisely through the contemplation of Śiva.

Through stabilization and so forth; although *āsvāda* (tasting) is an operation of the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*), it should also be understood as an operation of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) due to its proximity to the word *āmoda* (fragrance).
Thus, the word *āsvāda* is to be explained by means of both denotation (*abhidhā*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
"Of the senses" means of the sense of bliss (*ānandendriya*) and the others.

"Pride" (*māna*) is self-conceit, the function of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). "Illumination" (*prakāśa*)—for this is the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* respectively; that which is their equilibrium is *prakṛti*. [The rest begins with] "restraint" (*niyama*), etc.

And here, it should be explained by virtue of being established in identity with Śiva. "As if asleep" means the state of being incapable [of functioning]. Thus, the essential point is that their very purity consists in resting solely in Śiva; for this very reason, although these principles (*tattvas*) are impure, they are [regarded] as pure by him.

The wise have declared that both bondage and liberation depend upon the senses:
when restrained, they lead to bondage; when liberated, they lead to liberation. (17.112)
The Blessed One himself explains both the state of being restrained and the state of being liberated:

"When these [senses], along with the mind, are directed toward the pervasive reality (bhāva), they are liberated; however, when they are restricted to any particular object, they lead to bondage. (17.113)
Thus, in this way, the nature of the sense organs is declared to be twofold, according to the distinction between pure and impure, in the Siddhayogīśvarīmata. (17.114)
As it is said there:
"O Dear One, when these [senses] together with the mind are directed toward the pervasive reality (vyāpaka-bhāva), they should then be known by the wise as 'liberated'."
"But when they are situated in some object located in another region, then they are called 'bound'. (Mālatīmādhava 15.45). ||114||
The venerable teacher of the Vidyā has also spoken in this very way; thus he says: "In the *Pramāṇastutidarśana*, the illustrious teacher of the Vidyā said:
'Regarding this very matter, in order to state the rule for the application (*viniyoga*) of mantras, he says...'"
This rule is declared for all mantras during initiation.
In the purification at the end of Māyā, all rites should indeed always be performed with the Aparā;
but at the end of Sakala, with the Dvyātmikā, and in the Niṣkala, with the Parā alone.
At the end of the Īśa [mantra], one should recite the *pibanyā* and so forth; at the end of the Sakala [mantra], the five limbs (*aṅga-pañcaka*).
Having reflected upon this procedure, the most excellent Guru should perform the rite. || 17.117 ||
"All rituals" refers to those for which mantras have not been explicitly stated. Regarding the phrase "by means of the two-fold self"—that is, by means of the Parāparā [energy]. As it has been said:

"In all ritual acts, such as the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), for the sake of completely purifying the path up to the end of Māyā, the wise one should employ the Aparā [energy] in those rituals where mantras have not been specified."
And from Vidyā up to Sakala, one should likewise apply the Parāparā [Kalā];
above Īśvara, one should apply the group of eight beginning with Pibanī.
"And furthermore, the wise one should not perform any ritual enjoined by the injunctions in the Niṣkala [state] with the six limbs above the Sakala [state], using the Parā [mantra].
Thus [ends the verse]. 117.
He extends by analogy the number of oblations previously stated with reference to the predominance of the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) to the other paths, by adding further oblations:
"Whatever is this number of oblations on the path of cities (purādhvan), that same applies to the paths of principles (tattva) and phonemes (varṇa)."
One should double that very [distance] for the path of the *pada* [mantra], and quadruple it for the path of the *pada*.
In the path of the mantra-kalā, [the qualities] increase twofold by twofold in succession until,
upon the complete purification of the three principles (tattva), they become twentyfold.
For each ritual action within a triad of principles (tattvas), there should be sixty oblations;
however, they say that for a single principle, there are one hundred and eight oblations.

"This which is called 'number'" refers to that previously mentioned form consisting of three and so forth. "One should double it" means that because the worlds and other categories are included within the path of the *tattvas*, the number in the path of the *kalās* becomes sixteenfold in comparison to the path of the worlds—this is the intended meaning. "Sixty" refers to...
By multiplying the three oblations by twenty; "they say"—that is to say, for each ritual act—and this extension of the rule does not apply without distinction everywhere—thus he says:
"Those full oblations which are prescribed along with the reverse ritual."
When all these paths are completely purified, there is no change whatsoever in their number.
He concludes this very point with the first half-verse:
"Thus has this initiation been described, complete with birth and the other [stages]. (17.122)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Dispersed Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 17.
"Endowed with birth and so forth" means "expanded"—this is the sense. May there be auspiciousness. || 122 ||
Directing his gaze toward the expertise of his Guru regarding the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*),
one named Jayaratha composed this commentary on the seventeenth chapter.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Dispersed Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by Śrī Jayaratha. 17.
The Eighteenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
I bow to that infinite Balāvaha, the abode of Truth, who bestows strength.
He who, by His own majesty, favors this entire world without exception.
Now, in order to explain the abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣiptadīkṣā*) by means of the second half [of the verse], he says:
"Next, this abbreviated initiation, which results in the attainment of the state of Śiva, is taught.
He explains that very point as follows:
There is no requirement for dust, nor for a dwelling, nor for the possession of land;
having worshipped Śiva in whatever place the Guru may be, [he should perform the rite]. (18.1)

Having meditated upon the path with the mind, the Guru who has reached the further shore of reality should initiate [the disciple] by whichever path he [desires], [a path] which is indeed devoid of birth and so forth. (18.2)

"One who is permeated solely by the state of Śiva should perform [the rite] ending with a single *tattva* through the mind—meaning not by means of the conceptualization of binding threads (*pāśasūtra*) and so forth. 'One who has reached the further shore of the *tattvas*'—meaning one who has not failed to reach the further shore of the *tattvas*; for only such a person would have the qualification for this kind of ritual act."
This is the state of being. As he will say:

"In whatever measure the Guru is one whose knowledge is well-practiced and consists of identification with that [reality], in that same measure he should perform the rite in an abbreviated form, and not otherwise. (Tantrāloka 18.8)
Thus [it is said].
Having thus described the state of being devoid of birth and so forth, he states the division of mantras:
"Then, [the mantra] of this [deity] is the Parā-mantra; now, I purify its reality. (18.3)
One should utter "svāhā" for each respective principle (*tattva*); once purified, one should cast the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] with other mantras, either individually or collectively, as previously stated.
That which is called "enclosed by the *parā*" mantra ends with *svāhā* and begins with the nominative case;
one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with it a hundred, a thousand, or eight times, according to one's capacity. (5)
Therefore, such a supreme [initiate], who is devoid of that which is to be purified, is called "Full" (pūrṇa);
this is the rite of initiation taught therein by the Great Lord in various scriptures.

"By means of one's capacity alone"—that is, according to one's ability; the intention is that, in accordance with place, time, and other factors, either a hundred oblations or a thousand oblations should be performed. "Devoid of what is to be purified"—the meaning is that here not even a mental deposition of the paths (*adhvan*) or similar rites need be performed. "There, there"—means: [in each respective case].
In the *Kiraṇa* and other [Tantras], it is said:
"I shall now proclaim another initiation, which is fully endowed with the Śiva-tattva;
at the outset, it is joined with the *praṇava*, wherein the individual soul (*aṇu*) is denoted within the Śiva-mantra."
Having thus performed the naming [of the victim], Śambhu should then offer the oblation by enclosing [the name] within the mantra.
In this way, a thousand-fold oblation effects the severance from the three bonds.
"O Bird, this initiation, which is free from birth and the like, is difficult to obtain.
Thus [it is said]. (6)
Regarding this, he also states the division of mantras:
"One should purify the principles (tattvas) with each pair of letters of the Mātṛkā; or else, by means of the Piṇḍa-mantra. This is the rule for all mantras. (18.7)
"Yugma" (the couple) refers to that which consists of the forms of Mātṛkā and Mālinī. "This procedure" refers to the nature as it has been described above.
And this is not a task for the Guru alone; thus he says:
"In whatever way one whose knowledge is well-practiced becomes identical with that [knowledge]..."
The Guru should perform the ritual in such a way that it is concise, and not otherwise.
One might object: "In an extensive initiation, the teacher's state of having well-practiced knowledge is required;
what need is there for that in an abbreviated one? Anticipating this doubt, he cites the scripture itself as confirmation:
And it is stated in the Śrībrahmayāmala: "One should indeed contemplate the pervasion common to all the paths even in a concise [rite], but there is no elaboration in the sacrifice. (18.9)
Regarding the word "yāga" (sacrifice): it means within the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of the act of sacrificing (*yajikriyā*). || 9 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, what is the purpose of elaborate ritual action, which is accomplished only through great expenditure of wealth and effort? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One who performs scattered action that has not become identified with that [reality]..."
One should perform the prescribed rite for the distracted mind, thinking that it will gradually attain identity with that [object].
He concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson (āhnika):
"This concise procedure, which was spoken by Śiva out of compassion, has been stated [here], as it appears in the *Dīkṣottara*, in the *Kiraṇa*, and in various other parts of the teaching. (18.11)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Concise Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 18.
Thus all is auspicious. 11.
Jayaratha, preeminent in his mastery of the ritual of initiation for liberation in its condensed form, has thus explained this eighteenth chapter.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Concise Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the illustrious and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. 18.
The Nineteenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
[Salutation to] Him who is powerful through the differentiation of the various manifestations of worldly existence, and through the penetration and dissolution of their arising.
I bow to the powerful Lord, who [liberates] from the seizing of the planets of terrible form.
Now, with half a verse, he makes a formal promise to describe the initiation that bestows immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*):

"Next, the initiation that grants immediate departure [from the body] is described. But surely, this initiation is not the one by whose authority this treatise was originally set forth? To this he replies: "In that regard, this..."
Anticipating the objection, "It has not been stated with explicit syllables; therefore, what is the purpose of defining it here?", he says:
"At that very moment, or through enjoyment, upon the fall of the body, one shall go to Śiva."
Thus, by this statement, she was indicated by the Great Lord in the Mālinīśāstra.
Nor is this something we have stated merely as our own invention; thus he says:
"When the fall of the body is imminent, because of the manifestation of the descent of power (śaktipāta), having attained..."
Therefore, after the moment of initiation, one receives the Śāṅkarī initiation.
"By discerning the preceding and following [context], the meaning here—that one shall go to Śiva—has been explained by our illustrious Guru, who is the very embodiment of Śambhu. (19.3)
"Standing nearby" refers to that which exists in two, three, or more moments.
In this way, he demonstrates the diversity of the descent of power (śaktipāta):
"For when the descent of power occurs for one whose death is imminent, then, if it is weak, the end of life may come through service to the Guru and others. (19.4)
Or else, it may descend upon him through the mediation of kinsmen, friends, and so forth;
or perhaps he was previously a *samayin* who had not yet obtained the supreme initiation (*parā-dīkṣā*). (19-5)
Or, even if he has already received initiation, if he desires to cast off his life-breaths free from affliction,
the Guru should then perform for him the initiation of immediate departure (sadyautkrāntidīkṣaṇa).
"Life would reach its end"—the meaning is that when that [life] is exhausted, the initiate (*samayin*) is considered [to be in such a state].

"She" refers to Śakti; therefore, for one whose death is imminent, who lacks the capacity [for initiation] by himself despite serving the Guru, and upon whom the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*pārameśvara-śaktipāta*) has been marked through the entreaties of relatives, friends, and others, [initiation occurs] immediately.

The meaning is that the initiation of departure (*utkrānti-dīkṣā*) should be performed. By the term "one who observes the rules" (*samayī*), it is implied [this applies] when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is moderate; by "one who has received initiation" (*āpta-dīkṣa*), it is implied [this applies] when it is intense. The term "the last ones" means those desiring to depart [from the body]. ||6||

And this rite is not to be performed by them at an improper time; thus he says: "One should not effect the upward departure (utkramaṇa) when the impurity is not yet ripened, nor while the body still possesses residual karma; this is also established in the venerable Gahvara. (19.7)
Having seen the disciple seized by old age and afflicted by disease,
one should then cause him to ascend and unite him with the Supreme Reality.

"Unripe impurity" means one for whom the descent of power (śaktipāta) has not yet occurred. "Possessing a body of residual karma" means, in other words, one whose death is not imminent. And this is not established by mere reasoning alone; thus he says:
"In the venerable Gahvara. (8)

Nor is this scripture intended solely to declare that death is imminent; thus he says: "Because the status of qualifier and qualified is established according to one's preference, the collection of meanings previously mentioned has been set forth here by the venerable Śambhu. (19.9)
For when the disciple possesses the status of the substantive (viśeṣya) and [conditions] such as being seized by old age possess the status of the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa),
then for that disciple who has received initiation at the appointed time and so forth, there is either the initiation of immediate departure (sadyaḥsamutkrāntidīkṣā) or the former [initiation].

The two divisions beginning with "the initiate" (*samayī*) have been stated; however, in the case of the reverse order, the two divisions beginning with "for one who is seized by old age, through service to the guru and so forth" have been stated as being in the state of a disciple. Here, the venerable Śambhu has set forth the collection of meanings previously mentioned. ||9||
Thus, having regard for the appropriate time, he explains the placement of the *kṣurikā* and other [weapons]:

"Having performed the entire procedure previously described, according to the purification of the observance (*samaya*), one should place upon him the blazing *kṣurikā*, the cutter of the vital points (*marman*). (19.10)
This ritual placement (*nyāsa*) has been taught in our own tradition alone; thus he says:

"Having performed the previously mentioned placement, which possesses a radiance equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*), together with the pair of sacrificial ladles (*sruk* and *sruv*) according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*). (19.11)
Having performed the fire-element concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā), which inflames all the vital points (marmans),
one should fill the body with air from the big toes up to the crown of the head.
Having drawn that [soul] upward from the thumb to the top of the head by means of the [mantra] to be described hereafter,
one should sever its vital points (marmans) and release it through the aperture by means of Kālarātri.
"By this sequential method, even one who has been joined [to the practice] without performing oblations attains that initiation; thus it is stated in the venerable Mālinīmata. (19.14)
"By that which will be explained"—in the thirtieth chapter. "Devoid of oblations"—the meaning is: by mere mental contemplation (anusandhāna). || 14 ||
Right here he shows another alternative:

"From the sixteen supports, the six wheels, the three targets, and the five voids, [the piercing occurs] sometimes in one or another of these, or else as previously described for the bound soul's karma. (19.15)
Having entered [the root], cutting through the roots of the bulbous organs and so forth by means of the contemplation of oneness,
one should unite [the soul] with its own desired abode through the application of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
"In one place" means in a single location. "In either of these" refers to the twelve knots (*granthi*) and so forth. As it has been said:
"The *kula* is to be known below the penis; in the middle, it is designated as 'poison' (*viṣa*);
but at the root, it is called 'powerful' (*śākta*), which, through awakening, does not set [the breath] in motion."
Then, four finger-breadths above that is the one called Agni;
below the navel is the support of the wind (pavana), while at the navel itself is the one named Ghaṭa.
The one known as Sarvakāma is considered to be on the path of the navel and heart lotuses;
another, named Sañjīvanī, resides within the center of the interior of the heart lotus.
The tortoise is situated on the chest, and that which is called the "trembling" (lolā) is said to be in the throat;
above the lambaka is the essence of nectar (sudhāsāra), whose nature is nectar.
Relying upon that very root, gentle and resting on the gentle digits,
there is the expanse of the sky between the eyebrows, known as the lotus of knowledge (vidyā).
Raudra has its support at the base of the palate and is presided over by the power of Rudra;
another, named Cintāmaṇi, resides at the crossroads.
"Indeed, above the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), at the crown of the support of the fourth state (turyādhāra),
there is the supreme, subtle support of the channels (nāḍyādhāra), which awakens the pervasive density. Thus it is said.
The second void is within the navel called *janma*;
the third is in the region of the heart; and the fourth is from the center of the *bindu*.
That which is called *nāda* has been indicated; now the six cakras are described.
The cakra of channels (*nāḍicakra*) is in the [cakra] called *janma*, while the supreme one called *māyā* is at the navel.
The Yoga-cakra is situated in the heart; that which is situated in the palate is known as Bhedana;
the Dīpti-cakra is situated in the Bindu, and that which is situated in the Nāda is called Śānta.
And: "The internal object of focus, the external object of focus, and the middle object of focus as the third.
Regarding the word "previously"—it refers to the sixteenth chapter. Regarding the phrase "by means of the application of the full oblation"—the meaning is "in that same manner. || 16 ||
In this very context, he states another view as the primary one:
"Having visualized the blazing trident of knowledge, radiant with three flaming wheels, by means of this [mantra], one effects its piercing, awakening, and whirling. (19.17)
One should repeatedly perform kindling, striking, piercing,
and shaking within the cakras beginning with the *kanda*, especially in the heart-lotus.
Then, having brought [the breath] to the dvādaśānta, one should cast it into the pair of bindus;
or else, being united with the supreme Lord, one should cast it into the signless, supreme abode.
"One should not perform any funeral rite for him," the Lord has said in the Gahvara;
for what purpose would śrāddha and other rites be for one who is already full? Thus it is understood. (19–20)

Knowledge is supreme consciousness itself; that very [consciousness], through the differentiation of its respective supports and so forth, is the trident (*triśūla*). It is called "the three wheels" by way of the form of the three spokes consisting of *Parā* and the others. "By this"—that is, by the trident of knowledge. "Whirling" is the rotation in the sequence beginning with *Vāmā*. "Piercing" is the impelling. "Specifically"—for that indeed...

The primary locus of the individual soul (jīva) is that which resides within the pair of *bindus*—meaning, having the form of the junction between the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths. "Of him" refers to one who has attained supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*). || 20 ||
And this has not been stated only in our own scripture; thus he says:
"In the venerable *Dīkṣottara*, however, this procedure is encapsulated by fire:
*Haṃsa* is the Person (*puruṣa*), below which is Rudra joined with the Bindu. (19–21)
Having applied this [mantra] into the body of the disciple, one should recite it a hundred times without agitation.
Thus, having ascended upward in the blink of an eye, the disciple shall go to the Supreme.

Vahni is the letter *repha* (ṛ); haṃsa is *ha*; pumān is *ma*. "Of that" refers to the haṃsa encapsulated by the two fires (*vahni*). Rudra is the vowel *ū*; rahra is the syllable *ra*. This is the piṇḍākṣara. ||22||
He extends this very rule to another scripture as well:
"This same procedure applies in the venerable Siddhayogīśvarīmata;
and one who is not a yogin has no authority here"—thus he says.
This initiation of departure (utkrāmaṇī-dīkṣā) must be performed by the yogi guru.
How can one who has not practiced the movement of the vital breath perform this Brahma-vidyā which is about to be described—both with parts and permeated by the partless? (19–24)
The Guru should either recite this into his ear repeatedly or have him recite it;
furthermore, he himself should perform the rites such as the purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi).
By the power of the mantra-ritual, one should thus unite [the soul] with the Supreme through the *pūrṇāhuti*.

Having thus explained the movement residing within the body, he speaks in order to explain the procedure for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), beginning with the words "that which is to be described" (*vakṣyamāṇām*). "That which is to be described" refers to the thirtieth chapter (*āhnika*).
"Interwoven with the Niṣkala" means that it is interwoven— that is, encapsulated within every sentence— by the five-syllable Vidyā known as Niṣkala.
An objection is raised: "Has it not just been stated that this [rite] should not be performed by a teacher who is not a yogi?
Why, then, is it being taught right now? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even without having practiced yoga, the teacher [may perform it], which grants immediate departure [from the body]. (19.26)
By the power of knowledge, mantra, ritual action, and meditation, one may become a master capable of acting;
and here, even though knowledge and the other factors are present, it is the Brahma-vidyā alone that holds primacy—thus he says:
"By this [vidyā], the disciple is made to ascend by force alone in a single moment. (19–27)
If her enjoyment [of life] should exceed its allotted time, let it be but momentary; what of that?
Another [offering] grants immediate departure, in which one then offers the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 19-28 ||
One should give [the initiation] when his vital breaths are certainly desirous of departing.
"For even a single moment" means that after this very instant, his death would occur quite naturally—this is the sense. Now, one might object:
"...for that [karma] is indeed exhausted through experience.

Having raised the objection—how can there be the destruction of this karma, even if it is about to arise at that very moment, without its being experienced—he says: "Experience," and so forth. What follows from that?
Even while remaining,

there is no purpose for him when [the life-force] has almost entirely perished; "he should give then" means that at that very moment his vital breaths depart— and therefore, even for each single [recipient].
The sense is that there should be no transgression here of the characteristic of time.
He states that even by means of the abandonment of ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) alone possesses the status of a means here:
"Even without ritual action, by the power of the future knowledge of Brahman, the Guru... (19.29).

By means of the practice of whispering into the ear, one draws [the soul] out from the web of the sheaths of reality (tattva-kañcuka-jāla) into whatever is desired— whether the manifest (sakala), the unmanifest (niṣkala), or both.
Or one should gradually join the individual (pudgala) to reality (tattva) anywhere whatsoever;
by the phrase "anywhere whatsoever," the fact that it may be done according to one's preference is indeed reinforced.
It is not only by the avoidance of ritual action and so forth that she possesses the quality of being a means here;
it is even through the Guru—thus he says: "Whether one is a *samayin* or a *putraka*, one may likewise recite this Vidyā. (19–31)
The word "tathā" (thus) means: as one who is about to die might hear this.
Anticipating the question, "What would happen to him in this case?", he says:
"But by reciting that [mantra], he attains the state of being a portion of Rudra (rudrāṃśāpatti) as prescribed for a Samayin.
The word *tu* (but) indicates the reason; the meaning is that by this much alone, his initiation into the rules (samayadīkṣā) is accomplished.

Now, one might ask: "How is it proper for these two to recite this as if they were teachers? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because both of these are authorized for both the silent repetition (japa) and the formal study (adhyayana). (19.32)
"Neither in teaching nor in instruction is this [possible] apart from study.
He says, "This is [possible] apart from study," meaning that there is no recitation of these two other than through study;
the negative particle *na* is to be connected with what precedes.

Now, one might object: "If this recitation is indeed not of the nature of instruction and so forth, how could initiation into the *samaya* have been performed for him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But for these two who are reciting, that state [of attainment] occurs by virtue of the very nature of reality. (19.33)
He makes this very point clear by means of an illustration:

"Just as one who has renounced rites such as those for spirits, while reciting a mantra himself, does not incur a lapse even when someone else is possessed [by a spirit], because he has abandoned the sense of agency. (19.34)

And just as a practitioner of the observance, while reciting the scripture in an empty house, is not deprived [of merit] because of his benefit to the multitude of living beings residing therein; || 19-35 ||
Regarding the word "forbidden": as it has been said— “The recitation of mantras should not be performed because of the abandonment of the sense of agency”—
the meaning is that he possesses no such conceit [of ego] as "I am doing this."

By the word "empty" (śūnya), it is stated that what is intended here is precisely the solitude of people. Regarding the phrase "by way of benefit"—the sense is that the destruction of evil would occur merely from the hearing of the scriptures.
As it has been said:
The killer of a cow, the ungrateful person, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the guru’s bed,
the murderer of one who has sought refuge, and the betrayer of a friend’s trust.
"Even one who is wicked, of sinful conduct, a slayer of mother or father—
by the mere disposition of hearing this, they are liberated from all sins.
Thus [ends verse 35].
He applies this very point to the present context:
"Likewise, while reciting the Vidyā himself according to the nature of reality, he would not be deprived of it when that [teacher] is liberated, because he has contributed nothing here. (19.36)

Surely there must be no fault whatsoever in this, for there is a rule: "One should not recite the manual of the scriptures in the presence of those who are uninitiated. So how is it that one does not incur sin by reciting this Vidyā before such a person?
Thus he says:
"But surely, one should not recite the manual of the scriptures in the presence of those who have not been initiated. (19.37)
If that were so, then its recitation would never be possible;
therefore, why would even walls and the like not be present as uninitiated [listeners]? To this he says:
"He who is capable of hearing and comprehending by way of exclusion (paryudāsa)... (19.38).
It is that very [person] who is prohibited here, not walls, insects, or birds.

Now this is said: the prohibition intended here concerns those who are fit for hearing the scriptures and the like, being similar to the initiated, and not those who are inert like walls; thus he says:
"Now," and so forth.
If that is so, what purpose is there in violating the rule for one who is like a wall or on the verge of death even while he is reciting before him? To this he says:
"In that case, such a person is like a stone, his sensory functions having dissolved. (19.39)
"How can there be a transgression of the prohibition while he is reciting in her presence?
Surely, for one who is like a stone, what is the use of this recitation?"—to this he says:
"But he, by the very nature of reality, perceives even though his senses have dissolved. (19.40)
Indeed, independent of the senses and by means of his own self-luminous power of consciousness within, he was about to abandon the former body but had not yet entered the subsequent one. (19.41)
In the middle state, the individual (pudgala) may awaken through the power of an awakener.
Now, one might ask: "Who indeed is his awakener here, by whose power he might attain awakening in the interim? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Mantras consist of sound; by their very nature, they are essentially pure reflective awareness.
Appearing as the very essence of the object, they awaken one to that object;
therefore, for this person whose senses have ceased, awakening arises spontaneously.
"Self-awakening arises from the proximity of the contemplation (*amarśana*) of mantras that are of the same nature as one's own consciousness"— as he will state:
"Having heard which, even one who was helpless under the sway of great delusion gradually [attains liberation]."
Awakening itself approaches the presence of the speaker with impetuous haste.
(30 Ā. Thus it is said.
He illustrates this very point by means of an analogy: "For just as a wind of little speed, when mixed with its own kind... (19.44).
In the same way, the self, though its reflective awareness (*amarśa*) may be dormant, is awakened by that which is of the same kind— namely,
by [the breath] arising from the fan of the palms and so forth— and likewise by means of the contemplation of mantras (*mantrāmarśana*) and the like.
"In that case, does not a clear violation of the observance (samayalopa) necessarily follow from reciting the mantra in the presence of one who is uninitiated?"—anticipating this objection, he says:
"And he has become awakened; he is no longer called uninitiated. (19.45)
For initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed a purification (*saṃskāra*), and nothing else; and it truly belongs to him.

Initiation is a purification pertaining to mantra, and since that [awakening] would otherwise be impossible, it is established for him quite naturally through the contemplation of mantra (*mantrāmarśa*) and so forth. What [more could be said]?
The meaning of its name is the transgression of the commitment (samaya).
Thus, even by reciting scriptures and so forth for the benefit of others, there is no fault arising from the violation of his commitment (samaya); as it is said:
"For this very reason, he may recite his own scripture at any time whatsoever. (19.46)
Having heard that, if some fortunate person is liberated, there is no harm for him; "sāmaya" means "in one who possesses the samaya."
"Surely, in this way, the statement would be without a subject matter?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Let him not utter disparagement of the scripture, for it brings about the downfall of both. (19.47)
Thus, this [text] has that very purpose; one should not recite it in the presence of one who is uninitiated.
And here, with some hesitation, he says the following in order to awaken [the disciple] by means of his own entry into the *kañcukas*:
"And just as the initiate [performs] the application of mantra to a piece of wood or a clod of earth... (19.48).
Just as one who acts while moving upon that [ground] incurs no transgression, so it is here;
"on wood" refers to sacrificial fuel and the like; "on a clod of earth" refers to acceptable objects such as earthen lingas and the like; "here" refers to the person about to die.
He states the reason for this very point: "Because, for this initiate (samayin) who desires to attain the state of realization... (19.49).
For one who has proceeded by way of intrinsic nature, there is indeed no harm when that [nature] is liberated;
the means of realization is the resonance with the expansion of one's own mantra.

Now, it has been stated that for the Teacher there is no loss whatsoever in favoring others, and for the Samayin and Putraka, this occurs even as a secondary consequence; but what is the case here for the Sādhaka? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But the practitioner is always [bound] by the constraint of necessity regarding the fruit to be accomplished.
Even one who has heard the mantra from a fly should perform the appropriate expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
"The appropriate [expiation]" means according to the distinctions of intensity—mild, medium, and so forth. For this very reason, one should not show the dog-mantra or the rosary even to one's guru.

Thus it has been stated. Having thus spoken on this occasion, he states the subject at hand: "In this manner, the immediate departure [of the soul] which has been described—by the command of the Guru... (19.51).

Even one who has received initiation and so forth, having mastered the movement and return of the vital breath (prāṇa), should personally perform [the ritual] at the prescribed time for the sake of accomplishing the stated goal. (19.52)

Or even a Guru who has not yet performed his formal authorization (adhikāra) may [act] for the sake of purifying the pledges (samaya), provided he remains in a lower station and his consciousness is not yet kindled by gnosis (jñāna). || 19-53 ||
Regarding the phrase *akṛta* ("unperformed"): as it has been said—"If he does not exercise authority, he shall become a Vidyeśa upon the dissolution of the body.
Regarding the phrase *jñāneddha* ("kindled by knowledge"): for one established in supreme non-duality, [it is said]—“Do not renounce anything, do not grasp anything... and so forth.
According to this principle, since [the reality] is not an object of injunction or prohibition, what room indeed could there be for the violation of a convention?—
this is the intended meaning.
Now, there is no disagreement that this initiation characterized by immediate departure (*sadyaḥsamutkrānti*) is a task to be performed by a guru; however, one might ask:
what is the authority for its being performed by oneself? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, this immediate departure has been indicated in the *Mālinīmata*."
Either by oneself, or by the Guru, or by the Great Lord (Maheśin) as that which is to be accomplished.

He says that very thing: "If one should abandon the body, considering all enjoyment to be deformed, then by that means the initiate (samayin) is swiftly united with Śiva through that sequence. (19.55)
"One should abandon"—this refers to [the disciple] himself. "Has been joined"—this refers to [being joined] by the guru. As it is said therein:
"Or else, even while considering all enjoyment to be deformed, one who has abandoned his own body attains the eternal state. (17.25)
Thus:
"O Great Goddess, even one who is merely a *samayin*, when joined to the supreme state by this sequential yoga, attains the fruit described for initiation."
And thus it is said.
He concludes the subject of this daily lesson with the first half-verse:
"This immediate departure (sadya-utkrānti) has been described; it must be guarded by the wise like their own life-breath. (19.56)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Immediate Departure" (*sadyautkrāntiprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 19.
Thus all is auspicious. || 56 ||
Desiring to obtain the great heroic power of the mantra that bestows immediate liberation,
Jayaratha has indeed determined this nineteenth chapter.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Immediate Departure" (*sadyautkrānti-prakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmaheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. 19.
The Twentieth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
Victorious is the all-pervasive Lord, the bestower of strength, by whom the body is granted as a consolation for deluded people.
Though appearing to have an exterior, interior, and end, it is constantly manifest as empty of a middle.
Now, in order to explain initiation accompanied by causal conditions (*sapratyayā dīkṣā*) with the second half [of the verse], he says:
"Now I shall describe the initiation that grants consolation to the ignorant. (20.1)
Relief is confidence. || 1 ||
He says that very thing:
"In a triangle, the abode of fire, blazing on all sides with the color of fire, fanned by the city of wind, [placed] in the right hand, it shines intensely. (20.2)
Having taken some seed [of the mantra], one should likewise contemplate it within the heart and in the hand as being ablaze, while engaged solely in its recitation. (20.3)
Scorched by the stream of *phaṭ* syllables ignited by fire, the seed-syllable becomes seedless, rendered incapable of producing its own offspring. (20.4)
"In the abode of fire" means, by implication, facing upwards. "The color of fire" refers to the letter *ra*.
"The city of Vāyu" is the hexagon, which implies it is marked with the letter *ya*. "On the left" means on the right.
"Some seed" refers to grain and the like. "Joined with its exclusive recitation" [refers to that].
The meaning is: one who is intent upon the revolving of the letter *ra*, illuminated by the syllable *phaṭ*. || 4 ||

He explains precisely the incapacity for producing its own [further] birth: "By that very conviction, this [impurity] does not sprout; however, the impurities known as *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman* [are destroyed] through the power of mantra, meditation, and ritual action. (5)
"Burnt away, they no longer serve their own function; rather, this [state] is a condition devoid of seeds.
Thus did the illustrious and most gracious Śambhunātha explain it to me. (20.6)
In this regard, the application of the seed-syllable should also be performed through the grace of the Guru;
for initiation, being intensely radiant, can liberate even immobile beings. (20.7)

"For its own purpose" means for the binding of that which is to be bound. "Because of being well-ignited"—the intention is this: for if it were not ignited, even the joining of mobile beings would be impossible, so what need be said of immobile things? As it has been said:
"He should liberate even bears, winged creatures, rakshasas, and others, as well as immobile beings.
Thus [ends verse 7].
Therefore, he says:

"The guru who, having recognized within himself the perfection of recitation, fire-oblation, worship, and meditation, performs initiation—that initiation is known as 'with conviction' (sapratyayā). (20.8)
This procedure does not apply to one who is an Avadhūta, free from conventional conduct, and a knower of reality;
rather, it is the initiation possessed of visible signs of attainment that is performed by those who follow conventional conduct.
In initiation performed by one who is beyond conventional conduct (nirācāra), however, no external sign of attainment (pratyaya) is declared.

"This is the procedure" refers to the characteristics of initiation with signs (sapratyayadīkṣā). This [initiation] is for those who follow conventional conduct (sācāra) and prioritize ritual action. A visible sign of attainment consists of such things as the removal of the seed-syllable (nirbījakaraṇa) and so forth.
"By one who is beyond conventional conduct"—that is, by the man of knowledge (jñānin).
He establishes this very point through both reasoning and scripture:
"Since knowledge is self-evident, it does not require any further fruit. (20.10)
However, it has been stated in the *Siddhāmata* that meditation (*dhyāna*) and the like are to be accomplished through the fruit;

[the author] says "it does not deserve [to be so]," precisely because it is based on one's own direct realization (*svapratyaya*). By "through the fruit," he means by means of the practice of seedless absorption (*nirbījakaraṇa*) and other such methods.
Having thus described the examination of the qualified candidate, he now sets forth the procedure for the balance:
"Or one should perform the examination of the purity of the balance, which serves as a means of conviction. (20.11)
"Just as it was taught by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, [one might object]:
'But this is not stated in our own scripture; so what is the point of taking pride in the systems of other scriptures?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:"
And this has also been indicated by the Supreme Lord in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra.
Bliss, arousal, trembling, sleep, and the fifth, which is whirling—thus spoke [the author] while describing the gradations of power (śakti). (20.13)
Now, one might ask: "What is the point of even casting a glance toward the initiation by the scales (tulādīkṣā) here?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Arising occurs through lightness, due to the disappearance of the grasping of the body."
Now, one might ask: "How can there be the concealment of the body's grasp here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the body is primarily composed of earth; at that time, it relinquishes its primary nature. (20.14)
Having meditated upon the disciple as having leapt up by means of the mantra of "future lightness" (*bhāvilāghava*),
[the text says] "he abandons his status as the primary [object]"— because of the destruction of all fetters (*pāśa*). "Future" refers to the thirtieth [chapter],
where he will say:
Purity on the scales through lightness provides immediate proof;
the syllables *tā-ra-śa-ma-ra-ya* form the mantra, and the bowing consists of four syllables.
"The Śākinī-stobhana is the vital point, the heart, and indeed this is the life-force. (Tantrāloka 30.93-94).
"Leaped up" means having attained the nature of the supreme space by way of the disappearance of the conceit of being a physical body.
By which this [disciple] may attain equality with a flower on a scale. As it is said in the *Śrītantrarāja*:
"The disciple who has been initiated then becomes equal to space;
he indeed becomes Bhairava himself, with the bonds of saṃsāra burnt away."
Afterwards, one should offer the balance; having thus removed the stones, one should offer a garland made of twenty-seven flowers.
"When the practitioner becomes equal to that [Buddha], having abandoned all obscurations.
Thus it is said.
Now, one might ask: "Will initiation with full conviction not be accomplished by this very process alone as previously described?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, the Guru should perform all the rites previously mentioned. (20.15)

And here, although the consecration (*saṃskāra*) is mentioned in the list immediately after the examination of the qualified candidate (*adhikārin*), it is stated after the rule for the scales (*tulā-vidhi*) with the intention of expressing that it is subsidiary to both. || 15 ||
He concludes this very point:
"Thus has been described this initiation of the purification of the scales (tulāśuddhidīkṣā), which bestows [the fruits] individually.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The twentieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Tulā Initiation."
Thus all is auspicious.
He whose intellect is permeated by the conviction that the venerable Guru, the scriptures, and his own self are one—
this person named Jayaratha has thus explained the twentieth chapter.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Tulā Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 20 ||
The Twenty-first Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
I bow to that Lord of Power (*baleśvara*), who possesses the power to dissolve the manifestation of duality.
He who would establish the negation of limited selfhood even in both the totality and its absence.
Now, with the second half [of the verse], he promises to declare the ritual procedure for initiation when [the candidate] is absent:
"Next, the ritual of initiation for one who is situated out of sight is declared. (21.1)
"Of one who is situated beyond the senses"—that is, by way of space and time. (1)
Now, one might object: "But this initiation is not mentioned in our scripture. Let that be; on the contrary, there is a passage concerning a single, proximate subject:
"Pervaded by the power of Rudra, he who desires to go forth is led toward a true guru by the will of Śiva, for the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.44).
Such [statements] as these have been stated in contradiction [to one another]; how then is this [latter] proposed here?—anticipating this doubt, he says:

"For the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation, [the disciple] is led toward a true Guru"—in this statement from the *Mālinīvijayottara*, the word "toward" (*prati*) signifies "facing" (*sāṃmukhya*). (21.2)

And this "presence" (*sāṃmukhya*) of the disciple consists in being the object of his grace. Regarding the phrase "his grace": by the word "his," the Guru is meant; and the intention is that such grace is indeed no different whether [the Guru] is physically present or absent.

One might object: "Granted that this may be so, how can such passages as 'Having propitiated Him, and having received from Him, when He was pleased, the initiation of Śaṅkara' (1.45), which have proximity [to the deity] as their sole life-breath, be consistent here?"— anticipating this doubt, he says:
The statement "having propitiated him" is an indication of the cause for [his] compassion. || 21-3 ||
Regarding the phrase "due to compassion": the intended meaning is that, since he himself is thus non-existent, this [compassion] must arise through the mediation of relatives and others. || 3 ||
Not only is this understood from that [previous argument], but also from this—thus he says:
"Due to its connection, someone is liberated from that very moment";
for this is also the meaning of the excellent jewel of the *Mālinī* statement. (21.4)
He explains that this very sentence has precisely this meaning:
"At that very moment" means that for him there is no subsequent moment of desire to go and so forth;
rather, the Guru, overcome by compassion, should uplift him in this very way. (21.5)

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the moments of going and reaching that place and so forth are included. The sense is that this would not be possible for one who is dead or situated in another location. "In this very way" means independently, without depending on his own propitiation and the like. "Nighna" means dependent on another. || 5 ||
And who are the qualified candidates for this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"For one whose body has been worn away by service to the Guru, who has met death without having received initiation; or for one who, at the very moment of death, has spontaneously developed such a longing [for liberation]. (21.6)
Alternatively, for one who has received the purificatory consecrations (*saṃskāra*) of the initiations of the lower tantras and so forth,
but has not yet attained the supreme initiation (*parā-dīkṣā*) despite having entered the covenant (*sāmayika*), [the following applies].
Whether one has been killed by a child, devoured by a Yoginī, or died through malevolent magic (abhicāra), or was slain by a preceptor using yantras, tantras, and so forth; || 21-8 ||
"Even for one who has fallen from his own rule (svasamaya), having received initiation, [the grace] is exhausted"—this means for one who has served the Guru for a very long time. As it has been said:
"Even though he has received the supreme initiation and is devoted to the Guru with effort..."
Since his liberation is obstructed by time, how can it come to pass?
"What is the use of that affliction which was undertaken with liberation as its goal?
Is there any action whatsoever belonging to him that serves as a means to liberation? Thus begins [the text].
"Indeed, for one who is devoted to the guru, self-controlled, and intent on truthful conduct,
even if he has died, O Skanda, the rite of initiation (dīkṣākarma) is prescribed.
Regarding the phrase "at the moment of death"— for at that very moment, when his guru is pleased...
It has been stated that "the initiation of immediate departure (sadyaḥsamutkrāntidīkṣā) occurs"—otherwise, however, this [other type of initiation] applies; such is the distinction.
For this very reason, the phrase "one who has met death without having received initiation" must also be connected here.
"Lower Tantra" refers to the Vedic and so forth. "Supreme" refers to that which takes the form of the Putraka and others. "Of one struck down by a riot" means—

The meaning is: "of one killed by means of carts and the like, which are mostly inanimate. Regarding the phrase "by means of malevolent magic" (*abhicārataḥ*): it refers to [the use of] poison and so forth. A *yantra* is the arrangement of mantras upon birch bark or similar materials in accordance with the rite of killing;
a *tantra* is the corresponding ritual of worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so on. As it has been said:
Those who have rolled down from mountain peaks, those who have fallen from trees,
those who died by hanging, and those who were crushed by a cart;
Those who have been consumed by fire, those who died from the collapse of their houses,
and those evildoers who died in rivers, wells, or unfathomable depths;
Those women whose fetuses are stillborn, those who have died from miscarriage,
and those who have been killed by tamed buffaloes or other wicked creatures;
Those who have abandoned their lives by poison, those who commit suicide,
cow-slayers, slayers of Brahmins, and killers of fathers and mothers;
"And those who have died from diseases such as spider-bites and the like, O beautiful goddess, and by other many kinds of cruel [causes], whose number is not known.
Thus it is said. Likewise:
"In the case of those whose funeral cakes have been stolen by one who is without a protector, as well as for those killed by infants,
and for those who died through ill fortune, the initiation becomes 'dead' (ineffective). This has been stated generally, and it may apply to both the initiated and the uninitiated.
The word *alam* means "excessively," in the sense of being in the form of a spiritual son (*putraka*) and so forth.
"Surely, all such people die; therefore, should the Guru perform the initiation for the recovery of the dead for them without distinction, or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Due to the force of intense entreaties from relatives, wives, friends, and sons... (21.9).
Either by his own power, through the force of compassion arising toward that object,
or by recognizing the disciple as one whose nature has received a portion of the descent of power (śaktipāta) manifested through that [compassion].
The Guru should perform the initiation that rescues the deceased and bestows Śiva-hood. "Firmly"—that is, not superficially. "Himself"—the meaning is: without dependence on the request of another.
"By force"—and not by that alone. "Through his mouth"—[refers to the transmission of the teaching].
The meaning is: "by means of the entreaties of relatives and others. Regarding the word "partial" (aṃśa)—it refers to the distinction between intense, moderate, or mild [degrees of descent].
In this very way, because such entreaties from relatives and others would otherwise be inexplicable, it follows that these individuals have received the descent of power (śaktipāta).

The essential meaning here is that the Guru should perform the initiation for the recovery of the deceased (*mṛtoddhārī-dīkṣā*) only after reaching a firm decision. Furthermore, the prayers and other acts arising from relatives and others who are intent on rescuing the deceased are rooted solely in the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*parameśvara-śaktipāta*), and not merely in worldly affection; this applies in all cases.
Because such a perception is impossible; nor is there the fault of "different substrata" here,
since it is observed that effects arise from causes located in different places, just as, for example, the movement of a loadstone occurs toward an iron ball.
That primordial power descends upon a person in his final birth;
through its descent, his impurity—the cause of transmigratory existence—is dissolved.
"When that [ignorance] is exhausted, there arises a desire to go toward the supreme state of liberation.
Likewise:
"But by His grace alone, devotion arises in men."

"Just as those whose minds are absorbed in that [state] attain supreme perfection" (Mahābhārata), and so forth; since this refers exclusively to the individual soul (*jīva*) present here, there is no contradiction whatsoever with this [teaching].
Nor has this been stated by us as our own invention; thus he says:
"That which was spoken by the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Mṛtyuñjaya-siddha* and other [works]. (21.11)
He recites that very point according to its meaning:
"In the case of an uninitiated king and others, one who is indolent, one who has fallen, or one who is dead;
and in the case of a child, the sick, women, and the elderly—one should perform the 'Extraction of the Dead' (mṛtoddhāra). (21.12)
The entire procedure has been previously stated, yet it is intended here in brief;
for that [extensive rite], being devoid of the worship of the Guru and others, serves only for external enjoyment. (21.13)
The field for the ritual of endurance, the bed, and the preparation of the maṇḍala are not required here for the consecration of the disciple or for the vision in dreams. (21.14)

However, for the purpose of attaining proximity to the mantra and satisfaction through it, the mandala is required here; furthermore, on the following day, the worship of the deity is directly beneficial to him. (21.15)
As it has been said:
"O Goddess, when the king is uninitiated, as are his sons and the twice-born, or when [the rite] is obstructed by the defects of karma in those who are indolent regarding spiritual enjoyment..."
Neither ritual action was performed, nor austerity practiced, nor meditation cultivated, nor [virtue] established;
for those who die in a state of fallenness, their dwelling place is hell.
O Goddess, for many reasons— such as for the sake of rescuing women, children, the elderly, and the sick,
or for the sake of initiation when they have died— the Supreme Lord [acts].
"The deity is to be worshipped as before... (18a).

In this context, by the phrase "one who is uninitiated," three types of qualified persons are mentioned: the first two and the fourth. By the phrase "among the twice-born," the third is indicated. And by the phrase beginning with "through falling [from caste]," etc.,...

[The category] beginning with "slain by a child" (*ḍimbāhatādi*) has been described by others as "one who has fallen from his own observance" (*bhraṣṭasvasamaya*). For these [kings], because they fail to protect their subjects properly, because they are attached to sensual enjoyments, because they are obstructed by divine calamities and the like,
and because they lack the practice of austerity and so forth, it is necessarily to be expected that they have fallen from their observance.

In this regard, that which has been explained through a strained interpretation based on [the author's] own mental constructions (*unmeṣa*) should be disregarded, as it is intended merely to display his own dogmatic adherence. "That" refers to the previously mentioned initiation (*dīkṣā*) concerning a living person present nearby. "Maṇḍala" refers to [the area] outside the bed for the sake of protecting the disciple.
The arrangement of lines with ashes and other substances in every direction is as it has been said:
"One should contemplate a protective wall of weapons [formed] with ashes, yellow pigment (rocanā), and so forth.
It is not [merely] for utility—for the sacrificial pap (caru), the bed, and so on, are indeed for the purpose of purifying the disciple.
The meaning is: "Or for the purpose of seeing a dream, but since that very [object] is not present, what is the use of this?
The connection with the preceding [text] is that the mandala and the worship of the deity are useful once again.
As it has been said:

"The worship of Śarva should take place upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and there is no preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) therein. Regarding the phrase "not directly": the meaning is "by way of the proximity of the mantra, through a traditional succession"; for the intention is that he does not perform the visualization of the mandala and so forth himself. ||15||
And it is not the case that this alone is the cause for the presence of the mantra here; thus he says:
"By means of the ritual action, the implements, the place, the mandala, the form, and the mantra;
by means of meditation, yoga, exclusive devotion to that, knowledge, and the state of being absorbed in that. (21.16)
For anyone who has entered that [state], as well as for the disciples and the Guru,
these eleven are said to be the causes for the presence [of the deity].

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "These eleven causes for proximity have been taught by taking up, respectively, actions and so forth, as well as meditations and so forth, which are increasingly superior and, due to their intermixture, [varied]. The word "one" (ekā) means "principal. The phrase "of someone" (kasyāpi) refers to one who is negligent.
As it has been said:
"But for one who has entered [the path] through negligence, one should certainly not cause [him] to engage in investigation.
Regarding the phrase "successively higher": this refers to how, from ritual action (*kriyā*), there arises the instrument (*upakaraṇa*), and so forth. And these [factors], when combined—
He says that they are even "exalted"—namely, "by virtue of such intermingling."
Right here, he explains something that was somewhat unclear:
"The ritual action is exceedingly abundant; the flowers and other materials are of the highest quality and endowed with the proper characteristics. (21.18)
A place such as a solitary liṅga or similar site where the self becomes serene;
and the maṇḍala consisting of three tridents, lotuses, and wheels within the mantra-maṇḍala.
Even when not formally summoned, the establishment of one's status as a *samayin* is observed;
as it is stated in the *Mālinītantra*: "The *samaya-maṇḍala* is established. (21.20)
By the mere sight of which, from the two words "merely accomplished" (siddhamātra), the form is of a radiant nature; likewise, the mantra is intensely luminous. (21.21)
The remainder is clear; therefore, it is not described here again in detail.
The word "mātra" (only/measure) serves to exclude [other acts] such as worship and the like.
Having thus explained this as a digression, he states the subject at hand:
"Then, having constructed a mandala and worshipped the deity there with kuśa grass... (21-22).
One should fashion a figure out of cow dung and have the disciple lie down upon it. Then, within that figure, one should purify a single path through the contemplation of its pervasive presence.
Having cast [the essence] into the end of the *prakṛti*, one should again perform this rite by means of the application of the Great Net (*mahājāla*) from the midst of the entire path.
Having drawn the mind and made it abide there, that procedure is now described.
Regarding the phrase "the form" (ākṛtim)—it refers to one of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula). As it has been said:
"And therein, by way of distinction, is the form..."
It must necessarily be made of clay, similar [in shape], and twelve finger-breadths in length.
"O Goddess, it should be made from cow dung or purified with *kuśa* grass.

Regarding the phrase "up to the primordial nature" (*prakṛtyantam*): the intention is that the person who is to be drawn forth remains situated beyond this point. "Him" (*enam*) refers to what is about to be described. Thus, by this...
Immediately following the classification of the rules for the deceased and the living, the instruction on the Great Net (Mahājāla) has been briefly indicated.

He states the procedure for that very [practice]: "Having risen from the *mūlādhāra*, having forcefully ascended the staff-like path of the infinitely expanded and well-extended channels, and having projected it so as to reach the space of the nose, one is able to pervade [all things]."

This ritual application, named the "Great Net," consists of summoning the desired living being after covering the wheel of the path with a mass of flames that are exceedingly dense and beautiful with smoke. || 21–25 ||

In this context, this practice called the "Great Net" (*mahājāla*) is as follows: when the teacher, abiding within his own self through the nature of the identity of Śiva (*śivāhaṃbhāva*), arises from the *mūlādhāra*— the seat of birth— by repeatedly relying on the techniques of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*).

Having awakened the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) as the root cause, from that very source have issued forth— the infinite channels (*nāḍīs*), numbering three and a half crores, which are extensively spread throughout the entire body and serve as the cause for the upward and downward movement [of breath].

And because it has as its cause the nature of a clearly flowing stream, the staff (daṇḍa) is of the form of the path (adhva); the vital breath (prāṇa), taking that form by virtue of being situated therein, is [the object] which one, having overcome with vigor—
that is, with the power of Śakti— and having brought under one's own control, [proceeds] by the sequence of transcending the heart and the other centers.
Having reached the tip of the nostrils, while casting it outward and spreading it everywhere until— due to the absence of any specific limitation— it becomes capable of pervading the entire universe,
[the yogin perceives it] as consisting mostly of smoke, exceedingly thick and dense, because it still resides within the midst of the impure path (aśuddhādhvan).
By means of the multitude of his rays of sound, having completely covered the entire path and internalized it,

he quickly brings back the desired living soul as if catching a fish— meaning he draws it forth through the unification of the vital breaths, the senses, and so on; and this occurs through the reflective awareness of the seed-syllable *māyā*.
This one, named so-and-so, having first ascended by means of the sequence of withdrawal the staff (daṇḍa)— the letter *ra*—

by means of the potency (*vīrya*) consisting of the vibration of Śakti— the letter *ha*, and thereafter having reached the nose (*nāsā*), the letter *ī*, by means of the drop (*bindu*) which is a mass of crests in the form of light;

"Having covered [all else], he brings about the desired living state. As it has been said: "I am indeed the supreme Śiva—unwavering, possessed of all [powers], peaceful, the Supreme Self, omnipresent; by me the entire universe is pervaded."

Thus, remaining in meditative absorption, one should perform exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka); then, at the end of the breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should gradually expel everything through exhalation.

At the end of the exhalation (recaka), one should again perceive one's own mind, together with its power (śakti), at the "end of twelve" (dvādaśānta) in the form of a sprout, moving within all cosmic eggs.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should visualize consciousness joined with the subtle body (liṅga),
pure and in the form of a drop of water, situated within the stream [of the central channel].
"Having grasped it through its application with the great net (mahājāla) according to the proper method,
it should be placed within the heart, endowed with what is known as the seed-syllable (bīja).
Thus [ends verse 25].
Now, one might ask: "Does this [state] find its scope only in indirect initiation (parokṣadīkṣā), or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By this, that which is to be concealed first becomes subject to another and turns toward [the teacher]."
If [the soul] is brought back entirely from the end, or even from the middle of the path as desired—

whether for the purpose of attracting or extracting one who has passed away, or for the sake of a living person— I have described this method called the "Net" (jāla), as mastered through the tradition of the venerable Śambhunātha. || 21-26 ||
By this practice called "the Net," that wheel of the path which is to be covered—
being dependent on others and lacking autonomy— comes directly before the attractor; immediately thereafter, by means of this very [practice],
the entire multitude of living beings from within that [wheel] is brought into a state of unity exactly as desired.

When that [soul] is drawn forth, it is drawn out from the animal (paśu) during its extraction; likewise, in the case of the "revival of the dead" (mṛtajīvana), regarding the soul to be attracted in an indirect initiation (parokṣadīkṣā), this practice named "The Net" (jāla), obtained through the venerable Guru’s word, has been stated by me and taught to others.
This is the meaning. || 26 ||
Now, one might ask: "How can there be a unification here of the animal [powers] and the heavy [elements], such as the vital breaths and so forth? He dispels this doubt by demonstrating an analogy:
Just as two armies long separated meet again, the horses, elephants, and men rush toward their own respective kind with fervor.

Likewise, by means of the winds of the organs and the circles of the channels, having come together and brought into a state of oneness through their respective essences, they are to be brought under control by one's own net.

Just as when two long-separated bracelets are joined together again, the horses and other components join with their respective counterparts— horses with horses and so forth— likewise, through the power of the application of the *jāla* (net), the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other functions of the cow and other beings join with the breaths and other functions of the bound soul (*paśu*).
Such is the summary meaning. || 27 ||
An objection may be raised: "Surely, once dead, the soul attains various states such as heaven or hell according to the power of its own karma;
how then can it be drawn back? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The soul, drawn by the great net by one possessed of higher knowledge..."
At that very moment, he abandons his states of being as a celestial being, a hungry ghost, an animal, or a human.
He confirms this very point by means of an illustration:
"And this person, having attained that knowledge, mantra, and yoga, like a yogi, then abandons his artificial identity with the heart of the one to be mastered. (21.29)

Just as a yogi who has attained identity with the object of his practice during such acts as entering another's body immediately abandons that artificial identification once he leaves the heart of the victim, so too this [disciple],
having been drawn in by the knowledge and other qualities of the learned Guru through the application of the "net," [is likewise released].
The meaning of the sentence is that the soul of those who are ghosts, animals, and so forth, is the contracted self designated by the word "jīva. || 29 ||
And this is nothing unprecedented—thus he says:

"One should abandon the various states beginning with the stationary [plants], as well as the proximity to and residence in those worlds; that this occurs even through ritual action (karman) is not surprising. (21.30)

If even one who, by the power of karma, abandons those various states of existence (gatis) he has taken up—just as a man might escape from being dragged by a great net—is such a person, then what is there to wonder at?
This is the meaning of the sentence. || 30 ||
Furthermore, regarding birth as a human being, there is this distinction—as he says:
"But because it is a body qualified for spiritual office, when one is embodied in the human state, one is not liberated from the body; however, at the end of the body, one shall go to Śiva. (21.31)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, does this refinement produce some specific excellence in him regarding that [state], or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But in that body, a certain supreme power belonging to Śaṅkara arises for him."
And from wisdom that has grown through devotion, even if it has not been cultivated under a teacher. || 21-32 ||
Regarding the phrase "because it has not been practiced": the intention is that, due to the greatness of this [text], there is nothing else whatsoever here that needs to be adopted. || 32 ||
Now, one might object: "In that case, since this individual soul has not attained [the state of liberation] while still remaining in its body, for whom would there be consecration?
Thus, what is the point of indirect initiation (parokṣadīkṣā)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even though this soul remains situated within that body, by the power of the net..."
It pervades the body made of darbha grass and other materials by means of its own presiding presence, even while remaining unconscious.
Because its nature is all-pervasive, it cannot be that it does not have a substratum in both [states]; thus it is said:
"it pervades. "Even while not cognizing"—this is due to the power of non-manifestation (akhyāti). 33.
Or rather, by the power of the Guru, he may indeed abandon even the human body; thus it is said:
"Furthermore, by virtue of the great strength of yoga, mantra, ritual action, and knowledge, he immediately abandons even the human body at that very moment. (21.34)

Now, one might object: "This has been stated regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) that has assumed various births; but what is the case for one who has not yet taken on a body? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even that soul which is bodiless and as if asleep, by means of the net [of karma],..."
Drawn forth, he enters a body made of darbha grass or one consisting of fruit.
Now, one might object: "Was it not just stated that the construction of the body should be performed with *kuśa* grass or cow dung;

how then can it be said here that it may also consist of fruit? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Or the construction of the body may be done with whatever [materials] such as nutmeg (*jātīphala*) and so forth."
On the contrary, there is a distinction here—as he says: "Because of the appropriateness of both the internal and the external, that is said here to be the most excellent. (21.36)
Now, one might object: "If the individual soul (jīva) is present here, why do its powers of knowledge and action not manifest?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, that soul, brought [into the body] by the sequence of the network [of channels], remains as if asleep."
Because of the absence of obtaining the causal complex of the body and so forth, which is distinguished by the mind. || 21-37 ||
He does not throb, he does not know, he does not speak, nor does he desire;
for such a person, one should perform all the consecratory rites as before.
Having performed everything previously described by means of the seedless initiation (nirbījadīkṣā),
he should cast that [disciple] away along with the rite of union (yojanikā) and the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
When the body made of darbha grass and other materials has been offered into the fire along with the mantra and the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the soul,
