freed from its bonds, goes to Śiva, never to return again.
But wherever this body made of darbha grass vibrates with confidence, there it shall become so through the yoga of offering the vital breath, the mind, and the mantra. (21.41)
That which was stated regarding one who possesses practice is merely a source of encouragement by force;
it is not for the sake of such a person—meaning one who remains as if asleep. "Him"—meaning the body made of darbha grass and so forth. As it has been said:
"Thereafter, at the end, make the ladle filled with clarified butter into its original form."
"Standing with feet together [facing] the one who has arisen... and so on,
up to "...then one should cast the full [offering]."
"Having burned that image in the fire, one should unite it with the supreme abode;
he shall attain union with Śiva—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Thus [it is said]. "That" refers to the *spandana* (vibration). "Produced by that"—for this [attainment] does not belong to one who is merely initiated.
The intention is that it is some kind of mental formation (saṃskāra).
This very [rule] is extended by analogy even to the initiation of one who is alive but absent (jīvat-parokṣa-dīkṣya):
"By means of the same causes as those set forth for the rescue of the deceased (mṛtoddhāra), according to their availability. (21.42)
Even initiation for one who is alive but absent (jīvatparokṣadīkṣā) should be performed; however, that is "seedless" (nirbījikā).
In that case, when the representation is fashioned primarily from darbha grass, it is done through the application of the net (jālayoga). || 21-43 ||
By mere volition, the soul is drawn forth from the fear of death;
the rest is as previously described, except for the burning away of the forms arising from the kuśa grass and other materials. (21.44)

*Saṃbhūtiḥ* means origination. Although its seedless nature (*nirbījatva*) is established by the force of the extended application (*atideśa*) itself, nevertheless, lest anyone should harbor even a doubt regarding its having a seed (*sabījatva*) while it is still alive, it is stated: "but that [state] is seedless. Regarding the phrase "by mere volition" (*saṃkalpamātreṇa*), one should not place excessive emphasis on this point.
This is the meaning. ||44||
And this application of the net succeeds only within the domain prescribed by tradition and not elsewhere; thus he says:

"Because of limitation, because of a lack of sovereignty, and because of the constraint of destiny regarding the object to be accomplished, the drawing-in by the net does not arise without practice, nor from passion and aversion. (21.45)
For just as the drawing of a net cannot be accomplished without practice,
so too it is with passion and hatred. For how could a man acting in such a manner alter the goal constrained by destiny, since this—

Because its nature is contracted, it is not the Lord (*anīśvara*). Furthermore, it was stated previously that entities do not conform to His will; however, here, through the immersion (*āveśa*) into the state of the Supreme Lord, such a state indeed occurs.
For it is the Supreme Lord Himself who, by means of presiding over the body of the Guru, [acts].
He bestows grace upon those who are to be graced, and it has been stated more than once that his majesty is inconceivable. ||45||
Having thus imparted the instruction on the "Net" (jāla), he speaks in order to explain the consideration of the relative strength and weakness of the group of purificatory rites:
"If one has been initiated by means of unequal initiations while [the teacher] was out of sight..."
In that case, the higher [initiation] would be for the child, while the lower one is for the sake of purification.

Regarding the phrase "by incomparable [means]": because it is possible for initiations to be performed in this manner by many teachers— being requested by numerous sons and others— to uplift [the disciple] through various forms such as the *Kula-tantra* procedure and so forth.
For it has been stated thus: "The higher" refers to the Kaulika rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth; "the lower" refers to that which is taught in the Tantras. ||46||

Anticipating the doubt as to what would happen if an initiation of the same nature were performed again, he says: "But when an initiation that connects one to worldly enjoyment (bhukti) has been performed by many gurus in such a manner, there arises a variety of experiences due to the connection with a variety of causes. (21.47)

An objection might be raised: "Let this be so in this case; however, in the *mukti-yojanikā* (the initiation for union with liberation), since there can be no diversity in liberation, the diversity of causes would be useless.
Anticipating this, he says: "In the case of initiation by proxy (*parokṣa-dīkṣaṇa*), one who has transcended *māyā* should be joined to worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*)."
Indeed, the lack of desire for enjoyments is difficult to attain, even when it exists, for the purpose of abandoning enjoyments.

"For enjoyment"—but not for liberation. "Difficult to attain"—because the severance of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoyment is considered impossible. However, in the case of some great soul, the absence of desire for enjoyments, being possible, would lead only to liberation; thus he says: "Or, if it exists, for the abandonment of enjoyment. (48)

Now, one might object: "If, in the case of initiation at a distance (parokṣadīkṣā), such an act of unification (yojanikā) is performed even for the sake of worldly enjoyment (bhoga), then how could liberation occur for this person even when there is no desire for enjoyments?"— in response to this doubt, he states the resolution along with its supporting authority:
For it has been said: "Between one's own cognition and the cognition of another, one's own cognition is more powerful;
it acts as a sublater when there is a sublater, and likewise when there is equality or indifference. (21.49)

"More powerful"—the sense is that even if the Guru has performed the conjunction for enjoyment (*bhukti-yojanikā*), liberation alone will occur for him. Therefore it is said: "it is obstructive. "This one" refers to one's own consciousness (*svasaṃvit*). "Of equanimity and indifference" refers to those residing in the consciousness of both the Guru and the disciple.
"So be it"—the meaning is that it is indeed sublated. ||49||
Right here, he shows the specific detail taught by another teacher: the illustrious Dharmaśiva also said in his *Pārokṣyā-karmapaddhati*.
He states that very thing as follows:
If, during the rite of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the procedure for initiation in absentia, [an error occurs], || 21-50 ||
The fire emits a crackling sound along with smoke;
it assumes the hue of a dark cloud, repeatedly flaring up and then subsiding. (21.51)

If it spreads extensively, takes a terrible form, runs toward the earth below, or makes sounds as unpleasant to hear as those of a crow and other such birds, then the teacher should observe that [sign]. (21.52)
If he is burdened by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, or by association with those who commit minor offenses (upapātaka),
then his initiation must not be performed until this rite has been accomplished.
"In this"—that is, in what is about to be stated. ||53||
He states that very procedure:
"The *navātman* mantra, situated within the *phaṭ*-enclosure, followed again by five *phaṭ*s; then [the words] 'of such-and-such a person,' then 'I burn his sins,' and finally eight *phaṭ*s. (21.54)
Thus, a thousandfold oblation (sāhasrika-homa) should be performed with sesame seeds and rice;
at the conclusion, a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) must be offered, and then the Guru should initiate him.
One should perform the purification of reality up to the limit of the supreme union (*parayojana*).
The word "then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after such a procedure. He extends this very same rule even to one who is present and living—
Even for a sinful atom remaining within direct perception, [the power] consisting of the Blessed One [prevails].
One who has attained the supreme power (*jyeṣṭhā-śakti*) should perform the rite in this very same manner.
Regarding this, he states another alternative:
"Or else, if the teacher is not properly radiant, then that [rite] should be performed for him beforehand. (21.57)
Having performed purification through penances, gifts, and breath-control exercises, one should perform this rite of initiation without hesitation. (21.58)
"Of him"—that is, of the individual soul (aṇu) who remains even within direct perception. ||58||
Furthermore, for one who knows reality, this [world] is nothing at all to be accepted—thus he says:
"Even while acting in every way, the knower of reality may liberate bound souls;
being Śiva himself by his very will, one should therefore always worship him. (21.59)
One should not practice deceit in that regard; by doing so, the child would go to a lower state.
One should not proclaim his sin again; the one who proclaims it would go [to a lower state].
"Therefore, one should avoid hell"—this is the rule in the *Dīkṣottara*.
"In every way" means by whatever means possible. "Deceit" refers to doubt. "One should avoid" refers to the proclamation of one's sins.
He concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson:
"This initiation at a distance has been declared as twofold, according to the distinction between the living and the deceased. (21.61)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Illumination of Indirect Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus may there be auspiciousness.
This was indeed composed by Jayaratha in the twenty-first chapter of his commentary, with a mind agitated by the joy of desiring to uplift the entire world.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Illumination of Indirect Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. 21.
The Twenty-second Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
To Him who bears a countenance turned away from destroying the evil impressions of those of wicked conduct...
I reverently salute the god Amamda, who brings joy to the worlds. || 1 ||
Now, in order to explain the initiation known as the extraction of the *liṅga* (*liṅgoddhāra-dīkṣā*) by means of the second half [of the verse], he says:
"Next, we shall describe the one called the extraction of the *liṅga*, which is uniquely taught in the teaching of Śiva. (22.1)
"One [type of person]"— as was stated previously:
"For this very reason, in these Śaiva scriptures,
a purificatory rite (*sāṃskārika vidhi*) is prescribed for those who have no faith in the teachings of other systems."
Therefore, this Śaiva [path] is the most supreme; for he who has fallen elsewhere is indeed to be favored here, but one who has fallen from this [path] upward is never to be favored anywhere.

"For this very reason, nothing such as the extraction of the *liṅga* (*liṅgoddhāra*) and so forth has been recorded in their own scriptures by the omniscient ones, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others. (13.359) ||1||
Now, one might ask: "Is this initiation not mentioned in our own scripture? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It is indeed stated in the *Śrīmālinītantra*, after describing the meditative concentration on the earth (*pārthivadhāraṇā*):
'Whosoever is joined to whatever [level], from that he does not return. (22.2)
At the time of initiation, he should be appointed to that very task for which his instruction has arisen by the power of his inherent aptitude. || 22-3 ||
Having attained all the fruits, one who is devoted to Śiva is liberated;
even one who is not so devoted attains purification in the higher realms from the Lord of the World.
Purified and with the bonds of worldly existence burnt away, one attains the state of Śiva;
having thus described the meditation on the Puruṣa, this Vedic conclusion has been declared by me.
Thus it was told to Kapila of old in the first chapter;
by this sequential yoga, he attained the supreme state.
One no longer falls into the state of a bound animal (paśu), but abides in one's own pure Self;
this is the Vedic knowledge (Vedāntika)—that is, realization (vijñāna).

Now, one might object: "In this context of the discourse on the initiation of the extraction of the *liṅga*, why is this description of the Himavat mountain mentioned to one who is hesitant, as if it were for someone wishing to cross the ocean? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, this meaning is indeed implied even regarding those levels below the Śiva-tattva. (22.7)

For one who has been engaged with the principles (tattvas), there remains the possibility of being raised up again by that which bestows the discernment of the reality taught in all the scriptures. (22-8)
The Śiva-āgama is superior to all other āgamas;
and without the knowledge of Śiva, the state of being a bound soul (paśu) arises once again. (22.9)

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) refers to the three preceding statements. Regarding the phrase "in the lower [levels]" and "in the principles" (tattva), the meaning is: even while in the state of *māyā*. Thus, even one who remains within a lower system of philosophy, if he has received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), must necessarily be uplifted again by the Guru according to the procedure of the Śaiva Āgamas, just like the lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*).
It has been indicated: in that regard, it is stated everywhere that the *liṅgoddhāra* initiation alone is the means.

All the scriptures, such as those of Kapila and others, describe subjects such as the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; nevertheless, even through these, there is no liberation from *māyā*.

Because it bestows the discernment of the reality taught therein, the Śaiva Āgama alone holds primacy among all scriptures; consequently, the direct attainment of the supreme state occurs through that alone.
For those who have attained [the fruits] of other systems, there is indeed only the attainment of a lower state—this was stated previously.
Many times. || 9 ||
And regarding this, such is the sequence that must be observed—thus he says:

"The sequence consists of the descent of power, the removal of impurity, the desire to go forth [for liberation], initiation, awakening, the abandonment of what is to be discarded, and absorption into the nature of that which is to be accepted. (22.10)

The abandonment of the state of being an object of enjoyment and the bondage of the bound soul, the exhaustion of the agency of the Lord, and the abiding in one's own self—this indeed is the result of being established in other philosophical systems. (22.11)

For it has been stated that the state of being "to be uplifted" belongs to one impelled by Śiva and Śakti. "Desirous of going"—that is, toward the Guru. "Awakening"—because after initiation, one possesses the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. "To be abandoned"—referring to impurity (*mala*), karma, and the like. "The nature of absorption into that which is to be accepted"—that is, into the Supreme Reality.
The meaning is: "consisting of resting solely in Śiva, Śakti, and so forth. *Pāśava* refers to the *āṇava* impurity (*mala*).
Regarding the term *kartṛtva*: it consists of the impulse toward transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
Anticipating the question, "What is the duty for one upon whom the descent of power (śaktipāta) has thus occurred?", he says:
"Now, [the procedure] for those who abide in lower systems, beginning with the Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist tantras and ending with other such traditions... (22.12).
When the lotus of the heart has blossomed by the masses of rays from the sun that is Śiva,
then first comes the extraction of the *liṅga*, and after that, the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Even one who previously resided within another [non-Śaiva] school attains the state of Śiva through initiation;
this is the internal Siddhānta. For it was said previously:
"But by the sovereignty of the Great Lord, even they, if turned toward the state of Śiva..."
For these, there is a twofold refinement: first by the extraction of the *liṅga*, and then by initiation.
"When the foul odor has been removed, the jar is consecrated with flowers;
that consecration is double for it, but such a rite is not prescribed for a jar that is already pure. (13.283)
Regarding that, he now states the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga*:
"There, having made him fast, on another day, [he should perform the rite] with the *sādhāra* mantra. (22.14)
Having worshipped the Lord upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should cause him to hear his way of life:
"Previously this man was a bearer of the sectarian mark (liṅgin), but now he has been impelled by you. (22.15)
Being well-disposed, grant him this proper favor;
and let there be no penance for him arising from the fear of abandoning his own sectarian mark.
"May he, having soon become one with You, attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having received the command "So be it," he undertook that vow of his.
Having removed [the impurities] and cast them into the water, one should bathe [the deity] in the appropriate manner;
immediately thereafter, one should sprinkle the bathed [deity] with the waters from the arghya vessel.
Then one should offer him the five products of the cow and the tooth-stick;
thereafter, having led him in with his eyes bound, one should cause him to prostrate.
*Vartanī* means conduct. By the words "let it be so," the very purpose of the proclamation is authorized.

"He should bathe [the disciple]"—this is for the sake of removing any defects in his observance (*vrata*). "In a fitting manner"—the meaning is: according to the propriety of the vision he intends to bestow. ||19||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed are the common mantras here, from among which one may worship the Lord with any single one? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Praṇava, Mātṛkā, Māyā, Vyomavyāpin, and the six-syllabled mantra."
Bahurūpa and then Netra—these seven are the common [mantras]. || 22-20 ||
From among those, he should impart one mantra to him;
he too should mutter it for a full day and night, eating little or not at all.

Then, having entrusted the mantra to him, one should perform the purification of the vow in a fire consecrated by the common ritual procedures, after that mantra has been offered as libation (tarpaṇa).
"Enam" refers to any one of the common mantras. "Alpabhuk" and "abhuk" [are used] according to the capacity [of the practitioner]. (20–22)

Having thus performed its purification, he speaks in order to declare the removal of the transgression: "By means of the very mantra that has been worshipped, having placed the name of this [person] in the middle (saṃpuṭa), one purifies the penance through the application of the modification: *prāyaścittaṃ śodhayāmi phaṭ svāhā*. (22–23)

Having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations, and likewise a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the conclusion of the ritual procedure ending with "vauṣaṭ," he should invoke the Lord of Vows (Vrateśvara).
One should worship him with the mantra "Tāraḥ, obeisance to Vrateśvarāya," and one should proclaim: "By the command of Śiva, no task whatsoever shall be performed by you against him."
Then Vrateśvara is to be satiated with [mantras] ending in *svāhā*, and thereafter he should be asked for forgiveness and dismissed; following that is the dismissal of Agni.
The hearing of that [mantra] and the dismissal with the words "forgive me, O God";
*tāra* is the *praṇava*. "Enam" refers to Vrateśvara.
Having thus described the extraction of the *liṅga*, he now describes the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*):
"Then, on the third day, the entire procedure is prescribed as before. (22–27)
It begins with the *adhivāsa* (consecration) and concludes with the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) desired by oneself.
For it has been stated: "On the first day there is fasting; on the second, the removal of the *liṅga*"; thus, [the third day is mentioned].
Now, one might object: "If his initiation is to be performed according to his own preference, then is he also a fit recipient for all initiations? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For those who previously bore sectarian marks, the initiation for liberation is devoid of authority. (22–28)
Those who have returned to worldly life are not fit for the path of being a practitioner-teacher;
yet even those who have returned to worldly life may become a locus of guru-hood if they are kindled by knowledge.
"It is for liberation alone, not for enjoyment; yet it may also serve as a means for enjoyment.
Thus has the teacher Īśānaśiva stated in his own manual (*paddhati*). (22-30)
He is the one who correctly proclaims the reality taught in the *Yāmala* of the Śrīdevī.

Here, the reason for [his] unfitness is the state of being subject to rebirth (*punarbhavatva*). As it has been said: "Those who do not employ the *mantras* remain in the state of being subject to rebirth."
Thus it is said. And they are characterized as follows:

"One who was previously of another sect (*punarbhū*) and has now been established in the Śaiva [path], though bearing another sectarian mark (*anyaliṅga*). (23.10). They are "kindled by knowledge" (*jñāneddha*).
The sense is: for those whose very selves are illuminated by the supreme non-dual knowledge, how could there possibly be no qualification?
Regarding the phrase "by means of a method" (*abhyupāyataḥ*), the meaning is: in accordance with the systematic procedure of the scriptures which serve as the means to enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Nor is this [teaching] stated by him as being entirely without foundation; thus he says, "of the venerable Goddess," and so forth.

Thus, this consecration (saṃskāra) should be taught even to one who has reached the end [of his studies] but whose gaze is still directed downward and who remains lying [in ignorance]; so he says: "Even for one at the end [of his studies], whose gaze is directed downward and who remains lying [there], this consecration... (22.31).

"Having [initiated him], one should tell him the secret, and not otherwise, according to the Kāmika; indeed, the Kāmika text itself reads: 'Even if he has been consecrated in another tantra, one should not reveal the secret. (22–32)
This is not only the duty for one who abides in a lower doctrine, but even for one who abides in his own doctrine;
thus he says:
"Even if established in an independent [tradition], if he has relied upon an ignorant guru until the end, [he must act accordingly]."
If he is not confident there, he should perform the ritual even in that case.
Regarding "here"—it refers to when the guru is ignorant. ||33||

Now, one might object: "Granted that no merit may arise from resorting to an ignorant guru, but from where would a fault come such that even the extraction of the *liṅga* [of the disciple] would be required? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because this [ignorant teacher] bestows a mantra that has become devoid of potency, having come from the mouth of an unlearned preceptor..."
And that preceptor, having recited [the mantra] here, is not qualified [for the office] due to the aforementioned defect.
Then, having first performed his purification, one should thereafter perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "hi" (for/indeed). This is because of the aforementioned defect—namely, the characteristic of ignorance (*ajñatva*).
Having thus described this by way of the unity of vision, he speaks also by way of its differentiation:
"Previously initiated by a Guru established in the lower vision... (22.35).
Later, when he approaches a true guru by the power of intense spiritual energy (*tīvra-śakti*), then that true guru, having likewise performed purification for this disciple— || 22-36 ||

One should perform the entire ritual procedure, beginning with initiation, according to the prescribed injunctions by one who stands within the lower revelation— just as it is done by a follower of the Siddhānta within the Bhairava stream.

Now, according to the principle that will be stated later—namely, "They are not to be examined at the time of initiation; one should investigate them at the time of [receiving] knowledge" (23.21)—let initiation indeed be performed in this very manner for these [disciples]; however, as for the instruction...
Anticipating the objection, "How can it be performed without deliberation?", he says:
"Even if a true guru has been found, if he does not know the disciple's state of fitness... (22.37).
When the transmission of consciousness is to take place, that disciple should demonstrate his own fitness;
for in every way, he must neither remain silent nor speak what is contrary to the truth.
"Being ignorant in reality"—having abandoned that [ignorance], one should perform the rite in this manner.

"Without speaking"—this means in accordance with the observation of one's own fitness. "Contrariety"—the meaning is that which results in making known one's unfitness. "In reality"—and not [merely nominally].

Because it has been permeated by the power of dissolution and so forth. "That" refers to the communication of the state of being fit. Now, one might object: "Let there be no perception of its fitness; on the contrary, even its unfitness is observed.
Therefore, how can the prescribed rule be applied to this [state] which is almost entirely concealed? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
A person of intelligence should not entertain any doubt regarding its disappearance here. || 22-39 ||
The state of being "touched by the lower" is concealment (tirobhūti), not the discernment of the higher means;
for if this [individual] were in a state of concealment, there would be no longing at all for the discernment of the higher means—this is the sense.
He elaborates on this very point:
"In the Siddhānta, those initiated into the Tantra which has ten and eighteen divisions... (22.40).
One should initiate those bound souls (paśus) in the Bhairavīya system of sixty-four, as well as in the Trika, in the Siddhavīrāvalīsāra, and also in the Kula tradition of Bhairava. (22.41)

The initiation known as the Unsurpassed (anuttara), which is obtained through the sequence of the five initiations, has been investigated in the thirteenth chapter itself; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
This very point is applied to the present context:
"Therefore, even one who remains at a lower level is graced by the extraction of the *liṅga*. (22.42)
One should not resort to another teacher only when the current one is unsuitable, but even when he is suitable—thus it is said:
"Even he who, through the impulsion of the Great Lord residing in his heart, seeks a very extensive knowledge of the scriptures, he too should approach many teachers. (22.43)
One should also receive those initiations ending with the consecration (abhiṣecana),
for they are strengtheners of knowledge, performed by those possessing the respective knowledge.
Is it not said regarding the abandonment of the guru: "Death results from disrespecting the guru; poverty results from disrespecting the mantra;
and by abandoning both the guru and the mantra, even one who has attained perfection shall go to hell"?
Anticipating the objection— "Since a transgression is traditionally taught through such views as these, how can it be stated thus?"— he corroborates this very point with scripture itself:
"And it is said in the venerable Śrīmata and in various other scriptures in many places."
Just as a bee seeking fragrance goes from flower to flower, || 22-45 ||
In the same way, a disciple seeking higher knowledge [should go] from one guru to another guru.
In this regard, however, there is this distinction: that one should go to another guru with the permission of the previous guru.
As it has been said:
"But one should go [on pilgrimage] by the command of the Guru and must not abandon that Guru;
for even through ten million recitations, there can be no accomplishment if one abandons that Guru.
Thus it is said.
Now, one might ask: "Among these many gurus, is there some distinction such that for one person a certain [guru] is superior, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because among the many gurus, [the one from whom] the highest realization [is obtained is the best]. (22.46)
He who has attained this is his guru; for in this regard, initiation is not primary within consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "in this consciousness"—there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
And he must remain intent solely upon the propitiation of this [Guru]; thus it is said:
"Having obtained a Guru who is a treasury of all knowledge, one should remain well-established. (22.47)
The wise person, intent on investigating each respective [truth], should propitiate that very [guru];
by this much, the apprehension regarding going to another guru is addressed and removed.
Now, by means of the first half-verse, he concludes the meaning of the treatise while encapsulating the subject matter at hand:
"Thus has been declared the procedure for initiation, concluding with the extraction of the *liṅga*. (22.48)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Extraction of the Liṅga," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus may there be auspiciousness. 48.

Jayaratha, by name, has brought this twenty-second chapter to a conclusion, which consists of a thorough investigation through self-reflection that refutes the views of those who hold lower and even lower positions.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Extraction of the Liṅga," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 22 ||
The Twenty-third Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
Having assumed the form of Bhairava through the distribution of his own nature.
May that Sarvatobhadra bestow upon you auspiciousness in every respect here. ||1||
Now, with the second half [of the verse], he begins to describe the procedure for initiation:
"Next, the procedure for initiation according to the Supreme Lord is told. (23.1)

He says that very thing: "This initiation of the 'little son' (putraka) which has been described applies also to the Guru and the Sādhaka; it is the one that confers authority, provided it is conjoined with the sequential application of the principles to be experienced. (23.2)

Having recognized that he is a knower who has well-practiced [wisdom], is desirous of becoming [a teacher], and is a future [master] worthy [of the task], the guru should entrust him with his own office. (23.3)

Regarding the phrase "yaisā" (by which): this refers to the practice with seed (*sabījā*). Furthermore, the authority for these two arises from initiation (*abhiṣeka*), and since that must be granted after examination, he begins the examination of the teacher first, starting with the words "in due order" (*kramāt*) and so forth.

"Gradually"—the meaning is "beginning with hearing, reflection, and so forth. And this [process] is to be connected everywhere. "One who desires to exist" and "one who is about to become" refer to one whose state of knowledge has been well-practiced.

An objection might be raised: "Is it not stated everywhere that authority (adhikāra) arises from initiation alone? Therefore, let initiation alone be prescribed here as well; what is the use of considering such things as being a well-practiced knower?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One who does not know this, even if he has been consecrated, is not a teacher (daiśika) according to the sequence beginning with the initiate (samayin), as stated in the venerable Kāmika. (23.4)

"He who does not know the sixfold connection between the Vedas and the paths, situated both externally and internally—he, such a guru, cannot liberate," so it is stated in the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*. (23.5)
"Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, a guru who possesses knowledge is desired;
it is stated in the Śrīkacabhārgava that knowledge alone is the primary factor. (23.6)

The Guru is one who knows words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), is solely devoted to devotion to Śiva, understands the meaning of all the Śiva scriptures, and is compassionate. (23.7)
The connection is that even if he has been consecrated through the sequence beginning with the *samayī* initiation, he would not be a *deśika* (teacher).

Thus, by means of this corroboration with the meaning of numerous scriptures, it is demonstrated that when the guru possesses well-practiced knowledge, his authority is unimpeachable in all respects. || 7 ||
Even so, such [persons] as these should not be made gurus; thus he says:

"He is not self-born, and his characteristics have been declared by the Supreme Lord: one who is not a devotee, acting with the intent for livelihood, and lacking the presiding grace of the Lord. (23.8)
One who seeks to become a self-made ascetic by way of animal-like conduct has no authority anywhere;
likewise, the son of one who lives on ashes, the son of one who merely observes vows, and the son of a woman of ill character [have no authority]. (23.9)
The *Devīkhyāyāmala* states that the *kuṇḍa* and the *gola* are wicked;
as is the *punarbhū*, and he who previously bore another sectarian mark (*anyaliṅga*) but has subsequently been established in the Śaiva fold. (23.10)
"By means of the animal-self"—that is to say, not by virtue of being possessed by the Supreme Lord.
And "the remarried woman is wicked"—this connects with what was stated previously. (8–10)
But in our system, there is no such restriction as that [one must be a king]; thus he says:
"In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, however, no such restriction whatsoever has been enjoined:
'One who knows the collection of realities as they truly are is an illuminator for the disciple. (23.11)
Furthermore, the definition beginning with "he who knows all the principles" and so forth is likewise—meaning it is exactly according to the facts. As it is stated there:
"He who, moreover, knows these principles exactly as they are..."
That guru, who reveals the potency of the mantra, is declared to be equal to me.
Men who are touched, spoken to, or even looked upon by him with a joyful heart are liberated from the sins committed even throughout seven lifetimes.
"Furthermore, those living beings who have been initiated by him and impelled by Śiva,
having obtained the fruit according to their desire, proceed to the supreme state. Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: "Since the same principle applies here as well, why is the rule stated in other tantras not extended to this case too?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And in the practice of yoga, one should perform whatever is enjoined here in this tantra. (23.12)
"In that very way, this command (ājñā) has indeed been described for the sake of accomplishment. "One should practice"—this refers, by implication, to that very [command]. As it has been said:
"Since the division of the Tantras is traditionally held to arise from the distinctions of ritual action (kriyā) and so forth..."

"Therefore, whatever has been stated in a particular [text], that alone should be performed, and not according to another system. Thus, this rule regarding the guru applies not only because it pertains to the Kula traditions and so forth in other scriptures, but furthermore—
"One with a squint eye generates hatred, while one who is bald causes the destruction of wealth.
Thus [it is said]:
"Those born in Kāñcī, Kosala, Karṇāṭa, Kaliṅga, and Kāmarūpa..."
Those originating from Kuṅkuṇa, Kāvīrī, and the marshy region of Kaccha;
"These [places] are to be avoided, as well as others which a king should entirely shun"—
considering this and other such passages, [the impurity] exists even by virtue of being located within the region of the body.
Anticipating the objection, "Why then is this restriction not stated in our own scripture? he says:
"But for one who is an ācārya by virtue of being a ritualist (karmin), there [in that context] is the exclusion of those who are one-eyed and so forth. (23.13)

Since nowhere is there anything superior to the totality of causal factors (kārakasāmagrī) for the ritual action, there is the exclusion of Kāñcī and other such places in the *Devīyāmalaśāstra*. (23.14)
Because that fault is seen in anger and the like, how could it exist in one who possesses perfect knowledge?
"Because that fault is seen"—that is, because it is characterized by torment and so forth. As it has been said:
"One should know that there is torment in one who is prone to anger, and that fortunes are fickle in one who is unstable."
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that a person born in regions such as Kāñcī would, by their very nature, be subject to desire, anger, and so forth. "This" refers to anger and the like;
for one who possesses perfect knowledge perceives all beings as being exactly like oneself—this is the intention.

Nor has this been stated by us merely as our own invention; thus he says: "But the teachers [state that] in the *Yāmala* and other scriptures, [the worship of] Svayambhū and the rest is to be avoided. (23.15)
They explained that all of this is intended for the practitioner;
and whatever has been declared by the Guru, or by the Self-born One (Svayambhū) and others in the *Yāmala* and other scriptures as being to be avoided—
that too is entirely with the practitioner in mind— thus they explained, that is, they interpreted.
This is the meaning.
Therefore, the possession of knowledge alone should be accepted as the primary defining characteristic—thus he says:
"Hence, [one should disregard] the conceptualization of place, family, conduct, body, and physical marks. (23.16)
Disregarding even his own complete knowledge, the Guru should act as a teacher.
Regarding this very matter, he states the procedure:
"Having worshipped and offered oblations as before, and having made known what he intends to do... (23.17).
Then the Guru should consecrate that disciple once with sixty-four [vases] using the water of the essence of those mantras, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then, with great generosity, he should explain to him his own entire essence of what is to be done, which is the supreme secret of the scriptures.
"Sixty-four"—this refers, by implication, to sixty-four jars. "Once"—that is, with a single [jar]. And by this, because knowledge alone is primary, the inapplicability of ritual action is revealed;
as it says in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra:
Although the procedure for consecration has been mentioned by [the author] himself, it has not been set forth here in detail.
It states precisely what must be done:
"Disciples who are impelled by the power of Śiva should be favored by you.
But why is this examination performed at the very occasion of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), rather than earlier, at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*)?
To leave no room for the doubt—"How is this done?"—he cites the scripture itself as confirmation:
"This has been stated in the Jñānottara: [there are] Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. (23.20)
Eunuchs, women, Śūdras, and whoever else seeks that [initiation], they are not to be scrutinized at the time of initiation; one should examine them at the time of [receiving] knowledge.
"The Guru is said to have knowledge as his root; he should set in motion the Sevenfold Sacrifice (saptasatrī).
Regarding the word "said"—it was stated immediately prior. Now, one might ask: what indeed is this Sevenfold Sacrifice, and how should he set it in motion? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Initiation, exposition, compassion, friendliness, reflection on the scriptures, and oneness with Śiva. (23.22)
One should maintain these seven perpetual charities, beginning with the gift of food;
and during the rite of consecration, one should provide him with tools such as a chisel and chalk.
The entire collection of ritual implements should be offered to the wise one;
having been consecrated, he should afterwards honor his guru with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
As it has been said,
beginning with: "Having thus rebuked [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule, one should cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) to be bestowed," and so forth.
The uṣṇīṣa, the crown, and so forth; the parasol, the sandals, and the throne;
as well as the elephant, horse, palanquin, and especially the other constituents of sovereignty (rājyāṅga).

Having given a ritual knife, scissors, a whetstone, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a bundle of *darbha* grass, a book, a rosary, and so forth, he remains established in one of the four stages of life (*āśrama*).
"By the path of grace for those to be initiated, initiation and its exposition must always be performed by you;
from this day forward, this is your authority by the command of Śiva," and so forth.
"The disciple should worship the guru with extensive offerings according to his means," thus ends [the section]. ||24||
Now, one might ask: "Having bestowed this consecration upon him, how should the Guru subsequently conduct himself?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"A Guru who is a mere ritualist, devoid of knowledge, must not [retain] his own office after having handed it over."
Furthermore, one should not perform the authorization for initiation and other rites without his permission.
Thus he should cause [the disciple] to hear this; he too, having offered salutation, should rejoice.

Regarding the phrase "of him"—it refers to one who has been consecrated by himself. Furthermore, this verse was written by scribes in some places after the line "he should maintain the seven sacrificial sessions," due to confusion.
That should be disregarded.
Furthermore, this is the distinction regarding the Knower; thus he says:
"From that time forward, that former teacher has relinquished his authority. (23–26)
He may wander at will, free from constraints regarding exposition, initiation, and so forth; for by performing these he is not bound, being like one lamp lit from another. (23–27)

The continuity [of the lineage] does not lapse from its authority; one who does not perform [the rites] is not obstructed. Furthermore, it is stated in the Siddhāntatantra that one who performs [them] previously would be hindered. (23–28)

"Previous" means the first knower (*jñānin*). By the statement "whether acting or not acting, he is not bound," the very fact of being free from constraints is reinforced. "Like one lamp from another lamp"—the intention is that there is no difference whatsoever in the illuminating capacity of a lamp that produces another lamp.
*Cyavaḥ* and *pracyavaḥ*: [these two terms apply] when the governing authority (*adhikāra*) has not been superseded by a preceding rule.
He recites the very text found therein:
"One who imparts instruction according to the truth is called an Ācārya; and there must be no contempt at the time of the ritual action regarding the liberation from saṃsāra. (23–29)
A teacher who is possessed of the [true] principles should not initiate a disciple out of pride;
for he who does so shall dwell in hell and become afflicted by disease in this world. (23–30)
"Yaḥ" means one who is contemptuous and arrogant; "asya" refers to such a person. || 30 ||
Now, [the author] describes this teacher’s vow of learning (vidyāvrata):
"Having received initiation, that Guru should for six months meditate upon and recite the entire liturgy of mantras taught in the Tantras, until he becomes one with them. (23.31)

As soon as one has become identified with that [reality], one attains heroic power; therefore, one should exert effort in remaining established in that state of identification, whereby one may sever the bonds. (23–32)
"The entire mantra-paddhati" refers to the triad of goddesses, the four Bhairavas, and the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghora. As it has been said:
"The teacher, observing silence, should also recite [the mantra] every day for six months."
The fifteen mantras which were previously spoken by me to you—
Equipped with the previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa) and performing the fire-ritual three times a day, one should,
while observing celibacy, meditate upon the trident described earlier.
Having performed the previously described sacrifice within a circle marked by a trident,
the teacher should then consecrate himself both at the beginning and at the end.
"Having thus fulfilled his vows, the practitioner, the most excellent knower of mantras, performs the rites of restraint and grace without being obstructed. (Mā.vi.
Thus, he states the method for one who recites the mantra sequence while abiding in absorption in that [mantra]:
"Rising from the heart-cakra, subtle, resembling the moon or crystal, in the form of a line, consisting of sound, tranquil, and moving through the series of cakras. (23.33)
Established at the dvādaśānta within the suṣumṇā in the midst of the three paths, one should fill the heart-cakra there and recite the mantra, which possesses a blazing radiance. (23–34)
[The fire] resembling the submarine conflagration (aurva) flows through the apertures of the eyes, the pores of the skin, and so forth.

By the term "sauṣumna," the piṅgalā [nāḍī] is also indicated. "Therein" means when the vital power (prāṇa-śakti) has become firmly established at the "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta). "The heart-cakra" refers to it by way of its coming and going; therefore—
It should be understood that this extends from the heart-cakra up to the heart-cakra itself.

Because it carries forth flames through the apertures of the eyes and other senses, it is "equal to the submarine fire" (vaḍavāgni)—meaning it is extremely radiant. For this very reason, it is said to have a "blazing luster."
He demonstrates the very going and coming of the mantra:
"As far as it is strewn with peaceful crests, dissolving the clarified butter of the universe. (23–35)
Then, with the interior of the cavity of the navel satisfied by the stream of clarified butter, the mantras thus become bestowers of liberation—blazing, awakened, and perfectly pure. (23–36)

In the "peaceful" [state] at the *dvādaśānta*, due to the complete cessation of all mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*); for this very reason it is said: "that which dissolves the clarified butter of the universe. By the word "navel," the heart-center (*hṛccakra*) is indicated by proximity.
"Thus" means: through the upward movement (*uccāra*) as the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*). (36)
Thus, once the identity of the mantra and the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) is established, where indeed— in the wheels (cakras), the foundations (ādhāras), or elsewhere—
could this mantra attain its greatness, which consists in the penetration of its own potency? To this, he says:

It reaches the root, the bulb, the navel, the heart, the throat, the forehead, and the palate; it reaches the half-moon, the obstructress (rodhikā), the sound (nāda), its end (nādānta), and the pervasive power (vyāpinī-śakti).

Whether one recites [the mantra] in the wheel of Samana, Unmana, Śuddhātman, or Paracakra— by means of the distinction between the whole and its parts— in whichever wheel one may perform the recitation.
"In this regard, it is stated in the *Devīyāmala*: 'In each of those places, there is the Great Mantra.
Its end is the end of *nāda*. The supreme wheel is as follows:
'...at the end of *unmanī* is Supreme Śiva.'"

Thus it has been defined. And since the sequence is not intended to be significant here, there is sometimes an expression even without a sequence. By the sense of the word "japet" (one should recite), the mantra is meant, whose specific quality is its attainment within the respective wheels (*cakras*) and supports (*ādhāras*). Regarding the phrase "due to the piercing [of the centers] collectively and individually"—collectivity (*samastatva*)...
And the meaning is: "having resorted to the state of being separate."
He concludes the very subject at hand:
"This is declared to be the Vidyā-vow for the sake of attaining the potency of the mantra. (23-39)
And as it has been stated in the Spandaśāsana, that this is indeed identity (*tādātmya*):
"Having seized that power, mantras possess the power of the Omniscient One. (23.40)
They proceed toward their respective offices, like the sense organs of embodied beings. "That" refers to the vow; "identity alone" refers to [attainment] through the mantra.
And thus, only for one who has performed the vow of the sciences (vidyāvrata) does there exist eligibility for the seven sacrifices; so it is said:
"Having subsequently performed the vow of the sciences, [he may engage] in initiation, exposition, and all other such matters. (23.41)
One should [bestow this] upon worthy disciples, never upon those who are unworthy.
Regarding the examination of worthiness and unworthiness, he shows the reasoning by way of an illustration:
"O Brahmin, one should engage [the disciple] in the secret [teaching] after examining him; otherwise, [it would be] the reverse. (23-42)
"Even power [is attained] from right conduct alone, and not otherwise," as stated in the *Ūrmiśāsana*.

"From contrary conduct" means from that which contradicts the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, such as the drinking of wine and so forth. "In this way" means precisely from contrary conduct that is opposed to worldly norms, such as sexual intercourse and the like; for otherwise...
It has been stated that they should proceed through greed, passion, and so forth, and not otherwise.
Thus, being preoccupied with the benefit of others, he may perform even the daily rites and so forth in brief;
as it is said:
"He should perform the daily rites and so forth very briefly, as stated in the Brahmayāmala. (23.43)

"O Dear One, one who has fulfilled the observances of the Vidyā may recollect everything mentally. Now, one might raise the doubt: "But what if this person, though intent on examination, performs initiation out of negligence, not knowing the unfitness of someone? Is he at fault or not? Anticipating this, he says:
His omniscience is obscured by his connection with a physical body, and he is a vessel for hypocrisy.
Even if he initiates one who is unworthy, the teacher is never at fault;
however, having recognized the person's unfitness, he must not initiate him, for that would lead to sin.
In the absence of knowledge, the cause for the concealment of omniscience through connection with the body is [ignorance]. "One should initiate"—that is, out of greed and so forth. 45.
Even so, one should repeatedly examine the initiated disciple regarding the imparting of knowledge and other matters;
thus he says:
"Having understood him [to be fit] for knowledge, as well as for the attainment of the scriptures and the status of a guru, [one should initiate him] again."
One should examine him further still, ensuring he possesses the appropriate decorum for each occasion.

One should employ [the disciple] in this or that [practice], but never by way of the opposite. The word "parīkṣeta" (one should examine) is to be construed here with "viparyayāt" (from the opposite). "Tatra tatra" means in the scriptures of knowledge and so forth.
"Viparyayāt" means from that which is characterized by the absence of the aforementioned suitability.

One might object: "In this way, since the desire to know (jijñāsā) would otherwise be inexplicable, he must certainly possess the supreme Lord's presiding presence; and that itself is what is called 'fitness' (yogyatva). So what is the use of any further examination of fitness or unfitness?"—thus the objection is raised.
But surely, how can desire for that object arise in one who is unfit for it? (23.47)
The very will presided over by Him (the Lord) would indicate his fitness in that regard—in other words, in knowledge and so forth. Accepting this very point, he provides the rebuttal:
"True, that awakened will does not reach firm establishment anywhere. (23.48)
"Just as for one whose nature is sinful, [the desire] to abandon sin [does not take root];
surely, even though awakened by the presiding presence of the Supreme Lord, how could such a desire not attain growth?"— anticipating this doubt, he says:
Establishedness and non-establishedness [of a word] also depend upon his will, through the grace of Śambhu.
For this very reason, even when such a desire has awakened, one is not a fit vessel for knowledge and the like because that [desire] does not take root; thus he says:
"One whose such desire has not taken root is, for that very reason, not a fit vessel."
He who, having taken up right knowledge, is devoid of faith in the Guru. || 23-50 ||
"One might cause the world to perish; one should not impart knowledge once this [person] has been known.
Regarding "one might cause to perish"—this is due to contrary conduct.
Thus, when it is known that this person is unfit because their desire has not taken root, one should simply not impart knowledge.
Thus he says: "In this [there is] not," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding one who was not known at the time of the transmission of knowledge but is known at a later time—for such a person, one should indeed perform the withdrawal of that knowledge—as it is said:
"Even if [the disciple] was previously unknown, once he is known, one should carry out the withdrawal of his realization. (23.51)
This very point regarding the seizing of the *mātṛkā* is stated:
"When he has been known again and again as one devoid of trust, then one should meditate upon him in his entirety, flashing like the moon and the sun. (23.52)
Then, one should meditate upon the deluding Vāmā Śakti, who has risen from the sky of consciousness in the lotus of one's own heart and is as dark as Rāhu.
Having visualized her as having emerged according to the sequence of the left-hand path (vāmācāra) and proceeding toward the object to be accomplished (sādhya),
one should contemplate that [object] with its radiance swallowed by her.
By this sequence of application, for one of dull intellect and evil nature, knowledge, mantras, vidyās, and the like, bring about only harm. (23.55)
"Again and again"—the intention here is that even in this case, there should be no occurrence of "otherwise-ness.
"Vāmācāra" means by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). As it has been said:
"Having acquired knowledge through the [proper] method, one does not subsequently fall back from it."
Then, the wise one should perform the extraction of his consciousness.
Then, having observed that blazing light at the tip of his thumb, he should,
with one-pointed mind, gradually withdraw that radiance and lead it to the dvādaśānta.
Alternatively, having meditated on [the object] as having the luster of the solar disc, one should contemplate it being severed before one's eyes and swallowed by a power in the form of Rāhu.
By this method, for that dull-witted and evil-minded person,
knowledge, mantras, sciences, and the like do not provide any assistance.
"Even if there are a thousand offenses, one should perform this rite when possessed by great anger; it should never be done for the sake of mere sport. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 18.66) ||55||
But surely, since knowledge and action constitute the very nature of the self, the removal of its knowledge would result in the destruction of the self itself;
for we do not, like the followers of Kaṇāda and others, maintain a relationship of quality and qualified between the self and its knowledge— so how is this stated in our scripture?

Thus he raises an objection: "But how could consciousness, which resides within the self, be capable of being taken away? Therefore, how can the 'taking away of consciousness' be taught in the Śrīpūrva [Tantra]? (5.23–56)
To this, he provides the following rebuttal:
It is said that the knowledge of this disciple has not yet reached full maturity;
for if it were so, why would there be a "taking away" of one who possesses complete fitness? (23.57)

For this knowledge of the disciple has not yet reached its full maturity— that is to say, it has not attained purity. For if it had reached maturity, how could there be [any further need] for that knowledge which, by virtue of its capacity to achieve identity with the supreme, full abode, is itself already celebrated?
It would result in mere abduction; for in this way, it would amount to the very destruction of the self—this has already been stated. || 57 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the instruction for this has already been given, why has knowledge not become firmly established?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But this [disciple] has been rendered deeply deluded by the Lord through the power of Māyā."
Therefore, by its very nature, this [knowledge] and so forth is harmful to him. || 23-58 ||

Now, one might object: "If this [initiation] is by its very nature detrimental to knowledge and the rest because it is permeated by the power of dissolution (*vilaya-śakti*), why would the Guru perform the withdrawal of consciousness (*vijñānāpaharaṇa*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Guru, moreover, being non-different from Śiva, performs the fivefold action."
If he should perform it, then his qualification would be complete.

Therefore, just as [the Lord is authorized] regarding the creation, maintenance, and removal of impurity of the pure principles, the Guru is likewise authorized in the fourfold task of [bestowing] union and grace. (23.60)
One should perform that [activity] through non-difference from Śiva; likewise, this fifth activity called concealment (tirobhāva) is also performed by him whose very nature is Śiva-hood.

"From this"—because he possesses full authority by virtue of performing the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*). "That"—refers to the fourfold effect (*kāryacatuṣka*). Anticipating the question, "What would happen to him by thus performing the fivefold activity?", it is said: "In that way, he consists of the nature of Śiva. (61)
And because he is of such a nature conducive to the highest good, he would never become angry even in any circumstance—thus [the author] says:

"For this very reason, in the Śiva-scripture and in knowledge, he is a vessel of confidence; even if, due to the teacher's own delusion, he should become an object of anger, he is not [thereby] obscured. (23.62)

Therefore, precisely because the Guru is of the nature of Śiva, even though the disciple—by virtue of his former state—was a vessel for consolation in the Śaiva scriptures and so forth, yet has become obscured through delusion, he is not an object of anger; that is to say, the Guru should not direct anger toward him. ||62||
Now, one might ask: "What is this that has been said? If [it is the case], then only he whose teacher is angry is the transmigrating being who is concealed.
To this, he says: "For he whose teacher is angry is said to be concealed."

This is true; however, that Guru is indeed the Supreme Lord himself, supremely compassionate because he is intent on desiring to uplift the entire world, and since he consists of truth and knowledge, who could feel anger toward whom?
Thus he says:
For he is indeed a god who is still subject to saṃsāra, and not a guru who knows the falsehood [of worldly existence]. (23.63)
And for that very reason, even if the reviler of the scriptures and so forth is not consumed by the Guru’s wrath, he is nevertheless rendered invisible [to the divine grace]. (23.64)
The word *hi* is used for emphasis. "One who possesses false knowledge" (*mṛṣāvid*) means one whose nature is erroneous cognition;

the intention is that if this were the case, there would indeed be room for anger. "Therefore" (*tataḥ*) means precisely because of the absence of the nature of erroneous cognition. "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) refers to the greatness of the reality (*vastu*).
Because it is difficult to overstep. ||64||
This is also the view of our own teachers; thus he says:

"But this is the tradition of our teachers: when a disciple has become obscured [of his own accord], the wise teacher should neither be angry nor curse him, for he is always one who bestows grace. (23.65)
In the sense of "therefore" (tuh). ||65||
For there remains nothing else to be done by him here who intends to conceal himself of his own accord, such that it would have to be performed even by this [agent]; thus he says:
"If, impelled by the will of the Lord, he should press the noose against his throat."
What need would there be for the teacher’s cooperation in that regard?
"What would need to be done?"—the meaning is that here there is no purpose whatsoever for an auxiliary cause.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, why would his performance of the fivefold cosmic act (*pañcavidhakṛtya*), which is non-different from Śiva, not be undermined? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For although the Guru is non-different from Śiva, by worshipping the Lord’s primary power consisting of grace, he may grant grace in every way. (23.67)
As it is said there:
"One who has fallen from this method cannot be joined again by another through higher knowledge, until his own extraction is performed by that very same [teacher]. (Mālinīvijaya-tantra 18.67)
Thus [ends the verse]. ||67||
If one objects: "In that case, for what purpose would [the teacher] perform the 'stealing' of consciousness (vijñānāpaharaṇa)?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"However, such a thing is taught in the scripture solely to make known [the disciple's] absolute freedom (svātantrya)."
One must not provide a hand to those who are falling, nor should one tolerate their downfall.
Thus, he must be regarded as one solely devoted to compassion—so it is said:
"For this very reason, because of the sovereignty of his will, the Guru should, out of compassion, purify him through penances and then initiate him once he has turned his face upward again. (23.69)
"Because of her sovereignty"—for this indeed is her sovereignty: that she may bestow grace once again even upon one who has been restrained. || 69 ||

But has it not been said that one who has fallen from this [state] is indeed called "hidden"? In this way, having fallen even from that [higher state] due to a lack of confidence in the other, how could such a person, being deprived of both, be worthy of grace here as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Having turned toward the upward vision, if one remains thereafter without full confidence, even if one subsequently resorts to a lower scripture, one will not attain the state of being a fit vessel for the highest good. (23.70)
But one who has resorted to the downward vision with a mind lacking confidence in it,
yet partakes of the upward teaching, shall abandon that evil and become Śiva.
He illustrates this very point by means of an example:
"For even one who is a limb of the minister, if he bears malice toward the king, is destroyed;
but the reverse is not so. Thus, one should take recourse in the higher vision. (23.72)
For this very reason, our own scripture is also thus; so he says:
"In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra it was stated by him [the Lord] that [one is not liberated] until one has been extracted by Him alone. He explains this very point according to its essential purport:
For here, this meaning is augmented by all that has been previously stated. (23.73)
In this context, the word "that" (sa) refers back to the teacher;
the particle "tāvat" (firstly/indeed) serves to indicate the absence of any disagreement.
He also states the meaning of the word "only" (eva):
"By one who possesses such well-practiced knowledge and abides in the higher state. (23.74)
For one who has not been uplifted by another teacher, this [state] is not superior;
for this very reason, the analogy of the lotus and the sun is set forth here. (23.75)
Regarding the term *nirūpita* ("described"): this is explained in the *Pañcikā* itself. As it is said there:
"The lotus, though other planets and suns are present, does not attain full bloom because it lacks the downpour of the sun's rays; thus it remains contracted."
"In this way, the lotus-heart of the disciple, which had been closed when deprived of the Guru's feet, blossoms once again through the falling of those very feet. (75)
One might object: "Let him have another teacher as well; what is the purpose of that specific teacher?
Anticipating this doubt, he renders it untenable by means of another illustration:
"For the light of the sun, which illuminates the three worlds, is indeed one thing, and the light of the moon is another."
The knowledge of the teacher of the three [higher] lineages is of one kind, while that of those abiding in the lower [lineages] is of another.
Now, one might object: "If, in such a case, the meal for this teacher has already been finished, what then should be done by him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, when there is an absence of a previously existing teacher..."
Turning back toward it once more, he should take refuge in another who possesses those characteristics. || 23.77 ||
And its definition here is stated in [the Mālinīvijayottara-tantra] beginning with: "He, moreover, who [perceives] all the principles... (Mā.vi. 2.10). ||77||
But while he is alive, one must not abandon him—thus it is said:
"If, while he exists, one were clearly to turn away [from him] and abandon him, then there would arise a fault pertaining to one side or the other, which destroys one's authority. (23.78)

The essential point here is that one should take refuge only in a Guru who stands within the higher teaching (*ūrdhva-śāsana*). However, if a fault exists, even mutual abandonment must be performed; thus he says "if," and so forth. ||78||
Now, one might ask: "In this context, should the fault be understood as worldly or scriptural? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And here, a fault is not defined as a fault by virtue of its being situated in the world;
rather, it is considered to consist in the manifestation of ignorance and the manifestation of what is improper. (23.79)
For the disciple as well, the primary defect is the state of lacking confidence in such knowledge; for all other defects arise from that. (23.80)
He defines the nature of the fault that is strictly scriptural with the words beginning "ajñāna" (ignorance), etc.

From the word "api" (also), the word "guroḥ" (of the teacher) is understood; thus the connection is: "this is considered the primary fault of both the teacher and the disciple. In that regard, first, there is the ignorance of the teacher, even though he possesses knowledge.

[This refers to] the inability to explain [the teaching], or the explanation of a meaning that is improper even if it pertains to reality. "Others" refers to such things as the teacher's failure to perform prescribed duties and so forth, as well as the disciple's failure to accept a teacher and so forth.
The particle *hi* is used as an expletive for poetic ornamentation. ||80||

He confirms, by means of an example and through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that the failure to accept a guru is indeed caused by a lack of confidence in knowledge: "For who, once his disease has been destroyed, would hold a physician in high esteem?"
Surely one who is envious and whose disease has not been dispelled pretends to be healthy by force.
Thus, one who is fully confident in this knowledge—what would he not do for his guru? If he does nothing, then he is surely lacking confidence, even though he stands as if he were confident. (23.82)

For instance, everyone whose disease has been destroyed would show great respect toward a physician, thinking, "Our lives have been restored by your grace"; whereas one who is envious and jealous toward him would,
even though his own disease is certainly not destroyed and he is unwell, forcibly consider himself to be healthy.
Thus, what service indeed would a disciple who has full confidence in knowledge not perform for the teacher? But one who lacks confidence in knowledge—
even if in reality he is not confident— remains as if confident, thinking, "What business have I with my teacher?"
The meaning is that one would thus vainly maintain such a conceit regarding one's own self. || 81-82 ||
One might object: "What is the authority for the claim that only the scriptural defects of the guru are to be taken into account, and not his worldly ones?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"These defects of the guru, such as ignorance and the like, are indeed [scriptural] defects, not worldly ones."
Thus it was stated in the *Mālinīvijayottara* in order to make this known. (23.83)
One should not investigate his conduct, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
he alone knows what is appropriate or inappropriate. (23.84)
When he is attached to improper actions that deprive one of life or wealth, then he should be restrained by a wise man who bows before him. (23.85)
The qualification regarding improper acts was stated precisely with the aforementioned intention;
therefore, even if he is being strongly restrained, if he does not desist, [the following applies]. (23.86)
Then, having gone elsewhere to some other place, one should contemplate Śiva alone;
one should not search [for his faults], as it has been said:
"He who, while desiring to enter [the path], should search for the conduct of the Guru..."
Having approached a true guru, he shall swiftly attain Śiva.
"After falling at his feet, one should never thereafter seize upon any blemish;
for that would only soil the disciple's own radiant intellect.
Thus it is said: "He alone truly knows," because he alone has reached the further shore of the scriptures.
The phrase "the intended meaning has been stated" refers to the fact that the seizure of one's vital breath and possessions is a worldly matter.
Now, if this were so, he would not know the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; thus:
"Even for a guru who is conceited and does not know what should or should not be done..."

Anticipating the objection— "In view of such statements as 'The abandonment of one who has entered upon a wrong path is ordained,' let his abandonment alone be performed; what is the use of going elsewhere?"— he says:
For he would not incur that fault which belongs to one who performs cultivation on barren soil. (23.87)
He might act [thus], or he might go out at night; for such a person is a robber of wealth and life.
However, one who fears the displeasure of that person should instead behave toward him in a similar manner.
Thinking, "Lest he hear that which is unpleasant," it was spoken;
yet this has not been stated in our own scripture. To this he says:
"And that has been stated in the venerable Mātaṅga, but it was not studied [by us] for fear of its vastness. (23.89)
"Out of fear of prolixity"—this means for fear of excessive expansion of the text. Therefore, that [matter] should be followed from the *Caryāpāda* and other sections by oneself. ||89||

Now, one might ask: does the restriction "as long as it has not been extracted by that very [teacher]" aim solely to exclude other teachers, or does it also aim to prohibit independent discernment? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And that which was stated—that 'this much must be done'—is certainly [the case]."
For those seized by intense power, it will manifest spontaneously within their own hearts.
If this is so, has anything been accomplished by the Guru? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But this instruction is taught for the purpose of gradually kindling one's own power in those of dull or middling capacity; for in this way, that power truly blazes forth intensely. (23.91)
He illustrates this very point with an example:
"The entire essence of love, shining forth from within, is seen elsewhere for the sake of firmness in those who partake in the expansive intensity made beautiful by steadfast passion. (23.92)
"Elsewhere"—that is, in the case of one whose passion is not firm. ||92||
Now, surely this entire multitude of atoms manifests from consciousness alone, and that consciousness is undifferentiated everywhere;
so how is it that this inconsistent example has been cited— that for someone [the manifestation occurs] by itself?
Anticipating the doubt—"In this way, such a nature might manifest for one, but what of another?"—he says:
"But why is this an example? What inauspicious thing has been done by this [example]?
The vibration of consciousness (citspanda) is all-pervading; it appears in such and such ways due to different limiting adjuncts (upādhi). (23.93)

He explains this very point with the words beginning "What [is it]? and so forth. Now, what exactly has been rendered inconsistent by this illustration? The meaning is that although that vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) is undifferentiated everywhere, it may nevertheless assume various forms of diversity through the power of its association with various distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
He demonstrates that very variety:
"Someone who has become concealed might, even while turning his face upward again, be liberated by himself alone, just as before, even without a teacher. (23.94)

The phrase "even though" (*sannapi*) is to be connected with what precedes as well. "As before" (*prāgvat*) means according to the sequence taught at the beginning of the thirteenth chapter and elsewhere. || 94 ||
One might ask: "Even if [the soul] has become concealed, could it still possess innate knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But this method is not mentioned here, as it occurs through the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), being impossible [otherwise], like [the cases of] intense anger and favor. (23.95)
For this method characterized as "innate" (sāṃsiddhika) has not been described here in the context of one who is concealed; rather,

it is presented by way of mere possibility according to the context, meaning that this person, though concealed, has reached [the state of grace] through the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), being one who possesses a very slight descent of grace.

And this is inconceivable; for just as in the case of someone who has been made an object of intense anger by a king or similar authority, his favor would not return immediately without the intervention of another,
so too, how could this [favor] occur spontaneously without a guide?
Knowledge shall manifest. And by this much, the very theft of knowledge through the medium of the object has been distinguished. ||95||
And this must necessarily be observed by the Guru; thus he says:
"The Guru should observe this rule which has been declared for the Guru;
otherwise he would not go to Śiva," as described in the *Śrīmatsāra*. (23.96)
He recites exactly what was stated in the *Śrītrikasāra*:
"Those who act unrighteously and utterly disregard the meaning of the scriptures—those teachers have fallen from their observances (*samaya*) and go to the city of Ardhanārīśa. (23.97)
Regarding the phrase *ardhanārīśapure*: as it is stated therein—"Above is the principle of the Bindu (*bindutattva*); Īśvara is the deity there.
The rule (*vidhi*) for those who observe the covenant (*samayin*) has been definitively declared to you there."
Above that is Ardhanārīśa, filled with great worlds;
however, in the Skandayāmala Tantra, Ananta is proclaimed [to be there].
O illustrious one, it is the command of the Supreme Lord that [the disciple] should remain as a restrainer of those teachers who have fallen from the conduct of their commitments (samayācāra).
"Those who act unjustly and those who do not seek the true meaning of the texts— for them, who walk the path of injustice, shall be the dwelling place therein.
Thus [ends verse 97].
And this has not been stated only here, but also in other scriptures—as he says:

"Elsewhere as well, one should not abandon one's [spiritual] authority, for then one attains the state of a Vidyeśvara; otherwise, by abandoning the rule (samaya), one becomes a flesh-eating demon for a hundred years. (23.98)
As it has been said:
"If he does not exercise authority, he shall become a Vidyeśa upon the dissolution of the body.
Likewise:
"And by transgressing the rule of pacification, O Goddess, one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years," so it is said. (98)
Right here, through the intent of these three statements, he explains the division of the subject matter:
"The intended meaning therein is as follows: Unnaya is the Guru of the Siddhānta;
Piśāca is a Vidyeśa; but Tāntrika is indeed Śuddha. (23.99)
The teacher of the Trika (Ṣaḍardha) resides in the world of Ardhanārīśvara;
"Unnaya" means one who has transcended the conventional rules (samaya). This [term] is also to be applied later.
"Pure" means having the direct form of a Vidyeśvara. He is a Tantrika.
One who is devoted to the Bhairavīya system and other such traditions.
Regarding this, he states the division of the subject matter:
"This is said to be the path of teachers for whom ritual action (karman) is predominant. (23.100)
And it has been described everywhere that "this is not a bondage for the wise.
Now, in order to state the status of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), he extends the previously mentioned rule to his consecration (*abhiṣeka*):
"This entire procedure is said to apply even to the consecration of the practitioner. (23.101)
Regarding that as well, he states the distinction:
"In this case, there is indeed no conferral of authority (*adhikāra*), nor is there a vow of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*);
rather, there is the conferral of the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhyamantra*) here within the sequence of rites for one's own benefit. (23.102)
In all cases, there should be instruction and the offering of one's own implements.
Regarding "instruction," it has been said:
"To these two, one should fully and correctly impart the threefold knowledge."
"The yogi should give his own command regarding the performance of his own practice. Regarding "his own implements," it is said:
"One should provide the rosary and other items for the sake of the practitioner's qualification."
The ritual manual for mantras, a rosary, chalk, an umbrella, and sandals;
"Having offered [the initiation] while excluding the *uṣṇīṣa* and having entered into the presence of Śiva,
one should afterwards give the mantra of the sādhya along with flowers and water.
Thus it is said.
He concludes this very point with the first half [of the verse]:
"The procedure for initiation has been described by the Supreme Lord exactly as it was described. (23.103)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus all is auspicious. 103.
Jayaratha, whose conduct was rendered steadfast through the eternal practice of the nectar of service to the glorious True Guru, has composed this twenty-third daily observance with a pure intellect.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation" (*Abhiṣekaprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and most eminent teacher of Mahāmaheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. 23.
The Twenty-Fourth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
He who would unite even one whose life has departed with the supreme vessel of nectar in the transcendent abode—
May the auspicious form of Śiva, whose body is the very self of the world, bestow welfare upon you. || 1 ||
