Now, with the second half [of the verse], he begins to describe the procedure for the final rites (antyeṣṭi):
"Now, hear the secret final consecration as proclaimed in the Śāmbhava teaching.
(24.1) Therein, he first defines the nature of the qualified candidate:
For all those situated in lower stages, even if they have reached the status of a guru,
one should clearly perform the initiation for the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi-dīkṣā) following the previously described descent of power (śaktipāta).
And for those who follow the higher teachings but whose souls are impaired by their violation of the rules (samaya),
the initiation of the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi-dīkṣā) must be performed by a Guru who knows the reality (tattva).

"Of those situated below" refers to the Vaiṣṇavas and others. "Due to the descent of power" (śaktipāta) means by way of the intense entreaty of relatives and others. "Previously" refers to the initiation for the elevation of the deceased (mṛtoddhāradīkṣā).
"Of those belonging to the higher teachings" refers to the Śaivas and others. ||3||
Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", he says:

"For one who has indeed stumbled due to negligence regarding the faults of conventional conduct, the initiation of the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi-dīkṣā) must be performed; so it is stated in the venerable Dīkṣottara scripture. (24.4)

Regarding this very matter, he states the procedure: "Whatever was previously described in the rite called 'the extraction of the deceased,' all that should be performed here upon the corpse in place of the image. (24.5)
And here there is a specific distinction according to another scripture; thus he says:
"This procedure, as declared in the Śrīsiddhātantra, is now being set forth.
He states that very procedure:
Having made that which was last first, and that which was first last.
Having withdrawn each one individually, that rite which is performed is considered the final oblation (antyeṣṭi) for two types [of practitioners];
however, it is not for the adept (sādhaka) whose time has been consumed by worship, meditation, and recitation.
O Dear One, when an Ācārya who is perfected in reality dies anywhere, he becomes liberated from alms-food and the like, or he becomes a sky-walker. (24.8)
The funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) does not exist at all for one whose mind is pure and who stands at the summit.

In this context, that which consists of the syllables of the mantra and so forth— which was last becomes first, and that which was first becomes last— having thus reversed them and recited each one individually in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), this is the rite (*iṣṭi*).

The meaning is that the *iṣṭi* (sacrificial rite) begins from one end and extends to the other end. And that [rite] must be performed by the *samayin* and the *putraka* alone—thus he says, "the twofold view. Regarding the term *amūrdhani*:
since the word *mūrdhan* (head/summit) serves as an indicator for the body, it means "one who is devoid of identification with that [body]."
And regarding these two, the reason for the absence of the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) is presented by means of a qualification.
This [rite] is not to be performed only for those who have been harmed by the violation of their commitments (samaya), but also for others;
thus he says:
"And those who have been killed through the application of mantras, yogas, and so forth, are indeed in hell. (24.9)
The compassionate preceptor should perform their funeral rites here;
however, in this cremation ritual, there shall be no mandala or similar requirements.

Some have declared that even in the abode of the departed (the cremation ground), one should perform all that [is required] after having worshipped the All-pervading Lord; one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as previously described. (24.11)
By means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal, from the feet up to the top of the head;
in that very same way, one should awaken this [consciousness] through ritual action, knowledge, and meditative absorption.
He demonstrates the very process of action and so forth by dividing it according to the teaching of the *Śrīkulagahvara*:
"One should obstruct the reality-principle (*tattva*) with the Bindu; one should pierce it with the seed-syllable of Śakti.
One should strike it in the region of Nāda, and one should strike it with the Trident. (24.13)
By means of the emission (visarga) moving repeatedly within the suṣumnā, one should strike all the kalās; thereupon, that bound soul (paśu) trembles.
Or one may lift up the left hand and then join it to the Supreme;
for liberation without conviction is indeed untrustworthy to those who are deluded.
"For that purpose this was proclaimed, but this is not suitable for liberation"—thus the Supreme Lord spoke in the Śrī Kulagahvara scripture. (24.16)

In this context, the teacher should indeed restrain within his own heart— by way of non-difference from himself— the bound reality (pāśava-tattva) that has been drawn forth by the drop (bindu), by the vital breath (prāṇa), and through the sequence of the Great Net Yoga (mahājālayoga-krama);
thereafter, by entering the central channel (madhyadhāman), he should proceed upward from that very point.
One should interweave it with the seed-syllable of Śakti, which is an ocean of nectar;
thereafter, one should strike it at the locus of Nāda by piercing the fierce knot (raudra-granthi) and cause the vibration (spanda) to be grasped.
Then, one should strike it up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) with the seed-syllable of the trident (triśūla); thereafter, it becomes completely full.

One should repeatedly strike all sixteen digits (*kalās*) by means of the emission (*visarga*), which bears the lunar form and abides in the state that transcends all, according to the scriptural teaching: "In the Person (*puruṣa*) there are sixteen digits... and so forth.

One should assail [the victim] by means of one's own non-differentiation, whereby that sacrificial animal (paśu) to be extracted trembles or raises its left hand. Then, immediately after the arising of this sign of success, one should join him to the other—that is, one should perform his union within the Self of full consciousness—this is the meaning. || 16 ||
Anticipating the objection, "Even if this means of knowledge (*pratyaya*) does not have an absolute utility for liberation, what is the point of it?", he says:
"That which is beyond the senses, such as liberation and so forth, is to be accomplished through inference by means of these means of knowledge."
Regarding this, there is also a specific distinction found in another scripture; thus he says:
"And in the *Dīkṣottara*, the offering of the group of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) is taught here. (24.17)
He states that very procedure:
"In the lotus whose petals are the Vedas, one should worship the god Sadāśiva in the center, and the quartet of Īśa, Rudra, Hari, and Brahmā starting from the eastern direction. (24.18)
Having performed worship, one should offer hearing and touch, taste, smell, the two bodies,
intellect, ego, and mind to Brahmā and the others in their respective order.
Having performed the libation for these with one hundred oblations,
the preceptor [performs] this renunciatory initiation (sāṃnyāsikī dīkṣā), which purifies the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka).
"Vapuḥ" means form; one should sequentially project [it] into Brahmā and the others, according to the sequence.
As it has been said:
"At the conclusion of the purification of the kalās, [one should project] Brahmā, the lord of the causes."
Having first invoked them by their own names preceded by the syllable *praṇava*, one should satisfy them and then offer [the oblation].
"One should abandon sound and touch in this [state]...
and "...one should always offer taste, which is a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka*, to Viṣṇu."
Thus:
"Then, having invoked Rudra with the *praṇava* and other mantras, and having established him, one should worship him.
Then, O Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon his form and color, following the fixed oblation."
Thus,
having invoked the Lord with the name beginning with "Śva" and preceded by the *praṇava*, one should worship Him;
having worshipped, offered oblations, and performed the libation, one should [worship] the two portions consisting of intellect (*buddhi*) and ego (*ahaṃkṛti*).
"Then, having invoked Sadāśiva while reciting the root mantra, one should deposit the mind, which is a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka*, into the Lord of Causes. Thus [it is said]. (20)
Having thus described his *saṃskāra*, he states its purpose:
"In the absence of the *puryaṣṭaka*, there are no heavens, hells, and so forth;
having realized this, one should not perform even the slightest worldly action. (24.21)

It is stated in the Śrīmādhavakula: "Even for those who have died while remaining established in the teaching, one should avoid worldly customs such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the pouring of water (udaka), and the like. (24.22)
Regarding the word *hetau*: "in that manner" means by the method already described. || 22 ||
"One must perform only that which is prescribed by one's own scripture"—thus he says:
"Having fully worshipped Śiva, one should perform the worship of the Cakra according to one's capacity, sequentially on the tenth, thirtieth, and thirtieth days of the year. (24.23)
The mention of "the third" is an elliptical expression for the first and fourth; the mention of "the tenth" is likewise [an elliptical expression] for the eleventh as well. || 23 ||
He concludes this very point with the first half-verse: "Thus has been described this sacrifice of the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi-yāga) as spoken by the Supreme Lord. (24-24)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Last Rites," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 24.
Thus all is auspicious. || 24 ||
Jayaratha, whose victory was celebrated for his expertise in initiation (dīkṣā),
composed this twenty-fourth daily lesson (āhnika), complete with its commentary, with skill.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Last Rites" (*antyeṣṭiprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 24 ||
The Twenty-fifth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
He who, presiding over his formidable body, seems to contemplate Bhava (Śiva) on all sides.
May that Śiva, who bestows auspiciousness upon the hearts of the devoted, be the source of well-being for the virtuous.
Now, with the second half [of the verse], he speaks in order to state the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha*:
"Next, the procedure for the *śrāddha* as taught in the venerable *Ṣaḍardha* is being proclaimed. (25.1)

One might ask: "In which part of the Trika system is this ritual for the ancestral offerings (śrāddha) actually mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is indicated in the Siddhātantra, in the description of the worship of the forms (mūrtiyāga).
The word "indicated" means that it is not stated directly by its own name. As it has been said there:
"Or else, the 'hero's feast' (vīrabhojana) should be performed in the house of the deceased;
however, on the occasion of a śrāddha, it should be given... [as follows].
And thus it is said.
Anticipating the question, "For whom, when, and by whom should this be performed?", he says:
"The procedure for that [initiation] applies to both those who are well-purified by the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) and those who are unpurified. (25.2)
On the third day, on the fourth day, on the tenth day, every month, at the beginning of the year,
and every year— at all these times— he should perform that [rite] with his own people as before.
In that regard, one should worship the deity as before and likewise perform oblations in the fire.

"Of the impure" means by means of the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) alone, and not by initiation (*dīkṣā*) or other such rites. "By his own" means by his own [relatives], such as disciples, sons, and so forth—this is the meaning. "That" refers to the procedure for the *śrāddha* ceremony.
Right here he states a specific rule: "Then, having first taken the food offering (naivedya) within the reach of one's hand... (25.4).

The wise preceptor, having meditated upon the nourishing power consisting of food, which is of the nature of vital energy (vīrya), should contemplate that the person to be accomplished (sādhya) has been permeated by it. || 25.5 ||
Then, he should offer that aspect of his which is animal-like and consists of objects of enjoyment to the Enjoyer by means of the state of oneness; in this way, the disciple becomes Śiva. (25–6)

"Pervaded by her" means that [the individual soul] has attained a state of identity with her. "Him" refers to the portion belonging to the bound soul (*pāśava*), which is of the nature of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). "In this way" means through the attainment of oneness with the enjoyer (*bhoktr*) by abandoning the state of being a bound soul. ||6||
He demonstrates this very point by analyzing it: "The state of being an object of enjoyment, the other body, and the physical frame are considered to be of the nature of bonds.
In the Śrāddha rite, in the extraction of the deceased, and in the final sacrifice, there is their transformation into Śiva. (25.7)
"Anyā" means that which is distinct from the enjoyer by virtue of having the nature of an object of knowledge. ||7||

Now, one might object: "Since an initiated person becomes Śiva by his very nature immediately after the falling of the body, what is the use of funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) and so forth for him? Even in that case, let there be only a single rule for the purpose of avoiding the violation of the rules of conduct (samaya-lopa);
why these many?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
Although one's purpose may be accomplished by a single procedure alone, nevertheless, one should perform every rite for the sake of attaining complete identification with that [deity]. (25.8)
"One should practice"—this refers to the seeker of liberation. ||8||
For one who desires to enjoy worldly fruits, the abundance of ritual action and the repetition of practice are the causes for the abundance of results;
therefore, one should perform for him rites such as the *uddhāra* and *śrāddha* for the deceased.
And it has been said:
"Even for those whose souls have been purified by initiation and knowledge, and who are rendered stainless by the final rite (antyeṣṭi),
the Śrāddha ceremony as declared by the Lord must nevertheless be performed to complete the ritual injunction."
Thus, by this, the purpose of the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and so forth has been stated. || 9 ||
But for the knower of reality, none of this is at all to be accepted—thus he says:

"For one whose darkness has been destroyed by the sun of the knowledge of reality, no such thing as the ritual for the last rites, the ancestral offerings (śrāddha), or other injunctions is ever of any use. (25.10)

Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that even for those who possess knowledge (jñānins), great people perform rites such as the worship of the wheel (cakrārcā) on the anniversary of their death and other occasions? Why, then, has this been said? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But for them—namely, the gurus, their circles, their sub-circles, and their fellow-students..."
The day on which those who share that same lineage attain unity shall be a sacred festival day. || 25-11 ||

"Guru" is an adjective qualifying the specific festival day (*parvadina*). "His group" (*tadvarga*) refers to his wife, sons, and so forth. "A member of that group" (*vargya*) refers to the sons and others of those sons and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the day of oneness" (*ekyadina*): he states the reason for applying the word "festival" (*parva*) here to be the day of death, due to [attaining] union (*sāyujya*) with the Supreme Lord.
For when there is an overflow of consciousness (*bodha*), then it is called a *parvan* because of its filling.
The Supreme Lord says this: therefore, because it fills consciousness, it is called a *parvan*.
And for this reason, just like the day of [Śiva’s] union, his birthday as well is a festival (parvan) for those who belong to his lineage;
thus he says:
"Therefore, the day of birth and the day of union are both festivals by virtue of the attainment of awakening. (25.12)
Regarding this very point, he states a specific distinction:

"When even a spiritual son (putraka) becomes a benefactor to someone, then [the letters] belonging to the mother, the father, or the power (śakti) are situated in the left, right, and middle [channels]. (25.13)
One should cause the channels to flow and offer what has been presented to the deity.

By the word "api" (also), it is indicated that not only the Guru, but also the practitioner (sādhaka) [may do so]. Regarding the phrase "of the mother and the father"—this refers to the wife of the Guru as well.
And this was not stated merely as his own invention; thus he says:
"And that has been set forth by Śiva in the venerable Bhairavatantra. (25.14)
And he states the method for the flowing of the channels:
"One must attend to the timing of that flow for the sake of accomplishing its form; then, one should bring about its accomplishment through spontaneous freedom according to the future rite. (25.15)
Regarding those channels, such as the left (vāmā) and others: "On the day of the equinox, the right channel flows in the morning;
another flows in the evening; and at midday, it is the middle one; but for yogins, it is according to their own will."

The above has been stated with reference to the natural time of the flow; alternatively, having accomplished its attainment through one's own power according to the method to be described hereafter, one should perform the channel-activation—this is the intended meaning. || 15 ||

And in this matter, for everyone beginning with the initiate (samayin), the procedure prescribed in one's own scripture is the proper one, not the worldly one; thus he says: "Or, at the funeral rite (śrāddha) of anyone whatsoever, [one should perform] the satiation of the Guru, the deity, and the fire."
That would be a Śrauta sacrifice performed with a discus, but it would not be the ritual procedure for animal sacrifice.
In the absence of Vedic injunctions, the state of being bound by fetters (pāśavatva) is the cause. ||16||
Even so, in order to demonstrate the evidence for and against this point, he says:

"And likewise it is stated in the venerable *Mukuṭa*, a scripture of Śiva: 'He who, though established in the Śaiva teaching, believes in the Vedic [path], is like a broken bell—he possesses nothing at all. (25.17)
Thus, by means of the rites beginning with the worship of the deity and ending with the wheel-sacrifice (cakrayāga),
this living being attains the state of Rudra and enjoys divine pleasures.

"Like a broken bell"—the meaning is that a broken bell neither performs its own function nor is it iron; thus, it merely reaches a state of falling away from both. For this very reason it was said: "He is not anything at all. || 18 ||
He demonstrates that which was stated as "by the method of what is to be" (bhāvinā vidhinā):
"Now we shall clearly explain the movement of the channels for the sake of glorious success.
He recites the very text taught in the *Śrīsiddhayogīśvarīmata* by way of its meaning:
Whichever channel one wishes to cause to flow, that very one one should meditate upon.
When one becomes absorbed in meditation, that channel clearly carries [the breath];
or rather, whichever limb one desires to move, it is carried by that hand. (25.20)
Having pressed the abdomen, one should bend it; that channel (nāḍikā) will flow in an instant.

"Whichever"—meaning any one of them, such as the left, according to the intended measure (mātrā) and so forth. "One should contemplate"—meaning [the channel] as flowing. "Or else"—referring to the case of those who are not yogins. Having thus explained the procedure for the channels, [the text continues with] the śrāddha.
The state of being the cause for the granting of both enjoyment and liberation exists—thus he says:
"In this way, even by means of the *śrāddha* rite, there is the establishment of both enjoyment and liberation. (25.21)
"Śiva, the compassionate one, has stated in various places that [one] should perform [these rites].

Now, it has been said that initiation alone is the means for achieving enjoyment and liberation; how then can this result from mere ritual conduct (*caryā*) consisting of *śrāddha* and so forth?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
When the descent of power (śaktipāta) has arisen in a living being, by whatever means the teacher [acts], || 25-22 ||
He performs that very upliftment which conduces to his [the soul's] liberation.
He establishes this very point: "For he is the God of gods, the upliftor, and his power is inconceivable. (25.23)
One should resort to the means merely through the gateway of the guru’s initiation and so forth.
Nor is this reasoning our own invention; rather, the scripture also speaks thus—as he says:
"It is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* immediately following the question of the sage. (25.24)
In this regard, he first states the Sage’s question:

"If liberation arises from the discernment of the principles (tattvas), from initiation, or from yoga, how could it arise from mere conduct (caryā) alone? To this, the following is the uniform answer.
The Lord laughed and said: "Why do you have this delusion regarding the Supreme Ruler?
Indeed, let it be seen that his nature as the benefactor of all is well-established. (25–26)
As it is said there:
"Liberation [is attained] through the discernment of the principles, beginning with earth, by means of thorough investigation;
it is determined to be distinct from initiation, which finds its locus in the section on ritual action (kriyāpāda)."
The third [attainment] is also praised as being accomplished by rising from the stage of yoga;
how could the fourth be accomplished merely through conduct?

"One should attain [this] in the knowledge of Śiva; cut away the sprout of my ignorance. Thus—"after the question"; "equally"—meaning in accordance with [the truth]; "let it be seen"—meaning that there is no disagreement here by anyone. ||26||

He establishes this very point by means of an illustration: "For one whose death has arrived, poison, disease, weapons, and so forth are indeed the cause; whether that [cause] be small or great, in the same way, contemplation (anudhyā) is the cause of liberation. (25–27)
"However, these external signs are employed for the sake of liberation;
knowing this, a wise person should not entertain any doubt in this manner. (25–28)
Thinking, "How can liberation be attained by this much alone? one should take refuge in supreme devotion.

For just as in the case of one whose death is imminent, poison or the like—whether in small or large quantity—is not the direct cause of death; rather, it is simply the exhaustion of his lifespan, so too it is with liberation:
"But by His grace alone does devotion arise in men" (Mahābhārata).

Thus, by such a perspective, devotion characterized solely by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—that is, constant contemplation—is the primary cause. On the other hand, these external signs, such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, are merely metaphorically designated as means because they are [ultimately] of that same nature. And for this reason:

One should not doubt how liberation can come from the mere practice of rites such as the *śrāddha* for oneself; rather, in this matter, devotion alone must be resorted to with firmness so that it may be so. As it has been said there:
In the meantime, the Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, smilingly said:
"What is the cause here of this delusion, arising from the manifestation of contemplation?"
For the supreme Lord’s quality of being a benefactor to all is well-established;
indeed, the signs that the time has arrived are seen in many ways, just as they are.
Poison, disease, weapons, and the like are not the causes here;
for just as death does not occur when one's enjoyment is exhausted, it is certain that the same applies here as well.
Through the penetration of the power of contemplation, practices and the like are manifested;
these external signs, however, are employed as a means for the sake of liberation.
By that unswerving devotion, which is a manifest sign [of realization] from the very beginning,
the power of the disciple is constantly and unrestrainedly manifested.
"For indeed, when a person's state is serene, his nature as Śiva becomes manifest.
Thus [it is said].
He concludes this very point with the first half-verse:
"The rite of Śrāddha has been described, which crushes the terror of the poison of delusion. (25–29)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Śrāddha," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus all is auspicious. || 29 ||
This twenty-fifth daily lesson (āhnika) has indeed been determined by the wise Jayaratha, through his singular devotion to the various rites proclaimed in the entire teaching of Śiva.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Śrāddha," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the illustrious and great teacher of Maheśvara, the venerable Abhinavagupta, together with the commentary named *Viveka* composed by the illustrious Jayaratha. || 25 ||
The Twenty-sixth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
When, by the power of one's will, there occurs the worship of Śiva, the universal mark, in all directions;
He, being well-disposed, conquers the universe; he is well-disposed toward liberating those who have sought refuge. || 1 ||
Now, with the second half [of the verse], he speaks in order to describe the remaining conduct pertaining to those who have been initiated:
"Now the remaining conduct is being declared, which is useful for those who are living. (26.1)

Now, one might object: since it has been stated here that "Initiation alone liberates and leads [the soul] upward to the abode of Śiva," is there not fulfillment through initiation alone? What need is there for anything else?
Anticipating the doubt, "Is it by means of the instruction on the remaining mode of life?
he demonstrates its purpose by first stating the different types of initiation: "This initiation, which has been proclaimed as ending with the *śrāddha*, is of many kinds."
That [discipline] is for the sake of purification, for liberation, for enjoyment, or for both. || 26-2 ||
He elaborates on this very point:
"In that regard, the initiation which is for the sake of accomplishing purification does not liberate directly;
however, that which is 'with seed' (sabījikā) and [performed] by virtue of continuous contemplation (anusandhi) is directly liberating. (3)

The manner of life for those who have been initiated by either of these two must be explained to the spiritual sons (*putraka*) and others, in order to achieve the state of being identical with That. (26.4)
Among these four types, that initiation which is described as having the *saṃskāra* (purificatory refinement) as its primary motive—

pertaining to the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and others characterized by the desire for enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or the desire for liberation (*mumukṣu*)— does not directly grant liberation because enjoyment is predominant and thus acts as an intervening factor. And that which...
Because there can be no obstruction to enjoyment for one such as a "son" (putraka), she is directly the liberator (*mocitrī*) and the one who effects liberation (*mocikā*)—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, since that [liberation] could also be "seedless" (*nirbījā*), the term "with seed" (*sabījikā*) is stated in order to exclude that possibility; for in the seedless [initiation], there is no remaining worldly activity whatsoever, not even of the fetter belonging to the conventional [initiation].
Because they have been purified. And he will say:
"Who would speak of those two—the *sāṃsiddhika* and the *nirbīja*—for the sake of further practice? (verse 10).
By that initiation of the aforementioned nature, which is of two kinds, those who are *putraka*s and so forth...

The mode of life for those who have been initiated must be prescribed for as long as they live, so that their realization of identity with the One Consciousness may be accomplished without obstacle. (3–4)
Now, is this not what is called "subsistence through remnants" (śeṣavṛtti)—namely, the performance of obligatory and occasional rites for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation?
Therefore, does the seeker (sādhaka) or the spiritual son (putraka) perform this without distinction, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Whether for one desiring worldly enjoyment or for one desiring liberation, initiation has indeed been performed by the Guru for the sake of purifying the means of knowledge and so forth, based on one's own consciousness, the Guru, and the scriptures. (26.5)
Then, having realized himself to be fit for his own teaching through refinement,
he practices the performance of the things taught therein for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

For here, by the statement beginning with, "This knowledge is threefold in its source of authority... and so forth, the Guru— whether for one desiring worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*)— takes as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that which consists of one's own consciousness, the Guru, and the scripture.
The initiation that was performed for the sake of achieving purification (*saṃskāra*), from that initiation, he—
whether desiring enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*)— [attains] his own self in his own teaching, because it has been purified, [regarding] enjoyment and liberation.
Or, having recognized what is appropriate, one should practice the performance of the daily rites (*nitya*) and so forth as prescribed in one's own scripture;
that is to say, one should perform them without distinction. ||5-6||
Now, one might object: "In that case, should the 'remaining function' (śeṣavṛtti) be taught to one who lacks self-reflection (svaparāmarśa), or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even one who possesses enjoyment and liberation solely through faith in the Teacher..."
To prevent the arising of obstacles to that [practice], one should also explain its mode of conduct.
Thus, for one who possesses their own realization just as they possess the realization of the Guru, the same principle applies;
so he says:
"Even one who shares an equal realization of both their own consciousness and the Guru's consciousness..."
The remainder should be assigned as a livelihood for the sake of pacifying obstacles and other such hindrances.
But for one who depends exclusively on another, or does not depend at all, what is the use of a residual mode of existence?
To this he says:
"But he who, having entirely abandoned dependence on another, remains established in his own [nature]..."
And even one who has attained realization through conditions does so solely by means of the teacher's realization.
Who could speak of those two—the *sāṃsiddhika* and the *nirbīja*—for the sake of a residual practice?
"For the sake of a residual practice" means for the purpose of performing a residual practice.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then do these two behave like wood or a wall, or like common folk?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But those two are intent upon the means of becoming absorbed in that [Reality] through gradual stages and upon the worship of the Guru. (26.10)
In that regard, for the sake of their continued subsistence, these [virtues] are constant and occasional;
they are fixed, excluding those performed for specific desires, because desires are manifold and require manifold means. (26.11)

In that regard, the eternal rule consists of the performance of the twilight devotions toward the host of deities, worship of the teacher, the fire, and the scriptures together, and compassion for all living beings. (26.12)
But for all [these occasions], there is worship and recitation (japa) according to the specific occasion; furthermore, there is the sequence of rites for the sacred thread (pavitraka). || 26-13 ||
This initiation of the teacher has been analyzed in its many varieties;
furthermore, his duties such as exposition and so forth are certainly constant and occasional.
In that regard, at the outset, the Guru should clearly explain the daily ritual to the disciple, having observed his suitability for those whose natures are either expanded or unexpanded. (15)
Having observed the disciple’s fitness for the potency, pervasiveness, and other qualities of the primary and secondary mantras, he should bestow that very root-mantra upon him. (26.16)

"Devoted to absorption in that [reality], to the means, and to the worship of the Guru"—this is because of being intent on the reflective awareness of the Goddess of one's own consciousness (*svasaṃviddevī*) and due to devotion to one's own Guru. As was stated previously:
"He who possesses this right reasoning by himself is qualified in all respects."

"He is consecrated and initiated by the goddesses of his own self-awareness. (4.43) Thus, one should purify the bond of the conduct of tranquility (*śamayācāra*) in the seedless initiation (*nirbījā*).

"By initiation alone there shall be liberation, provided there is constant devotion to the Lord and the Guru. (15.31). Furthermore, the reason for the diversity of means is the diversity of desires; therefore, because these [desires] lack fixed causes, they are not mentioned here. Because sons and others lack the qualification for that [rite]. "Having observed their fitness" means that the extensive ritual procedure should be taught, or the primary mantra should be entrusted, only to a qualified disciple; however, in the case of another [unqualified person], it is otherwise. ||16||
For this very reason, he said:

"Indeed, one who has been initiated into that [lower] scripture, being apprehensive of conduct free from restraints, is not fit for the primary [path]; however, through service to another [the teacher], fitness may arise. (6.17)
Whether for a practitioner seeking enjoyment (bubhukṣu) or one destined to become a practitioner (sādhakībhāvin),
once the mantra has been mastered through the casting of the flower, it should be bestowed for the sake of accomplishing the goal.
Whether the prescribed rite is extensive or consists of subordinate elements, the Guru, having ascertained the disciple’s fitness, should perform for him the essential and concise ritual. (26.19)

In this regard, there is this rule: whatever form belongs to the mantra, the Guru should not manifest that by writing it down for the disciple, especially in the case of the Upper Teaching (ūrdhvaśāsana).

"Without restraint" means free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). "Another" refers to a secondary mantra. "Of the practitioner" (*sādhaka*) means one who has already received that initiation. "Of one becoming a practitioner" (*sādhakībhāvin*) means one whose initiation is yet to be realized. "Subordinate" (*guṇabhūta*) means not extensive. "Therein" means in the practice of the rule concerning the essence in this manner. "In the higher teaching" (*ūrdhvaśāsana*)—means...
In the Trikakula and other [tantras], || 20 ||
He establishes this very point:

"Mantras consist of phonemes, and those [phonemes] consist of reflective awareness (parāmarśa). If that [reflective awareness] is non-different from the consciousness of the Guru, then it would be transmitted to the disciple. (26–21)
A mantra that remains merely on paper is considered here to be devoid of potency;
its splendor does not manifest from a book through the power of convention. (26.22)

The word *sa* (he) refers to the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). The word *sā* (she) refers to the consciousness of the Guru, which consists of that reflective awareness. The word *tataḥ* (from that) means from the Guru. The term *nivīrya* (devoid of potency) is used because of the absence of reflective awareness; for he would indeed be non-different from consciousness—this is the intended meaning. ||22||
One might ask: "What is the authority for stating that the potency (*vīrya*) of mantras is not [to be found] in books? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, it is stated in the *Siddhāmata* that 'those who have learned the sciences from books' [are so described].
Thus, the intended meaning here is that the "binding of the burden" (*bharabandha*) must be performed upon the very potency of the mantras.
Therefore, he said: "But those who recognize the potency even in a mantra obtained from a book... (26.23).
These are declared to be the Bhairavīya saṃskāras, which are innate (sāṃsiddhika).
Having understood this correctly, the Guru, reeling with supreme bliss, [should act]. (26–24)
"Having worshipped in such and such a place, one should perform the ritual"—
the phrase "in such and such a place" means in a location suitable for a worthy disciple.
And in this matter, the Guru must be intent on secrecy; thus he says:
"Just as the practice of one disciple is not perceived by another disciple. (26.25)
The Guru should act accordingly, since the loss of secrecy is fraught with fault;
[he should worship] the triad of goddesses in their pure form, or else through their union as a *yāmala*. (26–26)
One should speak of either a single goddess who is pure, or one whose nature is dual (yāmalātmikā);
therein, the mantra clearly uttered by the Guru from his mouth, whether audibly or in a whisper.
Having ascertained that [object] through the process of engagement, one should practice it oneself with the mind;
thereafter, one should master the well-instructed triad of purifications: of the locus, of the body, and of the interior.
One should diligently perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), recitation (japa), mudrās, and worship.
Regarding the phrase "it is defective": it is with this very intention that it is said, "Success comes through concealment... [and so forth].
This and more has been stated elsewhere. "Pure" means solitary. "Manifest" means accompanied by sound. As it is said:
"That which is heard by oneself is known as *upāṃśu*; that which others hear, O Goddess, is declared to be *saśabda* (with sound). (Svacchanda Tantra 2.147)
Thus: "until the commencement" means until the time of beginning the performance;
"well-instructed" refers to the method explained in the fifteenth chapter.
Now he teaches the daily ritual:
"In that regard, having awakened at dawn, one should first remember one's own chosen deity. (26–29)
Having performed the necessary duties and become pure, he should then enter his house and,
facing the northern direction, [meditate] upon the three locations within the body.

Having performed the purification of the mantras, their placement in their respective locations, the display of mudrās, and meditation upon their nature in terms of both difference and non-difference. (26–31)
In the elements of body, vital breath, intellect, ether, and earth, one should perform worship there with the mind;
likewise, one should perform recitation (japa) here according to one's capacity and offer this to the God.
One should perform this at every junction of the day for the sake of attaining identification with that [deity].
Others, however, [perform it] in the four directions—east, north, west, and south. (26–33)
"This [term] *sandhyā* is said to be according to the Tantras; it is not our own opinion.
Furthermore, according to our own system, he says: 'That fourfold *sandhyā* which was previously mentioned in the section on Time (kālādhikāra) [is what is meant here]. (26–34)"
Having fixed that very [deity] within, one should perform the ritual of the twilight (sandhyā);
or else, a child may perform the duties of the four twilights in a single one.

One should be devoted to the study of one's own Veda, to specialized knowledge, and to service toward the guru; for otherwise, there would be a ruin of one's Vedic study and other duties—this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might ask: "How can the ritual to be performed during the four junctions (saṃdhyā) reach completion when it is being carried out at only a single junction? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By means of the technique of becoming absorbed in that [reality], which is infinite and arises from the meditation on the junctions. (26–36)
By the power of that purification, he shall indeed be absorbed in that at all times;
therefore, at whatever time desired, he [should perform] worship with flowers, wine, and other offerings. (26–37)

On a sacrificial mound or similar site, the initiate, having become thoroughly purified, should perform the entire ritual procedure, up to the end of the internal recitation (antarjapa), according to his means and capacity. (26–38)
Having first prepared the *arghapātra* (offering vessel) according to his own chosen mantra,
the wise practitioner should sprinkle everything— the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the flowers, and so forth— with that water.
Then, having mentally projected the sequence of the door, the seat, and the lineage of gurus right there,
one who is permeated by the state of Śiva should perform worship, preceded by the worship of his own body.
Then, having beheld that sacrificial ground— which is as pure as the clear sky or crystal, and whose nature is consciousness— therein [he perceives] his own host of deities.
One should perceive [the deity] as a reflection and through the realization of it as the original image;
this is the primary invocation, like the wind from a fan.

"Then" (*tataḥ*) means after the performance of the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth. By the phrase "on the sacrificial ground" (*sthaṇḍilādau*), it is indicated that the daily worship (*nityārcā*) on the sacrificial ground (*sthāṇḍilī*) has been introduced. By the word "internal" (*āntara*), it is hinted that one would have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to external sacrifice and the like without first performing the mental sacrifice (*manoyāga*). "In the city" (*pure*)—
In the fifteenth chapter and others: "vīdhram" means stainless. "Therein"—that is, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) whose nature is consciousness.

"One's own"—meaning that which one desires to propitiate. For it has been stated that consciousness itself, when reflected externally, surges forth in such and such a manner; thus it is said to be "as the original image" (bimba) and "as the reflection" (pratibimba). "This"—refers to the following.
The vision [of the deity] occurs by virtue of its nature as a reflected image. ||42||
He demonstrates this by analyzing the very example:
"Just as the wind, though omnipresent, becomes effective for one's purpose when fanned by a fan, so too the omnipresent wheel of mantras becomes [effective] through such established practice. (26.43)

This very reality is stated by means of the *Catuṣkapañcāśikā*. "By way of conventional usage" (*rūḍheḥ*) means: because it sprouts forth in this manner upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth. "In that way" (*tathā*) means: it is effective for the purpose.
"The *Catuṣkapañcāśikā*" refers to that which expresses the four objects of knowledge, beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
The meaning is: by a specific portion of the text of such a magnitude.
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well; thus he says: "And this very thing was declared by the All-pervasive Lord in the venerable Nirmaryādaśāstra. (26.44)
He stated that very point by way of its meaning:
"O Lord, how can the all-pervading, boundless Śiva be invoked or dismissed? Thus questioned, the All-pervasive One replied. (26.45)
O Goddess, the invocation is performed through latent impressions (vāsanā), and the dismissal is likewise performed through latent impressions;
in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), for the Lord, there is neither invocation nor dismissal.
"Without restraint" (nirmaryāda) means unconfined; that is to say, independent (svatantra).

He demonstrates here that [the deity] consists of nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā): "The Lord has been invoked by me, established upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), worshipped, and praised"—having rejoiced thus, one should dismiss the Lord. (47)
Indeed, for the sake of generating satisfaction in unawakened living beings, there is the invocation and so forth of those [deities]; otherwise, how could such activity exist? (26.48)
But in due time, those who have set out under the command of their Lord come to understand,
in proper sequence, the attainment of the God that precedes all worlds.
For those whose entire accumulation of ignorance has been destroyed by the radiance of the lamp of knowledge, from where is the Lord brought, or to where is He led? (26.50)

For He is established everywhere through the distinctions of gross, subtle, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "beginning with the worlds": "When [the mind] is fixed upon the Sustainer of the Worlds... (Mṛgendra-tantra).
By the force of the application [of the teachings] stated in such passages as "ityādi," the meaning is that [the practice] consists of the process of attaining each respective *tattva* and *bhuvana*.
To instruct on what is to be done immediately after the invocation, he says:
"When the assembly of mantras has been invoked, [one should proceed] with offerings of flowers and wine. (26.51)

And an offering of libations should be performed with incenses appropriate to one's faith, devotion, and strength, as well as with fermented liquors and meats for the blazing mantras such as Śakti, Nāda, and the rest. (26–52)
First, there is the satiation with blood, and afterwards, with an abundance of flowers, incense, and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "What is the authority for the claim that the satiation must be performed immediately after the invocation?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But if one does not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the mantra that has arrived, [the rite fails].
"He indeed takes away half the body"—thus it was said by Śambhu.
Now, while substances and so forth have been prescribed here for the purpose of libation (tarpaṇa), by which [means] should worship (pūjā) and the like be performed? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Whatever indeed bestows expansion upon his mind. || 26-54 ||
"He should perform the worship with that very [substance]; such is the firm resolve of Śambhu.
Now, if this is so, then how is it that for practitioners who desire worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), the rule is constrained by necessity? (26–55)
"For those seeking liberation who know the reality, that [liberation] alone is indeed unimpeded.
Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for such a distinction in the rule here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One desiring to produce a specific quality in the effect must employ a specific cause. (26.56)
Like one desiring red cotton seeds who finds a heap of those very seeds, there exist various specific differences in enjoyment, impelled by their respective causes. (26.57)
"Tulya" means "red" alone. || 57 ||
Furthermore, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding liberation; thus he says:

"Whether the ritual action be very slight or extensive, it is performed through considerations of place and time, and by means of qualities, substances, actions, and so forth, which bestow delight upon the heart. (26.58)
Whether constructed by external factors or by those born of mental construction,
such [causes] do not make a difference for one seeking liberation regarding the method for attaining the supreme good.

One might object: "How is it that here, whether an action be very small or very great, it is unable to produce any distinction? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For in Brahman, conditions of abundance or scarcity are not acknowledged."
Now, one might object: "If even an action conceived through various causes does not produce any distinction here, then why is it said that these [causes] primarily grant delight to the heart?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because consciousness has autonomy as its essence, it consists of a mass of bliss. (26.60)
Ritual action should be performed with those [means] that grant joy to the heart for the sake of becoming one with That;
"of That" refers to sovereignty.
For this very reason, their form, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss alone, is worthy of worship; thus he says:
"The multitude of objective existents, through the fullness of non-difference from Śiva, drips forth that essence. (6.61)
The wise man should offer that very [consciousness] for worship in the supreme abode.
And this has been stated by me at length elsewhere; thus he says:
"This has been declared by me in many ways in my hymns and in my daily ritual manual. (26.62)
Having stated this very point, he demonstrates it:
"Reposing upon the light that unfolds the expansion of ultimate reality, those who know the secret worship you with that vision of supreme nectar. (6.63)
Having made the foundational earth purified by the sprinkling of the nectar of wonder,
and having offered from the mind flowers of one's own nature that abound with their own fragrance,
through the sequence of the priceless vessel of worship— the one's own heart filled with the nectar of bliss— ...
I worship you, together with the Goddess, day and night within the temple of the body.

This supreme nectar of consciousness— which dispels death, old age, and birth— expands forth, having been squeezed out from this triple world of manifold tastes and flavors placed upon the machine of the heart-center, by the weight of the gravity of discernment applied from above.
With that supreme oblation, I shall satisfy you completely day and night.
Thus, contemplating within himself the meaning contained in these three verses,
he should satisfy the host of deities with whatever means available.
Thereafter, one should display the mudrā either mentally through yoga, or verbally through the application of mantra, or physically through the arrangement of the body. || 26.67 ||
Having performed the entire recitation, one should then offer it all to the deity;
this was stated previously in the procedure for determining the reality of the agent. (26.68)
Then the dismissal (visarjana) should be performed through the practice of identifying with the single nature of awakening;
or else, having performed the satisfaction of the mantra residing in the fire according to the prescribed procedure.
Except for the offering presented by the assembly of gatekeepers, the pedestal-deities, and the gurus, one should eat nothing else oneself; thereafter, one should cast it into deep water.

"By her"—that is, by means of the vision of supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*). "The support" (*ādhāra*) here refers to the support of birth. By the words "in the machine" (*yantra*) and so forth, even the worldly account of the potter is indicated here.
And since this has already been understood through the previous commentary, it is not explained here word-for-word.

"The meaning contained in the three verses" refers to that characterized by repose in supreme consciousness. "Previously" means in the ninth, thirteenth, and other chapters. "Other" means primary. || 70 ||
He states the reason for throwing this into the unfathomable waters:
"Aquatic creatures were previously initiated by Śambhu himself, according to the future rite established by the illustrious Mīnanātha, who has descended [to earth]. (26.71)
Regarding the word "bhāvini" (in what is to come): it refers to that which will be explained at the beginning of the twenty-ninth chapter and elsewhere. || 71 ||
There is a fault in consuming what has been eaten by another—thus he says:
"That which has been eaten by cats, mice, and so forth, or even by those who are uninitiated, leads to disease and to hell by causing the torment of doubt. (26.72)
As it has been said:
"The food that remains after the Guru and the deity have eaten is called *ucchiṣṭa*;
one should always protect it like a deposit and never give it to just anyone."
One who is self-restrained should cast [the food] into a pit, fire, water, or a well;
for when it is eaten by those who are uninitiated, the accomplishment of the mantra is destroyed.
If one who is not a devotee eats [the offering], there is danger from thieves; if a worldly person should eat it, deformity arises for him, and he is tormented by other birds.
If it is licked by crocodiles, O Goddess, there will be the loss of one's sons; if by rams, the loss of one's children;
and if by monkeys, there will be imprisonment.
If licked by a donkey or a camel, there is poverty; if by parrots, it increases sorrow;
and if by monkeys or horses, there will be the destruction of happiness and good fortune.
If it has been licked by a cat, disease will quickly arise;
there will be quarrels with female śārikā birds, and especially with sparrows.
If it is eaten by crows, there will be travel to a foreign land; if by a blue jay, death shall occur;
and if a rat should eat it, there will even be a loss of life-span.
When a dog eats [the offering], disease arises;
enmity with cows will occur, and from jackals, certain death [shall come].
If a boar should devour [the offering], there will be infidelity among one's wives;
if a mongoose should touch it, fear arises from thieves.
"When it is utilized by wicked women, men, and nihilists,
then even practitioners encounter all manner of sufferings. (72)

Now, one might object: "Is this not a conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*) between the initiated and the uninitiated? And since such a distinction is not appropriate for those who possess knowledge and are free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), how can this have been stated without qualification? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Therefore, even a learned man who knows reality and has destroyed the affliction of doubt should not perform such an act openly out of a desire to favor the world. (26.73)

"From this"—because eating [the flesh of] cats and so forth is thus a cause of transgression (*pratyavāya*). "Knowledge" (*vidā*) means cognition. "Manifestly"—the meaning is: in such a way that no one at all might see it.
For if that were the case, even worldly people with conceptual thought (*savikalpa*) would act in this manner, and thus the scriptural injunction (*śāstrīyo vidhiḥ*) would perish.
Or rather, he entertains doubt regarding the man of knowledge, thinking: "This person has performed an act contrary to the scriptures. || 73 ||
And this was not stated without foundation; thus he says:
"In the venerable *Matamahāśāstra*, that was spoken by the All-pervasive Lord himself.
He states that very thing: "But [the Lord] himself..."
Devoted to the extraction of the spike and the contraction [of the wound]. || 26-74 ||
It should be done in such a way that no suspicion arises in the minds of others;
then, having wiped it clean, one should bathe it and worship it with a flower.
One should cast all that [offering], such as flowers and so forth, which remained therein, into deep water.
"Then" means immediately after the consumption of the *naivedya* (food offering) and other rites.
He concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson:
"This sacrifice on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍilayāga) has been taught by Śambhu for the performance of the obligatory rite. (26.76)

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Worship of the Sacrificial Altar" (*sthaṇḍilapūjāprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 26.
Thus all is auspicious. 76.
Jayaratha, whose mind is delighted by having attained the true essence of worship through the grace of the illustrious Guru, has composed this commentary on the twenty-sixth chapter.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Altar Worship," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 26 ||
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
[Salutation to] the unborn Lord of the Foundation, the God who resides in the knot within the space of the wheel.
I bow even to that longing which is desirable because it is firmly rooted in the consciousness of others.
Now, with the second half [of the verse], he speaks in order to describe the worship of the *liṅga*, which consists of the remaining eternal form:
"Now the worship of the *liṅga*, as indicated in the *Mālinīmata*, is being told. (27.1)
It has been indicated by the passage beginning with: "One should worship the internal *liṅga* wherein the moving and the unmoving are dissolved" (18.3). ||1||
Now, one might ask: "Why has the worship of the *liṅga* not been explicitly mentioned here?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The installation of these mantras taught in the *Ūrdhvaśāstra* [is not required]."
Therefore, one should keep these secret, for they bestow accomplishment through their esoteric nature.
Now, one might ask: "What would be the purpose of these [mantras] being established externally? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"For those who bestow accomplishment by virtue of possessing entry into the majesty of the bliss of their own vitality (*vīrya*), their external nature is merely a deviation from their true form. (27.3)
There is also another sign here; thus he says:

"Furthermore, it has been stated that Śiva, when full of immersion, is of the nature of the enjoyer; when there is a cessation of enjoyment, He partakes in the intensity of longing for enjoyment and is of the nature of restraint. (27.4)
One might ask: "What would happen to him by virtue of this being of the nature of a defeat? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"The body, which is nourished by the hunger arising from the suppression of its state of tranquility, perishes for him when it is not fully expanded by that [consciousness] in which it is itself established. (27.5)
"He" refers to the self-established one. ||5||
And this is not merely based on logic alone; thus he says:
"And this very point has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Jñānottarā*:
'Since Śiva is fond of sacrifice, especially when situated in the midst of the subjects (mātṛs). (27.6)
Therefore, a wise person should never install outside those mantras which belong to the secret scriptures, especially those that possess a manifest form.

Therefore, the installation for the sake of one who has died, which is prescribed elsewhere, should not be performed here according to these scriptures; rather, that which is common [to all] should be performed. (27.8)
"For this very reason"—because of the prohibition against external installation. "Elsewhere"—in the *Śrī-mṛtyuñjaya* and other such texts.
As it has been said:
"Or rather, the installation should be performed upon a burnt lump in a cremation ground."
Thus. "Common" means [attained] by means of the Netra-mantra and so forth. ||8||
Thus, since our system negates any external, stable foundation, [the practitioner] must remain in motion alone; so it is said:

"Until the perfect realization of identity with That (tanmayatva) and until the arising of the desired fruit, the *putraka* and the *sādhaka* should clearly take recourse in either the manifest or the unmanifest. (27.9)
Anticipating the doubt as to whether the image here should be fashioned by the *putraka*s and others themselves, or not, he says:
"The *guru* should be requested by the *putraka*s, but the *sādhaka*, knowing [the procedure] himself..."
If he does not install it, then for that reason as well, the preceptor should be requested. || 27-10 ||
And here, regarding the time called "suppression" (nirodha), the Guru should speak thus to the pervasive one:
"While this [person] lives, you should remain until the fruit is attained," or "until the end of his life. (27.11)
And the *liṅga* may be made of stone, or of precious gems, or of pearl;
it may be made of flowers, or of food, or of cloth, or fashioned from fragrant substances. (27.12)
One should not conceive of a linga made of stone produced by an artisan;
and among those made of metal, one should avoid any other except that which is made of gold. || 27-13 ||
And in this matter, neither inferential signs nor authoritative testimony are of any use;
for that which is illuminated by mantras of noble potency is indeed what yields the fruit.
One should also perform the purification of that [altar] and so forth according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, there should be the offering of the mantra, and the restraint according to the stated method. (27.15)

There is also an extensive libation in the fire, especially a significant sacrificial fee for the preceptor, and the satisfaction of the poor and others according to one's means; such is the additional rule for the sacrifice.
In all cases where the signs are unmanifest, the primary principle should be understood as non-conceptualized;
for it has been stated thus in various places in the *Lakṣaṇa-pārameśvara*.
In the case of a scripture, a vessel, a banner, a garment, or that which is worshipped as self-arisen or as a divine arrow,
as well as that which arises from a river or a spring, there is neither invocation nor mental construction.
There is no restriction regarding the pedestal, the temple, the mantras, the time, and so forth;
[the image may be] clearly manifest in a painting, a book, or the like, or made of deodar wood or gold.
Then the Guru installs [the image] fashioned by a consecrated and skilled artisan,
or else one endowed with the proper characteristics and resting upon its skull-cup (karpara).
One should resort to the *tūra* according to the procedure for the *paṅkti*, *cakraka*, *śūla*, and *abja*;
I shall describe its characteristics as they are set forth in the venerable *Picuśāstra*. (27–21)
Yoga is always praised when performed on a *tūra* that is free from defects, for it bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*).
"He should establish [it]" means by himself. "If not" means if he himself is ignorant—this is the meaning.
"In this" refers to either the practitioner (*sādhaka*) or the spiritual son (*putraka*). "Until the fruit" means until the end of life. As it has been said:
"Until the complete accomplishment of identification with That (tanmayatva), and until the arising of the desired fruit.

The term *vāstra* means that which has been fashioned specifically from cloth and the like, but not from stone—the intention being that the latter is suitable for a permanent installation (*sthirapratiṣṭhā*). "One should avoid anything else"—by this [it is meant].

The meaning is that it must be made of gold alone; in this case, measurements and so forth are not required, which is precisely why one should not consider measurements and the like for those images established by the Siddhas.
Thus it has been stated. "Of that"—meaning of the *liṅga*. "As stated"—namely:

"You should remain in this [body] until the fruit is attained, or until the end of life. "Due to a great distinction"—and not merely due to some distinction. "Superior"—meaning superior to the *nitya* [liṅga].
"String" (sūtra) means on a rosary. "Vessel" (pātra) means a large one. "Banner" (dhvaja) means on a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and the like.

"Cloth" (vastra) means that which has been prepared for the purpose of sacrifice. "Head" (mūrdha) means unbroken. "Circular" (cakraka) means by way of a whirling motion. He recites that very [verse] beginning with "tūra," and so forth.
He describes the defects themselves:
"By means of lattices, worn-out [structures], holes, teeth that are deficient or excessive, and pain. (27.22)
If the *tūra* is employed, there would be loss; if it is omitted, the sacrifice is supreme.
Some authorities have maintained that the *tūra* is used only in optional (*kāmya*) rites. (27–23)

"By lattices" means by those that have recently emerged and are mostly subtle. "Tattered" means by those very same ones that have emerged long ago. "Deficient or excessive" refers to [a number] other than thirty-two. "By disease" means by that which takes the form of moisture and so forth.
"Devoid of that" means lacking lattices and the like. "Some" refers to the ancient authorities. || 23 ||
He states his own view:
"But the teachers explain that which was spoken by Picu—that 'one should carefully avoid defects in a rite performed for a specific desire'—does not apply to obligatory ritual action. (27.24)
And in the Śrīsiddhātantra, the supreme definition of the *tūra* is stated:
[it is found] in the single and so forth up to four sections, in the *gomukha*, and in the *pūrṇacandraka*. (27.25)
Resembling a lotus, gorocana, pearls, crystal, and rock crystal, auspicious, and endowed with one to five excellent apertures and lines of knowledge; || 27-26 ||
It is not rough, crooked, fragmented, long, depressed, or marked by spots;
here, it is clearly [depicted] with a smooth vajra-needle, accompanied by a host of goddesses.
One should draw everything to be worshipped, beautiful in all its limbs.
The term "cow-mouth" (*gomukha*) is employed for the sake of similarity in shape, while "lotus" (*padma*) and so forth are used for the sake of similarity in color.
Regarding the term "with excellent apertures" (*sadrandhra*): here, the existence of apertures is due to their state of being the cause for the exit of wine and other substances.

Regarding the term *vidyā*—there are fourteen [chapters]. As it is stated therein: "First, one should examine a skull endowed with the proper characteristics, whether it be in one piece, two pieces, or three pieces, and well-beautiful."
In a four-sectioned or cow-faced [mandala], possessing a radiance like the full moon,
resembling a lotus, the luster of yellow pigment (rocanā), the color of water, or the brilliance of a pearl;
Having the luster of coral and sapphire, resembling pure crystal,
endowed with lines of knowledge, and possessing one or two apertures.
O slender-waisted one, an image possessing auspicious characteristics should be made with three, four, or five [fingers]; it should not be rough, worn out, cruel, crooked, or long.
Never perform any ritual action in a hollow place studded with *bindus*;
rather, having recognized a skull that is completely pure in its characteristics, it fulfills all desires.
And there, in the upper section, one should fashion the image that resides in the mind;
having divided the field into four parts, one should draw a circle at its end.
In the case of the *vṛttānta* meter, it occurs again; the middle portion consists of three parts.
Having understood that there is a lotus again in its center, one should arrange the *cakra* accordingly.
"In the center, one should [visualize] the Goddess or the God surrounded by the Yoginīs;
and the arrangement of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) should be performed with a smooth vajra-needle," and so forth, in many such ways.
He extends this very [rule] to other cases as well: "This same characteristic is to be followed in the case of the arghapātra (offering vessel) as well. (27–28)
And likewise, there is also a scriptural authority (āgama) to this effect; thus he says:
"In the Śrībrahmayāmala it is also stated that the vessel with the face of a cow (gomukha) is the most excellent;
its base is like that of an elephant or a tortoise, and its shape is like a jar, a circle, or a trident. (27–29)
The secret born of power. ||29||
Having thus explained the nature of the *liṅga* in many ways, he now describes the rosary (*akṣasūtra*): "Then one should prepare the rosary; therein one should worship the sequence [of deities].
It may be made from the materials of heroes, minerals, water-born substances, pearls, gems, or gold. (27–30)
The rosary should be made of beads that are progressively superior, or especially of rudrākṣa seeds;
it should consist of one hundred and eight, or fifteen, or half of that [seventy-five]. (27–31)
Or else, one should fashion that [number] as fifty, or half of that.
"Vīradhātu" means a great conch shell. "Jalodbhūta" means lotus seeds. "Tithis" means fifteen. "Half of that" means fifty-four. "Half of that" means twenty-seven.
Right here he demonstrates the pervasion:
"The five faces [arise] from the conjunction of consciousness, vibration, knowledge, will, and action. (27–32)
The rule regarding the penultimate letter is that there is a fivefold unity between the beginning and the end;
therein, a twofold nature is declared through the distinction between Power (śakti) and its Possessor (tadvat). || 27–33 ||
Then, on a surface of double that measure, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) in two forms;
and on a surface double even that, one should perform it with the pair of emanation and withdrawal.
One should then perform the deposition (nyāsa) of either the Mātṛkā or the Mālinī in fifty [units];
however, in the highest [case], one should deposit both, having first performed the depositions previously enjoined.
In the initiation, the preceptor should primarily [teach] those fifteen mantras;
or else, [he may do so] by means of the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), kalās, mantras, words (pada), and phonemes (arṇa).
When the thread has been prepared according to various numerical divisions, the Guru should perform the respective ritual placements (nyāsa).
Having fashioned a rosary for it as well, everything for that too should be performed just as on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
And with that very [mantra] having been worshipped, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) without weariness;
this procedure has been declared by you in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*. (27–38)
That which one speaks while causing this [mantra] to revolve like a wheel becomes *japa*;
that which one beholds or offers as an oblation becomes so through its complete entry into the fire of awakening. (27–39)

"Fivefold" means that by multiplying the five faces with the five powers, beginning with *cid-śakti*, twenty-five arise—this is the meaning. "Unity" means a single form that transcends all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
for that [unity] is twofold: first, because the adjuncts have not yet arisen, and finally, when they have ceased.

"By means of the pacification of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Thus, there are twenty-seven. "Near the penultimate"—because it is situated near the final bead of the rosary, which consists of fifty beads. "Therein"—meaning in the twenty-seven. "In the double measure"—meaning in that which consists of fifty-four. "Of two forms"—means:
"Consisting of power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimad). "Twice that" means consisting of one hundred and eight.
"Khaśara" means fifty. "In the highest" means consisting of one hundred and fifteen.
"The two-fold" refers to the forms of Mātṛkā and Mālinī. "Previously" refers to the seventeenth chapter.
As it is said there:
"The goddess Parā likewise [drinks] the group of eight beginning with Piba and the group of six beginning with Astra.
(Tantrāloka 17.39–40)
Thus: "These [beads] should be fifteen. Regarding the word "or"—this refers to an alternative view. Regarding the word "stated"—it was stated in the nineteenth chapter. As it was said there:
"Then, by this procedure, one should fashion a rosary of seeds."
It is fashioned from gems, pearls, conch shells, and the like, as well as from lotus seeds and other materials.
Or else, a wise person [should fashion] one made of gold or other metals, measuring fifty akṣas,
so that it becomes bracelet-shaped and fits the length of one's own forearm.
Having taken that [flower], having anointed it and perfumed it with incense and fragrance,
and having worshipped the Lord of the Family, one should place the Śakti there.
One should utter each seed-syllable individually, enclosed within the seed-syllables of Parā;
one should then apply them all, shimmering with the syllable KṢĀṂ, into the first letter.
One should again contemplate the first syllable as all-pervasive and the presiding authority over everything;
for this rule is intended for both types of division among the syllables.
In the second [circle], one should place the second pervasive syllable as before;
this same procedure is prescribed for the third and subsequent syllables ending with *pha*.
Then, recollecting Śakti with a one-pointed mind,
he should visualize her as having the luster of a thread situated in the center of the beads for the purpose of perfecting the rosary.
Whatever he speaks here while causing this [wheel] to revolve like a wheel,
all that is fashioned as recitation for the sake of the complete accomplishment of the mantra.
"In the same way, there should be a *homa* when one is initiated, as well as when this object is being consumed [by fire]. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 19.74–83) ||39||
Now, even though the characteristics of the vessel have been stated, he states another alternative in order to demonstrate its various types:

"Alternatively, one should make a great vessel for the *argha* offering; that should be the northernmost and supreme [vessel], made either of coconut, or of bilva wood, or of gold, or of silver. (27–40)
This entire procedure, beginning with the installation (pratiṣṭhā) and so forth, is proclaimed for that [deity] as well.
Having filled it with the unshakable essences (rasas), one should perform the sequence of worship within it.
"By means of unshakable essences" (niṣkamparasaiḥ)—the meaning is: by means of the "heroic joints" (vīrasandhibhiḥ), such as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth. || 41 ||
Regarding this, he states the procedure:
"It should always be placed face down when worshipped; however, during the act of worship itself, that vessel should be turned face up, and one should not leave it empty in such a state. (27.42)
At the conclusion of the worship, having filled himself with that essence and having worshipped it while turned face downwards, the wise one should install it.
"Adored" means by means of the vessel, the vidyā, and so forth. "In the act of adoration" refers to the mantras and other elements as desired.
"Such" means facing upward (unmukha). (42–43)
To show other substrates for worship taught in various scriptures, he says:
"Or else, one should likewise make a sword, a small dagger, a pair of scissors, or a mirror stainless, as proclaimed from the mouth of the venerable Kālī. (27.44)
It is also stated in the Śrī Bhairavakula regarding the worship on the Kula festival days:
[the worship is performed] upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in fire, on a cloth (paṭa), in a linga, in a vessel, in a lotus, or in a mandala.
One should worship [the deity] in a physical form, a jar, a collection of weapons, a cloth, or a thread, using the respective offerings for each; one must avoid any confusion between them. (27–46)
"With their own respective [means]" means with those appropriate for householders and others. As it has been said:

"In the house, one should perform worship according to the rules with substances produced in the house; in the cremation ground, with those produced there. One should not practice a mixed [form of worship]."
Thus [ends the section]. ||46||
Anticipating the doubt, "But what is the need for multiple bases for worship such as sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila)?
he demonstrates the distinction between the domains [of these practices]:
"Just as mantras are used in water for the sake of pacification, so too they are certainly used in [the case of] weapons and other such objects."
Therefore, that which brings about the destruction of enemies and so forth is desirable, as it is free from the confusion of mixed motives.

"From this"—because these [elements] have their specific, restricted functions; therefore, one who desires peace (śānti) should perform worship in water alone, and not in the weapon-mantra (astra) or elsewhere. || 47 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, what is the use of these many [mantras] for one who is without desire? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"But for one who is without desire, those [mantras], by virtue of their respective locations and limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), certainly effect the severing of bonds, the purification of the principles (*tattva*), the nourishment [of the self], and so forth. (27.48)

Alternatively, even for a book that is well-purified, composed by one who has received initiation, and arranged according to the sequence of the scriptures on planetary deities (rahaḥśāstra), this same procedure is prescribed.

The word "or" (*athavā*) indicates an alternative view. Furthermore, because this [text] is woven together with the sequence of the scriptures on planetary influences (*graha*), its all-enduring nature (*sarvasahatva*) implies its suitability for all ritual actions (*sarvakarma*). The word "done" (*kṛtam*) means "written. (48–49)
Having thus described the nature of the *liṅga*, he speaks in order to describe the different types of worship:
"In this way, as long as there is stability in those [liṅgas] that are self-established, so long should there be satiation with offerings, purification, and the avoidance of interruption. (27.50)
Therefore, when the construction of the mandala takes many days,
one should perform extensive libations with abundant offerings day after day.
And in every case of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the Guru, having contemplated the supreme reality as previously described, should clearly effect its presence (*saṃnidhi*).

"Avoiding interruption" means having completely abandoned interruption—that is, [performing it] without interruption. "For this very reason" means because acts such as libation (tarpaṇa) must be performed without interruption. ||52||

Surely, according to such statements as: "Until the perfection of identification with that [deity] and until the arising of the desired fruit, the *putraka* and the *sādhaka* should clearly take recourse to either the manifest or the unmanifest" (*Tantrāloka* 27.9),
the *putraka* and others [must remain engaged] until the attainment of their respective desired accomplishments.
The recourse to the *liṅga* and so forth has been explained; now, raising the doubt as to what further should be done by these [practitioners], he says:
"But when the fruit of becoming one with That (*tanmayībhāva*) has been accomplished by the *putraka* and the *sādhaka*,"
That is entrusted to one of the other two, who are distinct from that pair. || 27-53 ||
This same procedure applies to that [image] as well; however, if it cannot be obtained at all, it should be cast into deep water after having been asked for forgiveness and formally released.
Thus, this procedure for self-installation has been described by Śiva;
[it applies] to a liṅga installed by another, one made of stone (bāṇīya), or one that is self-manifested (svayaṃbhū).
Having first projected [the deities] facing east according to the sequence for all the seats, one should perform the worship.

Anticipating the question, "If no one worthy of such an offering is found, what then should be done with them?", he says: "In the absence of those. By the word "svayambhuvi" (in the self-existent), the procedure is established by implication.
Thus, he says that very thing: "all," etc.
