Now, one might object: "Since Svayambhū and the others have descended from the midst of the path—whether from the pure or the impure—how can one worship here that which transcends all paths? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"All mantras born of the pure and impure paths, ending with Śiva, [are included here]. (27.56)
And since the path (adhvan) is said to reside here in the seat, one should worship this [mantra] everywhere;
however, one should perform the invocation and dismissal there as previously described.
And this is not established by reasoning alone; thus he says:
"It has been stated likewise in the *Svacchanda-tantra* by the All-pervasive Lord in the *Aghoreśa* [chapter]:
'Or else, it is prescribed every day according to the application of half of half the [prescribed] measure. (27.58)
Having constructed the desired mandala there, one should worship the entire sequence.
As it is stated in the *Ānā*:
"Thus, of this [mandala] measuring three cubits..."
Of that which has been stated in such passages as "three cubits" and so forth.
He summarizes this very point:
"The worship of the *liṅga*, which is divided into many varieties, has been described. (27.59)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Worship of the Liṅga," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus all is auspicious. || 59 ||
Skilled in defining the nature of the *liṅga* through its many diverse divisions and modes of manifestation,
the one named Jayaratha has expounded this twenty-seventh daily lesson (*āhnika*).

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Worship of the Liṅga," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by Śrī Jayaratha. || 27 ||
The Twenty-Eighth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
Difficult of access for all prosperity, with a terrifying form that shatters and destroys the violation of the rules of conduct (*samaya*).
May the Durga goddess, who is difficult to approach, unimpededly pacify for you the miserable states of existence that are so hard to traverse.

Now, concluding the rules for the daily rites (nitya-karma) and having reached the appropriate occasion, he promises to speak of the occasional rites (naimittika): "Thus the rule for the daily rites has been proclaimed; now the occasional rites are being described. (28.1)

In that regard, in order to characterize only that which is occasional (*naimittika*), he reveals how the definition [of permanence] proposed by others is vitiated by defects such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by means of their notion of "eternity": "When the rule is established that 'that which is certain to occur is eternal'..."
The state of being the primary [reality] is becoming one with That; therefore, everything is occasional (naimittika). || 28-2 ||

Now, if indeed that which is determined were itself eternal— since it would otherwise be impossible for it to be invariably manifest— then everyone would necessarily become absorbed in that very state day and night. For one who is engaged in bathing and such activities, there would never be any cessation at any time.

It might be argued that [something] is eternal because its arising is determined; however, this is not the case, for then nothing at all would be eternal, but rather everything would be merely contingent (*naimittika*). Thus he says: "Therefore, everything is contingent.
Now, if it is argued that eternality exists by virtue of the fixed determination of the conceptualization of days and so forth, as one might hope—

It says: "The evening and morning [rites], beginning with the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) and so forth—[this applies] when there is a fixed regularity arising from the conceptualization of days and so on; at that time, because of the fixed regularity of days, months, lunar mansions (ṛkṣa), years, and so forth, it is called 'all-encompassing permanence' (sarvanityatā). (28.3)
"In that case, since the necessity of conceptualizing [time] as days and so forth exists everywhere, everything would be said to be eternal"—to this he says: "Everything," and so forth. ||3||
Having thus refuted the characteristic of being caused by another through the gateway of permanence, he states his own view:
"That which occurs at some time or other, whose existence is necessarily certain and beyond doubt."
The wise declare this occasional [creation] to be non-restricted to any particular cognizer. || 28-4 ||
For the wise have called this "indicative" (naimittika); they have described its characteristic as follows:

that whose nature is such that it is not to be doubted, being certain, and therefore necessarily existent due to the compulsion of the desire to avoid transgression (pratyavāya). But is it not also eternal?

Is there not over-extension (*ativyāpti*) here as well, since [the definition] applies even to this? To this he says: "occurring only occasionally" (*jātucidbhavam*), which means "happening at certain times. But surely, even for that which is eternal, because it is restricted by time, it possesses this very same nature;
thus, does not that same fault remain? To this he says: "not restricted to a [single] cognizer. [This refers to] the eternal.
For [the initiation] of the four, beginning with the *samayin*, it is mandatory; however, this [present case] applies only to some.
As it has been said:
"The Guru and the practitioner alone should perform the triad beginning with the *nitya*."
"And another pair [of observances] must always be maintained for as long as one lives, by the command of Śiva.
Thus [ends the verse]. ||4||
Having thus characterized the occasional (naimittika) rite, he also characterizes the constant (nitya) one by way of digression:

"The worship on the junctions (sandhyā) and other festival days (parvan), as well as this sacred thread (pavitraka), is always constant; because it possesses a fixed form, it applies to everyone who has taken refuge in the teaching. (5)
For this daily [practice], such as bathing and the twilight worship (sandhyā-vandana), is always of a fixed form for everyone established in our system, beginning with the initiate (samayin). || 5 ||

This division between obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, which has been explained as dependent upon the cognizer and established through the force of logic, is in fact well-known everywhere according to the scriptural injunctions themselves. Among these, the division of the obligatory has already been explained at length; however, the division of the occasional is precisely what is being introduced here—as he says:
Likewise, there are the attainments of knowledge, scriptures, gurus, brothers, and their respective circles;
the various sacraments of their birth, and the celebration of one's own birth. (28.6)
The *śrāddha* rite as a remedy for calamity, joy from witnessing the marvelous, the gathering of *yoginīs*, and the meeting with one's own spiritual lineage and so forth. (28.7)
The exposition of the scripture, the beginning, middle, and end, the arising of the sequence, the vision of the deity in a dream, the command, and the atonement for transgressions of the rule. (28.8)
Thus, the occasional rites (*naimittika*), which constitute the basis for specific worship in twenty-three varieties, have been described in the illustrious *Tantrasāra*. (28–9)
Consecration (*saṃskriyā*) refers to the day of the guru’s initiation. Non-duality (*abheda*) refers to the day of his death, due to his oneness with Paramaśiva.
Festival (*utsava*) refers to worldly honors and the like. Calamities (*vipadaḥ*) consist of such things as the loss of one’s own power.
*Pramoda* (joy) arises from the recovery of what was lost and the like; *adbhuta* (wonder) arises from universal upheaval and the like.

By this fourfold set—including the counteraction of calamities and so forth—the occasional (*naimittika*) rite known as Śivarātri is also subsumed. For it is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) that on that occasion, this very [realization] occurred to the Lord.

And since this has been taught in all the scriptures as a universal principle, it is not stated here in my own words. "The lineage of one's own portion" means a fellow student of one's own monastic cell (*maṭhikā*). "Succession" (*krama*) refers to that which consists of the various previously mentioned wheels (*cakras*). "Vision of the deity in a dream" means...
The meaning is: "the vision of auspicious dreams. "The Command" (ājñā) refers to the day of one's own initiation.

"Expiation for the observance" (samayaniṣkṛti)—that is, the performance of penance—is the meaning. Having thus described the divisions of the occasional (naimittika) rite, he also states its purpose: "the basis for special worship" (viśeṣārcānibandhana). ||9||
This being so, because of its preeminence, he first states the divisions of the *parvan*s:
"In that regard, we shall explain the rule for the *parvan*s; the *parvan* is twofold: *Kula* and *Akula*.
The former, consisting of the eight *Kula*s, was taught in the *Śrīyogasañcara*. (28.10)
"Ocean, moon, sage"—this [number] belongs to the lineage of Brahmā through Māheśī;
for Kaumārī, it is the first and fifteenth days joined with six and three.
For the Vaiṣṇavī [mudrā], the number is the oceans (4), the protectors (9), and the moon (1); for the Astra [mudrā], it is thirteen;
for the Vārāhī, it is the apertures (9) and Rudra (11); and for the Caṇḍī, it is the Vasus (8), the eyes (2), and the pair (2).
For all [the goddesses], there are two lunar days each; however, for Yogeśī, it is the tenth.
Furthermore, because the eighth day belongs to her as well, she is proclaimed to have two lunar days.
And other non-kula parvas are characterized by the opposite; we call that a kula-parva, as it is stated in the Bhairava-kula.
In the Haiḍara, the Trikasadbhāva, the Trikakālīkula, and other such texts,
this Time which was previously described in great detail as residing within the vital breath (prāṇa) [is now discussed].
In the movement of the piercing of the wheels (cakras), he generates a certain self-awareness;
the moment of attaining the fullness of that self-awareness is called a festival (parvan). || 28-16 ||
The word *parvan* is derived from the root *pṛ*, meaning "to fill" (*pūraṇa*); thus, according to etymological analysis (*nirukta*), it is called *parva* because of that filling. (28.17)

In this context, the word *haiḍara* is heard in two forms: one ending in *-n* and the other otherwise. "The former" refers to the *Kulaparva*. "Abdhi-indu" is the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*); "muni" is the seventh day (*saptamī*).
"Of the lineage of Brahmā" means belonging to the *Brahmyā* [tradition]. "Rasa-vahni-yuga" refers to the pair consisting of the sixth and the third days.

*Abdhi* is the fourth; *akṣīndu* is the twelfth. *Astra* is the fifth. *Randhrarudrau* are the ninth and the eleventh. *Vasvakṣī* refers to the eighth and the second. Regarding the phrase "of that too"—it means not only [the eighth] of Cāmuṇḍā, but by that [statement], the eighth is common to both.
The meaning is this: whichever lunar day (*tithi*) someone was born upon, that is their *kulaparva* (family festival).
As it has been said:
"Whichever lunar day one is born upon, that is one's family deity (*kuladevatā*)."

Thus. "By way of reversal" means as in the case of "inauspicious-making" versus "auspicious-making"; the sense is that it may exist, in reality, within the *akula*, the bodiless (*aśarīra*), or the *śakti*. "Previously" refers to the sixth and seventh chapters (*āhnika*). He derives the word *parvan* for this very purpose with the words beginning "parva," etc.

Therefore, regarding the rule "parva pūraṇe," the word *parva* ending in *a* (akārānta) is derived from the root *pṛ* [meaning] "to protect" and "to fill" with the *uṇādi* suffix *vanip*, resulting in the word *parvan* ending in *n*. Furthermore, the etymological derivation is "parva [is so called] because of filling. This is likewise observed in actual usage—as he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "haiḍare'tra" and so forth: "here" refers to the *Bhairavakula* and other such texts. It is stated therein:
"By worshipping on the *Kulaparva* festivals...
and so on.
And also: "...by worshipping on the family festival days. Thus [it is said].
And those such as the Siddhas and Yoginīs who possess these higher knowledges (abhijñās) are intent on worship here—thus he says:
"Whosoever are perfected in the movement of that wheel, they are those of full consciousness. (28.18)
Joined with that assembly, they are always intent upon its worship;
even one who is not [naturally] absorbed in it becomes so at that time through the worship of his own sequence. (28.19)
Through the gathering of the assembly of yoginīs and siddhas, one becomes identical with that;
"not identical with that" means one who is unskilled in the movement of the wheels (cakracāra) and so forth.
He illustrates this very point with an example:
"Just as in a theatrical performance, [there is] the non-differentiation from the consciousness of each respective spectator... (28.20).
By entering that [state], one immediately attains that very self-awareness which is otherwise acquired through the gradual process of yogic practice and is thus full. (28.21)
They obtain this immediately upon entering into the unity of that consciousness;
and at that very moment, because consciousness is full, it possesses the quality of being a cow of plenty that milks all desires.
Therefore, by worshipping [the deity] at that time, one quickly attains those respective fruits;

for just as in the case of spectators at a performance and the like, even though [the aesthetic state] exists sequentially through the gradual dissolution of differentiation within that specific portion, it occurs immediately even for someone who has entered into that state at that very moment.
Just as non-dual consciousness arises [in that manner], so it is here in the present case as well.

For on festival days and the like, full consciousness possesses a nature like that of the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu), by virtue of which, through worship at that very moment, the respective fruits arise almost immediately.

One might object: "Granted that for accomplished yoginīs and others, there may be the respective fruits because consciousness is fully perfected on festival days and the like; but how could this be so for others?
To pacify this doubt, he provides an illustration:
Just as one who has long accumulated wealth performs a festival with great care, so [should one act]. (28-23)
He favors the guest who has arrived at that specific time;
likewise, the leaders of the Yoginīs and Siddhas [favor him] for the sake of attaining excellent fruits. (28.24)
Even those who exert effort are favored by him, who knows that specific time.
And this is not established merely through logic; thus he says:
"And it has been stated there by him here in this Kula as being common [to all]—enough [of further elaboration]. (28.25)
O Goddess, whatever mantra, yoga, or krama exists within one's heart by the command of the Guru shall grant success through worship. (28.26)
O Goddess of gods, one should worship according to family tradition for the sake of attaining perfection and liberation;
O Goddess of gods, on these festive occasions, one should especially perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
O fair-faced one, those wicked ones of evil conduct who, out of negligence, do not serve their gurus and deities are equal to beasts. (28.28)
Since there is no permanent worship [of a physical image], one must certainly perform worship in these [mandalas].
Wandering, which is proclaimed for the sake of attaining knowledge, power, and so forth, [is also required]. (28–29)
Furthermore, whatever Śakti-yāga has been taught— whether for subjugation, attraction, or killing—
all of that is accomplished without effort on the days of the festival (parva).
Thus, the festival (parvan) is described as sixfold by means of its general and particular aspects.

Regarding the word "therein"—it refers to the *Haiḍara*. Regarding "sixfold"—it is [divided] by way of the general, the general-of-the-general, the general-particular, the particular, and the particular-of-the-particular.
And by way of particularity and generality.
He demonstrates that very point:
"The first and the fifth day of the month are defined as the 'Auspicious Day' (śrīdina). (28–31)
Because it is preeminent, the day of the festival is spoken of with the prefix "Śrī"; for this is the rule: that which is secret should not be uttered without its [proper] title. (28–32)
The fourth, eighth,
and final days of each fortnight for both [the waxing and waning] sides are proclaimed here as the most general of general holy days (parvan).

If, during these very days, there should arise a particularity consisting of both future and present planetary states, that constitutes the nature of the general-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣatā). || 28-34 ||

And that [power], though one, has been declared by the All-pervasive Lord to be elevenfold in each [of the levels]; Śambhu has thus delineated it as being of the same kind yet progressively superior. (28–35)
"One should not speak [the name] without an *anupada*. As was stated previously:
"The name should be spoken preceded by 'Śrī'... "Another" refers to the ninth; "world" (*bhuvana*) refers to the fourteenth; and "final" (*carama*) refers to the fifteenth.

It is called "the commonality of the common" because it follows both positions; for this very reason, because it conforms to one position, the first and fifth [days] of the month are described as being common.
It is said to be "of a dual nature" because, even while being that day, there exists the particularity of the planets and so forth. "That" refers to—

Regarding the distinction: it is of eleven kinds—because on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, there is an absence of any specific [astrological] configuration such as that of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) or planets (*graha*). As he will state:
"There is no particular conjunction of lunar mansions and planets in Āśvayuja; therefore, that [day] is excluded."
"The calculation of the *velābhagraha* is stated for eleven months.
Regarding the phrase "in each one": this refers to the scripture. Regarding "of the same kind" (*sajātīya*):
for example, the ninth day of Mārgaśīrṣa; for although it is a general common festival (*parvan*), it [also] possesses this [specific quality].

It brings about a distinction; for this very reason, it is called "excellent" (utkṛṣṭā). The word "thus" (evam) refers to its nature as both general and particular, and as a particular itself. || 35 ||
He demonstrates this very point here:
"The pair of Kṛṣṇas, Fire-Sita (white), Śruti-Kṛṣṇa, and Vahni-Sita are the fortnights;
[the lords of the months] shall be Arka, Indu, Jīva, Candra, Budha, Yugma, Indu, Arka, Kavi, Guru, and Vidhu. (28–36)
The asterisms are Parigha, Citrā, Maghā, Tiṣya, Pūrvaphalgunī, Karṇa (Śravaṇa), Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī), Viśākhā, and that which is known as Śravaṇa. (28–37)
In the eighth [day] from the lunar day of the Sun, there is the eighth [day] of the Moon; in the sixth [day] from the eighth, there is the pair of the fifth and the eighth;
in the middle of the first night and the middle of the night, there are five [days] at midday; and sunrise is at midday. (28–38)
The time known as "the first night" occurs during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa;
the messenger (dūtī) is a woman of the Kanyā class, born of the lowest caste, a courtesan, full of passion, and a knower of reality.
In the ritual known as the *anuyāga*, they are to be worshipped in sequence, both in detail and in summary:
"Vahni" refers to three; "Śruti" refers to four; "Paraphalgu" is *uttaraphalgunī* (just as *rakṣa* means *rākṣasa*); "Caitra" is *citrā*; and "Prākphalgu" is *pūrvaphalgunī*.
*Karṇa* is the seventh [tithi]; *prājāpatya* is Rohiṇī; *randhra* refers to the two ninth [tithis];
*tithi* is the fifteenth; *arka* is the twelfth; *parā* is the thirteenth; *vasu* is the eighth; *śaśī* is the first;
*vṛṣāṅka* is the eleventh; *rasa* is the sixth; and *śara* is the fifth.

And here, from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa onwards, all [the details] beginning with the dark fortnights should be applied respectively throughout the twelve months; for example, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
during the dark fortnight, on a Sunday, under the lunar mansion Uttaraphalgunī.

On the ninth [tithi], during the first half of the night and the two [preceding] watches, there is the state of being a mountain (*parvatva*). Thus, in this context, because the four lunar days (tithis) known as *rasa*, *vṛṣāṅka*, *arka*, and *parā* consist of the constellations, planets, and so forth, they possess a specific form. As for the remainder, however—

Because the ninth day and those following possess a dual nature, they consist of both the universal and the particular. As it has been said: "On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the onset of night, for two praharas during the first half of the conjunction of Ādityā and Uttaraphalgunī..."
O Pārvatī, on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa,
at the arrival of midnight during the conjunction of the moon with the Citrā constellation, the second festival occurs.
On the full moon of the month of Māgha, at the arrival of midnight,
during the conjunction of the Maghā constellation and Jupiter, the third Kaulika festival occurs.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, during the conjunction of the moon with the constellation Tiṣya,
when the sun has reached the middle of the sky, the fourth festival is proclaimed.

One should consider the fifth festival on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, when the sun has reached the middle [of its course] and there is a conjunction with Mercury and Pūrvaphalgunī.

O fair-faced one, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, at midday, when there is a conjunction of Mercury and the Śravaṇa asterism, occurs the sixth sacred festival (parvan).
O Pārvatī, on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the middle part of the day,
when there is a conjunction with the Moon and the water-god (Varuṇa), it is the seventh festival.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, when the sun has reached the meridian,
the conjunction of the moon with the asterism Mūla is declared to be the eighth festival (parva).

O beautiful lady, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, during the conjunction of the Rohiṇī nakṣatra and the planet Venus, at dawn, occurs the ninth sacred festival (parvan).
O Goddess, when there is a conjunction of Viśākhā and Jupiter on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada at the time of midday, that is the tenth Kaulika festival.
O beloved, on that ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja,
neither the planets, nor the lunar mansions, nor the specific time of day is taken into account.
This is the eleventh chapter, which brings about the great arising of family-perfection;
[it was composed] at the beginning of the night on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika.
"The twelfth festival is proclaimed to occur at the conjunction with the moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Regarding the term "antyajā"—it refers to those such as fisherwomen (dhīvarī) and Mātaṅgīs. Regarding "tattvavedinī"—it means one who knows the rules (samayajñā).
As it has been said:
"And the worship of the Dhīvarī-cakra should be performed at night according to the prescribed rule;
O Goddess, one should worship the cakra born of the Mātaṅgī lineage.
Thus [it is said].
"And those Śaktis, who know the observances, sport at the end of the day," so it is said.

Now, one might object: "In this context, what is called 'worship' (pūjā) is said to extend from the initial sacrifice (ādiyāga) up to the concluding sacrifice (anuyāga), and since it is accomplished over a long period of time, how could it be perfected within such a brief duration on the festival days (parva)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And on every festival day, one should perform the cycle of the subordinate sacrifice with particular excellence. || 28-40 ||
It is complete through the sequence of ritual conduct (*yāgacaryā*) consisting of both secret and non-secret procedures;
indeed, the *anuyāga* (subsequent sacrifice) is the primary element in every application of ritual action. (28–41)
Therefore, one who is intent upon that [liberation] should strive to obtain the time for the *anuyāga*.

The sense is that the *mukhya* (primary sacrifice) is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to this [liberation], because it consists in the offering of substances that serve as the requisites for worship; thus, by that [means].
The essential meaning is that at the time of the [monthly] festival, the entire burden of the sacrifice must be performed.
Now, one might ask: "Why is the conjunction of the lunar mansions and planets not mentioned here for the month of Āśvayuja? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"There is no specific time for the absence of planets in Āśvayuja; therefore, that [month] is excluded. (28.42)
The calculation of the *velābhagraha* is stated for eleven months;
for this very reason, there is a state of being characterized by specific distinctions here.
In this way, he demonstrates the distinction between specific [days] elsewhere as well:
"The twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna is declared to be a sacred festival (parvan). (28-43)
This conjunction of piercing the first lunar day (agratithi) is the most important; this is the specific distinction here.
The first lunar day is the thirteenth (trayodaśī). As it has been said:
"In the month of Phālguna, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight should be joined with the lunar day of Monday."
"Even when success is achieved, there is this great distinction here regarding the portion for the guest.
Thus it is said.
It is not only here that there is this distinction of specificities, but rather everywhere; thus he says:
"Having divided day and night into three parts, [there is] the division into first, middle, and last. (28.44)

When that [day] is divided into three parts, the time for worship is the most excellent period; if the most excellent hour, the lunar mansion and planet, and likewise the astrological wheel (cakra), should coincide. (28–45)
That sacrifice is the primordial sacrifice; its desired fruit shall be accomplished through worship alone on the festival days (parvan).
Even there, the state of being gentle or fierce is determined by the calculation of the day, time, lunar mansions, and planets. (28–46)
Having understood this, the preeminent practitioner should perform each respective rite at its appropriate time. In this regard, one should indeed divide the desired day or night into three parts—
namely, the first, middle, and final portions— and [perform the rite] according to whichever of these three divisions is appropriate for the specific requirement.

Regarding the time of worship characterized by dawn, midday, and evening— even when that time is divided into three parts, the first, middle, or last portion is the most excellent time for worship according to its respective nature; it is precisely at that time that the circle of maidens, outcastes, and others is traditionally regarded as worthy of worship.

If the most essential factors— the time, the planets, and so forth— converge, then the sacrifice performed at that very moment is the "Initial Sacrifice" (ādiyāga), meaning it is the primary act of worship.
For that reason, on the festival days (parvan), even without [the presence of] yoga or knowledge, the desired result is attained through worship alone.

"Siddhyet" means that the desired accomplishment would be attained. "Tatrāpi" means even in that most primary time, which consists of specific variations. "Tattat" refers to [rites such as] pacification, eradication, and so forth.

Now, having raised the doubt: "Is it not the case that right here [in the previous section] it was divided [thus]: 'If the lunar day (tithi) and so forth should occur after the time for worship has passed, then what is to be done?'—anticipating this, he says:
"If the lunar mansion, planet, or lunar day should occur by transgressing that time for worship which has been stated... (28.47)
Some maintain that one should disregard the specific [lunar day] and prioritize the time (velā).
Regarding this very point, he states another opinion: "No; however, our teachers [hold otherwise], for here it is the lunar day (*tithi*) in its specific form that is essential, not the time. (28.48)
Now, one might object: "What indeed is this thing called a lunar day (tithi), such that it could possess the status of being a particular [object]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The portion of the moon, which is the nature of the object of consciousness, [is illuminated] by the mass of rays from the sun, which is the subject."
For as long as it is full, to that extent indeed is that lunar day (tithi) made manifest by the planets and constellations. || 28-49 ||
In this regard, it is said: "Thus, day by day, due to its particular position relative to the sun, there occurs an increase in the whiteness of the moon... (Vṛṣabha 4.4).
According to the perspective set forth in such works as the *Jyotiḥśāstra*, for whatever portion of the moon— which consists of the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—

constituted by each individual digit (*kalā*), there exists a corresponding time-period consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās* (plus or minus)— during which that portion is fully illuminated, whether in its visible part or its other part, by the rays of the sun— which consists of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It would be characterized by fully developed whiteness; for that is called a lunar day (*tithi*) which becomes manifest through the planets and stars—that is to say, it attains its specific distinction. || 49 ||
And for this reason, the lunar day (tithi) alone possesses primacy; thus he says:

"Therefore, here the lunar day is primary, and it is that which is qualified by its conjunction with planets and asterisms. Time (velā) is not the principal factor here; and this is logical, for the Supreme Lord [has said so]. (28–50)

In the Śrītrika, Bhairava, and Kula scriptures, it is stated that on festival days one should not observe any specific time-conjunction (*velā-yoga*) other than those arising from the conjunction of lunar days, asterisms, and planets. (28.51)
Regarding the cause: he states the following in order to establish this also through scripture—beginning with "And this is logical," and so forth.
It is said there:
"That which is the ninth lunar day (tithi) of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa..."
In the dark fortnight, it is joined with Uttaraphalgunī and conjoined with the Sun.
"In that [month], a special worship should be performed by the best of practitioners," and so forth, until:
"On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika..."
"One should worship the twelfth parvan when there is a conjunction with the moon and Śravaṇa. Thus ends [the section]. ||51||
And for this reason, the lunar day (tithi) alone possesses primacy as the object of worship; thus he says:
"In the absence of planetary conjunctions, the lunar day is to be worshipped because it is the primary form. The word "tu" (but/for) indicates the reason. As the Smṛti also states:
"...one should diligently perform the sacrifice on the lunar day (tithi).
By this, although the *parvan* days possess a specific character here, their general nature is also stated.
He illustrates this very point, which contains a principle well-known in other treatises:
"For they say that in the absence of a white [sacrificial animal], one should perform the immolation of a black goat. (28.52)

For the Mīmāṃsakas [hold that] when it is enjoined, "One should sacrifice a white goat," if the animal brought forward should flee, one should sacrifice another of the same color and the same age; and so forth,
if an animal of that very color cannot be obtained, then "qualities are substituted."

The meaning of the sentence is that, according to the principle beginning with "There are no [specific] species for goats and so forth," they declare that even a goat of a different color must be sacrificed; likewise, in the present case as well,
if the lunar day (tithi) were not qualified by the conjunction of a lunar mansion (bhaga), a planet (graha), and so forth, then this [day], being merely a Parvan, [would be insufficient].
"Grāhyā" (to be grasped). ||52||

Now, one might object: "How can the conjunction of the *velā* (the auspicious time), which was not mentioned by the Lord even in the *Śrītrikakula* and other such texts, be consistent with its being taught in the *Ūrmikula* and other scriptures? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Furthermore, although the *velā* is taught in scriptures such as the *Ūrmikula*, it is intended for those who pursue specific desires (*kāmya*)."
Having primarily prescribed the ritual procedure for that occasion on the full-moon day of the month of Pauṣa.
Just as an instruction given to one who has gone outside after performing worship at midnight, meditating,
and reciting mantras bears fruit, so too does the word from the Cakra bear fruit during the month of Māgha.
In the five [circles], there is the swift attainment of desired success, friendliness, wealth, and union.
In the location of the wheel, through wrath and the shattering of stone, there is the destruction of enemies. (28-55)
The attainment of the prophetic instructions up to the end of the path is described by the Lord.

He demonstrates this very point with the words "and likewise," and so forth. The term "in five" is to be applied according to the maxim of the crow's eye (kākākṣinyāya); thus, from the month of Phālguna until the end of Āṣāḍha, there is the accomplishment of one's desired goal within those five months.
In the months of Śrāvaṇa and Mārgaśīrṣa, one should practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] in sequence during five [periods].
As it is stated therein regarding the sequence beginning with the month of Pauṣa:
"O Dear One, worship should be performed there with diligence at the time of midnight."
Afterwards, one should be engaged in meditation and devoted to the recitation of mantras.
An instruction arises for him; having heard it, he should go outside.
There, O blessed lady, he shall attain his desired object; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [it is said].
At the time of midnight, due to the special worship performed there by the mantra-practitioner,
whatever word falls from the revolving wheel—
"Therefore, O Goddess of gods, without obstacle, it shall become fruitful within seven days," and,
"By worshipping there for half a day, one's desired goal is accomplished without delay."
Thus:
"Whatever accomplishment one may desire, that shall come to him before long."
"O Goddess, that which is prayed for is accomplished...
and, "O Dear One, one should worship the Cakra for the sake of attaining the objects desired by the mind."
"...by worshipping that wheel, one attains success.
Thus:
"For one who performs worship here at the beginning of the day according to the prescribed rule..."
"And all beings abide in a state of loving-kindness toward him.
Thus it is said:
"By worshipping there at midday, one gains good fortune, wealth, and grain."
"There is an increase, O Goddess of Gods...," and,
"But the melāpaka will take place everywhere on that festival day."
Thus:
"O Dear One, O Goddess, for whomever one strikes the ground in anger as a sign,
his head shall indeed shatter into seven pieces like a stone."
"But it shall burst open, O highly fortunate one; there is no doubt about this. By wandering through the sacred field at night, O Goddess, one shall obtain the instruction of the Siddhas.
Thus it is said.

Now, one might ask: "Even if there is an absence of asterisms, planets, and so forth on this lunar day, must the conjunction with the time (velā) be taken into account, or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the absence of a conjunction of asterisms and planets, one must certainly observe the time (velā) of the lunar day. (28.56)
For she, being thus manifest in form, would grant the arising of the lunar day's own nature.

Thus, on a day conjoined with the sixfold division [of the yoga], one should perform worship with great distinction—so he says: "The day that follows the portions of the asterisms, planets, lunar days, and time-measures is beautiful in all its limbs. (28–57)
If it should be obtained, then one should perform a most exceptional worship of it;
by the phrase "beautiful in all its limbs," its extreme rarity is revealed.

Now, one might object: "If the sacrifice is intended here solely with reference to optional rites (kāmya), then why has its connection been stated as being necessarily required even in this section on occasional rites (naimittika)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And this [prohibition] is not merely for the sake of desire, since it has been stated that [the result follows] from its avoidance alone. || 28-58 ||

In the venerable Bhairavakula and in the Ūrmiśāstra, it is stated that there is a violation of the samaya for those who are wicked, of evil conduct, equal to beasts, and who do not know the sacred festival days (parvan). (28–59)
He recites that very same point by way of its meaning: "For those who are wicked," and so forth. ||59||
Now, one might object: "How is it known that this was not already stated simply by the fact of the exclusive qualification for optional rites (kāmyādhikāra)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And there can never be any transgression (pratyavāya) from the non-performance of an optional rite."
What is the cause?
Having thus described the specific festivals, he speaks in order to discuss the *cakra* (the ritual circle):
"In that regard, the *cakrayāga* (the sacrifice of the circle) is now defined for the sake of accomplishing the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*). (28–60)
That which is called the "Sacrifice to the Embodiment" (mūrtiyāga) in the Śrīyogīśvarīmata—the daily and occasional rites taught here by the Great Lord—[is now described]. (61)
In all cases, the wheel-sacrifice (cakrayāga) is primary here, especially in rites for specific desires;
whether it be a man or a woman, a person who is wise and a yogi is [the officiant] in this rite known as the Mūrti-sacrifice.
"One should diligently employ [the disciple] in the sacrifice, for he is the unsurpassed vessel;
through contact with him, fullness arises"—so it is stated in the *Traiśirasa* and other scriptures. (28–63)
The word "that" refers to the knower of reality and so forth. ||63||

He recites that very [verse]: "Therefore, everything offered and performed—the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving—belongs to the one who gives or performs [the rite] for the man of knowledge or the yogi. (28.64)
And it is also stated in the Dīkṣottara: "Food is Brahmā, the essence is Hari, and the eater is Śiva. Thus, the man of knowledge may uplift even those who are outcaste dog-cookers.
If that practitioner eats while having become composed of all reality,
by that single act of eating, ten million have been fed.
Now, O beloved, if one who knows the reality should eat in this [context], no restriction would apply; so said the Blessed Lord Śiva. (28.67)
All that is to be enjoyed is of the nature of illusion; Śiva is the enjoyer, and he is also I.
He who truly knows this is a teacher who has reached the further shore of reality.
Seeing the God approaching, the medicinal herbs playing in their home said:
"Today we have indeed turned back from the deep ocean of worldly existence."
When [the breath] has reached his mouth, we shall go to the supreme state;
for others subsist on the downward breath (apāna), while the upward breath (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna) are directed downwards.
O Goddess of the gods, when that [deity] is the enjoyer, even hundreds of lineages of the donor are swiftly liberated from the ocean of torments such as hell. (71)

"He performs"—that is to say, service and so forth. "A crore"—that is to say, of Brahmins. As it has been said: "O Goddess, when the Teacher is fed, a crore of high-souled Brahmins who know the meaning of the four Vedas becomes fed."

Thus. "In this" refers to the *cakrayāga*. "Others" refers to those who have not reached the further shore of reality (*atattvapāragāḥ*). "Those who subsist on the *apāna*" means those who contemplate only that state of being an object of enjoyment which causes a downward fall—this is the meaning.
For this very reason it is said: "The *apāna* is downward-facing. As it has been stated:
"By means of dharma there is upward movement; by means of adharma there is downward movement" (Sāṃkhyakārikā).
Regarding that [state], it refers to the one who consumes vital breath and has crossed to the further shore of the principles (tattvas). || 71 ||

And the excellence of the man of knowledge is everywhere indeed beyond reproach—thus he says: "It is also stated in the venerable *Niśāṭana*: 'Even from the seeking of the teaching, once it has issued from the mouth of the Guru and reached within the ears... (72)
At that very moment, he is liberated, though the machine continues to stand;
this applies even to one who drinks liquor, a thief, a killer of a Brahmin, or one who violates the teacher’s bed. (28.73)
Whether an outcaste or a twice-born, whether a child, an old man, or even a youth—any wise person who dwells on the borders is a purifier of the country as well. (28.74)
The Lord is present there together with his consort and his attendants;
the point is that even his status as a great sinner—due to such acts as drinking liquor—is not to be taken into account.

And for this reason, one should perform the *mūrtiyāga* (the sacrifice to the form) by relying solely on a man of knowledge; thus he says: "Therefore, having primarily [chosen] a Guru who is proficient in knowledge... (28.75).
"One should perform the sacrifice of the image (mūrtiyāga); its procedure is according to the Yogīśvarīmata.
Regarding the word "procedure" (vidhi): it refers to ritual action (karma). For this very reason, the worship of the wheel (cakrārcana) is also implied by this.
And when should that be performed, and by what procedure? To this he says:
"At the Pavitrārohaṇa rite, at the Śrāddha, and likewise on festival days. (28.76)
During solar and lunar eclipses and other such worldly festival days (parvan), as well as during celebrations such as weddings and the sacrificial rites of Brahmins; || 28-77 ||
The Mūrtiyāga should be performed for the sake of initiation, for consecration, for the purification of the observances (samayas), and for the fulfillment of desires; it is fivefold.
"Utsava" (festival) refers to the anniversary of one's own guru's birth and so forth. || 78 ||
He demonstrates the fivefold nature [of the lineage]:
"The solitary, the paired, the mixed, the wheel-couple, and the hero-mixture;
the solitary is that which is joined with teachers who are themselves solitary. (28.79)
Furthermore, that *yāmala* (union) is of two kinds when performed by practitioners and others together with their wives;
it occurs either through union with one's own wife or through union with a courtesan acquired by purchase.

The Cakriṇī and other [deities] will now be described according to their appropriate association with the Śaktis; through union with them in the arrangement of the wheels (cakras), the sacrifice bestows all fruits. (28–81)

A sacrifice performed with all [of these] together is called a *vīrasaṅkara*. "Together with their wives" means—by implication—with the four [beginning with] the Guru. "Wives" refers to those who have been married.
"Will be described"—as follows:

"In the twenty-ninth chapter, [it is said]: 'The Mātaṅga, Kṛṣṇa, Saunika, Kānduka, Cārmika, Vikośin, Ghātu, Vibheda, along with the Mātsyika and Cākrika—their wives are nine here in the ninefold sacrifice. By the phrase "joined with the wheel" (cakrayukta), it means "possessing the wheel" (cakrayuk). By the word "by all" (sarvaiḥ)—
Thus it was said by those in male and female forms. Here, he shows the sequence for the seating:
"The Guru should be in their midst, and the group of Gurus should surround him. (28.82)
There are three outer enclosures ending with the *samayin*s in their respective order; or else, all of them may be arranged in rows, and the Guru is always in their center. (28.83)

Then, having worshipped each respective cakra according to its sequence with that [specific] scent, incense, garland, unguent, and garment, thinking "this is that very cakra," [he should proceed]. (84)

"Envelopment" (āvṛti) means the surrounding of the group of gurus. "Always" (sada) means at the time of the sequence of envelopment or the sequence of rows. "That respective circle" (tattaccakra) refers to that which is recognized as worthy of worship in the form of the gurus, practitioners, and so forth. ||84||
He illustrates that very point:
"One should contemplate the ritual of the Solitary Hero (ekavīra) in a wheel with one spoke;
the Couple (yāmala) in one with two spokes; and likewise the Triad (trika) in another, such as one with six spokes. (85)

One should worship the six Yoginīs and the group of seven in the seven-spoked [cakra], or the eight and the eight in the eight-spoked one; or whatever else is similar there in that cakra which possesses such a nature.
Then, when the vessel is filled with wine, the wise one should first worship the Cakra;
it must be accompanied by the Ādhāra (support), for there is never a libation (tarpaṇa) devoid of the Ādhāra.
Without a support, there is no falling away, nor do the rays find satisfaction elsewhere—that is, on the three-spoked [wheel]. "Of such a kind" means having that specific, fixed number.
"Previously" means first or primary. He demonstrates this very point:
The vessel shall be in the form of a preta, and the liquor shall be the nectar of Śakti.
But the power that is the enjoyer therein is Śambhu, the Supreme Lord;
having thus meditated upon the triad as merged—the individual soul (aṇu), power (śakti), and Śiva—[one attains liberation]. || 28.89 ||
Then, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed in sequence from one enclosure (āvṛti) to the next;
by means of the process of re-absorption (pratisañcara), he should cause [the soul] to enter back within once more.

"Indeed, that which extends as far as the presence of the Guru is called a complete circuit (*bhramaṇa*). 'From enclosure to enclosure' means from each of the four enclosures. 'In succession' means not by skipping the next [stage]. 'Pratisañcara' means moving back in the reverse direction."
For that is the "complete revolution," meaning it is a single movement consisting of both the sequence of emanation and withdrawal.
And regarding the libation (tarpaṇa), he states the sequence here:
"In that regard, first the deities are to be gratified, and then the heroes; such is the sequence. (28.91)
"Vīra and Vīraśakti—such is the lineage of our gurus.
Then [he served] various appetizers combined with meat, fish, and other foods. (28–92)
There, the best of practitioners should scatter [offerings] at the beginning until [the deities'] satisfaction is reached;
furthermore, in the absence of a vessel, one should use a *bhadra* or a curved shell. (28–93)
"The wise man should form [the gesture] in the vessel"—this is the sequence according to the Siddhāmata.
He demonstrates that very point:
"With the right hand, it should be auspicious; the 'waving' [gesture] is called the oyster-shell (śukti). (28.94)
One should place the little finger of the right hand over the left;
then, by joining the index finger and thumb, one should place the fingers of the left hand beneath the right. (28.95)
When these two [hands] are thus joined without any gaps, it is called the *vellitā* (waving) *śukti* (shell).
Those drops which then fall to the ground during the drinking [of wine]— [28.96]

For by those [offerings], the Vetālas, Guhyakas, and others, as well as the rays of light, are indeed satisfied; Bhairava is pleased by the stream [of offering], and after that, the supreme drinking from the hand.
No one whatsoever should be granted entrance here beforehand; however, if someone has entered through negligence, one should not subject them to any investigation. (28–98)
Having performed this in sequence, at the conclusion of the ritual, the wise practitioner should bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with unguents, betel, clothing, and other such items.
A wise person should not give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) less than half a rūpaka.
To those who have taken the pledges (samayins), it should be doubled successively, up to the teacher, where it may reach twice that amount. (28.100)
This is the Mūrtiyāga, which is the foremost of all sacrifices;
in the performance of rites for specific desires, it should be performed seven times in that same manner.
"By the right hand"—that is to say, by one whose fingers are closely pressed together, elevated, and contracted.

"By the union of the index finger and the thumb"—that is to say, by those belonging to the left hand; thus, the right little finger, resting upon the left [hand], is [grasped] by that very same index finger and thumb.
Having formed it into a bound shape, this arrangement should be made. As it has been said:
"Now, if the prescribed vessel is not available, then one should perform this rite;
either a *bhadra* or a *vellitaśukti* vessel is indeed recommended for drinking there."
O Supreme Goddess, with the right hand it should be auspicious;
and with both hands together, the great fruit-bearing *velli-śukti* [mudrā] should be performed.
O lady of excellent limbs, having placed the little finger of the right hand upon the top of the left hand, one should join the index finger and the thumb.
"Having placed the fingers of the left hand below those of the right, and having formed them into a seamless oyster-shell [mudrā], drinking [the nectar] becomes perfected.
Regarding "here"—it refers to the *cakrayāga*. *Rūpaka* means a *dīnāra* coin. ||101||
He states the purpose for performing [the rite] seven times:
"First they recognize the house, then its capacity; thereafter they perceive its strengths and weaknesses, and then the mothers are filled with wonder. (28.102)
Thereafter, they draw near and are gratified as givers of boons—both the goddesses and the Lord, together with their retinues. (28.103)
Therefore, this sacrifice to the Mūrtis should be performed by the wise man at night in a secret house; for there, O heroes, the Śaktis are fully capable of [acting] toward one another.
One should apply the deities by reciting their names, even without the use of conventional symbols. In the absence of the circle of images (mūrticakra), one should worship young maidens alone.

However, for the sake of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), one should not [marry] a girl who is deficient in limbs, nor one who has already reached puberty; likewise, [one should avoid marrying on] the first lunar day (*pratipad*), the days known as *śruti*, the fourth lunar day, and the three *uttarā* constellations. (28.106)
The fifth and sixth [tithis] are in Hastā; then the seventh is in Pūrvā-phalgunī and Punarvasu; the one following that (the eighth) is in Pitrya (Maghā); and likewise the ninth is in Rohiṇī.

O Brahmā, the twelfth lunar day occurs at the root (Mūla), the full moon on the day of Bhūtā (Aśvinī), and the new moon on Dhaniṣṭhā; this is the one consisting of eleven [constellations]. || 28-108 ||
Even if the day-count (ahargaṇa) is joined with any one of the three starting from Arka or with Śukra, it is renowned as a "yoga-parvan," whether occurring at night or by day. (28–109)
The Mūrtiyāga must be performed in every way during the Yoga-parvan;
for the wise man who honors all the days known as Yoga-parvan [attains the highest state]. (28.110)
Even without a mandala, he may become a *samayin* through the sacrifice to the Form (*mūrtiyāga*).
Such is the sacrifice to the Form according to the venerable *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*. (28.111)

"Samarthatām" means in rites such as sacrifice. "Balābalam" refers to capacity and incapacity regarding heroic deeds (*vīrakarma*). "Vismayante" means they regard it as a marvel, thinking, "Even mortals of this kind exist"—this is the meaning. "Mātaraḥ" signifies all [types of] connections.
As it has been said:
"In the first rite of the embodied form (mūrtiyāga), they recognize the house of the practitioner;
in the second, his capacity; and in the third, his strength and weakness."
O Goddess, in the fourth [month], those Mothers themselves are filled with wonder;
in the fifth, having gone there, they enter into the very midst of his house.
"In the sixth [recitation], they become pleased; in the seventh, they grant boons. They will bestow upon him his desire: the perfections of longevity and health.
Thus, from the recitation of the name of the deity, which is not joined with a conventional sign (*saṅketa*), it follows from some specific designation.
The meaning is that they are devoid of worldly verbal usage; for this very reason it is said, "hidden" (*gupta*).
Regarding "known by hearing" (*śrutisaṃjña*), it refers to the act of listening. Regarding "in the latter triad," the meaning is "joined with any one of those.
The same should be understood for the preceding [triads] as well. "That beyond" (*tatparā*) is the eighth [lunar mansion]; "pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*) is in the Maghās.

Regarding the word *brahma*: because the term *brahma* denotes the individual soul (*jīva*) in the statement, "In the eighth house from the center [ascendant], in the second, fifth, and third houses from Mars, [there is] Brahmā," the meaning is that it refers to the asterism presided over by that deity, namely Tiṣya (Puṣya).

"Bhūta" refers to the fourteenth lunar day (*tithi*). "The triad beginning with Arka" means the triad consisting of Arka (the Sun), and those following it—namely, the Moon, Mars, and Mercury. Thus, a day-count (*ahargaṇa*) characterized by the aforementioned lunar days and asterisms (*nakṣatra*), when conjoined with any one of these five planets, constitutes a "yoga-parvan."
The meaning is that its name is well-known; as it has been said:
"The ninth [tithi] in conjunction with Rohiṇī, the fourteenth with Puṣya, the fifth with Hasta, and the twelfth should be known to be with Mūla."
The first lunar day (pratipad) is established for the constellation Śravaṇa; the fourth is for the three Uttaras;
the sixth is a bestower of success in the Pūrvas; and the eighth is for Maghā.

The full moon day is to be known as occurring under Aśvinī, and the seventh lunar day is traditionally remembered as falling under Dhaniṣṭhā; likewise, O fair-faced one, the new moon day is to be known as occurring under Dhaniṣṭhā.
"On Friday, as well as on Sunday, Wednesday, and Mars (Tuesday),
the counting of the days of the week must be performed...
Thus [ends verse] 111.
Having thus described the worship of the wheel, he speaks in order to explain the procedure for the *pavitraka* (the sacred thread):
"Now the clear procedure for the *pavitraka*, as taught by Śiva, is being declared;
it has been further indicated in the *Śrīratnamālā* and the *Triśiraḥśāstra*. (28.112)
In this teaching on the essence of the *Mālinī* concerning the true nature of the illustrious *Siddhāṭana*, the procedure taught by the venerable Māla is stated here primarily. (28.113)
Regarding the phrase "it has been indicated": this is because it has not been explicitly stated in the *Śrīsiddha* and other such works. Regarding the phrase "primarily":
although there is no difference in terms of clarity, the arising of that [state] and so forth are described here with greater emphasis. || 113 ||

He says that very thing: "Stupefied by the sleep caused by the poison arising from the churning of the ocean of milk, the King of Nagas did not remain in his own abode during the rainy season. (28.114)
But solely pure, subsisting on air for a hundred years, he worshipped the divine lord Bhairava, who is ten times [more powerful than] the [other] lords. || 28-115 ||
And he informed that gratified Lord: "I am able to dwell in my own Pātāla during the rainy season"; and the Supreme Lord [granted him leave]. (28.116)
He placed the Naga upon the seat of his own matted locks;
thereafter, he was borne upon his own head by the entire host of gods.
For the universal worshipfulness of the great and the venerable is not at all surprising;
therefore, [this is seen] upon the head of Maheśvara and indeed upon all the deities. (28.118)
One should perform that purification for oneself preceded by a sacrifice; ten crores of other forms of worship are not equal to the rite of offering the *pavitra*. (28.119)
Initiation is in vain, knowledge is in vain, and even the propitiation of the Guru is in vain;
without this [rite of] *pavitra* and so forth, the serpent [Kāla] shall seize these by the command of Śiva. (28.120)
Therefore, it should be performed with every effort by those who know the Kula;
the meaning is that it is designated by the term "pavitra" (purifier). As it has been said:
"By that great-souled purifier, O Goddess, I have been propitiated."
Thus it is said:
"There is a lord of serpents named Pavitra, the elder brother of Vāsuki.
And regarding the reading *pavitreṇa*, it should be explained as meaning "with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth. They are equal.
"One hundred multiplied by ten" means one thousand years. As it has been said:
"The mighty one, subsisting on air alone, [should remain] for a thousand divine years.
The word "should perform" refers to the Guru and others. By the words beginning with "ten," the purpose is stated.
When should it be performed? To this he says:
"The rite [is performed] from the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha while the sun is situated in Gemini or Cancer. (28.121)
That [observance] should be performed without interruption until the full moon of Tulā;
the final day of Kārttika is considered to be marked by Tulā. (28.122)
Others, reciting the word *kula*, provide different interpretations.

The phrase "in the pair" (*mithuna*) and so forth is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it applies even when [the sun] is situated in Leo (*siṃha*) and other signs. "Without cessation" (*anirodhena*) means without interruption. "Of that which is indicated by Libra" (*tulopalakṣitasya*)—for indeed, in the month of Kārtika, [the sun] has entered Libra (*tulā*).
The meaning is that it becomes the sun.
He demonstrates that very difference in interpretation: "Those who know the Nityātantra [hold] Kṛṣṇa to be the final day of Kārtika. (28.123)
That is considered the state of fullness wherein the eternal wheel of the Kula resides.
As it has been said:
"This supreme ritual procedure should be performed on the festival of the lamp."
"Kula is declared to be power (śakti), and that is proclaimed to be eternal.
Having begun with these words, [the text continues]:
"Or, O Goddess, [one should recite] always in the middle [channel] for the cessation of all misfortunes."
"But by this procedure, one should worship the eternal wheel," thus ends [the passage].
Having thus presented one opinion, he states another as well: "The final day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is the Kula festival; such is that [other] view. (28.124)

The state of fullness of the moon therein is that lunar day (tithi) known as Kulapūrṇimā. Now, one might object: "Since the state of being the Kula-mountain and the fullness of the moon exist on other lunar days as well, why is it that only the full moon of Māgha is designated by the term 'Kulapūrṇimā'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Time, moving from south to north, is said to be of the nature of both Kula and Akula.
The completion of that family is said to occur on the final day;
here, beginning from the month of Phālguna, the rising of the seasons of the year lasts until the month of Śrāvaṇa, during which the six full-moon days constitute the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).

Starting from the month of Bhādrapada until the month of Māgha, there are exactly six full moon days that constitute the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). For it has been stated that the southern course, which is denoted by the term *kula*, reaches its completion on the final day of the month of Māgha; as the Śruti says:
"The full moon of Phālguna is indeed the mouth of the year.
Likewise:
"The full moon of Phālguna is for the establishment [of the fire]; this is the mouth of the seasons."
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, this is also stated—thus he says: "Consequently, the performance of the six-month period of the southern solstice is prescribed in the ritual injunction. (28.126)

Regarding the phrase "of Kṛṣṇa" [in the verse]: it refers to the path of Kṛṣṇa, who consists of *tamas*, for the purpose of establishing the luminosity (*prakāśatva*) of that path by means of the *pavitraka* rite, which removes the loss of the conventional order and so forth.
Having thus explained this as a digression, he speaks of the subject at hand:
"The Lord has described this very form, which is taught in many scriptures. (28.127)
In the *Śrīratnamālākulāgama*, it is stated with a single word that, in this very context, [the practice] consists of the fulfillment of all ritual procedures. (28.128)
The rite of the *pavitraka* must be performed in every way during the bright fortnight;
"extensively" means starting from the Vedic [tradition] onwards—this is the meaning.
But surely,

by the statement beginning with "In the middle of the two months of Nabhas and Anabhas, during the dark and bright fortnights," this procedure is prescribed as something to be performed even during the dark fortnight.
Anticipating the objection, "How is it stated here otherwise?", he says: "Filling [the petals] occurs through union with Śakti, and the white petal is of the nature of Śakti. (28.129)
Because it shares the same nature as the southern solstice, its procedure is described by that [term]:
"The great [vow] consisting of one, two, three, four, five, or six repetitions of the *laṭ*. (28.130)
One should prepare a sacred thread (*pavitraka*) made of pearls with knots marked by gold and gems;
for the Guru, it should consist of a triple-stranded golden thread with one hundred and one knots.
But for another Guru, [the distance] is four hundred and three; for a Parameṣṭhin, it is four hundred and six; and in the case of a Prāksiddha, an Ācārya, or a Yogeśvara, it is six hundred and three.
It is said that [the seat] of Śiva is eight [finger-breadths] more, filled with variegated jewels;
and for the Vidyāpīṭha, the rosary, and so forth, one should proceed as for the Guru and likewise for Śiva.
In the absence of gold for Vaṭuka, one should provide silver;
or else a thread made of silk, linen, or cotton, tripled three times over.
Therefore, from a ninefold thread, perform [the multiplication] in the sequence of threefold and so forth,
up to twelvefold (caṇḍāṃśu), or even triple that.
Therefore, that which arises from eighteen threads is considered inferior; furthermore, one hundred and eight is middling, while three times that [number] is held to be superior.
The knots are reckoned according to the number of principles (tattvas) by virtue of the calculation of the six paths;
alternatively, they are diverse through expansion and contraction, and filled with excellent fragrance. (28.137)
Having first worshipped according to the specific ritual injunctions,
one should then offer the *pavitraka* with the contemplation that it is completely filled with all the paths (*adhvan*).
Or else, [the descent] reaches from the knees of the Guru and the disciple up to the navel, the throat, and the crown of the head;
thereafter, a great festival should be performed, preceded by the worship of the Guru.
All those who follow the teaching should be gratified with sacrificial fees, garments, and food;
a great festival consisting of song and dance should be celebrated. (28.140)
The period may be four months, seven days, or even three days if [the full duration] cannot be obtained;
at its conclusion, one should ask the deity for forgiveness and dismiss the mandala and other elements.
And having performed the fire ritual, the wheel-sacrifice previously described should be performed;
the offering of the sacred thread (pavitraka) should take place month by month, every four months, or even once a year.
"It should be performed in every way according to the extent of one's wealth.
"The white petal"—the white fortnight (the bright half of the month). "It is said"—the intention is that such a scriptural statement exists in our own scripture (*asmacchāstra*).
"In the supreme Guru"—that is, in the highest teacher (*paramaguru*). "Beyond four oceans"—that is, [beyond] the four oceans.

The meaning is "four more. There are six *rasas* (flavors). "Filled with variegated jewels" means, by implication, at the location of the knots. "Silken thread" means, by implication, even in the absence of silver.
"Caṇḍāṃśus" (hot-rayed ones) refers to twelve. "Three times that as well" means—

The meaning is that it consists of three hundred and twenty-four [units]. Regarding the word "tantra"—it refers to whatever is intended in each particular case. Regarding "six paths" (ṣaḍadhvan)—by that, according to the number of *kalās*, there are five knots;
up to the number of worlds (*bhuvana*), there are one hundred and eighteen, by way of both detailed exposition (*vyāsa*) and summary (*samāsa*).
The meaning is that it is an *vyāsa* (elaborate exposition) according to the number of *tattvas*, whereas it is a *samāsa* (concise summary) according to the number of *kalās*.
It is called "variegated" (*citrā*) because it is reddened by saffron and other substances; for this very reason, it is said to be "filled with excellent fragrance.
"Cāturmāsya" means during four months.
He further reinforces the necessity of performing this rite in every way:
"In the absence of wealth, however, it should be performed even with *kāśa* grass woven together with *kuśa*. (28.143)
Furthermore, deceit when wealth exists leads to disease and to hell;
for it is said: "Indeed, in the absence of constant worship, one must certainly worship on these [specified days]."

Having raised the doubt—namely, that by such statements worship on the festival days (parvan) has been prescribed for the sake of constantly fulfilling omissions, so is that [fulfillment] also achieved through the Pavitraka rite?—he says:
"In the daily worships, fullness is attained through the fulfillment of the festival worship. (28.144)
In that regard as well, completeness [is achieved] through the worship of the *pavitraka*.
Anticipating the objection, "But what would happen if the *pavitraka* were omitted?", he says:
"However, upon the omission of the *pavitraka*, the wise one should recite the *prāyaścitta* mantra. (28.145)
"Being thoroughly purified, one should perform [the rite] once again"— this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Having thus stated the procedure for the *pavitraka* (sacred thread) in the *Śrīratnamālā*, he also speaks of that which belongs to the *Śrītriśirobhairava*:
Now, the clear procedure for that which was taught regarding Triśiras is being written down. (28.146)

He says that very thing: "In this system, the Śaiva [tradition]—which consists of three objects of knowledge, or five times five, or has ten and eighteen divisions—is said to have six streams (ṣaṭsrotas). (28.147)

"Of the three objects of knowledge" (triprameyasya) means because it consists of the nature of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva. "Consisting of five fives" (pañcapañcātmakasya) means that, according to the system of the Tantra, it is of such a form by way of being the [five] faces, and according to the specific system, by way of being Vāmeśī and so forth. "Of the six streams" (ṣaṭsrotasaḥ) means together with the Picu-face. (147)
In that regard, for the purpose of indicating the qualified candidates, he says:

"Those men who have fallen from their commitments (samaya), who revile the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth, and who are devoid of the daily, occasional, and other rites, as well as the junctions of the sacred festival days (parvan). (28.148)
Whether performed unintentionally or intentionally by those who engage in subtle sins, this purifying rite is performed, O Śivā, for the sake of their pacification. (28.149)

During the bright fortnight, which bestows auspiciousness, from the month of Śrāvaṇa until the end of Kārttika—and not during the dark fortnight, which brings suffering to the performer, the kingdom, the king, and others. (28.150)
By the word "subtle" (sūkṣma), its imperceptibility is expressed. In this very context, he specifies the time by means of the phrase beginning with "in Śrāvaṇa and so forth. || 150 ||
In order to specify its very nature, he says:
"The thread may be silk, or made of silk, or cotton, or even linen;
it has been spun and sprinkled by a woman of beautiful eyebrows belonging to one of the four stages of life. (28.151)
Having tripled the number [of strands] three times, one should cause the measurement to be made;
there should be one hundred and eight threads, or half of that, or half of that again.
The decrease from the previous number occurs sequentially by tens, or by nines, fives, or twenty-seven, starting from Śiva. (28.153)
One should make as many knots as there are arrangements of threads,
having smeared them evenly with four [substances], or else with saffron.

In the case of a manifest [liṅga], it should extend to the edge of the knees; in the case of a liṅga [installed in a pedestal], it should end at the base of the pedestal; and in the case of images, it is auspicious when it reaches the head, through the conceptualization of the three principles (tritattva).
Of the twelve powers of the knots (*granthi*), and also of the flames of the faces of Brahmā;
*kauśeya* is a type of silk cloth. "Of those belonging to the four stages of life" refers to the *samayins* and so forth.
"Of the previous number" refers to that consisting of one hundred and eight, etc. In that regard:

We shall explain that when one hundred and eight [threads] are reduced by tens, there are pavitrakas consisting of ninety-eight threads, and so forth. "In the manifest" (vyakte) means in an image (pratimā). "In the linga" means, by implication, in the unmanifest (avyakta) and the manifest-unmanifest (vyaktāvyakta). "In all forms of worship" (arcāsu) means in all [of them]. This has been stated by me:
"The triad consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva should be placed upon the head.

Regarding the phrase "of the powers"—this refers to Aghorī and the others. Regarding the phrase "of the flames of the Brahma-faces"—the meaning is "of the limbs and faces. This has been stated in that very same [text]:
"And together with the faces of Brahmā, I shall proclaim the ancillary limbs.
Thus [it is said].
In the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in the mobile liṅga, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), and in the assembly of gurus.

It is desired that [the ritual] be performed as is appropriate upon the bell, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the disciples and initiates, the gateway arches, one's own body, and the fire-altar. (28.157)
One should cause it to be made with nine colors in the temple and the sacrificial hall;
"on the seat of fire" means in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). "With nine colors" means having various hues.
In this very context, he specifies the knots: "In the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), however, there are fifty; those located in the image, the liṅga, and the seat. (28.158)

In the *vasu* [eight] and *veda* [four], there are eighteen arrows and eyes in the bell; in the *sruva* ladle, four and two; in the *sruc* ladle, thirty-six; in the temple (*prāsāda*), thirty-six; and in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), twelve. (28–159)

In the house of bathing, [the number of days] is one (rasa) and one (indu); in the house of meditation, four (abdhinetra); in the case of the Guru, seven; for the Sādhaka, five; for the Putraka, seven; and for the Sāmāyika, [seven]. (28-160)
There are four [knots] for one who follows another scripture; for a disciple, five are prescribed.
For those who bear the marks [of other sects], there is only the knot; one should arrange ten at the archway.

Having thus fashioned the *pavitraka* with eight knots at the gates, one should worship the assembly of mantras; then, having established them within that [the *pavitraka*], one establishes them within oneself.
Having prepared the purifiers (*pavitraka*), one should perform the consecration by sprinkling (*saṃpāta*).
Then, for one year, one should meditate upon Bhairava as the witness of one's imperfections (*chidrasākṣin*).
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, O Goddess, one should bow to Mantrabhairava:
"Oṃ, O Lord who fulfills all defects of ritual action, regarding this vow... (28.164)
O delighter of your mother, whatever evil has been done by me, whether unperformed or performed—may all of that perish through your grace, O Lord of Gods. (28.165)
In every way, O Lord of the Wheel of Rays, homage to you; be gracious to me.
With this [verse], one should offer the invitation-purifier (nimantraṇapavitraka) to the deity.
Then the Guru should offer the bali-oblation to the Yoginīs, the Kṣetras, and the Mātṛs;
meanwhile, the disciples should everywhere partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the tooth-stick.
The teacher should sleep and, having risen in the morning, perform his daily rites;
then, having performed the ritual worship, he should collect the sacred objects.
One should employ tooth-sticks, clay, dhātrī, and samṛddhātrī along with water, as well as the four equal parts (catuḥsama) and ashes, in these five [applications]. (28.169)
One should place these five purifiers in order upon the faces facing east, south, west, upward, and to the left, within the range of view of Īśa.
One should employ kuśa grass, fuel, and the five products of the cow before Śarva;
thereafter, one should offer the three kinds of food offerings (naivedya) combined with the left-hand nectar (vāmāmṛta) and other substances. || 28-171 ||
One should likewise offer blood, wine, and various kinds of drinks;
thereafter, there should be a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the flesh of a great beast mixed with sesame seeds.
Either with sesame seeds mixed with ghee, or with rice, or with grains,
all drenched in the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) combined with pieces of sugar-candy.
One thousand and eight recitations of the root mantra are prescribed for the Brahma-face of Triśakti;
then, one hundred and eight recitations of the *arciṣ* mantras, after which one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Then, having taken the purifier (pavitra) in his joined palms (añjali), he should recite this:
"O All-pervading Lord, whatever has been done by me, whether unintentionally or intentionally... (28.175).
"O Lord, by your command and by means of this purifier, may that [vow] of mine be free from flaw;
O Root Mantra, fulfill it"—thus [he says] regarding the rule of ritual action.
One should offer the purifying [mantra] ending with *vauṣaṭ* and concluding with the *bindu*;
likewise, one should sequentially offer the triad ending with *nāda*, *samanā*, and *unmanā*. (28.177)
In this manner, the householder should offer the fourfold set in direct order,
whereas the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) should offer the fourfold set of purifiers in reverse order.
Whatever various items there may be, such as garments, umbrellas, ornaments, and so forth—
these should be offered, as well as rows of lamps and vessels of gold and sesame seeds.
Provided with a pair of garments for the purpose of fulfilling all [desires], the devotees of Śiva should be fed and honored according to one's capacity. (28.180)
One should perform a great festival lasting from four, three, two, or one month down to a single day;
thereafter, they should never go to another place.
Then the preceptor, who is worthy of worship, should give him a new milch cow, adorned with gold, jewels, silver, garments, and other ornaments.
And the Guru should say, "May the rite be complete for you," and he should address the God of gods with the request for his return.
Then the dismissal should be performed; the teacher should take the secret ornaments and other items, and employ that offering for the purpose of the sacrifice. (28.184)
The *pavitraka* is remembered as common to all four [castes];
there is no vow superior to this—what more could be said in its praise? (28.185)
The remainder, however, one should cast into a fathomless flood of water and not keep it stable.
Kha-śara is fifty; vasu-veda is forty-eight;
śara-akṣi is twenty-five; veda-akṣi is twenty-four; ravi is twelve; rasa-indu [is sixteen].
Sixteen; and in the eyes of the ocean, twenty-four. As it has been said:
"In the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) there are fifty; in the image and the liṅga-seat, forty and eight respectively; and in the bell, twenty-five."
Eighteen [finger-breadths] are to be known for the *sruva* ladle, twenty-four for the *sruc* ladle,
thirty-six for the temple (*prāsāda*), and twelve indeed for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
Twenty-four [offerings] should be given in the meditation hall, sixteen in the bathing pavilion,
seven to the preceptor, and one should give five to the practitioner.
One should give seven [offerings] to the spiritual son (putraka) and likewise four to those who hold the pledges (samayin);
and one should give five to disciples (śiṣya) who have been taught according to other scriptures.
"For those possessing the *liṅga*, there is a single knot at the archway; then five pairs [of knots] at the gates;
one should place eight knots at the gates, O Mistress of the Mothers.
Thus it is said. The state of being situated therein and so forth has already been explained previously. "By this"—that is, by the mantra composed in verse.
"And one should perform the daily rite (*āhnika*)"—this is the connection with what precedes. "Then" means immediately after the daily rite.
"Having worshipped the ritual procedure" means having specifically honored the ritual procedure of Gaṇeśa and the others; this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
...one should perform the ritual worship according to the prescribed rules;
having first worshipped Gaṇeśa together with the three Gurus.
"One should subsequently bring forth the purificatory substances (pavitrāṇi) for the leader of the Mothers, Triśiro, who is joined with all obscurations.
By "by them"— it means by all [the items], beginning with the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha).
"Likewise, O Goddess, one should place the tooth-stick on the eastern face;
one should place the *dhātrī* fruit together with earth on the southern [face]."
One should apply clay mixed with *āmalaka* fruits on the western side;
water mixed with *āmalaka* fruits and endowed with the four equal ingredients should be given to one facing upward, along with ashes, wood, clay, and so forth.
"But the best of kissers should cause [the disciple] to give [it] to the northern face.
