Regarding the phrase "these"—it refers to the tooth-stick and so forth. "In the sphere of Īśa"—that is, in its corner. "This"—refers to what is about to be stated. Thus, in this context, this verse together with the *praṇava* (OM) constitutes the intended root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).
"Complete the ritual observance; *vauṣaṭ*—this is the modification (*ūha*). 'The triad' refers to the conceptualization of the *tattvas*;

the word 'fourfold' (*catuṣṭaya*) is to be understood as including [the phrase] beginning with 'thus' (*evam*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of returning': 'O You whose form is the universe, forgive all that was deficient, excessive, or performed contrary to rule by me.'"

"Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; salutations be unto you. Depart satisfied, so that you may return again. Thus it should be said. "Secretly"—meaning so that others, such as common folk, do not perceive his state of being overcome by greed and the like;
for this very reason it is said: "One should employ him for the sake of the sacrifice. What is the praise of this?
As it has been said:
"O Goddess, this supreme secret, the sovereign of all vows,
should be performed by those such as the Cumbakas for the sake of destroying adverse circumstances."
Having begun thus: "The fruit that is obtained by properly performing the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, as well as the Vājapeya, Aśvamedha, Sautrāmaṇī, and Atikṛcchra sacrifices..."
"The fruit of that [merit] is multiplied ten millionfold when the Pavitrārohaṇa has been performed.
Thus it is said.

Now, the occasional rite (naimittika-vidhi), which was previously indicated on occasions such as the family festivals (kulaparva) and so forth, is being described; thus he says: "Now, the occasional rite which was previously indicated by me... (28.186).
In that regard, it is said: "The worship of the Deity must be performed there with special care;
and the Cakra-sacrifice should be performed by the wise according to the previously stated procedure. (28.187)
In that regard, whatever—whether consisting of consciousness or the unconscious—is an aid toward one's own desired enjoyment or liberation, whether by way of succession or directly; || 28.188 ||
That [Reality] is to be worshipped, and its means are also to be worshipped for the sake of attaining identity with It;
even the means to that, such as the image, time, and ritual action, are to be fully honored.
"Consisting of consciousness and non-consciousness" means having the form of the self, the vital breath, and so forth.
"Its means" refers to knowledge, yoga, and the like. "Form" refers to the *liṅga* and other such icons; "time" refers to the *kula*-parvans and so forth;
and "action" refers to bathing, meditation, and the like. || 189 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not said that being a means (upāyatva) consists merely in being an instrument for that [end]? What, then, would be gained by worshipping that [means]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Being a means is the capacity to give birth to the goal; [this arises] from its worship."
Through becoming one with that very form, one shall swiftly attain the goal.

For this indeed is the very nature of a means (*upāya*) as a means: its capacity to manifest the goal (*upeya*) without depending on anything else. Because one honors that [means] which is itself the means to the goal, it is said:
"This worship is indeed absorption through reverence" (Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā 147).
According to this principle and others, because of dissolution (*laya*) right there [in the means], one may attain identification (*tanmayībhāva*) with that very means as if with the goal itself;
by so ascending step by step as appropriate, the state of being identical with the goal will be achieved without delay. ||190||
Therefore, he said:
"In whatever measure there is proximity to the means, to that same extent the necessity of the result is certain, especially in the case of worship and the like. (28.191)

Regarding the phrase "by way of distinction": for in the world, since there is a difference between the means and the goal, a transformation [of the means into something else] might be possible; here, however, the very attainment of the nature of the goal constitutes the state of being the means, so there is no room even for the suspicion of such a transformation—this is the intended meaning.
And for this reason, because the knowledge of the Self is the direct means to liberation and so forth, the day of its attainment is the primary festival; thus he says:
"The attainment of some form of knowledge that assists toward worldly enjoyment and liberation..."
When that very day is declared by the wise to be the primary occasional (naimittika) day. || 28-192 ||
The scripture is the means for that [realization], and the teacher who possesses those means is also instrumental here;
likewise, a brother-disciple who knows that [scripture] bestows knowledge through dialogue. (28.193)

Now, one might object: "In this context, it is logical to employ terms such as 'brother' and so forth with reference to a father; how then can it be said in the same way with reference to a guru? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The wife of the guru, as well as the brother, the son, and so forth—this is the group [to whom these terms apply]."
It does not arise by virtue of a connection through birth; rather, it is born from a connection through knowledge. || 28-194 ||
Now, one might ask: why is there no connection here by way of consanguinity? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Established in the egoity of a body that is a transformation of semen and blood, the lineages of those who benefit the body are firmly rooted in kinship. (28.195)
The continuum of the body refers to sons and the like; the continuum of assistance refers to servants and the like. ||195||
And for this reason, even the traditional law (smṛti) is logical; thus he says:

"Likewise, in the Smṛti scriptures, the inheritance of the lineage is indeed appropriate, for that [lineage] is said to be of such [a nature], due to the distinction of being distant or near. (28.196)

But those who have abandoned attachment to the body and partake in the state of "I am awakening" (bodhāhaṃbhāva) possess kinship with one another because of the two-fold continuity of the assistance toward awakening. || 28-197 ||

"Tāvān" (so much)—the meaning is that it exists in such and such a manner through the succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth. "Saḥ" (he)—refers to the father and others. "Due to the distinction of distance and proximity"—this refers to the characteristics of son, brother's son, and so on, with reference to which [the following] was intended.

"The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest *sapiṇḍa*," and so forth, as recorded in the *Smṛti*. "Having abandoned attachment to the body" means those who do not harbor the conceit of self (*anātma-abhimānin*) with respect to the physical body and other such things—this is the meaning. || 197 ||
Now, one might object: "How could his sense of 'I' regarding the body and so forth even fall away, such that he would have detachment toward them? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, when, as previously described, one whose vision and action have been opened by [divine] power should see thus..."
The word *ittham* means "in the manner that is about to be described."
He says that very thing: "This body, for its part, is constructed from successive prior material causes. (28.198)

The self is devoid of modification because it is eternal, and it is without cause. Regarding the phrase "each preceding one"—this refers to the father, grandfather, and so forth; therefore, [the body] is perishable because it is produced.
Now, one might object: "If the Self is changeless, how can it assume incompleteness even when it is complete, or assume completeness even when it is incomplete? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"However, by virtue of its own sovereignty, this [Self] remains as if concealed. (28.199)
Furthermore, having manifested again, he becomes a vessel for the state of Bhairava.

Now, if his state of being Bhairava were to occur spontaneously by himself, then what would be the use of this system of revelation currently under discussion? Moreover, it would not be logical for causes such as the ripening of impurities (*malaparipāka*) to be required.
Thus it has been said; yet we do not know which of these is the most appropriate means in this case.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, for the manifestation of this [Self], which consists of both enjoyment and liberation, intensely... (28.200).

That which is the appropriate means is this very continuum of knowledge (*jñānasantāna*). He demonstrates its status as the appropriate means [with the following verse]: "By means of a stream of similar cognitions that become increasingly clear in succession. (28.201)
"For that which is to be attained by casting off what is alien is indeed obtained quickly.
Anticipating the objection—"But even if there is such attainment of the goal, what would happen to him?"—he says:
"And thus, [there is the cessation] of the stream of consciousness appropriate to beginningless saṃsāra" (28.202).
Upon its destruction, supramundane gnosis would depend upon another continuum;
and this very thing is what has been called "the transformation of the basis" (āśrayaparāvṛtti) by other outsiders.

And although it has been stated that the causal efficiency belongs to the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*), nevertheless, because that [continuum] is merely a cooperative cause, it is not the primary one;
thus, there must be another primary cause. To this effect, he says:
"Of the noble continuum of such consciousness, which is appropriate for non-transmigration... (28.203)
That primary, original cause is the knowledge of the Guru residing within oneself;
"primary" means having the nature of the material cause—this is the meaning.
He establishes that very point: "Because of the complete projection of its own specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) therein, [it appears] clearly. (28.204)
For that [consciousness] is rightly considered the material cause (*upādāna*), even though there is a difference of bodies;
this is because of its "imparting" (*arpaṇa*) [its own qualities] therein—the sense being that the material cause must indeed be something that persists.
Now, one might object: when there is a difference of bodies, how can it be logical for one thing to impart its own specific qualities to another?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Difference and non-difference belong to the continuity of the body, [not] to the continuity of consciousness. (28.205)
"Not for the sake of suchness," as in the case of a body possessed by a child through the will of a yogin;
"not for the sake of suchness" means that in no instance whatsoever do these two act as the instigators.
And there is no disagreement on this point—thus he says: "The yogi [brings about] his own [power] in the production of life in another body and so forth. (28.206)
Is it not the case that for one who does not abandon the body, there is the state of being the material cause of various cognitions?
"Various cognitions" means those produced by the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth.
He concludes the very subject at hand: "Therefore, because of the primacy of the continuum of consciousness over the biological lineage... (28.207).
The lineage of gurus, one after another, who are firmly established in the knowledge of Śiva—this being the case, these three are the primary and auxiliary causes. (28.208)
"And the entity is both cause and effect"— this is the lineage of the Guru.
"Thus established" means that while the lineage of the Gurus is rightly primary by virtue of being the essential quality of the lineage of disciples.
He analyzes that very point: "In this context, the Guru is said to be the cause, and his wife is the auxiliary. (28.209)
Since this [individual soul], being devoid of power, would have no qualification for sacrifice, and since there is no harm even if an auxiliary cause should occasionally be absent—he says:
"Even without that external [auxiliary], because of the noble power of consciousness residing within. (28.210)
Just as the capacity of a yogin exists even without auxiliary causes, so too would there be brothers born of a single [cause]; whatever that may be, it is similar to that. (28.211)
Furthermore, due to their connection through the lineage, the group of gurus is also spoken of;
however, this primary lineage is always to be worshipped and honored. (28.212)
"Similar to that" means similar to the teacher's brother and so forth—this is the meaning. || 212 ||
Now, with the verse beginning "The attainment of some knowledge...
(192), he carries through the very theme introduced at the outset: the primacy of the occasion-specific day (naimittika-dina).
On the day that the teacher and others are born, on the day of initiation, and even on the day of death—
that very day is indeed the cause for the body and so forth, which serve as the means for higher knowledge.
Thus, one's own birthday is said to be a means for gaining knowledge;
it is the cause of the body, which is the basis for such enjoyments as well as liberation and so forth. (28.214)

The day on which the purificatory rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth were performed for one's own self shall be the primary birthday, because it is the birth of the continuum of knowledge. || 28.215 ||
That which is one's own day of death will become [the occasion] for others; because the deceased has become non-different from Śiva, it then becomes an occasional (naimittika) rite. (28.116)

"His own birth"—that is, [the day] of the disciple and so forth. This is the essential meaning here: whatever constitutes one's own birthday for all people is, first of all, the primary occasional (*naimittika*) occasion. For instance, if this body had not existed, that knowledge would not have existed either. The same applies to the birthday of the Guru.

In the absence of that [initiation], what would be the use of one's own birth-day, even if it were existent? Furthermore, since everything [else] is futile without the purificatory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*), that day too is indeed a primary occasional occasion (*naimittika*). That too [is so] because of the arising of the continuum of higher knowledge (*vijñāna-santati*).
The day of birth is indeed [the first]; the day of departure is likewise so, because here too there is the attainment of identity with Śiva.

However, this is the distinction: that both of those [days] pertain to oneself and others, whereas this [day of departure] pertains only to another. And thus, it is rightly stated that even these three days serve as the cause for the body and other factors which are the means to higher knowledge. || 216 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is called 'death,' in the presence of which even non-difference from Śiva occurs?
Anticipating this doubt, he first undertakes to describe the very nature of death as it arises in the present context:
In this context, as an incidental discussion, we shall clearly explain the nature of death,
following immediately upon the determination of the purposes for which one should worship on the birth, initiation, and death anniversaries of the Guru and others.
The examination of death as indicated by the secondary instruction has also been commenced. He says that very thing:
"Although Śiva is all-pervasive, due to being sealed by the contraction fashioned by His own will... (28.117).
"Under the influence of a flood of various karmic fruits, [the soul] assumes this or that body.

What indeed could be called its 'possession of a body'?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "And the possession of a body consists merely in this: that it enters a body while still in the womb. (28.18)

The first emergence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) belongs to consciousness that has ascended into the void (*śūnya*). And this "embodiment" of consciousness is precisely this: while resting upon the state of the void, its surging outward [results in] that which exists within the womb of the internal space (*udarākāśa*).
Having entered the body,

consciousness— according to the principle that "first, consciousness is transformed into the vital breath"— exists as the very nature of mere vitality, known by the name of the primary pulsation (*ādyaspanda*).
The meaning is: "having resorted to a state of solidification."

An objection may be raised: "How can the body already be present within the womb, such that the initial emergence of the vital breaths could occur as residing within it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Furthermore, its very sovereignty [is exercised] in the construction of the body situated in the womb. (28.219)
The Lord is so called because He is the agent of the body and other [manifestations] while remaining uncontracted.

"Of that very one" means of the very first emergence of vitalization (*prāṇana*). "Uncontracted" means not limited by the divisions of inhalation (*prāṇa*), exhalation (*apāna*), and so forth—this is the meaning. It is solely by virtue of Him that this...
The doctrine of the various teachers is that the Supreme Lord is the creator of the body, the instruments [of perception], the world, and so forth.
Furthermore, having undergone contraction, this [wind] must again be presided over by consciousness due to its insentience; thus he says:
"That wind-nature, within that firm machine of the body, [is presided over] by the conscious self. (28.220)
Driven by this, it moves about like the air from a bellows or a mechanical cow;
therefore, it awakens just as one who has been in deep sleep rises. (28.221)
Gradually, along with the body, the vitalizing power (prāṇanā) becomes stronger;
even there, by the force of the necessity of karma, that vitalizing power remains unimpaired.
One grasps [the breath] due to the predominance of the sensation of emptiness and resonance within the hollow cavities;
thus, in this sequence, the strength of the body and the vital breath becomes thoroughly nourished. (28.223)
He experiences the enjoyments produced by karma, residing in bodies born from a womb or not born from a womb.

"He" refers to the first emergence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Consisting of air" means that he has assumed limitations through the nature of the fivefold winds, such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth. Therefore...
Thus—by reason of the movement of this [embryo], whose nature is air; "it" refers to the body situated within the womb. As it was stated previously:
"That function of the vital breath (prāṇa) makes itself its own by means of the five forms, beginning with prāṇa."
"Because consciousness makes the body full, it shines forth through that [body]. (6.14).

Regarding the phrase "even there"—the meaning is: when [consciousness] possesses such power. The reason for the non-perception of the sense organs is stated as "void," and so forth; "void" refers to those things which consist of the substrata of the sense organs, such as the eyes, and so on.

The meaning is: because one who perceives the hollow channels experiences an abundance of the contact of consciousness, due to the presence of the consciousness-contact of the vital self (prāṇanātman) within the sensory channels in a state of excess—
even here [this is so].
"The cause is by the power of the necessity of karma," with this very intention [it is said]:

"The functions of the general instrument are the five winds, beginning with prāṇa" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 29), and so forth, as stated by others. "He enjoys"—by implication, this is Śiva himself who has assumed contraction.
Nor is this merely our own invention; thus he says:
"And it has been stated by the Moon-crested Lord in the treatise known as the Gahvara. (28.224)
Just as a householder, having completed a house, dwells within it, so too the embodied soul, having fashioned a body, remains devoid of qualities such as action and the like. (28.225)
That which was previously partless (niṣkala) is also called Śabda when it consists of mere slight vibration;
however, when the principles (tattva) such as the senses become manifest, it is called the Sakala Self.
"One should read much from that very source on what was stated in the *Śrīgahvara*," and so forth.
The intention is this: "One should read much from that very source"—however, we have not read it here for fear of excessive length of the book. Thus it is said there:
The entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including all that is mobile and immobile,
has indeed emerged from the principle of Māyā.
Then, bound by merit and demerit, the embryo arises;
from that, the odor produced from semen and blood arises.
From semen come the flesh, then the fat, marrow, and bones of embodied beings;
from blood come the skin, sinews, and flesh—thus this group of six constituents (dhātus) comes to be.
Semen and blood are said to consist of eight elements;
subsequently, endowed with the collection of primary elements, the body of embodied beings comes into being.
Just as a householder, having completed a house, subsequently dwells within it,
so too the embodied soul, having fashioned the body, remains as its sovereign lord.
The Puruṣa is indeed empty in form, inactive, and devoid of qualities;
he is said to be partless, consisting of nothing more than a slight vibration.
The Lord, the imperishable one of tranquil nature, is complete yet endowed with a portion;
likewise are the subtle elements, the gross elements, and the ten sense organs.
The senses, their objects, the mind, the intellect, and likewise the ego—
this entire aggregate is to be known as Śiva, established within the body.
"Among humans, animals, serpents, and aquatic creatures,

that which is called Śiva is indeed all-pervasive and remains established throughout the cycle of existence," and so forth, in great detail. Here, because [Śiva] exists as an inseparable concomitant of death...
He speaks these appropriate words, preceded by the mention of birth: "But when those karmas have been exhausted and the machine of the body has undergone change... (28.227).
The vital mechanism (prāṇayantra) disintegrates, and consequently the body becomes like a wall;
"of those karmas" refers to those that initiate the body; "consequently" means due to the disintegration of the vital mechanism.
He demonstrates that very dissolution:
"In the networks of channels (nāḍīcakra), contraction and expansion occur in reverse. (28.228)

Breaking, drying up, or moistening—through the decrease or increase of wind, phlegm, and the digestive fire; whatever [diseases] there may be of this kind that destroy the prior configuration [of the body]. (28.229)
The wise have described that very process as the "dismantling" (*vighaṭana*) within the machine of the body.

Regarding the phrase "in reverse": the contracted wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) expands, and the expanded one contracts. *Agni* is bile (*pitta*); by means of it, there is either an extreme depletion of even the three bodily constituents (*dhātu*), or...
From its accumulation, there occurs the breaking [of the body] and so forth, by which it undergoes a falling away from its former state.
What need is there for much? Indeed, whatever in this machine of the body destroys its prior configuration is called "dissolution" by the wise—that which is well-known in the world as "death."
And yet, by this much alone, there is no cessation of his transmigratory existence; thus he says:
"When that machine has been dismantled, that consciousness [attains] the nature of vital breath. (28.230)
Whether it be in a body born from a womb or another kind of body variegated by karma, that body then awakens like one who has risen from sleep. (28.231)
For him also, enjoyment, its loss, and death are exactly as before.

Regarding the word "yantra"—it refers to the body, and by the word "or" (vā), it also includes that which is not born from a womb. By the phrase "one should become awakened," his creation is stated. "Enjoyment and its loss" refers to the attainment and non-attainment of that [creation]; and this indeed is his [nature].
Abiding.

And these [acts] of his, such as creation and so forth, being brought about by the power of karma, possess their respective diversities due to dependence on necessity (niyati) and other factors; thus he says:
"Since these—emission, maintenance, and withdrawal—arise from the power of karma... (28.232).

Therefore, [if it were otherwise], grace would follow the diversity of necessity, time, and so forth, and would occur without even depending on karma and the like—thus he says: "But that which is grace occurs when one's own nature is expanding. (28.233)
How can that whose very nature is pure consciousness (jñaptyātman) await karma, necessity (niyati), and so forth?
One might object: "But what is the fault if even grace has karma and the like as its causes? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Since karma, time, necessity, and so forth, have their life in contraction. (28.234)
In this [process] consisting of the removal of contraction, how can there be a cause for grace?
Furthermore, grace is distinguished as being either gradual or intense. (28.235)
And since this has already been explained in detail, what is the use of further repetitions?
As was stated previously:
"In whatever [object] Śiva shines by means of his own nature..."
In that regard, for him who possesses knowledge, the impurity and karma are no longer to be taken into account.
Likewise, if its lack of intrinsic nature were abandoned, how could that which resides in it function as a cause?
Therefore, one must establish its independence from illusion.
"Therefore, the pure, self-luminous Śiva alone is the cause here. (13.116). "Previously" refers to the chapter on the examination of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
One might ask: "What would happen to him through such a favor? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By that [favor], his bonds of contraction are burnt away by initiation and the knowledge of Śiva. (28.236)
"At the end of the body, he is indeed Śiva; thus, there is no remaining in another body.
Now, one might raise the doubt: "If there is no production of another body in this way, is initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself the cause, or is there another cause? Anticipating this, he says:
And those who have entered into reality and follow the command of Śaṅkara. || 28-237 ||
Having died in the abodes of self-manifested beings, sages, celestial seers, humans, and others, they reach that city and are initiated by the lords of the city in due order.
Whether descending into the mortal world or not, they proceed to Śiva, from which there is no rebirth.
Among them, the self-manifested ones (svayambhuvaḥ) are of two kinds; some are solely intent upon bestowing grace.
Some [deities] come for their own ritual duties and occupy only their assigned places;
among those who have been commanded for the sake of bestowing grace, whichever man dies [in their presence], [he attains success]. || 28-240 ||
He clearly attains grace even without an incarnation as a mortal,
provided that while performing his own duty, he does not abandon that state out of fear of destruction.
Just as Gaurī, performing ascetic penance, resides in a cave in Kaśmīra, or likewise, as the all-pervading Lord Narahari is in Dhyānoḍḍāra; (28.242)
Terrifying the Daityas as he leads them toward the Vitastā, he rises up proudly,
like Viṣṇu at Śāligrāma or Śiva for his own devotees.
Likewise, Nara and Nārāyaṇa were performing austerities at Badarī;
such were the gods who remained established in their respective portions of duty.
When propitiated, they swiftly bestow the fruit appropriate to them;
and those who abide in their own allotted portion of duty proceed to the ultimate goal in that abode. (28.245)
Having enjoyed pleasures there in that manner, they descend even among mortals;
having descended among mortals, they become composed of those very [elements] and consist of their respective portions.
Through the sequence of initiation, knowledge, conduct, and so forth, they attain the nature of Śiva;
even the bound souls (paśus), beginning from stationary beings up to animals, who have died within these two [categories], reach that state. || 28-247 ||
Due to the impelling force of the impressions of their own past actions, beings experience diversity in that world.

Furthermore, although the worship of sacred fords and shrines is prescribed here immediately after the rite of the *pavitraka*, it has nevertheless been introduced following the examination of those [shrines] because of its utility at the time of death; thus, there is no contradiction.

There is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Regarding the phrase "intent on bestowing grace": by the command of the Supreme Lord, all eight groups [of deities] descended to the earth from the principles (tattvas) such as Water and the rest, solely for the purpose of bestowing grace—this is the intended meaning. The word "clearly" (sphuṭam) indicates that it was indeed for the sake of bestowing grace.

Because these [deities] have descended; by the words "practicing asceticism" (*tapasyanti*) and so forth, their own activity has been made known. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it is because they do not directly bestow grace upon those mortals who have descended into that state, as they remain intent on that [higher level]. "Those who possess such-and-such portions" (*tattadaṃśakāḥ*).

The meaning is: "the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in this pair": [they have] descended for the sake of bestowing grace and for the sake of their own specific tasks.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, and immobile beings and the like attain *sālokya* (residence in the same world), what then is the status of human beings? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And for men who are mere bound souls (*paśu*), there is *sālokya* due to a lack of discrimination. (28.248)
Regarding the phrase "of those who are merely animals"—the intention is that for others, even union (*sāyujya*) and so forth may occur.
Now, one might ask: "Do these [beings] possess a lack of discernment (*aviveka*), just like stationary objects and the like, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Non-discrimination [arises] from the non-emergence of its specific qualities, and likewise from delusion.

Regarding "from the non-emergence of its specific qualities": this is due to the rājasa nature of human beings. Regarding "from delusion": this is due to the tāmasa nature of stationary beings (plants and the like).
But is it not said elsewhere regarding stationary beings and the like:
"Those whose skins, even when dead, go to union in the abode of Śiva—
even the wood of trees— they too are Rudras, without a doubt"?

Thus it was stated that by such a vision, one would indeed attain the state of Rudra. But here, why is their *sālokya* (residing in the same world) mentioned instead? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Or [they may attain] the state of stationary beings and so forth, or the successive higher states. (28.249)
They do not attain that state of Rudra directly, but rather again through gradual stages.
"Such a state" means the form of immobile beings and so forth. "Successively higher" means by way of attaining the forms of male beings and so on.
Therefore, the scripture also says this:
"In [the lake] crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and filled with various clusters of trees. (28.250)

This has been stated in the Āgamas; therefore, from those very sources, I shall now declare the measurement of the sacred field (kṣetra) as proclaimed in the venerable Sarvajñāna-tantra and others. (28.251)
When a linga has been installed by a teacher, the sacred field extends one hundred cubits;
when it is self-manifested (svayambhū), it is one thousand cubits; and when it was established by a rishi, it is half of that.
When a preceptor who knows the reality installs a liṅga, the fruit is equal to that of a self-manifested (svayambhū) one;
but when a preceptor who does not know the reality installs a liṅga, then [the result is different]. 28-253.
Otherwise, the ritual injunction would become a defect, for it would corrupt both [the ritual and the object].

Now, one might argue: "Since self-manifested [liṅgas] and the like possess the nature of sacred fields (*kṣetra*) and so forth due to the direct presence [of the deity], what fault could there be if those who die in their house were to attain this [result]? But what about those [liṅgas] installed by humans and others?"

To pacify the doubt as to how this could be appropriate for the *liṅgas*, he corroborates it with scripture itself, beginning with the words "In the field" (*kṣetra*) and so forth. Here, the teacher (*ācārya*) is the one who brings about excellence (*utkarṣin*).
He demonstrates precisely this state of not knowing reality: "If there is the thought, 'I am one, the Supreme Self is another, Śiva is yet another'... (28.254).
Since everything is composed of the Self (ātman), one neither releases [the soul] nor is released;
therefore, whatever supreme *liṅga* has been installed by a knower of reality (tattvavid), [that alone is the true object of worship]. 28-255.
One should resort to that very [state] as the locus for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation. And thus the scripture also says this:
"Having known that the time has arrived," so it is stated in the *Śrīratnamālā*. (28.256)
One who seeks liberation should not experience fear; he should cast off his body without hesitation at sacred fords, shrines, or holy places, or else, O beloved, he should bide his time there.
This is the path for those who are not practitioners; a practitioner should bypass it through yoga. Being unable to bypass it, he should go to a sacred field or a sanctuary. (28.258)
Indeed, by resorting to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one undergoes deception;
for it is known:
"If, merely upon bathing, one's heart or feet become parched..."

"Or if smoke should vanish from the head, he does not live for ten days"— by such signs mentioned therein, one should "abandon" [the body] through the sequence beginning with *utkrānti* (the departure of the breath).
One who is unable to perform *utkrānti* and so forth should, however, abandon the body at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) or similar place by means of fasting and other methods, so that—
Furthermore, because he is no longer subject to birth and death, the deception of time (*kālavañcana*) is accomplished—thus he says "at sacred sites" (*tīrtha*), and so forth.

For this very reason, he says: "This is the path for those who are not yogis. Even by one who is unable to abandon the body through fasting and other such means, a sacred field (*kṣetra*) and the like must certainly be resorted to, by virtue of which [the goal] occurs naturally.
"It would be a deception of time upon the departure of the body"—thus he says: "But in deception... The single word *tu* (but) indicates the reason;
and he says that this alone is not what is to be expressed here, but rather something else as well: "And by this, through the yoga of practice upon the principles beginning with Earth... (28.259).
Thus, even for those who have attained supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the utility of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) for liberation has been stated.

For it is established that practitioners of *dhāraṇā* on earth and other elements attain those specific powers through the sequence of such concentration; however, the point is that liberation occurs through the service of the sacred field.
Now, one might ask: "In this way, is the utilization of the field (kṣetra) intended only for the ignorant, or indeed for the wise as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The account regarding the possessor of perfect knowledge will be taught further on. (28.260)
Now, one might object: "In that case, what is the status of those who are neither knowers (*jñānin*) nor bound souls (*paśu*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By virtue of their own fitness, they attain proximity to that Lord. (28.261)

Whosoever has a latent impression (vāsanā) produced in a particular [domain] by the power of their innate capacity, they should be appointed to that very [task], provided they possess higher purity through the Lord of the City. (28.262)
Thus it has been declared in the venerable *Pūrva* [Tantra] and also in the *Śrīmatsvāyambhuva*:
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular place, he is assigned to that very place. (28.263)

"By the power of the perfected mantra," and so forth, has been described elsewhere. "According to one's own suitability"—and not by virtue of suitability to a particular sacred field (*kṣetra*). The connection is that this has also been described elsewhere, in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*.
Furthermore, due to the suitability of the field (*kṣetra*), for those who abide by worldly norms, there may indeed be union (*sāyujya*) with that [deity]—thus he says:
"But those who abide in the knowledge of the respective principles (*tattva*), mantras, conduct (*caryā*), and so forth... (28.264).
"Those wise ones, having died there, attain union with that Rudra.
Now, one might raise this doubt: "Even so, do all of these descend as Rudras without distinction, or not? Anticipating this, he says:
Even for those who have attained union with them, [this occurs] due to their own residual conditioning (saṃskāra).
In such and such a manner, the descent from that portion [of the Lord] may be manifold;
"due to refinement" means due to the form of prior karmic impressions (*vāsanā*).
And likewise, there is also scriptural authority—thus he says:
"In the Siddhāntas and so forth, as well as in the Purāṇas, much is heard in this regard. (28.266)
"Even though they are equal in being incarnations of Rudra, there is diversity in their actions and experiences.
Anticipating the objection—"But how is this consistent if Rudra-hood is of a single uniform nature?"—he says:
"For the body of an entity is inlaid with manifold powers. (28.267)
"This [entity] is not something other than the powers; it cannot exist apart from their collection.
The word *yat* (which) refers to the cause and is displaced in its position; therefore, it should be construed immediately after the word *vapuḥ* (form).
Having raised the objection: "In that case, would the nature of the entity not result as being something distinct from those respective powers?"—[the author replies:]...

He says: "This [consciousness] is not something other than the powers. Anticipating the objection, "If it were something other than those, what would happen?", he says: "It would exist apart from their aggregate.
This refers to that which consists of the confluence of multiple manifestations.
Our established doctrine is that no form whatsoever can be maintained without being merged with its own manifestation.
Now, one might ask: "What would follow from this in the present context? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, from that [source] known as the aggregate of powers (śaktisamūha), by means of a certain portion beginning with Rudra... (28.268)
That appropriate task will be accomplished; that very portion clearly descends.

Therefore, from Rudra—who appears as a multitude of various manifestations—that specific manifestation-portion from which the respective effect is accomplished in accordance with prior karma, that alone [is the cause].
The aspect of manifestation clearly descends— meaning that one should directly assume the very form of those respective Rudras.
Right here, in order to show another variety [of practice] arising from the difference in qualified practitioners, he says:
"And those who have received initiation at a lower level, yet have not abandoned their devotion to it, [are initiated] by others. (28.269)
Those who have died while established in reality (tattva) attain excellence even in a lower state, like wood;
however, those who have abandoned that excellence partake in what lies beyond it.

Even those who have received initiation into the higher principles (ūrdhvatattva), though they may not yet possess discernment (viveka) and have only reached the lower limits, are still fortunate recipients of the fruits of that initiation.
For you have not abandoned your attachment even to that initiation prescribed by the scriptures;
without discrimination, you have resorted to such attachment based on worldly renown. (28.272)

And those who, being merely worldly-minded, have achieved union with the lower levels such as the *aptattva* and are devoted solely to them, while others— having descended into the respective *tattvas* such as the *tejaḥ-tattva* which are higher than those—
die without even performing the *sandhāna* (reintegration) into any one of the places among the eight extremely secret [levels] and so forth; they [are as follows].
In that regard, even those in a lower state partake in excellence;

the meaning is that they become enjoyers of experience by virtue of their distinction from other practitioners who have died while remaining in that state. Furthermore, there are those who have received initiation precisely within the element of water (aptattva) and so forth.

In that regard, even those who have thus failed to show due respect, having died in this manner, become enjoyers (*bhogin*) precisely within the principle of fire (*tejastattva*) and the others above; they attain that very state—this is the meaning. Furthermore, even those who have received initiation in the higher levels, such as the principle of fire and so forth, [may fall] due to delusion into the principle of water and so forth belonging to Svayambhū, who has descended [to those levels].
Even those who have met their death while situated in a lower, related station fully enjoy the fruit of that very initiation; for,
having placed their trust even in such an initiation,
they followed the crowd out of mere worldly renown and took refuge in a lower abode and so forth.
For they do not possess such scriptural discernment as would lead them to follow only the location appropriate for initiation. ||272||
Anticipating the question, "What is concluded by this much? he says:

"The Supreme Lord has declared that for a mere animal [devotee] there is *sālokya* (residence in the same world); for one who is initiated, *sāmīpya* (proximity); but for one intent upon That, *sāyujya* (union). (28.273)

"Of one who has been initiated"—meaning, by initiation into the worldly dharma. "Devoted to that"—meaning, even though he has been so initiated, [this applies] to one who dies in such places and so forth.

For one who has been initiated into higher and higher Siddhāntas and the like, yet lacks conviction therein and resorts instead to external holy places (tīrtha) and so forth, everything becomes utterly useless— thus he says:
"But he who has gone to the higher scriptures and there abandoned his conviction due to doubt..."
One who goes to a place of worship does not obtain any fruit at all. || 28-274 ||

And regarding that subject, it has been stated at length by the God of gods that for such a person, initiation, knowledge, and likewise pilgrimage to sacred sites are all in vain, and so forth. (28.275)
As it has been said:
"The initiate who, having performed the rites such as the worship of the Guru according to the Śiva-siddhānta,
finally departs for a sacred ford (tīrtha), a temple, or the like— "
"In vain is his initiation, in vain is his knowledge, and likewise his propitiation of mantras;
all that has been abandoned by him who desires only the fruit of visiting sacred fords. (275)
But he who, though currently unfit, remains thus in the abode of Śiva, shall later enjoy the fruit to that same extent through the binding force of his established conviction.
"Until he is unfit" means for as long as he lives; "afterwards" means at the very moment of death; "until then" means until it is complete. || 276 ||

One might object: "Why was it stated that this occurs only for those who die in places such as Svayambhū, when elsewhere it is declared that even places like Antarvedī are sites of death? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That merit which consists primarily of rivers, mountains, and lakes does not [lead to the highest state] upon death;
however, for those who die there, it is excellent, as they enjoy the pleasures of heaven. (28.277)
Furthermore, those who have attained discernment regarding consciousness at the time of death, yet still rely on a basis in the lower realms, remain hidden here. (28.278)
Anticipating the doubt, "Is there any atonement for these [transgressions], or not?", he says:

"The sin that may indeed belong to them, as described in the context of the defilement of that knowledge, shall be destroyed by the sequence beginning with initiation (dīkṣā) by the Lord of that respective city; such is the established rule. (28.279)
But those who, with their minds, revile the knowledge of the seats of initiation (dīkṣāyatana), and practice [actions] contrary to it here—all of them go to hell. (28.280)
Now, one might object: "If these are seen practicing [the path] directly, how can their specific distinction from others be known? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The loss of commitment toward the locus of knowledge, initiation, and so forth..."
They are to be known by their activities and utterances, and those too are of two kinds.

In this context, there are two kinds of activities and utterances: those belonging to the side of saṃsāra and those belonging to the side of liberation. Among these, their engagement occurs sometimes in accordance with [prior] mental synthesis, sometimes not in accordance with it, and sometimes without any mental synthesis. Of these, the first—

The first path is indeed clear, because activities and so forth occur in accordance with the underlying intention (*anusandhāna*). The second, however, is perverted, since activities and so forth are observed to be the reverse of that intention. But the third is not of this kind—thus he says:

Those [sensations] which never again arise even when one is in a state of health, but arise only from an imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātu) during ill-health, consist merely in the experience thereof. (28.282)

Those [impressions] which are of two kinds— pertaining to saṃsāra and pertaining to liberation— are set aside by activity and are never aroused during a state of equilibrium; for example, those pertaining to saṃsāra in the case of the knower,
and those pertaining to liberation in the case of the ignorant person, during a state of disequilibrium.
Furthermore, those [experiences] that arise by the force of the humors (dhātu-doṣa) are merely the enjoyment of those [past actions];

at that time, for these [beings], there is only such an experience brought about by the power of prior karma, but there is nothing therein that performs a new good or evil action—this is the meaning. || 282 ||

Now, one might object: how can it be said that this is merely a matter of experience (*bhoga-mātra*)? For even in the case of a knower (*jñānin*), since the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of transmigratory existence occasionally manifest within, he would appear to be ignorant; and likewise, even in the case of an ignorant person, because the impressions appropriate to a knower arise, he would appear to be a knower.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"And due to the defects of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of transmigratory existence are awakened;
yet even when they enter through the openings, they do not take root, being mostly burnt away by knowledge. (28.283)

However, those latent impressions (saṃskāras) conducive to isolation (kaivalya), which are always unmanifest during states of well-being, become manifest during states of ill-being through the descent of grace (śaktipāta). (28–284)
"Mostly"—the intention is that their knowledge is indeed powerful. "Unawakened"—this means, by implication, those who are ignorant. || 284 ||

One might object: "Even though there is no difference in their physical health, why is it that these latent impressions (saṃskāras) are awakened by a disorder of the bodily humors (dhātudoṣa) for the knowers (jñānins), whereas for others they are awakened by the descent of grace (śaktipāta)? From where does this distinction arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because those belonging to saṃsāra are refined by the impressions of intense past habituation"—thus spoke the Lord of Serpents, according to the aphorism: "In their lapses... (YS 1.30).

However, those cognitive states conducive to absolute liberation (kaivalya) are never practiced due to the persistence of worldly existence; therefore, these [states] arise through the descent of power (śaktipāta).
And he says, "Thus," etc., to show that this is not our own invention alone. Regarding the phrase "in those gaps," it refers to the *sūtra*:
"In those gaps, other cognitions [arise] from latent impressions" (YS 4.27).
This is the meaning; for [this concerns] the activities and so forth of those involved in worldly existence.
There must exist a cause consisting of intense practice from a previous birth by virtue of which these [states] arise;
however, for others among transmigrating beings, there is no such practice, yet their occasional arising is observed.
Therefore, there must be some cause in this case, and it is logical to state that this is indeed the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Thus, these [states] are described.
The formative impressions [arise] from the descent of power. || 285–286 ||
Now, one might object: "In that case, do not even these latent impressions (saṃskāras) of the Knower arise solely from the descent of power (śaktipāta) that causes their concealment?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By those [impressions] which are obstructed by [current] activities and provoked by the imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātudoṣa)..."
By those who have not attained certainty or reflection, and who are like those who are asleep or intoxicated. || 28.287 ||

Even by those who are perverted, who revile knowledge, initiation, the guru, and so forth, concealment (tirobhāva) is not to be understood [as occurring], because of the absence of firm rooting in the heart. (28.288)

"By those who have not attained certainty or deliberation"—this is because [the meaning] is otherwise established. "Due to the absence of conventional usage"—the sense is that for this [word], there is a much firmer habitual application elsewhere. ||288||
And for this reason, he possesses other worldly impressions (*saṃskāra*) as well; thus it is said:

"Therefore, even though awakened, one who dwells in a body may experience perceptions such as those of the servants of Yama or serpents, which arise from karma and take the form of objective enjoyments. (28.289)
If one asks, "In that case, what is the nature of his liberation?", [the author], having raised this doubt, says:

"He is not unliberated merely by this much; for death is an experience just like birth, and like [the state of] abiding, therefore death is twofold, consisting of both suffering and pleasure. (28–290)
Therefore, just as the various experiences of pleasure and pain do not strike at the state of liberation while one is awake, so too they do not strike it even at the time of death.
"From this"—because death, like birth and so forth, consists essentially in a particular experience (bhoga). || 291 ||
Furthermore, for yogins, there is even greater excellence at the time of death than for those possessing mere knowledge—thus he says:

"But as for those who are yogins, in whichever reality (tattva) they have well-cultivated their minds, they place their consciousness right there and, free from doubt, attain that very reality. (28–292)
"They cause [the mind] to settle" means for the purpose of the departure [of the breath] and so forth; "unafraid" means due to the absence of the suffering of death and the like. || 292 ||
And thus the scripture also says this; so he says:
"In the Śrī Svacchanda, it is declared that those who have died [by means of] the concentration on scent (gandhadhāraṇā)...
and so forth, as well as the fruit of the concentrations in the Mālinīśāstra. (28–293)
As it has been said:
"Having abandoned their vital breaths in the subtle element of smell through dhāraṇā, those yogins attain a form such as that of the earth, the supreme body of the Earth. (10.788)
Thus:
"Having indeed performed the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) correctly upon the subtle element of taste alone, they have reached the supreme source of the waters... (10.799).
And so it is said; however, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, this has been explained in detail from the twelfth chapter onwards, and thus it should be understood from that very source. || 293 ||
Now, one might object: "If death is inevitable for yogins, then they must also experience its enjoyment consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
why then was this said? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But for those who [have cast off] the body, there is no experience known as death."
By means of dhāraṇās, they quickly abandon [the body], like entering another's body. || 28-294 ||
Now, one might object: "How small indeed is that experience called death which they do not possess? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"For the experience of death consists in this: a delusion residing in the senses that cuts the vital points (marmans), and a turbidity of darkness in the mind; and that does not exist in these [beings]. (28–295)
"That" refers to [the piercing of] the vital points (*marmaccheda*) and so forth. ||295||
He establishes that very point: "For indeed, one maintains mental effort through the ascent of the 'I'-sense into another body until the movement of the intellect occurs. (28-96)
The wheel of vital breath (prāṇacakra), though dependent on that [central channel], moves along its path;
therefore, by means of that very [path], one should awaken the wheel of the senses (akṣacakraka) in another's body.

For if indeed there were pain in the vital organs, delusion in the senses, and a state of darkness in the mind of the yogi while abandoning his own body, then how could he have performed such acts as entering another's body, which are accomplished through mental effort? [Such acts] depend entirely upon the exertion of the mind.
For indeed, there is a movement of the intellect, vital breath, and so forth into the body of another by the yogi, by means of which the sprouting of the sense of "I" occurs therein. ||297||
Now, one might ask: "Why is it that the wheel of the senses, beginning with the vital breaths, follows the mind alone?
He pacifies this doubt by means of an illustration:
"Just as flies rise up after the king of the flies has risen."
And likewise, all the functions of the senses enter into the mind as it remains [in that state]. || 28-298 ||

Thus, even upon the departure from the body, for yogins there is no cessation of the senses in the intermediate state as there is for others; so he says: "Therefore, in his movement into another body and so forth, there is no merging [of the senses]."
Subtle and situated in the midst of the senses, this [self] is again like the body.

Regarding the word "ataḥ" (therefore): it is because of the absence of the experience of death. Now, one might object: "In this very body, a merging of the senses could occur merely by a severe blow to a vital organ; how then can there be such a merging through the abandonment of that [body]? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "This may be subtle, like this body again."
He concludes this very point by means of an illustration:
"In this way, for yogins who move within the bodies of various *tattvas*, just as for those who move within the bodies of others, there is no state of delusion. (28–300)
And they too should be known as being of two kinds: worldly and likewise initiated.
The former are Śivas in due order; the latter [are so] merely through the experience of that [worldly state]. (28–301)
Initiation (dīkṣā) as well, by virtue of its application to various distinctions of upper and lower levels,
becomes manifold for yogins and yields diverse fruits.
"Those" refers to the yogins; "worldly ones" refers to those established in the systems of Patañjali and others. || 302 ||
Having thus described the account of the death of the yogin, he speaks also of the man of knowledge (jñānin):

"But those who possess realized knowledge (vijñānin) are here of two kinds, according to whether they are trembling or otherwise. Among them, those whose realization is trembling clearly become Śivas at the end of the body. (28–303)
He establishes this very point:
"Because the cognition that has arisen regarding these [objects] is not perfectly clear, nor is its nature completely uprooted through the association with other conceptual constructions. (28–304)
Therefore, the conceptual construction arising from negligence regarding the body will necessarily perish upon the fall of the body; and that supreme knowledge is also realized.
And it is not "very clear" because it is obscured by conceptualization arising from the strength of the body. "By another conceptualization" means by a contradictory one. || 305 ||
Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be the cessation of conceptual construction upon the fall of the body, but what is the cause for the arising of manifest knowledge?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That which remains established within as a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), having been rendered non-existent by [the power of] creative imagination (*kalpanā*)."
For when its ripening has reached the point of being experienced in an unfortunate rebirth, that karma indeed shines forth.
But those whose consciousness is always thoroughly cultivated as consisting of Śiva, they are indeed liberated while living; for them, there is no further deliberation whatsoever regarding death.
"Reached its full maturity" means having ascended to the supreme limit.
"Of the concealer" refers to the body, which acts as a coverer. || 307 ||

Now, one might object: "Is there no inquiry regarding the death of the knowers [of reality], since even they, at that time, are just like common folk—possessed of bodies and so forth—or are they not? Anticipating this doubt, he speaks by means of an illustration:
"For just as there is no inquiry concerning the state of those liberated while living,"
In states of pleasure, pain, or delusion, as well as even at the time of death, that [consciousness] does not exist in such a manner.
And thus it is stated in scripture:
"The Supreme Lord spoke this in the Śrīratnamālāśāstra, and the Lord of Serpents, the bearer of the burden of the support of the universe, spoke it in his own scripture as well. (28–309)
"In one's own treatise" means in the *Ādhārakārikās*. || 309 ||
He recites that very [teaching] in sequence:

"Whether in the middle of a street, amidst urine and excrement, in the house of an outcaste, in hell, or in a cremation ground—the man of knowledge, whether possessed of thought or free from thought, attains liberation even at the end. (28)
"In hell" means in a degraded place; such is the meaning. || 310 ||
He explains this very point in brief:

"Moreover," [the text] says, "the resonance (dhvani) proclaims his state of liberation while living; the statement regarding being both with thought and without thought indicates the extent of his possible condition. (28–311)
It is not only at the end that the man of knowledge attains liberation; rather, he does so even while living—this is the meaning.
"To this extent" means as long as he is free from attachment. || 311 ||
Regarding the other case as well, he first states the intended meaning:
"Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, even one who has lost consciousness may cast off the body;
liberated simultaneously with the arising of knowledge, his sorrow destroyed, he attains absolute isolation (kaivalya). (28.312)
And this [bond] is said to be of infinite duration; it is indeed called a bond. One might suspect that its good and evil deeds belong to it, yet they do not belong to it. (28–313)
The intended meaning here is that for the knower (*jñānin*), since there is no karma that binds, there is no distinction whatsoever in dying at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or elsewhere. (312–313)
He explains that very point word by word:
"By the word 'api' (even/also), it is indeed possible [that death occurs] through unimpaired memory;
however, death belongs only to one whose memory is lost—let that [memory] exist prior to death, for what is the use of it then? (28–314).
The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), as it is indeed possible that this [liberation] might occur;
and that [suffix], expressing time, declares that death is not the cause of liberation. (28–315)
In this context, death occurs only for one whose mindfulness has perished;

thus, even if mindfulness were possible prior to death, it would serve no purpose. By the use of the word "api" (even), the meaning is that if mindfulness has not perished, the very possibility [of its utility] is virtually fruitless. The term "liṅgi" means "one should abandon."

"This much is possible"—for the knower (jñānin), whether his memory has been lost or not, may abandon the body anywhere. Regarding the statement "death is not the cause of liberation": the intention is that he is liberated by the very attainment of knowledge; what need has he for [the state of] recollection? (314–315)
Now, one might object: "If he is liberated at the very same moment as [the arising of] knowledge, why was it said that he 'goes to isolation' (kaivalya)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And even that body which was the basis for the doubt regarding isolation..."
By destroying even this [notion of difference] through its very nature as a bestower of division, he attains freedom from sorrow.

"A point of doubt" means: at the very moment of realization, [the question arises] whether this person is liberated or not. For this very reason, it is said that he is "one whose grief is destroyed" and "free from doubt. ||316||
Now, what is this ground for suspicion? For nothing such as the body and so forth constitutes a bond for the knower;
as it has been said:
"Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, dharma and the rest cease to be causes [for bondage]."
"By the force of residual impressions (saṃskāra), he remains holding the body like the whirling of a potter's wheel" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 67)?— having raised this doubt, [the author] says:
"Just as his connection with another body and so forth is not a cause of differentiation..."
Likewise, although the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) still possesses a connection with his own body, [he remains free].
Therefore, there is no distinction for this one who has transcended all forms, whether he is within a body non-different from Śiva or even in the absence of such a body. (28–318)

Nevertheless, because there remains the possibility of doubt regarding the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous distinctions, "isolation" (*kevalatva*) has now been described; or rather, it is so called by virtue of its reliance on another factor (*mātrāntara*). (28–319)
They do not perceive him as distinct; therefore, he is said to be liberated by them.

For here, for the knower, the connection with his own body—just like the connection with another’s body—is not a cause of bondage, because for one who is non-different from Śiva, whether the body exists or does not exist, there is the state of being the form of the universe or being formless.
Although there is no distinction [between the two states], nevertheless, as long as the body exists, even the suspicion of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of duality may arise;

therefore, it is said that he attains absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) immediately upon the fall of the body. Alternatively, even while living, because his body has become liberated, for other subjects (*pramātṛ*), at that time—
"But now, knowledge is indeed knowledge. And thus, scripture also speaks in this way; so he says:
"It is also stated in the venerable *Traiśirasa*: [in that state] devoid of the casing of sun and moon... (320).

In that state where the sense of revulsion has collapsed, which stands firm as a pillar in every respect, which is free from all calamities, and which transcends the means of valid cognition and their objects; || 28-321 ||
Dissolved within that state of awakening, the agent of action is likewise untainted;
it is like the primary matter, the pot, or space—the Self remains as the sky even when the pot has perished. (28–322)
In that very same way, he does not perish; the knower becomes identical with Śiva, established as autonomous, and may expand into all things. (28–323)
Its state is neither existence nor non-existence, neither configuration nor conceptual construction.
The meaning is that the "primary" (prādhānika) body is that which is commenced by the primary cause (pradhāna) through the relationship of cause and effect;
thus, there is an equality between the body and a jar, and between the self and space. Just as when a jar is destroyed...

The space delimited by that [body] does not perish; likewise, even when the body has perished, the Self remains, but rather consists solely of its own undelimited essential nature. Thus, although it performs various specific actions, it is manifested therein as the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*). Therefore...

Thus, because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), it transcends the categories of means and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇapratyaya*) and is therefore not an object of cognition; for this very reason, it is devoid of the pair of sun and moon and is not delimited by the dyad of means and objects of knowledge. Consequently, it exists in the state where both the loathsome (*jugupsā*)—that is, a loathsome object—and the non-loathsome (*ajugupsya*), which is the absence of such an object, have been shattered.

Free from the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted, you alone shine as the support of the universe, standing in the center like a pillar of gold, having simultaneously cast all powers— perception and the rest— outward toward their respective objects of knowledge.
By such statements as these, [the Self] stands everywhere like a pillar; for this very reason,

because it cannot be conceptualized as existent, non-existent, and so forth, and because it cannot tolerate contact with words, it is free from impurity (*anañjana*)— having dissolved into another consciousness within the non-conceptual Self— and is thus its own essential nature, a single mass of pure, unconditioned consciousness.

This is the meaning. Therefore, the knower who has thus realized the truth, established in his own sovereignty, may extend himself into all things and abide everywhere through the very state of oneness with them; for this is not [otherwise] for him.
The meaning is that there exists some real conceptual construction characterized by birth, death, and so forth.
Other scriptures as well are thus—so he says: "Having taken this very point into account, the Guru spoke [it] in the Gītās. (28.324)
He says that very thing:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state. (Bhagavad Gītā 8.6)
Therefore, at all times, remember Me and fight.
Desiring to explain that very point, he first summarizes the meaning of the Gītā in order to establish the introductory framework (pīṭhikābandha), stating "When... and so forth.
But when one has dissolved into the increased state of *sattva*, then one goes upward.
In due order, one who is dissolved in rajas or tamas enters a womb of action or a state of delusion;

for when, through the lifelong practice of someone, whichever among sattva, rajas, or tamas becomes predominant at the time of dissolution, then, by the very fitness of that [state], it occurs for him.
The meaning of the statement is that there would be a transition into forms such as human or stationary beings— as it has been sung:
"When the embodied soul meets its dissolution while goodness (sattva) is predominant,
then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest."
"Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action;
likewise, dissolved in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded. (Bhagavad Gītā 14.15).

Now, one might object: even if beings possess the nature of *sattva* and the other qualities at the time of death, they must all necessarily be in a state of delusion due to the helplessness caused by labored breathing, hiccupping, stammering, and so forth; and if that is the case, how can their transition to another body—characterized by an upward movement and the like—be logically consistent?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that state, there is delusion of the senses and being overwhelmed by the exhaustion of labored breathing. (28.327)
This experience of death is not the actual casting off of the body.

Here, that which is called the delusion of the senses and so forth while the body still exists is designated by the term "casting off the body" through a figurative usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*); it is the experience of death, but not the literal abandonment of the body itself.
Because even at that time, it remains in a state of manifest clarity.

Now, one might ask: "If this is so, when will there be the direct abandonment of the body? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But that which is the single, final moment consisting of the vital breath... (28-328).

That momentary fraction of time at which this body becomes like wood or a wall immediately after [the realization of truth] is the "digit" (kalā) of the time of abandoning the body, characterized by separation from the body. (28.329)
For that very reason, she is indeed devoid of the pleasure, pain, and so forth belonging to that body;
yet, due to the awakening of prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), she remembers whatever [she experienced] therein.

Due to causes such as the abundance of unseen impressions (*adṛṣṭa*), repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and so forth, that very same form attains the states of being happy, miserable, or deluded. (28–331)
Furthermore, this very moment is singular; because no other subsequent moment arises immediately after it, it is without companion.

For this very reason it is the final one, and for this same reason, because the division of inhalation, exhalation, and so forth has been severed, it is a moment whose nature consists of a contracted consciousness characterized by the act of breathing.

When, immediately thereafter, the body is observed to be on the same footing as other objects of measurement such as wood or clods of earth, that [moment]— which is directly denoted by the term "abandoning the body" and perceptible to all people— is also a fraction of time.
The *kalā* is of the nature of a partial aspect (*aṃśarūpā*); because of the loosening of the bond that provides its firmness, it becomes separated from the body.
For this very reason, it is devoid of the pleasure and other experiences bound up with that [body], and consists solely of contracted consciousness—this is the meaning.
And precisely in that final momentary state, due to the force of causes such as the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth...

The meaning is this: before the awakening of past latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), whatever [entity] characterized primarily by *sattva* or other qualities is remembered as being attached to another body, that very thing becomes his form, supported by the first consciousness. || 331 ||
Having thus described this as the domain of the ignorant, he further describes it according to the distinction between knowledge that is well-practiced and knowledge that is not:
"Or else it is devoid of pleasure, pain, and so forth; or else it is of the nature of bliss."
"Free from pleasure, pain, and so forth" means that its nature is consciousness transcending the universe.
"Consisting of bliss" means that it is of the essence of the full Supreme Brahman. As it has been said: "Where there is neither pain nor pleasure, neither the object of perception nor the perceiver."
"And even the state of delusion does not exist; that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality. (Sampuṭa-tantra-kalpa 1.5). "Bliss is the nature of Brahman."
And thus it is said.
One might object: "Why should this [object] attain such a form through mere recollection alone?
Anticipating this doubt, he provides the following response with the words beginning with "tadeva" (that very thing):
"Why? Because that very [object] is what he remembers within consciousness. (28-332)

For here, in the final moment, due to the abundance of practice and other factors, there must necessarily occur the awakening of that very latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by means of which one is to become [the object] hereafter; through its power, there arises the recollection of that [object],
and by means of that recollection...
The attainment of that state. || 332 ||
Now, since consciousness (*saṃvit*), whose nature is eternally undiminished, cannot possibly be dissolved,
its state of being "the body" consists simply in its being the substrate (*adhiṣṭheya*) [of objects]; and since that status is no different for blue, yellow, and so forth,
how can it be consistent to speak of the dissolution of the body alone, by which [you would establish this]?

Might there not also be a consideration of memory and so forth? Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which shines forth more prominently at first is the body, because it is presided over by consciousness. This means that here, prior even to [the perception of] blue and other objects, [the body appears] by virtue of being presided over by consciousness.

The meaning is this: although it does not function as anything additional [to the Self], this body—which, while resting in the state of the subject (pramātṛ), is designated by that term—manifests with an appearance of excess, like a reflection in a mirror.
Now, one might ask: "What is the significance of 'dissolution' (pralīnatā) in this context? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That which was previously the locus [of consciousness], by virtue of its functioning through identity with the intellect (citi). || 28-333 ||
That very state is here called "dissolution" (līnatā) with respect to the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

For that which was previously the presiding ground (adhiṣṭhāna) by consciousness is precisely what is here called dissolution with reference to sattva and the others; what indeed is inconsistent about this?—this is the meaning. Now, [an objection]: here...
The entire collection of objective phenomena (bhāvajāta) attains existence only by virtue of being presided over by Consciousness; otherwise, nothing at all could be perceived.

Therefore, if dissolution means simply being presided over by Consciousness, what difference is there between life and death?—anticipating this doubt, it is said: "by way of functioning as identity" (tādātmyavṛttitaḥ).

The essential meaning is this: although the body and so forth exist in a state of identity with consciousness (*saṃvit*), it is precisely through its sovereignty that their manifestation as something other than the self—predominantly as if they were not the self—is "life"; otherwise, when they are designated by terms such as "dissolved," it is "death."

Now, one might object: "Let this be; but what is the basis for the claim that the body is the primary substratum for consciousness prior to [the perception of] blue and other such objects? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because, in the case of objects of knowledge such as blue, yellow, and so forth, the body is first conceptualized... (28-334)
"Consciousness, having itself presided [over the body], fully effects that very presiding.
For this very reason, even though there is no difference in the fact that both are objects of consciousness's presiding, the body possesses a distinction from [objects] such as blue"— thus he says:
Therefore, even though the body is merely that which is presided over, it is distinct from a wall. || 28-335 ||
The body possesses a specific distinction, namely that it is the first among all things to be presided over [by consciousness].

Now, one might object: "Even so, since there is no difference in their being objects of consciousness, why is it not stated that blue and other such objects have also dissolved? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The occurrence of identity in other things is not perceived there, even though it exists.
However, because the body is eternal and non-deviating [from its nature],

that [consciousness] belongs to the body; therefore, although other objects of cognition such as blue and so forth may exist within consciousness— which is by nature the cognizer— [they do not constitute its essence] due to reasons such as the body's prior state of being the locus of superintendence (*adhiṣṭheya*).

The occurrence of identity is not perceived in those [objects], because they are apprehended as "this" (idantayā). On the other hand, although the body is an object of cognition, that [identity] is at all times non-deviating, because it is compatible with the apprehension of "I-ness" (ahantā), owing to the non-falling away from the nature of the subject.
Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for such a state here?", he says:
"And that [state] belongs to that very body through its previous death and subsequent birth. (28-337)
"By memory"—that is, by the variety of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by previous experiences;

"as such"—meaning, through the function of identification (*tādātmyavṛtti*). For it is in that state that, at the final moment of departure from the previous body, there arises for that [Self] whose nature is eternal and non-deviating consciousness, [an experience] originating from the impressions deposited by prior experiences.

The cause is the remembrance of the body itself; for whatever object one has constantly cultivated within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), that very thing one remembers at the time of death, and one attains its very state. Therefore:
"...for he remembers that very [state] within consciousness," as was stated immediately thereafter in verse 332.
For this very reason, our own teachers have also spoken most appropriately; thus he says: "By this reasoning, that which was [stated] by Kallaṭa, the teacher of our lineage... (28–338).

It has been stated that the cause for the firmness of what is called "vital breath" (prāṇa) despite the lack of distinction between bodies is that [firmness] itself; otherwise, what would be the reason for the firmness of the vital breath in one case and not in another? (28–339)
Even though there is no difference in the state of being a body, this question does not cease:
namely, that which was stated by the venerable Kallaṭapāda, "The grasping of all bodies [occurs] through the body, blue, and so forth."

By such statements as these, although there is no distinction in the fact that both are bodies, it is the physical body (*deha*) alone that is the basis for being [an object of perception] in that way; furthermore,
