by the statement beginning with "the firmness of the cause known as *prāṇa*," the firmness of *prāṇa* is stated to be the cause, which [is now addressed] by this immediately following statement.

This is logical by virtue of the reasoning set forth in the aphorism beginning with "Consciousness first transforms into the vital breath," which is characterized by [consciousness] being the prior substrate of everything that is to be presided over;
for otherwise, even though there is no distinction [between them], what would be the reason for the firmness of the vital breath in one specific case? This [objection] is difficult to resolve.
Such would be the question.
Now, one might object: "Granted that there is recollection at the final moment, but how is it known that this [recollection] is the cause of a future body? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Recalling"—the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) indicates the cause; thus, one attains that form. (28.340)

Now, one might object: "If only that which is remembered is attained, then even the memory of blue or other objects occurring at that very moment would be the basis for such attainment. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Since the body is remembered first, it is first illumined by the consciousness presiding over it."

He attains that very form previously called "the body," which at the final moment is the body itself as it was formerly presided over by consciousness prior to [the perception of] blue and other objects; therefore, while manifesting, it is remembered— it comes to become an object of memory— this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "What is the proof for the existence of such a recollection at that time? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, that final recollection which occurs among subjects who are not omniscient... (28-341)
Since the determination of another body is never within its range,
therefore, that recollection which— by persisting through the state of separation from the body— is not attached to another body,
does not fall within the range of non-omniscient cognizers when it is joined with the connection to a body.

The meaning is: since instruction is futile for those of limited vision, how could others understand that? Now, one might object: "Is this statement not contrary to experience, given that even at the final moment, the memory of relatives and the like, or of drinking cool water and so forth, is indeed observed?"
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But as for that clear recollection of kinsmen, beloved ones, sons, drink, and so forth... (28.342).
It is not connected with another body, nor is it its final [moment], since it would otherwise be so;
the sense is that it is not final, but rather this experience of death occurs at the penultimate moment.
But surely, just as memory, so too experience would serve as a cause for attachment to a future other body;
for instance, a certain sage [reared] a fawn of the hermitage that had lost its mother, bringing it up as if it were his own son.
The knowers of ancient lore say that, seeing his life departed by the strike of a Śabara’s arrow,

he was released from his vital breaths while mourning him with great sorrow and thus attained the state of a female deer; having raised the doubt— "How can such a state be said to result from mere remembrance?"— [the author proceeds].
He said:
"But for someone, whichever latent impression (vāsanā) awakens at the end of the body..."
When there is a living body, a clear experience arises due to its suitability, as described in the Purāṇa regarding the thirst for a fawn. (28.344)

A certain sage, having been perfumed by his past impressions, assumed the state of a doe; for whatever latent impression has been cultivated through many births will awaken at the end of that body for anyone whatsoever.
It will awaken in the form of memory as the cause for attachment to another body;
accordingly, even while this [present] body exists, there would be a clear experience [of that future state],
with which very intention [the author] refers in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts to one who is "perfumed" by the thirst for a fawn.
The narrative concerning how a certain sage attained the state of a female deer.
He clarifies this very point:
"In that case, that experience is not the cause for the production of another birth. (28.345)
The cause of this [experience] is that latent impression (*vāsanā*), occurring by chance like the "crow and the palm fruit" maxim;
"of this" refers to another birth, and "this impression" refers to that which is about to awaken at the end of the body; "it" refers to the experience.
Now, if the recollection of being a deer is indeed the cause for attachment to that body,

then— since recollection must necessarily be preceded by experience— an experience itself must be stated as the cause for the production of another birth; for if there were no restriction regarding the object established by experience, anything at all might be recollected, yet there is a definite rule.
From where [does this arise]?—thus he raises an objection:
"But why does he remember that very thing? To which he replies: "Because it is always [present]. (28-346)
In order to show that even without direct experience, there is a restriction of the object of memory by way of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he says:
"Because he is permeated by that state, he remembers that alone sufficiently.
This means: since he is always permeated by that state, therefore he remembers that alone, and that is sufficient.
The Blessed One said; that is to say, he spoke.
One might object: "Would not the cultivation of that state (*tadbhāvabhāvana*) also be designated as experience (*anubhava*) itself? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The thought 'I am thus' and 'I shall be thus'—this is called that state. (28.347)
One might object: "How can there be such a rule that a latent impression (vāsanā) must pertain only to a future object?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is the becoming of what is yet to be that is projected, never that of what already exists."
"Not of what exists"—the sense is that for that which has already come into being, there can only be experiencing (*anubhavana*), not cultivation (*bhāvana*).
He clarifies that very point:
"The process of making [the object] manifest through successive stages is proclaimed as 'bhāvanā' (creative contemplation). (28.348)
And the experience of that which is already manifest is not "cultivation" (bhāvanā); this is clear.
Now, for those who—due to profound delusion—have no opportunity for cultivation even for a moment, how could there be a connection with another body in the absence of a final recollection?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of a child born on that very day, or of a beast, an insect, or a tree... (28–349).

Even though there was delusion at that time, the previous cultivation indeed became manifest; through the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it arose at the end of that deluded body. (28.350)
By means of memory, it yields the fruit of the diversity of that body;

for even though infants born on that very day and others are then in a state of ignorance, a clear mental cultivation (bhāvanā) must certainly have occurred due to constant practice in a previous birth; therefore, of that [cultivation] which has been set forth—

The meaning of the sentence is this: at the end of the body of one who is deluded, that very cultivation (bhāvanā) shall yield its fruit in the form of the variety of appropriate bodies, by means of memory awakened through the activation of latent impressions (saṃskāra).

Now, one might object: "In this case, how could a latent impression (*vāsanā*), situated in another body and thus distant and obstructed, undergo awakening, such that the memory arising from it would also yield results in the form of the diversity of that [present] body? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Even when separated by distance and other factors, this is because the latent impressions (vāsanās) have been thus described. (28-351)

Because memory and mental impressions (saṃskāra) are of a single nature in their uninterrupted succession, there is thus a cultivation of even that which is vivid, through its not being established as a direct experience. (28-352)
Being cultivated, does it not produce a body similar to its own continuum?
For even when separated by space and time, there is an immediate succession among latent impressions (*vāsanās*), as stated:
"There is an immediacy even for those [impressions] separated by space and time" (Yoga Sūtra 4.9).
Because [the mind] is of a single nature with the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) described by these and other [arguments], awakening must necessarily occur;
and by virtue of that, memory [occurs].
Thus, it is rightly stated that memory (*smṛti*) and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) bestow as their fruit the variousness of those respective bodies. In this way...
Even in such experience, contemplation (*bhāvanā*) alone is primary— thus he says "therefore," and so forth. Therefore,

from the reason of the aforementioned distinction between contemplation and experience, because experience sprouts with firmness through a form appropriate to contemplation, even in the case of a manifest object...

Furthermore, future existence (*bhaviṣyattā*) must be something that is being cultivated (*bhāvyamānā*), not something currently being experienced (*anubhūyamānā*), because experience has as its object that which has already come to be. And why does such a future existence, when being cultivated, not produce another body in accordance with its own continuum? There is no [reason] here [to prevent it].
The meaning is: "there is some misconception."

Now, one might object: "If indeed the arising of another body is brought about solely by mental cultivation (bhāvanā), then would this [new body] be accessible only to the one who performs the cultivation—just like grief and other such states—or is it perceivable by all people? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Together with such kinsmen, sons, friends, and others of that kind. || 28-353 ||
It also appears in the other world according to the sequence of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like a dream;

such a body, appropriate to that particular conception, appears through the sequence of latent impressions just as in a dream, even together with relatives and others who have attained forms corresponding to it in another birth.
The meaning is: it should be perceptible to all people.

"Is this not an unequal analogy? For even those such as kinsmen who appear in a dream are indeed ignorant of their own circumstances. To this he replies: "But is it not the case that [the dreamer] is likewise [unaware] of his other kinsmen, sons, and so forth? (28.354)
"It is experienced—that is, the object of the dream. 'In that way' means like the dreamer. 'Nothing is experienced' means it is not known at all. To this, he says:
"Who said this? He himself must know its state of being experienced."
But surely, who says this? That dreamer knows that the object of his dream is perceivable by all people; as for whether others actually perceive it or not, that is another matter.
But surely, since relatives and others are separated by space, time, and so forth in a dream, they are not actually present;
how then could one know even their perceptibility? Or rather, this is merely an illusion.
But if relatives and others appear there, how can they be non-present? For that which appears cannot be non-appearing.

[Otherwise] it would be so; for in that case, even while awake, there would be a total absence of those [objects]. If it is argued that in that case (the waking state), there is a powerful inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their existence because of the observation of activity, speech, and so forth, then here too it is the same—thus he says:
In the multitude of other objects of cognition, which are to be known through a mass of activities and verbal expressions, || 28-355 ||

"The statement 'he does not exist in the dream' is devoid of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "He" refers to the collection of other cognizers. "Devoid of valid means of knowledge" means that there is no means of knowledge whatsoever there that can establish his non-existence; this is the intended meaning. Even though [the dream] is an error...
Dreaming is indeed no different from waking; that even waking is merely an illusion—on this point, everyone has already exerted their efforts, so enough said.

Now, one might object: "Even so, since the firmness and lack of firmness in waking and dreaming states are well-established everywhere as constituting reality and unreality respectively, how can this be denied? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But these very things which are seen in the waking state are perceived by me [in the dream]. (28.356)
"Let this [dream] be false; let it be so," [he says] by virtue of the speech of those perceivers.

"This—that is to say"—the meaning is the conceiving [of them] as one [with oneself]. "By virtue of the speech of those perceivers"—for those waking perceivers [ask], "Indeed, what was seen by you yesterday in the dream in my presence?"
When questioned, they would simply say "no" in reply.
Now, one might object: "In a dream, there are certainly certain relatives and others; for those cannot possibly exist as a duality [of subject and object] for him.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Those whom I saw in the dream as perceivers were none at all. (28.357)
Regarding the statement, "They do not grieve and they do not perceive me," what proof is there for this?
For as to the claim that those cognizers who are seen in a dream—such as kinsmen and others—are none at all, what proof is there?
The meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever that makes known their non-existence; on the contrary, [the opposite is the case].

By the statement, "The inference that establishes their existence has been stated here; and they neither grieve for me nor look at me," it is made known that [these things], although they perform purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*), [are nevertheless devoid of self-awareness].

Now, one might object: "Inference is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and that [means] is subordinate to its object of knowledge (*prameya*); yet, in this case, there is no such object of knowledge characterized as another cognizer. What, then, could serve as its objective support (*ālambana*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For all inferences are established upon self-awareness. || 28-358 ||
The existence of other subjects is grounded in consciousness, not in those [subjects] themselves;
for in this system,
the determination of objects is indeed grounded in consciousness.

According to this principle, since all inferences lack the capacity to impart any excellence to the object and possess their fruitfulness solely within the cognizer, their final rest occurs only by ascending into the consciousness of that [cognizer]. Thus,
even the existence of other cognizers who are being cognized is established as resting therein alone, and not otherwise.

Since [the reason] resides in the very nature of the object to be inferred (anumeya), what is the use of investigating its existence or non-existence? Furthermore, since this has been extensively elaborated elsewhere by others, let it be; what is the point of such digressive discussion here?
Not only is inferential cognition thus, but even perceptual cognition is so; as he says:
"The existence of a jar or the like is established in consciousness, but not residing in that [object]. (28.359)
In the same way, this [cognition] regarding another object is grounded in consciousness (*saṃvit*) and does not reside in that [object].
He applies this [principle] even to an inferable object with the words "in the same way" (*tadvat*), etc. The word "this" (*eṣā*) refers to existence (*astitā*).
He pacifies [the doubt] exactly as it was explained: "Therefore, this is established: whatever is meditated upon, that very thing indeed [comes to be]. (28.360)
If one does not awaken at the end of the body, there will be another kind of awakening;
"another kind" means that it is indeed indefinite—this is the meaning.
He reinforces the very dependence upon cultivation (bhāvanā):
"For thus, at the final moment, one is refined by the hearing of the knowledge of Brahman. (28-361)

It has been stated that a living being is liberated due to the power of prior impressions (*saṃskāra*). However, when there is a constant cultivation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward what is unreal, an unfortunate rebirth (*asadgati*) occurs; therefore, for the sake of dispelling that [unreal cultivation], even if it is weak, one must cultivate that which has reality as its object.
In order to instill strength,

at the final moment of the highly powerful Brahma-vidyās, as stated in such passages as, "The power of mantra is indeed inconceivable, arising from the mouth of the Supreme Lord," [the following occurs].
The Blessed One gave this instruction for the sake of purification, so that there may be liberation for him alone.
And this has not been stated as being devoid of literal meaning; thus he says:
"Because of the two particles, because of the word 'end' (anta), because of the recollection [of the scripture], and because of the four ends. (28.362)

From the entire preceding verse and from the half-verse immediately following it, as well as from the word *līna* (or *laya*), all that was stated regarding the true nature of reality (*arthasatattvaka*) is [to be understood]. (28–363)
In this context, the word "vā" (or) indicates the inclusion of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) from previous births for trees and other such beings;
and the word "api" (even) indicates the impossibility [of such cultivation] despite the strength of the experience.
Regarding the phrase "from the word 'anta'": the word "anta" is intended to exclude the penultimate moment and those preceding it.

"From remembrance"—that is, from that which has the form of *prakṛti*. "From the suffix" (*śatuḥ*)—that is, from that which has the form of a grammatical suffix (*pratyaya*). "Ultimately from the quarter"—as it is said: "When one is permeated by that state... (8.6).
Thus [it is said].
"From the whole"—this is like the "crow's eye" (a term for something that serves two purposes simultaneously). "From the half-verse"—namely:
"Therefore, at all times, remember Me and fight" (Gītā 8.7).

Thus it is said. For by this it is stated that one must always cultivate a meditative realization (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the real. Regarding the word "līne" (in the dissolved state)—it is derived from the term "pralīna" (dissolved). By this, the state of being single-mindedly intent upon the object being meditated upon is reinforced.
However, those ignorant of this meaning have explained it otherwise; thus he says:
Not understanding this, everyone clings to mere straws;
some invert the order of "yat" and "tat," while others follow a different sequence altogether. (28.364)
They explain that the two particles have a reversed order and that "he abandons" takes the locative case;
however, all of that is not useful for the application of the stated [reasoning].
Regarding "the inversion of *yattad*": it means "remembering whichever state he attains, that very one.

Regarding "of a different kind": this is simply due to the reading itself. Regarding "the reversed order": it refers to "or remembering. Regarding the locative case: it means "while he is casting off the body in the final moment. || 365 ||

Now, one might object: "Having restated such an interpretation, why was it not refuted? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that [interpretation] shown is not false, for it does not cause delusion within one's own mind."
Now, one might object: "What is the use of this investigation into the true nature of death based on mere speculation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, this reality of such a departure [from life] was [received] from the venerable Śambhunātha. (28–366)
"Having realized what has been declared by him, fear of death perishes.
Anticipating the objection— "But how can that fear be pacified merely by the statement of the true nature of death?"— he says:

Having realized the true nature of death, the gods here swallowed the Kālakūṭa poison, thinking it to be nectar produced from the churning of the potency of the moving heart out of the ocean of consciousness.
If you drink it then, your state of Śiva-hood is certain. || 28-367 ||

Thus, having weighed the true nature of death by this measure, the gods are limited subjects who act within the path of *māyā*; yet, because they are of the very nature of the eternal and infallible vitality (*vīrya*)— which consists of the supreme reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*)— they are drawn upward by ascending to the supreme stream.

That which is "pressing out" (niṣpīḍana) is the acceptance [of reality] as its essence; by virtue of that, there arises from the ocean of consciousness an ambrosia consisting of the wonder of supreme bliss, which is fullness (pūrṇatva).
Through the cognition of that, time—which effects various divisions—is the entire expansion of bonds extending up to the level of *samanā*. That very [time] is...
When that which consists of the nature of non-apprehension— which is essentially a false inversion—

is swallowed by the realization of one's own self-consciousness and brought to the state of being composed of perfect apprehension; if, right here in this liberated and immortal Self, you begin the act of drinking, then indeed, at that very moment—

The meaning is: "What further use is there for this repeated drinking of nectar [if] you were already possessed of full consciousness? The essential point here is this: for one who constantly practices the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaita*), at the end of life, there will surely be the attainment of identity with that very [consciousness]; what [need is there for anything else]?

There is no room for the fear of death for such great souls. Nevertheless, when the gods, having descended to the mortal realm, perceived this [poison] that had arisen from the churning of the ocean by dragging Mount Mandara and from the exertion of their own prowess as being nothing other than nectar, they consumed the *kālakūṭa* poison— if [they did so].
If you drink the nectar of immortality, then it is certain that you will attain equality with the Blessed Lord Śiva himself, who has swallowed the unbearable poison. ||367||

Having thus explained the nature of death as a digression, he speaks of the subject at hand: "For even any worldly festival produces a state of exhilaration that resembles a wave in the ocean of consciousness; that too is like a sacred occasion (parvan). (28.368)
By this, the [rites] for the destruction of calamities, for rejoicing, and so forth, are explained; therefore, in those cases as well, there is especially the worship of the deity. (28.369)

Whatever wonder arises from the agitation of the city [of the body] and so forth, that is the bestower of firmness in the sovereignty of one's own consciousness; therefore, on the day of its attainment, there is a special worship. (28–370)
"It gives birth to exhilaration" means because it produces repose within one's own self.

"That too"—the meaning of the word "too" (api) is that not only should the day of death be like a festival day, but this [day] as well. "By this"—by the principle of analogy characterized by the production of exhilaration.
"By means of the cause"—this is the meaning. Regarding "the attainment of that": the word "that" (tat) refers to the sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*).
Now, he speaks in order to indicate the meeting with the Yoginīs (*yoginīmelaka*) and so forth, which were mentioned immediately after the examination of death:
"The meeting with the Yoginīs is twofold: by force (*haṭhataḥ*) and likewise by love (*priyataḥ*)."
One should guard against vulnerabilities in the east, and against acting according to one's whims in the north.
And both of these will be shown in the context of extracting the mantras:

"in the former" refers to *haṭhamelāpa*; "in the latter" refers to *priyamelāpa*. Whether there is freedom of action (*kāmacāritva*) or the guarding of vulnerabilities (*chidrarakṣaṇa*), this is already understood by the very words *haṭha* and *priya*.
"Dvaya" means "consisting of two parts. "In the context of the extraction of mantras" refers to the thirtieth chapter (*ahnika*).
Now, one might object: "Let it be so; but from where does its status as an occasional (*naimittika*) rite arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And from the *yoginīmelaka*, he necessarily attains knowledge. (28-372)

By that [means], there is likewise the union with one's own lineage and so forth on that festival day. "By that" means by the attainment of knowledge which is necessarily destined to occur; "likewise" means like the gathering of yoginīs.
Now, one might object: "If it is said that this [yogin] necessarily attains knowledge from the *yoginīmelaka*, what is the proof for this necessity? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Consciousness is the soul of all; yet, due to the differentiation of bodies and so forth, it becomes contracted. (3.373)

In this context, although consciousness is all-pervasive, it becomes contracted due to the differentiation of bodies; yet, when there is a *melaka* (union), through the mutual friction and the resulting reflection—
that is, through reciprocal transference— it becomes fully expanded.
The meaning is that it becomes full by casting aside contraction through blossoming.
Now, one might ask: "How could she attain such blossoming by this alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"With her own mass of rays surging forth, she is reflected within the cognitions. (28-374)
It shines like many mirrors, effortlessly manifesting everything;
for the mass of rays from the senses as they project outward toward any external object is reflected within those very cognitions belonging to the Yoginīs and others, which resemble multiple mirrors.
The meaning is: being ignited and attaining expansion on all sides, it would, even without effort, protect everything and reach a state of omniformity.
And its very state of possessing all aspects is its full form, overflowing with supreme bliss—thus he says:
"Therefore, in a large assembly during the singing of songs and so forth... (28.375).
That bliss which arises from identification with everything (*sarvatanmayībhāva*) does not belong to a single [entity] alone.

"Therefore" means: precisely because she possesses all forms (*sarvākāratvāt*). "Identification with everything" means that within those respective portions, the differentiation of all things has dissolved.
But surely,

according to the principle stated in such passages as, "Even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its omniformity and is inconceivable," consciousness is filled with bliss in every single instance; so why [is this being said]?
Anticipating the question, "By what means does it become identical with everything? he says:
"That consciousness, filled with bliss, attains oneness with each [object] in that same way. (28.376)
When directed toward objects such as dance and the like, it attains full-blown bliss.
Now, one might object: "Even so, since the contraction of the body and other such limitations have not dissolved, how can these [beings] possess the nature of full-blown bliss?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because there is an absence here of causes for contraction such as envy and malice, that [state] exists. (28.377)
"Flourishing, unobstructed, and united with the bliss of consciousness"—
having raised the doubt, "Will those who do not possess the absence of contraction such as envy and the like ever attain this state of being composed of consciousness, or not?", he says:
But when some object that is not identical with it stands there, [the mind] is repelled. || 28-378 ||

The phrase "standing as something of a different nature" means existing like the sensation of a rough surface; that is to say, not having attained the state of being composed of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*). For this very reason it was said:
"standing as something of a different nature. Regarding the expression "like the sensation of a rough surface"—for example:
Just as there would be an obstruction of touch upon a low spot in an uneven object, so too is it here with consciousness— this is the meaning.
In this very way, entry must not be granted at all to one of such a kind during the gathering (*melaka*) and other rites; thus he says:
"Therefore, in the worship of the *cakra* and so forth, [one should exclude] one who is of a different class and not absorbed in that. (28.379)
One should not at all allow entry [into the body], for that is the cause of the contraction of consciousness.
The absence of such entry is the reason why it is the cause of the contraction of consciousness.

Thus, because entry is prohibited for one who is not identified with [the deity] during the *melaka* and other rites, even when entry is permitted, he says—[in order to highlight the distinction]—that only those who are identified with [the deity] should enter here:
"However many bodies there may be, they should be as perfectly full [of the deity] as one's own limbs. (28.380)
Having entered into a single consciousness, one should worship as many [forms] as there are.

By the phrase "bodies," it is indicated that, in reality, there is no distinction whatsoever among the embodied beings here. For this very reason, it is said: "having entered into a single, perfectly full consciousness."
And [the rule] "as if it were one's own limb" (svāṅgavat) also [applies].
Now, one might ask: "If someone who is not of that nature should enter a *melaka* or similar gathering through negligence, what should be done then? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If one has entered through negligence, one should not fall into contraction (*saṅkoca*) because of it. (28-381)
One should practice one's own conduct together with him who has been introduced [to it].
Anticipating the doubt—"In this way, will there be some benefit for him, or not?"—he says:
"But if he is pierced by the power of grace (anugraha-śakti), he shall become identical with that. (28.382)
But one who is pierced by the left (vāmāviddha) would revile that [teaching] and might even cause its destruction.

"That" refers to the secret practice and so forth found therein. "Revile" means out of envy and the like. "Cause its destruction" is because such is the traditional injunction regarding the *samaya*. As it has been said:
"One should cause those who break the rules of discipline and those who act contrary to proper conduct to be executed.
Thus [it is said].
And this has not been stated by us merely as our own invention; thus he says:
"It is also stated in the venerable Picumata that one should protect [it] with effort from the very beginning. (28.383)
One should not cause [the disciple] who has entered the entrance to engage in deliberation;
and this should be understood as referring to one who is qualified even when not yet absorbed in that state—not otherwise—as he says:
"But he who remains established in worldly conduct, when such a person has entered... (384).

Without performing that customary practice, one should again worship the *cakra*. "In such a case" means when [the disciple] remains established in worldly conduct. "He" refers to the worshiper of the *cakra* and so forth. "That" refers to what is prescribed for the *melaka* and other occasions. "Again" means when he has departed, or on the following day.
Now, he makes a formal declaration in order to explain the method of exposition which has come in due order:
"Now I shall state the method of exposition of the scripture as taught by the Guru. (28-385)
In the Devyāyāmala-śāstra and other texts, the Lord whose crown is the moon has said the same:
"One who knows the Kalpas, one who knows their collection, one who knows the Śāstras, and one who knows the meaning of the Saṃhitās. (28.386)

And the Guru who is versed in the meaning of all the scriptures is taught as distinct [from others]. "The collection thereof" refers to many indefinite ritual procedures (*kalpa*s). A scripture (*śāstra*) consists of several definite ritual procedures. A *saṃhitā* consists of four quarters (*catuṣpādā*). "Of all the scriptures" means—
The meaning is that the Guru is taught in the *Śrī Devyāyāmala* as being fivefold, namely the fourteen fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). As it is said therein:
"I shall fully describe the Teacher (*ācārya*), who is proficient in all the scriptures."
He was proficient in the Saṃhitā consisting of four quarters and was skilled in the section on ritual procedures (Kalpaskandha).
"Or one who is capable of practicing the conduct even within a single portion of a single kalpa of the scripture.
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might ask: "If it is explained in this way, who has the authority [to do so]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whoever possesses well-practiced knowledge of a particular scripture, let him provide the commentary upon it. (28.387)
If it were not otherwise, and that [knowledge] were absent, then even he would act [otherwise];

"not otherwise" means one whose knowledge is unpracticed. Now, if the Guru were not one whose knowledge is thoroughly practiced in every respect, then even he—being one whose knowledge is unpracticed—would perform the exposition; it is not thus.
The meaning is: "there is some fault."
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well; thus he says:
"And in the Śrībhairavakula, such knowledge of the Kalpas and so forth is described. (28.388)
Now, one might ask: "Even so, why is the entire burden placed solely upon the teacher's state of well-practiced knowledge?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The defining characteristic of a teacher is precisely this: his state of complete and perfect knowledge."
Even there, that [activity] of his which consists of the functions of consciousness and action is merely intermediate.
Now, one might object: "In that case, would he not lack the status of being an agent (karmin)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therein," and so forth.
Even in the state of possessing complete knowledge, there exists for this Guru a distinction characterized by his being both a knower and an agent, and so on.
The meaning is that this too is a subordinate form. And this has been stated by the venerable Goddess in the *Yāmala* itself;
thus he says:
"That was stated in the fifty-second chapter (*āhnika*) of the *Devīyāmala*."
He states that very same point by way of its meaning:
"The Lord himself, desiring to abide in the form of the Guru, becomes tenfold. (28-390)
He demonstrates the tenfold nature [of the lineage] as follows:
Ucchuṣma, Śavara, Caṇḍagu, Mataṅga, Ghorāntaka, Ugra, Halahala, Krodhin, Huluhulu—these ten gurus of the East are composed of the essence of Śiva. (28–391)
By means of the sequence of their own partial mental fluctuations, they assume human bodies;
though their cognitions and actions are distinct from one another, they are completely full of knowledge.
All are devoted to the consumption of meat, wine, and sexual intercourse, as well as to the study and practice of ritual manuals;
yet there is an internal distinction based on pride, the absence of anger, forbearance, and so forth. (28.393)
Antaka is Yama. As it is stated therein, beginning with: "The ten highly fortunate Rudras are remembered as the preeminent gurus in the Tantra."
He wore a crown of matted locks and was constantly devoted to the worship of the Liṅga.
Constantly devoted to wine and meat, firm in his vows regarding the practice of mantra,
he should also take pleasure in his own power and diligently study the scriptures.
The teacher, born from a portion of Ucchuṣma, has mastered the scriptures;
born from a portion of Śavara, he is one who relies upon the path of reality.
He constantly practices secret conduct, engages in sexual intercourse with his wife in secret,
is prone to anger and exceedingly fierce, and is always devoted to liquor and meat.
He was a portion of the fierce-rayed Sun and a preceptor who always bestowed initiation and grace;
he was patient yet fond of meat, and a slayer of sacrificial animals in the rite.
Born from a portion of Mataṅga, the Guru is a knower of the meaning of the scriptures,
yet he is conceited, prone to anger, and always devoted to sexual intercourse.
One who is well-concealed, extremely skillful, and fierce-rayed is known as a Guru;
he is devoted to the practices of recitation and fire-offerings, and delights in the worship of the Liṅga and other sacred objects.
That portion which the teachers have declared to be harsh in the rite of initiation—
namely, alchemy, mercury and the like, and elixirs such as medicinal herbs— is [to be avoided].
The yogi, intent on bestowing grace upon his disciples, should always and constantly serve him who is called Ugrāṃśa by the gurus and is known as Halahala.
Anger arises everywhere in one who is proud, even though he is always devoted to yoga;
he regards everything as mere straw and thinks that nothing is equal to himself.
Difficult for all people to propitiate and arduous for worshippers to serve,
yet constantly bestowing grace upon his disciples, he is proclaimed as an aspect of Krodhin.
One who is proficient in the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), who always consumes wine and meat,
and who is born in the *hulahula* lineage, is proclaimed as a teacher (*daiśika*).
These ten are declared to be the gurus, proud of their knowledge of their own true nature;
they have arisen from a portion of that [Supreme] and follow its inherent disposition.

"But those who are favored by them indeed abide by that conduct," and so forth, in many such ways. And this has been written here by selecting [passages] as needed for fear of excessive length; therefore, one should follow it according to one's own inclination from that very source. || 393 ||
In this very manner, such a guru should be requested for the purpose of exposition—thus he says:
"Having understood this always, the wise disciple, desiring to request a guru who has mastered the complete scriptures for the sake of exposition, should do so preceded by worship. (28.394)
He too, whether it be one belonging to his own sect or even a disciple of another,
should provide an exposition of such a scripture when the listener is fit for it, even if that listener belongs to a lower tradition, such as the Vaiṣṇavas.

Furthermore, the Guru, filled with the essence of compassion, should bestow initiation even upon a base person, avoiding only those who are devoid of the vital points [of spiritual capacity], for he must take into account the diversity of the descent of power (śaktipāta). (28.396)
By this, the injunction for hearing (śrutavidhi), which is connected to the method of exposition, has also been briefly indicated. Regarding the phrase "he too":
out of compassion, the Guru may provide an exposition even for one who is inferior, such as a Vaiṣṇava;
however, he should do so while avoiding the vital points (marmasthāna), because that person has not yet directly received the descent of power (śaktipāta). || 396 ||
Right here he states the procedure:

"On the ground smeared [with cow dung], one should draw three lotuses upon a square pedestal (*pīṭha*) located on the lotus-diagram; this shall be the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring sixty-three finger-breadths. (28–397)
Having worshipped Vāgīśānī in the center, the Gurus and Gaṇeśa in the south and north, and Kalpeśvara in the lower lotus, with offerings of water for honor, flowers, and libations; || 28-398 ||
Then, having properly gratified the maṇḍala by means of the general rite involving the argha vessel,
the wise one should deliver the exposition preceded by the [establishment of] connection.
The term *kajage* is an adjective qualifying the pedestal (*pīṭha*); its meaning is "situated upon the lotus located within another pedestal below. As it has been said:
"One should draw a lotus beneath the pedestal."

Thus [it is said]. "Rasa-vahni" refers to thirty-six. "In the middle" means in the central lotus (*madhyapadma*). "Below" means situated beneath the pedestal (*pīṭha*). As it is stated there: "In the middle is the worship of Vāgīśī."
"On the right, on a lotus, are the Gurus; on the north, however, is Gaṇeśvara.
One should worship Kalpeśa on the lotus that is beneath the pedestal.
Thus [ends verse 399].
Demonstrating that [the text] must necessarily be preceded by a connection [between its parts], he teaches the method of exposition:

"By means of the arrangement of the sequence of the aphorisms, words, sentences, sections, and the entire treatise, one should lead [the student] through the sentences by means of their connection, having augmented them so that the preceding and following parts are not contradicted. (28.400)

One should apply the meaning of the treatise without confusion, ensuring that the preceding and succeeding parts are not contradicted, by means of the appropriate logical methods such as "leaping like a frog" and "the lion’s glance. (28.401)

By means of logical arguments such as *tantrāvartana*, *bādha*, and *prasaṅga*, one who knows how to employ sentences should state the actual object, establishing its distinctness from other objects. (28.402)
Whatever comes within the range of verbal expression, that very thing one should firmly establish through more robust arguments, even if it is something yet to come into being. (28.403)
"Padeti"—the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) consists of the word and so forth. "Granthakrameti"—it takes the form of the feet of the *Vidyā* and the rest.
As it is said there:
"In this context, O Dear One, there is one connection consisting of the feet (*pādika*), and another consisting of the sequence of recitation (*pāṭalika*)."
The meaning of the words, the meaning of the sūtra-sentence, and this fivefold relationship constitute [the subject matter].

As long as the Saṃhitā consists of four quarters, one should cause the continuity of the meaning to be grasped through its beginning, middle, and end, according to how each quarter has been explained.
Having understood how they may be non-contradictory through mutual non-distinction, the Guru describes them as they exist within the quarters.
That which is a *pāṭalika* object should be delivered at the end of the chapter;
because it intends another chapter, this is known as a *pāṭalika*.
Whatever category of meaning may be approached,
the Teacher provides an explanation of it as determined by that specific category, distinguishing each from the others.
This one, known by the name Pādārthika, listen now to another [work] contained within the Sūtra.

this Sūtra should be investigated as established by the statement.
With conditioned objects of speech that flow like the current of a river,

In this case, there is indeed the "leap of the frog" and then the "glance of the lion";

The teacher provides an exposition according to the nature of the subject matter, or according to the division of the chapters, or in whatever manner he has been requested by the questioner.
"Such [a teaching] should be spoken by him for the sake of preserving the stability of his own tradition.
Thus,
like the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings which are auxiliary parts of the *paurṇamāsa* sacrifice consisting of three sacrifices, it is a single entity common to many.
*Tantra* (common procedure) is as follows: *Āvartana* (repetition) is the repeated performance of an action for the duration of the substance, such as threshing and so forth.

*Bādha* (sublation) is the prohibition of what was not [otherwise] prohibited, such as in the case of the *camasa* cup or the *godohana* vessel. Like the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), that which falls within another [rite] proceeds by means of another's *tantra* alone, independently of its own *tantra*.

Accomplishment (*sampādana*) is the incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Reasoning (*tarka*) is a cognition consisting of a state of necessity that exists within the interval between doubt and certainty. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [methods such as] extended application (*atideśa*) and so forth are included. "Real" (*sat*)—the meaning is: by means of those which are distinct from worldly maxims such as the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluta*) and others. From another entity...
By the phrase "establishing solitude," the very state of being unmixed is reinforced. "It might become corruptible" means it would assume a future state of corruption. || 403 ||
Now, one might object: "What is the purpose of first establishing the strength of that which is to be refuted at a later time?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The reality that is to be expressed must be done so by way of uprooting the previously firmly established prima facie position."
When he ascends to the level of the disciple's mind, he is then free from doubt and error.
Whether it be through language, logic, debate, dissolution, or sequential order— whatever serves as a means for the disciple's awakening, in that very manner the Guru should employ the exposition.
Having completed the subject matter to be expressed, there should be gratification and worship within the maṇḍala;
furthermore, one may speak of other subjects, but one must not speak beyond the chapter.
At the conclusion of the exposition, having asked for forgiveness and dismissed [the assembly], one should cast everything into deep water.
One should perform worship especially at the beginning, middle, and end of the scripture.
One should perform special worship for the sake of atonement for the transgressions of the *samayas*.

Language (*bhāṣā*) is divided into six types, such as Sanskrit and others. Logic (*nyāya*) is as previously described, whether worldly or scriptural. Debate (*vāda*) has the nature of resulting in the ascertainment of reality (*tattva*).

The adoption of a position and its counter-position; absorption (*laya*)—the practice of exposition characterized by being absorbed in the subject matter to be explained; sequence (*krama*)—the specific order of the text and its meaning; "the subject matter to be expressed" refers to the root sūtras and so forth; "another subject matter" refers to another sūtra. As it has been said:
"One should conclude after explaining three root-sūtras, two, or even just one; for if one speaks further, one is indeed afflicted by obstacles."
And it is said: "I shall go beyond the chapter...

Thus, by the phrase "and for the atonement of the *samayas*," it has been indicated that the twenty-third occasional rite (*naimittika*), previously mentioned as the "atonement of the *samayas*," is now about to be explained.
"Is it not the case that convention (*samaya*) is indeed the scriptural restriction consisting of 'this is to be done' and 'this is not to be done'?
And since that does not exist for those who are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), how can this have been stated without qualification?"— anticipating this objection,
he says:
Even though there may be no penances for one whose mind is free from conceptual construction, [the following applies].
Nevertheless, for the sake of favoring those who do not know reality, one should act in that manner.
Anticipating the objection—"But what is the authority for acting in this way?"—he says:
"O All-pervasive Lord, if even the mere recollection [of the deity] destroys sin, as stated in the *Śrīpicu*, how much more so [the actual practice]? (28.409).
When the Goddess had thus urged, "The rule for atonement has been proclaimed," [he replied]:
"It is true; even a single recollection here, when chanted once, brings about liberation. (28.410)
Although one who knows the subtle essence of the reality of mindfulness is free from the entire web of karma,
nevertheless, the prescribed rule must be performed for the sake of maintaining the established order.

"Of memory"—that is, of mantras and so forth. By the phrase "one who knows the principles and digits of memory," the state of being a knower (*jñānitva*) is indeed reinforced. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of protecting stability," it has been said:
"Whatever a superior person practices, that very same thing other people do."
"Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that. (Bhagavad Gītā 3.21). ||411||
For those who do not know reality and are solely intent upon mere conduct, a loss of knowledge arises when their minds waver. (28.412)

And thus, if this [state] were not concerned with conventional reality (saṃvṛti) precisely because it is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), then one would not engage in any social interaction whatsoever with those who do not know reality. If, however, one does so, one must also perform expiation (prāyaścitta)—

Therefore, if one is free from conceptual construction and has desisted from conventional reality, one should avoid any confusion with those who are always dependent upon the conduct prescribed by the treatises. (28.413)
Or he may seek out a mixture [of offenses] and perform the expiation in such a way that their minds do not become wavering regarding the meaning of the scriptures. (28.414)

"Ceased from conventional practice" (*saṃvṛtyuparata*) means that *saṃvṛti* is concealment; the meaning is that he has ceased from or desisted from it. "Always dependent on the conduct prescribed by the scriptures" means being perpetually subject to the constraints of the scriptures. "Of them" refers to those who do not know reality (*atattvavid*).

He demonstrates the very expiation for such transgressions by way of an illustration: "Whatever [sin] was previously impelled [to be committed] in the rite called 'The Hand of Śiva' (śivahasta), one is released from it after reciting this Weapon-mantra (astra) a hundred times—except in the case of killing a woman. Now, in order to state the procedure for the worship of the Guru, which was indicated immediately after the rule concerning what has been heard [the scriptures], he says: "At the conclusion of the rites for initiation, consecration, and occasional ceremonies, there is the worship of the Guru. (28.423)
On the following day, the task must always be performed according to the Siddhayogīśvarīmata;
[the officiant] should be a poet endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and a knower of the true reality of the Trika.
That guru is always to be accepted, even if one must abandon another who is established therein;
"kavi" means "one who speaks correctly. "Established therein" (tatsthitam) means "established and well-acquainted with that very [system], such as the Trika philosophy"—this is the meaning.
And how should the worship of the Guru be performed here? To this he says:
"Having made a svastika in the mandala, one should place there a seat made of gold or other materials. (28.425)
Having performed [the ritual], one should worship the Path situated there, which brings an end to all things;
then, with devotion, one should request the Guru to preside over it.

There he is to be worshipped with his own mantras, with extensive offerings of flowers, incense, and water for the guest (argha), followed by ointments, fine garments, food offerings, and libations in due order.
Having worshipped this Āśānta, the disciple should sacrifice with ritual fees;
being purified in spirit, he should bestow all his possessions upon him, even his own self. (28.428)
But by failing to satisfy the teacher completely with ritual fees (dakṣiṇās),
even one who knows reality remains subject to the bondage of debt and thus lacks the requisite qualification.

"Sakala" refers to Sadāśiva; by this, the placement (nyāsa) of the seat-division ending with him has been described. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of presiding over that"—the word "that" (tat) refers back to the aforementioned division of the seat ending with the Sakala.
Regarding "by their own [mantras]"—this means by those [mantras] one desires to propitiate. By the term "as far as Āśānta," his...

thereafter, as one qualified, he attains liberation—so it is stated in the Skandayāmala. (28.430)
Therefore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must certainly be given again to the preceptor. Indeed,
once consecrated by the preceptor, one should subsequently honor the preceptor with sacrificial fees.
An objection is raised: "Since the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth has already been mentioned previously, what is the purpose of stating it again here?
Anticipating this, he says: "For that was previously declared as an ancillary part of the sacrifice (yāgāṅga), but this [present statement] is for the sake of his satisfaction. (28–431)
Then, having obtained his permission, the child himself should eat what has been enjoyed by him;
thereafter, he should worship the cakra according to the extent of his available means.
"Tajjuṣṭam" means "served by that"—this is the meaning. ||432||
He confirms this very point by way of its contrapositive:

"Since even that which has been performed is as if unperformed if the sacrifice to the Guru is not performed, therefore the sacrifice to the Guru must be carried out with effort according to one's capacity. (28.433)
"According to one's ability" means without stinginess regarding wealth and so forth. || 433 ||
If the Guru is not present, what should be done? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even though the Guru is not there, he should be worshipped by means of mental visualization as before;
then one should employ that substance for the service of the deity or toward the devotees. (28.434)

The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Parvan, the Pavitraka, and Other [Rituals]."
"This is karma"—this is what is meant by implication; may there be auspiciousness.

Thus, by Jayaratha, through his charming conduct characterized by skill in the discussion of daily rites such as the constant worship of the deity's image, this twenty-eighth chapter has indeed been elucidated here.

"Viveka" (Discrimination).

Now, with the second half [of the verse], he makes a formal promise to state the procedure for the secret discourse:
"Next, the procedure regarding the secret is stated here with reference to the qualified practitioner.
Regarding "the secret": it refers to the Kula method. Regarding "procedure": it refers to the sacrifice (yāga).
He analyzes this very point:
"Now, this entire worship is described according to the Kula method. (29.1)
Likewise, that which is appropriate for the Guru and disciple who have ascended to the state of *dhārā*— namely,
"one should worship by means of the *Kula* method"— this is the meaning of *kulayāga*. By the phrase "likewise for those who have ascended to the state of *dhārā*," [the author indicates] this.
By stating that [the state] has reached a stage of near-perfection through its abiding in a non-conceptual state that has attained the ultimate limit (*parakāṣṭhā*),

the distinction among qualified practitioners (*adhikāribheda*) is also suggested. Furthermore, in this context, the word *atha* is employed to illuminate the fact that this work is essentially a commentary (*vārtika*) on the aphorisms (*sūtra*) of his own *Pratijñā*.

Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the distinction of the Kulaprakriyā from other methods such that even a difference in the qualified practitioners (adhikāribheda) is intended here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And it has been stated by the Supreme Lord that the essence [of all practice] lies in the worship of the Krama. (29.2)
He says that very thing:
"That which may occur for one who is engaged in the lineage of the Siddhas in a single month, that would not happen even in thousands of years through various multitudes of mantras. (29.3)

Regarding the term *siddhakrama*: it means in the *kula* method (*kulaprakriyā*) that has come down through the lineage (*tatparamparāgata*) of the Siddhas—such as Śrī Khagendranātha and others—who have descended according to the sequence of the Kṛta Yuga and so forth.
Regarding the word *vividhaiḥ*: it means by those [methods] taught in various other specific systems (*prakriyā*).
As it has been said:
"Those mantras which are proclaimed in the Siddhānta and other Tantras are all devoid of potency, because they are bereft of the splendor of Śakti."
"But the Kaulika mantras, by their very nature, possess blazing splendor;
they flash forth with divine luster and produce immediate conviction.
Thus [ends the verse]. (3)
In this regard, he first explains the word *kula* mentioned in the phrase "by the lineage-method" (*kulaprakriyayā*):

"The *kula* is the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord; it is capacity (*sāmarthya*), upwardness (*ūrdhvatā*), autonomy (*svātantrya*), vigor (*ojas*), and virility (*vīrya*). It is the mass (*piṇḍa*) and the body of consciousness (*saṃvit*). (29.4)

"Potency" (sāmarthya) means the capacity to cause both dissolution and emergence. "Verticality" (ūrdhvatā) means existing above all things as their cause. "Sovereignty" (svātantrya) consists in being the agent of all things and so forth. "The Body" (piṇḍa) is so called because the universe abides within it in a state of aesthetic integration (sāmarasya). "Consciousness" (saṃvit) is the Self. As it has been said:
"For the *kula* is indeed the supreme power...
and "...the arising and dissolution [of all things] is the nature of consciousness; therefore, it is called *kula*."
Thus,
in its own nature, the stainless consciousness is the cause everywhere within the Kula.
"O lady of excellent complexion, that Kula is the creator of all, all-pervading, and subtle.
Thus, O Goddess, the Kula of Śarveśa is everything, established within all things.
"That energy is supremely terrible...
[thus it is said].
Know that the all-pervading Kula is the potency residing within the sphere of Śakti."
Thus:
"The Kula is that supreme bliss... and so forth.
"The Kula is indeed the nature of the Self...
and "Kula is said to be the body..."
Thus [ends the fourth].
Having thus explained the word *kula*, he speaks in order to explain the word *yāga* as well, which is suggested by words such as *vidhi* (injunction) and *upāsā* (worship):
"For one who perceives all classes of entities as being thus [as identical with the Self]..."

Whatever a hero may perform, that is remembered as a Kulayāga.
Having thus stated its true nature, one might ask: "What is the substratum of this sacrifice? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Externally, in Śakti, in the couple (yāmala), in the body, on the path of the vital breath (prāṇa), and in the mind—thus the worship in Kula is sixfold, distinct according to each division. (29.7)
"In the *Yāmala*" means in the couple (*mithuna*) mounted upon the primary sacrifice (*ādyayāga*). "In the path of breath" means in the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*).
"In the doctrine" means in the intellect (*buddhi*); the sense is that even by means of the respective determinations (*adhyavasāya*), the attainment of that [state] may occur.
"Dividing according to each division" means just as [the elements] such as earth, cloth, and so forth exist externally.
The divisions. || 7 ||

Now, one might object: "In this way, just as there is a difference in the substrates, does the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) here differ slightly from the *tantra* method, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which consists of bathing, the mandala, the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), and so forth, as well as the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) and the like—that is not [required here]."
Something might be useful here, or perhaps what has been done serves for refutation.
The meaning is that one should perform this as one desires. As it has been said:
"In this [practice], nothing such as a mandala or a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is required;
nor is there any prior requirement for ritual placement (nyāsa), bathing, and so forth, according to one's will."
Thus [ends the eighth].
Now, one might ask: what is the reason for the impossibility [of performing] external bathing and so forth in this context? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Free from the six mandalas and devoid of all veils, consisting of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, the Kaula is proclaimed in the Traiśirasa doctrine. (9)

In this context, the Kula-knowledge, which consists of the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti, is free from the proliferation [of conceptual constructs] because it is liberated from the cakras described in such passages as: "The mastery over the six cakras of the Lord has been taught in the Traiśirasa doctrine" (1.114), which are defined by the six dharmamaṇḍalas. Therefore...
Therefore, knowledge—which is free from all obscurations—is an outward-turned awareness whose nature is that of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), such as blue or pleasure, is the object of experience (*vedya*) consisting of that [knowledge]. All this, beginning with the object and the subject, has as its very essence the expansion (*sphāra*) of that [knowledge]; there is nothing whatsoever apart from it—this is the meaning. Thus it has been said:
"As long as these are not the knower, how can they be the knowable, O beloved? But the knower and the knowable are one; therefore, there is no impurity in reality. (9)

And therefore, because everything has pure consciousness alone as its essence, both purity and impurity do not exist in reality; to indicate this, even their distinction is not intended here. Thus he says:
"In this sacrifice, whatever substance is prohibited in the continuous tradition of the scriptures..."
The wise one should join that very [channel] which is overflowing with the nectar from the left.
As it has been said:
"This sequence is to be worshipped with substances that are loathed by the world, excluded from the meaning of the scriptures, and considered disgusting and censurable."
Thus [ends the tenth].
Now, one might object: "Granted that this substance is excluded from the scriptures and so forth, what purpose does contact with wine serve for it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the venerable Brahmayāmala it is also stated that wine is the external essence of Śiva."
Without that [practice], there is neither enjoyment nor liberation; nor can it be attained through flour, honey, or molasses.
Taking the forms of female, neuter, and male, it bestows enjoyment in both the present and the future;
yet the supreme splendor arising from the grape is Bhairava himself, free from all conceptual construction.
This is itself the pure essence, consisting of light, bliss, and consciousness;
it is eternally dear to the deities. Therefore, one should always drink this. (29.13)
Regarding "the nectar of Śiva," it has been said: "Wine is the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), and liquor is called Bhairava;
the Self has been made into a liquid form by the Great-Souled Bhairava."
Thus [it is said]: "Without that, there is neither external enjoyment nor liberation. As it has been stated:
"There is no liberation devoid of this; there is no goal devoid of this."
"Without this, there is no accomplishment, especially in the Bhairava-āgama.
Thus [it is said].
"O Maheśvarī, by whomsoever it has been smelled, heard, seen, drunk, or touched..."
"And it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation for him...

Thus it is said. And that [enjoyment] is twofold: artificial (*kṛtrimā*) and innate (*sahajā*). Among these, the artificial is threefold—made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), honey (*kṣaudrī*), and molasses (*gauḍī*)—whereas the innate is only one, arising from grapes (*drākṣottha*).
He says that [the Supreme] is designated by such terms as Bhairava and so forth, and possesses supreme excellence—thus he says "piṣṭa" and so on.
Furthermore, it is stated that in relation to the male (puṃs), the female and the neuter are merely objects of enjoyment—thus he says "bestowing enjoyment before and after.
"Free from conceptual construction" means free from fixed conceptual constructions in the form of female, neuter, and so forth.
The meaning is that it is abandoned as having the singular form of the supreme subject. As it has been said:
"The wine made from flour, from molasses, and likewise from honey is known as artificial liquor;
through its nature as female, male, and neuter, it bestows enjoyment upon the practitioner."
Thus:
"The grape-wine (mārdvīka) and the innate (sahaja) are one; their splendor is of the nature of Bhairava.
It is neither female, nor neuter, nor even male—the supreme, all-pervading Lord."
Thus: "The Gauḍī, the Mādhvī, and likewise the Paiṣṭī; above is Ānandabhairava.
Thus it is said.
"This Dharma is fourfold, a method equal to the four ages;
it is the bliss of the four intoxicants, intent upon peace.
Thus [it is said].

And precisely because it possesses the power of another (*paratejas*), this very essence of the other (*pāratīya-rasa*) has a majesty equal to that [original substance]—this is the meaning. "Pure" (*śuddha*) means not mixed with any other substance serving as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
for if it were so [mixed], its power would necessarily be restricted—this is the intention. Therefore, it has been said:
"Consisting of light, bliss, and consciousness. As it has been said:
"Just as Śivabhairava is the leader among the circles of Bhairavas, so is the supreme Kālāntakī among the multitude of divine circles."
"Likewise, two are declared to be the leaders among all the lords of mercury (rasendras):
Madyabhairavanātha and the lord of mercury from Pāraṭī.
Thus it is said: "It is dear to the deities. As it has been stated:
"It is eternally dear to Bhairava and to the multitude of Mothers.
Therefore—because it possesses such majesty, and not out of greed or the like as do bound souls (paśu).
As it has been said:
"Even a hero, having drunk according to the rite of *paśu-pāna* without having worshipped the god Bhairava and without having performed the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) of the mantras, shall go to hell.
Thus, "one should drink" is the injunction. For this very reason, there would also be transgression (*pratyavāya*) from not drinking. As it has been said:
"When a Brahmin or even a Kṣatriya who is endowed with family conduct is not touched by liquor, then he should perform expiation. Thus [it is said].
And it is said: "When the mouth becomes empty due to the influence of liquor and meat, then one attains the state of a beast; at that time, one should perform an expiation.
The word "always" (sadā) refers to the occasion of the sacrifice; for otherwise, if one were to abstain from drinking liquor even for a single moment [at other times], [it would be a fault].
Otherwise, a transgression would ensue. Therefore:
"A man shall perform penance for abstaining from the drinking of wine for one day, half a day, half of that, or even half of that again."
Thus, this should be applied specifically with regard to the time of the sacrifice. As for the statement:

"The drinking [of wine] at the parvan festivals is always best; it is middling if done once a month; it is inferior if done only once every month; and after a month has passed, one becomes a sacrificial animal."
and so forth; this was stated with reference to times of distress. As for the statement:
"O Beloved, [the bath] for Brahmins is with sandalwood paste, for Kṣatriyas with saffron, for Vaiśyas with camphor-water, and for Śūdras with mud."
Thus:
"At the time of initiation for a Brahmin, at the ascent to battle for a Kṣatriya, at an auspicious rite on the earth for a Vaiśya, and at the funeral rites for a Śūdra."

What has been stated above refers to those who have not received initiation (*adīkṣita*); however, in the previous context, the scope is further extended to include those who possess faith in the worship and libations (*arcā-tarpaṇa*) as described by us. Otherwise, the distinction between castes (*jāti-bheda*) would be difficult to maintain. "At the time of initiation" (*dīkṣā-kāle*)—referring to the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice and others. For this very reason...
From the time that [the Veda] was corrupted by the preceptor of the Daityas,
from that time onwards the distinction between the names of the social classes (varṇas) was displayed.
It is prescribed for the drinking of Brahmins at the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
for Kṣatriyas in a great battle; and for Vaiśyas in the work of agriculture.
But during a great festival, when there is a gathering of kinsmen and friends.
O auspicious lady, this distinction regarding drink is for Śūdras at the edge of a cremation ground, at a wedding, or upon the birth of a son— for those beings of deluded minds. However,
this does not apply to those who have been initiated into the Śāṅkara Tantra and the Devī Tantra.
"Those who are devoted to the command of the Guru, who are guarded [in conduct], intent upon mantra-recitation and worship,
skilled in theoretical and practical knowledge (jñāna-vijñāna), and whose intentions are not corrupted by greed—
for those twice-born ones, O Beloved, there is never anything forbidden."

Thus it has been said; enough with these intermediate details. In this way, the following has been introduced by him: that even if a collection of substances excluded from the scriptures and so forth is gathered, it is not a cause for the perfection of the sacrifice without wine (*madya*); however, wine alone—even without such a collection of substances—is [sufficient].
In this context, "the sign" (nimitta) refers to that by which it was said: "One should join [the breath] with that which is overflowing with the nectar of the left.
As the scripture states:
"All other movements are on one side; the nectar alone is on the other."
"One should never perform worship devoid of wine, even if it is devoid of *caru*.
Thus: "In the absence of these substances, worship is ordained as being performed constantly [with substitutes]."
"Without that one Lord of Wine, even [all else] would be fruitless.
And: "O fair-eyed one, if there were no offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth..."
"One should satisfy the mantra with honey...
Thus: "O Goddess, what is the use of other collections of substances intended for the sacrifice?"
"And with even a single drop of the left-hand nectar, they do not equal a sixteenth part [of this].
Thus:
"The water offering (argha), flowers, incense, lamp, and food offering (naivedya) likewise..."
"Whatever exists, such as the substances of heroes and so forth, all is established in wine.
Thus:
"By means of wine alone, one [worships] Śaktīśa, who is joined by the Śaktis."
"One who desires her presence, O Dear One, should always and in every way perform sacrifice.
Thus [it is said].
"He who worships the lineage of the sandals (pādukākrama) without wine (alī),"...
"The yoginīs become despondent toward him and consume his juices and meat.
And:
"O Goddess, those who are devoid of liquor do not attain accomplishment in the Western [Tradition]."
"And: 'The self-born ones (Svayambhus) are eternally fallen from their lineage in Thohakāsama.

Thus it is said. Here, since the performance of all [rites] is dependent solely upon liquor, we have placed our emphasis on this agreement with the Āgamas; therefore, one should not be envious of us. || 13 ||
Thus, although this [the Krama] is preeminent, other things have also been declared as preeminent in another scripture with respect to particular intermediate subjects— so he says:
"And in the Śrīmatkramarahasya, it was delineated by the Supreme Lord."
The vessel for the guest-offering (arghapātra), the sacrificial abode, and the lamp—these three are so designated.
In the Kaulika sacrifice, the secret consists of the *argha* [offering] arising from union with Śakti;
and the abode known as Earth, Vessel, Body, and Seat possesses excellence in successive order. (29–15)
"Lamps arise from ghee, and cows are indeed remembered as deities moving upon the earth; knowing this, a Kaulika should be diligent toward these three. (29.16)
Regarding the word *tatra*—it signifies the selection of one out of three. Regarding *argha*—it refers to a specific substance known as *kuṇḍagolaka*.
Regarding *śaktisaṅgamāt*—it means from the first sacrifice (*ādyayāga*) which will be described. *Kāyapīṭham* refers to one's own head or that of another. As it has been said:
"The head is held to be the support of all the deities;
that place is Devīkoṭṭa, and one should worship there eternally.
Thus, it attains excellence through the sequence—likewise, from the earth comes the garment, and from that, the skull (muṇḍa).
Regarding the phrase "arising from ghee"—this is said because of its preeminence; by implication, those arising from oil are also included. As it has been said:
"One should prepare lamps with red wicks, filled with ghee or oil.
And the reason for this very preeminence is stated here: "The cows are remembered as deities who move upon the earth."
As it has been said:
"For the sake of benefiting the world, the deities beginning with Brahmā move upon the earth having assumed the form of a cow; therefore, one should procure that substance [from her]."
Thus: "one who is diligent" means that one should possess faith in the gathering of those [requisites]; the meaning is that one should not entertain doubt on this account. || 16 ||
For in our system, the *argha* alone is primary;

therefore, the Supreme Lord has prescribed even other substances appropriate to it. Consequently, one should not have any doubt regarding them. Indeed, it has been stated many times before that doubt itself is a great defect.
Thus he says:
"Therefore, having understood the preeminence of the argha vessel, one should employ those substances which have been prescribed by Śambhu;
here one should be free from hesitation, for doubt is indeed a defiler. (29.17)

"Those substances" refers to the five jewels and so forth. As it has been said: "Semen, the water of Śiva, flower, alkali, and likewise *nālājyaka*; that which originates from man, from the earth, from a goat, from fish, and that which comes from birds."
"Onion and garlic, as well as the twelve auspicious substances.
Here, "in this regard" refers to the enumeration of the substances. || 17 ||
Having thus established the introductory framework for the Kulayāga, he begins to describe its specific sequence:
"Having entered the sacrificial chamber, which is richly provided with perfumes and incense, facing either the east or the north..."
Or else, with the Mālinī [varga], either in reverse or in direct order. || 29-18 ||
One should perform the purification consisting of burning and nourishing, according to the distinction between the radiant and the gentle,
either in sequence or by means of the mantra of the true nature of the Mothers.

"Having entered"—meaning preceded by the worship of the threshold alone. "In reverse order"—meaning by the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra), from the feet up to the head. "In direct order"—meaning by the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭi), from the head down to the feet.
It has been stated that they are "blazing during combustion" and "soothing during nourishment," which refers to this sequence. (18–19)
Furthermore, there is a distinction between the occasional (*naimittika*) rite and the regular (*nitya*); thus he says:
"If one desires to perform initiation, then the arrangement for the placement of the path to be purified must be made;
thereafter, by means of Power (*śakti*) alone, one should lead the objects to be purified to the state of immortality. (29.20)
The path to be purified consists of any one of the levels beginning with the *bhuvana*s. "From that" means immediately after the purification of the body and so forth.
"Having purified" [refers to this] because if the sacrificial implements—consisting of the *argha* water, flowers, and so on—were not themselves purified, [the rite would be defective].

The meaning is that [the disciple] would not possess fitness for sacrifice. "By means of power alone" (śaktyaiva) means, however, not by means of the previous methods such as sprinkling with drops from the arghya-vessel and so forth. ||20||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Three mantras have been mentioned here; how, then, is their application (viniyoga) to be understood? Anticipating this, he says: "Either enclosed within the Para-mantra, or else enclosed within the Mātṛkā-mantra."
Or else, Mālinī alone [is used] in all ritual acts. (29.21)
In all ritual actions (*karma*), such a *mālinī* should be joined with the object and so forth by one seeking liberation;

it should be encapsulated (*sampuṭita*) by the true being of the Mother (*mātṛsadbhāva*) for one seeking both [liberation and worldly enjoyment], and by the Supreme (*parā*) for one seeking that alone. Even in the case of the two [mantras] taken individually, the application is exactly the same for the Supreme and the true being of the Mother. As it has been said:

"One who knows the ritual procedure should employ Mālinī situated in the middle of the *parāsaṃpuṭa* for all rites, or else, O Dear One, the supreme [Parā] alone. Here, by the word *parā* itself, the author has also explained the *mātṛsadbhāva*.
This very [power] is indeed the supreme, the most transcendent form. || 21 ||
Is it not said: "Whatever brings delight to the mind and whatever increases one's good fortune—
having adorned oneself with that, one should always worship the Lord"?

By such statements as these, it is stated everywhere that whatever collection of substances consists of bliss (ānandamaya) should be employed as an implement for worship. Yet, why is it said here that this [substance] is to be loathed?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
One should fill the arghya vessel with substances that are the causes and fruits of bliss (*nanda*);
that is, with the causes of bliss such as wine and the like, and with the fruits such as *kuṇḍa*, *golaka*, and so forth.
For this very reason it has been said:
"He whose essences produce supreme bliss in the state of purification—
he is meditated upon and remembered in the Bhairava Tantra by the Destroyer of Existence (Bhairava).
And as for the tradition regarding the completion of this [verse] here, it remains secret because of its esoteric nature.
Furthermore, this has not been revealed by us here out of fear of violating the *samaya*; it is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone. As it has been said:
"The sacrificial pap (*caruka*), the tradition (*sampradāya*), the realization (*vijñāna*), and likewise the assembly (*melaka*)."
"And the procedure for the sequence of worship resides in the mouths of the Yoginīs.
Thus [it is said].

Because of such statements as, "Whatever sequence of worship or recitation one might perform with a non-divine body, all of that becomes fruitless for him," it follows that sacrificial rites and the like performed with a non-divine form would not yield their fruit. In this regard:
The practitioner should cultivate the state of Bhairava within his own self; thus he says:
"Therein, through identification with the aforementioned mantra, one should bring about the nature of Bhairava. (29.22)
The true nature of the Mothers and so forth has been explained. For he will say:
"I am not, nor does another exist; I am solely the powers.
One should thus cultivate this mental impression at all times through mere remembrance. (29.64)
Thus [ends the section]. || 22 ||
And by means of such meditation in this very way upon the body and so forth:
