"The formless goddesses, having resorted to a form, abide within the physical body;
they sport with various states of being out of a desire for the most excellent substances."
By such statements as these, all the deities, beginning with Karaṇeśvarī, become present through their eagerness for worship; thus, regarding these [deities]:
"If one does not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for a mantra that has arrived..."
"One takes away half the body...
and so forth; by such statements, it is said that the libation (tarpaṇa) must necessarily be performed—[therefore he says]:
"By that [libation], one should fill oneself completely, both externally and as present within the primary and secondary wheels (cakras)."
One should satisfy [the deities] with droplets [of water] above and below, and by drinking from within. || 29-23 ||
"By that" means by the reason of bringing [the soul] to the state of being Bhairava. "Of the upper and lower" implies, by extension, also the transverse direction. As it has been said:
"Therefore, O Dear One, droplets should be offered upwards, downwards, and likewise transversely."
Thus, outside of that, one should satisfy oneself—accompanied by the circles of various deities—with droplets [of nectar] falling from all sides and drinking; this is the meaning. || 23 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, the *kulayāga* is established by this much alone; what else remains? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that way, the flood of rays of the full sound [emerges] by virtue of the surging state of its activity."
Desiring to see such a Self externally, one should perform external worship.
Likewise, when the practitioner— having fulfilled the circle of deities such as Nijakaraneśvarī according to the sequence just described, and though resting in his own self alone—
[perceives] that "just as a she-donkey or a mare [enters] her own abode, the temple of bliss,"

"Having entered [the heart] consisting of expansion and contraction, one rejoices within the heart. (5.59). According to the manner expressed in such passages, when the functions of the senses have blossomed, the Self—desiring to behold itself as full even externally—manifests as the Supreme Consciousness itself, even in its external form, according to the analogy of the original object and its reflection.
When one reflects in this manner, then one should worship externally; even there, the sequence of worship is the proper method—this is the meaning. As our own teachers have said:
"O Lord, when everything within the entire universe is directly composed of Your own nature..."
"For those who possess devotion, in what sacred field would this mantra not be effective? (Uṣṭo.
Thus [ends the verse]. || 24 ||
And where is that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"On an auspicious red cloth measuring twelve finger-breadths, or twice or thrice that size;
or in the sky, beautiful with vermilion, or else filled with lapis lazuli. (29.25)
In a vessel made of coconut, filled with wine, or else in a combined form situated within a mandala of that same nature. (29.26)
The wise one should perform the sacrifice; the sequence for this is stated as follows:
*arketi* means twelve; *vyomnīti* means, by implication, situated on the earth. And it has been said:
"One should fashion the orb of the sky with the pigment *rājavarta*."
One should draw a red line in the sky using vermilion.
"Or else, a white line in the sky should be drawn in the reverse manner.

Thus, it is not only the abode known as Earth, Cloth, Body, and Seat that exists individually, but even collectively—as he says: "or rather, in the form of a composite whole. Therefore, on the surface of the earth...

Above that is a red cloth, and upon that is the so-called *kāyapīṭha*, which consists of the syllable *ka* and so forth, or else a skull belonging to Viśvāmitra as its substitute. "Of such a kind" means that although they are indeed combined, they are situated within the mandala; thus, the mandala has a configuration being carried upon the ground, and therein—
On some base there is a red cloth, and upon that, the letter Kā and so forth.
He states that very sequence:
"In the northern direction, from the northeast corner to the northwest, [one should worship] Gaṇeśvara. (29.27)
One should worship Vaṭuka, the three Gurus, the Siddhas, the Yoginīs, and the Pīṭha;
thereafter, one should worship them beginning from beneath Gaṇeśa in the eastern direction.

The Siddhacakra [is to be placed] in the four directions, ending with Gaṇeśa at the bottom. "In the north" means according to the order of Prajāpati. "Gaṇeśvara" is for the sake of removing obstacles; and he, by implication, is accompanied by his beloved. The same applies to Vaṭuka as well. "The three Gurus" refers to—

The Guru, the Paramaguru, and the Parameṣṭhin; "the Siddhas" refers to Anādisiddha and others; "the Yoginīs" refers to Anādiyoginī and others. Regarding the "Pīṭha": it is Jālandhara, because from there this system (darśana) descended through the lineage of those Siddhas and Yoginīs. Therefore, [it pertains] to the maṇḍala.

Outside, in the northeast corner of the square, one should worship Gaṇeśa; then, from Vaṭuka and the three Gurus down to the Pīṭha, the Anādisiddha, and the Anādiyoginī, following the sequence of rows from top to bottom until the northwest corner, one should worship the threefold lineage— divine, accomplished, and human— according to their respective divisions.
Regarding the phrase "the group of gurus," it has been said:
"Having worshipped Gaṇeśa at the door for the pacification of obstacles,
one should then worship the lineage of gurus, beginning with one's own guru."
Thus [it is said]. Likewise:
"Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, the Siddhas, and likewise the lineage of gurus.
And this is stated with reference to a practitioner facing east, by which it is on his left.

"It shall be worshipped"— this [rule] regarding one facing north should be applied with respect to oneself, so that what is to its left would indeed be worshipped. Furthermore, at the door, Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka are to be worshipped first,
externally on the northwest and southwest corners of the square itself.
This is established by the sense, such that Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka should be located on the right and left sides of the sacrifice. As the Gurus have said:
"Externally, Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka are situated in the two corners to the right and other than right, preceded by the Śruti [corner]...
Thus, after the worship of the Guru, one proceeds to the east, outside the square.

Starting from the second square, which occurs immediately after the one situated below Gaṇeśa located in the northeast (rudrakoṇa), and proceeding in the order of the cardinal directions (pūrvādi) in a clockwise rotation,
[the arrangement continues] across the four directions until reaching the very position below Gaṇeśa in the northern direction (saumyadik).

By implication, this means that one should worship the four Siddhas—who have descended in the sequence of the Kṛta and other ages—within the four quadrants joined at the corners; that is, one should perform their worship according to the sequence to be described hereafter. As it has been said:
"Below Gaṇeśa, one should worship the entire collection of mantras;
thereafter, one should fully worship the group of their presiding deities in that very same place.
Thus [it is said].
He says that very thing: "The Lord of Birds (Khagendra), together with Vijjāmbā, along with Illāri Ambā. (29–29)
In the beginning, Vaktraṣṭi was pure and joined with Anantamekhalāmbā;
[then came] Kūrma with the power Maṅgalā and with Illāri Ambā. (29–30)
Jaitra is in the south, as is Avijita, along with Sānandamekhala;
Meṣa is with Kāmamaṅgalā, together with Ambā Kullāri. (29–31)
Vindhya, Ajita, together with Mekhalā, Ajara, Macchanda, and Kuṅkuṇāmbā—this pair of six possesses authority. (29–32)
In the north, Marutta; and ending with Īśāna, such is the second row.
These six are, in order: Amaravara, Deva, Citrāli, Vindhya, Guḍikā, and [the last]. (29–33)

"Pureti" means in the east. "Yāmye" means in the south. "With the girdle ajarayā" means with the girdle ajarā—this is the meaning. "Pare" means in the west. Thus, [it refers] to the triad of directions beginning with the east.

The sequence consists of the Siddha, his wife, and two sons. Furthermore, regarding the northern direction, there is this distinction—as he says—"six pairs. This means the twelve [deities] consisting of the six pairs related to the sons and their wives. "The second" refers to—
This is with respect to the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*). By this, it is indicated that worship should be performed even in the four directions according to the sequence of the lineages alone.
He states that very same group of twelve:
"Sillāri with Eruṇā, as well as Kumārī and Bodhāri, along with Mahālacchī and Aparamekhalā—these are the six Śaktis. (29–34)
The meaning is: together with Eruṇā and Aparamekhalā. ||34||
He reveals their very state of possessing a mandate:
"For these are the authorized ones who are to be worshipped, whose manifold lineage—consisting of disciples and grand-disciples—is diverse and uninterrupted. (29–35)
He demonstrates its very diversity:
"The series of blisses ending with Bodhiprabhupāda, and those ending with the word 'Yogī'—these are the *ovallis*;
this is the group of six mudrās in sequence. (29–36)

From the right thumb to the little finger, and then from the left little finger up to the end of the twelve [fingers], [the sequence is]: the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī, the Bindu, the Heart, the Navel, and the Kanda; these are the secret signs (chummās). 29–37.
Śabarāḍabillapaṭṭillā, Karabillāmbiśarabillā, Aḍabīḍombīdakṣiṇabillā, Kumbhārikā, and the one called Akṣarā. (29–38)
Devīkoṭṭa, Kulādri, Tripurī, Kāmākhya, Maṭṭahāsa, and Dakṣiṇapīṭha—this group of six belongs respectively to the Gharapallipīṭhas.
The *ovallyas* are the streams of knowledge (*jñānapravāhas*). "In sequence" refers to the subject matter of the *mudrās* and *chummās*.
*Baindava* is this place known as Bindu, located between the eyebrows. *Śabara* refers to the place called Pulinda. *Ambī* refers to Ambilla. *Dakṣiṇa* refers to Dakṣiṇāvarta.
*Kulādri* refers to Kaulagiri. *Tripurī* refers to Tripurottara. *Kāma* refers to Kāmarūpa.
As it is said in the *Śrīkulakrīḍāvatāra*: "Their mudrās, chummās, pallīs, and ovallis,
as well as the sequence of pīṭhas and the gharas, were likewise distributed by the Father."
Having begun thus:
"Bodhi and Amarapāda, Prabhu and Varadevaka, Citra and Pāda, Saṃkalpa and Ākṛti, and indeed Ali and he named Ānanda."
"And Vindhyapāda the yogi, as well as Guḍikāvali. Thus [it is said].
And starting from the thumb of the right hand up to the little finger—
Listen now to the detailed description of the mudrās of Vāma across the six [deities].
The thumb belongs to the eldest son, the index finger to the second,
the middle finger to the third, and the ring finger to the fourth.
"The little finger indeed belongs to the fifth, and the little finger to the sixth.
Thus I shall fully explain the *chummakās* as they exist in the *Kulāmnāya*.
The past belongs to the first, but the second is Kuṇḍalinī.
The junction of the third [channel] is indeed between the eyebrows; the navel belongs to the fourth;
the support of birth belongs to the fifth; and the sixth is the foundation of birth.
Thus: hear the sequence of the houses for the six princes. For Amara, however, it is Paṭṭilla; Dakṣiṇāvarta is Pallikā.
In Varadeva, Karabilla shall be the hamlet; Kumbhārikā shall be [the hamlet] of Citra, O slender-waisted one, and Ambilla as well.
Bilva shall be the hamlet of Citra.
When Alinātha is Pulinda, Aḍabī is called Palli;
when Śarabilla is Vindhyanātha, Palli is designated by the name Akṣara.
O Beloved, the house of Guḍikānātha-pāda is Aḍabilla;
and the village of the Ḍombīs is likewise indicated.
Thus,
they know that the abode in Tripurottara is a place of accomplishment (*siddhisthāna*),
O lady of beautiful hips; it belongs to the immortal Varadeva, whose form is desire (*kāmarūpa*).
"Aṭṭahāsa of Citra, likewise Devīkoṭṭamala, the southern [peak] of the Vindhya, and Guḍikā at Kaulagiri. Thus [it is said]. (39)
Now, one might object: "What is the purpose of such instruction regarding the *vallī* and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"If one who knows these conventions wanders through the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) desiring supernatural powers (*siddhi*), he will before long obtain from the mouths of the *yoginīs* whatever is to be attained. (29–40)

For the practitioner who thus knows the conduct regarding the mudrās and so forth, by wandering through the sacred seats (pīṭhas) out of a desire for their respective accomplishments, the yoginīs— recognizing him through the sequence of displaying those various mudrās and so forth as his own respective lineage— swiftly become bestowers of all accomplishments.
This is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Whichever deity is the lord of a particular lineage, that is proclaimed as its mudrā;
having extended the hand and displayed [the gesture], they are endowed with the syllables of their names."
By that sequence, they will gradually come to know their own family lineage;
he who points upward should point to his own [lineage].
"Among all those beginning with Kauṇḍilya, whoever shall point out [the lineage] for each person,
by this knowledge of the lineage they shall know their own family.
Thus [ends verse 40].
Having thus described the group of six princes together with their specific offices, he now describes those who are without office:
"Bhaṭṭa, Indravalkala, Ahīndra, Gajendra, and Samahīdhara—these six are chaste ascetics (ūrdhvaretas) who have abandoned the station of office. (29.41)

Now, one might ask: "What indeed is this 'qualification' (adhikāra)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For qualification is the flow of virility along the path of Kula. By virtue of the non-flow of that [virility], they are called 'those whose semen flows upwards' (ūrdhvaretas). (39.42)

For "authority" (adhikāra) indeed refers to the expansion of vigor associated with mantra and mudrā, as well as the final element; its "flow" (prasara) is its transition into the disciple upon the path of the family (kulavartman), into the bodily path beginning with the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), and into the primordial foundation of the Śakti. Since they lack that very [flow], these [are not entitled].
The meaning is that those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas) are said to have as their very essence a state of resting solely within their own Self.
Indeed, in the *Śrīdevīpañcaśatika* and other texts, it is said:
"Niṣkriyānandanātha together with Jñānadīpti form one [pair];
Vidyānanda and Raktā form the second; this has been told to you."
Based on such statements as, "Śaktyānanda, Mahānandā, the third honored by the Siddhas,
Śivānanda, and likewise Samayā should be known as the fourth," other gurus accompanied by their consorts have been mentioned; how is it that here too [they are treated] in the same way?
Anticipating the objection, "Are they not mentioned? he says:
"And others—the Gurus and their wives as proclaimed in the venerable Kālīkula—sport without hesitation, assuming various bodies while remaining bodiless. (29.43)
When the Kaula [reality] arises from those whose such-like will has been awakened, it shines forth; therein, the state of being a Guru is defined by that very form. (29–44)
These [deities] are not to be worshipped with specific offerings; they are merely to be remembered.
Then, from the interior, together with the Mātṛkā, [one should worship] Vāyu and Agni.
The Mālinī [alphabet] is to be worshipped in sequence, and thereafter the internal wheel of mantras (antar-mantra-cakram).

Furthermore, those other gurus mentioned in other scriptures who are accompanied by their wives have not assumed a physical body because they do not take on a specific, limited corporeal form; for this very reason...
Because they are not perceived by anyone else, they remain unsuspected; through the method of entering another's body (*parapurapraveśa*),

they sport with various bodies belonging to men and women whose desires for the objects of play have been awakened, experiencing the play of sexual enjoyment, such that [the child] is born from such a union.

Through the process of transition—at the very moment of entering the womb, at the time of birth, or at some subsequent time—the Kaula knowledge manifests; for it is precisely because of this that they possess such authority. This is the scriptural tradition established by the Yoginīs of the venerable *Rahasyarājikā*.
Through the grace of the Bhagavatī’s own nature, knowledge was seen and obtained from her form;

it was transmitted by them to those situated in the womb within their own family; it was seen by them from the womb, seen by others as soon as they were born, and by yet others after twenty-seven [days].

The meaning is: "It is seen at the end of the *samāna*s. Because they are formless (*amūrta*), they are here merely to be remembered; they are not to be worshipped with specific [offerings], for they were not so instructed by the former gurus.
Alternatively, [the deities] beginning with Viśvayoni are to be explained. As it has been stated by this very [author]:
Then the entire world-existence, and thereafter the lineage of Prajāpati;
ending with the word *yoni*, this is declared to be the pentad of gurus.
Vigor, agitation, seed, emission, and creation—these are said to be the powers (śaktis). Excessive enthusiasm, power, the union with patience, the surging forth, and arrangement [are also powers].
It is said that these very powers, together with the expansive [consciousness] of their own Guru, assumed some external body here and there; for the arising of independence is not [otherwise],
since, by the mere power of will, they indeed occupy a pair whenever they so choose.
"In that regard, those longing for play [attain] the knowledge of the supreme state as the fruit in reality.
Regarding "from there"—it means from the second square. Regarding "internally"—it means in the void (*vyoman*).
Regarding "gradually"—it means starting from the wind-corner (*vāyukoṇa*) up to the fire-corner (*vahnikoṇa*), in an upward sequence.
The Mātṛkā is to be worshipped, while the Mālinī is worshipped starting from Fire (the southeast) down to the end of Air (the northwest), proceeding downwards in sequence; this is established.

"Then" means after the worship of the Mātṛkā and Mālinī. "Inwardly" means in the triangle situated within the sacrificial ground, which corresponds to the position of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). There, in the eastern, southern, and northern corners, [one should worship] together with Bhairava.
The triad of goddesses beginning with Parā, and Kuleśvara in the center; as he will state:
"Having worshipped the pair of Kuleśas in the central position, [one worships] the goddesses in the three circles.

And thus, explaining the etymological significance here, he states the primary application of [the goddess] Kuleśvarī in worship: "That which resides in Kula, consisting of mantra, the perfected [state], vital breath, consciousness, and the instruments... (3.46).
Consciousness, which is the sovereign mistress, is said here in this system to be the Mistress of the Kula (Kuleśvarī) whose nature is the Wheel;
she is the venerable Goddess Parā in the center, whose form is the true essence of the Mothers.
Then she is to be worshipped as Aparā through the superimposition of that [nature], or else as Parāparā;
and she is to be worshipped as Ekavīrā, or alternatively as Sakuleśvarā.

She who is indeed sovereign because she is the locus of rest within the Kula— the assembly of the worshipful and the body of the worshipper— which consists of the wheels, and because she is the essence of the supreme mantra-siddhas and so forth, as well as the essence of the vital breath, intellect, and the instruments of perception.

Consciousness (citi) is said to have as its true essence nothing but full radiance; it is that very consciousness which, because it is the Mistress of Kula (kuleśvarī), is designated by that term—this is the meaning. The phrase "due to the superimposition of that" is to be connected with each [instance].
Therefore, whichever [deity] one desires to worship according to the falling of the flower and so forth, she is [to be worshipped] by him.
The intention is that they are likewise worthy of worship. || 48 ||

Now, one might ask: "What is the distinction between worship according to the sequence of the Solitary Hero and the sequence of the Couple? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The power (śakti) swells forth, and Bhairava, moreover, becomes radiant with joy."
In this manner, one should worship the couple through the repose in the bliss of their union. || 29-49 ||
One should worship here that very mass of rays belonging to consciousness—which is of the nature of great light—just like sparks [of a fire]. (50)
For when Śakti flows forth toward Bhairava, and Bhairava, in turn, turns toward Śakti, then, through this mutual orientation, by their friction— that is, their union—
there arises this bliss which is the wonder of one's own self; by resting in that, the couple [is realized].
One should worship [it] with the thought:
"By bliss alone perfected, one abides as Brahman itself.
Thus, according to such statements, its true essence is solely the nature of the Supreme Brahman, which is a single compact mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*).
The meaning is that one should connect [it] with the *Yāmala*. "That very [one]"—the meaning is that it is not something additional to that. || 50 ||
He says that very thing:
"The inner group of twelve is to be worshipped, and then the eight groups of eight;
or the fourfold [group], or as one desires—what indeed is the fixed number regarding the rays? (51)
"Twelvefold" refers to [the group] beginning with Sṛṣṭidevī, or that which will be described in the chapter on "Unification" (Ekīkārāhnika).
"Fourfold" refers to [the group] beginning with Siddha, or [the group] beginning with Jayā. "As desired" means established according to one's own practice. 51.

Now, it has been stated that the rays are indeed infinite, and since they are described in various ways in other scriptures, neglecting them would be entirely groundless; for if everything were treated in such a manner, there would be the undesirable consequence of total confusion, and the performance of those [rituals] would become unstable.
Why has it been stated that this "inner twelvefold" (*antardvādaśaka*), which is not prescribed in the [primary] scripture, is to be worshipped, and so forth? It is true that this is so;

however, this has been demonstrated as being the intention of other teachers. Therefore, according to the primary mode of practice, only the two groups of eight mentioned by [Abhinavagupta] himself are to be fully worshipped in the sequence of the *Yāmala*—thus he says:
Māheśī, Vairiñcī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī are in the four cardinal directions; Aindrī, Yāmyā, Muṇḍā, and Yogeśī are in the corners starting from the northeast.

In this group of eight, beginning with Aghora and ending with Pavana, each pair should be worshipped in sequence as having become a *yāmala* (united couple) through the vision of the bliss of their union.
For even in the ritual procedure detailed in various ways under the name *Aṣṭāṣṭaka*, this very same rite is prescribed; the number of lamps in that [rite] should be [eight times eight].

"Gradually"—meaning: outside the triangle, upon an eight-petaled lotus, one should worship the group of four beginning with Māheśī together with Aghora and the others on the petals in the east, south, west, and north; and on the remaining petals, from the northeast to the southeast, one should worship the group of four beginning with Indra, together with Bhūmi and the others. As it has been said:
"In the directions of the east, south, west, and [north], there is the tetrad beginning with Māheśī;
likewise, starting with Indrāṇī, they extend from the northeast to the end of the southeast petal.
Thus it is said.
And it is said: "Thereafter, one should worship the group of eight heroes (vīrāṣṭaka) according to the procedure prescribed by Śakti.
Regarding this:
"When the field is divided into eight parts, in the middle, from two parts, there is a pit within it."
Thereafter, one should make it triangular by dividing it into three equal parts on all sides.
Then, there is a lotus with eight petals; furthermore, by means of a [single] division, there are four sky-quarters (nabhaścatuṣkikā) at the four corners.
Then, in the directions of the four-cornered [figure], there are divisions reaching toward the ears (śruti).
"In this way, from the two sides, this mandala is square according to the lineage tradition.

Thus ends the summary of the mandala. Regarding the phrase "elaborated in many ways through various names"—this is because the Kula scriptures are infinite and their names are likewise diverse. For it is not...

This [set of names] of the former teachers has been mentioned here as being worthy of honor, so that by tradition there may be a fixed adherence to those names; however, it is with the intention of merely demonstrating the pervasiveness [of the principle], and thus their names should be adopted according to one's own preference. As has been stated by this very author elsewhere:

"But as for the names of the eight groups of seven, they may be taken from other family scriptures according to one's preference; thus, those respective names should be taken from the various family scriptures."

And here, by the mention of "eight groups of seven," it is clearly indicated that eight groups of eight are intended as the objects of worship. For otherwise, there would be no basis for the separate worship of the eight groups according to the sequence of their enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), and this would contradict the scriptures; so, enough of this prolixity. This—
"Thus"—meaning characterized by the *Yāmala*. Here, as far as it says:
"Once the host of mantras has been invoked, an offering of satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed with flowers, wine, food offerings, and incense, arising from the power of faith and devotion."

"By means of the liquors and meat-offerings of the blazing mantras such as Śaktinātha, one should first perform the libation (tarpaṇa), and afterwards the elaborate offering of flowers, incense, and so forth. According to such statements, the libation must necessarily be performed within the Kula tradition; and therein—

Because it serves as the representative of the Great Animal (mahāpaśu), the lamp-caru alone holds primacy; thus, he first declares that very thing as what is to be offered: "There should be a garland of lamps of that same number.
By the phrase "of that same number," the extension from eight times eight is here indicated. And this...
Regarding the subject of consecration (abhiṣeka). || 54 ||
Regarding this, he states another method:
"In the Śrīratnamālāśāstra, however, the wise man should count the number of phonemes of the Vidyā that is primarily to be worshipped as 'illuminators' (pradīpaka). (5.29–55)
As it is said there:
"O fair-faced one, when the evening has faded, the mantra-practitioner should offer lamps;
O noble lady, he should place them, numbering according to the syllables, in the four directions."
Thus [it is said].
Since it was introduced with the words, "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme worship of Mālinī," Mālinī is the primary object of worship; [this refers] to the number of her phonemes.
Fifty lamps have been mentioned; therefore, it is established that as many lamps as there are syllables in the root-vidyā should be prepared therein. || 55 ||

Having thus explained the lineage-succession (kula-krama) of the Siddhas' consorts by this much, he says the following in order to outline the modes of worship (arcā-prakāra), stating even another opinion along with its corroboration:
"Or one may perform the Kula-worship together with the sacred seats (pīṭha), fields (kṣetra), and so forth."
Just as it was spoken by the Supreme Lord in the Śrīmādhavakula. || 29-56 ||

"In the Śrīmādhavakula" means: in that which constitutes a portion of the venerable *Tantrarāja-bhaṭṭāraka* text. For here exists the tradition of certain teachers through the synthesis of the meaning of the *Śrīdevyāyāmala* and the *Śrīmādhavakula*.

It has been suggested that the worship of the Kula lineage (kulakramapūjana), endowed with the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth according to the sequence to be described by the illustrious Mādhava, should be performed. He states that very point:
"The fourfold sequence named emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, and [the nameless]."
One should worship [the deity] together with the pīṭhas and cremation grounds for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Regarding the phrase "of enjoyment and liberation"—the meaning is "for the sake of those two. As it has been stated there:
"The sequence of emanation is the first, the descent is the second, withdrawal is the third, and the inexpressible is the fourth."
Having begun thus:
"One born of the Śākala family should clearly cultivate the visualization.
So it is said.
"And the tradition established by Saṅkarṣaṇī through the sequence of the pīṭhas—without those, there can be no accomplishment; therefore, I shall tell you that state.
Thus it is said.
For in the *Śrīdevyāyāmala*, there is a quartet consisting of the three goddesses and Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇī.

In that regard, it designates the locations of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) within the body: "One should meditate upon this [quartet] as belonging either to the Self, or to the Power (*śakti*), or to the Wheel (*cakra*)."
One should perform the supreme lordly ritual of placement (nyāsa) within the body known as the sacred seat (pīṭha).
"This" refers to that which is about to be described. ||58||
He speaks of that very [sequence]:
"Aṭṭahāsa in the place of the crest-lock (śikhā), Caritra in the aperture of the crown;
Kaulagiri in the ears, and Jayantikā in the two nostrils. (59)
Ujjayinī is at the two eyebrows, Prayāga is in the face, Vārāṇasī is again in the heart, the Śrīpīṭha is on the pair of shoulders, and Viraja is in the throat.
One should worship Eḍābhī in the belly, Hālā in the navel, Gośruti in the bulbous root (kanda),
Marukośa in the generative organ, and Nagara Pauṇḍravardhana in the anus.
Elāpura, Purastīra, Sakthi, Ūru, Dakṣiṇa, Kuḍyākeśī, Sopāna, Māyā, Pū, Kṣīraka, and likewise [the others]. (29–62)
One should worship the knees and shanks as the two palaces of King Tāmraka,
and the pair of ankles as Vairiñcī, who supports [the world] from the feet up to the limit of Kālāgni.
Regarding "Aṭṭahāsa"—the connection with the preceding [phrase] is "one should remember it as being that which is to be deposited.

The same applies to what follows. "In the place of the crest" (śikhāsthāne) means "in the dvādaśānta," which consists of the state of resting in the power of the vital breath (prāṇaśakti). "In the mouth" (vaktre) means "in the face. "Hālā" means "the city of bees" (alipuram).
As it has been said:
"O Supreme Goddess, the city of letters (lipura) is at the region of the navel, above the *kanda*.
Regarding the phrase "gośruti"—it means *gokarṇa*. Regarding "of the thighs and the shanks"—it refers to the knees and the calves—and "the pair of ankles."

And the phrase "to the south" (*dakṣiṇataḥ*) should be connected everywhere [in the following list]. Thus, on the right thigh is Nagara, on the left Pauṇḍravardhana; on the right upper leg (*ūrū*) is Āvelāpura, on the left Purastīra; on the right knee is Kuḍyākeśī, and on the left Sopāna.
In the right calf is Māyāpurī, while in the left is Kṣīraka; in the right ankle is Āmratakeśvara, and in the left is Rājagṛha. As it is stated there:
"In the right thigh is the city [Māyāpurī], and in the left should be Pauṇḍravardhana."
On the left thigh is Purastīra, while on the right is Melāpura.
Kuḍyākeśī is on the right knee; Sopāna is remembered on the left. Kṣīraka is on the left calf, and Vāmapurī is on the right.
Āmratakeśvara is at the left ankle, and the auspicious Rājagṛha is on the right.

Thus. Regarding the term *vairiñcīm*—it means Brahmāṇī; and the meaning is that her sacred seat (*pīṭha*) is the one called Śrīśaila. As it is stated in the *Śrīkulakramodaya*: "Brahmī resides on Śrīśaila..."
Having begun with these words, [it continues]: "The Brahmic [power], situated upon the support of the feet... ||63||

And one should not remain here by way of identifying with those [objects], but rather one must contemplate: "I alone am the seat and the powers that preside over it," whereby accomplishment (siddhi) may occur— thus he says:
"I am not, nor does another exist; I am merely the pure powers (śaktis).
One should always cultivate this mental impression (vāsanā) through mere remembrance. (29.64)
As it has been said there:
"I am not, nor does another exist; there are only the powers (śaktis). If one should contemplate this innate state of rest here, even for a moment,"
Then, having become a sky-walker (khecara), he shall obtain union with the yoginīs.
Thus [ends verse] 64.

Now, an objection might be raised: "Is it not stated everywhere that accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs through the constraints of place, time, vows, and so forth? How then can this be so here merely by means of mental focus (*anusandhi*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Neither the lunar day (*tithi*), nor the asterism (*nakṣatra*), nor fasting (*upavāsa*) is prescribed."
One who delights in worldly pleasures shall indeed attain success by constant recollection.

"Delighting in vulgar practices"—the meaning is that his livelihood is such. And since this has already been stated in the first chapter (āhnika), it should be understood from that very place. || 65 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is that *cakra* for which this procedure called the 'pīṭhas', intended as a placement (*nyāsa*), is meant? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The outcaste, the black [smith], the butcher, the bow-maker, the leather-worker, the sword-wielder, and the metal-smelter."
The beloved wives of the fishermen, cartwrights, and others are their consorts here in this ninefold sacrifice. (29.66)

*Kṛṣṇa* refers to the *kajjala* (lamp-black) maker, that is, the *ḍomba*. The *vikoṣī* is the liquor-seller who carries a banner. The *dhātuvibheda* is the bone-breaker, the *kāpālika*. As it is said therein:
"The *mātaṅgī*, the *kajjalī*, the butcher (*saunī*), the bow-maker (*kārmukī*), and the leather-worker (*carmakāriṇī*)."
"Dhvajinī, Asthidalanī, Dhīvarī, and Cakriṇī, O Beloved.
Regarding the phrase "in the Navayāga"—the meaning is: in the sacrifice of the nine wheels (*cakras*). This has been stated therein:
"Just as the goddesses devoted to the nine-fold sacrifice worship the Lord,
so too should this ninefold worship directed toward the nine wheels be performed.
Thus [ends verse 66].
And those very houses are the *pīṭhas* by virtue of being places of convention (*saṅketa*). Thus he says:
"Saṅgama, Varuṇā, Kulagiri, Aṭṭahāsa, Jayantī, Caritra, Āmraka, Koṭṭa, and Haimapura as the ninth—among these, Cakriṇī is the principal in the center. (29.67)
As it is said there:
"O fortunate one, Mātaṅgī’s abode is celebrated as Prayāga;
Kajjalī is known as Varuṇa, and Saunī is Kulagiri, O beloved."
Kārmukī, Cāṭṭahāsa, Jayantī, Carmakāriṇī,
Caritra, Dhvajinī, and Ekāmrasthividāraṇī are proclaimed [as the goddesses].
"Devīkoṭṭa, Dhīvarī, and Hiraṇyapura—this is the ninth Cakriṇī-pīṭha, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. Regarding "of them"—it refers to Mātaṅgī and the others. (67)
He demonstrates her very preeminence:
"There, Kuṇḍalinī—residing in the *kanda* and leading to the three-and-a-half seats—revolves everywhere, crushing the seed by separating the juice from the husk. (3.68)
Having thus performed the worship of Cakrodaya, Kuleśvarī is to be worshipped in the center;
at the very end of that is Saṅkarṣiṇī, who effects both withdrawal and nourishment.
Whether she is the solitary heroine (*ekavīrā*) joined with the wheel (*cakrayuktā*), or even situated in union with the wheel (*cakrayāmalagā*),

she here indeed abides in a state of direct confrontation within the *kanda*— the supreme subject whose nature is light and who is the root-source of the manifestation of the entire universe; for this very reason, she contains the totality of the universe within herself.

When the Supreme Power (parā-śakti), in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, desires through her own sovereignty to manifest the appearance of duality, she becomes the leader [of the breath] within the three-and-a-half seats.
Assuming the state of being a subject through the body and so forth, she wanders everywhere—

she manifests all around as the very nature of this or that blue object, pleasure, and so on. Then, once again striving to cause the universe to rest within herself alone, she presses the seed apart from its husk and essence.

The meaning is this: by means of the process of suppressing the state of being a subject (pramātṛtā) relative to the body and so forth, she enhances the essence of supreme consciousness and thereby eclipses Māyā, the cause of the universe. Furthermore, that very [power], residing in the support of the kanda and having the form of the Prāṇakuṇḍalinī, is the Seed (bīja).

The meaning is as follows: food and other substances consumed for the sake of flowers and so forth are transformed into the forms of essence (*rasa*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*); by means of this, she—impelling the support of the body—circulates everywhere and remains as the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇana*) within the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) and elsewhere. Furthermore, externally, she is the one who belongs to the wheel (*cākrikī*).
Impelling a wheel of approximately three and a half cubits in circumference, she stands in its center and revolves in every direction,
toward all quarters; by this very revolution toward all quarters,
the *kuṇḍalinī* seed is pressed like sesame seeds and the like through the separation of juice and husk.
The meaning is that she squeezes [the substance] until the separation of the oil and the oil-cake is achieved.
As it has been said: "That which is the ninth, the possessor of the wheel (cakriṇī), revolves while situated in the center of the universe."
She crushes every seed by means of the division between the juice and the husk.
"And that [power] named Kuṇḍalinī has emerged from the enclosure of the *kanda*.
Thus, "the arising of the wheel" (*cakrodaya*) means the wheel that has arisen. *Saṅkarṣiṇī* consists of seventeen syllables. As it is said in the *Śrīdevyāyāmala*:
The syllable *ṅā*, the syllable *śārṇa*, the *nitamba*, and the *prāṇa* joined with half of *śūla*;
having extracted the *nitamba* and the *prāṇa*, [the latter] is conjoined with the color of milk (*kṣīravarṇa*).
He has three eyes, the color of a parrot, and his right arm is joined [in a gesture].
Having extracted the third letter from the dental series and placed it well upon the right knee,
one should fix the staff of the trident between the two tongues at the secret throat.
The second letter of the Śiromālā [mantra] is again joined to the two hands;
likewise the eye, and thereafter the head in the same manner.
Then, one should join the left foot placed upon the skull in five ways;
this seventeen-syllable Vidyā is to be worshipped even by the gods.
"...she who is known by the name Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī.
And this very Vidyā is also [taught] in the Śrīmādhavakula:
"One should join Mohinī, Kāla, Ātman, and Vīranātha."

By the passage beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "madīyabhūṣaṇairyuktaṃ pañcadhārārdhamuddharet," it is stated that this alone is the tradition of the Guru (gurvāmnāya). Regarding the phrase "tadantānte": the end of that wheel is the rim consisting of the spokes; at the end of even that [rim] lies that which consists of the supreme reflective awareness of the Full "I" (pūrṇāhaṃparāmarśātman).
The meaning is: "in the abode of rest. As it has been said:
"Having thus known the arising of the wheels, knowledge in the center cuts through time;
that which resides at the very end of its end is remembered as Saṅkarṣiṇī."
Thus: "situated in the *cakrayāmala*"—the meaning is that which is the couple (*yāmala*) within the wheel (*cakra*), situated therein according to the sequence of the couple, joined with the wheel.
Anticipating the question, "How are the seats (pīṭhas) to be worshipped here in conjunction with the [deities]? he says:
"Starting from the northeast, they are located in the directions of Ishana, Indra, Agni, Yama, Kravyād, Kava, Vāyu, and Varuna. (29.70)
One should worship these three triads, conjoined with their respective future triads.

Thus, in the northeast corner, one should worship the triad consisting of Aṭṭahāsa, Caritra, and Kulagiri; and so on, until in the north, at Āmratakeśvara, there is the triad consisting of Rājagṛha and Śrīparvata.
And one should not worship each of these seats in isolation alone; thus he says, "conjoined with the future triad," where "future" refers to that which is about to be described.
He says that very thing: "The heart, Kuṇḍalinī, and the middle of the eyebrows—these three, respectively. (29.71)
"One should worship the cremation grounds and, in due order, the group of Sadyoginīs born of the *kṣetras*";
the connection here is with what precedes. "Born of the *kṣetras*" means that which is produced from the *pīṭhas*.
Thus it has been said:
"...starting from the northeast (īśakoṇa) in sequence:
the directions that are east, south, west, and north, O Dear One.
Thus [it is said].

"The cremation ground (śmaśāna) is the region of the heart; the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) is the kuṇḍalinī; and the field of the Yoginīs (yoginīkṣetra) is the space between the eyebrows—this is to be known within the lineage of the Yoginīs.
Thus it is said.
When the worship has been performed, it is absolutely necessary that it be accompanied by an offering of food (naivedya); thus he says:
"Eight finger-breadths high, upright and round, with slender waists... (29.72).
One should prepare lamps of ghee with red wicks for the "ears and eyes"—that is, twenty-four. As it has been said:
"One should cause twenty-four lamps to be offered in the four directions."
And those consisting of flour should be well-rounded, with their bases, middles, and tips of equal measure.
"They should be eight finger-breadths in height, beautiful, and four finger-breadths in width; they are provided with ghee lamps and placed upon red wicks.
Thus it is said.
Right here he states another alternative:
"Or else, one should worship whatever [deity] is in the center as one's own practice. (29.73)
"Non-duality alone, not duality—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, the mantras taught by the Siddhāntins, Vaiṣṇavas, and others are possessed of impurity. (29.74)
In this non-dual state, they would become lifeless due to their inability to endure that splendor.
"Whatever it may be"—this is what is intended. As it has been said:
"Whoever, through the application of mantra, stands in the stage of the conduct of the Tantra..."
Having begun thus, [it says]:
"One should perform the sacrifice in the middle according to the dog-rite (śvakrama), but one should avoid the dualistic practice (dvaitācāra).
Having said this...
The Siddhānta-Vaiṣṇavas, the Buddhists, the Vedāntins, and the followers of the Smārta systems—
these should be avoided with effort, for they are remembered as mere beasts.
"Through contact with the fluid of non-duality, they abandon their proximity;
they turn away, becoming lifeless and devoid of the individual soul.
Thus it is said.
Therefore, having abandoned that collection of ritual implements, one should resort here only to that by which accomplishment may occur without effort—thus he says:
"The jar, the binding of the eyes, and so forth; the mandala, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the fire. (75)
Having abandoned [worldly concerns] here, success is found in the true wine; one should worship Kṛśā in the middle of the vessel.
For one performing this sacrifice for a day and night, on the following day— || 29-76 ||
When the *vīrabhojya* (hero’s feast) has been performed, the mantras will certainly be accomplished without effort.
In this sacrifice called "Bringer of Fortune," one should recite the *pīṭhastotra* (hymn to the sacred seats).
"On another day" means when the night has turned to dawn. As it has been said:
"One should dispense with the water-pot, the blindfold, the mandala, and so forth;
even without these, success is attained through the fire, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and other such implements."
"O Mother of the Gaṇas, the slender-waisted goddess is to be worshipped in the midst of the aforementioned vessels filled with wine, which are said to consist of elixirs (*rasāyana*).
Having begun thus...
Whether in the forenoon or the afternoon, one should recite the Pīṭhastotra throughout the day and night; at night, one should perform the recitation (japa) with a concentrated mind.
"At dawn, when the sky is clear, one should cause the Vīrabhojya (hero’s feast) to be performed;
through this, the rise of great fortune occurs, and at the end of his reign, he shall become a Khecara (sky-walker).
Thus [ends verse 77].
Alternatively, one may worship the *krama* alone, omitting the mandala and other elements—thus he says:

"Or else, the wise man should worship in due order the very forms (mūrtis) themselves, which exist in pairs, have the nature of heroes (*vīra*), are liberated (*avadhūta*), and are beyond conventional conduct (*nirācāra*). (78)
Regarding the phrase "only the forms" (mūrttīreva): by the word "only," it means the powers alone. Regarding "having the nature of heroes" (vīrasvarūpiṇīḥ):
they are the solitary heroines (ekavīrāḥ). "The Avadhūtas" means those free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpāḥ). || 78 ||
Now, one might object: "How can worship reach fulfillment if only Śakti exists? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Furthermore, the Lord of Kaula, though being himself only one, becomes as many [as those forms]."
One should satisfy the powers through the yoga of union, like Viśvarūpa.

Then, having become himself alone as the Guru— the Lord of the Kula (Kauleśa) due to his identity with Kuleśvara— he, being thus the universal form itself, should satisfy even those numerous powers through the yoga of union (*yāmala-yoga*).
For these powers have as their sole true essence the repose within one's own self, consisting of the state of aesthetic flavor (*sāmarasya*) born from the bliss of the friction [of union].
One should perform [this]—such is the meaning. || 79 ||

Now, one might ask: "Why is a specific time not mentioned here for the Kulayāga, as it is in such passages as: 'The installation and consecration (sthāpanādhivāsa) should take place during the northern solstice (udagayana), on an auspicious day, under a fixed zodiacal sign (sthiralagna)'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In consciousness, which consists of light, there can be no such thing as succession;
for there is indeed no absence of consciousness, and therefore its gratification is timeless.
"In this regard,
this Self is manifested once and for all"—
according to this principle, consciousness, consisting of the Great Light, has proceeded from the very beginning, without there being a "first time."
It manifests through a form that is uninterrupted; it does not do so with intermittent breaks like a flash of lightning.
Therefore, no such thing as "sequence" exists here, for sequence depends upon differentiation.
Consequently, since time itself has that [sequence] as its sole life-force, time also does not exist here; thus, the libation is said to be "timeless."
The intention is this: how can that which does not fall into something else attain the status of a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*) therein?
For this very reason, there is no spatial sequence here either; thus he says:
"In this sequence, because the tree of duality has been uprooted along with its roots, there is no discussion of the position of a seat."
It is not logical for [the Lord] to be separate, for the Supreme Lord indeed rests within the abode of His own power (*svaśaktidhāman*).
Regarding the phrase "within the abode of His own power": "His powers are the entire universe... (as stated in the *Śiva-sūtra-vimarśinī*).
Indeed, according to such statements, everything is that very [reality]; what place, then, could there be apart from it that might serve as its seat?
Having thus described the procedure for worship, he determines the nature of recitation (*japa*) which is closely connected to it:
"Thereafter, recitation should be performed according to the divisions of three hundred thousand and so forth;
it has been stated in the *Śrīyogasañcāra* that it possesses a manifold nature. (3.82)
Anticipating the objection, "What is the proof for its division into three hundred thousand [verses] and so forth?", it is said:
"It is stated in the *Śrīyogasañcāra*. He recites that very passage: "And that [scripture] has a manifold nature. (82)
He demonstrates that its very nature is manifold: "At the rising, the union, and the cessation, the recitation is said to have three characteristics;
[it occurs] in the mouth, in the going and coming, in the thread, in that which is called Haṃsa, and in the pair of Śiva. (29.83)
These five hundred thousand [recitations] have been declared; one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as a tenth part [of that].
[The mantras are placed] in the eyes, in the coming and going, in the mouth, in the *haṃsa*, and in the rosary.
In the union of Śiva and Śakti, a recitation of six hundred thousand is prescribed;
O beautiful lady, [this occurs] in the eyes, in the coming and going, in the ears, in the *haṃsa*, and in the mouth.

Japa is said to be of seven kinds: with the hands, with the two arms, with the eyes, with the coming and going [of the breath], with the ears, with the mouth, and that which is secret and most secret. (29.86)

O beautiful lady, this recitation situated upon the hundred-spoked and thousand-spoked wheels constitutes one hundred thousand repetitions of Rudra; the fire-oblation here is likewise a tenth part of that.
One should practice twice over the eyes, the incoming and outgoing breaths, the ears, the mouth, the interior of the Brahma-aperture, the breasts, the hands, the feet, and the secret wheel.

"At the rising" (udaye) means: in the foundation of birth (janmādhāra), which is the locus of the arising of the vital power (prāṇa-śakti). "At the junction" (saṅgame) means: in the heart (hṛdaya), which possesses the convergence of various channels (nāḍī). "In the state of peace" (śāntau) means: consisting of intense, simultaneous concentration for the purpose of arresting the breath (prāṇa-nirodha). "In the coming and going" (gamāgame) means—

In the form of the flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Regarding the word "in the thread" (*sūtre*)—it refers to the ground of the threads of the wheel of the channels of the senses. Regarding the phrase "called Haṃsa"—it refers to the heart, which illuminates the Self. Regarding the word "pair" (*yugmake*)—it refers to the foundation of birth (*janmādhāra*), whose nature is the union of Śiva and Śakti, or else to the *dvādaśānta*. [This is] the secret.
The support of birth. Regarding "the secret" (*guhyaka*): that which exists in the cave (*guhā*) is the secret (*guhya*), namely the aperture (*randhra*);

by that [aperture] is characterized the *ka*, the aperture of the ear, which is to say the *brahmabila*. In the hundreds of spokes, in the thousands of spokes—in such countless and numerous channels—the central one.

The "places" are the heart and the navel—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "here too there is a fire-oblation" (*homa*), the word "too" (*api*) indicates that a ten-part oblation (*daśāṃśa-homa*) must be performed everywhere. As for "in the secret wheel" (*guhyacakre*):

this refers to the *janmādhāra* (the source of birth) and the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve fingers), which are also known by the synonymous terms *yoginīvaktra* (the mouth of the Yoginīs) and *ājavaktra* (the mouth of Āja). This is the recitation (*japa*).

"Sixteen lakhs" is to be understood according to the previously stated method; for in such places as these, the vital breath (prāṇa) should circulate twelve times—this applies to all the remaining cases. || 88 ||
He explains this himself:
"Wherever the eye has gone, wherever the mind has gone—there the *haṃsa*, consisting of expansion and contraction, should be practiced twice. (29.89)
Wherever the eye or the mind has gone—to a place such as the mouth or elsewhere—it is precisely there that the yogin focuses his attention.

There, the *haṃsa*—the vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose nature consists of abandoning and taking up, and which is characterized by expansion and contraction—is to be practiced twice; that is to say, it is solely intent upon exiting and entering. This is the meaning.
Therefore, one must contemplate the cessation of these aforementioned paths, such as the mouth and so forth, by which means,
being blocked from all sides and having no other way of going, he enters precisely into the central abode; for once he has entered there, [he attains] oneness.
Uttering the mantra, the yogi shall attain each respective accomplishment. As it is said elsewhere:
"One should mutter [the mantra] in equilibrium with the vital breath; then, success will arise in solitude.
And for the sake of attaining this very state, it has been stated that one should perform sixteen hundred thousand recitations, and so forth.
As for the deficiency in the respective characteristics that was mentioned, the cause therein is the varying degrees of the yogins' contemplative realization. || 89 ||

Thus, through the cessation of the apāmārga [channel], the vital breath (prāṇa), having attained its growth within the central channel (madhyadhāman) due to the overflow of the nature of consciousness (saṃvidrūpa), reaches the state of being the self of all (viśvātmakatā). As it is said:
"That Self is the Goddess Mātṛkā; Śiva is established within the body."
Although situated within the body, that *haṃsa*— having attained identity with the deity of the mantra— is the Self (*ātman*) whose nature is contracted and atomic.
"The power (*śakti*), however, is to be known as Mātṛkā, and she is to be known as having Śiva as her essence."

By such statements as these, the meaning is that the Goddess Mātṛkā— the supreme power of the Lord— and Śiva Himself manifest as that very same reality, consisting of the nature of Nara (the individual), Śakti (power), and Śiva (the Absolute).

For this very reason, one who has attained identity with that mantra—namely, the vital breath (prāṇa) and the self (ātman)—should not entertain any notion of difference regarding the one who recites the mantra; thus he says: "One should not entertain the conceptual construction (vikalpa) that 'he is one and I am another. (29.90)
For one who conceptualizes, accomplishment and liberation are very far away.
Now, regarding the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for sixteen hundred thousand [breaths] and so forth, as previously stated: [29–91]
"A mantra separate from the mantrin never succeeds;
all this has its root in knowledge, otherwise it does not succeed at all"—
it is with this very intention that [this is stated] in all the scriptures.
"...one should begin the recitation (*japa*) in a secluded place," and so forth, as stated [in verse 91].
For in its primary sense, the very cessation of conceptual construction is called "exclusive devotion" (ekānta). Thus it is said:
"The abandonment of pure and impure conceptual constructions is called exclusive devotion.
Abiding therein, he himself indeed offers oblations and performs recitation as well. (9.92)
Recitation (japa) is the activity of internal discourse, whose nature consists of the awareness of the primordial sound (nāda).
The dissolution of that which has been thus perceived into the fire of consciousness is proclaimed as the oblation (homa). || 29-93 ||
And the "grasping" (āmarśa) was previously described as consisting of the twelve goddesses;
therein, the two final consciousnesses constitute the act of offering the oblation in the form of dissolution.

The venerable Śambhunātha, the moon for the ocean of the meaning of the Trika, has thus instructed that in the case of *homa*, the other ten [deities] are included as part of those [ten], thereby constituting the state of being a tenth-part (*daśāṃśatā*).
"And that [twelvefold group] exists there [in the Trika system], because everything is included therein" (4.123).

"Therein" means from within the twelvefold group. "The two final consciousnesses" refers to those whose nature is the power of the sovereignty of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*). And these two alone are the autonomous [powers] in our own philosophical system.

By the statement "Awakening is the ultimate reality," and so forth, it is said that this is the place of rest for the sake of the means [to that end], because rest in the supreme subject has been described as occurring through the sequence of the rungs of the ladder consisting of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and so on. And this has been explained in detail in the chapter on the Empowerment of Energy (*śāktopāya*). Therefore...
This is how it must be understood. Thus, regarding the state of the *homa* being one-tenth [of the recitation], this is the intended meaning—so say our teachers. 95.
Having thus described the ritual of worship ending with recitation and fire-oblation,
he begins to describe the procedure for the messenger (dūta):
"When, however, he should worship this [deity] together with the external Śakti..."
Then this secret procedure, spoken by the Supreme Lord, is being declared.
"Although this supreme power (parā śakti) is eternally manifest, nevertheless, for one devoid of external conduct, the Kaulika rite is difficult to attain.
By such statements, it follows that one must necessarily engage in external conduct. And therein also:

Without a messenger (dūtī), there is no accomplishment whatsoever—thus he says: "together with the power (śakti) residing externally. As it has been said: "A messenger must be employed in every respect; one devoid of a messenger does not possess success."
Thus it is said:
"Just as a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice in the ritual with his wife,
so too should a messenger be understood to be present in a family where the ancestral tradition is eternally established."
Thus [ends the verse]. 96.

Is it not the case that, without distinction everywhere, for one who worships the Blessed One, [it is said]: "Free from hypocrisy, devoted to the guru, a celibate student, with senses conquered, intent on the worship of Śiva, observing silence, and turning away from liquor and meat"?

Such are the characteristics that have been stated. [The author] now provides the introductory framework for this injunction, removing any room for doubt by means of the Supreme Lord’s own words regarding the objection: "How is it said here that one should perform worship together with the Power (śakti) residing externally? [He says: "... and so forth. This characteristic has been declared. How then is it said here that one should perform worship together with the Power (śakti) residing externally?—anticipating this doubt, he establishes the foundation for this injunction by means of the very words of the Supreme Lord.

It is stated in the *Śrīyogasañcāra*: "One should maintain stability in celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Now, one might ask: what indeed is this so-called *brahman*, that one should maintain stability even in its practice? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Bliss is the supreme Brahman, and it resides within the body in three ways.
In that regard, there are two types of benefactors, and the other fruit is of the nature of that [benefit]. As it is said: "Bliss is the form of Brahman...
By the word "supreme," its necessity for being cultivated is stated; and that is not merely...

He says "in the body" to show that the distinction between the supreme Brahman and so forth resides within the self itself, as well as in external forms such as the physical body—which are not the self. The word "therein" means from among the three;
"two" refers to wine and meat; "the other" refers to sexual intercourse.

It has been stated that "one whose physical constituents (*dhātu*) are nourished by the drinking of wine and the eating of meat, while sporting, would attain bliss"—this is referred to as "the benefactor" and "the fruit. For this very reason, it is described as being "of that nature" (*tadātmaka*), serving as the remainder for everything.
And here, by the word "that" (*tat*), there is a reference to bliss (*ānanda*).
Thus, because these are composed of Brahman, one who performs this practice is called a *brahmacārī*. So it is said:
"He who practices the triad of the final labials is called a *brahmacārī*. (29.98)
The labial class consists of the *pavarga*; its final letter is *ma*. These three—characterized by wine, meat, and sexual intercourse—are [the objects of enjoyment]. || 98 ||

"But is it not said: 'There is no fault in eating meat, nor in wine, nor in sexual intercourse; for this is the natural inclination of living beings, yet abstention from them yields great fruit'? (Manu Smṛti 5.56)
According to such statements, the scripture is the motivator for the cessation of meat-eating and similar acts, but not for their engagement,
because the latter occurs spontaneously; for one does not say, "A dirty person should bathe," or "One who is hungry should eat," and so forth.
In some places, the scripture has been applied [differently]. Anticipating the objection, "Then why was this said?", he says:
"Those bound souls (paśus) who are devoid of that [knowledge] are bereft of bliss;
those who perform the wheel-sacrifice (cakrayājaka), being deprived of it, have artificial food as their source of bliss. (29.99)

"Both go to the terrifying Raurava hell. This means that those here who, even though they have entered the Kula practice, do not— out of greed or doubt— offer this [substance] prescribed for the Cakra-sacrifice and so forth, whether to themselves or to another, are indeed mere *paśus* (bound souls).
The meaning is that they are devoid of the bliss arising from that [Supreme Brahman] which has become their very self,
and have instead grasped the ego-identification with the body and so forth alone. As it has been said:
"Those who are attached to the family traditions (kulāmnāyas) but are excluded from these substances are designated as 'beasts' (paśus); one should not associate with them.
Furthermore, there are those who, out of their own greed and for the sake of pleasure, take the three measures themselves—

They partake of the three *makāras*, whereas those who perform the sacrifice with the *cakra* do so by excluding them through greed and other such motives; they too are indeed merely sacrificial animals (*paśu*), as connected with the preceding [text]. Thus it has been said:
"O Supreme Goddess, like a fool, without the Guru and without the Deity..."
"Those who constantly consume liquor and meat are undoubtedly beasts.
Thus, because they fail to perform what is prescribed and perform what is forbidden, both groups go to the terrifying Raurava hell, where they experience thousands of torments— this is the meaning.

Thus, having entered this path of the Kula, one should practice it solely with the aim of manifesting the bliss of one's own self in every way, and not out of craving for it; for if that were the case, what distinction would there be between this and worldly people? As they say:

Therefore, one who is liberated from craving for sense objects should withdraw all that by means of taking refuge in that form known as the bliss of Brahman, which is indeed attained through such reliance.
That bliss which spreads forth from desire, from delusion, and from being deeply rooted in states that are not distinct from sense objects— that too is common here even to bound souls (paśus).
"That very object which, being distinct from pure consciousness, manifests as the revealer of cognition,

and which appears in a fit form within the self of the enjoyer through constant non-difference— that alone is said to be the object; though appearing divided, it has attained a state of non-difference."
Thus:
"Even though the cognition of objects is not separate from them and does not deviate from its own nature, it is indeed experienced;
these are the observers of the Hero's Vow who have ascended to the Great Sequence."
Established in the hundred-thousand-fold recitation, rooted in mantra-repetition, devoted to discipline, his mind tranquil through celibacy;
even when encountered in conflict, he remains steadfast, a man of great dignity with a perfectly peaceful body.

He who is the Great Perfect Buddha, who always remains established in his own nature as pure consciousness alone, effects a gathering [of disciples] through the rules of conduct and the laws of the pledge taught in the Atimārga and Vinaya.
For the sake of accomplishing the realization of his own Self, he does not touch sense objects out of a sense of longing;
for, being free from the state of a bound soul (paśu), he is truly intent upon the Great Path.
He who maintains a state of constant vigilance within himself, even in the midst of worldly affairs,
remains forever unerring in his observance, even when engaged in the practice of unconventional conduct.
He who, at the emission of the final element, within a mere fraction of a moment, through his own self-perception, causes all mental functions of the mind to suddenly cease.
And it is said: "The arising of the consciousness of bliss is declared to be the form of that Brahman."
Now, let it be granted that the consumption of liquor and meat is easy here; however, the other [practice] is difficult even for the immortals, let alone for mortals who possess such misfortune.
Therefore—
Then, one should bring there a beautiful female messenger whose eyes are rolling with intoxication,
who has lips like the *bimba* fruit, lovely teeth, and a face marked by a frown.
Her eyes resembled those of a frightened young deer, she possessed a beautiful smile,
and her mass of hair shone like a swarm of shimmering bees.
Her tremulous eyes were like the curved bow of Kāma,
and she was like a waveless river with the complexion of molten gold.
She was most beautifully adorned with hundreds of exquisite splendors from her ear-ornaments,
and her noble neck was graced by excellent ornaments resembling a fine conch-shell.
She was bent by the weight of her breasts, which were as unruly as the frontal globes of an elephant;
she was adorned with the sprout-like arms that were well-rounded and full in form.
She is resplendent with fingers resembling five true hoods,
and her toes are beautified by rings of shimmering jewels and variegated scales.
Her face possessed the exquisite beauty of the full moon, captivating the heart;
she stood in the midst of the best of Hari’s weapons, the great lion, and the pipīlava tree.
She walked with a languid gait, her hips possessing the beauty of three folds and a fine orb;
her thighs were shaped like plantain trunks or the trunks of elephants, and her shanks were excellent.
Her feet were beautifully adorned with toes like the spokes of a chariot wheel and ankles like its hub.
She was resplendent with long-hanging golden ornaments and strings of necklaces,
while the sound of her girdle was made resonant by the tinkling of her shimmering anklets.
Her gait was slow due to the tinkling sound of her bracelets and bangles,
and she possessed a deep navel and a stride resembling that of a rutting lordly elephant.
She spoke auspiciously with a voice as sweet as a swan’s and like the sound of a flute,
and she was adorned with armlets, strings of pearls, and fragrant garlands of flowers.
She was intensely longing for the excellent betel-roll pressed between her great five-hooded serpent hoods;
she was enveloped by the playful coquettish gestures of dancing, singing, hissing sighs, and amorous dalliance.
The Goddess, whose mind is dedicated solely to the One, who is waveless and of uniform nature,
whose consciousness is utterly free from greed and delusion, and whose very essence is pure awareness.
"She is the messenger, the seal of enchantment (*mohanīmudrā*), whose sole nature consists in the savoring of the unique wonder of Bhairava, within this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Thus it is said in the venerable *Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka*.
She is auspicious, truthful in character, and follows the commands of her teacher;
she speaks kindly, possesses a beautiful form, is of a sattvic nature, and is free from attachment.
Endowed with the conduct of Bhairava, longing for the nectars,
always devoted to non-duality, established in practice, and firm in their vows.
One who is pure-minded should look upon all women as one's own daughter and not feel revulsion;
she should be born of a family of virtuous conduct, be childless, and possess beautiful hair.
Her limbs were soft from indulgence in wine, she was rich in semen, possessed of a charming smile,
very affectionate, humble, and always well-disposed toward guests.
Her essential nature is entrusted to the mantra; she is stainless and free from egoism.
Abiding in the lineage of succession, she nevertheless conforms to worldly conduct.
Constantly engaged in both the regular and occasional rites during the successive festival days,
she was devoted to the practices of the Kāma-tantra, knowing well how to satisfy the deities.
"...contented in all states...
Thus, as described in the venerable *Triśirobhairava*, the external power (*bāhyā śaktiḥ*) characterized in such a way is indeed unattainable;
for qualities of this kind, when all gathered together in one place, never occur at any time or place.
[Such women] have been observed. As it is said:
"............ Where, indeed, are all qualities found everywhere? Furthermore, a messenger (dūtī) who is not of this kind is to be avoided. As it has been stated:

"A sacrifice without a messenger (adūtika) is better than one corrupted by a bad messenger. However, the intention here is not to establish the state of being without a messenger as such, like the statement regarding the consumption of poison. Rather, this is an injunction for performance due to incapacity, meaning: "A sacrifice without a messenger should not be performed, yet such a messenger cannot be found."
Having raised this doubt, he says:
"The definition of power (śakti) is precisely this: its non-differentiation from that which possesses it. (3.100)
One should make her such by that [means], and there is no regard for [her] caste or other qualities.
Even for one who is inferior in power, manifold accomplishment may arise. As it has been said:
"If the female messenger (dūtī) of the practitioners should indeed be devoid of auspicious marks..."
"With a mind focused solely on the Hero (Vīra), unwavering in all actions—thus it is understood.

Regarding the castes (*varṇa*): these are the Mātaṅgas and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the entire range of characteristics beginning with age is included. This is the characteristic of *Śakti*: non-difference from that [Hero]. Therefore, nothing else is to be taken into account.

[This refers to] age, caste, and so forth. For this very reason, it is said that by relying precisely on identity with those [attributes], she is everywhere differentiated by their respective distinctions.
Thus it is said:
"Because of the union with both the worldly and the non-worldly natures, due to an identity that is superior [to them]. (3.101)

In the teaching of the Guru, that [causality] is said to be threefold— arising from an effect, from a cause, or as co-emergent— and furthermore, it is threefold again as being direct, through a lineage, or as equivalent to those.

Indeed, here in the teaching of the Guru, in our own philosophical system, that very power is said to be threefold according to its primary function— as the generated (*janya*), the generator (*janikā*), and the innate (*sahajā*)— because herein its identity (*tādātmya*) exceeds [that found] in worldly relations, whether through sexual union (*yauna*) or through the extraordinary relation of gnosis (*jñānīya*). For elsewhere, however...

Attachment belongs only to the knower; thus, there is no identity [between them] in that regard. And so, this power, being twofold—either directly or through a lineage—has six aspects. As it has been said:
"Because it arises as an effect, a cause, or simultaneously, it is threefold; and then, otherwise, [it is threefold] directly."

Thus [it is said]. The connection through succession (*pāramparyayoga*) is as follows: it may be an effect of an effect, a cause of a cause, or an effect of that which arises simultaneously. For this very reason, their equality to that [original category] is stated here. [As it is said: "Is she a dog's mate, a sister, a mother, a daughter, or a beautiful friend?"

By such statements, one might ask why even one’s own wife is not included here, since there too exists a twofold union—both worldly and unworldly. Why, then, is she said here to have only six varieties? True; however, in this case, it is not out of a desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*) as in the worldly sense.

This has been stated with the following intent: that [the activity] is not merely a worldly engagement, but rather arises from the intensity of immersion (*āveśa*) into the nature of unconditioned supreme consciousness (*anavacchinna-parasaṃvit-svarūpa*), according to the perspective that will be explained hereafter.
For otherwise, there would even be room for the possibility of a desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*) toward one's own wife. As it has been said:
"One who seeks to accomplish his purpose should employ a female messenger, but not one who is deluded by lust;
for the sake of stability, he should delight his beloved, never out of lewd desire."
Thus:
"One should contemplate the mutual form consisting of Śiva and Śakti;
one should not harbor a sense of duality joined with passion, delusion, and the like."

"Everything should be performed by the best of practitioners through the cultivation of knowledge. Thus it is said. In this very context, even the contradiction with other scriptures is resolved; for there too, it is so taught out of a desire for the goal, while avoiding the desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*). As the Smṛti says:
Having anointed his limbs with clarified butter, or even with oil or ghee,
he should avoid touching face to face and limb to limb.

"When only a remnant of the family remains, one who has been appointed by his elders for the sake of progeny, and not out of lust, may approach the wife of his younger brother. Thus, in this way, only those great-souled knowers of reality (*jñānin*) whose mental activity is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) possess the qualification [for this practice].

For those who, by rejecting their own worldly conduct, possess a continuous inquiry consisting merely in the examination of whether the mind is one-pointed or not within the non-duality of consciousness itself—it is with this very intention that it is said: "Conduct is not taught as being for the sake of enjoyment; it is declared to be the embodiment of desire."
"By examining one's own mind, is the mind stable or is it moving? Thus it has been said. || 102 ||
And this is not our own invention alone; thus he says:
"In the *Śrīsarvācārahṛdaya*, this very point is summarized:
'These six powers have been declared to bestow the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation. (29.103)
"Vegavatī, then Saṃhārī, Trailokyakṣobhaṇī,
as well as Ardhavīrāsanā, and Vaktrakaulā is the fifth"—
such [classifications], though each may exist as a variety of sub-divisions, are not mentioned here because of their infinite number.
It has been calculated. || 103 ||
Now, one might ask: "Let this be; why was it said that 'one should worship together with the power residing externally'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But from the two [powers] come emanation and withdrawal; therefore, their union (melaka) is supreme."

Indeed, at the moment of their union, when the two—the Power and the Possessor of Power—act as causes, creation and withdrawal occur through their primary mutual orientation and repose within their own respective natures.
Therefore, the state consists of both, while its manifestation occurs in the fourth part; thus, it arises from its own inherent essence.
That which arises from this is the supreme union (*melaka*), because it bestows the attainment of the supreme state; that is to say, it effects identity (*tādātmya*).
This is the meaning.
And how is this to be performed? To this he says:
"Having brought her [the Śakti] and having worshipped each other mutually, they should satisfy one another. (29.104)
The worship of the primary wheel (mukhyacakra) is performed precisely through the internal sequence.

Regarding the phrase "having worshipped"—it means [worshipping] in the state of Power and the Possessor of Power (śakti-śaktimad-pada). Regarding the phrase "the worship"—it means it is the task to be performed.
Anticipating the objection—"What indeed is this intermediate sequence, and what is that primary wheel?"—he says:
"That which is the mass of bliss is indeed the internal aspect of consciousness. (29.105)
That would be the primary wheel (cakra), and the others are subordinate wheels (anucakra).
"The others" means that they do not possess such an abundance of bliss.
Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for the application of the word *cakra*? he says:
"Because of expansion (*vikāsa*), because of satisfaction (*tṛpti*), because of the cutting of bonds (*pāśotkartana*), and because of the power of action (*kṛtiśakti*). (29.106)
The word *cakra* is said to be derived from the roots *kas*, *cak*, *kṛt*, and *kṛ*.

The word *cakra* is derived from the application of the meanings of four verbal roots: *kasī* (to expand), *cak* (to satisfy), *kṛtī* (to cut), and *ḍukṛñ* (to do). Thus, it is called *cakra* because it expands (*vikasati*), satisfies (*cakati*), cuts (*kṛntati*), and acts (*karoti*).
Is it not the case that,

according to the principle beginning with, "That which generates bliss, is worthy of worship, and captivates the heart," the characteristic of the collection of substances suitable for worship is their quality of being a mass of bliss?

It has been stated everywhere [that this is so]. But here, one might raise the objection: "How can that [sacrifice] be said to belong specifically to the primary wheel (*mukhyacakra*) and other objects of worship?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And sacrifice (*yāga*) as well as libation (*tarpaṇa*) are proclaimed to be external expansion. (3.107)

Even externally, what is called sacrifice (yāga) is said to be a satiation (tarpaṇa). And that [satiation] is the expansion of consciousness through the production of its state of self-sufficiency—the meaning being its nature as an overflowing surge. || 107 ||
Now, one might ask: "How could there even be an external satiation from which the expansion of consciousness might arise?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
