"From that which resides within the primary and secondary wheels (cakras) and is fashioned by the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān)..."
And also from food that flows with bliss, even when it has entered the vital breath. || 29-108 ||
From external objects such as perfumes, incense, and garlands, there is an upward surging of consciousness;

by means of that [consciousness] projected by the possessor of power, one should contemplate oneself as completely filled with it, extending outward to the primary wheel (*cakra*) and its subordinate wheels (*anucakra*).

"One should satisfy with drops [of nectar] the upper and lower [centers] within, and with affection," according to this principle, from the drinking and so forth occurring within the primary and secondary wheels (cakras), [it is said]:
"The wind arises from the void; there shall be the arousal of the penis."
The meaning is that through the union of the vital breath (*vāyu*) and the penis (*meḍhra*),

as seen in such passages, there occurs an "upward surging" or expansion of consciousness (*cita*) due to the external consumption of fragrant substances, incense, garlands, and the like— which are of the nature of stimulating that [breath]— and which cause the flow of bliss.
Thus, in order to attain identity with the primary wheel, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) in the secondary wheels; so he says:
"In this way, the libation in the secondary wheels is performed with portions of substances appropriate to each. (29.109)
They should perform [these acts] here for one another in order to achieve the unification of their facial wheels (*mukhacakra*).

"An object appropriate to oneself" refers to any one of the [sensory qualities] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, within the "subsidiary wheels" (*anucakra*)—that is, in the form of the sense organs such as the eyes;
and furthermore, it refers to an object appropriate to oneself, such as embracing, kissing, and so forth. As it has been said:

What is the object of worship? Who is the worshiper? What should the invocation be like? What are the flowers, the incense, and the sacrificial porridge? And what is the mantra and the recitation itself?
"What indeed constitutes the sacrificial pit? What is the fire, and what is the wood or even the clarified butter?
O Maheśāna, what is *samādhi*? Tell me this, O Three-eyed One. Thus begins [the passage].
Women are indeed worshipped, and the man is the worshipper;
their invitation is the pleasure, and the flower is the wound from fingernails.
Incense is said to be an embrace; the sacrificial oblation (caru) becomes the thinning of the body;
the mantra is the web of words of one's beloved; and the recitation (japa) is the nectar of her lips.
The vulva, the sacrificial pit, the small ladle, the linga, the fire, and the sprout of the vulva, as well as the clarified butter and the seed— these are said to be "bhaga" in the Bhairava Agama.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
at the time of the joy of emission, the continuum of the object exists in these five ways.
"O Maheśānī, having realized that samādhi, one shall attain Śiva.
Thus it is said.
Anticipating the objection, "But how can identity with the primary wheel (*mukhyacakra*) arise from the satiation of the secondary wheels (*anucakra*)," he cites the scripture itself as confirmation:
"And it is said in the *Triśirastantra*: 'The sphere of the pure seat (*vimalāsana*),' [verse 29.110]."
One should enter the station of Rudra in the midst of the six senses;

for here, among all the wheels whose nature consists of the subordinate wheels, even while bringing forth the various objects as appropriate during their agitation, one remains pure due to the absence of attachment to them.
Being established in that state of abiding which is free from the stain of helplessness,

one should enter the station of Rudra through resting in one's own true nature by withdrawing its agitation; the meaning is that one becomes a participant in the state of the supreme subject, whose essence is the primary wheel.
He elaborates on this very point:
"In the reflective awareness of one's own essential nature, which unfolds through the full expansion of each respective enjoyment. (29.111)
Gradually, the goddesses of the subordinate wheels (anucakradevyaḥ) enter the central wheel of consciousness (saṃviccakraṃ).

This occurs because one's own nature as the subject (nijasya pramātṛrūpasya)— which is characterized by the tendency to expand through an outward surging form via the enjoyment of various objects such as form and so forth, each according to its own specific mode of perception— [is withdrawn].
When there is the touch of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the unfolding of the wonder of one's own self (*svātmacamatkāra*),

the goddesses of the secondary wheels, such as the Eye and the rest, each according to their respective order, proceed toward the central wheel of consciousness— the primary reality consisting of supreme bliss (*paramānandamaya*), which is the true nature of the subject (*pramātṛsatattva*) and the locus where all consciousnesses come to rest— right there.
They attain rest—this is the meaning.

One might object: "In that case, since at the time of perceiving each respective object the identity with the primary wheel (mukhyacakra) would be established for everyone without distinction, what is the purpose of this instruction? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But for another whose body is [not] self-abiding, those [powers] exist because they have abandoned the presiding over the body. (29.112)
Because they "sit" [there], one who possesses that [egoity] is neither full nor overflowing.
On the other hand, for the other—the healthy-bodied one—there is a state of being merely peripheral due to the absence of such reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
This is because the goddesses of the secondary wheels, such as the [powers of] sight and so forth, sit there having left the body which serves as their substrate. In that regard:

They take recourse in indifference; consequently, they possess the sense of "I" only in that very body—having grasped the conceit of identity there—but they are not yet full, because their sensory functions have ceased due to the exhaustion of all desires.
Nor do they surge outward, even though longing remains, because of the indifference toward the functioning of the senses such as sight, which would otherwise be directed toward the external world.
The meaning is that he would certainly not be one who has fallen away from both.
One might object: "In this way, what would happen to these two [the central deities] through the repose of the subordinate wheel-deities within the principal wheel?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having attained potency through the complete filling of the rays consisting of the deities of the subordinate wheels. (29.113)

That pair of Power and the Possessor of Power becomes mutually oriented toward one another through the rays that take the form of the goddesses of sight and the other senses, such that: "By whichever sensory path whatever object appears..."

According to the principle expressed in such passages as, "By the power of his own self-confidence, the yogin becomes absorbed in that [object] and identified with it," there occurs a state of fullness; through this, having attained its own inherent self-confidence, that couple consisting of Śakti and Śaktimān, in the form described above, becomes mutually face-to-face.
The meaning is that one should attain union.
Now, one might ask: "Even so, what would happen to this [consciousness]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That pair, having experienced the agitation born from the contact of entering the upper abode... (29.114)
At that time, even the subordinate wheels (anucakras), being identical with that [central wheel], do not exist separately; for at the moment of union,

through the varying degrees of immersion into the primary wheel— the supreme blissful state consisting of the mouth of the Yoginī within the upper abode— there arises [a state] characterized by the complete disappearance of identification with the body and so forth.

The meaning is: how could one not perceive that couple— characterized by power and the possessor of power— as being of one essence, such that it stirs even the subordinate wheels (anucakras), which possess an intensity of self-delight characterized by agitation and fullness?

One might object: "When one has entered into that state by setting aside the identification with the body and so forth, what purpose could there be for the subordinate wheels (anucakras)? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "At that time, those [wheels] are identical with that [central reality], not separate from it.
Furthermore, in this regard:
Agitation is characterized by mutual striking, embracing, kissing, and so forth.
One might ask: "In this case, would there not be the arising of another consciousness [rather than one's own]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this way, that very couple (yāmala) exists wherein all talk of duality has dissolved. (29.115)
Indeed, through the application of the gradation of the sequence, that very consciousness is the union of emission;
it is the supreme abode of the eternal, which is both the world and the noble bliss of the Self. (29.116)
It is neither quiescent nor arisen; it is the supreme Kaula, the cause of the birth of both the quiescent and the arisen.
"The union of emission" (visargasaṅghaṭṭa) means that emission whose nature is union.
"Consisting of both" means having the form of the bliss of the world, which consists of the state of essential identity (sāmarasya) between Śiva and Śakti.

"Quiescent" (*śāntam*) means transcending the universe; "arisen" (*uditam*) means consisting of the universe. "The supreme Kaula" means that its nature is exceedingly secret, because it cannot be designated by terms such as "quiescent," "arisen," and so forth.
Furthermore, because there is no occurrence of emission (*kṣepa*), it is not quiescent; and because of its rest in its own essential nature, it is not arisen.
But the meaning is this: its true nature is uninterrupted pure consciousness alone, which is the cause of these two states.
And regarding this immersion, one must certainly pay close attention—thus he says:
"One who desires the unconditioned state should always make that consciousness one's own. (29.117)
For the form of the Goddess of Consciousness is, in ultimate reality, indeed undivided.

Raising the doubt, "How then can immersion (āveśa) be accomplished here?", he says: "By means of the full description of the dissolution of states consisting of the arising and subsiding of such-and-such and so-and-so-like [experiences]. (29.118)
The fortunate one should enter the unconditioned, innate state of emission (vaisargika),
for the two forms of tranquility and emergence— whether they be of such-and-such a kind— are essentially nothing but one's own direct experience, and thus cannot be described as "this" or "that."
The dissolution of existence (*bhāva*) is non-arising (*anutpatti*). Regarding this, [it is said]:
"When existence is abandoned, consciousness, having ceased, does not go to another state of being;
then, through that intermediate state, supreme contemplation (*atibhāvanā*) blossoms. (Vi.bhai. 62)

Thus, by means of this method— through a thorough and all-encompassing grasping— the fortunate one shall enter the unconditioned, naturally emergent abode; the meaning is that he shall achieve the direct realization of his own consciousness as the nature of the full, supreme consciousness.

Now, let it be so; however, how can there be the emergence of the two forms—the quiescent and the arisen—is it solely by virtue of being located in the power (*śakti*), or rather solely by virtue of being located in the possessor of power (*śaktimat*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Then the dyad consisting of the quiescent and the arisen emerges simultaneously in both the power and the possessor of power. (29.119)
The word "atha" is used in response. ||119||
However, there is this distinction here—as he says: "The arisen form resides in the abode of the other, while the tranquil form resides in itself alone.
For the arisen form does not transcend its mutual orientation toward both power and the possessor of power."

It should manifest by embracing the unity of the respective primary abodes known as the cakras; furthermore, it is quiescent and resides within the Self alone, for in that state, supreme rest arises within one's very own self.
Now, one might object: "In this way, would not the identity of power and the possessor of power (śakti-śaktimatoḥ) as previously stated be lost? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In reality, both indeed constitute a couple (yāmala); thus it is said to be both manifest and quiescent. (29.120)

In reality, even though this pair characterized as power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) does not abandon their single essential nature (*ekātmya*), both must rest within the Self in a state of quiescence (*śāntatā*), and not through the intention of mutual difference.
Thus, the meaning is that the quiescent form, existing as inherent to the Self, has been described. || 120 ||

Even so, there is this distinction between these two—as he says: "Power nourishes an appropriate creation, but not the possessor of that power, even when there is a state of equilibrium in the reflective awareness of both forms, consisting of the quiescent and the emergent. (3.121)
Regarding this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the two forms consisting of the quiescent and the emergent, even though there is an equality in their union,

it is the *Śakti* alone— and not the possessor of power (*śaktimān*)— who, as before, nourishes the creation that has blossomed in accordance with her own appropriate nature and gives birth to the embryo; this is the distinction of hers.
This is the meaning. || 121 ||
And because she conceived [the embryo] from that very moment, it is stated in every scripture that her middle state (*madhyadhāma*) is fully radiant; thus he says:
"Therefore, in the scripture, Śakti is described as having a middle state that is fully radiant."

It is with this very intention that it has been stated elsewhere: "The practitioner who observes his vows with strict discipline may remain for a full year; yet whatever accomplishment he attains thereby, women achieve in a single day," and so forth.
And for this reason, she alone is fit for the transmission of knowledge; thus he says:
"The Guru should properly transmit the Kula-doctrine to her alone by means of that [initiation]. (29.122)
And by means of that [channel], one should cause [the breath] to circulate among men according to the stated sequence.

"By means of that" means for the reason that the central channel is fully expanded; "by means of that" means through the mouth of Śakti. The underlying intention is that for human beings, there is no expansion of the central state (*madhyapada*).
"It is precisely with this intention that the wise man should place [the mantra] in the mouth of the woman, O beloved, and cause it to be received from the mouth of the woman.
Thus [it is said].
"And from the mouth of a woman, success (siddhi) arises; that state is perfectly established within them.
Thus it has been said. And this has also been stated by the Gurus—as he says next: "One who is permeated by a reality superior to one's own body," and so forth. (29-123)
The venerable Kallaṭanātha has uttered this statement for the sake of attaining all the aforementioned goals;
indeed, the venerable Kallaṭanātha [spoke thus] immediately after [the teaching] beginning with the definition of Śakti,
in order to summarize the entire meaning even from his own body.

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: the Guru should make the *śakti*—which has been cultivated (*bhāvitā*), that is, refined (*saṃskṛtā*), by means of a state (*bhāva*) that is truly existent because it shines forth with an intensity exceeding its natural middle state—into such a condition; this is what the sentence declares.
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"That primary wheel, the mouth of the Yoginīs, has been described by Maheśa. (29.124)
In this regard, the following is the tradition: from that, knowledge is obtained.

Thus, by the manner described, the Blessed Maheśvara has stated that the primary wheel (*mukhyacakram*) is indeed the "mouth of the Yoginīs" (*yoginīvaktra*), which is synonymous with the "mouth of Picu" (*picuvaktra*) and other such terms. It is precisely there that this [knowledge] has been taught, or will be taught.
The tradition must be practiced because from it knowledge is obtained, and its immersion in supreme consciousness arises— this is the meaning.

"Now, let it be told: what kind of knowledge is obtained from this?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "This very [knowledge] is said to be unwritable; it resides in the mouth [of the teacher], and is transmitted from mouth to mouth according to the logic already stated. (29.125)
"The face is the primary wheel; how can one's own consciousness be painted?"—the meaning of "unpaintable" is that it is impossible to conceptualize.
Now, one might object: "Since this resides from mouth to mouth, how can it be said to be 'unwritable'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It is said," and so forth.
And as for the "mouth" (*vaktra*), it is said by the Great Lord: "Indeed, that which is called the 'mouth' is the primary *cakra*."
By the reasoning stated in such passages as "the mouth of the Yoginī...
and so forth, the primary wheel is described; therefore, how could that consciousness—which arises from the friction of those two and whose very nature is pure self-experience—be depicted?
Anticipating the question, "How was this stated?", he says: "Now, those who contemplate this twofold creation, which consists of the states of the quiescent and the emergent... (3.126).
Established in that unconditioned state where the existence of emission (*visarga*) prevails in the east,
the word "atha" (now) serves as a response; by means of it, [the transition occurs] into this reality just described, which is of two kinds— quiescent and emergent.

"...the Self liberated through its own sovereignty" (1.5.16). According to this perspective, within the realm manifested by oneself during creation, there is the primordial [state]: "The supreme Kaula, the cause of both the quiescent and the emergent birth" (1.16).

By such statements as these, they contemplate the reality of emission (*visargasattā*), which consists of their union and serves as the cause for the arising of these two states; they realize that "all this is indeed the essence of its expansion," and thus they are established in the undivided plane— the meaning being that they rest in the full plane.
Having thus stated this regarding those who desire liberation, he now speaks also regarding those who desire worldly enjoyment:
"Those who wish to attain supernatural powers (siddhi) should, moreover, assume the form that has arisen. (3.127)

Those who desire to attain accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as the state of being established in the body (*piṇḍastha*) and so forth, should worship with that very [substance] which has the most pure nature due to its proximity to consciousness (*saṃvit*). They should take up that form which has arisen from it and is designated by terms such as *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*. Now, with that very [substance] thus arisen...
By virtue of its form, because of the proximity of consciousness to the state of being composed of bliss, as stated in the Śruti: "Bliss is the form of Brahman... and so forth.
"Therefore, one should take up that which is not too far removed from consciousness;
by this principle, they should worship with a most pure body— the meaning is that they should satisfy the circle of goddesses (devīcakra)."
And how could there be "bringing forth" (āharaṇa) and so on in this case? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Moreover, that [speech] also indeed arises mutually from the speaker; for it is said that, primarily, it resides in the speaker. (29.128)
"The supreme [elixir] known as *kula* is intent on bestowing the state of agelessness and immortality;
moreover, that exalted form is the excellent and auspicious *rasāyana* substance residing within one's own body."
By such a perspective, because [the deity] resides within the body itself, it is designated as *kula*; for this very reason, it is supreme. For this very reason, it is said:
"Śiva is eternally praised; that which is called worship is honored by the gods.
By merely consuming it, a human being becomes immortal."
Alternatively, O Goddess, the man who constantly consumes [the substance] mixed [with others] becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair and becomes dear to the Yoginīs;
by such a principle, [this teaching] primarily issues from the mouth as a means for bestowing the state of being ageless and immortal.
"From the mouth of the Yoginī" means from one another's mouth; "spoken" means declared in all the scriptures—this is the meaning.
For this [knowledge] indeed passes from the mouth of the Yoginī into one's own mouth, from there into the mouth of the Śakti, and from there back into one's own mouth.
"Then one should cast it into the *argha* vessel and so forth—thus say the Gurus. As the scripture also states:
"O slender-waisted one, having caused the *golaka* and the *kuṇḍa* there to dissolve, take that great substance situated therein with your mouth, O slender-waisted one."
Then, having placed that [substance] in his mouth and again having brought it back to his own mouth,
he should fill the vessel with that, mixed with great quantities of water.
"With that, one should prepare the vessel of honor (arghapātra), which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
Thus,
"Having gathered the great essence through the application of mouth-to-mouth,"
"With that, one should satisfy the wheel [of deities] together with the gods and heroes.
Thus,
"Then, having aroused the messenger (dūtī), whatever desire arises..."
"One should cause the accumulation of wealth arising from that to be shared mutually," and,
"In the same way, one should worship the mantra-vidyā with the power arising from both."
Thus [it is said].
Having thus described this regarding the sphere of the Knower (jñānin), he also speaks regarding the sphere of the Ritualist (karmin):
"Even those who have not attained awakening, yet are firmly rooted in the sacrifice that has blossomed forth... (29.129).
The deities situated within that imagined wheel attain consciousness.
"Those who have not attained awakening" means those whose knowledge has not yet taken root and who are established on the path of wonder—this is the meaning.
In that very context, he demonstrates the conceptualization of the deities residing in the wheel:
There, in that wheel of powers (śakticakra), they [are] externally composed of that very essence of bliss.

Having worshipped everything in the four directions according to the stated sequence, beginning with Gaṇanātha, one should worship the couple Kuleśa and Kuleśvarī in the central square, and the goddesses during the three moments of haste.

"Externally, on each spoke, there is indeed a tetrad; thus is the wheel of rays (*raśmicakra*) consisting of twelve [spokes]. Then the Sage should worship in sequence the various groups of eight and sixty-four within the wheel of power (*śakticakra*).
Regarding "in the wheel of power": this refers to the primary wheel, which pertains to Power and consists of the faces of the Yoginīs.
Such is the meaning. "By that very [form]" means by the form that has arisen. "As stated" refers to the occasion of describing the daily worship (nityārcā). "Arkāra" means twelve-spoked. || 132 ||
This is not to be worshipped only in the wheel of powers (śakticakra), but likewise within one's own self as well; thus he says:
"In the very same way, one should practice worship in the abode situated within one's own body.
Now, for those who contemplate emission (visarga), which consists of both [aspects] arising from their union (saṅghaṭṭa) and is uninterrupted—

It has been stated that "growth" (praroha) and the attainment of consciousness (vijñāna-prāpti) occur in the *pada*; however, one might raise the doubt: what is the destiny of those who have grown [in consciousness] within the emission (*visarga*) of the tranquil self (*śāntātman*)? Anticipating this, he says:
"That which is the tranquil form—by means of that practiced through the consciousness of the heart... (29.133).
He indeed attains the peaceful state of Śiva, which resembles an ocean whose waves have subsided.
The word "attains" implies one who has practiced the nature of peace. That very state of peace is made explicit by the phrase "resembling an ocean whose waves have subsided."
Now, one might ask: "If this were so, what would happen to him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because of his immersion in that state of peace, the entire host of deities residing within the wheel [becomes tranquil]. (29.134)
"He remains with his functions ceased, resting upon the void, devoid of bliss.
Regarding "with his functions ceased"—this is because of the complete dissolution of all objective states; for this very reason it is said, "resting upon the void," and for this same reason...
"...the supreme Śiva is without support.
By this vision, through resting in the state of Śiva, he is beyond [limited] bliss (nirānanda).
It is not only the host of deities situated in the central wheel who abide in this manner, but even those situated in the subordinate wheels; thus he says:
"Even he who possesses the nature of the subordinate wheels, such as sight and the rest, is dependent upon that [central wheel]. (29.135)

Therefore, he remains immersed in bliss, desiring bliss; "partaking of the nature of the subordinate wheels, such as sight and so forth"—that is to say, the host of deities. "Dependent upon that" means being under the control of the host of deities residing in the primary wheel. "By that" means by virtue of being dependent upon that.

Now, one might object: "In that case, let even the host of deities of the subordinate wheels (anucakra) rest in a state devoid of bliss; what need has this [host] for a longing for bliss? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Without the union with the nature of that Supreme Reality, this host of rays of the instruments... (29.136)

For this host of deities presiding over the senses, such as sight and so forth, remains devoid of its own specific form while being oriented toward the attainment of that essential nature; indeed, it abides within the Supreme—
the Self of the subject who is the very essence of consciousness— which, being filled with its own bliss, is the most excellent, and whose true reality has just been described.

The meaning is: without rest, being devoid of its own nature and incapable of performing its respective functions such as grasping objects, it remains intent on attaining its true nature and thus becomes desirous of bliss.
Anticipating the question, "What would such a collection of rays of the instruments do?", he says:
"By virtue of chewing external objects that are filled with its own essence, through the relish of longing. (29.137)
Having attained a certain state of rest within itself, it then offers [the object] back to its own self.

For this collection of rays of the senses, through attachment to desire, performs a "chewing" (carvaṇa) of those objects which— though filled with their own essence— are manifested externally solely by virtue of being composed of one's own consciousness.

Attachment (*rakti*); by its power, having attained a certain locus of rest consisting of self-reflection, it immediately— by implication— offers up the entire multitude of objects already relished within itself, in the self-contemplation of its own nature which unfolds through the full expansion of its respective enjoyments.

The meaning is that, according to such views as [verse 112], "Gradually the goddesses of the subordinate wheels enter the central wheel of consciousness," one attains rest within the primary wheel of consciousness, which is the self of the knower.
Now, one might ask: "What would happen to this [consciousness] through such repose in that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By the offering of its own object, there is a downpour of fully surging consciousness. (29.138)

The Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara), his vigor stirred by the fulfillment of the hosts of deities of the subordinate wheels, also surges forth with impetuosity according to the previously stated method. (29.139)

For the Lord, as the cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*), because he is the locus of rest for the wheels (*cakras*), is filled by the host of deities of the subordinate wheels (*anucakra*) through the offering of their respective objects;
thereby, his vital energy (*vīrya*) is stirred, and his own self-support (*avaṣṭambha*) becomes manifest. For this very reason:

First, there is the downpour of fully surging consciousness, which has attained vigor through the complete filling of the rays consisting of the deities of the subordinate wheels; that pair of Śakti and Śaktimān then becomes mutually oriented toward one another. (113)
By the reasoning stated in such passages, "one would leap forth with impetuosity"—meaning one would suddenly become oriented toward the external—this is the sense. || 139 ||
He concludes the very subject at hand: "In this way, the threefold emission (visarga) has arisen as both the 'clashing' (saṅghaṭṭa) and the 'tranquil' (śānta).
He shows the reason for the application of the term *visarga* across these three modes:
From which manifold creation is emitted, and wherein creation has ceased. || 29-140 ||
The word "yataḥ" is used in the sense of a reason. ||140||
And this is not our own invention alone—thus he says:
"That has been taught in the *Śrītattvarakṣaṇa*, the *Śrīnigama*, and the *Triśiromata*. Therein..."

Since the *Tattvarakṣāvidhāna* has already been cited previously with the words, "Therefore, the threefold emission is taught in the *Tattvarakṣāvidhāna*," etc., [the author] does not quote that text,
but rather corroborates it by citing the *Śrīgamaśāstra*:
The sacrificial pit is Śakti, Śiva is the Liṅga; their union is the supreme state.
In the *Gama*, emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), and their emission (*visarga*) are threefold according to two [principles].

The *kuṇḍa* is the form arisen from the power of the Lord (*bhagavat-śakti*); *Śiva* is the quiescent (*śānta*); and *melaka* is the union (*saṅghaṭṭa*). Because of its very state of arising, it is [the source] of emanation through Power; because of its very state of being quiescent, [it is the source of withdrawal].

Through the term "the supreme state" (paramaṃ padam) referring to the withdrawal by Śiva, there arises the Unnameable (anākhyam) due to the absence of all limitations through their union; thus, in the Gamaśāstra, this emission (visarga) is threefold.
Having thus brought the *Gamaśāstra* into agreement, he also brings the *Śrītriśirobhairava* into agreement:
"The awakening of the upper and lower wheels is the culmination of the two currents. (29.142)
And [he knows] the resting place and the immersion, as well as that of the channels and the vital airs;
and the absence of division in the mechanical organs, the joints, and even the vital points.

In the body of seventy-two thousand channels and in the thousand-petaled lotus, Śiva eternally brings about the union of the two cognitive faculties through their mutual movement and withdrawal. (29.144)
Through that effort, one should always abide in the state of Bhairava, which is the friction [of the two];
its characteristic is the attainment of the formless state of both. (29.145)
Free from the division of measures and clearly illuminating the manifest meaning,
it is here [the teaching] on the distinctions in the movement of the wheels, the channels, the instruments, the joints, the vital points, and the winds that reside eternally above and below.

Having brought about the awakening, resting, and immersion of the two currents of one's own right and left channels until their culmination— that is, up to their repose within the central channel— in the body consisting of seventy-two thousand locations;

By the statement beginning with, "There are seventy-two thousand channels in the navel-cakra," and so forth, [the yogi], having attained immersion into Śiva within by means of severing the prāṇa and apāna in the region of the navel— which is permeated by those channels— unites the two cognitive states consisting of the quiescent (śāntā) and the emergent (uditā).

One should become intent upon the essential nature of the union of those two; then, one should always remain with effort in the state of *saṅghaṭṭa*, which is the form of perfect consciousness— the meaning is that one should be attentive precisely there—
since it consists of the two forms characterized by quiescence and emergence.

Because it is devoid of the delimitation of all forms and so forth within its own specific locus, it possesses the true nature of being formless; for this very reason, because it is partless, it is free from any division of measure;
and thus, it is the illuminator of the object—which is perfectly manifest, consisting solely of the nature of one's own self-experience.
The meaning is "that which manifests."
And in this very context, firmness must be cultivated; thus he says:
"One should practice the consciousness of being by means of the withdrawal from all objective states. (29.146)
Having restrained the sun and moon by way of dissolution and emission,

having turned back from all states of being such as the cakras and so forth, and having blocked the prāṇa and apāna through the right and left paths, [one perceives] that which is woven through all states within the central abode.
One should practice that consciousness which consists of their union and has the nature of the subject— one should be intent solely on the reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) of that—
this is the meaning. However, if the reading is *vittīḥ*, it should be explained as "those [consciousnesses] whose nature is both quiescent and emergent."

Thus, in this way, whatever spontaneous reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) flashes forth for those who possess immersion (*samāveśa*) within these three kinds of emission (*visarga*), that alone is the supreme vitality of mantra (*mantravīrya*). Thus he says:
"In this manner, that which arises in the abode of the attainment of immersion into the threefold reflective awareness... (29.147).
Sound, whose essence is the reflective awareness of consciousness, is precisely what constitutes the potency (*vīrya*) of mantra here.
One who is eager to obtain such a fruit as has arisen therein [should contemplate] his own mantra. (29.148)
He who always remains in contemplation indeed knows the arising of the mantra;
whoever possesses such an immersion into emission (*visarga*) experiences that [state] at the moment of union (*saṅghaṭṭa*), as it is an object accessible solely through direct experience.
If one, being eager to attain that fruit which is full of bliss and impossible to describe,

remains constantly— rather than for a mere moment— intent upon the desired mantra within that very resonance (*dhvani*) consisting of the self-reflection of consciousness (*saṃvitparāmarśa*), which is composed of the wonder of "I" (*ahaṃcamatkāra*), then he [is a true practitioner].
In that context, one knows the "arising of the mantra"—the meaning is that his mantra becomes arisen.
And one who is intent on meditation should practice this very point again and again, so that one-pointedness may be accomplished in the central wheel alone; thus he says:
"One should perform recitation (japa) right here, upon the arrival of the consciousness of the unity of the subordinate wheels. (29.149)
"Simultaneously expanded through a hundred thousand divisions by means of the very activity of *nāda*,
the goddesses of the subordinate wheels (*anucakra*) gradually enter the central wheel of consciousness.
(112) According to this and other such perspectives, [the goddesses] enter into the form of the primary wheel as the unity of the goddesses of the subordinate wheels simultaneously.
When there is an arrival at consciousness— that is, a state of rest— it occurs right here within the mantra, which consists of the reflective awareness of consciousness,
by virtue of being composed solely of the reflective awareness of the *nāda*.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) as elaborated through the various types of *lakṣas* mentioned in such passages as, "At the arising, at the union, and at the cessation, the recitation is said to consist of three *lakṣas*";
that is to say, one should repeatedly carry out the contemplation (*anusandhāna*). This is the meaning.
And it is stated elsewhere that this alone is the supreme vigor even among the mudrās; thus he says: "In the *Śrīyogasañcara* as well, this mudrā is said to be supremely dear to the Yoginīs. (29.150)

In the lotus that covers the mandala which is eternally oriented toward the interior of the three corners, there is a stalk that is never separated [from it], its excellent root formed by a sixteen-petaled lotus. (29.151)

Through the process of the friction of the pair of lotuses joined by the central stalk, and through the collision of the streams of digits of the full, beautiful moon and the sun situated in the center within the fire; || 29-152 ||

From the contact with the red, three-petaled energy (*vīrya-kalā*), the sprout— the creation— emerges in the center. That which exists within the three corners, eternally upward-facing and always blossoming,
is the "three-petaled lotus of the womb" (*bhaga-padma*).

By such statements as these, the three-petaled covering of the mandala—the *bhaga-kamala* (vulva-lotus) belonging to the male or the female—is joined with the letter *sa* (*sataviyuta*) due to its quality of providing nourishment, according to the verse: "That which is semen, that is the Moon... and so forth.

By such statements as these, [the center] is characterized by the sixteen-petaled lunar lotus; for this very reason, because it is replete with bliss (*ānanda*), it is "existent" (*sat*); for this very reason, it is the root and the abode of origin of the emanation whose nature will be described hereafter, which is the stalk consisting of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*).
"Let the left [channel] be the carrier of water (ambuvāhā), the middle the carrier of semen (śukravāhinī),
and the one situated on the right the carrier of blood (raktavāhā)..."— by this statement, that which is strung together or woven by means of that central stalk...
The pair of lotuses pertaining to woman and man, through the process of their mutual friction—

the moon and the sun, consisting of semen and menses, who are situated between them, full, unimpaired, and therefore beautiful due to their nature as bliss— arise from the conjunction of their digits.

By the statement, "The fire named Śuci arises from the friction of the sun and the moon," when the fire— which is of a single nature with the subject (pramātṛ)— has shone forth, that which consists of the expansion of consciousness arises from the union of the energies of *rajas* and *retas* in the center of the three-petaled lotus.
The sprout is capable of containing the universe within itself; that creation likewise manifests externally—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Fire resides in the *bhaga*, and the Sun resides within the *liṅga*."
"The wise one is situated above; from the friction [of the union], the essence (rasa) emerges.
Thus, "That is the seat (pīṭha) in the wheel of the Śākinīs; that is the creation, including the moving and the unmoving."
That is the field for the king of seeds, which arises during the proper season.
[He saw] Hāṭakeśvara, the golden [linga], situated in the center of the pericarp, belonging to the lineage that enjoys the pollen and flowers, both of the noble and the ignoble.
"And: 'The supreme Śiva, non-dual, is dissolved within the interior of the lotus of power.
Thus it is said.
Now, one might ask: "What would happen to him by binding this mudrā? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, by the mudrā of the union of the Moon, the Lord of Day, and Citragu, [he attains it] instantaneously. (29.153)
Bringing the sequence beginning with emanation (sṛṣṭi) within, one attains stability in the fourth state (turya).
By the word "conjunction" (saṅghaṭṭa), its possession of the arrangement of the six spokes is indicated.

Having thus described the nature of the mudrā by means of the extension of the mantra’s potency, he speaks again in order to demonstrate their mutual state of fusion and to extend that potency back into the mantras:
"In this penetration of the Khecarīmudrā, there is [the union] of the Power and the Possessor of Power with one another. (29.154)

That which consists of discernment during drinking, enjoyment, play, laughter, and so forth, [manifests] through unarticulated sounds, resonance, outbursts, audible sounds, and the various stages of sound up to its final cessation. (29.155)
The potency of those mantras would consist in their having the nature of an uninterrupted, unstruck sound (*anāhata*).
When there is immersion (*āveśa*) into this *khecarīmudrā*, which is characterized by the seal of six spokes,
that experience which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśātmā*) arises from the mutual drinking and enjoyment of the Power (*śakti*) and the Possessor of Power (*śaktimān*).
If that were to arise, it would be the mantra-power (māntra-vīrya), whose nature is the awareness of the supreme sound (paranāda) divided into eight forms beginning with the unmanifest (avyakta).
"The attainment of that [state] occurs through repeated cultivation right here"—thus he says:
"Thus, established upon the eightfold wheel and performing the innate recitation (japa) in the supreme abode... (29.156).
One attains that state of the eight Bhairavas which is differentiated by the eight kalās;
"differentiated by the eight kalās" means it is divided— i.e., distinguished— by the eight kalās beginning with Ardhacandra and ending with Unmanā.
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is this 'eightfold wheel' (cakrāṣṭaka) mounted upon which one should perform recitation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When going and coming have ceased, in the ears, the eyes, and in contact with the two organs [of generation and excretion]," (29.157).
In the conjunction of their union (*tatsaṃmelanayoga*), which is called the "end of the body" (*dehānta*) and constitutes the *yāmala* wheel;

[this occurs] during the coming and going of the *apāna* together with the *prāṇa*—such is the meaning. When the resolve has reached its limit—that is, when the intellect (*buddhi*) has completed its determination—there is "contact" (*saṃparka*), which is merely a touch. This is what is meant by "in the conjunction of their union."
The meaning is: "at the time of their union," that is, at the occasion of the friction (*saṅghaṭṭa*) of those two signs;
"in what is called the end of the body" means in the *dvādaśānta*; "in the *yāmala* wheel" applies as a remainder to all [the preceding].
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the locus of the eight Bhairavas here, which could be differentiated by the eight digits (kalās) beginning with the half-moon? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is unmanifest, residing in the throat, from the region of the heart between the breasts down to the lips. (29.158)
Having heard that which resides between those two wheels at the moment when agitation ceases, they attain extinction right there; and thus, the supreme eightfold Nādabhairava [is realized].
That supreme pervasion of mantra, produced by light, sound,
and breath, is said to extend from the region of the heart and the center of the breasts up to the lips and the interior of the throat.
"That which is the supreme, unshakeable syllable arising from the throat of the Beloved, called the innate sound (nāda), is the eternally manifest reality; that is recitation.
Thus [it is said].

That which arises as the two syllables "hā-hā"—a state that is almost unmanifest and whose nature is described in passages such as, "From the tasting of the essence of eternal bliss, 'hā-hā' resounds within the hollow of the throat; it is the self-existent, the utterance that bestows happiness, and the revealer of the reality of Kāma. That [is what is meant].

At the moment of the cessation of the agitation whose nature consists of mutual friction, having discerned that which has come to rest within the primary wheel consisting of the mouth of the Yoginī, all attain extinction— that is,
they find repose— in that very state which is the nature of Nirvāṇa.

Thus, by way of having the unmanifest (avyakta) and other forms, it is eightfold; for this very reason, it is the radiance of the eight digits (kalās) beginning with the half-moon (ardhacandra); for this very reason, it is the supreme Nādabhairava. That supreme mantric pervasion (vyāpti) is said to be everywhere—this is the meaning of the sentence. Light (jyotiḥ).
The half-moon is the resonance, the sound; the wind is the power whose nature is touch; and it is established by implication that what is below is pervaded by the moon itself.

And here, raising the doubt as to what that group of eight Bhairavas is and what the mantric pervasion (vyāpti) consists of, he says: "The Sakala, Akala, Īśa, Śūnya, Kalāḍhya, Kha, Amala, and likewise Kṣapaṇaka. (29.160)
The internal [phoneme] is gutturo-labial; thus, from the Moon (C) up to the end of Unmanā, there is pervasion.

Since these arise at the moment of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śakti and the Possessor of Śakti (*śaktimān*), it is inappropriate to designate them by either one of those two; therefore, their neuter gender alone is appropriate, as indicated by that grammatical gender.
The exposition.
Thus, through the cultivation of this pervasion, his state of supreme Bhairava will arise everywhere; so he says:
"In this way, remembering the pervasion in every single action, wherever it may be... (3.161).
One who is eternally untainted is liberated while living and becomes the Supreme Bhairava.
And at such an occasion of union (*melaka*), one who has taken birth is most excellent—thus he says:
"Whoever may be in the womb, his body adorned by the bud of such a union. (29.162)
He, born of the Yoginīs, is himself Rudra, the vessel of gnosis;
for even as a child still in the womb, he is of the nature of Śiva, according to the venerable Vīrāvaliśāstra. (163)

Now, one might ask: "What is the reason for applying the term *ādiyāga* here, given the statement: 'Thus, O Goddess of the God of Gods, the *ādiyāga* has been described by you'?"—anticipating this doubt, [the author says]:
He said:
"Because the essence is taken from this, and because it is the primary [sacrifice], and because it is the principal sacrifice, it is therefore known as the Ādiyāga. (29.164)
And in various treatises, the All-pervasive Lord has praised its essential nature in the *Śrīvīrāvali*, the *Hārdeśa*, the *Khamata*, and those existing within the *Arṇava*. (29.165)

In the Śrīsiddha, Utphulla, Maryādā, Hīna, Caryā, Kula, and other [tantras], it is the essence—consisting of the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) and characterized by nectar (*amṛta*). Therefore, it is both "the beginning" (*ādi*) and "the sacrifice" (*yāga*);
that is, it is the sacrifice of the "beginning," which is the primary wheel (*mukhyacakra*). For this very reason, it is present in all the scriptures (*sarvāgama*).
The supreme excellence—thus he says, beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth. *Hārdeśa* is the Lord of the Heart (*hṛdayabhaṭṭāraka*).

*Khematam* is the *Khecarīmata*. *Arṇava* is the Ocean of the Womb (*yonyarṇava*). "Residing therein" means, by implication, within certain portions of those texts. *Utphulleti* refers to the *Utphullakamata*. It is devoid of conventional constraints (*maryādāhīna*).
The scripture is without boundaries. As it has been said:
"This Kaulika sacrifice of yours, which bestows the supernatural powers of yoga immediately, has been declared as the supreme secret, utterly bewildering to those who hold to duality."
For heroes, it bestows both suffering and happiness, and through the playful application of the union of yoga,
the fire sacrifice on the day of worship is prescribed.
But for the deluded who stand on the path of beasts and perform evil deeds,
O Goddess, it must always remain unrevealed, just as one would keep some great treasure hidden.
And here, the supreme sacrifice is not situated in external nature, yet it is of great success;
there is no sacrificial pit, no fire-offering, no ritual of oblations, and no mandala.
In this [rite], there is no invocation, nor indeed any dismissal;
there is no performance of the image-sacrifice (mūrtiyāga), nor any other seat.
Free from the practice of vows and devoid of external substances,
it is filled with the nectar of one's own bliss and bestows the attainment of great bliss.
And when only the Self exists, it is Śiva, consisting of all powers,
possessing all forms yet formless, the source of the self, both supreme and non-supreme.
The great yogi should meditate upon that and worship the Lord of the Wheel;
this is the supreme secret, the most profound mystery, and the application of the highest [practice].
This Kaulika tradition, which vibrates with brilliance, has been imparted today out of affection for you.
You must always keep it well-guarded; O lover of heroes, it must not be given away.
It is certainly not for dualists of limited intellect, whose minds are afflicted by greed,
nor for those who employ illusion, those of cruel nature, or even for those merely seeking knowledge.
Even if one who knows the mantra should dwell on the surface of the earth like a mute after having given away the entire earth, then he attains success and shall obtain the assembly of the Siddhas.
"Released from all diseases, one attains perfection with this very body;
by means of this path of yoga, I speak no falsehood.
Thus [it is said].
In this [system], the scripture consists of four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*) by virtue of its nature as knowledge (*vidyā*), mantra, mudrā, and maṇḍala.

Among these, the tradition concerning the two seats consisting of mantra and mudrā has already been stated. Now, here [we shall explain] the tradition of this very [scripture] regarding the remaining two seats, which consist of knowledge and the maṇḍala.
He explains:
"By the grace of this couple, one who is devoid of vows and yogic practice [attains the goal]. (29.166)
Having maintained constant mindfulness and being solely intent upon the primordial sacrifice (ādiyāga),
one should project the Vidyā and the Kūṭas in their proper sequence onto the body of Śakti within oneself.
Having meditated upon the lotus resembling the moon and oneself as possessing the radiance of the sun,
one should here itself unite the two seats consisting of the Vidyā and the Mantra.

By the grace of this aforementioned pair of seats (pīṭha), which consists of mantra and mudrā, the Guru— through mere contemplative realization alone, independent of vows, yoga, and the like— is at all times devoted to the primordial sacrifice (ādiyāga); he is Śākta because his lotus [of the heart] is filled with bliss.

Having meditated upon oneself as resembling the moon yet possessing the brilliance of the sun due to its capacity to bring about expansion, one should sequentially project the desired mantra— predominantly *śakti* in nature— into one's own body, which is of the nature of *śakti*, and the *kūṭa* (syllabic cluster) or mantra, which is predominantly *śiva* in nature, so that right here [in this very state],...
Through the varying degrees of application to the reasoning just stated, even the two seats consisting of *vidyā* and *mantra* shall become merged. || 168 ||
And because this is an extreme secret, we have not explained it by breaking it down into parts; therefore, it must be understood by oneself—thus he says:
"Furthermore, because of its secrecy, it is not recited by me in explicit words."
But one who is curious should discern [the truth] simply from the thorough study of the stated scriptures. || 29-169 ||
In this very context, in order to also describe its nature as the maṇḍala, he says:

"That which all [beings] always worship, and by virtue of which the Lord and the deities exist—that is the supreme wheel (cakra), which brings about the presence [of the deities] at the goddess-worship and other rites. (29.170)
The body itself is the supreme *liṅga*, the auspicious (*śiva*) essence of all principles (*tattva*);
frequented by the circle of deities, it is the most excellent abode for worship. (29.171)
That very mandala is primary, consisting of three tridents, lotuses, wheels, and space;
right here one should always worship the circle of deities, both externally and internally. (29.172)
Preceded by the reflective awareness of their respective mantras, one should touch [the object] with the aesthetic flavors (rasas) born thereof—
which abound in bliss— by means of the process of emanation and withdrawal.

"Yadvān" means possessing the primordial support (*ādyādhāra*). "And the deity" implies, by implication, that she possesses it. "The wheel" refers to the primary wheel. For this very reason, it is said: "The supreme [wheel] consists of three tridents, a lotus, a wheel, and space.
Regarding the phrase "in the triple-trident": here, within the seven-spoked [wheel], it is joined from the center.

The meaning is that its form consists of seven lotuses, wheels, or voids, according to the principle that will be stated later [in 31.28]: "There may be seven of lotuses, wheels, or voids. The phrase *svasva* means "of each respective [desire].
The phrase *tajjanmabhiḥ* means "by those born from it," namely, by the *kuṇḍa*, *golaka*, and so forth, which have emerged from the primary wheel (*mukhyacakra*).
"By the method of emission and withdrawal"—the meaning is: "by means of the sequence of the quiescent and the emergent. || 173 ||
And what would happen to him in this case? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Lord of that wheel of consciousness, awakened by the intensity of contact with that [object], attains the supreme abode, having satisfied all the deities. (3.174)

According to the procedure prescribed for the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga), one should satisfy [the deities] within by means of substances that captivate the heart, likewise through the application of their respective reflective awarenesses (kāmarśa). 29.175.
"According to the procedure taught for the *anuyāga*," as was stated previously:
"Whatever indeed bestows expansion upon his mind, with that very thing he should perform the worship; such is the settled conclusion of Śambhu. (26.55)
Having begun with these words, [the text continues]:
"The wise one should offer back into the supreme abode that very rasa which flows forth from the multitude of entities due to their being filled with non-difference from Śiva" (26.61).
Thus [ends the verse]. ||175||
And in order to illuminate this excess of reverence, he corroborates it with a portion of his own hymn that was previously cited:
"Having made the foundational earth washed by the momentary sprinkling of the essence of wonder..."
With the flowers of my own nature, which are naturally fragrant and abundant with their own scent,
and by means of the priceless offering-vessel of my own heart filled with the nectar of bliss, I worship you, O God, together with the Goddess, day and night within the temple of the body.
Nor has this been stated by us as our own invention; thus he says:
"In the collection of scriptures such as the Śrīvīrāvalī and the Amaryāda, this very supreme sacrifice was praised by the Moon-crested Lord. (29.177)
"This" refers to the body; with this very intention it was stated elsewhere: "One should go to one's own body as the abode, and not to any other abode," and so forth. ||177||
And this [rite] should be performed not only in the body but also in the vital breath (prāṇa); thus he says:

"Alternatively, the Guru should perceive the entire host of deities residing within the function of the vital breath by means of the very method previously described, and worship them right there. (3.178)
And how is worship to be performed here? To this he says:

"The satiation of the goddesses who reside in the vital breaths is accomplished by means of the lunar wheel of the apāna [breath] entering through the cranial apertures that pierce the Brahma-nāḍī and the others. (3.179)
"Brahma" refers to the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā). ||179||
And what would happen for him in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this manner, by means of the sequence of the vital breath (prāṇa) alone, one should satisfy the host of deities;
then, through their grace, one quickly attains the perfections of knowledge. (29.180)

Or rather, what is the use of the body and so forth, which are not of the nature of the Self? One should satisfy the circle of goddesses (devīcakra) by means of its very abiding in consciousness—thus he says: "Or, the circle of goddesses, which resides in pure consciousness alone, [is satisfied] through the offering to consciousness."
It should be satisfied by the wise one through the application of universal enjoyment.

It has been explained that [the world appears] "through the offering of consciousness" by means of the application of the universal expansion; for this very reason, it is called "the All-knowing One" (vipaścit). || 181 ||
Now, one might ask: even for the wise, while the body and so forth still exist, how can the wheel of goddesses (devīcakra) abiding in pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra) be satisfied? To this he says:
"In that [state] where all things go to dissolution, the accumulations of the principles (tattva) are consumed."
Behold that funeral pyre situated within the body, possessing a radiance equal to the fire of time.

Behold that consciousness residing in the body, which possesses a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction because it effects the dissolution of the entire universe; therein all subjects, beginning with Sakala, and all objects of knowledge, consisting of past and future entities, attain identity with it— consciousness alone, even while the body and other such things persist.
The meaning is that she alone vibrates everywhere. || 182 ||
He clarifies this very point:
"In this cremation ground, whose nature is emptiness, frequented by yoginīs and siddhas, a place of play that is most fierce, wherein all formal structures have subsided. (183)

In that which is filled with circles of light rays, in which the succession of darkness has been destroyed, which is liberated from all conceptual constructions, and which is the absolute state of bliss; 29.184.
In this cremation ground, terrifying with its funeral pyres and filled with countless mounds, which person who has entered this support of all deities does not attain accomplishment? (29.185)

In this body—which is filled with countless states of consciousness consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth; which is for that very reason most terrible because it inflicts the torments of saṃsāra; and which is, for that same reason, like a cremation ground because it must be abandoned—what person who has entered within and turned inward does not attain perfection?

Such is the connection [of the words]. And of what nature is this? Because of its inward-turned state, it is of the nature of emptiness (*śūnya*) due to the dissolution of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*) therein; for that very reason, it is the cessation of the forms of all [entities], beginning with the *sakala*; and for that very reason, it is that which has destroyed the succession of darkness.
In that which has utterly destroyed the darkness of duality, and for that very reason is liberated from all conceptual constructions;

and for that very reason is filled within itself—and not externally—with the circle of rays consisting of the assembly of deities of the senses such as sight; and for that very reason is served by yoginīs and siddhas, and is the support of all deities; and for that very reason...
"The goddesses, situated within the *piṇḍa*, sport through various states.

Thus, this is the place of their play; for this very reason, it is the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) as the locus of the convention (*saṅketa*) of all deities; and for this very reason, it is consciousness (*cit*), which effects the withdrawal of all things and is of a single nature with the subject (*pramātṛ*).
In the terrifying, and for that very reason, in the state of absolute bliss which rests solely in one's own self—this is the meaning.
Nor is this our own invention; thus he says:
"In the venerable Vīrāvalīśāstra, Bhairavī spoke as follows:
'Here, the sequence of consciousness consisting of practice (caryā), though already alluded to, is now set forth separately because of its extreme secrecy.'"
Since it was not stated separately, the learned should not harbor resentment toward us.
Thus, concluding the sequence of the *Rahasyopaniṣad* connected with the procedure for the messenger (*dautavidhi*), he introduces the ritual of initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*):
"Having first performed the sacrifice in this manner, [one should initiate] one who possesses such fitness. (29.186)
One should initiate that disciple who has reached the state of "one in a hundred thousand" within such a sequence.

The term "one in a hundred thousand" refers to one who has been repeatedly tested and found worthy; for this very reason it is called "one's own disciple," meaning one who possesses such worthiness. "Within such [a sequence]"—that is, within a process of that nature.
In this way, their essential nature has been defined.
He says that very thing: "Having sprinkled it with the power of Rudra (rudraśakti), one should place it in the presence of the deity. (29.187)
Having gazed upon his two arms, he should inflame them with the power of Rudra;
with that very power, he should place a flower upon his hands, which have been smeared with fragrant unguents.
Having established those two as being without support,
he should contemplate them being drawn forth by the power of Rudra in the form of a blazing goad.
Then, having personally taken up the cloth, he should blindfold his eyes;
and he himself should cast down a flower, and from its falling, one should discern the *kula*.
Then, having opened his mouth, one should cause him to prostrate at the feet;
and upon his hands and head, one should worship the circle of goddesses.
The *mālinī* [mantra] is encapsulated by the power of Rudra (*rudraśakti*) through the supreme state of the Mothers (*mātṛsadbhāva*).

"It should inflame" means that one should stimulate the mass of powers residing in the heart, which has emerged through the gateway of the fingers, by means of the process of drawing it forth. "By that very [power]" means by the power of Rudra.

"Without support" (*nirālambau*) means that because their own worldly, artificial powers have dissolved away, they are as if lifeless—this is the sense. "In the form of a goad" (*aṅkuśarūpayā*) is used because it is appropriate for drawing [them] toward oneself. "From that" (*tataḥ*) refers to the reason of contemplating the two arms as being drawn by the power of Rudra.
"One should observe"—for in this way his own lineage will be accomplished without effort.
"One should prostrate"—[this refers to] Śakti alone. || 191 ||
Anticipating the question, "And how should one worship the wheel of goddesses (devīcakra) here?",
he says: "By means of the relationship of attractor and attracted, and of impeller and impelled—
one should worship the wheel of goddesses in the hands as the object to be impelled, and on the head as the impeller."

Since that which is to be attracted is the attractor itself, thus, by the power of the circle of goddesses worshipped at the crown of the head, the two hands are drawn forth; falling right there, they attain the state of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta). As it has been said:
Then, having worshipped the wheel on his head and in his two hands,
the knower of yoga should impel those two hands with power until they reach the end of the head.
"The ritual of Śiva’s hand has been proclaimed, which produces immediate conviction.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, when this procedure for the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta) should not succeed, then one should follow the sequence from another scripture; thus it is said:
"In the venerable Ratnamālā, it is stated that the navel is enclosed by the staff. (29.192)
Adorned with the left [hand], the ornaments, the shanks, and also the hips,
one should apply the *codanā-astra* (the impelling weapon) into the hand of the disciple which holds flowers.
Until he reaches a state of trembling and falls down of his own accord,
this very Hand of Śiva spontaneously produces immediate conviction.
By this very procedure, the Guru should have the disciple take the sacrificial pap (caruka) and the tooth-stick; their falling [of the tooth-stick] is exactly as before. (29.195)

The navel is *kṣa*. The staff is the letter *ra*; by this, it is "enclosed," meaning joined above and below. The left ornament is *ū*. The left shank is *au*. The hip is *m*, which, by implication, is in the form of a bindu. Thus, [the mantra] is *rakṣtrauṃ*. The word "that" (*sa*) refers to the hand of Śiva. As it has been said:
In that regard:
"Having extracted the root-staff, one should extract the phoneme situated at the navel;
it is seated upon the trident-staff-throne and joined with the left ornament."
"Joined with the left shank and adorned by the hips, O beloved—
this supreme divine weapon is clearly not obtained by one who lacks merit. Thus it begins.
"O Maheśānī, one should apply this peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) to the hand of Śiva; O Goddess, as soon as he utters it, that [hand] moves of its own accord.
Thus, it is said to "produce immediate conviction"—wherever in the wheel of the body the hand is applied, [it occurs] instantly.

"The Guru says that one should remain intent on practice right there where [the drop] falls. By 'by this very [means]'—it means by way of the relationship characterized as attractor and attracted. 'The sacrificial pap (caruka)'—that is, having caused it to be offered before the Goddesses. 'By the disciple'—this is the instrumental case used for the indirect agent (*prayojyakartṛ*). 'Just as before'—"
As stated in the Fifteenth Daily Lesson (Pañcadaśāhnika). || 195 ||

Now, one might object: "Since his possession by power (*śaktyāveśa*) has already been indicated by the single paralysis of the hand (*karastobha*) consisting of the seizing of the eye-cloth, what is the purpose of mentioning that [possession] again? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The paralysis of the hand, indeed, [is that which occurs] from the seizing of the eye-cloth onwards."
One should observe therein the limit up to the taking up of the tooth-stick. || 29-196 ||
"In that manner" refers to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) characterized by distinctions such as intense or mild;
"in that place" means in such a paralysis of the hand (*karastobha*). "In that manner" means distinguished as intense, mild, and so forth.
This is the underlying intention here: for when the falling of the flower occurs in a particular wheel (*cakra*), it is precisely there [that the initiation takes place].

Prostration, the offering of *caru* at that very spot, and the receiving of it from that same source—by such signs as these, one should recognize whether the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is intense; otherwise, it is considered mild. As it has been said:
"From their movements, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should examine the descent of power."
"The wise one [should know that] it is weak, intense, and so forth, according to the distinction of being weak, intense, and so forth.
Thus [it is said].
Thus, by this much, the initiation of the *samayin* has been described in our system; so he says:
"In this way, he is declared a *samayin* in the *Śrīpūrva* [Tantra] by virtue of the trembling of the hand. (29.197)
And this has not been stated here as something previously unknown; thus he says:
"But the initiate [attains it] from the paralysis of the hand," according to the *Śrībhogahastaka*, as stated in the *Śrīpañcāśikā*.
"But by the shaking of the hand with the mudrā, one becomes a *putraka*," and so forth.
Right here, he states another procedure:
"Or rather, the Guru should give [the substance] smeared with the nectar of the left. (29.198)
By receiving [the teachings] without hesitation, one becomes a Śaktigotra who is freed from illusion;
however, by receiving them while trembling, one becomes a Samayin in matters such as recitation and so forth.
"Through purification of the paths over time, and by maintaining the observance of the rules through protection, one is called a 'vessel for accomplishment' in the venerable Ānandeśvara. (29.200)
Regarding the word *caru*: it consists of the five jewels and so forth. As it has been said:
"I shall describe the *caru* residing within the body, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain:
the water of Śiva, semen, and blood; the stalk, the clarified butter, and the emergence of the universe."
"Therefore, according to the prescribed ritual, one should have the sacrificial pap (caru) taken while it remains within the body.
The phrase "of the Śakti-lineage" means having the nature of a constituent part of Brahmyā and the others. For this very reason, by taking [it] without hesitation, one is freed from Māyā.

The meaning is that one becomes a direct realization of the reality of non-conceptual, effortless consciousness (*anupāya-saṃvitti*). For this very reason, it was previously stated that the consumption of the sacrificial pap (*caru*) and so forth constitute the auxiliary (*parikara*) of the effortless means (*anupāya*). Furthermore, one who takes up this [practice] while still possessing doubt would be a fit initiate (*samayin*) for the recitation, hearing, and other such rites, by which—
Subsequently, one whose intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*) has been indicated by the observance of the respective conventions of those scriptures shall,

through the complete purification of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidha-adhvan*) according to the sequence of the *putraka* initiation, become a vessel for the attainment characterized by the fortune of liberation. And this is not...
He states that this was indeed spoken by himself: "It is called the venerable Ānandeśvara. (29-200)
Having thus explained the initiation of the *samayin*, he begins to describe the initiation of the *putraka*:
"But when one would make someone a *putraka*, then one should perform the initiation.
Here, first of all—

"O Dear One, he who performs initiation for someone without the initiation of piercing (vedhadīkṣā)—both of these go to hell; such is the certainty of the Śākta tradition. According to such statements, initiation must not be performed for a disciple without [an experience of] possession (āveśa); thus, first comes possession.

In this very way [the disciple] is to be produced, so that once his fitness for initiation is known, the Guru may perform the ritual procedure for it; otherwise, however, because of the absence of eligibility for initiation, he is simply to be abandoned. As it will be said:
"But for one who might still think thus even so, one should not abandon him here [in this practice].
To demonstrate that immersion (*samāveśa*) is taught without contradiction across all scriptures, he states its definition according to the sense as it is expressed in the *Śrīratnamālā*:
"It is stated in the *Śrīratnamālā* [that one should contemplate] the [alphabet] from *na* to *pha*, blazing with light... (29.201).
One should perform the deposition up to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); by that, one falls [into the state of Rudra], and thus such a sequence occurs here.

"By that" means by reason of such a deposition. "Falls" means that, through the abandonment of the grasping of the body and so forth as the self, one enters into the power of Rudra itself—this is the meaning.
Thus it is said there:
"Then one should project Mālinī, the Mother of the World, who resembles a blazing fire, upon the disciple from the feet up to the top of the head."
"By the recitation of the letters from *na* to *pha*, one causes [the disciple] whose senses are agitated to fall;
this is initiation, O Beloved, in the *Mālinīvijaya* by the Great Goddess.
Regarding the word "by that" (*tena*)—it should be applied like the eye of a crow (to both preceding and following terms); thus, "by that" means "by the cause of falling. Herein:
Regarding the initiation of a "son" (putrakadīkṣā): "of this kind" means as will be described hereafter. He states that very point:
"Of the child who has been sprinkled with water and upon whom the sequence of the paths to be purified, as previously mentioned, has been projected... (29.202).
The Guru, becoming one with that [power], should contemplate the Śakti as straight-bodied, having reached from the feet to the top of the head, blazing brightly and burning away the fetters. (29.203)
Having sat down, one should then meditate in succession on the fire burning from the root to be purified up to the very end of the limit of what is to be purified at the conclusion.
In this manner, having burned all the principles (tattva) and so forth to be purified as previously described,
one should meditate upon them as dissolved into Śiva, whether he be considered partless (niṣkala) or with parts (sakala).
When joined with the path by the yogin, it nourishes that which is of the same nature, while it utterly consumes the entire collection of that which is of a different nature. (29.206)

"Consisting of that" means consisting of the radiant power (*dīptaśakti*). "From there" means immediately after arising. "The root-purification" refers to the first purification, such as *nivṛtti* on the path of the kalās; "the end-purification" refers to the final purification, such as *śāntyatītā* in this very context. "In this manner" means beginning from the root-purification and ending with the end-purification.
"Pure," as stated in the section on the initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*). "In the partless" (*niṣkala*) refers to in relation to the spiritual sons (*putraka*) and others;

"in the with-parts" (*sakala*) refers to with respect to the aspirant (*sādhaka*). "On the path" (*mārge*) means in the central channel (*madhyadhāman*). "Of the same genus" (*sajātīya*) is consciousness (*caitanya*); "of different genera" (*bhinnajātīya*) are the impurities (*mala*) and so forth. || 206 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the fruit of this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"For the disciple being purified by this [initiation], through the various degrees of the descent of power (śaktipāta), such as the intense and so forth, his bodies—consisting of consciousness, space, breath, and those internal and external [to the body]—" (29.207)
Entering [the body], the power of Rudra gradually produces these fruits:
bliss, arousal, trembling, sleep, and a whirling sensation within the body. (29.208)

Thus, for this disciple whose bonds have been burnt away, Rudra’s power—entering his consciousness directly through an intensely intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—begets bliss; whereas, [that same power], entering the body through a very mild descent of power, begets a state of reeling (*ghūrṇi*). For:

Bliss is appropriate for the *cit* because it is of the nature of bliss; emergence is appropriate for the void (*vyoman*) which is the self of the *śūnya*, because of its capacity to provide space; trembling is appropriate for the wind which is the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because of its agency;
and sleep is appropriate for the internal body, the city of the intellect (*buddhipuryaṣṭaka*), because of the cessation of the various functions of *māyā*.
The sense is that because the obstruction in the external [channels] has been shattered, there is a "whirling" [of consciousness];
thus, the teacher may have confidence that initiation has truly taken place for him. || 208 ||

One might raise the objection: "In this way, since his bonds have been stunned and he has been joined to Śiva alone, would it not follow that the fall of the body occurs at that very moment? Anticipating this, he says:
"Thus, for the self whose bonds are stunned and who has been joined to Śiva..."
For the sake of remaining enjoyment, one should perform the creative act directed toward the completely purified reality-level.
"Of the remainder"—that is, of the karma that initiated this body. "Creation"—meaning, specifically the creation pertaining to this very body. (209)

Even so, if for someone whose descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is weak this immersion does not arise due to the non-appearance of these signs, then one should perform another purification for him; thus he says: "Or else, if for someone there is no such immersion, one should burn him."
Thus, by the aforementioned power, he would fall to the earth both outside and inside.
However, one for whom even this [instruction] might not suffice should not abandon it here; rather,
he should visualize a triangle facing upward with masses of fire rising and falling simultaneously,
seated within which is the [seed-syllable] encircled on all sides by the letter *ra*, consisting of a mass of flames through its power (*śakti*).

"One should burn [the impurities] both externally and internally"—thus say the Gurus. "It may not be so"—this refers to the *āveśa* (spiritual immersion). "Like a stone"—the meaning is that, because the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has not occurred, there is a state of dense insentience.

For a disciple who has been thus abandoned continues to sink and surface within the cycle of existence (saṃsāra); therefore, with the intent to favor him, he speaks of another unimpeded initiation (dīkṣā) established through both the Guru and the scripture:
Now, I shall describe the initiation accompanied by conviction, as taught by the wise and satisfied [teacher].
"Taught by Śambhunātha and seen in the *Sadbhāvaśāsana*.
Regarding the phrase "in the *Sadbhāvaśāsana*": it refers to the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*.
He states that very same thing: "The nectar, fire, and wind; the slow, supreme, and fire-winds. (29.212)
Fire, temple, pleasure, peak, fire, and wind— each of these, together with the sixth [syllable], is said to be one of the three clusters that effect *stobha*.
*Sudhā* is *sa*, *agni* is *ra*, *marut* is *ya*; thus, *sryaṃ*. *Manda* is the letter *ḍa*;

the one following it is the letter *ḍha*, which is denoted by the word *phaṇabhṛt* (serpent); *kāla* (time) is *ma*, the ender who pacifies the vital breath (*prāṇaśamana*); *agni* is *ra*, and *vāyu* is *ya*; thus, *ḍḍhmyraṃ*.
*Vahni* is *ra*; (*saudha*) *soma* is *sa*; *asu* (vital breath) is *ha*; *kūṭa* is *kṣa*;
*agni* is *ra*; *vāyu* is *ya*. Thus: *rashkṣyūī*. Here, the *dvandva* compound is used in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*).
"All" refers to all three *piṇḍas*. "With the sixth vowel" means they are situated upon the seat of the vowel *ū*.
