"And marked with the *bindu* and so forth. "Each one" means individually or separately. As it is said there:
"Now, even so, for one whose soul is defiled by impurity (*kaśmala*), there may be no immersion (*āveśa*)."
One should lead that [consciousness] by means of one [of the three] from the triad of clusters to the state of awakening.
First, one should extract a single mass from the Moon, Fire, and Wind;
the second [mass] is joined with the Serpent, the Vital Breath, the Subduer, Fire, and Wind.
The third [set] consists of Śikhin, Soma, Āsuka, Kūṭa, Agni, and Samīra;
O beautiful one, all these seats are marked with the *tilaka* sign.
"By these three taken separately, there occurs an immersion of power (śaktyāveśa) residing within the body.
Thus [ends the verse]. || 213 ||
Right here he states the procedure:
"That which is known as the seed-syllable of Śakti should be deposited over all the limbs;
the mantra adorned with the twelve vowels is to be deposited in the heart-cakra. (29.214)
In the center of that is consciousness, resembling a hibiscus flower;
it is a wheel impelled by the wind and illuminated by fire. (29.215)

One should meditate upon that and recite the mantra through the method of interspersing it with the disciple's name; within half a blink of an eye, the disciple will undoubtedly experience a state of paralysis (stobha).

The seed-syllable of Śakti is the letter *ī*, which is the triangular seed-syllable (*trikoṇabīja*) due to its phonetic union; and Māyā is that which is denoted by the word *ḍambara*. "One should perform the placement upon all limbs" means that one should contemplate the person to be initiated between these two seed-syllables. As for the term "mantra," it refers to the letter *ha*, which is the universal essence of all mantras.

"Of that"—meaning, of the mantra which exists in the form of a wheel because it is interpenetrated by the twelve vowels, excluding the neuter ones. "That wheel"—the meaning is: the entire collection of mantras, such as the *vāgbhava* and others, contemplated both externally and internally for the one to be initiated (*dīkṣya*). By means of that, this [is performed] with the wind (*vāyu*).

One should meditate on [the deity] surrounded on all sides externally by the letter *ya* and the fire-repha (*ra*), by which, being thus inflamed, it attains the boldness for the manifestation of *stobha*. Regarding the word "mantra"—it refers to any one of the three clusters (from among the three). By the application of the name interspersed [with the mantra], first comes the mantra.
Then follows the name of initiation (*dīkṣya*), and again the mantra. As it is said there:
"One should install the leader of the mantra within the heart-cakra, joined with all its limbs, accompanied by the *ḍambara* and the triangle, and interpenetrated by the twelve vowels."
One should move the *jīva*, which resembles the rising sun, by means of that [breath];
one should illuminate it with fire alone and awaken it with the wind as well.
"O beautiful lady, one should recite the name of the disciple, interspersed with the mantra;
then, being intent upon that, he enters into possession at that very moment.
Thus [it is said]. (216)
And what is his experience like in this state? To this he says:
"O Goddess, being joined to each successive principle (tattva), he perceives the Self;
but when he has reached the supreme principle, then he does not see [it]. (29.217)
By this sequential yoga, he perceives the entire path.
"He perceives" means—in due order—that which is pure; "he does not perceive" means that he becomes one whose very nature is the Seer alone. This is the meaning.
Not only does such an experience arise for him as the cause of conviction within himself alone, but it occurs even for both himself and others—as he says:
"Or else, at that very moment, he causes all the scriptures to be grasped. (29.218)
"All scriptures" means those not previously seen or heard, by implication. (29-218)

If indeed there should be someone who desires specific enjoyments, then one should perform for him initiation corresponding to that very [desire]; thus he says: "For one who is subject to the power of his fitness, the perfected yogi should perform initiation according to the rule of the individual principles (tattvas) by means of the practice of those principles."
Thus, for this seeker of liberation who has been duly initiated,
the Kula-krama-iṣṭi, endowed with five states, should be prescribed for his remaining conduct.

"Capability" means that for some there is a desire for the state of being a lord of the world within the earth-principle (*pṛthvītattva*) itself, while for others it is for the state of Sadāśiva. "By the method of practicing the principles" means by means of the respective meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth—this is the meaning. "For the sake of remaining as a remnant" means for the purpose of the residual function—this is the meaning. (220)

He explains that it is indeed endowed with five states: "Just as consciousness may remain unfailing throughout the waking state and the others, so too should the Kula-sacrifice, which resides in the mouth of the Yoginīs, be taught. (29.221)

Regarding the term *anapāyinī* ("non-departing"): the meaning is that it proceeds in an uninterrupted form, according to the principle stated [in the Spandakārikā]: "There is no state which is not Śiva" (SpKā 3.2). || 221 ||
He says that very thing:
"Everything that is to be done in the waking state is [performed] in the dream state within each individual mantra;
having warded it off in deep sleep, that which is called the Root [mantra], augmented by its own power, [remains]. (29.222)
In the Fourth state there is only one called the Messenger (dūtī), while in that which transcends it, she is the Mistress of the Kula;
thus proceeds the worship for those who are completely filled with their own power.
Indeed, here in the states such as waking and so forth, there is a corresponding disappearance of difference and the emergence of non-difference; thus,
in the waking state, the entire collection of mantras should be applied as objects of worship.

It is the same even in the state of dreaming; however, the meaning is that it refers specifically to a single mantra, such as Parā, which one desires to propitiate individually. But in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), having set aside the entire collection of mantras that constitute the retinue, there remains the triad of Bhairavas conjoined with the triad of powers beginning with Parā.

The Kuleśvaras should be worshipped as a pair; likewise, in the Fourth state (turya) there is only one Kuleśvarī, and in the state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta), there is only the Kuleśvara. || 222–223 ||

He extends this very principle elsewhere as well: "One should describe to him that aforementioned fivefold state—beginning with *piṇḍastha* and ending with *sarvātīta*—along with its stated divisions. (29.224)
"Previously"—in the tenth chapter. "The aforementioned division"—by virtue of being the object of the knowledge of yogis and jñānins.
"To him"—to that seeker of liberation who has been thus initiated. (224)
Now he also describes the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the practitioner (sādhaka) and the teacher (ācārya), which was indicated immediately after the initiation (dīkṣā):
"For the practitioner who desires enjoyment (bubhukṣu), there is the consecration of perfect yoga.
Having worshipped the God there with riches, [using] an image made of gold or other materials, free from blemish... (29.225)
One should light eight lamps, filling them with ghee and red wicks;
they, as well as the two Lords of the Kula, should be worshipped within a conch shell by means of the eight families.
Having been consecrated by means of that [liquid] which is filled with the nectar of bliss, according to the path taught by the Hand of Śiva,
he should thereafter perform the practice for the realization of the mantra.
This is the consecration of the Ācārya, which carries with it authority;
he should prepare sixty-four lamps for him using flour and other such materials.
They should be worshipped with eight times eight [offerings], and in the center, as before, the two Lords of the Kula;
by the very method taught for the Hand of Śiva, one should also consecrate the Guru.

"Yoga" means that which has that as its primary focus. "Therein" refers to the consecration of yoga. "In the conch" means in the great conch (*mahāśaṅkha*). "By the path described for the Hand of Śiva" means by the sequence consisting of the drawing forth of power (*śakti*).
"By that" means by the conch. "He" refers to the seeker (*sādhaka*) who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*). "With flour and so forth" means...
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), clay from an anthill and so forth are included. "As before" means by way of being situated within a conch shell. || 229 ||
Desiring to dispel the doubt— "What would come of these two through such an initiation?"— he recites the scripture itself:
"These two, thus initiated by the entire host of yogis..."
Once they have been recognized by you there, the Guru shall become the bestower of liberation.

Right here, in order to explain the intended meaning of the fourth quarter, he says: "The intended meaning of this quarter is that the Guru who was previously a *sādhaka* bestows the supernatural powers (*siddhi*s); any other [Guru] fully grants liberation. (29.231)
To these two, he should fully explain all three types of knowledge and bestow his own command regarding the performance of their respective duties. (29.232)

The essential point here is this: between these two, he who was previously a practitioner and then became a teacher bestows only supernatural powers (*siddhi*) upon others; whereas the other, who was a teacher from the very beginning, bestows even liberation (*mokṣa*) with extreme excellence, preceded by the granting of supernatural powers.

This is the meaning. Although it is traditionally taught that the status of an *ācārya* belongs only to one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*) and has been initiated through initiation with seed (*sabīja-dīkṣā*), nevertheless, that refers to the domain of ritual action (*karmin*);
this [present case], however, refers to the domain of the man of knowledge (*jñānin*). Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. It is of three kinds—
It consists of the forms of Āṇava, Śākta, and Śāmbhava; its own activity consists of initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth.
He expresses this very point also through an internal sequence:
"The group of six known as the Causes, together with Paramaśiva and Lord Bhairava—that is declared to be the group of eight. (29.233)
Perceiving the universal selfhood of each [sense] and directing that state toward the Self, the Guru should transfer it to whichever sense organ, such as the eye, he intends. (29.234)
That very [rite] is known as the supreme consecration with full jars;
it is said in the *Śrīvīrāvalibhairava* that this occurs even without external [implements]. (29.235)
(The Hexad: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Anāśritaśiva;
Paramaśiva is the thirty-sixth. Bhairavanātha is the full form, designated by terms beginning with the thirty-seventh. That which belongs to this...
The sixty-fourfold activity of each of the eight [deities] manifests as their universal self-nature;

having established that within oneself, the Guru should transmit it— through the channel of one's own respective sense organ— into whichever sense organ, such as the eye and so forth, of the disciple who is to be consecrated, thereby effecting the attainment of identity with that.

He should perform it; that very [initiation] is considered by our teachers to be the supreme consecration (*parābhiṣeka*), because it is filled with the essence of consciousness even without external [vessels], and because its internal jars are full, being distinct from external ones—
the meaning is that this is intended as what is to be practiced.
Having thus described the procedure for initiation (*abhiṣeka*), and desiring to determine the nature of the Creator (*vedhas*) as previously mentioned, he begins to explain that initiation:
"But for one who desires immediate enjoyment, the most accomplished Guru [is the means] through yoga."
One should immediately perform the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣaṇa), which bestows the desired fruit.
"Most perfected through yoga"—the meaning is that one who has well-practiced yoga is the qualified person here.
As he will say: "And that [practice] must be performed by one possessed of practice... (29.237).

Thus [it is said]. "Piercing" (vedha) means the piercing of the centers (cakras), supports (ādhāras), and so forth, by means of the power of the central breath (prāṇa-śakti) through ascending higher and higher. As he will say:
"[... by which, through entry higher and higher..."
"The disciple's realization of the piercing of the wheels (*cakrasaṃbheda*) arises with certainty.
(29.237) It is with this very intention that it is said:
"Having taken recourse to the jewel (*maṇi*), one should place the power (*śakti*) in Heruka."
"The act of severing the bonds is designated as 'piercing' (vedha)," and so forth, as has been stated. || 236 ||
He says that very thing: "And the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣā) has been described in various places in many ways;
and it must be performed by one who possesses practice, so that [the soul] may enter higher and higher. (29.237)
The disciple’s conviction regarding the piercing of the cakras arises certainly;
"by which" means by virtue of possessing [the power of] practice.
Anticipating the question, "What would happen to him by such [a means]?", he says:
"By which the perfection (siddhi) beginning with atomization (aṇimā) [is attained]...
Otherwise, however, in the absence of entry further and further upward, one would become a vessel for obstacles and the like.
As for the scriptural authority, he says:
"And she is impelled in the *Śrīmālā*. (29.238)
In the absence of the stage of the upper wheel (*ūrdhvacakra*), that is indeed a possession by a *piśāca*.
As it is said therein:
"O fair-faced one, when the lower states migrate upward..."
That alone is the state of the station of liberation; that alone is the vessel for knowledge.
"When states belonging to the upper wheels arise even from below, that is the Paiśāca possession; it is indeed the cause of an obstacle.
Thus [it is said].
He explains what was stated as "in many ways" [in verse 28]:
"It consists of mantra, nāda, bindu, śakti, bhujaṅgama, and parā. (29.239)
The Supreme Lord has taught the initiation by piercing (*vedhadīkṣā*) in six ways in the *Śrīgahvara*.
As it is stated therein:
"The piercing by mantra, that which is called the piercing by sound (*nāda*), and beyond that, the piercing by the point (*bindu*)."

"The Śākta piercing by means of the serpent (bhujaṅgavedha) is declared to be the supreme sixth. And the reason for its being sixfold here is that it incorporates the purification of the paths (adhvaśuddhi). As it has been said:
"O Dear One, one should purify the paths through the awakening of the sixfold piercing."
Thus.
He recites the very text from that [source], both in meaning and in words:
"The wheel consisting of eight spokes and so forth, filled with flames, as described in one's own scripture. (29.240)

Having meditated, by means of that [wheel], there is the piercing of the mantra through the piercing of his heart-center (*hṛccakra*). "By himself" (*sva*) means as something to be performed. "By that" (*tena*) means by the eight-spoked wheel and so forth. "Heart-center" (*hṛccakra*)—by virtue of being located therein, the Self, whose consciousness is uncontracted, is indicated. As it has been said:
Then, having meditated upon an excellent eight-spoked wheel,
or even a twelve-spoked one, filled with flames, according to the application of the rules of one's own scripture.
"The piercing of another's mind is declared to be the 'piercing by mantra'.
Thus it is said.
He states this very point by means of another sequence as well:
"Having projected the form ninefold within the body, one should then transfer it. (29.241)
By means of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should unite the disciple— who is blazing with great radiance—
into the Supreme Reality through the paralysis of his bonds.

Thus, the procedure seen in the Dīkṣottara was taught to me by Śambhu: "By means of the utterance of Nāda, that which is called Nāda [arises] through the application of the sequence of emanation. (29.243)
One should pierce the mind with the sound; this is declared to be the piercing by sound (nādavedha).
The mind, situated in the location of the bindu, is established on the path between the eyebrows.
Or, O Great Goddess, [one should visualize] a drop (bindu) with a radiance filled with flames at the target of the heart;
by means of that, one awakens the person to be acted upon (sādhya). This is proclaimed as the "Drop" (Bindu) method. || 29-245 ||
O beautiful one, through the utterance of the Śakti and the powerful one, by means of the utterance of the scent,
[one perceives] that which is crooked and coiled in form, seated upon the throne of the Śṛṅgāṭaka.
By pronouncing [the mantra] without vocalization, one should pierce the entire universe;
thus, piercing by means of the "bee" (bhramara) is declared to be the piercing of Śakti (śāktavedha). (29.247)

"Ninefold" means due to the division of the apertures (*randhra*). "In the body" means, by implication, in one's own body. By means of the application of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), it shines forth ninefold once [the body] has been abandoned. By the term "possessing great radiance" (*mahārciṣam*), its capacity for the paralyzing of bonds (*pāśastobhana*) is indicated.
This has been shown. Regarding the phrase "by the utterance of *nāda*": by the word *nāda*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the long vowel is meant.

Regarding "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*): it is characterized by the letters from *na* to *pha*. Regarding "by *nāda*": it is in the form of the vowelless *kalā* (the bindu), which is self-uttering in nature. As it has been said:
Having uttered the long *nāda*, one should fully ascend from *nāda* into *nāda*.
Having uttered [the consonants] from *ṅa* to *pha*, one should purify the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*).
"One should pierce by means of the *nāda*; this is declared to be the piercing by *nāda* (*nādavedha*).

Thus it is said. The state of being situated in the location of the *bindu* is explained by the passage beginning with "between the eyebrows" (*bhrūmadhya*) and so forth. "The mind" (*citta*) refers to that which belongs to the disciple, and by implication, it is permeated by the *bindu*. "The *bindu*"—by implication... [the rest of the sentence].
Having meditated upon that, it is said:
"By meditating on the *bindu* either between the eyebrows, in the heart, or at the *kanda*,
one should enter the disciple's mind and pierce it through the piercing of the *bindu*."
Thus, and as it is said:
"The exceedingly terrifying [power] leaps up from the contraction of the *mattagandha* (intoxicated scent)"— according to this view,
by means of the upward movement resulting from the force of yoga applied through the pressing and so forth of the *gandha*, that is, the *mattagandha*.

Having attained the state of perfect identity with the Supreme Foot within the possessor of power (Śaktimat), whose nature is Śiva and who abides at the limit of the twelve (dvādaśānta) as the power of the Middle Energy (madhyaśakti), [one perceives Him] seated upon the throne of the triangle (śṛṅgāṭaka) in the foundation of birth, coiled in form through non-differentiation from the vital energy (prāṇaśakti), because He is perpetually arisen there.
Having uttered the crooked mind (manas) by means of non-utterance—
since it is of a nature that utters itself independently of the effort of utterance— one should fix one's attention upon the natural utterance of both self and other,
and thus pierce the entire universe through its movement to various respective locations.
The Śākta piercing is said to be that which produces a state of delusion. || 247 ||
Now, in order to explain this related "snake-piercing" (bhujaṅgavedha), he says:
"And that very supreme power, which causes bliss to blossom, adorned with five hoods, goes beyond the place of birth. (29.248)

The word *param* refers to the Possessor of Power (*śaktimant*) who resides at the *dvādaśānta*. As it has been said, beginning with: "Thus the five-hooded Goddess emerged from the lower sphere (*adharamaṇḍala*)."
"She has gone to the supreme space, the supreme maṇḍala of nirvāṇa.
Thus [ends verse 248].
He elaborates upon the very fact that [the Goddess] is adorned with five hoods:
"The *kalās*, the *tattvas*, the [five] Nandās and so forth, the voids (*vyoman*), the *kulas*, the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, and the senses—she consists of these five groups. (29.249)
Thus, that [energy], having emerged from the station of Brahmā in five forms,
shines forth as it enters the station of Brahmā, merged like a flash of lightning.
Having entered, one should pierce the body and cause the self to break through;
thus is the "serpent-penetration" (bhujaṅgavedha) described in the Bhairava-āgama.
One should cultivate the mind until the mind has reached its exhaustion;
O Goddess of the Gods, when the mind is exhausted, supreme bliss (*parānanda*) is proclaimed. (29-252)
The *kalās*—the five beginning with Śāntyatītā; the *tattvas*—earth and the others;

the *nandā*s and so forth—the lunar days (*tithis*); the *vyoma*s—the locations of the birth, navel, heart, and bindu; the *kulas*—those known as Mahākaula, Kaula, Akula, and Kulākula; and the causal deities beginning with Brahmā.
"Ending with Sadāśiva" refers to the senses—the organs of perception and the organs of action.
"In the abode of Brahmā" means from the support of birth (the *janmādhāra*); "in the abode of Brahmā" also means at the *dvādaśānta*.
The intention is that both of these are his primary seats (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "The body" refers to—

It has the form of the wheel-base (cakrādhāra) and so forth. Now, one might ask: "What would happen to the self through the piercing of the body? To this it is said: "One should pierce the self. And it has been stated:
"Coiled like a serpent, it is situated below the navel."
Fully awakened, she should move like a serpent, adorned with five hoods.
"From the pentad to the pentad, until the piercing known as the serpent.

Thus, "when exhausted" means through the abandonment of the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). "Supreme bliss" (*parānanda*) refers to that which consists of the wonder of the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). || 252 ||
For this very reason, there is for him a dissolution of all differentiation; thus he says:
Neither the senses, nor the vital breaths, nor the domain of the internal organ; neither the mind, nor that which is to be thought, nor the thinker, nor the act of thinking. (29.253)
The supreme piercing (paravedha) is declared to be that in which all states of being are completely exhausted.
He shows its manifold nature through another method [of classification]: "due to the divisions of Manu, Śakti, Bhuvana, Rūpa, Jña, Piṇḍa, Sthāna, Nāḍī, and Para" (29–254).
Other teachers who know the secret teach this Veda in nine ways.
He characterizes this very [system] in sequence:
"In a triangular mandala joined with the mass of fire-syllables within the womb of Māyā... (29.255).
Having meditated, one should pierce the knots with that [flame] which is formidable with its blaze;
one should strike with flowers and unite [the disciple] with the Supreme—this is the procedure known as Mantra.
Having entered through one of the two channels, [the practitioner] concentrates the consciousness in the abode of the *kanda*,
causing it to whirl forcefully by means of the fivefold and eightfold *śikhā*.
One should direct [the consciousness] to some wheel reached by the tip of the spear of power (śakti);
this is the piercing by power (śākta-vedha), which produces immediate conviction. || 29-258 ||
By means of a flame, white as moonlight, which has emerged from the base with impetuosity and dissolved into the sky by way of the seat at the root of the disciple’s big toe; || 29-259 ||
Having purified the body and recollecting the previously mentioned series of cities from *kṣa* to *a*, one who pierces the worlds reflects them through meditation upon his own maṇḍala. (29.260)

One should meditate with identification upon some beautiful form within the station of the Bindu arisen between the eyebrows, and afterwards, one should make the disciple consist of that very essence.
Thus has the piercing of form been described; and here that very form comes into the range of vision.
In the end, the disciple, having become one with it, attains union (sāyujya) with it. (29–262)

The consciousness, which is eightfold—beginning with that termed the sense of smell and ending with the instrument of cognition—one should cause it to circulate within the disciple according to the sequence of the threads of their respective channels. (29.263)

The piercing known as *vijñāna*, by means of the process of binding through the firmness of self-conceit, instantly brings about the rising of the sun of divine knowledge within the void of the heart. (29.264)
The *piṇḍa* is supreme, consisting of *kalās*, subtle; externally it is the *puryaṣṭaka*, which is gross.
That shadow-self (*chāyātman*) is known to be turned away [from the object], yet facing forward in a mirror and the like. (29.265)

Thus, one should forcefully dissolve each successive division of the *piṇḍa* into the one following it; through that gradual dissolution by means of the piercing of the *piṇḍa*, the supreme state is attained. (29.266)
Whichever cakra is in the body, having arrived there and rested in sequence, one should cause that cakra to blaze; this is the piercing known as "the place," which bestows its specific fruit.
There are three principal channels, while those contained within them are innumerable;
here, piercing the channels by unifying with them produces that specific result.

When the flow [of consciousness] moves through the desired channels—primarily those established in the eyes and other sense organs—the attainment of their awakening occurs through the piercing of the channels (*nāḍīvedha*) in various and manifold forms. (29.269)
Like one possessing the strength of a tail’s form, the great yogi, having struck another channel encircled by his own channel, forcibly casts even a perfected being down to the earth. (29.270)
Perceiving non-duality within all the cakras during the supreme piercing (paravedha),
the Guru brings about Supreme Śiva, which bestows the attainment of the state of Śiva.

*Māyā* is the seed-syllable of *māyā*. "Fire-colored" refers to the letter *ra*, which is triangular—meaning, with its apex facing upward. "Having meditated" means, having meditated on the disciple seated within it.
"By that" means by the triangular mandala. "By either one" means...

"By means of one [of the channels] from the midst of the triad of channels beginning with Suṣumṇā"—that is, having withdrawn [the senses] from all sides. "Having whirled around"—in that very place, by way of a clockwise rotation with great velocity.
[The senses consist of] the five organs of action, the eight [organs of perception], the five cognitive faculties, and the three internal organs.
And: "Power" (śakti) refers to that characterized as Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā. "Somewhere" (kvāpi) means in whatever [place] is desired.
"Realization" (pratyaya) is characterized by possession (āveśa). "By the crest-lock" (śikhayā) means by the power (śakti) whose form is that [crest-lock].
By the phrase "pure as moonlight" (jyotsnāvadātayā),...

Its luminosity and purity have been made known. And precisely because of this suitability, it is said: "having purified the body. "In the sky" means at the *dvādaśānta*. And that state of dissolution is to be contemplated either from the seat at the base of the big toe or from there.

"By way of the sequence starting from the base of the thumb"—this refers to the letters beginning with *kṣ* and ending with *a*, according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). "Previously"—in the beginning of the eighth chapter. "One's own maṇḍala"—one's own body. "It reflects"—the meaning is that one should likewise make the disciple [reflect] in that same manner. "A certain"—[refers to...]

[She is] in the form of one's chosen deity (*yatheṣṭadevatārūpā*). Furthermore, raising the doubt, "What is the fruit here?", he says: "And she," and so forth. He clarifies her eightfold nature with the words beginning with "nose" (*ghrāṇa*) and so on. "Internal" (*antar*) refers to the triad of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "Heart" (*hṛdaya*) is mentioned because it is the place where all the channels (*nāḍī*) are manifested.

*Piṇḍa* means the body. *Kalā* is an indication of the five *kañcukas*. *Yaḥ* refers to that which has been described as threefold. *Uttarottare* means that the gross [merges] into the subtle, and the subtle into the supreme.
*Kramaśaḥ* means according to their respective degrees of firmness. And here, in the interval...
The imagined [nature] is described as: "That shadow-self should be known as facing away [in reality], yet facing forward in mirrors and the like.
Because this is half-contradictory and thus largely redundant, it should be disregarded.
Let it suffice if this reaches consistency for those who are obsessed with explaining things exactly as they stand.

For us, however, there is no such [limited] view. "The wheel" (cakra) is an elliptical expression for the support (ādhāra) and the rest; "gradually" (kramaśaḥ) means beginning from the network of channels (nāḍī-cakra) and so forth.
"One should cause it to blaze" means one should make it radiant by turning it toward consciousness—this is the meaning. "Its fruit" (tatphala)— [Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence.]

It consists of the act of making [the channel] radiant. "Contained therein" means because they possess its shadow-like nature. "By them" refers to the other innumerable channels. "Its fruit" is characterized by unification.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says "abhilaṣita... and so forth, using the term "lāṅgūlākṛti" (having the form of a tail).
Just as some great creature fells trees and the like by the lashing of its own tail, so too does this one.

The word "supreme" (param) is used elliptically. The term "great yogi" (mahāyogī) should be understood as applying to all [the preceding titles], namely, the Guru who bestows the attainment of Śiva-nature. || 271 ||
And this has been stated thus even in the Āgama; so he says:
"In the venerable Vīrāvalikula, it is likewise described in this way.
He states that very point:
It should be known as entirely indivisible; having realized the middle, one is not stained.

The Guru, established in the sequence of its division, may liberate the bound souls (paśus). Here, that which cannot be pierced by those lacking yoga must necessarily be known through the sequence of yogic practice and so forth—the "middle," namely the central vital energy (madhya-prāṇa-śakti); having known it—

Having experienced that which flows unimpeded through the piercing of the various cakras and so forth, he who is not tainted— that is, he who does not remain submerged in the movement of both prāṇa and apāna— therefore,
by means of firmness in that very sequence of division previously mentioned, which consists of mantra and the rest, within the central power (madhya-śakti).
Having attained experiential realization, he—the teacher of the ultimate reality—shall liberate the bound souls (paśus);
that is to say, he shall cause them to emerge from their respective centers (cakras), supports (ādhāras), and so forth.
And how should the Guru perform this? He says: "The disciple should enter before the Guru; he should pierce mouth with mouth. (29.273)
Form [should be dissolved] into form through the sense objects until they reach a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhavet*).
For the disciple seated upon his own head, the Guru [places it] in the mouth— indeed, it is said here that "the Śiva-mouth is the entrance" (Vijñānabhairava Tantra, verse 20).
By such statements as these, one should pierce one's own central power (*madhya-śakti*) into that [deity's] central power;

one's own form of the eye-faculty into that faculty which perceives its form; and likewise, indicated by this, one should pierce one's own respective other faculties into those various other faculties [of the deity], for that purpose.

One should apply [these means] until, by means of these being made objects of perception, one becomes of equal flavor (samarasībhavet)—that is to say, one should attain identity (aikātmya). This is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection, "Even so, what would happen? he says:
"When the mind has become equanimous [in flavor], there is the state beyond the mind (unmanasī) for both. (29.274)
And at that moment, through the movement of the *unmanī* state, one becomes initiated in both [the disciple and the teacher];
when the moon and sun are conjoined, the individual soul attains identity with That. (29.275)

"Initiated"—this means, by implication, the disciple. For when he attains identity with that [state] through yoga—which consists of the state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) achieved by completely shattering his own limited nature within the central power (madhyaśakti) situated between the moon and the sun, i.e., the prāṇa and apāna—he shall reach absorption in that; the meaning is that he shall attain that single central point. ||275||
And this is also an object of aspiration even for the causal deities; thus he says: "In this [system], Brahmā and the other gods, desiring liberation, [strive] for the sake of release.
Anticipating the objection, "But why is it so?", he says:
Having ceased the wheel of rays, both one's own enjoyment and liberation [are attained]. (29.276)
If he swallows that, it is proclaimed as the initiation of Śarva.

Indeed, if such a teacher and the like, having restrained his own mind and the circle of rays [of the senses], swallows both enjoyment and liberation—which are mutually exclusive—even while in the state of enjoyment; |||
Therefore, this initiation of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī dīkṣā) is proclaimed as "liberated"; the meaning is that it is renowned for bestowing liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Therefore, he said: "This very liberation, which is vibrationless, has been described as existing in all living beings. (29.277)
By striking and merging the portions of Agni and Soma, one should remove vibration.

"Vibrationless" (niḥspanda) means having an unchanging form even in all states. For one who is thus initiated, [the state arises] from the portions of Agni and Soma, which consist of the prāṇa and apāna and are composed of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the objects of knowledge (prameya).
By repeatedly removing the nature of the affliction through resting in the very form of the subject,
one should take away its vibration— that is, one should pacify its outward orientation— this is the meaning.
And how could this be so for him? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The external breath, having gone outside, by means of its connection with the form of darkness... (29.278).
Having emerged through the pores of the skin and wandering by means of all the causal factors,
one should cause it to revolve while abiding in the middle which is beyond definition, and then release it from there.
By means of the yoga of friction and upward extraction, one should pierce the five knots;
one should contemplate the pair of functions of friction within the central abode. (29.280)
One should not perform the conjunction of the self, the void, the external mantra, and the body;
this initiation bestows the attainment of the state of Śiva upon all living beings. (29.281)
In this context, although the apāna— which by its very nature consists of objects of cognition (prameya)— tends to flow outward,

it is "intermediate" (madhya) because it is oriented toward resting within the prāṇa; for this very reason, it takes the form of flowing everywhere through the channels consisting of the pores of the skin.
"Beyond the differentiation of the 'I' there is no further suffering, for darkness does not exist within non-dual concealment.

By such statements, [the soul]— having assumed the form of a cognizer in the shape of a cataract (timira)— though wandering through the locations presided over by the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, is [trapped] due to the obstruction of upward movement.

One should cause [the breath] to revolve in whichever [place] by resorting to the abandonment of other objects of meditation; and after such revolving, one should release it so that, through the upward movement of the union of prāṇa and apāna,
one may pierce the five knots presided over by their respective causes.

One should contemplate the pair of prāṇa and apāna as having become unified within the central abode; there alone one should remain with focused attention, whereby [one perceives] from the limited self— the void— from the exterior.

Because it holds the reflection of external objects such as blue and so forth, one should not practice the conjunction of the intellect—which speaks in secret—and the body; rather, one should experience direct realization within the Self alone, by which the attainment of the state of Śiva is said to be conferred through this initiation. || 281 ||
Having thus described the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣā) in its many varieties, he also states the remainder of the procedure for it:

"At the conclusion of the initiation, having cooked the lamps, the sacrificial porridge (caru)—which destroys even the greatest sins—should be consumed by the Kula-teachers together with all the practitioners. (29.282)
Thus, in the *Śrīratnamālā*, whatever deficiency or excess occurs in the ritual procedure—that itself is a transgression; this [following] is proclaimed as its pacification. (29.283)
And this was not stated according to my own imagination; thus it was said: "In the *Śrīratnamālā*—as it is stated therein:
'At the conclusion of the initiation, lamps should be prepared by the practitioners together with [the teacher] after having cooked [the offerings].'"
"The sacrificial oblation (caru) should be consumed by the family preceptors; it destroys even the greatest sins.
Now, one might object: "As long as not all are knowers of reality, one should not show the lamp."

According to the principle thus stated, the consumption of the sacrificial pap (*caru*) is indeed forbidden for those who do not know reality (*atattvavid*); furthermore, for those who know reality (*tattvavid*), there is not even the slightest apprehension of being touched by sin. With what intention, then, was it said here that [this practice] "destroys great sins" (*mahāpātakanāśana*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "deficient," and so forth. (283)
In this very context, he states another procedural requirement for the sake of completeness:
"On the following day, a sacrifice must be performed for the Guru; for without it, the rite does not reach completion. Therefore, one should perform it with effort. (29.284)
Whatever may please the Guru, that one should offer to him;

by the statement "the ritual does not reach completion [without this]," its status as an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*yāga*) is declared, but not its being merely something that causes his satisfaction.
And what rule is intended here, by which its fullness would be achieved? To this he says:
"The rule for this [practice] is said to be its movement within the course of the wheel. (29.285)
Having beheld the vessel of wine, perfectly full and held in the hand of the Lord of Heroes (vīrendra), which is the Supreme Brahman, one should drink it by the command of the Guru. (29-286)
Having gratified the beings, he should offer [the remainder] to the Guru.
"Of this"—that is, of the initiation. "The Lord of Heroes" (vīrendra) refers to the Ācārya.
This very point is taught here: having prostrated on the ground before the Guru, and having taken [the substance] and gratified the sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs). || 29.287 ||

Having bowed to one's own mantra, and then to the messenger (dūtī), Gaṇapati, the gurus, the guardian of the field (kṣetrapa), and the assembly of heroes (vīrasaṅghāta), in the proper sequence beginning with the guru; || 29-288 ||
One should drink the substance personally touched by the hero, and never otherwise.
"Having made [himself] on the ground"—this means that one should prostrate before the Guru after falling to the ground; this should be construed as: "having saluted and taken up that vessel of wine."
"Toucht by the hero" (vīraspṛṣṭam) means that which remains after being drunk by all [the initiates] in the sequence beginning with the Guru.
And this must be performed only with those who know the reality and are initiated, not with others; thus he says:
"Those who do not know the Supreme Brahman and are devoid of the scriptures and their transmissions... (29.289).
And those who indulge in greed, delusion, pride, anger, passion, and deceit—one who desires his own welfare should not associate with them. (29.29)
Anticipating the question, "And when is this rite to be performed?", he says:

"At the beginning of the sacrifice, during the sacrifice, at the end of the sacrifice, during the worship of the Guru, and during the prescribed occasional rites, the disciple should perform this procedure. (29–291)
"In those previously mentioned"—that is, in the twenty-eighth chapter. ||291||
He concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with half a verse:
"Thus has the secret procedure been thoroughly examined, made perfectly clear through the experiences from the mouth of the Guru.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda.
The twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Secret Method."
Thus all is auspicious.
Jayaratha, whose Kaula experience was transmitted through the succession of the teachings of the illustrious Guru,
has thus explained this twenty-ninth daily lesson (āhnika).

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Secret Rite," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, the illustrious Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by the illustrious Jayaratha. 29.
The Thirtieth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination). [He] whose body is purified by the great potency of the nature of innate self-reflection;
I bow to that [deity] who fulfills one's desires, who is the means for accomplishing what is sought, and who follows the mind; I bow to Him who is the follower of the mind.
Now, with the second half [of the verse], he speaks in order to define the mantras: "Next, the collection of mantras appropriate for the practice of the Trika and Kula traditions is defined.
Anticipating the objection, "But what is the purpose of defining this?", he says:
For those whose intellects have not yet ascended to such discernment, [the following is taught] for the sake of its attainment, in due order. (30.1)
"Tāvān" means full. "For the sake of that accomplishment" means for the purpose of attaining the ascent of the full self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*)—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Now, one might ask: "How could that be so by means of this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For those mantras are awakened, having as their sole essential nature reflective awareness (vimarśa).
But was it not stated previously that having reflective awareness as one's essential nature is possible only for an agent?
Anticipating the objection—"Since mantras are of the nature of instruments (karaṇa), how is it logical for them to be so [i.e., agents]?"—he says:
"Because of the sovereignty of the independent abode of consciousness itself, they consist of agency. (30.2)

Now, one might object: "If this is so, how can the teacher's agency in performing initiation, grace, and so forth be logically established? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that [power] which enters the teacher, through its firm establishment in identity with him..."
Even the instruments, when made independent, attain the status of the agent.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, how can their status as agents be possible without the presence of instruments? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Even the instruments attain the state of agency. For the mantras indeed attain the state of agency while not relinquishing their own nature as agents.
The meaning is that they take on the state of being instruments. || 3 ||
Now he describes the very nature of the mantras:
"In the Ādhāra-śakti [is] *hrīṃ*; but in the fourfold [series] beginning with Earth, they say the four syllables are, in order, *kṣlāṃ*, *kṣvāṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *kṣam*. (30–4)
Haṃ is in the stalk; likewise, yaṃ, raṃ, laṃ, and vaṃ are in the four [petals] beginning with Dharma;
and ṛṃ, ṝṃ, ḷṃ, and ḹṃ should be in the [next] tetrad in reverse order. (30.5)
Oṃ, auṃ, and ha—these three constitute the triad of Vidyā, Māyā, and Kalā;
the anusvāra and visarga belong to the two principles (tattva) of Vidyeśa and Īśvara.

The letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha* are placed upon the filaments; the vital breath (*prāṇa*), joined with the eight vowels and the nasal bindu, is then placed upon the eight petals, illuminating one's own name.

In the three circles, one should place the nine powers along with the *śaṣasa* syllables; one should arrange the letter *kṣma* with the bindu upon the corpse, and *jūṃ* upon the prongs of the trident.
In the worship of individual seats, these mantras are prescribed in sequence;
however, in the abbreviated worship, one should use the first and the last seed-syllables.
Having taken [the seed-syllable], one should worship [it] from the foundation-power (ādhāra-śakti) up to the tip of the trident,
together with fire, wind, earth, water, the sixth vowel, and the bindu.
The mantra of Ratiśekhara consists of his faces and limbs formed by the short and long vowels;
[the seed-syllables] are fire, breath, fire, withdrawal, time, Indra, water, and wind. (30-11)

The sixteenth vowel (au), the bindu, and the half-moon, and so forth, belong to the Ninefold Self (navātman) in the sequence beginning with Earth— that is, in the Earth, the ocean of nectar, the pot, and the bulb (kanda). Therefore, the seed-syllable of Māyā resides in the Power of the Foundation (ādhāraśakti), whereas elsewhere it resides in the navel, from the left breast and the milk.

[The vowel *i*] is joined with the throat and nose, while [the vowel *u*] is alone; however, in the boat (*pota*), there is the throat and the fire (*tejas*) everywhere. Regarding "in the stalk" (*nāle*)—that is, in the staff (*daṇḍa*)—therefore, here the vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses vigor (*ojas*). Regarding "in the opposite"—that is, in unrighteousness (*adharma*) and so forth—therefore, here the four semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) are permeated by vigor (*ojas*).
And [the form] of the neuter [principles]. "Vidyā" refers to that which consists of the *asūraka* (architraves) in the form of a quadrangular frame (*catuṣkikā*);

"Māyā" refers to the form of the lower covering; "Kalā" refers to the form of the upper covering. The *Īśvara-tattva* is the immediate upper level belonging to Vidyā itself; therefore, the two shanks (*jaṅghā*) are located here.

"And the vital breath (prāṇa) with the visarga. Regarding "the lords of knowledge" (vidyeśa): the locus presided over by the Lords of Knowledge is the principle of Īśvara (īśvaratattva), which is shaped like a lotus. Regarding "Īśvara": this refers to Sadāśiva. For the pervasion consisting of the pure enclosure and so forth resides in the pericarp—this is the intended meaning. "From *ka* to *bha*" means:
There are twenty-four [petals], and thus there is one color for each filament (*kesara*). *Prāṇa* is the letter *ha*.

The eight vowels are *ā, a, i, ī, u, ū, e, ai*. Now, from the statement "of the nine" (*atha... navakasya*), it follows that even in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), *prāṇa* itself is differentiated by the ninth vowel. As it has been said:
"In the filaments [of the lotus] are the letters ending in *bh*, namely *haṃ*, *hāṃ*, *hiṃ*, *hīṃ*, and likewise *haṃ*;
and on the petals are *hūṃ*, *heṃ*, *haiṃ*, and *hoṃ*—thus the Śaktis are present with their own respective names.
Regarding the phrase "in the three mandalas"—this means including the presiding deities; therefore, in the Āgneya mandala...

The secret [syllable] is for the Sun (Saura), the belly for the Moon (Candra), and the "Jīva" (the letter *j*) for the Preta. When the vital energy (*ojas*) is divided, the navel and the hips [are assigned]. Regarding the spikes of the trident (*śūla*), the trident consists of the staff (*daṇḍa*) together with the bindu. "The first" refers to the seed-syllable of Māyā (*māyābīja*), which denotes the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*). "The last" denotes the sound of the trident (*śūlārava*).
The syllable *jūṃ*; with that, the modification is: *hrīṃ jūṃ āsanapakṣāya namaḥ*. Fire is the letter *ra* (repha); wind is *ya*; earth is *la*; water is *va*; the sixth vowel is the letter *ū*.
The five short vowels are *a, i, u, e, o*. The six long vowels are *ā, ī, ū, e, au, aḥ*.
Thus, by the statement at the very outset, it has been indicated that this same principle applies elsewhere as well to the limbs (aṅga) and faces (vaktra):
fire is *repha* (r), breath is *ha*, fire is *repha* (r), dissolution is *kṣa*,
time is *ma*, Indra is *la*, water is *va*, wind is *ya*, and the sixth vowel is the letter *ū*.
And regarding the *bindu* and other [principles], there is a different designation elsewhere; thus he says:
"The pervasion of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth, is as it is taught in the venerable *Traiśirasa* system. (30.12)
Then, [the stages] designated by the names *kṣepa*, *ākramaṇa*, *cidudbodha*, *dīpana*, *sthāpana*, *tatsaṃvitti*, and *tadāpatti* [are described]. (30.13)
This much is proclaimed here as the "Great Pervasion" (*mahāvyāpti*) by way of its formal manifestation (*mūrtitvena*).

Furthermore, the pervasion of the *bindu* alone extends from the *ardhacandra* up to the *nirodhikā*; thus, immediately following that [in the sequence], there is the mention of the *nāda*. Such is the case with the *bindu*.
Because of the statement, "And the *bindu* itself is indeed Īśvara" (*Svacchanda Tantra* 4.264), regarding the state of being Īśvara, [it is said]:
"Īśvara is the external unfolding... (*Riju-vimarśinī* 3.1.3).
By saying this, it is stated that the very essence (*satattva*) is the outward manifestation itself; this is the "rejection" (*kṣepa*). And regarding *nāda*, [it is said]:
"Sadāśiva is to be expressed in *nāda*" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.265).
"...the internal *nimeṣa* is Sadāśiva. (Rijuvimarsinī on Parātrīśikā 3.1.3).

By this statement, it is shown that the very nature of the universe as it unfolds externally is its inward progression; thus, it is called "ascension" (*ākrānti*). Even so, within the *nādānta*, which consists of the emergence of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*) through the submergence of the "this-ness" (*idantā*), [the state is attained].

The awakening of consciousness itself, which is of the nature of the subject, is what is meant by "the awakening of the *cit*. Thus, there is an intensification of awakened consciousness in the state of *Śakti*; even when there is some degree of intensification in the state of *Vyāpinī*, it remains exactly as it was, up until the stage of *Samanā* for yogins.

The direct realization of that [state], and its identity with it on the plane of *unmanā*—this is what has been stated. "To this extent" means up to the attainment of identity with *unmanā*. As it is said there:
"The casting forth, the ascending, the awakening of consciousness, and the illumination..."
Establishment, as well as consciousness, and likewise its attainment.

"O beautiful goddess, in this scripture, by means of the sequence of causes and through the relationship of support and supported, the form is traditionally taught to be sevenfold," thus beginning [the text].
"Projection (kṣepa) is said to be the point (bindu); pervasion (ākrānti) is called resonance (nāda).
The awakening of consciousness (cidudbodha) is the supreme state (parāvasthā); illumination (dīpana) is called power (śakti)."
"Sthāpana is said to be Vyāpinī, while Saṃvitti is remembered as Samanā;
Unmanā is the attainment of that—this is called the Mūrti.
Thus it is said.

This extent of pervasion belongs not only to the physical form, but even to the salutation (namaskāra) intended as the illuminator of the mantra; thus he says: "Salutation is said to be its transformation and its dissolution. (30.14)
This [mantra], with its three syllables omitted from the bottom and joined with the six long vowels, one should assign as its six limbs, beginning with the heart, and its faces. (30.15)

By means of the seed-syllables *kṣaya-rava-la-ba*, which are radiant and adorned with the nasal bindu, [one obtains] the *jhakāra* (the letter jha), the dissolution, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), together with the sixth vowel and the bindu. (30.16)
This is the true nature of Bhairava, adorned with the crescent moon and other ornaments;
the mantras of Mātṛkā and Mālinī have already been fully described. (30.17)

The syllable Oṃ, followed by the name in the dative case and the word "namas," should be the mantra for Gaṇeśa and the others in this sequence; however, for those among them for whom a seed-syllable (bīja) has not been specified, [this formula alone shall apply].
The first letter of each name is illuminated by the vowel *ā*, the bindu, the crescent moon, and so forth;
for all seed-syllables (*bīja*), that [first letter] is joined with the fourteenth and the sixth vowels.

The vocatives for the triad beginning with Aghorī are formed by the seed-syllables (bījas) uttered in sequence; [the first is] Māyā with the visarga, [the second is] *huṃ*, and [the third is] the letter *ha* with the visarga. (30.20)
Furthermore, there are three successive vocatives for the triad of goddesses;
in the second word, the letter *a* is traditionally held to represent the letter *e*.
Then, the mantra for the two Śaktis has its final syllable omitted;
both [syllables] "he" and "agni" (ha) are joined with the fifth vowel (ū), each separately.
The syllable *va* joined with the letter *ka*, followed by *huṃ ha* and the visarga;
then again the syllable *śa*, together with the *tāra* (oṃ), increased by two syllables consisting of eight, three, and half [of the same]. (30.23)
This is the Vidyā of the goddess Parāparā in the illustrious Trika teaching;
it consists of words composed of syllables numbering five, six, five, four, two, three, and two. (30.24)
In the group of seven beginning with Aghorī, there is the remainder of Pibanī;
this is also stated in the Siddhayogīśvarīmata to apply to each individual syllable. (30.25)
The arrangement of the circle of deities is not affected by its multiplicity;
the mantra consisting of *māyā*, the *visarga*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ* is of the nature of Aparā. (30.26)
The pervasive power (parā) has been described as having pervasion on the left; the individual soul (jīva), together with that [power], is the fourteenth.
That [pervasive power] is said by the Great Lord in the *Triśiraḥśāstra* to have many divisions. (30.27)
Although its nature is diverse and its composition is crowded with many elements,
this entire pervasion is universally recognized as a "homage" (namaskāra) by virtue of being a genus (jāti),

insofar as it effects the assumption of the state of the conscious subject (cit-pramātṛtā) by withdrawing the state of the limited subject (pramātṛtā) consisting of the body and so forth from the one who offers the homage.

"Transformation" (pariṇāma) is so called because it is like a transformation resulting from that very activity (*tatkarmyat*). Even so, one might think that its non-deviation from its true nature (*tattva*) is not possible; thus he says: "and its dissolution therein" (*tallayaśca*). "Devoid of three phonemes" means lacking the [phonemes] *va*, *ya*, and *ū*. "By means of seed-syllables" (*bījaiḥ*)—means...
"By those conjoined with the five short vowels, which take the form of ether, air, fire, water, and earth;

'blazing'—the ancients [hold] that because the short vowels beginning with *o* and those beginning with *a* possess a fiery nature, they consist of light (*tejomaya*); while the venerable Lakṣmaṇaguptapāda [holds] they are 'with the letter *ra*' (*sarepha*)."
As it is stated in the scripture:
"O Pārvatī, the supreme seed-syllable consisting of twenty-six [phonemes], joined with the letter *ra* and provided with the bindu,
is the eastern face of Maheśvara and likewise of the goddesses."
Ending with the letter *ma*, accompanied by the nasal bindu and the letter *ra*, and having the form of Bhairava,
that shall be the right face of the host of gods and goddesses.
Furthermore, the auspicious twenty-eighth syllable is the great seed-mantra of Indra;
it is endowed with the letter *ra* and the nasal dot (*bindu*), and is the auspicious western face.
"The supreme seed-syllable of Varuṇa, pierced by the seed-syllable of Agni,
conjoined with a Bindu at its head, is the auspicious northern face.
Thus it is said.
The letter *jhakāra* is intended as the right finger; *saṃhṛti* is *kṣa*; *prāṇa* is *ha*.

The sixth vowel is the letter *ū*. Regarding the word "previously"—this refers to the fifteenth chapter (*pañcadaśāhnika*). It was not enjoined—meaning in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*—therefore, the practical application begins with *oṃ gaṇeśāya namaḥ* and so forth.

"Regarding 'the first letter of the name'—it refers to *ga* for Gaṇeśa, or *vā* for Vāgīśvarī. By this, the practical application is as follows: *oṃ gaṃ gaṇeśāya namaḥ*, *oṃ vāṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ*, and so forth.
Regarding 'that'—it refers to the first letter of the name. The fourteenth [vowel] is the vowel *au*; the sixth vowel is [also *au*]."

The letter *ū*; by that [is formed] *gūṃ* (namely, *gaṇeśāya namaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in Aghora, O you of terrible form": the seed-syllables are those mentioned in their proper sequence—meaning they are indicated at the end. Because of the statement "possessing the visarga," *māyā* here is without the *bindu*. Thus: *aghorai hrīḥ*, *paramaghore* [is] the armor-seed (*kavaca-bīja*), and *ghorarūpe*.

"Haḥ. There are three further vocatives: "Ghoramukhi," "Bhīme," and "Bhīṣaṇe"; however, in this second vocative word, the letter *a* should be substituted for the *e* so that its form becomes "Bhīma. The invocation of the two powers is "Vamani" and "Pivani. As for "the last":

The word *nityakṣara* [means] "eternal syllable," by which [it is meant] "vama piba" (vomit, drink). Following that, *prāṇa* joined with the right knee [is] *agnivarṇau*—that is, two *repha*s (the letter *ra*). The fifth vowel is *ukāra*. *Parau* means the same as *agnivarṇau*. *Astram* is *phaṭ*. After that is the seed-syllable of armor (*kavaca*) with the *visarga*.
Furthermore, *prāṇa* (h) and *śara* (s)—this is the second weapon (*astra*). "By *tāra*" means by the *praṇava* situated first.
"Vasvagni" refers to thirty-eight. "Half-syllable" refers to the vowel-less letter *ṣ*. Thus it has been said.
In the *Triśirobhairava*:
"Thus the goddess Parāparā, adorned with eight words,
consisting of thirty-eight syllables— she is the Supreme Goddess who has been extracted."
"And two half-syllables of this [mantra] should be known by those who know the reality.
Thus [it is said].

Regarding "five": as in *oṃ aghore hrīḥ*, this is the [mantra] of Aghorī. "Vedas" means four; "eyes" means two; "fires" means three; "eyes" means two. The "remainder" is a word of eleven syllables consisting of two and a half phonemes. As it has been said:
The eight Yoginīs of great power, born from the limbs of Parā and Aparā,
consist of five, six, five, four, two, three, and two syllables respectively.
"The [mantras] are to be known as having seven, eleven, and two syllables, accompanied by one and a half syllables" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.60).
Regarding the phrase "the wheel of deities"—it refers to that which consists of forty [deities]. As it is said therein:
"The god Bhairava resides in the pericarp within the *praṇava*."
With eyes wide open at the syllable *a*, she has full breasts at the syllable *gho*.
In the syllable *re*, she has the form of Tvaṣṭṛ; in the syllable *hrīḥ*, she has the form of a tiger;
in the syllable *pa*, she has the form of a lion; and in the syllable *ra*, she is intent on drinking.
Then, following in sequence, the Rākṣasī is likewise in the syllable *ma*;
the Māṃsabhakṣī is in the syllable *gho*, while the Raṇāśinī is in the syllable *re*.
In the syllable *huṃ* she is Retovahā, and in the syllable *gho* she is remembered as Nirbhayā;
in the syllable *ra* she is Ghoradaśanā, while in the syllable *rū* she is Arundhatī.
Having placed these [syllables] in sequence: she who speaks kindly is in the syllable *pe*;
she of fierce form is in the syllable *haḥ*; and she of naked form is in the syllable *gho*.
In the syllable *ra* is Raktanetrī; in the syllable *mu* is Caṇḍarūpiṇī;
in the syllable *khi* she has the form of a bird; and in the syllable *bhi* she is radiant with nourishment.
In the syllable *ma*, Māraṇī is proclaimed; in *bhī*, Śivā is remembered.
Having placed these in their proper sequence, Śākinī is remembered in the syllable *ṣa*.
In the syllable *ṇa*, she is Yantralekhā; in *va*, Vaśakārikā;
in *ma*, Kāladamanā; and in *pi*, she is known as Piṅgalī.
In the syllable *va* she is Vardhanī, and in *he* she is Himasītalā;
by the syllable *ru* she is Rukmiṇī, and by the syllable *ru* she is Halāyudhā.
By the letter *ra*, she is the form of fire; born from the letter *ra*, she is the form of radiant energy.
By the letter *pha*, she is the form of the womb; by the letter *ṭa*, she possesses the supreme form.
"In the syllable *huṃ* she is called Hutavahā; in the syllable *haḥ*, she is Varadāyikā;
by the syllable *pha*, she is Mahāraudrā; and in the syllable *ṭa*, she is Pāśadāyikā.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the phrase "due to its abundance"—this is because of the fear of excessive prolixity in the text, for [all this] is indeed contained within the commenced Śrīpūrvaśāstra.
The intention is that this worship has not been prescribed. The term *aparātmaka* means "pertaining to the Aparā [level]. As it has been said:
"First, one should install the Aghora [mantra] ending with the letter *ha*; then again, the *prāṇa* [the letter *ha*] joined with the *bindu*."
"Having placed [the vessel] accompanied by the *vāmamudrā*, one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) as before with the [mantra] beginning with 'ka'. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.51).

Thus it was said—previously. That is the individual soul (*jīva*). It is the fourteenth vowel, *au*. Although there is no difference in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), the reason [for its mention] is provided by way of the qualifier "a composition crowded with many varieties" in the teaching of its manifold forms.
He recites this very point by means of different terminology:
"In this context, the individual soul (jīva) resides within the vital breath (prāṇa), or the vital breath is situated within the individual soul. (30.28)

The term *jīva* (the individual soul) thus includes the fourteenth [tattva]. The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed [therein]. As it has been stated there: "The Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), being impelled by the will of Sāvitrī, [manifests as] the *jīva* residing within the *prāṇa*, or the *prāṇa* residing within the *jīva*."
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, it is "shauḥ hsauḥ."
And revealing the intended meaning behind this reversal of the relationship between locus and located,
he clarifies the qualification itself:
"Because of the connection with inseparable concomitance through the relationship of locus and located."
The *haṃsa*, situated in the midst of nectar, is pierced by Kālarudra.
Joined with the head of Bhuvaneśa and conjoined with two Anaṅgas,
it should be known as more radiant than the radiant when applied according to the sequence of the six cakras.

The vital breath (prāṇa), established in the staff-posture (daṇḍāsana) and joined with the will of the secret power (guhyaśakti)—this is declared to be the supreme vocal [utterance] by virtue of its nature as the Great Knowledge (mahājñāna). || 30-31 ||
This supreme single-syllable knowledge, however, is clearly the heart of Bhairava;
it is the pure nectar abiding in the void, or else it is joined with the Sāvitrī.
Endowed with the union of the two voids, this supreme heart of Parā should be accomplished through the yoga of the couple by those who know reality. (30–33)
There are also others who consist of a single syllable; according to the procedure for the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra), they are secret and most secret, being devoid of limbs and lineage.

Those established in the Kula, who bestow accomplishments, should be worshipped by the foremost of practitioners according to the ritual procedure of the Kula lineage and through the yoga of subtle discernment. (30–35)
O Goddess, these [rites] should always be performed by a woman or a man.
The syllable *sakāra* joined with the six long vowels constitutes the limbs and the faces. (30–36)
That same mantra, when further joined with the five short vowels and the letter *kha*, becomes the Heart-mantra of the limbs of the Vidyā through its five *oṃ* syllables. (30–37)
The Praṇava, Amṛta, Tejomālinī, together with Svāhā, constitute the eleven-syllable Brahmaśiras according to the Mālinīmata. (30–38)
"Vedavedani hūṃ phaṭ," joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning, is for the *śikhā*.
"Oṃ vajriṇe vajradharāya svāhā," preceded by the syllable oṃ, [is for the kavaca]. || 30-39 ||
The eleven-syllable armor-mantra is remembered as "puruṣṭuta":
Tāra (oṃ), dvijihva (pha), kha (kha), śara (i), svarayuk (e), and jīva (sa). (30–40)
This eye-mantra is known to be of the nature of light and common to all; the weapon-mantra is *tāraḥ ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ*, consisting of six syllables. (30–41)

Indra and the other [deities], as well as their weapons, are formed by the long vowels joined with the consonants *la*, *ra*, *ṭa*, *kṣa*, *va*, and *ya*, together with the bindu; Viṣṇu and Prajāpati are formed by the short vowels.
In the Smṛti, within the lotus and wheel [mantras], there are two short vowels, the fourth and the second;
likewise, the "births" (jātis) are *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *haṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
Then, in the six limbs in succession,
one should likewise identify with those [mantras] during the rites of recitation, fire-oblation, nourishment, eradication, and pacification.
And in the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), there are the classes of mantras beginning with *namaḥ*;
they consist of the six vowels, the five groups of consonants, and the second [consonant] of each group, together with the nasal drop (*bindu*). (30–45)
The true nature of the Mothers is Kālakarṣiṇī, by means of the syllable of the Yoni;
it is considered to be either devoid of the first [syllable] or even devoid of the last. || 30.46 ||
The *jīva* (life-force), situated within the hollow of the vital breaths, possesses a radiance equal to the fire of time;
it is exceedingly brilliant, its left foot adorned by a *bindu* upon the head.
This one resides on the right knee and is worshipped by the entire host of Mothers;
by him all are sustained, and he bestows the desired fruit. (30.48)
For this is the supreme state of being of the Mothers and of Bhairava;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should recite this if he desires the highest accomplishment.
The immersion in the power of Rudra is eternally established here, because this supreme power is proclaimed as distinct from any other. (50)

Whatever accomplishments (siddhis) exist in the Tantra, she indeed brings them all about; and her limbs and faces are likewise [assigned] according to the application of vowels as previously described. (51)
The staff (daṇḍa), the living being (jīva), and the trident (triśūla) are located in the right finger, the other breast, the navel, and the throat;
the visarga is accompanied by the wind (marut) and Rudra along with the trident.
He is declared to be the sovereign of all the circles of yoginīs;
by the mere utterance of his name, the aforementioned realization shall arise. (30.53)
"Mahācaṇḍā," "Yogeśvarī"—this [mantra] consists of eight syllables.
This nine-syllabled [mantra] is more secret; it is the True Being (sadbhāva), Kālakarṣiṇī. (30.54)

In the Śrīḍāmara Mahāyāga, the seed-syllable (bīja) arising from that which is higher than the highest is proclaimed as being composed of *sudhā*, *chedaka*, *ṣaṇṭha*, and so forth, with the vowel of *chedaka* being devoid of sound (*asvara*).
In the Mālinīmata, Kālarātri is one and a half syllables long and is a razor-sharp mantra;
indeed, by reciting it a hundred times, pain arises in the head. (30.56)
Having thus reflected upon these conditions, one who desires long life, O Goddess, should take recourse in the meditation that conquers death; he should not utter this [mantra] otherwise.
Dvirdaṇḍa, Agni, Śūla, Nabha, Prāṇa, Chettra, Anala, Kūṭa, and Agni—these five, along with the Visarga, are likewise [to be applied] in the five [sections]. (30.58)
"In the voids," so it was said by Śiva in the *Tantrasadbhāvaśāsana*;
this is the razor that cuts, by which one is joined to the Supreme. (30.59)

One should meditate upon this blazing weapon-mantra, joined with the Bindu, the Indu, the Anala, the Kūṭāgni, the Marut, the Ṛṣṭha, and the Svara, extending from the soles of the feet to the top of the head.
Then, one should perform the contraction of the fingers and subsequently the impelling;
from the knees up to the outer wheel, one should contract wheel after wheel.
Thus has been told the supreme secret, which brings about immediate liberation;
now the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is being declared, which grants immediate realization.
Śiva, the illustrious Bhūtirāja, bestowed this [teaching] upon us for all living beings when death has arrived. (30.63)
By reciting which, the individual soul (jīva), having transcended, goes to the stainless state (nirañjana).
Regarding the term "inseparable" (avinābhāva): it is because of the identity (aikātmya) between Śakti and the pure Self (śuddhātman). As it is said there:
"O Goddess, because of the inseparability of Śakti with the pure Self..."
One should know Śiva as Śakti, and Prāṇa as that which is designated as the Pure Self (śuddhātman).
"Because of its single form, and because of the connection between the object of knowledge and the support and the supported.
Thus [it is said].

And regarding this final seed-syllable: "The letter of the heart and the letter of the hips, O Dear One, situated on the right knee—that is the Goddess, that is Śiva, and that is the universe; everything else is its expansion."
One should contemplate this as the essence of thousands of millions of books.
"The power of this [text] could not be described even in hundreds of aeons"—
thus is its majesty declared in the *Śrīdevīpañcaśatikā*. Furthermore,
regarding the fact that there is a different tradition here due to a variation in the reading by the venerable Ojarāja, his own teachers alone are the authority.

Haṃsa is *ha*, amṛta is *sa*, Kālarudra is *ū*, Bhuvaneśa is *au*, the two Anaṅgas are the visarga, and *shsūḥ*. It is called "Six Wheels" (*ṣaṭcakra*) because it consists of six parts. Prāṇa is *ha*, Daṇḍa is the letter *repha* (ra), Guhyaśakti is *ī*, and Icchā is *aḥ*; thus, *hrīṃḥ*. Amṛta is *sa*, and *kha* is [the letter *kha*].
The seed-syllable of space is *ha*; likewise, *sha*. Here, the *bindu* (dot) must be implied because of its inseparable connection.

Alternatively (*yadvā*), in another view: *sāvitrikā* is *au*, by which there are two voids (*śūnya*) [forming] the *visarga*; thus, *sauḥ*. The pair-offering (*yugmayāga*) is the *yāmala*. And although this is so...
Although this was extracted immediately following [the verse beginning] "The soul, together with the fourteen...
(verse 27), it has been stated again here for the sake of conforming to the arrangement of the *Śrītriśirobhairava* text; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
"Others" refers to those mentioned in the passage beginning with:
"The individual soul resides in the vital breath... (verse 28). "By the lineages" means by the speakers. "That very one" refers to the letter *sa*. "Kha" refers to—
The Bindu. As it has been said:
"The Jīva [is formed] by the six long vowels combined with their respective classes [of consonants];
the limbs of the three Vidyās [are formed] by the short [vowels], and the faces by the five [long vowels]. (Mālinīvijaya Tantra 3.61)
Thus [it is said].

And regarding this, the followers of the venerable *Triśirobhairava* maintain that the seed-syllable of the armor (*kavaca*) is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); those who rely on the venerable *Devīyāmala* maintain it is four-syllabled; however, our own teachers uphold the second position alone, since here [is mentioned] the eye-mantra (*netramantra*), even though it was not taught in the venerable *Pūrvaśāstra*.
Since this is stated according to the method of the *Śrīdevyāyāmala*, setting aside the doctrine of the *Śrītriśirobhairava*, it is that very meaning which is intended here.
And so says the *Triśirobhairava*:
Having divided the Gāyatrī into five parts and conjoined it with the Śukriyā,
this mantra beginning with "to the heart" (hṛdayāya) is the omniscient, supreme heart.
Having taken Vāgīśī alone, one should draw her hip;
having placed her in the state of Nivṛtti, Tārā follows immediately after that.
Applying it in two ways and joined with the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), one should extract the trident;
having rendered it devoid of the staff (daṇḍa), it is then endowed with the Gāyatrī.
Mahākālī is joined with *payas*; Pūtanā is indeed through the power of *māyā*;
Nādinī is joined with the tongue; and Paramā is conjoined with the throat.
Having made that [offering] endowed with milk, Ambikā was joined with milk;
this is declared to be the fulfillment of the head of the Lord of the Three Peaks (Triśira).
The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), however, resides in the throat; one should deposit the solitary burner (dahanī).
Having joined it in two ways and inscribed it, one should thereafter [place] Nādinī.
Then there is Māyāyuktā, followed by Mohinī accompanied by Ambikā;
next is Śukrādevī, and after that, Pheṅkārī.
And at its end is the *kapāla*, devoid of half a vowel;
O Goddess of the Gods, this is declared to be the *śikhā*, known as the primordial awakening (*anādibodha*).
One should offer Śikhinī alone; Jayantī is joined with Daṇḍa;
Saṃyojyā is joined with Jihvā; and Janārdanī is joined with Dṛk.
Śikhinī is to be extracted alone; it is a trident joined with a staff.
From Priyadarśanī comes the staff, which is endowed with milk.
Vāyuvegā is supreme when joined with Śikhinī and milk;
Ambikā, likewise joined with milk, is known as an impenetrable armor.
One should then extract Cāmuṇḍā, the supreme Śakti, and Ambikā;
all of them are accompanied by Sāvitrī and adorned with the Bindu.
The three eyes of the God have been explained to you, O lady of virtuous vows;
they are Kusumā, Pūtanā, and Guhyaśakti.
One should offer the head together with Śukrā, and the heart alone;
the secret place with Mohanā, and Ambikā conjoined with Bindu, which is indivisible.
Mounted upon the power of wisdom, one should quickly join the syllable *pheṃ* with the Skull-Bearer (*kapālinī*) who is broken apart, as the weapon possessing a radiance equal to the sun.
"It is known as the Mahāpāśupata, which destroys all supernatural attainments.
Thus [it is said].
The *Śrīdevyāyāmala* also states: "The heart of this [mantra] is fivefold, beginning with that which is remembered as the first syllable;
then the syllable of speech (*vāk*), the hip, and the garland of heads situated at the beginning."
Having divided the thigh, which rests upon the right knee, into two parts on all sides,
one should thereafter extract the syllable [HRĪM], illuminated by the trident and the syllable OṂ.
The *nitamba* is joined with *kṣīra*, while the third is the *śiromālā*. That which begins with *praṇava* and is adorned with it is declared to be the *śiras*, ending with *svāhā*.
Having placed the Praṇava and the letter of the throat upon the right knee,
and having then divided [the body] into two parts, one should subsequently place the left foot in the middle.
Then, having extracted the left foot together with the letter of the tongue (jihvārṇa) joined by the crest (śikhā),

one should join the two final letters of the other [group] and extract the crest of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (vajrin). One should then extract the letter of the throat (kaṇṭhārṇa) and the trident (triśūla), and thereafter the two eyes.
In the ocean of milk, the staff of the trident [is placed], with "svāhā" at the end; the armor-mantra follows next.
The Praṇava, colored like a trident and adorned with an earring,
joined with the right hip and possessing the Visarga, should be applied as the Self.
This is the Eye of the Goddess; it is the supreme bestower of victory over death.
It consists of *Ślīṃ*, *Paśum*, preceded by the *Praṇava* (Oṃ), and followed by *Prāṇa*.
One should properly apply [the mantra] everywhere as an ornament for the left ear;
one should join the syllable at the end of the crest-lock, [ending with] the most terrible weapon-mantra.
Thus [it is said].

*Tāra* is the *praṇava* (OM); *dvijihva* is *ja*; *kha* is the *bindu*; *śarasvara* is *u*; *jīva* with the *visarga* is *sa*. Regarding "with *rasa*"—it means six; for the letter *ṭa* is not counted here because it lacks a vowel.
"With the long vowels" means joined with the previously mentioned group of six long vowels; however, for Kubera and Īśāna, [the vowel] is the sixth.

And by the second long [vowel], the *sakāra* and *makāra* are conjoined; thus it is said, "by those joined with *sūma*. Regarding the phrase "by short [vowels]": this means by those corresponding to the long ones. As it has been stated:
"Pūtanā, the staff of the trident, the skull, and the navel itself..."
Śikhinī, Vāyuvegā, Paramā, and Nitambakā.
"And they should be known, O Great Goddess, as joined with the long vowels and accompanied by the bindu;
but the mantras of the world-protectors [and] their weapons are devoid of the long vowels.
Thus it is said.
"By the fourth and the second"—that is, by the letters *ṛ* and *a*. "By the two short ones"—that is, by the letters *i* and *a*.
"In the same way, Viṣṇu and Prajāpati are to be conceived from the nose and the milk."
"But the first and third [of these] vowels are the denoters of the lotus and the wheel.
The term "in the six" is to be applied according to the maxim of the crow's eye (kākākṣinyāya). For indeed, the ritual actions (*karma*) are also of exactly six kinds.
This is what was intended to be expressed. "Consisting of that" means "having the nature of the sequence.
