He demonstrates this very state of being composed of that with the words beginning with "in the recitation" (*jape*). "Akṣi" refers to the second *ka*-group (the *ca*-group). "The second [vowels]" refers to *kh*, *ph*, and *ra*.
With the "vulva-syllable," which is the letter *e*, [this forms] the Lord of the Five Clusters (*pañcapiṇḍanātha*). As it has been said:
The second [hand] should likewise be placed on the left foot with the row of teeth; below that, joined with the right knee, it should be positioned as if holding a staff.
"Marked by the *tilaka*, it bestows all accomplishments.
Thus [it is said].

"By the first"—that is, by the letter *kha*; thus [the syllable] is *phreṃ*. "Also by the last"—the meaning is that not only by the first letter *kha*, but also by the last letter *ra*; thus [the syllable] is *pheṃ*. That is the *jīva*.
The enclosure of the two *ha*s is the two vital breaths (*prāṇa*). *Kālānala* is *ra*. The left foot is *pha*.

Excessively radiant by means of the *repha* (the letter *r*) situated below; the right knee is *e*; "vowel" (*svara*) refers to the distinction between short and long; the staff (*daṇḍa*) is *ra*; life-force (*jīva*) is *sa*; the trident (*triśūla*) is *ja*;
the right finger is *bha*; the other... [is *pa*].
With respect to the right side, the left breast is *la*; the navel is *kṣa*; the throat is *va*; Marut is *ya*; Rudra is *ū*;
the Visarga is *aḥ*; and the trident is *au*. Furthermore, it has been declared in the *Sahitā* that the eighth letter here is *śa*, as found in the *Śapaṭha* and other sources. Thus it is said:
The syllable *kāla*, likewise the all-pervading (*sarvagata*), with the head seized by *dāraṇa*,
the first of the third wave, and joined with the vital point (*marman*) of the *ḍākinī*.
The *pavana* (ya) is joined with the ninth [letter] (na), and from that, the seventh [letter] (sa) is subtracted;
then, having extracted the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī (la), it is conjoined with the Lord of the Oceans (va).
"Having extracted the seventh from the Moon (S), the nine-syllabled Kuleśvarī [is formed].
Thus it is said.

*Kāla* is *ma*; *sarvagata* is *ha*; *dāraṇā* is *ā*. And the first of the third [vowel group] is *i*. *Taraṅga* is *ṇa*; *ḍākinīmarma* is *ḍa*. *Pavana* is *ya*; the ninth is *o*. From that—meaning from the vowel *e*—the seventh is *ga*; *e* is the vowel *ekāra*. *Lakṣmībīja* is *śa*; *udadhīśa* is *va*. From *soma*...
From the letter *a* [the seventh is] *ṛ*. This consists of nine syllables.
By the statement, "..................Ṣadbhāva is Kālakarṣiṇī" (verse 46), the meaning is that it is together with any one of the [states] beginning with Ṣadbhāva. And by this much, of these two—
The equal pervasiveness of the two *piṇḍas* with the Lord of the *piṇḍa* has been made known. Regarding the phrase "beyond the beyond of the supreme"—as it is stated therein:
"That Goddess Saṅkarṣiṇī is established as transcending the supreme."
Thus [it is said].
*Sudhā* is *sa*, *chedaka* is *ka*, and *śaṇṭhādya* is *ṛ*; since *chedaka* is without a vowel, it is the vowelless *ka*. Thus, *skṛk* is formed. As it has been said:
"The *jīva* [the letter *ja*] mounted upon the first of the twice-born [the letter *ra*], joined with the garland of heads [the letter *u*]."
Having done that, he should then place before him the foremost twice-born man who does not live by the profession of a physician.
Thus has been described this Kālarātri, the cutter of the vital points;
O Goddess, he who desires long life should not utter her name.
"By the practice of reciting fifty [times], a sensation arises at the crown of the head.
Having observed this sign, one should resort to the meditation that conquers death. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 17.31) Thus it is said.

*Daṇḍa* is *ra*, *agni* is *ra*, and those two are doubled; by that, *raraḥ raraḥ*. *Prāṇa* is *ha*, *nabhaḥ* is *kṣa*, *śūla* is *ja*; thus, *hkṣjaḥ*. *Chettṛ* is *ka*, *anala* is *ra*; thus, *kraḥ*. *Kūṭa* is *kṣa*, *agni* is *ra*; thus, *kṣraḥ*. *Bindu* is the dot (*m*), *indu* is *sa*, *anala* is *ra*.
Kūṭa is *kṣa*, Agni is *ra*, Marut is *ya*, and the sixth vowel is *ū*; thus, [the mantra] is *srakṣyūī*.
He demonstrates that this very [teaching] produces immediate conviction:
"Even for a man of knowledge who has fulfilled all his duties, once it has been heard... (30.64).
It instantly dispels the agony of death born from the severance of the vital breaths and other functions;
having heard it, even one who was helpless under the sway of great delusion gradually attained [liberation]. (30.65)
Awakening approaches you of its own accord with impetuosity through the presence of the speaker;
you have come here from the supreme state—you are eternal—so abandon the end of the body.
O All-pervading Lord, from the big toe upwards, there is indeed a fierce binding;
this statement of the Noble One was previously [taught] with words named after the worlds. (30.67)
Abandon the binding [tendency] located at the ankles, reaching the knees, situated in the collarbone, and likewise in the genitals;
abandon the foremost city and its center; arise from the heart-lotus! (30.68)
With these many words, this second Āryā verse [is completed]:
"O Haṃsa, O Hayagrīva, O All-pervading Lord, you are Sadāśiva; you are the Supreme, known as the individual soul (jīva)."
"O you whose body is the *bindu* produced by the union of the Sun, Moon, and Fire—haha! Arise!
This is the third statement in Āryā meter, consisting of words numbering one more than the preceding count. (30.70)
You are the eternal one, consisting of the great mantra of Haṃsa, observing the auspicious and the inauspicious;
seated in the center of the maṇḍala, you are the great purpose who acts as the bridge of power.
"O deity-body, enter into awakening, seated upon both lotuses.
This noble statement consists of eleven words. (30.72)
In his exhalation, however, there was the sound "upa" in place of the incorrect word;
[the deity said: "Out of ignorance you were bound; being awakened, arise, O Devāde! (30.73).
This shall be the fifth half-verse of the Āryā, consisting of seven words:
"Go to the great door called the Palate, which is struck by the Udumbara. (30.74)
"Having reached it, go indeed, O friend! Go indeed to the state of Vāmadeva!"—this is the sixth Āryā verse, consisting of fourteen words.
O Lord of the knots, Supreme Self, peaceful one! Having reached the great cavity of the palate, ascend! O Lord of the body, go quickly to the stainless state of Śiva. (30.76)
The seventh noble utterance consists of fourteen words; the reading "prabhañjanastvam" (you are the destroyer) is found in the *Niḥśvāsaśāsana*. (30.77)
Having ascended the middle path and having withdrawn the prāṇa and apāna breaths, and having abandoned both merit and demerit, O Nārāyaṇa, go to the limit of peace.
This eighth noble statement is proclaimed with nine words:
"O Brahman! O Viṣṇu! O Rudra! You are Śiva; you are Vāsudeva. (30.79)
"O Great Space! Abandon this eternal lump of clay consisting of Agni and Soma"—this is proclaimed as the noble statement (āryāvākya) counted among these worlds. (30.80)
The three words "sanātma," "tripiṇḍam," and "mahākośam" are established in the *Niḥśvāsa*, *Mukuṭottara*, and other [Tantras]. (30.81)
"O you who are as subtle as a thumb! Abandon the stainless veil!"—this tenth noble utterance is expressed in six words. (30.82)
"Enough, twice; and thus it is subtle," so it is said in the Śrīmukuṭottara:
"O Puruṣa, you are bound by the threads of egoism and by bonds consisting of Prakṛti. (30.83)
"O non-becoming, O ever-arisen, O Supreme Self! Abandon the path of passion!
This would be the thirteenth line, an excellent verse in the Āryā meter. (30.84)
"O you whose body is the mantra *hrīṃ hūṃ*, come quickly without delay to the end of the body"—this half-verse of the Āryā constitutes the supreme twelfth six-footed [stanza]. (30.85)
Therefore, abandon this body of yours, composed of the qualities [of the elements] and consisting of the six sheaths.
Such would be the thirteenth half-verse of the Āryā, consisting of seven words. (30.86)
Do not grasp at this body composed of the elements; rather, let the eternal great body be taken up.
This fourteenth noble half-verse consists of that many words. 30-87.
"Having pierced through this stainless, infinite mandala that exists in three ways, go forth"—this is the fifteenth noble half-verse, consisting of eight words. (30.88)
This entire Brahmavidyā consists of fifteen clear statements;
however, its partless (niṣkalā) form is proclaimed by means of five syllables.
"That which is recited with [the syllables] joined at the beginning and end of every response" refers to those called "worlds"—that is, fourteen. "By this many" means by exactly fourteen.
"By the previous number plus one" means by fifteen. "By the number of Rudras" means—
[It is] by eleven [syllables]. Regarding "he approaches"—therefore, the reading here is *śubhāśubhopekṣī*.
Regarding "in the Niḥśvāsa-śāsana"—for there, indeed, the reading is *utkrama he deheśa prabhañjanastvaṃ prayāhyāśu*, while the division of the words (*padapravibhāga*) remains exactly the same.

"By nine"—this is because [the word] "having gathered together" (*samāhṛtya*) is intended as a single unit. "Numbered by the worlds"—that is, by fourteen. "The eternal lump of clay of Agni and Soma"—this is indeed a single word.
"The Ārya-verse"—by implication, this is the ninth. "Three words"—for in the *Niḥśvāsa* and other [scriptures],...

The reading is "O Great Treasury, abandon the triple-piṇḍa which has the nature of Agni and Soma"; by this, it is established that there are fifteen words here. "Āryāvākya" means half [of a verse] by implication. "Twice" means two times; therefore, here [the instruction is]: "O [Lord], abandon the covering, even that which is as small as a thumb!"
The reading is "mahāsūkṣmam. "Āryāvākya" means the eleventh [chapter] by implication. "By so many" means by seven. "By fifteen verses" refers to twelve and a half Āryā verses.
He points out the partless Brahmavidyā itself:
Tāra, Māyā, Vedakala, Mātṛtāra, and Navātmaka. (30.90)
Thus, there are five syllables according to the stated pervasion:
the Bindu, Prāṇa, Amṛta, Jala, and Marut, conjoined with the sixth vowel. (30.91)
By means of this seed-syllable situated in the utterance of power (śakti), the bound soul (paśu) is seized;
having first performed the rite of initiation, even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified. (30.92)
Through lightness, the purity of the balance provides immediate conviction;
the mantra consists of the syllables *tā-ra-śa-ma-ra-ya-i*, with *piṇḍa* and *nati* as the four-syllabled [formula]. (30.93)

This is the vital point for paralyzing Śākinīs; it is the heart and the very life itself, consisting of the sixth [vowel], the vital breath (prāṇa), the three peaks (trikūṭa), the raised arms, the one called the spear (śūla), and the bindu. (30.94)
Adorned with moon-segments facing downward and devoid of vowels,
this heart known as Bhairava is the cause of the dissolution of all things.
Vedakala—consisting of four parts (catuṣkala). Mātṛtāra—the sound "Phreṃ".
Navātmā—the [syllables] located in the bindu, the vital breath (prāṇa), the staff (daṇḍa), the navel, the hips, the left breast, the throat, the left shoulder, and the left ear.
It is not composed of syllables. And this [work],

consisting of twelve Āryā verses along with [the commentary], has not been set forth word-for-word because its true nature— the meaning previously explained— can be understood by oneself, and out of fear of excessive prolixity in the text.

This has been explained; therefore, the wise should not be resentful toward us. Bindu is *śūnya* (the void), *prāṇa* is *ha*, *amṛta* is *sa*, *jala* is *va*, *marut* is *ya*, and the sixth vowel is *ū*; *prāṇa* is *ha*, *trikūṭa* is *kṣa*, *ūrdhvabāhu* is *jha*, *śūla* is *au*, and *bindu* is *śūnya*.
The vowel-less is the *nāda*; the nose is the *śakti*; and the downward-facing crescent moon is the *ardhacandra*.
Thus: *hūrkṣjhūṃ*.
He demonstrates his very nature as the destroyer of all:
"Scorched by the fire of Bhairava situated in the center of the circle of fire, the Śākinīs come under control if one should burn this place with it. (30.96)
One should dismiss them first; otherwise, they cause harm. [This is done] with these syllables—*hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *vleṃ*, *kleṃ*—adorned with the twelve vowels. (30.97)
One should recite the heart-mantra named *Priyamelāpana* in the *sampuṭa* (enclosed) form;
the supreme procedure is to do so either for each [mantra] individually, for two together, or with all of them.

"Come under control" means they effect a union by force; "first" means immediately following the union. "By these syllables" means by the two seed-syllables of Māyā and Kāmarāja, which are conjoined with the bindu (the nasal drop) on the left breast and the right knee, respectively.
"By means of [the syllables] beginning with *kaṇṭha* and ending with *danta*, and in such forms. "Each individually"—for example:
*klaṃ vlaṃ klaṃ hrīṃ klaṃ vlaṃ klaṃ*. "By means of two"—for example: *vlāṃ klāṃ hrīṃ klīṃ vlāṃ klāṃ*; or *hrīṃ kliṃ vliṃ kliṃ hrīṃ klīṃ vleṃ*.
*Kleṃ kliṃ vliṃ kliṃ hriṃ*. Thus, it should be understood that this applies even when adorned with other vowels.
In this very context, he shows the two traditional authorities (*gurvāgama*) from the *Śrītantrasadbhāvaśāsana*: "The yoga of the balance-meeting (*tulāmelakayoga*)."
That which was taught by Śambhunātha has been shown by me in due order.
Now, for those who are truly destitute of wealth and have sought refuge, but who—due to defects such as place and time—are not so resolute; || 30.100 ||
The initiation (dīkṣā) that is to be performed, as proclaimed in the Śrīsantatyāgama, is now being told, as requested by Hāṭakeśāna, the Lord of Pātāla. (30.101)
He says that very thing: "O Śrīnātha, O Noble One, O Blessed One, this triad indeed resides in the *kanda* at the foundation (*ādhāra*).
Varuṇa, Macchanda, and Bhagadatta—this triad is in the heart. (30.102)
The four designations for the groups beginning with Dharma, located in the region of the throat, are to be worshipped;
all of them are preceded by *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*, possess the word "sambodhi," and end with the word "pada. (30.103)
Then, one should meditate upon the three vidyās at the crown of the head with mental application, either with flowers or with joys, or even by means of pure contemplation alone. (30.104)

If a disciple whose heart is set solely on liberation is [initiated] by a Guru who knows reality, this initiation, which is skilled in bestowing liberation alone, is called the "Supreme Secret" (paropaniṣad). || 30-105 ||

One who has been initiated by this initiation, remembering these three vidyās within the heart, indeed goes to the supreme abode at the end of the body, even without external worship and the like. (30.106)

Regarding the phrase "in the group beginning with Dharma": this refers to the fourfold aim (*caturvarga*) characterized by virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*).
By means of these, there are Dharmanātha, Arthanātha, Kāmanātha, and Mokṣanātha.
"Sambodha" means an address or invocation; by means of that, the sequence begins with *hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīnāthapāda* and so forth. Thus it has been said.
—consisting of the higher, the lower, and so forth. "Bhāvi" means that which is about to be described. "Atha" (now/then) refers to the context of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"By the application of the mind" means by the firmness of continuous contemplation (*anusandhāna*). "By joys" means by wine and other things that produce them. By the phrase "the supreme abode," it is indicated that this [state] pertains exclusively to those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
It has been extinguished.
He points out this very triad of vidyās:

one should place at the beginning the three syllables—the Praṇava, Māyā, and the Bindu—at the end of which is the beloved of Agni (the syllable RA), following the five words joined with their vocatives. (30.107)
The Praṇava is Oṃ; Māyā is Hrīṃ; the Bindu, by virtue of its four parts, is Hūṃ; and the beloved of Agni is Svāhā. || 107 ||
He explains the five words themselves: "First, Siddhasādhani; O you whose nature is the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman);
and together with the word 'Samastabandha', [the word] Nikṛntani. (30.108)
And that [seed-syllable] is addressed as "O Awakener, O Mother of the True Being of Śiva.
Then there is a sequence of five words consisting of five, eight, nine, three, and eight syllables respectively.
This auspicious knowledge of the Supreme Brahman consists of five syllables beginning with *kha* and bestows liberation;
it is composed of the letter *gha*, which is the final of the consonants, followed by the thirteenth vowel.
At the end of these three phonemes, there is the tetrad of the semivowels;
then the first of the consonant groups, the horse (ha), joined with the triangle (e) and the bindu (m); and after that, the three phonemes ending with pa.
The seven syllables beginning with *mahāhāṭakaśabdā* and ending with *īśvarī*, followed by the three-syllable vocative *kṣamasva* and *pāpāntakāriṇi*. (30.112)
Then follows the six-syllable mantra, which is the word for deluding [the senses] regarding evil speech and so forth;
then the ten-syllable phrase "pāpaṃ hana dhuna" repeated twice. (30.113)
The six-syllable mantra ending in the fifth case (dative) arises through the power of Rudra and Śakti;
thereafter, that which is the single syllable is proclaimed as the Brahman of the Visarga.
One should recite it by merging it with the syllable *tadanackatakāra*.
This Vidyā consists of forty-nine syllables and is celebrated as the Dīkṣāvidyā.

The six-syllable mantra of Māyā, the four-syllable mantra of the Supreme Brahman, the three-word mantra of the Fourfold Knowledge (Caturvidyā), and then the eight-syllable and five-syllable mantras known as Yogadhāriṇī. (30.116)

The three words consisting of the forms of the individual self (ātmā), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman), ending in the vowel 'e' and situated in the state of awakening, are proclaimed as the ten-syllable mantra. (30.117)
"Rudraśakti" consists of four syllables; then "rudradayite," and "pāpaṃ daha daha"—this is the twelve-syllable mantra of four words. (30.118)

In the auspicious Sadāśiva, there is a pair and a hexad; the bearer of the drop and the arrows [is] that group of four and a half syllables. Thus, this [mantra] is the destroyer of worldly conventions (samaya). (30.119)
That supreme Vidyā of the Lord consists of fifty-five syllables.
He also explains the division of the syllables of the five words, beginning with "five" and so forth: "randhra" means nine;
"khapañcārṇa" means fifty syllables. Thus: *oṃ hrīṃ hūī bodhani oṃ*.

*Hrīṃ hūī śivasadbhāvajanani svāhā*. The unsurpassed is *a*; desire is *i*. The end of the gutturals is *ṅa*. The thirteenth vowel is *o*. The semivowels are *ya-ra-la-va*. The first of the classes is *a*. The horse is *ṇa*. The triangle joined with the bindu is *e*; the end of the labials is *phaṃ*, thus *pheṃ*. The emission is Brahman (*visargabrahma*).
That, with the *randhra* (the letter *ha*) and *abdhi* (the number four), makes forty-nine. Thus:
*aiṃ oṃ ya ra la va aṇa phaṃ mahāhāṭakeśvari kṣamasva pāpāntakāriṇi pāpavimohini pāpaṃ hana hana dhuna dhuna rudraśaktivaśāt sat māyārṇaṃ hīm hrīṃ*.
That which ends in the vowel *e* is situated in the *bodhana* [mantra]; by that, [the mantras] are *ātme*, *antarātme*, and *paramātme*.

"Four-footed" (*catuṣpadī*) refers to the single word *daha daha*. A "pair" (*yugma*) refers to two words. A "sixfold" (*ṣaṭka*) refers to six syllables. *Bindu* is *hūṃ*. An "arrow" (*iṣu*) is *phaṭ*. *Sāvahā* is *svāhā*. *Khaśarā* is...

Fifty [syllables]. The letter *ṭ* with a half-vowel (*sārdhārṇa*). Thus: *hrīṃ pare brahme caturvidye yogadhāriṇi ātme antarātme paramātme rudraśaktirudradayite me pāpaṃ daha daha saumye sadāśive hūī phaṭ svāhā*. And this [mantra] belongs to us.
The teachers have taught this; thus he says:
"This triad of vidyās was elucidated by the illustrious Bhūtirāja. (30.120)

The illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha, who directly assumed a human body—surely, the nature of the mantras has been shown here; but why has their potency (vīrya) not been stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In this regard, vigor has already been mentioned; the teacher should apply it everywhere.

In accordance with the entry into the seed-syllables of meaning, their internal [visualization], their recitation, and so forth, there is indeed nothing whatsoever that has not already been described previously. (30.122)
Furthermore, fruitless repetition never pleases us.
Anticipating the objection—"Is it not the case that his power (*vīrya*) is of many kinds? By what kind is this [to be understood]?"—he says "artha" and so forth.
He summarizes this very point with a half-verse:
"In this manner, the essential nature of mantra, vidyā, and so forth, has been described. (30.123)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Mantras and Other Means," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus, may there be auspiciousness.
Satisfied by the nature of the mantra obtained through the instruction of the illustrious Guru,
this man named Jayaratha has thus concluded the thirtieth chapter.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Mantras and Other Means," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 30 ||
The Thirty-first Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
This [work] consists of seven paths, having as its nature the triad of Vidyā, Māyā, and Prakṛti.
Victorious is Kauśika Śambhu, who causes the universal trident to blossom on all sides.
Now he begins to explain the true nature of the mandala according to its essential meaning:
"Next, the reality of the mandala is described in brief.
In that regard, he first states the accomplishment of the square:
Having established the eastern direction, one should stretch the cord evenly.
Having divided that [line] in half, one should again mark the middle, the east, and the west;
then, by measuring half of that and half of that again, [one marks] the east and the west.
One should mark it with that [measurement] and draw two intersecting lines;
thus, there shall be two "fish-junctions" (matsyasandhi) in the south and north.
In the middle of that, one should drop a thread for the sake of establishing the south and north;
or else, by means of a thread equal to the east-west line, [one establishes] the north and south.
One should mark from the other mark and likewise from the eastern one;
then, one should cast a long thread through the center of the fish, extending it toward the south and north.
Then, using half the measure of the deceased's field, one should mark the cardinal directions from the center;
by means of two threads arising from two directions, there shall be a fish-mark at each corner.
In the fish-shaped diagram, the Vedas and the Sūtras form a square;

having established the east and west directions— meaning the eastern direction by means of the equinoctial shadow of the gnomon and so forth, and the western direction by inference— at both evening and morning, one should proceed toward the equality of the desired field of four cubits or other dimensions.

One should lay down a thread extending from the eastern to the western direction. Having divided that equally, one should mark the middle in the eastern and western directions—meaning one should indicate it by means of three lines.
Immediately after that, [one should mark] the half which consists of four parts in relation to the entire thread.

Taking as the measure that which consists of one-eighth [of the whole], half of that (one-sixteenth), and half of that again (one thirty-second), one should mark the front and back; the meaning is that one should draw six lines in each of the two directions by moving outward. From there, by that same amount...

Having placed markers on the left and right at each respective location using a cord measuring the two halves of the east-west axis, one should successively apply two circles in the southern and northern directions, so that therein—

There should be two fish-junctions (matsyasandhi) shaped like the feathers of a crow. By casting a thread through the middle of those two fish-junctions, extending from south to north, the establishment of those two directions is achieved. "Or else" (*yadi vā*)—this marks the beginning of an alternative method. "Equal to the east and west" means by means of the entire [compass].
"From the western mark and also from the eastern one"—by this mark, the instruction is stated as being the remainder of all [the others].

"In the same manner" means as was just mentioned. And thus, with reference to the center, the two lines that serve as the cause for establishing the four directions take the form of four cubits and so forth.
One should mark the desired field with measurements along the cardinal directions— in other words, one should draw four lines there in order to produce equality on all sides. Then,
from the marks situated in the four directions, using two threads originating from two directions...

The fish would be situated in each intermediate corner: in the southeast from the east and south, in the northeast from the east and north, in the southwest from the west and south, and in the northwest from the west and north. And in those four [fish] situated in the intermediate corners...
One should place four Veda-units at the corners—thus is the accomplishment of the square.

An objection may be raised: "Are there not many mandalas in each respective scripture? Which ones, then, are said to exist here? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that although these [mandalas] differ according to the specific scope of their own scriptures, [they are nonetheless included here].
It serves as the cause for the various types of spear-rotations (*śūlavartanā*) described, which depend upon specific mandalas that constitute the primary basis;
for indeed, "effort applied to the principal [factor] becomes fruitful."
With this intention, he promises to first describe the mandala of the triple trident as revealed in the *Śrītrikasadbhāva*, since the mandalas are said to range from one up to a hundred:
"Since the mandala is taught to begin with one and end at a hundred... (31.7)
In the Siddhātantra, it is said that there are one hundred maṇḍalas at that pīṭha;
among them, the three maṇḍalas situated in the center are considered the principal ones. (31.8)
The middle trident, the triple trident, and the nine-pronged trident are clearly [described];
therein, the ritual procedure for the trident has been stated through infinite varieties. (31.9)
We shall describe that maṇḍala which has that as its source, as shown in the sequence of the true state (*sadbhāvakrama*).

Regarding the phrase "on that seat" (*tatpīṭhe*): it refers to the seat of the maṇḍala. Regarding "in the middle of that": the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the hundred maṇḍalas. Regarding the phrase "it has been said": this means, by implication, in the *Siddhātantra* itself. As it has been stated:
"Now listen, O beloved, as the mandala and the seat are being described.
A hundred mandalas have been proclaimed in the Siddhātantra, O fair-faced one."
"I shall declare their names; listen with a one-pointed mind, O lady of excellent hips, as they proceed in order up to a hundred mandalas. Thus he begins.
"Hāhārāva, Ghanaruddha, Sāmaya, Citrakaṇṭaka," and so forth,
up to: "Madhyaśūla, Tritriśūla, and likewise Navaśūla."
Thus ends the middle section, concluding with: "It is considered to consist of a hundred mandalas joined with the sacrifice of time (adhvamedha).
He states that very point:
In the case of a square [mandala] based on the Vedas, one should set aside one-third from all sides.

One should divide that respective field into sixteen parts. "In a four-cubit [area]" means in one consisting of ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). "A third part" means thirty-two finger-breadths. "On all sides" means in the four directions; therefore, in each direction...

One should discard sixteen finger-breadths each— meaning one should set them aside for the sake of the door and so forth. Therefore, because of that discarding of one-third, the entire remaining field is to be used for the drawing of the three tridents (triśūla) which will be described.

The meaning is that one should divide [the area] into sixteen parts; sixty-four square inches (256 *koṣṭhakas*) are to be made. For when the entire field is divided into twenty-four parts, there are five hundred and seventy-six (576).
There are squares because, by omitting four parts in each direction for the sake of the doors and so forth, three hundred and twenty (320) squares remain— thus it is said.
This is the intended meaning. Therein, he begins the procedure for drawing the trident itself:
"Now, the center of the two Brahma-threads is clearly the Brahma-pada. (31.11)
Then, having established a limit and a target, one should first draw the fourth thread;
thereafter, one should proceed transversely with the fourth thread immediately following that.
One should draw two moon-lines within the square from the outer edge by half a part;
their point of intersection lies on the third vital point (marman) from the Brahma-line.
And another [mark] at half a square; thus there shall be a pair facing inward.
From the Brahma-sūtra, on the second cubit, it should be fixed upon the vital point (marman). || 31-14 ||
Having drawn a pair of full moons, the wise one should rotate [the lines] from the third transverse division on the sixth part situated along the Brahma-thread.
Having placed a thread at the center of the half-square, suspended from the tip of the full moon,
one should rotate it upwards until it reaches the two fire-parts (three-quarters) of the pair of crescent moons.
Having set aside two horizontal parts from the western side of the crescent moon,
one should likewise form a corner up to that point and create two curved segments.
That single horn arises with an extremely sharp and curved tip;
this same clear procedure is declared for the second horn as well. (31.18)
Then, when the middle prong is to be made,
there should be two inward-facing half-moons in the third upper cell and in the fourth half-cell.
And just as that single full moon previously described would be reached, through the joining of mutual knots, the state of being bound arises. (31.20)
Thus, on its second side, by means of the two curved segments of a crescent moon,
one should join the *gaṇḍikā* with the two middle [lines] and lead it forward with the other two.
The sūtra on both sides [of the central axis] is that by which it becomes sharp at the middle peak;
subsequently, the second Brahma-sūtra is placed below both sides. (31.22)
Having been carefully grasped by the preceptor who understands the *ūha* method,
the practitioner of mantra should subsequently turn westward toward that Brahma-thread.

"Excluding the middle prong, the entire procedure previously described [applies]. The word 'thence' (tataḥ) means starting from the level of Brahmā, which has been established as the limit. The word 'cord' (sūtra) refers to a line and not a square. The word 'from the beginning' (āditaḥ) means in an upward sequence. The word 'thence' (tataḥ) refers to that which has been made the target."

From the fourth sūtra. "Tiryañc" means by way of a lateral movement. "In that which is immediately following it" means situated in its vicinity; thus, having placed the left hand upon the vital point (marma-sthāna) consisting of the fourth sūtra, [one proceeds] with respect to the fourth [sūtra] situated above that vital point relative to the Brahma-sūtra.

Starting from the middle of the square and extending outward as far as the square below it, one should draw two moons by means of a circular motion, but not by relying on a measurement of half a portion of the inner section.
"Situated at the third vital point (marman) from the Brahma-thread" means that it is situated by taking that [point] as its support.

Having placed the right hand upon the third vital point (*marman*) and the left hand upon the square and its half, by means of their rotation, one should produce another pair of moons joined together— facing inward, not outward— immediately following those two moons.
And with reference to the Brahma-sūtra itself, having firmly placed the left hand on the second vital point (marman)—
that is to say, on another full [circle] joined to the first two moons, and not on a pair of half-moons occurring immediately thereafter— one should proceed. By that—

One should lead [the line] upward from the Brahma-sūtra to the end of the second part, so that the joining of the *gaṇḍikā* may occur here according to the sequence to be described. For this very reason, it is said, "by the wise one.
Regarding the phrase "from that which is situated on the Brahma-sūtra"—this means starting from the Brahma-position as the limit.

This is the meaning. "From the sixth part" refers to the sūtra, while [the seventh] is from the seventh. "In the third" means by way of upward movement. "Full" is in relation to the second moon of the previous [fortnight]. As he will state: "from the western [part] of the crescent moon," therefore...
Having placed the right hand on the back of the thread at the second half-square,
starting from the tip of the inner full moon and facing upward, one should extend the thread up to the portion characterized by the number three, which is marked by fire.

One should rotate it. How? He says: "joined with a half-moon"; that is to say, it is joined with a half-moon, meaning it possesses that shape. Furthermore, from the third half-cell, having omitted two horizontal parts—that is, on the back of the middle of the line of the second part of that [cell]—one should proceed.

Having placed the right hand at the west, one should rotate [the cord] again starting from the tip of the crescent moon until reaching the corner in the form of the extremity of the edge of the crescent moon situated immediately adjacent to that thread, so that by such rotation it becomes joined with a crescent moon; thus is the crescent portion formed.

But it should not be full; one should make two curves so that there may be a horn with an extremely sharp and curved tip. Regarding the readings *tataḥ* and *ādyāt*: from *tataḥ*, it means starting from the western crescent moon (*khaṇḍendu*); and from *ādyāt*, it means from the first-formed crescent moon.

It should be explained as "up to the corner," in the same manner as [the phrase] "prior to the village"; it does not refer to "two moons" in the preceding sentence, because— as stated later in passages such as "one should draw two revolutions for the pair of moons from the western and the first half-moon"— only two moons are to be drawn.
Because the first word has already been introduced, it cannot be referred back [to], and because it would be purposeless;
he extends this very point to the other horn as well with the words "in the second," etc., but here the specific difference is that the placement of the hand is otherwise. Thus...

Having described the formation of the two side-peaks (*pārśvaśṛṅga*), he also speaks of the formation of the middle peak, beginning with the words "the middle," and so forth. "The third" refers to it in relation to the Brahma-thread (*brahmasūtra*). "Upward" means not horizontally.
"Inward-facing" means not outward-facing. "That" refers to the pair of half-moons. "One" refers to—

"One by one"—the meaning is that by that [process], even two full moons [are formed]. He states the purpose for this very point with the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth. He extends this same [rule] to the other side as well with the words "in the same way" (*evam*) and so forth. "Of this"—that is, of the middle peak. "Joined" (*śliṣṭa*)—by means of the union of the upper and lower [parts]. "One should lead"—[this is the ellipsis].

The end of the field. Having thus described the procedure for the preceding field, he begins to speak of the subsequent one as well with the words beginning "pārśva" (the side). "The second" is said because it occurs in the latter half.
"By one who knows how to infer" means by virtue of skill in determining the meaning through extension (*atideśa*) and so forth. And thus, what [is achieved] by this?
Regarding the task to be performed, he says: "It should be," and so forth. This means excluding the middle prong, because a staff (daṇḍa) will be fashioned in its place.
Now he describes the formation of the peaks on the southern and northern sides:
"Then, that pair of upward-facing half-moons which was previously mentioned... (31.24).
Then, by means of two [lines], a well-connected *gaṇḍikā* should be made within;
by means of two further leading lines, there shall be a pair of middle *śṛṅgas*.
"Pureti"—at the time of drawing the previous trident (*triśūla*). "Susaṅgateti"—referring to the two side-prongs.

(25) Having thus drawn the three tridents here, he speaks in order to draw the lotus and other elements situated below them: "Below this, by increasing the portions, [draw] a lotus consisting of four circles."
Then that wheel is of two kinds: one with sixteen spokes and one with twelve spokes.
In the center is the station of Kuleśvarī, which may be the void, or a tilaka, or a lotus, or a six-spoked wheel, or the twelvefold sky. || 31.27 ||
In this [mandala] with three triple-tridents and seven spokes, by merely joining them together at the center,
there shall be a group of seven lotuses, wheels, or voids.
Or it may be mixed or combined through the divisions of concise and detailed treatment.

"Below this"—that is, below the trident (śūla); as for the staff (daṇḍa), it is above. For its proper position is indeed only below. Therefore, there is an internal covering for these by means of the trident, but by these [others], however—

Regarding the word *daṇḍasya* (of the staff): for this very reason it has been said—“...the five parts thereof are concealed by the lotus-seat. Regarding the phrase *bhāgavṛddhyā* (by the increase of parts): [this occurs] in the sequence of one, two, and so forth. Regarding the phrase *dvidhā tat* (that is twofold):...
"Having twenty-four spokes"—meaning first twelve spokes, then sixteen spokes, and then twenty-four spokes.
"A tilaka" means a mere dot (bindu). "Merely by being joined" means not by way of covering.

The word *vā* (or) indicates an alternative. Here, "intermixture" (*saṅkara*) refers to the state of being combined when the lotus, the wheel, and the void are taken together, or when they are separate within a single spoke—either the lotus and the wheel, the lotus and the void, or the wheel and the void. "Mixture of positions," however, refers to their abiding in separate spokes. By that [method], starting from one up to six, they are placed in pairs in the subsequent [spokes].

Thus, there are six varieties among the single units. Likewise, there are exactly six [varieties] for the triads when combined with the single units. Similarly, there are also six for the dyads when combined with the triads. When the three are mixed together, such that one remains as fivefold—namely, a triad in one place, a dyad in another, and single units in five places—this constitutes one [variety].

In one place there is one [unit] and in another three; in five places there are two [units] each—this is the second [arrangement]. In one place there is one [unit] and in another two; in five places there are three [units] each—this is the third. Thus, there are three [arrangements]. Regarding the fourfold arrangement, however:
in one place there is a triad, in two places there are dyads, and in four places there are single units—this is one [arrangement]; in one place...

The first [case] is: two [groups] of two, and four [groups] of one; the second is: one [group] of two, two [groups] of three, and four [groups] of one; the third is: one [group] of one, two [groups] of two, and four [groups] of three; and the fourth is:
one [group] of one, two [groups] of three, and four [groups] of two.

The fourth [arrangement] consists of three [units] in one place, one in each of two places, and two in four places; this is the fifth. Two in one place, one in each of two places, and three in four places—this is the sixth. Thus there are six. However, when situated in three ways: two in each of two places, three in each of two places, and one in each of three places—this is the first; two in each of two places... [and so on].

There are three [arrangements]: the second is "two [groups] have one each, and in the three [remaining groups] there are triplets"; the third is "in two [groups] there are triplets, and in the two [remaining groups] there is one each, and in the three [remaining groups] there are pairs. Regarding the threefold placement of two [groups], there is one [arrangement]:

"in one [group] there is one, in the three [remaining groups] there are pairs, and in the three [remaining groups] there are triplets," and [another where] in one [group] there is a pair, and in the three...

The second [arrangement] consists of single units in three groups of three; the third consists of a group of three in one place, groups of two in three places, and single units in three places—thus there are exactly three [types], making thirty-three in total. These are formed in such ways as: first the lotus and then the wheel, or first the wheel and then the lotus, and so forth.

Since there would be the contingency of numerous varieties if one were to specify the distinctions— such as when, due to the transposition of the sequence and so forth, pairs alone are mixed together within the seven spokes in cases of *saṅkara* and the like— one variety is presented. Thus:
When there is a mixture of the three triads through a permutation of their sequence, there is one [configuration], making thirty-five.
When these very [configurations] are fixed in position upon the seven spokes (*arā*) and multiplied by seven, they become two hundred and forty-five. These are the solitary lotuses (*padma*).
There are three modes: that wheels or voids exist everywhere; that all three exist everywhere;
and also the mode that pairs [of these] exist everywhere.

Since specifying individual distinctions would result in an infinite variety of types, and because they are all identical as a pair (*dvikatva-sāmānya*), these unmixed variations remain one; thus, even within the seven spokes (*arā-saptaka*), due to their uniformity and lack of distinction, there are five [types], totaling two hundred and fifty. And among these modes, regarding the triads (*trika*) and so forth, through the inversion of sequence and other permutations...

Because there is an infinite variety arising from the mixing of three, two, or one [of these factors] in their various combinations, they are not enumerated here. Now, he speaks in order to take up the field (*kṣetra*) consisting of three parts, which has been established on all sides:
Then, one should add an additional area there, measuring half of the original field.

Then, immediately after the drawing of the trident, lotus, wheel, and so forth, one should add further ground to the area already taken—which consists of sixty-four finger-breadths divided into sixteen parts;
that is to say, one should take it for the purpose of drawing the intended staff, gates, and other features. Now, [one might ask]: "But..."

Anticipating the doubt—“What is meant here by ‘more’? Is it intended with the specific intention of having previously abandoned the entire field, or otherwise?”—he says: “by the measure of half the field,” referring to the field that was originally demarcated for the purpose of drawing the trident and other figures.

The meaning is: by that measure which constitutes half of the thirty-two finger-breadths (dvātriṃśadaṅgula) consisting of eight parts. By that, there are four sections of sixteen finger-breadths in each direction—this is the intended sense. || 29 ||
When the field has been cast in this manner, what should be done? To this he says:
"In that regard, the staff (daṇḍa) is said to be one part, consisting of six spokes and a pure hub;
with an extremely sharp point and a beautiful red luster, it effects possession in an instant. (31–30)
That goddess Kuṇḍalinī, known as the wave and possessing great surges,
resides within the bulb (kanda) in the form of a hexagon, embodying the six deities.
It should be eight parts in width and half of that in length;
from that, the doors should be fashioned in sequence according to the rules of variegated proportions.
Regarding the term *bhāga*—he states the pervasion [of the parts] by means of the *daṇḍa* and *amalasāraka* through the words beginning with *yā sā*.
It is characterized as being hexagonal (*ṣaḍaśreṇa*). It consists of six deities, as it has been said:
"Hāhārāvā, Mahārāvā, Ghoraghoṣā, and Bhayaṅkarī..."
"Pheṅkāriṇī and Mahājvālā [are located] in the bulb (kanda), and they are greedy for the six flavors.

Regarding the phrase "by eight parts"—the word *bhāga* here denotes a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); therefore, the meaning is "by two parts. Regarding the word "extended"—this refers, by implication, to the *amalasāraka*. Half of that...
"Thus"—by means of four finger-breadths. "Then"—immediately after the drawing of the staff (daṇḍa). || 32 ||
He demonstrates the very same variegated arrangement:
whether the forms are triangular or circular, and the arrangement of the staff and the door will occur right at the front; therefore, it is not divided here.
This has been explained.
Now he points out the varieties of the *śṛṅgavartanā* by way of its divisions:
"Then one should make the horn clearly [shaped], or else in the opposite manner. (31–33)
Or, having divided a pair of upward-facing crescents (unmukha), one should make four;
they are curved in the middle, clearly visible, downward-facing, and situated on the sides. (31–34)
The *uttāna* (upturned), *ardha* (half), *asama* (uneven), *pūrṇa* (full), *śliṣṭa* (joined), and likewise *granthigata* (knotted)—thus the twelvefold turning of the moon destroys delusion. (31–35)
Furthermore, that [triangle] is considered to be of two kinds by virtue of being inward-facing or outward-facing.
"With a clear peak" means it is fashioned with three parts facing the eastern direction, like the middle peak.
"By way of the reverse" means it is indistinct, as in the case of the east. "The pair of moons facing upward"—
It is drawn by being attached to the fourth vital point (*marman*). "Having broken" means having divided it into two.

"The fourfold" refers, by implication, to the moons. "Crooked in the middle" means that even within its interior it has the shape of a half-moon. "Clear in the middle" means it retains the very form previously drawn.

"In the middle" means like the eye of a crow (which looks both ways). "Facing downwards" means its tip, shaped like a half-moon, is somehow hanging outwards. "Situated on the side" means it is turned toward the south and north, like a clearly defined horn. "Upright" means—
"Facing upwards. "Half and uneven"—meaning, by its half it is unequal, having the nature of a single moon and consisting primarily of lines.
"Full"—because of its distinctiveness. "Interlocked"—meaning, it has been formed from the base upwards through mutual connection. "Situated at the knot"—meaning...
It is fashioned precisely by the joining of the tips of the edges of half-moons; thus, there are twelve modes of fashioning.
If a further differentiation were made even among these divisions, there would be an infinite emergence of variations of mandalas; thus he says:
"From the differentiation of those [mandalas], there would be an incalculable expansion of variations. (31–36)
[The design] arises from the pedestal, the path, the outer ground, the neck, the ears, and the cheeks;
through the combination of primary and secondary ornaments, and through the various arrangements of lines representing the qualities. || 31–37 ||
Through the distinctions beginning with the pair of svastikas and extending up to the group of eight,
and by means of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, the mandalas are infinite.
Then powders should be offered according to their beauty:
vermilion, lapis lazuli, and excellent white chalk. (31–39)
In this world, the supreme colors arise from the union with the triad of deities:
the Supreme (Parā) is radiant like the moon, while the Higher-Lower (Parāparā) is red.
She is the other, supreme Kālī, the terrifying Caṇḍayoginī; for indeed,
as previously explained in the first group of six types,
when pairs of identical forms are mixed with identical single units, starting from one of the two wheels, the lotus and the disc.
There are six [combinations] up to those situated with the lotus, the wheel, or the sky, making eighteen.

Thus, there are eighteen types for the lotus and the sky, and eighteen for the wheel and the sky, totaling fifty-four modes. When these are multiplied by seven, according to the fixed rule of the seven [groups of] enemies (arā), [the total becomes three hundred and seventy-eight].
Three hundred and seventy-eight arise. By multiplying those by two, due to the division of the doors, seven hundred and fifty-six arise.
By further multiplying those by twenty-four, due to the division of the moons—
There are eighteen thousand one hundred and forty-four;
by the presence or absence of their pedestals (*pīṭha*), there are thirty-six thousand two hundred and eighty-eight; and by the presence or absence of their pathways (*vīthī*) for those as well—
Seventy-two thousand increased by five hundred and seventy-six— thus, through these alternative calculations, three crores, seventy-one lakhs, fifty-eight thousand,
nine hundred and twelve arise. And in this very same place, all together:

In the lotus-wheel (*padmacakra*), by means of the combination of the whole and the parts— such as [the pair] "lotus and space" in one place, "wheel and space" in another, "lotus" in one, "wheel" in another, and "space" elsewhere— and so forth, through the mixing of various pairs and single units,
the resulting divisions are multiplied by seven and so on, according to the aforementioned method of the non-regularity of spokes (*arānaiyatyādi*).
As for the question of how many there are, one must ask Śrīdhara himself. "Then" means immediately after the turning at Dvārakā. "Kālī" refers even to Kṛṣṇā.
For this very reason, its majesty is so great—thus he says:
"Having seen that maṇḍala, all the goddesses dance there at all times. (31.41)
Even if [the deity] has not been worshipped, one should be initiated by the Mothers when [the deity] is seen by one who is uninitiated.
Having thus established the infinity of the mandala and, as an incidental discussion, having defined the offering of colored powders (*rajas*) and so forth,
and because the trident alone is predominant here despite its infinite varieties, [one should perform] the principal [rites] based upon it.
He enumerates the divisions in brief:
"Or what is the use of saying too much? [There are] those with three tridents and seven spokes. (31–42)
Thus, there are six thousand and two hundred and fifty Śūla-yāgas.
Or rather, what is the use of this demonstration of the infinity of mandalas?
[As it says: "In this three-trident with seven spokes... (31.28).

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: the two hundred and fifty varieties introduced by the words "ityādi" (and so forth) are multiplied by twenty-four— according to the aforementioned method, by means of the twenty-four divisions of the moon based on the support of the seven-and-a-half [syllables]— resulting in six thousand Śūlayāgas.
"There would be six thousand minus two hundred and fifty.

Regarding the word *ūnam* (minus): *ūnā* (feminine) is indeed a corruption, because it lacks syntactic connection and because the ablative case is inappropriate where the instrumental case is required. Furthermore, in this context, two hundred and fifty is the quantity to be multiplied.
The twenty-four lunar divisions, obtained by taking seven spokes as the divisor, are the multipliers;
the resulting product is six thousand. This [calculation] would become rootless in the reading that omits the term "multiplier" (*guṇya*), for no multiplier has been mentioned here previously.
Let this matter rest; for generally, this verse would be more logically placed before the verse beginning with "tato rajāṃsi deyāni... (verse 39), so that everything would be consistent.
Now, one might ask: "From where does such majesty as this arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That Goddess who is the supreme power (parā śakti) is established as the flow of the vital breath (prāṇavāhā). (31.43)
That [energy], coiled in the form of a spiral within the universe, is present here directly;
the principles (tattvas) and the goddesses of the principles, as well as the entire universe, are established within this.
He shows this very point in part:
"Here, above, by means of a mere thread, three spokes of the trident are situated; as the seat, they consist of Icchā and the others, and are the accomplishers of enjoyment and liberation. (31–45)
But for one whose sole desire is liberation, these [rites] have their centers pierced by the spokes of the trident;
therefore, one should perform this great sacrifice with extensive displays of great wealth.
Whether desiring prosperity or seeking liberation, the wise man should worship [it];
by the mere sight of it, bhūtas, vetālas, and guhyakas [are subdued].
They flee in the ten directions and Śiva himself becomes propitious through the worship of this maṇḍala, even for one who is pierced by the power of dull faculties. (31.48)
Constantly, within six months, he attains the threefold knowledge;
having attained which, he himself discerns what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.

"At the end of the body, one becomes the self of Bhairava; moreover, one who desires accomplishment attains it by means of the *tantu* alone"—that is to say, by means of the expanding form. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis, meaning that those very [powers] beginning with Will (*icchā*) are meant. "With the center pierced by the spokes of the trident."
This means they have the form of the three lotuses of the Unmanā state. As it was stated previously:
"These very [energies], when the expansion of duality has dissolved, gradually attain blossoming;
yet, while remaining unmixed with one another, they then become free from differentiation as the three nights dissolve."

"The three lotuses and the state beyond mind (*unmanasī*)—this very thing shall serve as the seat. (15.341). "Therefore"—meaning, for the reason that it is presided over by the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), and so forth.
Not only does he possess such majesty, but even one who has mastered this [mantra] likewise—thus it is said:
"He who knows the pervasion of this mandala and the very placement of its deities... (31.50).
He who understands the practice within the Trika teaching is a guru;
the dust of his feet should be borne upon the head by one who desires Śiva. (31.51)
Here, one should worship all three—creation, maintenance, and destruction—in their proper sequence;
however, the fourth [state] is either in the center or is the fulfiller of them all.
"Here"—that is, in the three tridents. "In the middle"—that is, in the place of Kuleśvarī. "In all"—that is, in all three sequences. || 52 ||
By means of this very extension, he speaks of another sacrifice:
"Or one should perform the sacrifice of the four tridents with the hidden staff;
there, one should properly worship that clearly manifest fourfold sequence. (31–53)
Regarding the term "hidden staff" (guptadaṇḍa): the sense is that its middle prong would indeed be located in that very place.
And this is precisely the distinction between this [mandala] and the previous one. || 53 ||
And this which has been described by us is also stated in other scriptures; thus he says:
"This has been told in the secret *Ṣaḍardhahṛdaya*, the supreme [scripture];
it is proclaimed in the *Ṣaṭka* and indicated in the *Śrīsiddhayogīśvarīmata*. (31.54)
Having first delineated the mandala that grants all desires, it should be provided with a great trident and adorned with lotuses, wheels, and other symbols. || 31-55 ||
One should draw a trident at every door, except for the western one;
furthermore, in the corners, one should fashion the great trident accompanied by trees.
On the tip of the trident, there should be three groups of three lotuses born from the waters of nectar;
thus the trident should be fashioned in eight ways or even in three ways.

Thus, the divine city of the *khecarīs* has been indicated in this secret and esoteric scripture, namely in the *Hṛdaya of the Three-and-a-Half [Āgamas]* (the *Trika-hṛdaya*). It is "indicated" (*saṃsūcita*) rather than explicitly stated. He cites the very passage from that work, beginning with "in front," etc., up to "the western."
Regarding the phrase "having excluded": that which exists as the locus of worship is [indicated by] the verse beginning, "The western [door] should be made open...
The term *amṛtāmbhobhavārīṇām* refers to the one born from the waters of nectar, namely the Moon (*candra*). Of him...
The meaning is "of the enemies' lotuses. The terms "eightfold" and "threefold" refer, respectively, to the intention of having four and one prongs on the tridents.
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well; thus he says:
"It is also taught in another place, in the teaching of the Śrīsiddhātantra. (31.58)
He says this very thing:
"In the center is a lotus; with half of that [measurement], the prongs of the trident are formed.
The mandala should be fashioned as marked by a trident, and marked by a lotus during the filling. (31.59)
Having thus explained the arrangement of the lotus and trident as taught in the *Śrītrikasadbhāva*,
he now begins to describe that which is set forth in other scriptures: "Now, the arrangement of the lotus and trident [is taught] in the *Śrīpūrva* and the *Triśiromata*."
In the Siddhātantra, the Trikakula, and in the Devyāyāmala and Mālā; || 31-60 ||
As it has been stated in the *Sāraśāstra*, the *Tantrasadbhāva*, and the *Guhyatantra*, so shall it be clearly demonstrated here, even though it follows the sequence already mentioned. (31.61)
Although the arrangement of the trident (śūla) has already been understood through the method just described, nevertheless,
it is now clearly demonstrated for the sake of easy comprehension, exactly as it is taught in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* and other texts, by employing certain specific details.
The meaning is: "it is expressed. || 61 ||
In that regard, because of its preeminence, he first demonstrates exactly what is taught in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"On the ground based on the Vedas, measuring three cubits, one should first divide the eastern half;
having set aside half a cubit on all sides—extending toward the east, north, and south—" (62).
With squares measuring three finger-breadths each, arranged eightfold both vertically and horizontally,
one should again set aside two parts each on the southern and northern sides.

The intention of the phrase "previously, at three cubits" is that by subsequently adding one cubit for the sake of the door, it will become four cubits; thus, since it will be stated later that "one should divide this into squares of three finger-breadths," it is established that one should divide it into thirty-two parts.
In this manner, having likewise set aside twelve finger-breadths from each of the three directions starting with the east,
one should divide the eastern half— by means of eight squares measuring three finger-breadths each moving upward and sixteen squares moving sideways— from that previously divided eastern half.

Furthermore, on the right and left sides, one should omit two squares each in a row-wise sequence so that twelve squares remain by way of the side-movement; by this much alone, the *śūla* [diagram] is accomplished. || 63 ||
First, he describes those situated at the sides: "On both sides of Brahmā, from the fourth *jīva* line toward the east, there are two pairs of crescent moons, each measuring half a *bhāga*. (31.64)
Here, excluding the Brahma-thread, the threads designated by the term "jīva" are those on both sides; starting from the Brahma-thread, that which is the fourth jīva-thread from it—
toward the east (pūrva), in the eastern direction— and likewise, that which is the very same fourth jīva-thread from there.
By means of a cord measuring one part and a cord measuring half a part, there shall be two half-moons;
however, the instruction "two by two" is given in the distributive sense with reference to both sides. || 64 ||
How so? He says:
"Between those two, on the third [line], on the right and left sides, the wise man should fashion a pair of crescent moons from the inner rotation. (31.65)
One should draw two pairs of half-moons, positioned at the tips of the two crescent moons, facing outward and located at the other vital points (*marmastha*) of those two.
In the same way, one should fashion [the third line] in the Brahma[-line], measuring one part and half a part.

For it begins from the fourth life-line by moving along the side, and it comes to rest at the second life-line because its measurement is one part; that which is between those two life-lines is the third.

The *jīva* (the life-line) is, by implication, the fourth line from the front; there, having placed either the left or right hand according to propriety, the wise person—skilled in its drawing—should fashion two semi-circular segments on the inner side of both flanks, and not by wandering outward. However, this is for the measurement of the half-circle.
Regarding Khaṇḍacandra, according to the method to be described, this is the distinction:
that the drawing begins from the fourth part. On both sides of those two, by means of an inward-entry movement on the third *marman* relative to the fourth—
Placing one hand so that its two tips are joined to the ends of the two crescent moons turned immediately adjacent to it, one should rotate it outward— not inward— twice, so that in both instances...
Two pairs of half-moons should be rotated. "In that manner" means:

having placed one hand on the second *marman* (vital point) on both sides—specifically the one following the third—and [having it] reach the tips of the two half-moons by being joined with a thread extending vertically from south to north, therefore...
In this way, one should create two inward-turning curves so that there may be two pairs of crescent moons, each having a measure of one part and a measure of half a part.
Thus, after describing the side-turning (*pārśvavartanā*), he describes the horn-turning (*śṛṅgavartanā*): "Then, at the end of the second part, on both sides of the Brahma-line... (31.67).
Two lines should be drawn forward by the wise, divided into three parts and reduced by one-third;
they should meet at the upper tip of the single half-moon and join with the end of the Brahma-thread.
One should draw two lines for the purpose of establishing the middle peak;

furthermore, from the two sides of the Brahma-line, proceeding upwards, those which are the second parts on the east— having been so stated— one should, by virtue of being wise, [draw them] from their base to their end.

By joining the tips of two crescent moon-shaped portions, two lines should be drawn so that they taper by one-third of the width. With that [same] measure, there should be a *gaṇḍikā* (joint) three fingers wide and three fingers long;
for one [of these] is joined with the *gaṇḍikā* of the other.

Starting from the upper extremity of the moon, which measures half a portion, one should fix two threads reaching to the tip of the Brahma-thread, by means of which the central horn shall be accomplished.
Now he describes the drawing of the side-ribs:
"A thread held at intervals from the *jīva* at the ends of those sides [is used]. (31.69)
One should draw [the line] from the corner of the first half-moon segment to the [opposite] corner;
likewise, from the other chord of those two, starting from the corner of the first half-moon segment. (31.70)

In that very same way, one should lead the thread for the sake of accomplishing the two horns. Taking as a support that which is the fourth *jīva*— meaning the two sides situated at the tips of that central horn which have entered the mandala— one first establishes the second [line] externally with respect to the internal [space].
Starting from the tip of the crescent moon that is being divided,
one should draw a line as far as the end consisting of the sixth part between the southeast corner and the northeast corner, since it is held at a point separated by one such part.
"...reaching the fire-portion" (verse 16)—

by this view, the meaning is that it is situated in a space measured by three parts. From the other *jīva* located at those same front and side [points], with respect to the fourth as the third, according to the stated method...

From the eastern side, starting from the midpoint of the fourth part of the first circle drawn internally— which measures half a part— one should lead the cord toward the corner in the same manner as previously described, extending it only as far as the sixth part, whereby the accomplishment of the lateral horn is achieved.
Having thus drawn the trident in the eastern half of the field, he says [the following] in order to draw the staff and so forth in the other half as well:
"In the other half of the field, the staff is two cubits long and consists of five concealed parts. (31.71)
It should be six finger-breadths wide and four long; below that is the stainless core (sāraka), and below that, the base is desired to be four finger-breadths with a sharp tip.
One should construct four doors in the cardinal directions of the primary field;
they should be one cubit in height, or half of that, and their width should be equal to that [height].
One should make it double in size on the outside; then listen to how the lotus is to be made.
One should construct circles according to the Vedas, with each having the measure of one unit.
Furthermore, one should lay down sixteen life-lines (jīvasūtra), eight in each of the directions;
then, again, in the middle of each pair, one should drop lines equal in number to those [already laid]. (31–75)
One should perform a rotation equal to the side-life-line (pārśvajīva), situated on the third circle;
having completed this end, one should then bring forth the tip of the life-line (jīvāgra).
Wherever there is attachment, once that connection has been stabilized, the practitioner should apply it there to bring about the success of the tips of the petals. (31.77)
On each petal, one should fashion three filaments;
likewise, the triad of horn-like buds should be made with double the eight-finger measurement.

"Two cubits" means together with the door-area that will be described hereafter. "Five concealed parts" means that this [area] consists of four divisions and one part concealed by the pedestal (*pīṭha*). As it has been said:
"It is two cubits; those five parts are hidden by the five pedestals."
"The remainder would be the other visible part, measured by its width and divided into sections. Regarding "four finger-breadths":
when fingers are mentioned, the *āmalasāraka* (the central stone) is six fingers wide and four fingers long. "Sharp-pointed" means having the shape of the letter *E*.

"Of the primary field" means of that which measures three cubits (*hastāyāma*). "A cubit in length" is because, by taking four parts on each side of the central lines, half of that—namely half a cubit—is the width of the door, as it is extended by exactly four parts. "Twofold from the outside" means—

This is because four additional parts are added to each side. "Equal to that" means that, like the neck, the cheek is also extended by exactly two parts. Now, he describes the drawing of the lotus situated within the four parts of the *aṇḍa*-field—therefore:
And so forth. "Like the Vedas" means four. "In the middle" means equidistant from both sides.
"Numbered as such" means sixteen. "Of these" refers to the sixteen lines that have been drawn again.
"Third" means, by implication, within one of the sixteen lines drawn again that are situated on the third circle.
Having placed the hand outside that [circle], starting from the tip of the third part— aligned with the life-line situated at its side—
one should rotate [the compass] until reaching the end of one of the sixteen lines previously laid down for it.

One should bring that [line] into proximity with the life-thread (jīvasūtra) situated at its side—thus one should produce sixteen half-petals. Here, by the phrase "in some lotus" (*atraiva kutracit padme*), which implies an impossibility [of otherwise], this is made known: for the sake of accomplishing the half-petals...

It was stated that one should make a rotation by placing the hand in the middle of any one of the sixteen lines given again in the third turn; it is exactly the same here as well, but with a reversal. "Having made firm" means mentally. "There" means at the place of contact. "Having done" implies [placing] the hand. "One should lead" means—
That is to say, [it refers to] the delusion. "Three by three"—this is by taking recourse to the three lines situated there.

"In that same way"—by means of the aforementioned method of drawing; however, it is double eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas). For that indeed consists of twenty-four finger-breadths. Thus, in the preceding case as well, it is by means of exactly four parts.
It should be understood that the lotus, the wheel, and the void are the effects. || 78 ||

Right here he states the rule for the pollen: "The pericarp is yellow; according to the division of base, middle, and tip, the mass of filaments should be made white, red, and yellow respectively. (31.79)
The petals are white in color along with the protective rim;
likewise, the pedestal is quadrangular, extending outward to a measure equal to half the pericarp.
One should [draw] its four feet starting from the southeast in the sequence white, red, yellow, and black;
likewise, the four corners are drawn with all four colors, and the circle is desired to be made with three.
The staff should be blue-red; the *āmalasāraka* [wood] should be yellow. One should fashion the red trident, which was previously described. (31.82)
Afterwards, having left a space of four finger-breadths to the east of the door,
the door— whether quadrangular, circular, or oval— should be decorated with various designs.
One, two, or three *purāṇi* may be equal, whether on the sea or on both [sides];
they are highly adorned with many features such as the beauty and embellishment of the cheeks and the neck. (31.84)
It has a manifold form and configuration, endowed with creeper-like subtle chambers.
There is a circular line situated at the tip of the petals of the *prativāraṇa*. "In that same way" means it is white.
One part is half of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). "Its feet" refers to the feet of the pedestal (*pīṭha*). "By three" means—
"Free from red dust"— this refers to the exception to the rule of two cubits, namely, that one should leave aside four finger-breadths.
He demonstrates the variety mentioned in other scriptures concerning the door as well, which is supplementary to this,
beginning with the words "the door," and so forth.
Although the arrangement of the lotus on the trident has been taught for all the scriptures mentioned, nevertheless, whatever specific distinction exists, that alone is demonstrated here; thus,
even by deviating from the sequence, he sets forth that arrangement as stated in the *Śrīdevyāyāmala*:
It is stated in the Śrīdevyāyāmala that when the field (kṣetra) is situated in the form of a square (vedāśrita): || 31-85 ||
Having divided half [of the space] into twelve parts both horizontally and vertically,
the Guru should cause one part to descend toward his own side above.
One should rotate both [lines] at the end of that middle third;
then, having left aside one part, one should rotate again in the middle of that.
From the upper part of the third portion, one should rotate upwards as far as the end of the fourth portion;
then, from above that, one should again join it downwards.
Having rotated upwards from that measurement, one should join it with the fourth [line].

By the statement "having divided the half into twelve parts," it is established that the entire field must be made into twenty-four parts. "Transversely and upwards"—that is, "on all sides"—therefore, in the four directions.
Having set aside six parts on each side, a field measuring twelve parts should be taken in the middle; therefore, because it is situated on one side of that, the Guru himself,
by means of the very side associated with that part, [should place] one horizontal part upwards in the sequence beginning from the top.
"One should cause it to descend"— the meaning is that one should direct it so as to cause it to revolve. By this,
having placed one hand on the second vital point (marman) with respect to the plane of Brahman, one should [direct] that entire portion—
that is, its own third part— and not, as before, half of it.
One should rotate both of these at the end of that Brahma-thread, starting from its proximity,
so that two crescent moons are formed. Then, by moving sideways,
one should leave aside one part situated above the second part— that is, on the third [part].
Placing one hand upon the *marman*, one should rotate within that very portion already abandoned,
as before, so that two half-moons (*khaṇḍacandra*) may be accomplished. That pair of half-moons which has just been rotated—

Starting from the fourth part—that is, proceeding diagonally in sequence up to the corner of the field—one should join it by moving upward and downward; this is the accomplishment of the horn (*śṛṅgasiddhi*). He extends this same rule to the other side as well, beginning with the word "again" (*punaḥ*), stating: "And again, that very same..."
Relying on the measurement just mentioned, one should rotate three pairs of crescent moons upwards as appropriate, joining them together on all sides,
and having delineated [the form] by means of that, one should also [proceed] with the fourth [pair] which initiates the horn.
"One should join with a pair of half-moons"—the meaning is that one should make it joined with those.
Having thus described the side-circling, he speaks in order to describe the middle-circling as well:
"One joins the thread from above down to the Brahma-thread in sequence. (31.89)
Having first made it wide according to the sequence, one should then gradually reduce its portion;
the staff is desired to be half a part in measure, while the other [part] is twice that.
Again, starting from above the crescent moon that is currently being turned for the first time in its third part,
and extending the thread up to the Brahma-thread, one should join it by gradually reducing the width bit by bit— attaching it right there.

One should act so that its tip becomes sharp—this is the accomplishment of the middle prong (*madhyaśṛṅga*). And thus, in this case, it should be less than [the others] on both sides at the middle prong; this is also the distinction from the previous [case]. "Half" (*ardha*) refers to the two halves belonging to the two parts.
The meaning is that its measure in parts is four *aṅgulas*. Regarding the term "twofold":
by adding half of the field to the six remaining parts (which were left after taking half of the field), its measure becomes twelve parts—that is to say, two cubits (*dvihasta*). || 90 ||

Right here, one prepares the *āmalakasāraka* (the essence of the myrobalan): having taken one part from each of the two [substances], one should roll it like a leaf of the *pippala* tree; this preparation should be placed below. (31.91)
One should draw a lotus in the sixteenth part by omitting twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Here, the word "part" (*bhāga*) signifies a finger-breadth; thus, having taken one finger-breadth from the area on both sides, [it takes on] the shape of an *aśvattha* leaf.

Regarding "the arising of the whirling": this is the downward extension of the staff (*daṇḍa*) by which the base of the *amalasāraka*—which is six finger-breadths wide—is four finger-breadths long and has a sharp point at its lower end.
"In sixteen parts" means in a field divided by sixteen lines.
"By reducing twelve finger-breadths"—that is, in each direction, by which there would be a cubit-sized lotus.
And where should one write that? To this he says:
"Above that, in the middle portion, one should draw a lotus. (31.92)
Then, one should draw the third [lotus] at the end of the middle prong;

"above that" means above the staff. Regarding the phrase "in the middle part"—this is with reference to the mandala. He says "middle," etc., to indicate that one should not only draw the lotus here, but also above it.
He connects the very meaning of the third word [“middle”] with the passage beginning with “in the middle,” and so forth.
In the same manner, one should likewise draw two lotuses situated at the hips on the left and the right.
The pericarp is yellow, and the filaments are red, yellow, and white;
the petals are located outside the lotus, and the protective wall (prativāraṇī) is white.
The trident is marked with black powder, while the Brahma-line is white again;
the tip of the trident is endowed with flames, and the shaft of the trident is yellow.
One should always worship Īśa in the lotus that is in the center of the trident;
above him, the wise one should worship Parā, on his right the other [Parāparā], and on his left Aparā.

"Likewise"—the meaning is: "by means of the removal of exactly twelve finger-breadths. "Petals"—meaning, by implication, white ones. "The line of Brahmā"—the central portion of the spokes. "Endowed with a flame"—due to the application of red powder. "Īśa"—Sadāśiva in the form of the *paitṛka* (ancestral/fatherly). "Above"—[refers to the upper part].
Of the middle peak. "The other" refers to Parāparā. || 96 ||

Now, one might object: "Has not the Goddess Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, who is even higher than the Parā and designated by such terms as 'the true being of the Mother' (mātṛsadbhāva), been mentioned here? Where is she to be worshipped? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That Goddess who is the ender of time (Kālāntakā) is established as transcending even the Parā."
She always seizes the wheel of pain by her mere will.
As it is said in that very same place:
"In the middle of that is the Supreme Goddess (Parā), on the right is the Intermediate (Parāparā), and on the left horn is the Lower (Aparā); now hear concerning the top of the central horn."
"That Goddess Saṅkarṣiṇī, who is established as transcending the Supreme.
The word "devours" (grasate) means she assimilates [all] into her own self; by this, the intended meaning is that all this is indeed composed of her alone. || 97 ||
He states the pervasion of these very [energies] through their elaboration:
"This energy (kalā) is indeed of the nature of Śānti; it becomes supreme (parā) as Vidyā;
