the non-supreme (aparā) is Pratiṣṭhā; and Nivṛtti is the intermediate (parāparā). (31.98)
Now, one might object: "The powers (kalās) such as Śānti and the rest have been described as belonging to Sadāśiva as his energies (śaktis).
How can they possess such an extensive pervasion? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The staff of Bhairava, standing upright, is the form whose nature is that of Sadāśiva."
Its powers are fourfold in their gross form, but subtle, they are manifold.

For that very form of Bhairava, which is full and situated above the trident characterized by the staff (daṇḍa), is of the nature of Sadāśiva; within its own grossness there are many powers such as Śānti and so forth, whereas otherwise these [powers] are different—this is the intended meaning. 99
Having thus explained this as an incidental digression, he concludes the subject at hand:
"This sacrifice, known as the Ḍāmara, which possesses the three powers, has been fully described.
Now, he begins to describe the arrangement of the trident and lotus according to the Triśirobhairava system:
Now, the procedure for the trident and lotus as seen in the *Traiśirasa* is being inscribed here.
He says that very thing:

"One should worship the ground, the colored powders, the measuring cord, and the chalk with the root mantra, using the primary purifiers such as the beautiful nectar of the left [hand] and others. (31.101)
In the center of a square measuring four cubits, there is a trident with three prongs;
its staff is two cubits long, extending from top to bottom, and it is broad, supported by a pair of pedestals.
It should be made eight finger-breadths in length and provided with three lines;
at the base of the staff, there should be a pedestal measuring twelve finger-breadths.
In length it is four finger-breadths, and in height it is ten finger-breadths.
The middle of the pedestal (pīṭhī), situated at the base of the trident (śūla), measures forty-eight finger-breadths from the root—

“from the root” meaning by means of the root-mantra (mūlamantra). Regarding “in a four-cubit [pedestal]”— even though it is divided twenty-fourfold according to the method to be described later— the division for the three cubits alone is such that the staff (daṇḍa) is two cubits.
"Vasvaṅgula means 'broad'—that is, eight fingers in width. As it is said there:
'The breadth, however, is eight fingers... Thus, the reading 'vimala' (pure) is a corrupt reading because it lacks scriptural authority. The same applies elsewhere as well."

Because they are not found in the original transmission (*anāgamika*), corrupt readings have been rejected and will continue to be rejected; therefore, one should not think otherwise. "Khābdhi" means forty. In this [mandala], there is a covering of eight finger-breadths by means of the *vidyā*-lotus, and one finger-breadth by means of the sky-line (*vyomarekhā*).
Its visible extent is thirty-one finger-breadths.
Concluding this and beginning the procedure for drawing the trident (triśūla), he first describes the field required for it:
"Having made the staff of the trident, [one should divide it] on all sides into three parts. (31.105)
It should be one cubit (hasta) in measurement on all sides, consisting of parts each measuring eight finger-breadths (aṅgula).
"By three parts" means stacked one above the other. "One cubit on all sides" means it is a perfect square.
He divides these very three parts according to their respective locations on the trident:
"The tip of the trident, the middle of the trident, and its base—that is how they are. (31.106)
An altar should be constructed in the center, measuring six finger-breadths on both sides;
it should likewise be twelve finger-breadths long on both lateral sides.
One should fashion an altar at the base with a height of four finger-breadths;
likewise, on both sides, it should be shaped like a half-moon.
One should rotate the chalk-line and fashion the waistband, O Goddess, measuring two finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in length.
One should arrange it on the left side exactly as it is on the right;
in the middle, from the width of the tip of the trident, there is one finger-breadth both below and above.
The *gaṇḍikā* should be made according to its own form, with a width of four finger-breadths and a height of six finger-breadths.
O lady of excellent vows, the base of the trident should be fashioned above the pedestal;
the tip of the trident should be made six finger-breadths long and very sharp.
"The center of the spokes should be made, and the space below the spokes is six finger-breadths.

Regarding the phrase "the altar" (*vedī*) and so forth: here, in the middle portion of the finger-breadth, with respect to the Brahma-thread, the area measuring six finger-breadths at both ends on both sides is intended by implication.

Having relied upon that method of six fingers in width, a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) twelve fingers in length should be constructed; therein, a central arrangement in the shape of an altar must be made—meaning that two inward-facing crescent moons (*khaṇḍendu*) should be drawn on both sides. The same applies to the base as well.
That is to say, having set aside half a part from the proximity of the Brahma-line to be used for the *gaṇḍikā* as will be described,
one should construct an altar (*vedī*) on both sides at a distance of one and a half parts,
measuring four finger-breadths in height, with an upward-facing crescent-moon shape; then, from that point as well— meaning:

Placing the hand at the tip near the *brahmasūtra*, one should rotate the thread from the second tip up to the tip of the crescent moon (*khaṇḍendu*) situated in the middle part, so that [the line] is of the required length.
A configuration measuring four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) and shaped like a hip (kaṭyākāra) may be established on both sides;
and in that case, the width is two finger-breadths. He extends this same measure of two finger-breadths even to the middle part, stating:
"because of the width of the tip of the trident in the middle. And it is not the case that this applies everywhere without distinction.

"The width is two finger-breadths"—thus he says—"and below, one finger-breadth. By this, a reduction of the half-moon should be made at the end of each finger-breadth from the edge of the hip, as appropriate.
Now he describes the tip of the trident, beginning with "from above," and so forth. Immediately after that...
Furthermore, because of its width in the upper portion, it measures four finger-breadths;

this is established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the placement of the three lotuses of twelve finger-breadths each to be described later, as well as the inclusion of a field measuring one cubit on all sides.

The meaning is that, from the edge of the side of the spike-field up to its height, a pedestal (*vedī*), waist (*kaṭi*), or spoke (*arā*) measuring six finger-breadths and one and a half parts should be made on both sides. In this way, he also fashions the side-peak (*pārśvaśṛṅga*).

By the words "gaṇḍī" and so forth: first, the base of the spike (śūlamūla) should be made consisting of a knob (gaṇḍikā) whose height is equal to two parts, with three spokes joined at the top, situated above the pedestal;
immediately thereafter, it should be one finger-breadth in width at the tip, and for that very reason, it must be very sharp.
By leaving two finger-breadths above the third part, there is a space of six finger-breadths in the middle and the same measure below; thus, up to the tips of the two half-moons,
it is eighteen finger-breadths in length.
The middle peak should be there. Regarding this very point, he states its breadth:
"One should fashion the middle part so that it is four finger-breadths deep. (31.113)
That very same [line] from east to west is here [the first]; the trident, however, is outside of that.
One should cause it to be made with three threads and should rotate each one individually.
The three lotuses at the tips of the trident are twelve finger-breadths [in diameter] with four parts;
they have three, eight, and twelve petals respectively, located in the right, left, and middle positions.
The triple wheel, the city of wind, and the lotus with eight spokes—known as Vidyā—are at the base of the trident; thereafter, one should cast down the *rajas*.
One should fill the trident up to its handle with lapis lazuli; behind the three lines, there should be three white spokes.
With white *rajas*, there should be a lotus of knowledge at the base of the trident;
the three upward-pointing lotuses are, in sequence, red, reddish-black, and white. (31.118)
With white [pigment], a line for the sky (vyoma) should be made; due to its thickness, it extends one finger-breadth outward.
Having set that aside, the altar (vedikā) should be constructed with a measurement of one cubit.
The square enclosure wall should be three times its width in length; furthermore, there should be gates on all sides in the cardinal directions, each measuring one cubit.

Having divided it into three parts sequentially according to the measurement of twelve finger-breadths, one should fashion the neck, the cheek, the primary ornament (śobhā), and the secondary ornament (upaśobhā) at its end.
Then, one should cause a square enclosure to be made, provided with the earth-lines, using powders that are white, red, yellow, and black.
One should fill the center with red powders according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
regarding its pervasion, that which was previously stated should be followed therein.

Thus, with reference to the middle shaft (*madhyaśūla*), one should fashion the middle portion, extending from east to west, as being depressed according to the measure of four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)—this is the connection [of the sentence]. This is the meaning here: [the depression] extends as far as the inclusion of the *gaṇḍikā* above the two tips of the half-moons.

The width is four finger-breadths; starting from the middle section, there is a reduction of one finger-breadth for each of the four [sections] respectively until only one finger-breadth remains. Regarding the drawing of the three lotuses above that, he says "tadbahiḥ" (outside of that), and so forth; by the inclusion of the additional area, [the lotuses are placed] even upon the tips of the tridents.

The meaning of the statement is that one should form three lotuses with three revolutions, and each one should be drawn with four [revolutions] of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) each. "With spokes eight finger-breadths long" means that the spoke connected to the shaft is eight finger-breadths in length and has eight petals. It is called "the triple spoke" because it pertains to the shaft (daṇḍa).

"Red-black" means dark brown (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*). "In sequence" means in the right, left, and middle [channels] as previously mentioned. "The line of space" refers to that which pertains to the lotus of *vidyā*.
"Dividing it threefold in sequence" means according to each respective part. "In the city" means—
On the occasion of the mention of the "three tridents," he briefly clarifies its very sequence. || 123 ||
He says that very thing:
"The division into three spokes, the entry, the exit, and the revolution;
the pervasion of the plane of the Unstruck (anāhata), and the supreme arising of Kuṇḍalī. (31.124)
The goddesses have gone to the place of the heart in the well-proportioned middle of the trident;
the shaft of the trident resides in the navel, while the base of the trident is situated in the heart.
One should contemplate the three wheels at the extremity located in the station of power (*śaktisthāna*).
Regarding the term "unstruck" (*anāhata*): this is because the arrangement of the spokes, whose nature consists of the rotation of entry and exit, has this very form.
It is stated that such is the awakening of the power (*śakti*) in the form of Kuṇḍalinī—by means of Kuṇḍalī.

"Arising as supreme" means that they have gone to the location of the heart, because of the manifestation of will and the other powers in the form of the enemy (arā). "Situated in the navel" means that from that very place, the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti) arises in the form of a staff (daṇḍa).
[The word] "in the heart" [is used].
By the statement beginning with, “The heart is the thread of power...,” [it refers to] the birth-support (janmādhāra), which is the locus of the arising of power. For this very reason, he says:
“the limit situated in the place of power. Regarding “at the limit” (prānte)—it means at the “end of twelve” (dvādaśānta).
Regarding the method for its emergence from the base of birth up to the *dvādaśānta*, he says:
"Lifting it up again and again by means of the *kalā* from the nature of the center of the body. (31.126)
One should enter the range of the center of the trident situated at the end of the staff of the trident;
one should enter the root, the middle, and the end within the abode of Śakti at the limit of the limit.
Anticipating the question, "How even this [is possible]?", he says: "Having made the instruments motionless, one should at one time engage in vibration;
having pressed upon the root-bliss, one should enter the state of the three powers. (31.128)
There, by worshipping with diligence, all accomplishments arise through the union of all paths and the state of pervasion by the sixfold path. (31.129)
With such efforts as these, beginning with the entire circle of mantras,
one should contemplate the trident composed of the thirty-six principles.
The arrangement of mantras by one situated at the equinox should be performed in this supreme mandala; when it is worshipped, one shall attain the state of the Lord of All.
"Root" means consisting of the scent of intoxication (*mattagandha*). "By one situated in the equinox" means by means of the equilibrium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—this is the meaning.

Having thus described the distinction between the trident and the lotus, he now defines the *svastika* of the Lord of Space: "Now, it should be performed with the *svastika*; its procedure is stated as follows."

Regarding the phrase "it must be done": by the force of the statement, "Now the true nature of the mandala is briefly described," it refers to the *maṇḍala*. "Endowed with a svastika" means because of its connection with the svastika.
The meaning is: "that which is designated by that name. As it has been said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Mātṛcakra, bestower of the refuge of the Unmanā state!
[You are] the auspicious Svastika, which brings peace and nourishment, is blessed, and grants all desires."
O Supreme Lord, that which has been indicated in all the Tantras but not explicitly stated—
by the omission of its aphorisms, there arises the conceptualization of the lotus of delusion.
"Speak that which is great, which pacifies the flood of obstacles and brings about nourishment.
Thus [it is said].
Regarding the state of being the Svastika of Vyomeśa, however,

[it is established] by the Lord Navātman, who is designated by the etymologically meaningful term *Vyomeśa* according to such statements as: "One should offer the incense of the body to the Great Liṅga of Vyomeśa."
In order to define the state of being that which is to be presided over, he states the procedure for it as follows:
"First, one should establish the channels (nāḍikās) according to their measure, [amounting to] a muhūrta. (31.132)

The *nāḍikās*—that is, the threads—are situated in the directions of Śakra (East) and Varuṇa (West), as well as extending toward the South and North. "Muhūrta" refers to thirty [units]. "Śakra" means those extending from East to West; "Yāmya" means those extending from South to North.
And what would happen in that case? To this he says:
"There would thus be twenty-nine lines, proceeding both straight and oblique. (31.133)
The "lines" (vaṃśāḥ) are the divisions. "Straight" means extending from east to west; "transverse" means extending from south to north. || 133 ||
He summarizes this very point in order to make it clear to the heart:
"Eight hundred and forty-one *marmas* arise.
Here, "*marmas*" refers to the constituent parts (*bhāgas*). For, when twenty-nine is multiplied by twenty-nine, [the result is as stated].
It would be so.
He analyzes this very point:
"The lotus has stalks numbering the objects of the senses, and its circle consists of two moons. (31.134)
The *svastika* pedestal, which grants all desires, should consist of six parts;
with eight parts, there are the doors and the pathways—such is the arrangement of the divisions.

Regarding "viṣaya"—there are five. And this is on all sides, so that there would be two and a half parts on each flank. The same should be understood for what follows. The phrase "yugmendumaṇḍala" (the pair of moon-maṇḍalas) and "svastika" are qualifiers of the lotus itself; their inclusion here is to manifest its preeminence.

It is said that [the mandala] "bestows all desires. By this, it is stated that there are twenty-nine divisions: five parts for the lotus, two for the moon-maṇḍala, six for the pedestal (pīṭha), eight for the pathway (vīthī), and eight for the gate—thus making twenty-nine divisions. In this manner...
This is the "distribution of portions. || 135 ||
Therein, he first describes the door:
"O beautiful one, one should erase nine, five, five, and three [units] from the exterior to the interior in sequence;
likewise, the vital points (marmāṇi) in the four directions from the center [should be erased] at the doors. (31.136)
One should erase the vital points (marmāṇi) within the cities located in the external and internal wombs of Fire, Earth, Sage, and Space, excluding the internal channels (nāḍis). 31.137

Nine apertures (*randhra*), seven sages (*ṛṣi*), five arrows (*śara*), and three fires (*agni*). Here, with respect to the center, in all four doors starting from the outside and proceeding inward, portions numbering nine and so forth are to be erased in sequence, so that here—

The arrangement of the layout on the floor of this particular temple known as Meru should be as follows: the five elements, including space— which indicates the apertures by way of its void-like form—
thus constitute the collection of portions beginning with fire (vahni) that extends from the outside to the inside on both sides of the door.
One should omit [the lines] so that the arrangement, being at the very threshold of the gate, becomes inward-facing and takes the form of a city (*puryākāra*).
Having thus described the drawing in the four cardinal directions, he speaks also regarding the corners:
"In the corners of the gates and the enclosure wall, [one should place] two, three, five, and six [units]."

There are two eyes and six seasons. Thus, in the door-corners, beginning from the second, third, and fifth squares respectively by omitting one square at a time, one should erase them; however, those numbering the seasons (six) should be taken separately and erased entirely.

When, through the merging of the two types of beauty arising from both directions, an arrangement resembling the *gomūtrikā* (cow-urine) pattern emerges in the corners— this is the junction of the doors (*dvārasandhi*).
Now, he speaks in order to describe the drawing of the grid (vīthī):
"The channels of the Brahma-lineage are to be erased, starting from the eyes and extending to the sixth position. (31.138)
The two eyes and the fire [2] from the fire [3] are to be deleted; from the Vedas [4], the pair of eyes [2];
from the flavors [6], the eye [1] situated in the north; and from the east, the Vedas [4], the fires [3], and the flavors [6]. (31–139)
There, on the right side of the Brahma-line fixed at that door, starting from the second part which is the *netra* (eye), six parts situated in the *rasa* (sixth) position are to be erased;
above that, starting from the third of the *vahni* (three), five parts—namely, *netra* (two) and *anala* (three)—are to be erased; and likewise above that.

Starting from the fourth [square] from the Veda [four], there are four [squares]—two eyes (2), two yugas (4), and again two eyes (2)—which means that above that, starting from the sixth [square] from the Rasa [six], two parts (2) of the eyes are to be deleted. He extends this very same rule to the left side as well with the words beginning with "saumya" (northern). Thus...

The meaning is that one should erase the collection of parts beginning from the second part of the "eye"— the first previously mentioned— moving gently toward the "fire"— the third— from the "Veda"— the fourth— and from the "flavor"— the sixth— according to the principle that "the sequence of meaning is stronger than the sequence of recitation."
Because one follows the sweeping of the entire area of the *vīthī* (path) that will be described hereafter, the erasure (*lopa*) within that [area] is also established. || 139 ||
Having thus described the arrangement of the city, he also speaks of the drawing of the *svastika*:
"Leaving aside the channels situated in the world, [the squares are] two, four, and three in sequence; then five, three, and one; then a pair, two, and three from the sixth. (31.140)
From the eye and from that which has gone to the east...

having set aside seven portions of the world starting from the lineage of Brahmā, one should rely upon the ninth portion, which is the eye; and the four Vedas, being three [portions] closely adjacent to it, [make up the remaining].
The sections, which produce beauty by forming a single unit with the svastika according to the perspective of the omissions to be described hereafter, are to be deleted.
Immediately after that, starting from the ninth section designated by the word "netra" (eye)...
By the word "with arrows" (śaraiḥ), it is indicated that three parts—the fire-altars (*agnayaḥ*)—are to be erased together with the fifth part belonging to the second row which has been turned back.
This is the son of Daśaratha, Rāma... [text continues].

The sandhi in the phrase *vedāgnayaḥ* is like that in *itivat*. Furthermore, from that which is designated by the word "arrow" (*śara*), one should eliminate the pair—the second part—along with the three parts joined with fire; this is the meaning.
Then, sequentially, from what remains after the one designated by the word "yoke" (*yuga*) and the two eyes (*netra*) [from the previous total], one should proceed.
The eye is the second part and the three fires are the parts to be erased; thus is the accomplishment of the *svastika*.

This should be understood likewise for the other directions. Here, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), having drawn two *svastikas* from the east, they should be drawn from the west so that there is symmetry in the arrangement on all sides.
It may be so.
And showing both of these arrangements, he concludes: "..................Mount Sumeru is designated as the gateway; and the beautiful city Svastikā—both are situated in the four directions. (31.141)
"Both" refers to the city of Svastikā and Mount Sumeru. ||141||
Now, one might ask: "In how many parts does the removal of the path (vīthīlopa) occur? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"And having cleared away two hundred vital points (marman), as well as the directions multiplied by the sages (seven), and the [parts] beginning with the eyes, from the middle of the path, O beautiful one. (31.142)
Regarding "the directions" (diśaḥ)—meaning ten—when multiplied by the seven seers (ṛṣis), seventy are produced. There are two eyes.
Thus, having performed the elision (lopanā) within the field of the path (vīthīkṣetra), which consists of two hundred and seventy-two [units], the Guru...
One should construct the street known as Svastikāpuri—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 142 ||
Now he describes the lotus:
"In the center, made by three sages (ṛṣi), the pericarp (karṇikā) should consist of the sense-objects.
The phrase "made by three sages" means it is divided twenty-one times.
He analyzes this very point:
"The wealth made into leaders is the leaf; the leader is divided once. (31.143)
Having placed the fire (three) in the eighth position (sixteen), one should erase those situated in the moon (one).
"Doubled" means multiplied by two. For, out of the five parts allotted on all sides for the sake of the pericarp, exactly sixteen parts remain for the purpose of drawing the petals.

The word *bhāvaḥ* means "they become. For, since the tip of the petal is to be drawn up to the end of the seventh division in each direction, the leaf would consist of exactly eight divisions, including the space-line (*vyomarekhā*).
How so? He says: "the eye," and so forth. "The eye" refers to the second division.
"Divided once" (sakṛdvibhājitam) means made into two parts by a single line alone—this is the meaning.

In this way, [one obtains] the fire—the third part. Having divided these two parts, which extend through the eight [squares] to the end of the entire field, into two [again], one should erase those situated at the moon.
The meaning is that one should provide three circles in the shape of a crescent moon for the sake of achieving the filaments, the petals, the junctions of the petals, and the tips of the petals.
How so? He says:
"From the midst of the fires, arrows, and sages, [the letters] are to be deleted up to the moon of the sacred seat (pīṭha). (31.144)

The meaning is that, starting from the region of the pericarp (karṇikā) in the middle— which is delimited by three, five, or seven parts— up to the moon-maṇḍala attached to the pedestal (pīṭha), this much is to be erased. This is the essential point here regarding the third circle.

Starting from the sūtra included within the second division and extending to the middle of the Brahma-lineage, one should draw a circle to produce sixteen half-petals; in the same manner, one should also produce the tips of the petals, but with the reversal as previously described. || 144 ||

Having thus described the arrangement of the lotus, he speaks also of the pedestal: "From the Brahmā [square], one should remove two [units] from the range of the eyes; from the eyes, one should remove four and three; having erased two from the ocean, the channels (nāḍīs) are situated in the eastern direction. (31.145)
From the second part, which is the eye of Brahmā starting from the station of Brahmā (brahmapada),
there are five objects; starting from Brahmā as the sixth part,
those situated therein are arranged in rows according to the lines to be described.

In a location other than the area for the *svastika* that is to be drawn, one should erase five parts from both sides of the eye (*netra*), as no other erasure has been prescribed. Likewise, one should remove exactly five parts from both sides of the four and three parts belonging to Brahmā, even though they are situated within seven parts. From that very point, [one proceeds] to the fourth ocean.

The second part is for Netra, and the fifth part belongs to Brahmā; one should erase exactly five [units] on both sides of those as well, so that in the eastern direction there is a pedestal provided with three lines, white, red, and yellow. (31.148)

The meaning is that, according to the view to be explained below, there are three channels (nāḍikā) in the form of strips (paṭṭikā). Since the "eastern" direction is mentioned as an illustration, this same procedure applies to the other directions as well.
Having thus described the drawing out [of the lines] in the cardinal directions, he speaks also regarding the corners:
From the fifth [square] of the true eye, one should erase [the numbers] from the head, the eye, two, three, fire, and sight;
then from the left side, one should erase them in all four corners of the seat.

By moving toward the corner of Brahmā or by moving along the side, one should erase those three parts belonging to the second position— namely, the fifth part which is the "element" (bhūta), not by its upper region above the head but by its side and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "from the eye, two and fire"— by the power of the word "two," [one proceeds] even from that which was mentioned as the "element."

The second part—meaning that third part connected with it—should be deleted along with that [second part]; likewise, that second [part] should also be deleted along with the third part. In this way, by the phrase "the triad of eyes," that [third part] should also be deleted along with the second triangle;
thus is the accomplishment of the *svastika*. In this manner, it proceeds from the left.

The meaning is that the Guru should erase [the marks] in all four corners of the pedestal, beginning from the svastika located in the southeast corner, by virtue of their being situated in the direction immediately following one's own. || 146 ||
Right here he describes the application of colors (rajaḥpāta): "The petals are to be made with white [pigments], the filaments with red and yellow;
the pericarp is like gold, and the tips of the sprouts are red. (31.147)
The sky-line (vyomarekhā) should be well-measured and blue at the center of the circular lotus;
the pedestal (pīṭha) is endowed with three lines, being white, red, and yellow in color.
The svastikas are of four colors, located in the quarters from Agni to Īśāna; the pathway resembles coral, and the weapons are on the outside in their respective directions.
The vajra is like sapphire; the śakti has the luster of a lotus-gem;
the staff resembles gold; and its face is exceedingly red. (31.150)
A sword with a luster like that of the blue [lotus], a noose with the brilliance of the vatsaka flower, and a banner endowed with flowers and fruit and adorned with five colors. || 31-151 ||
The mace, resembling gold, was exceedingly fierce and adorned with various jewels;
the trident was like a blue lotus, with a crest of blazing, fierce fire.
Above that is a white lotus with a slightly yellowish-red luster;
the wheel is like gold, radiant, and its spokes are like lapis lazuli.
The center of the courtyard should be a beautiful yellow, and the exterior should be reddish like a flame;
such is the temple of the God of gods, which bestows the fruit of all desires. (31.154)

"Svastikas" refers to those located on the pedestals and those situated along the walkways. "Resembling coral" applies to everything except the svastikas. "From the outside" means even from the doors. || 154 ||

Thus, having described the *vyomeśasvastika* in connection with the teachings of the venerable *Triśirobhairava*, he now describes the *śūlābja* (trident-lotus) as taught in the venerable *Siddhātantra*:
"In the venerable *Siddhā*, the procedure for the trident is first [performed] upon a square field."
"The procedure for the trident" (śūlavidhi) is thus stated by implication.
He states that very procedure:
"One should divide it into three parts, each a cubit in measure, so that there may be nine sections. (31.155)
In the center there is a trident; therein, one should thus divide the central portion into three parts.

In a square field—on all sides—one should take a field measuring three cubits (tri-hasta), excluding twelve finger-breadths from the sunward side [the east], so that it may be divided into three parts according to the measure of a cubit. As follows:

By dividing [the area] three times, it shall consist of nine parts for the elephant-formation (hāstika). And therein, one should fashion a trident in the center—this is the implied remainder, according to the manner that will be described below.
He analyzes the middle [mandala] itself:
"Then this procedure is stated as being joined with nine compartments. (31.156)
Having set aside three middle sections,
one should rotate a thread below those two middle sections so as to take the form of a crescent moon.
One should rotate it in both directions there so that the shape of the letter *hā* appears at the front; then, having placed a thread at that corner, one should lead it to the previous line.
Leaving four finger-breadths to the east of the western door,
the wise one should erase the line so that it takes the form of a trident.
Having left a space of half a cubit at the tip of the trident, one should fashion lotuses;
below that, in the middle of the cubit, there should be a lotus with its pericarp and three prongs.

The meaning is: one should divide that central portion, which measures one cubit (tamekahasta) and is composed of nine squares, into three parts, and then divide it again in two ways—that is, divide it sixfold on all sides—thereby making it consist of thirty-six squares, each measuring four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula). This is "this" [referred to].

This will be explained [later]. He states that very point, beginning with "in the middle" and so forth: having set aside the three parts below the middle and taking hold of the station of Brahmā, one should place the hand upon the second vital point (marman) in the center of the two parts on both sides.
Below, one should double the thread in the shape of a half-moon, as previously described; there too,
having placed the hand at the third vital point (marman) to the east of the central thread,
one should draw it in the form of a crescent moon, facing inward and moving upward, between the two parts.

One should rotate [the cord] so that the arrangement takes the form of two curves (*dvikubjākāra*). Then, from the cords joined together at the tips (*koṭi*)— which are of the nature of the beginning and the end— located at the two sides of the letter *ha*, one should [draw] the first [cord] on both sides.

One should lead the line, previously determined at the time of the ninefold division, along the central peak-thread toward the western door according to the perspective to be described, for as far as half a cubit of the upper ninth part. How? He says: "having abandoned," and so forth.

One should eliminate the line arising from the tip of the edge of the crescent moon situated within, starting from the base after leaving a space of four finger-breadths; one should diminish it according to the circumstances by the power of one's own wisdom, so that the sharpness of the tips of the prongs is produced. Thus.

The accomplishment of the three prongs (*śṛṅga*). Then, on the tip of the trident (*śūla*) which has been fashioned with a half-cubit (*ardhahasta*), one should—having omitted the upper half-cubit as a matter of course—construct three lotuses measuring twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*) as before; furthermore, below the three prongs, there should be a lotus measuring one cubit (*hāstika*).
Having thus described the drawing of the trident, he speaks also of the staff:
"One should hold the thread at the tip of the face and let it fall at a distance of three cubits;
having placed the thread at the tip of the middle prong's face, one should let it fall at a distance of three cubits."
One should lead [the line] from the center, avoiding the outer twelve-finger space on all sides.
Having thus described the length, he states the width: "Then one should make two finger-breadths at the bottom, and likewise in the middle and above. (31.161)
One should draw two lines so that they form a trident;
from the lower part upwards, a line is extended there.
Then, having aligned the cord, one should likewise draw two lines on the upper part.
Thus, at three places, one should draw two lines on both sides with a distance of two finger-breadths between them,
so that there is equality on all sides with the lower and middle parts above.
Having made the lines equal, one proceeds; then, in that same manner, one should drop two vertical lines so that a trident with its staff is formed.
And it is not the case that the covering by the stalk of the central lotus should be performed in this manner; thus he says:
"O illustrious one, the central lotus is to be established beneath the trident. (31.163)

And here, in this field divided into twenty-four parts, everything beginning with the doors should be laid out as previously described; however, let it suffice to note that the Blessed One has made the primary allocation of divisions specifically within the central *hasta* used for the half-moon [mandala]. || 163 ||
He concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with a half-verse:
"Thus has this procedure for the mandala been declared by the great gurus through the method of abbreviation.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The thirty-first chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Maṇḍala."
Thus all is auspicious.

Jayaratha, who is eloquent in the exposition of the scriptures of Śiva— such as the *Svastika*, *Śūla*, *Abja*, *Naya*, *Durga*, and *Mātaṅga*— has thus explained this thirty-first daily lesson (*āhnika*).

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Maṇḍala," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. 31.
The Thirty-second Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
It seals the entire universe within the two caverns of the distinction between the pure and impure paths.
May he who, by virtue of being the nature of consciousness, perceives the faults of the virtuous, be Time itself.
Now he begins to explain the procedure for the mudrās:
"Next, I shall describe here the procedure for the mudrās as sung in the tradition of the Guru. He states that very procedure:

And in the venerable *Devīyāmala*, mudrā is said to be of the nature of a reflection (*pratibimba*), based on the scriptural teaching regarding the arising of the original image (*bimba*), through the discernment of these two meanings. (32.1)

In that regard, from the *Śrīdevyāyāmala*, based on the scriptural statement regarding the emergence of the prototype (*bimba*)— namely, "Mudrā is the emergence of the reflection"— which functions through the door of a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound with the sense of a fifth-case [genitive] bahuvrīhi;

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: based on the distinction between two meanings of the term *pratibimba*, the *mudrā* is said to be of the nature of a reflection because it takes the form of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*). And here, these are the two meanings:

the prefix *prati* signifies "facing toward" (*abhimukhya*); therefore, having made the proximity of the original object (*bimba*) the cause, there is an arising that is restricted solely to that original object.

By the phrase "of which," it is stated that the original object (*bimba*) is the cause for the arising of the reflection (*pratibimba*); since the manifestation (*udaya*), characterized by the appearance of the original object, has gone toward or reached [the reflection], this indicates that the reflection serves as the means for cognition (*jñaptyupāya*). Alternatively:
"The mudrā is named Bimbodaya...
Since this is heard in the scripture *Bimbodaya*, it must be explained by setting aside the literal meaning of the word "prati" (counter-). ||1||
He states that very point by way of its underlying purport:
"That from which the emergence of the original image (bimba) occurs is called 'reflectedness' (pratibimbatā);
that from which the emergence of the original image occurs is called 'the means thereto' (tadupāyatā). (32.2)

"Arising" (*samudaya*) means origination. "Of which"—referring to the *mudrā* whose nature is a reflection—this is the sense of the genitive case; and "from which"—this is the sense of the ablative case. "Emergence" (*udaya*) means cognition; thus, "the means thereto" means the means to the original object (*bimba*) by way of cognition. || 2 ||

Having thus demonstrated the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word *mudrā*, he now demonstrates its etymological derivation (*yoga*): "Because it bestows (*rāti*) or offers (*arpayati*) joy (*mudaṃ*)—known as the attainment of one's own true nature—to the selves by means of the body, it is described as *mudrā* in the scriptures. (32.3)
And although it is said here: "With this intention, the mudrā releases [the self] from the entire web of bonds;
likewise, one should dissolve the bodily impressions of the *puryaṣṭaka* by means of the mantra."
"Yoga seals [yoga], ritual action (kriyā), and conduct (caryā) by means of their identity with that [reality].
From such perspectives, yoga may arise in many ways;
nevertheless, it is stated only this much: that this alone is primary because it bestows the nature of being filled with supreme bliss (parānanda).
First, he demonstrates the relationship of primary and secondary among these very [powers]:
"Among them, the venerable Khecarī is the primary one, consisting of the deity;
she is renowned as Niṣkalā (the Partless) in her aspect of transcendence, and as Triśūlinī (the Trident-Bearer) in her aspect of totality. (32.4)
Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, Lelihānikā, Mahāpretā, Yogamudrā, Jvālinī, Kṣobhiṇī, and Dhruvā. || 32-5 ||
Thus, this very Śrī Khecarī is celebrated in many such forms.

The term *dhruvā* (the fixed) is an epithet of Khecarī; for even when she assumes all forms, such as the Trident-bearing Goddess (*triśūlinī*) and others, there is no falling away from her partless (*niṣkala*) nature—this is the intended meaning. For it has been said:
"This is that Khecarī Mudrā, proclaimed as partless (niṣkalā); its manifest form (sakala) exists through various distinctions. Thus [it is said].
One might object: "Since other mudrās, such as the Triśūlinī and others, also exist as constituent parts of this [rite], why are they not mentioned here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But other [mudrās] that are its constituent parts, such as the Padmā and so forth, are [described] in the Mālinīmata. (32.6)
Because of their great number and their primary status, they are not described here.
Now, one might object: "In the Śrī Mālinīmata, the venerable Khecarī is indeed mentioned alongside the Padmamudrā and others;
so how can it be said that she alone is the principal one? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Whatever place one who is possessed by the illustrious Khecarī may resort to, [that becomes like the sky].
For the sake of the Goddess's presence, that alone would suffice; what is the use of vain displays?
"Alam" means sufficient.

But surely, since these [mudrās] also have primacy with respect to the practitioner (sādhaka), according to such statements as, "Protected by which the mantra-practitioner (mantrī) shall attain the accomplishment of the mantra," how can it be said thus?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"In the case of optional ritual action, those [qualities] might occasionally be primary for someone. (32.8)
"Of someone" means of the practitioner alone, and not of the spiritual sons (putraka) and so forth. "At some time" means not at all times, as if it were a constant rule. || 8 ||

Furthermore, since this treatise is devoted to establishing the primary goal known as liberation, rites performed for the sake of specific desires (kāmyakarma) have not been mentioned; so what is the purpose of describing mudrās, which are useful for those [desires]? To this he says:
"And that has not been stated by us; so what is the use of what is useful for that?"
And in order to state their essential nature by way of indicating their divisions, he says: "Mudrā is fourfold, through the distinction of body, hand, speech, and mind. (32.9)
In this regard, I shall describe *khecarī* itself in its complete form.
The word "speech" (*vāk*) refers to that which consists of the dissolution of mantras. As it has been said:
"Through the dissolution of the hands and body, and by entering into the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)."
"The mudrā should be known as fourfold... beginning thus, [it continues]:
"By means of the different placements of the fingers, the hand-born [mudrā] proceeds through many paths."
The physical mudrā is a mode of conduct that maintains a single form in all circumstances.
This vow, which involves wearing the five seals, is practiced by the Siddhas.
The seal consisting of identity with the mantra is proclaimed as that called "dissolution."
"The mental mudrā is proclaimed to be the state of being absorbed in the object of meditation.
Thus [it is said].
"By the full"—the meaning is "by all four kinds as well."
In that regard, he first describes her form primarily according to what is taught in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the yogi should cast the Lord of the Eye into the navel. (32.10)
One should lead that [wind], shaped like a staff, as far as the three voids; having restrained it there, one should quickly impel it through the three voids.
"By binding this [channel], there shall be movement in the sky," so it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana*.
Indeed, the yogi, seated in a firm and comfortable posture, having risen from the *janmādhāra* and fixed the mind in the region of the navel,
should cause it to circulate repeatedly in that very place through unification with the central power of breath (*madhyaprāṇaśakti*).

Having led [the breath] in the form of a staff as far as the three voids (*kha-traya*) characterized by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*) at the crown of the head, and having restrained it right there through the practice of *kumbhaka* (retention),
one proceeds swiftly with an upward movement by means of the three voids consisting of *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, and *samanā*.

One should impel [the consciousness] by means of the ascent through the state of *unmanā*, leading it toward the presence of Paramaśiva, so that by relying upon this, one may attain the state of moving within the sky of supreme awakening.
He points out the form described in the *Śrī-yogasañcāra* for this very [state], together with its internal subdivisions:
"The mind, joined with sound, light, and wind, comes to rest above. (32.12)

By means of this practice of yoga, having pierced through Śiva, one shall go to the Supreme. Sound is *nāda*, light is *bindu*, and wind is *śakti*; by that [means], one reaches the "twelve-finger limit," which is the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Thus, from the foundation of birth onwards, this mind is joined with these three voids.

The meaning of the statement is: having performed [the piercing] right there through intense meditation alone, the yogi, by means of his power, gradually pierces even the three upper voids consisting of *śakti* and proceeds to the Supreme Śiva.
Following this penetration, he describes the form of Triśūlinī as well: "Having placed both hands below the collarbone, and the left foot upon the right... (32.13).
The wise one should open the mouth with the two little fingers, the nose with the two middle fingers, contract the ring fingers, and form a frown with the two index fingers.
The mantra-practitioner should move the tongue and utter the sound "hā hā";
by means of the application of the trident, he arrives at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 32-15 ||
Having abandoned that very spot, one immediately leaves the earth.
Here, by the word *jatru*, the throat is indicated; thus, the meaning is "below that.
Regarding "the nose"—it refers to its two apertures. "One should move" is to be applied to all three [actions], beginning with the knitting of the eyebrows.

"Only that" (tanmātra) is established. "He leaves the earth" means that by casting off the ego-identification with the body and so forth, he becomes a wanderer in the space of supreme consciousness—this is the meaning.
He teaches the very practice of the trident:
having brought the wind and fire into a single staff within the dissolution of the void and the non-void. (32.16)
One should recognize that trident as being connected with the three powers and presided over by the three deities, by means of which the wise man may fly up into the sky. (32.17)

In this manner, having rendered the wind and fire— the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths— into a state of equal flavor (*samarasita*) within the central breath (*madhyaprāṇa*), and because of that very process, as they spread upward from the *mūlādhāra*,
when that [central breath] has become rod-like (*daṇḍākāra*), this trident (*triśūla*) is thus employed.

One should understand that by means of this, his flight into the void occurs; he specifically characterizes the central breath (*prāṇa*) as having the form of a single staff— presided over by the three deities,
meaning it is presided over by the triad of causes known as Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Anāśrita, which reside in the space between the eyebrows and other locations.
This is the meaning: likewise, when one is connected with Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā, and has attained union with them, then,

precisely because of the attainment of the supreme state (parapada), there occurs the dissolution of both the void and the non-void, wherein linguistic conventions such as "existent" and "non-existent" have fallen away.
This is the meaning. || 17 ||
And he does not fly up into the sky by this much alone—thus he says:
"Having abandoned the state of space and arrived at pure existence, having made the trident of one flavor, he remains like taste within taste. (32.18)
O Dear One, having recognized that trident with its single staff as moving through the sky,
and having bound the khecarī mudrā and meditated upon himself as Bhairava, [he should proceed].
One who is joined with the wheel of the *khecarī* instantly leaves the earth.

Thus, having understood the single-staffed trident that moves through the sky (*khacara*), which bestows the severance of those very [notions], and having abandoned even that mere existence, that wise one enters into the binding of the *khecarī-mudrā*.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having become established in the nature of supreme space (*parākāśa*), and remaining right there, having rendered even the piercing pain (*śūla*) into a state of equal flavor (*samarasīkṛtya*) like one taste within another, and having meditated upon himself as Bhairava attended by the wheel of sky-faring goddesses (*khecarīcakra*), he abandons the earth immediately.
Anticipating the objection, "But what would happen to him if it were so?", he says:
"Having abandoned all parts [of worldly conduct], free from ritual observances, devoid of doubt, and shunned by the world. (32.20)
An Avadhūta, free from conventional conduct, contemplating "I am not," being solely devoted to the mantra, perceives all the deities residing within the body. (32.21)
In joy, agitation, egoism, anger, sleep, sexual intercourse, and envy;
or in regard to form and the other [objects], and in all cases regarding the agent, the object, and the instrument. (32-22)
Thinking "I am not [this]," and contemplating that which has become one,
[he perceives] the host of deities situated in the wheel of the ears, eyes, mouth, nose, and so forth.
Constantly perceiving the grasper, one clearly attains perfection through the Khecarī [mudrā].

"Having abandoned the parts" means having attained partlessness. Regarding "beyond conduct" (nirācāra): it should be understood as that from which conducts have departed, or that which has departed from conducts.

"Perceiving all the deities residing in the body" means knowing the Self as consisting of all the deities. By the words "hlāda" (joy) and so forth, specific modifications of the mental faculty (*cittavṛtti*) are indicated.
"In form and so forth" refers to the fivefold objects of the senses. "The grasper" refers to that which has the singular nature of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*).
This is the meaning.
He confirms this very point by way of its contrapositive:
"One who doubts the Vidyā, doubts the impurity, or doubts the scripture does not attain success. (24)
Regarding "vidyā"—it is the auspicious Vedic knowledge. ||24||

Now, one might ask: "Why would this not be established in such a way? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Śiva is the sun; Śiva is the fire, for he is the cooker and thus the domestic priest (purohita).
All the deities residing therein illuminate the entire universe. (32.25)
The sun is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), fire is the knower (*pramātṛ*), and for this very reason, the domestic priest is the sacrificer—this is the meaning.
"Because of being the cooker" (*paktṛtva*) means because everything consists in the act of assimilating [it] into one's own self; "they remain illuminating"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
For in this way, since Śiva alone is everything, what room is there for doubt? This is the intended sense.
Having thus described the form of Triśūlinī, he speaks also of Karaṅkiṇī:
"Having torn open the mouth with the little fingers, likewise the two eyebrows with the index fingers;
one should touch the palate with the tongue upon the face, using the ring and middle fingers. (32.26)
This is the goddess Karaṅkiṇī; now hear of Jvālinī.
With the hands placed on the jaw and forehead, the fingers are extended and clearly visible.

The wise one, knitting his brows, should cause [the victim] to tremble with the force of the wind; having opened his mouth wide along with his tongue, he should cause him to utter cries of "Hā! Hā! 32.28.
This is Jvālinī in the fire-wheel; if one recites her mantra one hundred and eight times, then the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, shall be mastered.

"By the little finger"—meaning by that which belongs to both hands. "In the mouth"—that is, having placed [it] there. And here, the masters maintain that the underlying connection with the binding of the *khecarīmudrā* must certainly be kept in mind. "The jaw"—this is the reading; by this, [the area] from the jaw up to the forehead is indicated.

The meaning is that they should be held in that position. "With fingers extended" means with the fingers stretched out. "Internally" means between the two hands. "In the fire-wheel" (agnicakra) means, having meditated upon the inner self within an upward-facing triangle. || 29 ||
He demonstrates the very accomplishment (siddhi):

"One should see oneself within the bodies of others, and the other [person] within one's own body, moving about, established in the state of coming and going through [the processes of] abandonment and acquisition. (32.30)
And that which has entered the nine apertures, resounding, all-pervasive, and eternal—by means of this, the Śrīyogasañcāra is said to be the mover in the void. (32–31)

"By the resonance of 'Hā'"—the meaning is: by the resonance, that is, the utterance, of the syllable *hā*. "Going and coming"—that is, from one's own body to another's body, or from another's body to one's own body. By the term "moving in the void" (*khacārī*), the penetration of the *khecarīmudrā* bandha is also indicated. || 31 ||
Now he describes the procedure for this [rite], which is also taught in the *Śrīvīrāvalī*:
"Having bound Kulakuṇḍalikā, who knows the interior of the atom, she is intent upon the withdrawal of that which is left-handed (vāma) in this world. (32–32)
Having attained rest in its own place, consisting of the essence of the nectar of gnosis,
it should proceed to the state of the *kanda* in the center, having made soundless sound.
As long as one lives, the alms-bowl is four-cornered and desired;
having awakened her there and understood the destiny that has come down through the lineage, [one should act]. (32–34)
But one should [visualize] the goddess, bound by both wheels and hanging from the tip of a branch,
so that she may tear asunder the knot of darkness starting from the root-place.
One should pierce the base of the *liṅga*, which has emerged from the center of the corner, with that which is called the *vajra* born of gnosis, likewise from both ends of the branch. (32–36)
There, the pair of wheels, when struck together, shines as a unity;
however, by reversing that process and casting them apart, they consequently attain a state of duality.
She should cast [the breath] from the thighs down to the big toe, as far as the Kālāgni;
she, as the possessor of the mark (liṅginī), moves through the coming and going of its circulation.
In that state, through the union with that [supreme] state, she brings about the blossoming [of consciousness];
he who knows this shall attain perfection in the withdrawal and emission of the vital essence (rasa).
This place is with attachment, yet it is the supreme unfolding of the waves;
this is the sequence, and beyond that is the other, the reversal—the supreme Khecarī.
Renowned as the "Support of the Womb" (yonyādhārā), it is called the "Root of the Trident" (śūlamūlā);
there, the castes (varṇas) attain dissolution into that which is beyond caste (avarṇa), yet possesses the form of all castes.

Having ascended here the central vital energy (madhyaprāṇaśakti), known as Kulakuṇḍalikā, which knows the interior of the subtle atom (aṇu), moves within, and has attained identity with that [reality], and having reached the bliss consisting of the attainment of oneness with Her in Her own place— the foundation of power (śāktādhāra)— which destroys ignorance;

By the statement, "But at the root, the Śākta [power] is said to be non-impelling due to its awakening," because it does not impel due to awakening, one should produce the sound (nāda) which is the resonance (rāva) of a peaceful nature, acting as the restrainer within the middle channel and the locus of the poison.
"...greedy for the six flavors in the *kanda*.

By this phrasing, the word *kanda* refers to that which consists of the essence of the nectar of knowledge (*jñānāmṛta-rasa*), which is the *kāma* (desire-granting) term denoting all desires; it is the *jīva* (life-principle) called *sañjīvanī-amṛta* (the life-restoring nectar), so called because it resides at the crossroads.

The quadrangular [mandala] called Cintāmaṇi extends as far as the *paiṇḍa* body, which is the support (*ādhāra*). Having awakened that Kulakuṇḍalikā who has descended through the sequence into those supports,
starting from the root-place (*mūlasthāna*), she is interwoven with the two wheels consisting of the prāṇa and apāna.

Having known her as she goes as far as the *dvādaśānta*, just as this yogi, by the majesty born of knowledge alone, would pierce the knot of ignorance— which is called "vajra" because it is difficult to break— and the central channel (*madhyamā nāḍī*), so too [he pierces] the two branches consisting of prāṇa and apāna.
Relying on the end, one should pierce even that which has emerged from the center of the triangle— the support of birth—
and is therefore called the "root of the *liṅga*," the support of *akula* situated below the *meḍhra*;
for there, indeed, the pair of wheels consisting of *prāṇa* and *apāna* [is dissolved] by the breaking of their own respective forms.

The meaning is that, being struck together as one, it shines forth; from that very power of the central breath (*madhyaprāṇaśakti*), there arises its emergence. Therefore, from the state of *Akula* called the root of the *liṅga*, she again undergoes a twofold division by casting herself downward through the reverse process.
The meaning is that if she were to cast herself as the cause for [the body] from the thighs down to the big toes, she would assume that very form. For that Kulakuṇḍalikā,
disregarding the upward and downward movement, [is characterized by] the prāṇa and apāna.
Having attained cognition by encompassing the possessor of the marks (*liṅgin*) through the two marks (*liṅga*), she should proceed;

by means of the distinctions of their respective supports and so forth, she should ascend to the central abode (*madhyadhāma*). For in that central abode, she brings about the expansion of consciousness (*saṃvit*) through the union of the two stages of the prāṇa and apāna. And that which...
He who knows this supreme state— which is of such a nature, permeated by all existents, the unfolding of waves, and which brings about the expansion of supreme consciousness—
shall achieve mastery over the withdrawal and emission of the essence of consciousness, and thus possess the power of creation and dissolution.

The meaning is that capacity arises. And the meaning is that this aforementioned sequence—consisting of the movement through various supports and so forth—is her natural flow (*vāha*). Furthermore, another sequence, even one that is non-consecutive (*vyutkrama*), is possible for her, provided she is *parā*.
Khecarī is renowned as the support of the womb; having arisen from there, she is immediately designated as the "Root of the Trident."

The meaning is that she has reached the station of the *dvādaśānta* because of her union with the triad of powers consisting of *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, and *samanā*. For there, in that state which consists of the cessation of all [duality]— even though external reflective awareness (*bāhyāmarśa*) is embraced—
it is within the unmanifest (*avarṇa*), whose nature is solely self-reflective awareness (*svāmarśa*), that the letters (*varṇāḥ*), which are external reflective awarenesses, go to their dissolution.
The meaning is that they become truly at rest therein—thus it is said. || 41 ||
Now, one might object: "Granted that this be so, how then does the yogi effect its awakening?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having uttered [the alphabet] from *na* to *pha*, [one should contemplate] Kauleśa, who is identical with the body."
Having first ascended the wheel in the sky, it is pressed down by the foot upon the machine.
Indeed, from the *nāda* which contains the essence of Śakti, the state of Kaulinī arises from that essential womb,
by means of the movement of the five seed-syllables and through the sequence of piercing the trident.
One should awaken the power of the Consciousness-Rudra through the piercing of the knots and the sharp pains in the heart;
[one should awaken] the navel-mandala called Bindu, which resides within the wheel of the vital air (vāyu-cakra).
One should go to the station of Lambikā, which has emerged from the twelve channels;
one should enter the cage of the elements by means of the reverse order of the lunar wheel.
Furthermore, she performs her play within the cage of Māyā;
again, creation and withdrawal are performed by Khecarī, according to the wise. (32–46)
This is the procedure for the Khecarī [mudrā] in the illustrious Vīrāvalīyoga.

"Cid" refers to the pure Self; "Kauleśa" is that which consists primarily of secret knowledge, and for that very reason, it contains within itself the central Power (madhyaśakti) in the form of the letters from *na* to *pha*, having the nature of the friction-stick (*araṇi*) for all mantras.
Having uttered that very *nāda* as non-different from one's own body, and thus uttering the *nāda* together with the "womb" (*sagarbha*),
with reference to that *nāda*, [one reaches] the vital point (*marman*) of *Kaulinī*— that is, of the *Kula-kuṇḍalinī*— which is in the sky (*khe*), whose nature is the space of birth (*janmākāśa*).
Having afflicted with a quarter—that is, a one-fourth portion—the first wheel consisting of the channels (nāḍī), which was described as: "The wheel of channels called 'birth'... and so forth.

Therein, having somehow restrained the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) and having ascended through all five remaining wheels (*cakras*) by means of the sequence of transcending the five causes beginning with Brahmā, [one reaches] the twelve knots of the trident (*śūla*)— which consists of the three channels (*nāḍī*) situated in the heart and revolves around the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
By means of the process of piercing the trident whose nature consists of Śakti and the rest, one should awaken the power of Rudra (rudraśakti),

whereby this [practitioner], starting from the place of birth up to the end of the wind-wheel (vāyucakra) which is the support of the vital breath, reaches the navel-mandala situated in close proximity, which is the support for that [piercing] impact.
The location of the *lambikā* (the uvula) is situated above that, the support known as the *bindu*,

which holds the nectar and resides between the eyebrows; it is called the lotus of knowledge (*vidyā-kamala*), the source from which twelve knots of the channels emerge, and it transcends all connections.

The meaning is that one should proceed straight and gradually as far as the station of the *dvādaśānta*, and there one should rest. Furthermore, from that point, having turned back from the lunar wheel located at the *apāna*, one should enter one's own body by way of a reverse sequence, whereby this—

One should conduct oneself in accordance with the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Therefore, for the knowers (*jñānin*) who have attained the penetration of the *khecarīmudrā*, there arises the capacity to perform creation and withdrawal through the constant alternation of the opening and closing of the internal and external [senses], like the incessant flow of a stream—this is the summary meaning. Regarding the word "in yoga" (*yoge*):
"At the occasion of his speaking"—that is to say.
He also describes its form as stated in the Śrī Kāmika: "That supreme reality which is heard with a mouth in the shape of a kiss. (32.47)
"By swallowing this entire universe within the hollow cavity of the moon and sun, one becomes a traveler through the sky; thus it is stated in the venerable Kāmika. (32.48)

By means of this mouth— which is of the nature of a kiss, shaped like the beak of a crow, consisting of the unstruck (*anacka*) kalā, and which, though supported by the central vital power (*madhyaprāṇaśakti*),
assimilates this entire universe— consisting of both means and objects of knowledge— into its own self, it is therefore supreme.

The reality whose sole form is the subject is heard and directly realized within the central abode, in the cavity of the pair of prāṇa and apāna which forms the enclosure of the moon and sun; from that very source, its movement through the void occurs—this is the meaning of the sentence. || 48 ||
Now, in order to describe her specific form as taught in the *Śrīkulagahvara*, he says:
"Indeed, mudrās are powers (śaktis) that, having abandoned worldly existence, dissolve the fetters.
Of these, Khecarī is the primary one; and she is threefold according to the mode of utterance, being vocal (*vācikī*). (32.49)
O Goddess, the *triśiromudgara* is recited as belonging to the body (*kāyikī*).

Therefore, the powers (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī*) themselves are said to be the *mudrās*, for their etymological definition (*nirvacana*) is that they liberate bound souls (*paśu*) from transmigratory existence and dissolve their fetters (*pāśa*). As it has been said:
"They liberate [beings] from the most terrible ocean of saṃsāra, the abode of sea-monsters;
they dissolve the bonds of the bound soul (paśu); therefore, the mudrās are indeed powers (śaktis).
Regarding the phrase "by means of utterance" (uccāreṇa)—it refers to mantras and so forth. Regarding "the mallet of the three heads" (triśiromudgara)—it refers to...

According to the principle expressed in the passage beginning, "preceded by will, knowledge, and action," because it consists of the three powers (*śaktitraya*), the Triśiromudgara "pronounces joy"— that is, supreme bliss (*parānanda*)— by reflecting upon it within its own self; this is the meaning of "supreme consciousness" (*parasaṃvit*).
In this very way, supreme consciousness has manifested as the body—thus he says:
"The nose, the two eyes, and also the heart and the two breasts. (32.50)
Having reached the body at the two testicles and the penis, she has entered it;
one should determine the state of existence and the state beyond existence through exhalation.
This one is Mānasī; other than her are the eight mudrās beginning with Padmā. They belong to the family of the Mātṛvyūha and are her attendants.
The entire body, which has the form of the *kūṭākṣara*,
is this *mudrā*, the *mahāmudrā* of Bhairava, according to the *Gahvara*.

Regarding "in the heart" (hṛdi)—it refers to the form of the stalk of the heart-lotus. Since the true nature (satattva) of this has been explained in various scriptures, it is not elaborated upon here due to its extreme secrecy; that must be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone.
"The state of existence is the body, while the state of non-existence is through upward utterance" (uccāra).
"O Dear One, know that the lotus here is the heart-lotus itself, the trident is the three channels,
the navel is the wheel, and Śakti is the form of the end of sound (nādānta)."
The staff arises from the region of the *bindu*, the vajra is the indivisible mind;
O highly fortunate one, the fangs and tongue, as well as the skull, are the mandala of space.
"By moving through these locations, the mental [power] is proclaimed.
According to this principle, the meaning is "by upward movement," that is, by going upwards. Regarding the word "eight"—as it has been stated:
"The retinue of Khecarī is proclaimed to consist of eight mudrās."
O Goddess of gods, they are also remembered as being within the group of eight Śūlas and the assembly of Mothers (Mātṛvyūha).
"The lotus, the trident, likewise the discus, the spear, the staff together with the thunderbolt,
the fang, and the skull— thus everything is established therein.
Thus it is said.
The "peak syllable" (kūṭākṣara) is the letter *kṣa*. Its true nature has already been explained extensively before.
By this, the definition of the Bhairava-mudrā, which was previously mentioned, has also been stated. || 53 ||
To demonstrate that this very [method] is uncontradicted everywhere, he describes its form along with its divisions even according to another scripture:
"Seated comfortably upon a lotus, with the rays of his fingertips smiling..."
With rays suddenly rising while turned away, they remained positioned behind [the object]. || 32-54 ||
This internal abiding is Khecarī, known as Saṅkocā and Śaśāṅkinī;
from that very state, having raised the arms and bent them inward.
Because she is established correctly within the voids, the Khecarī is considered to be named "the Void" (Vyomākhyā);
because of the clashing of two fists at the heart, she is called "the Heart" (Hṛdayā).
That which is called Śāntā has both hands raised, one above and one below; it is to be gazed upon with an even gaze, with the palms joined outwardly. (32.57)
This very same [mudrā] is the Śakti-mudrā if the hands are extended downward,
immediately after the ten fingers have been formed into a fist.
By a swift upward throw, the goddess Khecarī is considered to be the fivefold Kuṇḍalinī;
indeed, this very same gesture is the Saṃhāra-mudrā if it is thrown upwards.
The *utkrāmaṇī* [mantra] instantly severs the bonds of bound souls (*paśu*), as if suddenly casting one's own self into a very deep abyss. (32.60)
With the two hands drawn together through a forceful entry, the gaze is habitually directed downward and endowed with a correct vision. || 32-61 ||
This Khecarī, known as Vīrabhairava, which increases awakening, has thus been described in eight ways in the Śrī Bhargāṣṭakaśikhākula. (32–62)

In this context, when the yogin seated upon a lotus or other posture is characterized by the rays of the moon emerging externally— rays which, because they are directed backward due to his being positioned behind [the moon], are like ropes consisting of the fingers at the tips of his hands— he [attains realization] instantly.

Through the withdrawal of the external, one comes to abide within and rests in one's own self alone; at that time, because the moon has been thus cultivated within, she is called Śaśāṅkinī, and because the external has become contracted, this single Khecarī Mudrā is known as Saṅkoca. Thus, that...

Relying on the positioning of the fingers of the hands and so forth, having properly bent the two arms and supported them by clasping them in the form of a *svastika*, [one recites]: "The infinite sky, called Māyā..."
In the five voids mentioned above, according to the correctly stated sequence,
the second [void] is called *vyoma* (the void) due to its location and firm support; likewise,
it is formed by the right fist placed below with the thumb pointing upward, while the left [hand] has the thumb raised above.
From the clashing of two fists, characterized by the mudrā of the fist, at the heart, that third [khecarī] is called "Heart. Likewise, by the word "hand," the arms are indicated;
thus, when the pair of arms is positioned with the left below and the right above, and the palms are turned inward toward each other—
When this same [mudrā], called Śāntā, has the hands raised upward and is viewed with the gaze directed toward it, then it is the fourth, named Śāntā. Likewise,
even in this same configuration, if it is one where the hands are extended downward, then it is called Śaktimudrā.

The fifth [mudrā]: likewise, immediately after clenching the fists of both hands, by the sudden horizontal casting out of all ten fingers, because each hand takes on the form of five *kuṇḍalinīs*, it is called the sixth, the *pañcakuṇḍalinī*. Likewise...

If, in this manner, there is the upward casting of all ten fingers, then this very same [mudrā] is the seventh, known as the *pañcakuṇḍalinī* or the *saṃhāramudrā*. Its status as the *saṃhāramudrā* has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "the one that causes [the soul] to ascend" (*utkrāmaṇī*). Likewise, because it has the nature of looking downward...

When the yogi, endowed with a vision that correctly perceives the internal target, joins his two hands in a contracted gesture and, as if suddenly casting himself down into a vast abyss through the entry of the seal of daring (*sāhasamudrā*), becomes one whose awakening has increased— then indeed this [seal] occurs.
The eighth is known as Vīrabhairava; thus ends the venerable Bhargaśikhākula. 62.
Concluding this, he introduces the praise of Vīra:
"Thus, relying upon various kinds of divisions, she who remains as one alone is the venerable Khecarī; possessed by her, one attains the supreme seed-syllable. (32–63)
"Of various kinds" refers to [the goddesses] such as Triśūlinī and others.

The essential nature of all these, beginning with Triśūlinī, has not been stated here because the intent is to show their lack of distinctness. "The supreme seed" refers to the supreme seed (*parā-bīja*) consisting of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). For in reality, there is no difference between these two.
This is the state of being. As the scripture says:
"The one seed-syllable consisting of emanation, and the one mudrā, Khecarī—whosoever knows these two as one is indeed worthy of worship in the Kulāgama."
Thus [ends the verse]. 63.
For this very reason, he said:
"There is one seed-syllable consisting of emanation, whose potency resides in all mantras;
there is one mudrā, Khecarī, by whom the entire multitude of mudrās is enlivened. (6.42–64)
And for this reason, the very penetration (*āveśa*) [of that state] is the reality of all mudrās; thus he says:

"In this way, whatever form should manifest when one is established in the wheel of the *khecarīs*, that alone is to be considered the mudrā; everything else is merely a physical transformation. (32.65)
"Remainder" means one who is devoid of that immersion. ||65||

And in order to determine the specific timing for the binding of these very [mudrās], he says: "The occasion for the ritual of mudrā is at the beginning of the sacrifice, in its middle, at its conclusion, during the contemplation of knowledge and yoga, for the pacification of obstacles, and for the severing of bonds. (32.66)
Now, one might ask: "What would be the purpose of binding the mudrā at such a time? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Penetration into awakening, presence through oneness, dismissal, attainment of one's own true nature, the shattering of doubt, and the radiance of the arising of the wheels—these are the functions [of the mudrās] in their respective order. (32.67)

Regarding "the radiance of the arising of the wheel": according to the state established in the seventh chapter, this means the radiance—that is, the kindling—of the mantras that have arisen. || 67 ||
He concludes this very point with a half-verse:
"Thus has been declared the rule of the mudrās, which is well-guarded and bestows the fruit.
Thus [ends] the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The thirty-second chapter, titled "The Revelation of Mudrās."
Thus all is auspicious.
Jayaratha, whose immersion in consciousness has been awakened by the profound contemplation of the true nature of the venerable Khecarī,
has completed this thirty-second chapter.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Illumination of Mudrās," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 32 ||
The Thirty-third Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
Though this entire external world shines forth, it is a treasury of the nectar of supreme bliss.
Resting all beings within the Supreme Self, the Lord of the Universe is victorious.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since here there exists only a single consciousness whose essence is the reflective awareness of the universe (*viśvāmarśana*), the very relationship between the object of worship and the worshipper is not logical; even so, what distinction is there among the objects of worship?
Why, then, has this state of consisting of multiple wheels (*cakra*) been taught?"—thus incorporating this doubt within itself.
With the second half [of the verse], he speaks in order to explain that very unification: "Now, the unification which has reached its proper occasion is being declared.
He explains that very thing:
As it was said: "The triad, together with the division of the wheels, is to be worshipped.
In this regard, this unification of the divisions of the wheels is [achieved] by this method. (33-1)
"It has been stated"—in the first chapter and elsewhere. And so it is said there:
"The Solitary Hero, the Couple, then the Three-Powered, and the Fourfold Self," and so forth.

"In this way, up to the thousand-spoked wheel or even the innumerable-spoked wheel, the Lord Maheśāna, whose power is the universe, unfolds within the universal wheel"—thus [the text] continues at length until the end of verse 1.112.
"By this" refers to that which is about to be described. (1)
In that regard, he first demonstrates the breaking of the wheel (cakrabheda):
"Viśvā, Tadīśā, Hāraudrī, Vīranetrī, Ambikā, and Gurvī—these are the goddesses in the six-spoked [wheel] as shown by the venerable Siddhāvīra. (33.2)
Māheśī, Brahmāṇī, Skāndī, Vaiṣṇavī, Aindrī, Yamātmikā,
Cāmuṇḍā, and Yogīśī— these are the eight, or alternatively, Aghorī and the others.
Accompanied by Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Īśa, and the Mothers, they are twelve in number:
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Kālī, Karālī, and Vikṛtānanā.
Kroṣṭukī, Bhīmamudrā, Vāyuvegā, Hayānanā, Gambhīrā, and Ghoṣaṇī—this is the procedure for the twenty-four-spoked [cakra]. (33–5)
Success, growth, splendor, fortune, intelligence, beauty, nectar, fortitude, radiance, nourishment, intellect, fame, stability, a good state of being, mindfulness, and memory. || 33-6 ||
Suprabhā and Śoḍaśī are the powers (śaktis) beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha;
[the lords are] Bali, Balinanda, Daśagrīva, Hara, and Haya. (33–7)
Mādhava is on the six-spoked wheel; those [others] are recorded as being on the twelve-spoked wheel:
Dakṣa, Caṇḍa, Hara, Śauṇḍī, Pramatha, Bhīma, and Manmatha. (33.8)
Śakuni, Sumati, Nanda, Gopāla, Pitāmaha, Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Śaṃbareśvara. || 33-9 ||
