Arghīśa, Bhārabhūti, Sthita, Sthāṇu, Hara, as well as Jhaṇṭhi, Bhautika, Sadyojāt, Anugraha, and Krūra-sainika [are present]. (33–10)
Those who are joined with that which consists of sixteen parts and is immortal, possessing the appearance of being full and flowing with liquid,
have bodies that are like waves of the current, moving, and composed of limbs, with their faces turned upward as they sing aloud.
The lords of the forms for the sprinkling of the body, and another who bears all nectar;
through the recitation of the Śrīpāṭha, these sixteen powers are proclaimed. (33-12)
Saṃvarta, Lakulin, Bhṛgu, Sita, Baka, Khaṅgin, Pinākin, Bhujaga, Bali, Kāla;
Dvija, Chagala, Aṇḍa; Śikhin, Śoṇa, Meṣa, Mīna, Tridaṇḍin, and Āṣāḍhin. (33.13)
Devīkānta, Tadardha, Dāruka, Halī, Somanātha, Śarmā, Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanta, Ajita, Sujaya, Jayarudra, Kīrtana, Āvaha, and Kā—[these are the names]. 33-14.
Tanmūrti, Utsāha, Dava, Vardhana, Bala, Subala, Bhadradāvaha, Tadvān, Dātā, Īśa, Nandana, Sama, Bhadra, and Tanmūrti. (33.15)
Śivadāsūmanas, Spṛhaṇaka, Durga, the one named Bhadra, Kāla, Cetā, Anuga, Kauśika, Kālaviśva, Suśiva, and another, Kopa. (33-16)
These [syllables] consist of the vowels (śrutis), the fire (agni), and the r (ra); these are the Śaktis because they are recited as feminine.
"Her Lord" refers to Viśveśvarī.
"Vīranetrī" means the leader of heroes (vīranāyikā). As it has been said:
"Viśvā, Viśveśvarī, Hāraudrī, Vīranāyikā, Ambā, and Gurvī—these are the Yoginīs... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 20.60).
Thus [it is said]. These [deities] are taught not only in our own system, but elsewhere as well—as he says:
"shown in the venerable Siddhāvīra. "Skāndī" means Kaumārī. "Yamātmikā" means Yāmyā.
Regarding "Aghorī and the others," it is stated in the venerable *Triśirobhairava*:
Aghorā, Paramāghorā, Ghorarūpā, and likewise Parā;
Ghoravaktrā, as well as Bhīmā, Bhīṣaṇā, Vamanī, and Parā.
"And the eighth [tithi] is declared to be Pibanī... thus it is said.
"Followed by" means, by implication, by Māheśī and the others.
As it has been said:
"Or, O Dear One, the four corners beginning with the southeast are occupied by Brahmaṇī and the others" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 20.45).
Thus: "The rule for the twenty-four-spoked [mandala] is by means of the conjunction of the twelve [deities] beginning with Māheśī.
As it has been said:
"In the twenty-four[-spoked one]..."
"Listen: all [the goddesses] beginning with Nandā, and likewise those beginning with Brahmaṇī, follow in sequence. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 20.53).
And this has been stated here for the purpose of relying upon the goddesses situated within the twelve spokes; it is not...

The objection regarding the reversal of the sequence may be raised. Furthermore, in the two groups of eight [spokes], only the Aghoras are the possessors of power (*śaktimant*), yet they have not been mentioned here because they were already indicated previously. As it has been said:
"In the eight-spoked [wheel], the deities beginning with Aghora and those beginning with Aghorī [are located]."
"O Goddess, [the goddesses] beginning with Māheśī are likewise... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 20.53).
"Sadyojaḥ" means Sadyojāta; "Anugraha" means Anugraheśvara; "Sainika" means Mahāsena. As it has been said:
"...Ṣadyojāta, as well as the other [Vāmadeva], Anugraheśvara, Krūra, and Mahāsena as the sixteenth. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 20.50).
By the word "by that"—meaning by the nectar—the sequence beginning with "of the color of that nectar, shining like nectar," and so forth, [is established].
"Vaktra" means the mouth; "secanā" means sprinkling. As it has been said:
"He is nectar, full of nectar, resembling nectar, the flow of nectar;
he is the flood of nectar, the wave of nectar, and another is the vehicle of nectar."
"Amṛtāṅga, Amṛtavapu, and indeed Amṛtodgāra;
Amṛtāsya, Amṛtatanu, as well as Amṛtaniṣecana; Tanmūrti, Amṛteśa, and likewise Sarvāmṛtadhara. (Mālinīvijayottaratantra 3.19)
Thus [it is said]. He indicates the possessors of power (*śaktimant*) who follow in sequence on the twenty-four-spoked [wheel], beginning with the words "Saṃvarta" and so forth.
"Lakuli" refers to Lakulīśa. "Sita" means Śveta. "Kāla" means Mahākāla.
"Dvi-chagalāṇḍau" refers to Dviraṇḍa and Chagalāṇḍa. [This concludes] the pentad beginning with Śikhin.

The *dvandva* compound is used in the sense of a collective. "Śoṇa" means red. "Devīkānta-tadardha" refers to Umākānta (the beloved of Umā) and Ardhanārīśa (the Lord who is half-woman). "Halī" means the wielder of the plow (Balarāma). "Somanātha" refers to Someśa.
As it has been said:
Śaṃvarta, Lakulīśa, Bhṛgu, Śveta, Baka,
Khaṅgin, Pinākin, Bhujaga, and the ninth, Bali.
Mahākāla, Dviraṇḍa, Cchagalāṇḍa, and likewise Śikhī;
Lohita, Meṣa, and Mīna; and those named Tridaṇḍin and Āṣāḍhin.
"Umākānta, Ardhanārīśa, Dāruka, Lāṅgalin, as well as Someśa and Śarman—these are considered the twenty-four. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 20.56).
"Ajita" means Aparājita. The word "aja" is connected to all three [of these]. Therefore...

"Jayarudra, Jayakīrti, Jayāvaha"—by the word "tat" (that), there is a reference back to the word "jaya. By that [logic], [the names are] Jayamūrti, Jayotsāha, Jayada, and Jayavardhana. "Subala" means "Atibala" (Extremely Powerful).

The term *bhadra* is connected with each of the three words *bala*. Thus, [the names are] Balabhadra and Balāvaha. *Tadvān* means "possessing that," i.e., Balavān. *Dātā* means "giver of strength," i.e., Baladātā. *Īśa* means "lord of strength," i.e., Baleśvara. *Samabhadra* means "auspicious on all sides," i.e., Sarvatobhadra. *Tanmūrti* means "having an auspicious form," i.e., Bhadramūrti.

"Śivada" means the bestower of auspiciousness (*śiva*). "Bhadrākhya" means the auspicious time (*bhadrakāla*). "Ceto'nuga" means following the mind (*mano'nuga*). "Viśva" means the Lord of the Universe (*viśveśvara*). "Śrutyagnyara" means having thirty-four spokes (*caturtriṃśadara*).
As it has been said:
Jaya and Vijaya, Jayanta and Aparājita,
Sujaya, Jayarudra, Jayakīrti, and Jayāvaha.
The embodiment of victory, the enthusiasm for victory, the giver of victory, the increaser of victory;
strength itself, exceeding strength, Balabhadra, and the bestower of strength.
He who brings strength, the powerful one, the giver of strength, the lord of strength;
the delighter, auspicious in every way, the embodiment of goodness, and the bestower of welfare.
Sumanas, Spṛhaṇa, Durga, Bhadrakāla,
Mano’nuga, Kauśika, Kālaviśveśa, Suśiva, and Kopa.
"These thirty-four [mantras] are proclaimed as having arisen from the womb. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.24).
In this very context, he states the division of the mantras: "The syllable *juṃ* and then the wife of Agni—these six, excluding the neuter [vowels], are in the six-spoked [wheel]. (33.17)
In the twelve-spoked [cakra], the consonants together with those [vowels] are placed; in the sixteen-spoked, the vowels in sequence;
in the double of that [thirty-two-spoked], the consonants; and in the eight-spoked, the letters from *ya* to *ha* according to the Tantrika system.
"Agnipatnī-svāhā"—by this, each syllable is [accompanied] one by one. "Together with those" means together with the neuter vowels. "Twofold that" means in the thirty-two-spoked [mandala]. || 18 ||
Right here he states a specific distinction:
"In the thirty-two-spoked [cakra], the final letter is the Bindu; it is on the head of all.
He says that by this very sequence, the other cakras should also be conceptualized.
In this manner, one should devise many other such divisions of the wheel from this [text]. || 33-19 ||
"From this"—that is, from the aforementioned division of the wheels (*cakrabheda*). "Many others"—meaning sixty-four and so forth.
By the word "one should fashion," their lack of ultimate reality is revealed. || 19 ||

In reality, there exists only the single light of consciousness (citprakāśa), of which [the universe] is merely a designation as power (śakti) and its possessor; thus he says: "This very one, the conscious self (cidātman), is the essence that reflects upon the entire universe."
Therefore, Śakti and her possessor (tadvān) are proclaimed as the Mother and the Mass of Sounds (śabdarāśi).

But when there is a differentiation between those two alone, through the conceptualization of power (śakti) and its possessor (tadvat), the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) and Mālinī constitute such a body whose nature is agitation (kṣobha). (33.21)

"From this"—because the division between power (*śakti*) and its possessor (*śaktimān*) has been indicated by the aphorism. "The Mother" refers to *Mātṛkā*. "Of those two"—of *Mātṛkā* and the collection of sounds (*śabdarāśi*). Now, one might ask: what is the reason for *Mālinī* being considered power?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Such is her body, consisting of agitation. (21)
The differentiation of the wheels (cakrabheda) arises from the various forms of reflective awareness (parāmarśa) rooted in each of these two; thus he says:

"Likewise, when the internal reflective awareness is differentiated, there are in reality three [aspects] called Anuttara, Icchā, and Unmeṣa, from which the entire universe proceeds as reflective awareness. (33.22)
When conjoined with the waves of the vowels (ānanda-īśa), that group of six is proclaimed;
when conjoined with the semivowels and sibilants (antaḥstha-uṣman), that group of eight is proclaimed.
Then, in the absence of the fourfold [group] of immortals, there would be a group of twelve;
through their conjunction, there would be what is called the sixteen-fold, and so on until there is an infinite number.

Likewise, when the reflective awareness of "I" (ahamparāmarśa), which exists internally in identity with the subject through the nature of power and the possessor of power, is differentiated, it is said: "That very triad they call the supreme majesty of Bhairava."

According to the method stated in such passages, in reality there exists only the triad known as Anuttara (the Supreme), Icchā (Will), and Unmeṣa (Expansion), from which arises this full reflective awareness that "I am all this. Furthermore, when that very [triad] is joined with Ānanda (Bliss) and the others, the aforementioned group of six is illustrated, by means of which this differentiation of the wheels (*cakras*) occurs.

Thus, with reference to the two groups of four known as the internal semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) and sibilants (*ūṣman*), there would be an octad, by which it is said that the letters beginning with *y* are in the eight-spoked [cakra]. "The group of four nectars" refers to the four neuter vowels;
the meaning is "when they are deficient," that is, when they are excluded. "In their conjunction" means—
The meaning is: "in being accompanied by the four nectars. "Innumerable" means:
through the conjunction and disjunction of those respective reflective awarenesses. 24.

Now, one might object: "In this [reality], which is of an undivided, single, and compact form, how can there be infinity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because it clearly endures the entire universe from its capacity for a single, supreme awareness onwards, since it ultimately endures even the subtlest perceptions of parts and sub-parts. (33.25)
Therefore, there is the oneness of the fifty [phonemes], the diversity of vowels and manifestations,
the eight groups (vargas), the differentiation of letters, and the arising of the eighty-one kalās.
This has been demonstrated previously.

"The universe" (viśvam) means everything. "Identity with the fifty" (pañcāśadaikātmyam) means having the nature of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa). "Manifestation" (vyaktiḥ) means the act of making manifest. "Kalā" refers to the half-measures (ardhamātrāḥ). "Previously" (pūrvam) [refers to what was stated] before.
In the third, sixth, and other such chapters.
Is it not said:
"A short vowel should be one mātrā; a long vowel is said to be two mātrās;
a protracted vowel is to be known as three mātrās; whereas a consonant consists of half a mātrā"?

Having stated this, one might raise the objection: "It is appropriate to say that consonants can endure half-measures (ardhamātrā), but since vowels conform to a single measure (ekamātrā), they cannot; how then does the emergence of eighty-one kalās occur?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
...because of its capacity to endure half-morae;
for even a vowel has a half [of a mora], since the *svarita* [accent] possesses half a mora. (33.27)
The knower of words has stated that its beginning is acute (*udātta*).

Here, because vowels can endure for half a *mātrā*, they are also considered to have the duration of half a *mātrā*; for Pāṇini [says]: "A combination of *śa* and *ma* is circumflex (*svarita*)" (1.2.31).
Thus, while it is stated in the rule that the *svarita* consists of a collection of acute (*udātta*) [elements],
the rule "its first half-mora is acute" (Pāṇini 1.2.32) also establishes that the initial acute portion possesses a duration of half a short mora (*hrasva*).
He concludes the very subject under discussion:
"In this way, this consciousness consists of the reflective awareness of the nature of that which is to be sacrificed. (33.28)
This circle of wheels of consciousness is non-different from consciousness itself;
one should employ it in many ways according to the distinctions of the Lord and the veils.
The word "that" refers to the circle of the Cakravāla mountains. ||29||
One might ask: "But what is the difference even from the Lord? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The other, the intermediate, and the supreme [powers] are the emanation, maintenance, and concealment;
but that which consists of the true being of the subject is called the fourth, the repose. (33-30)
"Anyā" means the other [power]. "Tirodhi" means withdrawal (saṃhāra). || 30 ||
Now, one might object: "If the Fourth (turya) alone is the place of rest, why has it not been described by dividing it [into stages]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And that Light, residing in the speaker, has indeed been indicated at every step."
"One should find rest right here"—thus he says: "Rest should be established in the Fourth state, which flows from the true being of the subject. (33.31)
And here, raising the doubt, "What would arise from resting [in this state]? he says:
"In that way, the universe appears to him as having attained identity with his own self. He concludes the subject matter of this chapter with a half-verse:
Thus, this unification of the meaning of the scripture has been declared as taught by the Guru. (33.32)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Illumination of Unification," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus all is auspicious. 32.
Having been bound by the continuous connection with each respective wheel, which is of the nature of non-dual supreme consciousness,
this one named Jayaratha has thus explained this thirty-third chapter.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Illumination of Unification," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 33 ||
The Thirty-Fourth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
May the Great Sound, the auspicious Śiva, be ever more auspicious for the virtuous again and again.
That which, though manifesting externally, has not departed from its own nature.
Now, one might raise the objection: "If this Supreme Lord, the conscious Self, is indeed one alone, then what is the purpose of the variety of means such as the *āṇava* and the rest?
Anticipating this doubt, the author begins the second half of the verse to explain that entry [into the Self] occurs precisely through this very process, by way of doors and doorkeepers.
Now, the entry into one's own true nature is described in accordance with the sequence.
He explains that very thing:
"That which has been taught in many ways as the *āṇava* [means] for the attainment of Śiva-hood."
In that regard, one should enter at intervals and rest upon the proximate word.
Then, by abandoning even that [āṇava level], one should take refuge in the śākta stage;
and from that, likewise, in the śāmbhavī stage—clearly according to this progressive sequence.

"In many ways" means by way of forms such as meditation (*dhyāna*), recitation (*uccāra*), and so forth. "In between, in between" refers to [the sequence] among the phonemes (*varṇa*) with respect to their respective positions, and with respect to those, it refers to the organs of articulation (*karaṇa*) and so on. "In the vicinity" refers to one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
From that...
"Thus"—that is, immediately after resting in meditation and the like which abide in proximity to one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

"Due to the abandonment of the individual means (*āṇava*)": the intention is that when the object of knowledge is discarded, one must establish rest in knowledge itself. "Even from that"—that is, immediately after taking recourse to the level of the empowered (*śākta*), for indeed [the nature] of conceptual construction...
The reality is rest in the non-conceptual state alone. "Śāmbhavī" refers, by implication, to the ground.
"In this way" means through resting progressively higher and higher. "Clearly" means one's own true nature; the word "becomes" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Now, one might ask: "If this is so, what would happen to him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this way, he partakes in the state of Bhairava, whose expanding flow is completely filled by the great rays of awakening that arise in succession."
Without requiring any preliminary means, it eternally enters its own self, which contains the form of the entire universe.
"By way of independence from means"—the meaning is: by the sequence of non-means consisting of a single teaching and so forth. And for this reason, it is rightly said:
"The wise should not conceive of any difference here in the fruit, which is consciousness."
Thus [it is said].
He summarizes this very point with a half-verse: "This entry into one's own true nature has been taught by the Supreme Lord."
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of One's Own Nature," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus all is auspicious.
He who knows the reality of the relationship between the means and the goal as proclaimed from the mouth of the illustrious Guru—
this one named Jayadratha has thus explained the thirty-fourth daily lesson (āhnika).

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Entry into One's Own Nature," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, the illustrious Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by the illustrious Jayaratha. 34.
The Thirty-Fifth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
That which, indeed, having brought down the essence of the Mātṛkā in its entirety through various distinctions...
Victorious is the all-knowing Lord Kopa, the author of the treatise and the savior of the world.
Now, by means of stating the unity of all scriptures, he makes a formal declaration with the second half [of the verse] to establish the authority of all the Āgamas:
"Now, the synthesis of all the scriptures here is being stated."
In this regard, he first states the general definition of scripture (āgama): "In this world, this entire ancient worldly transaction... (35.1).
And that very [notion], following established consensus (*prasiddhi*), is called "scripture" (*āgama*).

Here, first of all, this entire worldly transaction proceeds by following an ancient consensus that has long been firmly rooted because it has not been uprooted by any other consensus— all [of these] indeed.

The meaning is that they conduct themselves in such a manner. And that very established usage is called *āgama*—the meaning being that it should be subject to the linguistic convention of that term (*tacchabda*). As it has been said:
"In the world, established usage is *āgama*..."
Thus it is said.
But is it not said: "Upon seeing one thing, when another unseen thing is seen, and failing to see it when that other is not seen,
a person infers the effect even without instructors"?

Having raised the objection— "What is meant by saying that 'all this worldly transaction proceeds' based on the consensus of those who, having understood the relationship between the probandum and the probans through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*) according to such principles as these, engage in their respective transactions?"— he says:
For positive and negative concomitance are dependent upon established usage. || 35-2 ||
If those two were dependent on themselves, what would be the status of those two with respect to a multitude of individual instances?

For it is only when a thing is already established that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) can serve as the basis for understanding the relationship between the probandum and the probans; otherwise, this would not be possible.

If those two [the perception and the recollection] were independently determinative, then, because they arise in relation to each individual instance, the determination of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) would have to depend on each individual object;
yet this is not the case. Therefore, even in that regard, established convention (*prasiddhi*) alone is the root. And so it is with smoke.

Although specific qualities such as paleness and the like follow the positive and negative concomitance of fire, they cannot be inferred as being invariably concomitant [with it] because they lack established recognition as such.

Establishment [of a cognition] is not the basis only in the case of inference, but even in perception; thus he says: "Perception, too, arises from the specific [contact] of the eye, the self, light, the object, and so forth. (35-3)
In that case, it depends upon that very nature of the established [form] at its root;
even perception, which is produced by the totality of causes such as the sense organs, depends there— upon the root consisting of the sense organs and so forth—
upon that [established form] which consists of the reflective awareness of that very nature.

The meaning is that [the means of knowledge] depends upon that well-known consensus which serves as the basis for all worldly transactions; without it, since there would be no impulsion of the sense organs and so forth, nothing at all could be established.
He clarifies this very point by way of contrast:
"A child born alone, surrounded on all sides, is hungry. (35-4)
What could he do, what could he grasp, with what could he see, or where could he go? For a child born on that very day, standing in a place filled on all sides with a multitude of various objects,
though hungry and full of longing, being alone and having received no instruction from others— what indeed could he do without it?

The meaning is that for a child, there would be no linguistic practice consisting of the rejection or acceptance of determined objects, which presupposes a well-known cognition whose essence is self-reflection.
"In this case, the establishment [of the reason] through being otherwise established (anyathāsiddhi) is not applicable"—thus he says:
"Indeed, even in a place crowded with hundreds of objects, that which indeed... (5).
Whether seeing, smelling, or even touching, the mind becomes serene; having immediately grasped that very object, it partakes in positive and negative concomitance.

For on the very day of birth, when a child first engages with its environment—even in a place crowded with hundreds of objects—that very thing which, having come within the range of the eyes and other senses, produces clarity of mind is to be accepted; by implication, everything else is to be rejected. Immediately thereafter, however, [the child] quickly and repeatedly...

The meaning is this: his linguistic usage is rooted in positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), brought about by the excellence of practice regarding the parts of that concomitance. || 6 ||
Now, he teaches with reproach as to where even this clarity of mind (*cetaḥ-prasāda*) comes from:
"Alas! Even that clarity of mind which pertains to a particular object is itself fashioned by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose form is prior latent impression (*vāsanā*). (35.7)
[It is] not born from external means of knowledge such as perception, inference, and so forth;

for is it not the case that mental clarity (*cetasaḥ prasādaḥ*) is merely intuition (*pratibhā*), whose nature is a flash of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) arising at that moment, and thus constructed by a reflective awareness in the form of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?— having raised this doubt:
He said:
"This is merely intuitive flash (pratibhā), subsisting upon prior latent impressions; it is not [the ultimate reality]."
A man does not develop a desire to consume raw meat like a child;

this clarity of mind conforms precisely to prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and is not accidental or a mere flash of intuition. For it is thus that a man who has somehow grown up from childhood [retains such dispositions].

Just as with breast milk and the like, there might even be a desire to consume clay through a lack of awareness of its true nature; yet since this is not the case, the root cause here is simply prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of reflective inquiry (*vimarśa*). As for the consumption of clay by infants and others, that is merely imagined out of a simple hunger (*jighatsā*), and thus it is nothing of consequence.
There is a fault.

Now, one might object: "Granted that mental clarity may indeed be constructed by prior latent impressions (vāsanā) in the form of reflective awareness (vimarśa), but what room is there for it to be established [as a valid means of knowledge] on that basis alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "If reflective awareness depends upon prior latent impressions, and those latent impressions... (35.9)
If this well-known ancient tradition has come from the East, then surely,
if prior latent impression (*vāsanā*) alone is the cause of the clarity of consciousness,
and if that prior latent impression is indeed reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), then this very thing— the ancient tradition that has arrived— is that [awareness].
This alone is its true nature—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"The sacred tradition (āgama) is reflective awareness (vimarśa); that is the well-established consensus free from contradiction."
Now, one might object: "What is the use of established consensus? Let this conventional usage be based merely on the clarity of the mind.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the entire course of worldly transaction does not depend upon the clarity of the mind alone. (35.10)
Let it be accepted that well-known consensus is the root and the authority in all cases;

for the entire worldly transaction consisting of rejection, acceptance, and so forth, would not be established by mere clarity of mind alone, since in that case the process of rejection and so on could not be carried out. Therefore, in every worldly transaction consisting of rejection, acceptance, and so forth—
The meaning is this: let it be accepted that established usage (*prasiddhi*), being the very root, is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for this has come about by force. As they say:
"The entire course of worldly transaction proceeds solely through established usage of a similar kind."
"For everyone, even the most ancient latent impression (vāsanā) remains established from the past.
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "Is it not established that every worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) subsists precisely by depending on those who were more learned in the past? And since this infinite regress does not destroy the very root [of knowledge], what is the need for a basis in traditional consensus (*prasiddhi*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
When investigating whether each preceding [factor] serves as the basis for the subsequent one, that [basis] exists in some cases by itself.
For indeed, in the beginning, that well-known state shines forth without doubt in a single omniscient being;
even when searching for the path of subsistence based on each preceding [source], that renown exists in some single omniscient one at the primordial stage, which is of a supreme nature.

The meaning is that it shines forth without hesitation, being self-sufficient and independent of anything else; due to its subtlety, it remains unmanifest [as an object], yet it vibrates as the essence of the supreme awareness (*parāmarśa*).

Now, one might object: "In this way, let all this worldly transaction proceed entirely on the basis of depending merely upon what has been established by each preceding stage; what is the point of postulating an omniscient being as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For no single conventional usage whatsoever is fully present in the mother.
Therefore, this [scripture] is not established merely by the fact that it was preceded by one who is not omniscient;
for the meaning is that in no case whatsoever does any worldly transaction fail to occur among a non-omniscient cognizer simply because of his non-omniscience. And thus, this...
The meaning is that if this well-known consensus were established as being preceded by one who is not omniscient, it would not be capable of sustaining all worldly transactions.

Now, one might object: "Even so, let the proof of an omniscient being be established simply by his having another omniscient being as his predecessor, just as [the existence of] non-omniscient beings is established;
what is the point of insisting on this specific manifestation [of his being preceded by a single omniscient being]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And there is no evidence whatsoever for the existence of many preceding omniscient beings. (35.13)
"There is no pride"—because of its futility and so forth.

And for this reason, he says that there is only one Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), who consists of the supreme reflective awareness of "I" in its fullness, who is omniscient, and who is the foundation of all established knowledge:
"He is adorned by hundreds of established instances of enjoyment, liberation, and their causes."
That Supreme Lord Bhairava has the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa). || 35-14 ||
And this [power] has proceeded from the Supreme Lord in two ways as the basis for worldly transaction; thus he says:

"Therefore, through the connection of parts and sub-parts, that established tradition, having spread by relying on either the lineage or the scripture, causes the worlds to engage in worldly transactions. (35.15)
"Portion by portion"—due to distinctions such as region (*deśa*) and lineage (*kula*), or due to distinctions such as worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*).
"Tradition" (*paramparā*)—meaning established in the form of oral succession. "Scripture" (*śāstra*)—meaning a formal composition (*nibandhana*).
"Extensive" (*vitatā*)—because there is no internal contradiction. As it has been said:

"The supreme speech of the Lord is thus that which sprouts from the contemplation of scriptures ranging from the worldly to the secret, and whose essence consists of the established tradition known through the oral transmission of the masters. (15)
Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so, what is the reason for accepting only the fixed (niyata) scriptures? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By means of that very [scripture], all virtuous people who abide by the laws of worldly conduct have lived since childhood upon the primordial Śaiva scripture alone. (35.16)

But others are incomplete because of that, and thus they do not partake in the fruit of liberation; "the wise" means those who possess discernment (*vivekin*). By the terms "Śaiva" and "the primordial," its quality of expressing the complete meaning is revealed. As they have said:
"Therefore, he who establishes himself in the supreme non-duality of perfect awakening and perceives the meaning of all principles—that is the supreme scripture.
Regarding the word "supreme" (*pare*): it refers to those who are not [so]. Imperfection has been explained by that; therefore, it is not [the case here].
"Those who partake in the fruit of liberation."
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then what was the purpose of establishing the authority of all the scriptures?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "To the extent that they subsist [upon them], to that extent they partake in their fruit. (35.17)

The word *tu* (but) indicates a reason. *Yāvat-tāvat* means limited. For this very reason it has been said: "those who partake of that fruit," meaning they attain a fruit that is strictly determined; by which [it is meant] that "the Buddhists, abiding in the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*)... and so forth.
Thus and so forth has been stated. || 17 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that for a child who has not yet understood positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and so forth, [the use of words] may be based on mere conventional renown;
but how could this be so for a discerning person? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even when childhood has passed, the reason this person proceeds to eat food is..."
That [self] is established by that very [scriptural authority] alone, and not through perception nor through inference, because [the latter] is impossible. (35.18)
For even in the case of a non-ignorant cognizer, activity toward food and the like is based solely on conventional consensus (*prasiddhi*);

because in that instance, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not possible—since its object is the food itself, and not its "edibility," as the latter does not produce any modification (*vikāra*) in the cognition of it. Therefore, how could this [be perceived]?

It would have to be an instigator with respect to an object that has not yet attained the status of being an object; nor can it be inference, for that is rooted in positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and it has been stated that the basis for these two is precisely established cognition (prasiddhi).
How, then, could this [inference] possess such a nature while abandoning the established cognition that constitutes its very foundation?
It is precisely with this intention that it has been said: "In worldly convention, indeed, the fool and the wise man are alike," and so forth. (18)
Nor is it logical to assume any other sign here—thus he says:
"And there is no expectation of any defect here, because doubt has been removed;
for even one who is somewhat afflicted by hunger and the like does not act elsewhere [than toward what is desired], to that extent."
Because certainty is impossible once defects such as hunger have been removed.
"Now, if this is so, why would such a doubt not arise even for one who acts on the basis of what is well-known?"—anticipating this objection, he says:
"And well-knownness is a cognition arising from non-discrepancy, consisting of verbal designation. (35.19)
It is the very nature of a mother that he never suspects her;
for Śaṅkara, the omniscient one, acts solely by virtue of his own autonomous power. (35.20)
For *prasiddhi* (established conviction), because it is perpetually arisen and shines forth without contradiction,
consists in the cognizer’s own nature as a realization whose essence is self-reflection; thus, within that *prasiddhi*,
[the subject exists] as the agent of the act of reflective awareness.
Precisely because of his own self-made nature, this cognizer never doubts or hesitates;
for he is Śaṅkara, the omniscient one himself—in reality, he is of that very nature—this is the meaning. || 20 ||
Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so when [the soul] possesses the nature of the Supreme Lord; but otherwise, how can this be consistent? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But as long as it does not possess the state of Śiva, [it remains bound] to that which follows its own [limited] self."
To that same extent, he does not doubt this well-established conviction.
"One might be suspicious of another" means one regards her with great esteem.
"To that same extent"—meaning as limited as that. "Of another"—meaning of one belonging to another.
"More"—meaning excessively. "Her"—meaning the well-known reputation that conforms to one's own self. "Regards highly"—means...
Because it is non-deviating.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how is it said that the wise rely solely upon the Śaiva Āgama? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, one who is destined to become Śiva certainly regards this as established tradition. (35.22)
"Thus"—as is well known to oneself. "This"—the Śaiva [tradition] under discussion. || 22 ||

An objection might be raised: "Since this [notion of liberation] is well known in many ways through the divisions of Śaiva, Buddhist, and other traditions, why is there such great esteem for the Śaiva tradition alone regarding the inevitable attainment of the state of Śiva?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This is indeed the one and only scripture shown by the all-pervading, all-seeing Lord; it stands established upon both the path of worldly engagement and the path of renunciation. (35.23)
"In the state of active engagement" means in the form of karma and so forth; "in the state of cessation" means in the singular form of knowledge alone. || 23 ||

Now, one might raise this objection: "If this single scripture was revealed by the All-pervasive Lord, then what is the cause for the diversity in the nature and results of the four aims of human life—beginning with dharma—which are presented differently in each individual treatise?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says:
He said:
Regarding the diverse fruits—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—which differ according to whether they are complete or incomplete, the Śāmbhava Āgama is the sole means. (35.24)

Now, one might object: "If this [scripture] has a single author in this way, why would these various instructions not contradict one another? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that [scripture], which bestows diverse fruits due to the distinctness of its subject matter..."
Even the instruction on diverse means would not entail contradiction. || 35-25 ||
Even though that scripture was composed by the one Śambhu alone, the teaching of diverse means such as dharma and so forth is not [redundant],
because it yields diverse fruits by relying on differences in the object, such as place, time, and the qualified recipient.
The meaning is: it would result in contradiction—that is, it would not become a cause for invalidity. || 25 ||

One might object: "What is the proof for the claim that all this was composed by Śambhu alone, setting aside the authoritative teachers such as the Buddha, Arhat, and Kapila? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The worldly, the Vedic, the Sāṅkhya, Yoga and so forth, and the Pāñcarātra..."
The Buddhist, Ārhata, and Nyāya treatises, which establish the sequence of categories (padārtha). || 35-26 ||

Since all [teachings], such as the Siddhānta, Tantra, and Śākta, originate from Brahman, they are proclaimed in the *Śrī-svacchanda* and other scriptures according to the divisions of Sadyojāta and the rest. (35.27)

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: for it is declared in the Śrī Svacchanda and other scriptures that everything, beginning with the worldly [level], has emerged from the faces of Śambhu himself—specifically from the Brahmās [faces] distinguished as Sadyojāta and so forth. As it is said therein:
It has come from Śiva, the supreme cause, with an invisible form;
it is in the nature of sound, extremely subtle, perfectly pure, and endowed with great radiance.
That very same [reality], in another form, is Śiva, the Supreme Self,
seated upon the throne of mantra, whose great essence consists of the five mantras.
Having swiftly deliberated upon the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), one should examine the various means—
ranging from worldly matters up to Śiva— for the sake of attaining both higher and lower manifestations,
within the respective spheres of experience for those who are fit to receive such grace.
"Bound by the *anuṣṭubh* meter, it consists of thousands of millions of billions [of verses]," (8.31); likewise:
"O Goddess, worldly knowledge has emerged from Sadyojāta."
The Vaidika [mantra] comes from Vāmadeva, while the Ādhyātmika comes from Aghora.
"And from Puruṣa, O fair-faced one, that which is called Atimārga has emerged; but the great knowledge known as Mantramārga has emerged from Īśāna. (11.45).
Likewise:
"O Goddess of gods, worldly knowledge is indeed bound by virtue alone;
however, the Pāñcarātra and Vaidika systems are bound by both virtue and knowledge."
O lady of excellent vows, O Pārvatī, both the Buddhist and the Māhārata [systems] are based solely on dispassion; indeed, the Sāṅkhya knowledge is bound to both knowledge and dispassion.
Knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are established in the knowledge of yoga;
it is proclaimed as that which has transcended the states of the intellect and surpassed all paths.
"And that knowledge transcends the world; it is remembered as being beyond the path. (11.182) ||27||
Now, one might raise this objection: "If the Śaiva, Buddhist, and other scriptures are indeed [all] *āgamas*,

then why is it stated that for those following the Buddhist and other systems, when they turn toward the Śiva-scripture, there must also be another purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) such as the removal of their sectarian mark (*liṅgoddhāra*)?"— this doubt is addressed by means of an illustrative example.
It pacifies [the impurity]:

"Just as even in a single tradition such as the Veda, there are various purificatory rites for those entering different stages of life (āśrama), so too here [in this system], there are rites such as the extraction of the *liṅga*. (35.28)
"It is another conditioned phenomenon"—this is stated by implication. ||28||
One might object: "Even if this entire scripture has indeed arisen from Śiva alone, why does the nature of Śiva not likewise arise from the Śaiva, Pāñcarātra, and other [scriptures]?
Taking this doubt as a point of comparison, he speaks by means of an illustration:
And just as in that case one does not attain the fruit of the higher stage from the previous stage, so too in the Pāñcarātra and other systems, one does not attain the nature of Śiva.

Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): it means in one [place], namely at the beginning of the Vedas; and regarding "in the preceding stage of life" (pūrvasminn āśrame): this implies that he remains [in that state] rather than proceeding to a subsequent stage of life, such as that of the householder. || 29 ||
Thus, this very scripture established by the Lord is one alone, wherein everything from the worldly treatises onwards finds its ultimate rest; so he says:
"Therefore, there is only one scripture, [which includes] therein the worldly treatises."
Indeed, everything from the Vaiṣṇava up to the Buddhist and Śaiva systems is established therein.

One might object: "Even for such a scripture as this, what is the goal to be attained? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That supreme abode which is to be reached by it is designated by the term 'Trika'.
Now, one might ask: *Note: The word "nanu" at the end of the provided fragment indicates the beginning of a further objection or inquiry.*
"Know that Kula, O Omniscient One, to be devoid of Śiva and Śakti, wherein this variegated universe arises and wherein it sets"—
by such a view, it is stated that Kula alone is the locus of the repose of all things. That...
Anticipating the question, "What is this that is being called? he says:
"Because it does not cut off any differentiation whatsoever, that very [reality] is called Kula. (35.31)

Just as there is a single vital breath throughout the various parts of the body, whether they occupy higher or lower positions, so too, according to the scriptures, the Trika exists as one within all things.
And it is stated in the venerable Kālīkula that this is proclaimed as the essence of the ten and eighteen divisions, being devoid of the five streams (pañcasrotas). || 35-33 ||
Just as fragrance resides in a flower, oil in sesame seeds, the soul in the body, and nectar in water,
so too is the Kula established within the scriptures.

Indeed, that very triad appears everywhere—in space, time, and so forth—as being nothing but non-dual consciousness (*saṃvid-advaya*), because there is no division or interruption [of its nature]. It is called *kula* because it follows the meaning of the verbal root *kula*, namely "to contract" or "to gather"; the sense is that it is designated as such in common usage. This alone—

He establishes [the point] by means of an illustration, beginning with "Just as" (yathā). This is established not only through reasoning, but also through scripture; thus he says, "The venerable," and so forth. || 34 ||
He concludes the very subject at hand: "Therefore, this single scripture is manifold for a manifold qualified practitioner.
Regarding the word "manifold," he states the reason: "for a manifold qualified practitioner."
Now, one might object: "How can it be that [the teaching] is both single and manifold due to the difference in qualified recipients?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that very same way, that well-known tradition indeed extends to both those within one's own school and those belonging to other schools. (35–35)

For indeed, that very same conventional renown (*prasiddhi*)—which consists of diversity—is established even in the case of unity, by virtue of being categorized as belonging to one's own group or another's group. For there is no such scriptural tradition (*āgama*), such as that of the Buddhists and others, which, despite being a single entity, is not diverse due to the difference in its intended recipients (*adhikārin*). || 35 ||
Not only is oneness established here through reasoning, but also through scripture; thus he says:
"One should not disparage Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, nor the Vedas themselves, because they have all originated from Śiva," so it is stated in the *Svacchanda-śāsana*. (35–36)

Now, one might object: "If all these, such as the Sāṃkhyas and others, have indeed arisen from Śiva, then why are they not well-known simply as 'Śaiva'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And from a single scripture, these [systems] have been extracted as fragmentary pieces."
There may be scriptures in the world, and by them people wander, deluded. || 35-37 ||

"Extracted"—by Kapila, Sugata, and others. "Deluded, he wanders"—the meaning is that, considering those [teachings] to be mutually contradictory because they were composed by various [different authors], one would not be a seer of things as they truly are. || 37 ||

Now, one might object: "If there is only a single scripture, then since an option (vikalpa) is possible according to the principle that 'there is an option for those among the learned who possess equal authority,' what is the purpose of distinguishing between different subject matters? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even in the view that there are many scriptures, the distinction of subject matter must be stated."
Necessarily, for the sake of establishing validity, there must be a state of being situated one above and the other below. || 35–38 ||
Otherwise, the validity of nothing whatsoever would certainly be established.

Even if there is a lack of unity among the scriptures, for the sake of establishing their validity, it must necessarily be stated that they possess distinct subject matters through their arrangement in a hierarchy of higher and lower levels; otherwise, the validity of no scripture at all could be proven.
The certainty is that validity would simply not be established due to mutual contradiction; therefore,
the meaning is that a scripture which teaches a specific means for a particular qualified person— viewed from the perspective of "thereby enjoining someone to something"— is indeed authoritative.

One might object: "If the authority of scripture is established by its very eternality and non-contradiction alone, what is the purpose of stating the distinction or non-distinction of its objects? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Eternality and non-contradiction are not the grounds for [scriptural] authority. (35–39)
There is no ground for pride—because validity is described even in the case of perception and other means despite their impermanence;
because it is impossible [to find such validity] in the case of space and so forth despite their permanence;
and because validity is accepted even in the case of statements regarding heaven and the Agnihotra sacrifice, despite the absence of any observed non-discrepancy.
Since in cases such as "there is water in the well," even when that [water] is sometimes seen, validity is not established, he says— having granted [the opponent's position] for the sake of argument:
"In this respect as well, validity would belong to that very [cognition] alone, because it was stated in that manner."

Even if one were to accept this portion which constitutes the cause of validity— characterized by its constancy and non-contradiction— the validity would belong to this Śaiva [tradition] alone, because it teaches such a state of being;
for even the Vedas and other scriptures exist only as part of the Śaiva [revelation].
He is the one who describes the supreme speech solely for the sake of awakening the inner essence,
and he is refined by the fundamental impressions of the unartificial penetration of the Supreme.

"The meaning of the scripture culminates in the worldly [level], while in the supreme, all-pervasive [state]— the thirty-seventh," according to the reasoning stated in such passages, there is permanence upon resting in the ten states beginning with Parā;
thus, "The Śiva-āgama is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) for that."
Thus, non-contradiction would be established even in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like.
One might object: "Even if there is a lack of correspondence with reality, there are indeed other ways to interpret statements such as *arthavādas*;
so what is the point of this [criticism]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the case of [interpreting them] otherwise, or in the assumption of a different meaning, or in their being untrue, or for the sake of persuasion... (35–40)
If one must necessarily accept this means of knowledge called "scripture," then there would be the over-extension [of the argument], which would subvert all scripture whatsoever. (35–41)
"In other ways" means by way of definition (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth. "In [the case of] established [meaning]" refers to the primary meaning (*vācya*) itself.
"In [the case of] unreality" refers to instances such as "Rudra because he wept" (*rodanāt rudraḥ*). "In [the case of] persuasion" refers to through praise, censure, and so forth.

Otherwise, by the implication that [the Buddha's] predictions and so forth are not [authoritative] for anyone else, the validity of the entire scripture would necessarily be destroyed; therefore, one must either abandon the authority of that scripture or accept the true nature of the reasoning we have stated— one must not remain in between— thus he says:
This determination of the culmination of the scripture must necessarily be accepted.
"This" refers to that which has just been stated.
Now, one might object: "Since all scriptures possess equal authority, why is there such an excess of reverence for the Śaiva alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For, in reality, effort directed toward the primary member [of a whole] is what yields fruit. (35–42)
Therefore, someone impelled by Śambhu should be diligent in this matter;
and likewise, there is also scripture to this effect—thus he says:
"In various scriptures here and there, it was described by the Great Lord. (35–43)
It is clear that such a qualified person is rare;
as it has been said:
"O Goddess, he who knows this Siddhātantra in its entirety [is rare]."
"That guru, who delights the heart of the Yoginīs, is said to be difficult to find.
Thus [it is said].

He concludes this very point with a half-verse, preceded by a demonstration of the Guru’s instruction: "In this manner, the venerable Śambhunātha has taught me the integration of the scriptures. (35–44)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Integration of the Scriptures," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 35.
In this manner, by the way described, there has been a "conjunction of scriptures" (śāstramelana) for me; that is, the scripture has been integrated by me—this is the meaning.
And this is not my own invention, as stated by the venerable Śambhunātha. May there be auspiciousness!
Having traversed the path of the meaning of the entire range of scriptures,
Jayaratha, by ascending to the broad ground [of understanding], has explained this thirty-fifth chapter.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Integration of the Scriptures," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 35 ||
The Thirty-Sixth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
Since all this has clearly descended through the sequence of parts and sub-parts...
May that Śāstra—the mass of sounds consisting of the awareness of perfect I-consciousness—protect you all.
Now he begins to describe the sequence of the transmission of this treatise, which has been introduced as the resting place for all scriptures:
"Next, the transmission of the scripture is told, as it has arrived at its proper occasion."
He says this very thing: "Bhairava, the Goddess Bhairavī, Svacchanda, Lākula, and Aṇurāṭ are designated in the Śrīsiddha[tantra] and described by the Gurus. (36.1)
Gahaneśa, the Lotus-born (Brahmā), Śakra, and Guru [each] studied it by subtracting ten million [verses] at a time; thus, it was mastered in nine stages, its extent being ninety million verses.
Thereupon, the Guru bestowed one quarter from that ten-million-fold amount upon Dakṣa and the others,
and likewise two quarters upon Saṃvarta and the others.
One quarter [of the merit] goes to Vāmana and the others; half a quarter to Bhārgava; one-eighth to Bala; and whatever other one-eighth remains [is for the rest]. || 36-4 ||
From what remained after giving half to Siṃha, two portions were given to Vinatā’s son;
one quarter was given to the nāga Vāsuki—these are the seventeen divisions.
Then Rāvaṇa seized half of heaven; Rāma, in turn, obtained even that half from Vibhīṣaṇa through the traditional succession of preceptor and disciple.
Then, it was divided into nineteen parts. Aṇu, Ananta, Abjaja, and Brahmā— by subtracting ten million [each], nine crores were indeed studied by Bhairava,
eight by Bhairavī, and one crore by the Guru, in succession.
Thus—from Bhairava to Bhairavī, from her to Svacchanda, and so on down to Śakra and the Guru.
By these, namely Bhairava and the others, is the scripture [received]; as it is said in the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*: "The *Siddhayogīśvarīmata* was obtained by Bhairavī from Bhairava."
Then, by the god Svacchandadeva, [it was bestowed] spontaneously by Lākula.
From Lakulīśa [it was received] by Ananta; from Ananta, the Lord of the Gahana;
and from the Lord of the Gahana, O Goddess, [it was received] by the Grandfather, the Lord of the Gods.
"It was heard by all the mighty ones, such as Svacchanda and others, through a reduction of ten million from the Grandfather [Brahmā] to Indra, and from Indra to Bṛhaspati.
Thus, "one quarter" means the fourth part, which is twenty-five lakhs. "Both"—meaning...
By this [expression] "the two feet," it is stated that the duality is conditioned by the coexistence with the preceding foot;
for otherwise, since duality would already be established by the dual ending itself, the word "both" (ubhau) would be redundant, as its purpose is merely enumeration.
And it would not contradict [the calculation]. "Half a quarter" means twelve and a half lakhs.
"A quarter of a quarter" means six and a quarter lakhs. "Another quarter of a quarter" consists of exactly six and a quarter lakhs. "Then, half of that" means—

It consists of three hundred thousand and twelve thousand five hundred [verses]. Regarding the phrase "from what remains"—that is, from the second half of such a form. Regarding the phrase "two parts"—this refers to the two portions consisting of fifty-six thousand two hundred and fifty verses, as will be described later, which were carried away by Rāvaṇa.

The meaning is that, in comparison with the second half of the measure of one hundred thousand (*alakṣa*), [the first half] has a magnitude of one hundred forty-one thousand and sixty-seven (*141,067*).
"A portion" (*bhāga*) refers to the third part, which consists of fifty-two thousand and eighty-three (*52,083*).

This is the meaning. Regarding "seventeen"—this is together with the nine previous sections. This concluding summary is intended to illuminate that these [sections] have a divine subject matter. "He took half of heaven" means that he obtained it by way of a forceful union (*haṭhamelāpa*). Therefore—

"From the half taken away by Rāvaṇa"—the term "half" refers to that which consists of seventy-eight thousand one hundred and twenty-five units. "Through the lineage of gurus and disciples"—this applies to all [the remaining parts]. "By nineteen sections"—referring to the seventeen [sections] belonging to the ancients.

And in order to demonstrate that these two sections have the world of mortals (bhūloka) alone as their domain, they are specified by a number separate from the seventeen. It is with this very intention [that it is said]:
"The remainder will be in the land of Kumārikādvīpa, in the house... and so forth.
Thus it has been said. Regarding the word "that": it refers to the *Siddhayogeśvarīmata*, which has an extent of ninety million verses.
As the scripture states: "Therein, the illustrious Bṛhaspati then began the exposition."
Having begun with these words, [the text continues]:
"Dakṣa, Caṇḍa, Hari, Caṇḍī, Pramatha, Bhīma, Manmatha,
Śakuni, Sumati, Nanda, Gopāla, and then Pitāmaha."
O Goddess, having heard this tantra, they departed for the Yogīśvarīmata;
from among ten million [verses], they clearly established one quarter of it as firm.
O Bhairavī, O lady of excellent limbs, the two feet were established by Vīreśa and others beginning with Saṃvarta;
the single foot was known by Vāmana and others.
Then Śukra obtained half of that; Balinanda, half of that;
Siṃha, half of that; and likewise Garuḍa obtained a mere hundred thousand.
The lordly Mahānāga, named Vāsuki, the king of the Nāgas, protects Pātāla; having taken half a lakh [of them], he always worships [the Lord].
"Then Rāvaṇa, the thorn in the side of the gods, having seized all that remained of it with a wicked mind, departed for Laṅkā. Thus [it is said].
Thus, it came to the mortal world from the realm of Indra,
having descended through a succession of lineages and brought down by Rāvaṇa.
Then, [it was said]: "Vibhīṣaṇa has arrived; therefore, go to the son of Daśaratha.
And:
"It has been divided into nineteen sections by those desiring to hear it."

And it is said: "Extending up to ninety-nine million verses, [it contains] the Siddhayogīśvarīmata. Here, by the word *mātra* in the phrase "only one hundred thousand" (*lakṣamātram*), the meaning is "fifty thousand" (*lakṣārdham*).
Furthermore, by the word *ardha*, which denotes an unequal portion, there is the acceptance of a number slightly exceeding that.
Since the author has cast a sidelong glance toward its elucidation, he has merely performed a division of parts; and here, within each section, there is an eightfold nature—thus he says:
"Each section is eightfold, according to the divisions of the previously mentioned quarters and so forth. (36–7)
He points out the very feet and so forth:

"The foot (pāda), the root-extraction (mūloddhāra), the subsequent (uttara), the great-subsequent (vṛhaduttara), as well as the ritual manual (kalpa); the compendium (saṃhitā) and the trunk of the ritual manual (kalpaskanda), the unsurpassed (anuttara), and the pervasive (vyāpaka)—thus threefold are the three. (36.8)
The goddesses are described here in a progressively expanding form;
however, in the ninth station, no calculation is mentioned, as it is devoid of any division.

These technical designations, beginning with *pāda*, refer to specific, fixed quantities of text. Now, one might ask: if all three goddesses are here described as being threefold in their manifestation as the nature of the *prapañca* (the cosmic expansion), why is it not stated that each one possesses nine divisions (*navakhaṇḍatva*)?

Anticipating this objection, it is said: "The Absolute (Anuttara) is all-pervasive. For this very reason, it is stated that no numerical calculation is mentioned regarding the ninth state, which is devoid of differentiation. As the scripture says:
"The foot, the root, the extraction, the Absolute, and the Great Absolute."
The Kalpa and the Saṃhitā have indeed been told to you, O lady of virtuous vows.
O lady of beautiful hips, I shall tell you the ritual procedure for Skanda in brief:
the foot is reckoned at fifty [verses], and the root-mantra at one hundred.
Know that the *uddhāra* is twofold, while the subsequent one is considered fourfold;
this other [method], O fair-limbed lady, is devoid of half-syllables.
Thus has the *Uttaratantra* been described in the *Mūlabhairava*;
when it is devoid of the six parts, O Varārohā, it is the *Aparā*.
Then it would indeed be "Vṛhaduttara" because of the exclusion of the syllable *amṛta*;
the definition of a hundred syllables is thus declared.
O illustrious lady, that [Kalpa] of Aparā is reckoned at one thousand [verses],
consisting of fourteen thousand and sixty-two verses.
Then that Saṃhitā is to be known according to the doctrine of the Siddhayogīśvara;
the Kalpaskandha previously mentioned shall be twice the size of a Kalpa.
Thus, the classification of the tantras has been explained by me in great detail. (9)
Now, one might object: "Was this not obtained by Rāma from Vibhīṣaṇa; did someone else obtain it from him again, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From Rāma it went to Lakṣmaṇa, from him to the Siddhas, and from them also to the Dānavas."
Then from them [came] the Guhyakas, and from them the yogins, and from them the best of men.
As the scripture states: "The success of those things spoken by Vibhīṣaṇa to Rāma, by Rāma to Lakṣmaṇa, and by Lakṣmaṇa [to others], is indeed inferior."
The Dānavas [attain it] from the Siddhas; the Guhyakas from the Dānavas;
the Yogins from the Guhyakas; and the best of men from the Yogins.
"He has arrived by the command of Bhairava, O Bhairavī, through his fierce asceticism. (10)
Having thus explained the method for transcending Māyā as taught in the Śrīsiddhātantra, he speaks in order to describe that which has been set forth by the Gurus:
"When, in the course of time, [the transmission] among them has fallen away from the middle of that sequence..."
Then, by the power of the command of Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the Siddhas descended.
The venerable masters known as Tryambaka, Āmardaka, and Abhikhyā are, respectively, experts in the non-dual, the dual, and the dual-nondual [teachings] within the Śiva-scripture. (36.12)
And from the first [lineage], a second was born through the succession of daughters;
that lineage, known as the Ardhatryambaka, became well-established.
Therefore, there are three and a half monasteries here,
expanded through the lineage of disciples and grand-disciples established in a hundred branches.

"In the non-dual" (advaye) means in the *Trikula* and other such systems. "Half" (ardha) is said in relation to a daughter. "Three and a half" (ardhacatasraḥ) means four less a half, that is, three and a half—this is the meaning. || 14 ||
Now, one might object: "In this context, it would be more appropriate to speak only of the Traiyambika lineage, through which this scripture has come down;
what is the purpose of describing other lineages? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The extraction of the essence, which is the vital sap of the streams of the three-and-a-half lineages..."
Having been established, this Tantrāloka flows forth with all its streams.
Concluding this and introducing another topic, he says: "The manner of attainment has been stated; now the state of being worthy of acceptance is determined.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sequence of Succession."

In order to demonstrate the mutual continuity from one daily lesson (*āhnika*) to the next, although separate conclusions and openings have been composed for the beginning and end [of each] by means of a single verse, [the author] now [proceeds] at the end of the book.
Therefore, in order to illuminate their union most intensely, they are depicted simultaneously by means of a single half [of the body];
may there be auspiciousness! || 15 ||
This thirty-sixth chapter has been definitively established by Jayaratha through the secret tradition transmitted via the sequence of the three-and-a-half lineages.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Sequence of Transmission," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. 36.
The Thirty-Seventh Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
By means of the realization that "this entire universe consists of Me," everything attains the state of being supremely worthy of acceptance.
Victorious is the illustrious Goddess Mālinī, the weapon that destroys the various states of existence.

Thus, in order to determine the worthiness of this very treatise as something to be adopted, he first establishes the introductory framework by relying on what has preceded it: "When all worldly transaction proceeds exactly according to the method already stated..."
Since established consensus must be relied upon, scripture (āgama) must necessarily be accepted. (37-1)

In this context, when universal linguistic practice has been set in motion, the scripture (āgama) must necessarily be accepted as the basis for established usage according to the principle stated in the thirty-fifth chapter; otherwise, nothing at all would be established.
Now, one might object: "Granted that for an entity within the scope of worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), its establishment may be based on common consensus;
but how could this be so in the case of Śiva, who is beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition and inaccessible even to yogins?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Just as, according to worldly perspective, one partakes of other fruits through their established consensus, so too, by engaging in correct worldly practice, one partakes of Śiva through His established consensus. (37-2)
"Anyā" means the unseen (adṛṣṭa). ||2||

Now, one might object: "Since scripture (*āgama*) is thus established as having many forms, which among them must necessarily be accepted? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that scripture which must necessarily be accepted, which teaches its own specific portion..."
That which yields even a slight fruit is most worthy of being adopted; the opposite of that is not. (37-3)
Just as poison is destroyed by the state of being the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) due to fearlessness, so too the persistence of karma perishes through fearlessness born of the state of Bhairava. 37–4.

That which is stated in the Ṛṣi scriptures as a cause for downfall is, in this Vāma teaching, for the sake of swift accomplishment; for everything pertaining to the Ṛṣis resides within the belly of Māyā. (5)
The opposite of that—namely, the contrary—is of great fruit. ||5||
Anticipating the question, "And what is this of such a kind?", he says:
"And what might that be which is seen by every omniscient being?"—
this being preceded by the doubt, "What might even that which is seen by every omniscient being be?"
He demonstrates its essential nature: "When, through the entirety of the instruction, the unsurpassed fruit is produced... (37.6).
And here, two verses have been written otherwise in the lower [manuscript] by way of transposition; since they ought to be in the correct order, we shall explain them in that very place. || 6 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is this complete instruction by which [the reality] would become such as this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Just as through the restatement of the true nature of things taught by each progressively lower [level of authority],"
The answer has been stated: that which is established by consciousness must indeed be so. || 37-7 ||

Just as here the reality of entities such as ritual action, as stated by the Vaidikas and others, is restated and then excelled [by this teaching], so too knowledge-yoga and the like, established through one's own experience, have been declared. || 7 ||
For this very reason, it is determined that the lower scriptures were not composed by an omniscient being; thus he says:

"Because they describe objects established through a consciousness superior to what is stated [in them], it is known that the teaching in the lower scriptures was proclaimed by one who is not a fully perfect omniscient being. (37.8)

Now, one might object: since even in the lower teachings (adhara-śāsana) knowledge and so forth are taught through such statements as "The self is to be known, it is to be reflected upon," why then is [the latter] considered to have been composed by one who is not omniscient?

Anticipating the objection, "How is this known?", he says: "Even when the portion of the reality of the higher teaching has been seen and yet abandoned, the nature of Māyā is perceived in the lower scriptures through their concern for creation and preservation. (37.9)
Regarding the word "samujjhite" (in the abandoned): it is because there is no further growth in that very place. Regarding "sargarakṣaṇāt" (for the sake of protecting creation):
the meaning is "for the purpose of protecting the world. || 9 ||
Furthermore, what is the authority for this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And it has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Ānandaśāstra* and other works:
'The word of the sages involves much affliction, yields unstable and meager results, and is limited. (37-10)
A wise person should not treat [other scriptures] as authoritative; he should take refuge in the Śaiva Āgama alone.
Now, one might object: "If the treatises of Manu and others are not to be accepted, would this entire system of conduct not fall into ruin? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That which was stated in the Ṛṣi tradition as a cause for downfall is [the same] in this Vāma teaching. (37-11)
"For the sake of swift accomplishment, since everything pertaining to the Ṛṣis resides within the belly of Māyā.
Regarding the phrase "stated as the cause of downfall" (*pātahetu*): the meaning is that it refers to the speech uttered by the gods and others for the purpose of causing downfall.
However, "stated as the cause of sin" (*pātakārya*) is the clearer reading. As for the phrase "residing within the belly of Māyā":
Because he is devoted to the protection of the world.
One might object: "In that case, would not the stability of karma be destroyed? He dispels this doubt by first presenting an illustration, beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā):
"Just as poison may be neutralized through the state of fearlessness regarding the power of the Queen of Birds (Garuḍī). (37-12)
"In that same way, the persistence of karma reaches its exhaustion through the state of Bhairava, free from doubt.

Now, one might object: "Granted that this occurs through the attainment of the state of Bhairava, on what basis can it be said that his scripture must necessarily be accepted? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In the inferior teaching, which is bitten by ignorance and the lack of a true instructor.
By the reversal of this [dualism], the teaching of Śiva must necessarily be grasped;
and therein, the two authoritative ones are the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha and Lakuleśvara. (37.14)
This treatise has two streams and bestows perfect liberation;
yet, for the former [stream], the capacity to grant desired enjoyments also remains. (37-15)
And that [teaching] is declared to be fivefold, variegated by the diversity of powers;
it is called the "Five Streams" (Pañcasrotas), the glorious ordinance of Śrīkaṇṭha.
The fivefold stream, which is tenfold and eighteenfold, is further distinguished by sixty-four divisions; it is the most excellent, known as Bhairava. (37–17)
"Because of ignorance," meaning it has been bitten—that is, touched—by one who teaches erroneously.
"Therein" means in the teaching of Śiva. "Of the former" refers to Śrīkaṇṭha. "Fivefold" is due to the distinctions beginning with consciousness (cit). || 17 ||
Right here, in order to determine that [the lineage] consists of four seats (pīṭhas), he says:
"Indeed, it was stated by the Blessed One in the venerable Ānandaśāstra and other works:
'This seat is a collection, and it is twofold, according to the right and the left. (37-18)
Mantra is *vidyā*, and therefore the dyad belonging to the mudrās and maṇḍalas [is also so called].

It is said that in the Āgama, the Lord has designated the *pīṭha* by the word "assemblage" (*samūha*); this is the meaning of the definition. Regarding the phrase "on the right and left"—this is by way of being the forms of Śiva and Śakti.
This is the meaning: for the mantra has the nature of Śiva, and the vidyā has the nature of Śakti.
"Therefore" means from the two seats (pīṭha) which consist of mantra and vidyā.
He explains this very point in sequence:
"That which bestows both reflection (manana) and protection (trāṇa), and is called 'mantra', [is realized] therein through knowledge (vidyā). (37.19)
Strengthening is nourishment, for that [nourishment] illuminates the object to be known;
the mudrā is the counterpart of the mantra, and it is that which effects its nourishment. (37.20)
Indeed, the Maṇḍala is declared to be the essence (sāra), and by the term *maṇḍa* it is called Śiva;
thus, the four seats (pīṭha) function through mutual interpenetration. (37.21)
Therefore, in reality, everything exists within each and every sacred seat (*pīṭha*). This is the reinforcement and nourishment [of that truth], as it was stated in the aphorism:
"The secret of the mantra is the existence of the body of the Vidyā. (Śivasūtra 2.3)

Thus [it is said]. It is called "illuminating the object of knowledge" because its nature is that of power (*śakti*). It is called "maṇḍala" in the sense that it takes (*lāti*) the essence (*maṇḍa*), which is named Śiva. Now, one might object: "If a single seat (*pīṭha*) is thus the soul of all, then what is the purpose of teaching these separately? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Furthermore, the distinctness of each respective entity arises from its predominance.
This has been taught for the sake of the accomplishment of various objects for the foremost of practitioners;
each of these consists of four parts: the mandala and likewise the mudrā.
The mantra, the vidyā, and the pīṭha are each increasingly superior.
"Each individually" means one by one. Regarding "each subsequent one is more excellent":
therefore, from the maṇḍala-pīṭha comes the mudrā-pīṭha, from that the mantra-pīṭha, and from that the vidyā-pīṭha.
And so it is said.
He brings this very point to rest in the present context:
"And the Siddhayogīśvarīmata is the preeminent seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha). (37.24)
The supreme essence of that [scripture] as well is the *Mālinīvijayottara*.
Furthermore, what is the authority for this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And this has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrīratnamālā*. (37.25)
The essence of all Tantras without exception, based upon both the Left and the Right,
is united in one place as the Kaula within the teaching of the venerable Trika (the Three-and-a-Half).
In the Siddhānta, ritual action (*karma*) predominates and is defiled by impurity (*mala*) and *māyā*;
the Right Way (*dakṣiṇa*) is rich in fierce rites (*raudrakarman*), while the Left Way (*vāma*) is filled with supernatural powers (*siddhi*). (37.27)
Abandon from afar that discipline which possesses little merit, is fraught with much affliction, is devoid of personal realization, and is lacking in the knowledge of liberation. (37.28)
"Raudra" refers to [rites] such as killing and eradication. "One's own realization" means one's own direct experience. "Vinaya" is the scripture in which the Tantras are predominant. || 28 ||
Now, one might object: "In this *Śeṣavṛtti* as well, a multiplicity of objects such as the 'object of action' (*karman*) has been mentioned; so why was that not stated here?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And at whatever time the Guru has revealed the state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*)."
At that very moment, he is liberated, and the machine remains alone.

Now, one might ask: "What is the nature of these other currents, such that it is appropriate to describe this [current] as superior to them and thus worthy of being adopted? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "I shall describe the nature of these currents from the eternal state of the Unsurpassed (Anuttara)."
This has been explained in detail, beginning from [verse 37.30], in the *Mālinīślokavārtika*.
One who desires to know is therefore capable of ascertaining this;
we, however, do not value the mere repetition of what has already been said, for it is fruitless.
Thus, because it expresses this very same meaning, this treatise composed by us is indeed to be accepted;
so he says:
"In this way, bestowing effortlessly the great fruit of liberation while living..."
It is established as the bestower of great enjoyments according to one's desires. || 37-32 ||
This true scripture, the essence of the Trika (Ṣaḍardha), is clearly worthy of being adopted.
And by this [work], the wise person who always [recites] these thirty-seven [verses]...
One who practices these daily rites thoroughly shall become Bhairava himself.

The great purpose, which was introduced by the verse beginning with, "When one becomes Bhairava through the complete awakening in the thirty-seven [principles], what wonder is it that even individual souls (aṇu) attain the state of Bhairava by his glance? (1.289), has thus been fulfilled.

The author, having established his familiarity with the scriptures along with their limbs and sub-limbs, now sets forth his own life story— recording the sequence of his country, lineage, and teachers— in order to demonstrate his own fitness for composing this work by means of highlighting his excellence.
Although this infinite series of worlds was produced by the power of the thirty-six principles,
the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is exceedingly beautiful.
For there is no state of being beautiful apart from variety. || 37-33 ||
Even though that [city] is filled with the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr, I consider its second floor to be the abode of happiness;
