for where else could there be such a place, adorned by the sun and moon moving in their wondrous courses?
The division of the enjoyment of the progression of day and night is the ornament. (37.34)
And even there, the land called Kumārikā is indeed superior to the other continents, which yield a rain of highly precious celestial enjoyments.
"The second world" refers to Bhuvarloka. "Therein" means in that second world.
The Varṣas are Ilāvṛta and the others; the Dvīpas are Śāka and the rest. He demonstrates their very superiority:
where, from the lowest of the lower levels up to the supreme level ending in Śiva—
Even the authority to ascend [this mountain] is priceless for those who are accomplished.
He establishes this very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"Of what use is birth in a state of being fit for the enjoyment of animal-like fetters (paśu) resulting from past karma, even if it were in a realm consisting solely of happiness?"
For everyone indeed attains the highest satisfaction when their future prospects are honored, but not while the present moment is fleeting.
Even in this world called Kanyā, that country alone is most venerable where the supreme scriptures are indeed the eyes;
who would not censure one born in a house of those blind from birth?
In the light emanating from the face of the sun, which resembles crushed collyrium.
Indeed, Madhyadeśa is the abode of all scriptures without exception; in that land was born a certain twice-born man of preeminent virtues,
whose lineage was etymologically defined by the name Atrigupta.
He belongs to the lineage of Agastya, who arose like the churning-stick for the ocean of the scriptures.
Then King Lalitāditya, out of the impetuosity of his affection, led him to his own city named Kaśmīra, situated upon the crest of the Himalayas,
where Gaurī’s beloved dwells with his [four] hands, such as Vijaya and the others.
To simultaneously savor the entire essence of enjoyment from its very source.
Since all the sages have made their dwellings in various places here, and since the Moon-crested Lord himself resides at every step,
I believe that this place is not for the attainment of even the most desired of perfections.
Furthermore, after Kaśmīra, there is the city of Pūrṇavr̥tti, which does not bring satisfaction. || 37-40 ||
There, she who is as radiant as the autumnal moon and renowned among people as Śrī Śāradā,
is perfectly pleased by the essence of Śāṇḍilya’s service.
He unites all people with his own riches. || 37-41 ||
Possessing a luster as crimson as an orange, a complexion as pale-white as a blossoming balla flower,
a radiance as delightful as the golden hue of a freshly emerged, pure mātuluṅga fruit,
and shining with a dark splendor resembling the tresses of a kerī plant;
In which the great Bhairava liquor is perfectly radiant with the fourfold power. || 37-42 ||
The multitude of Madana’s arrows, dissolved here by the flames of the Great Three-Eyed One’s wrath, now manifests under the guise of wine.
Otherwise, how could passion, delusion, intoxication, and the fever of love arise?
Acting incessantly, he brings the world under his control through the afflictions of desire. || 37-43 ||
That which bestows maturity upon the loving words of beloved women; that which unimpededly shakes off all trepidation during the act of love;
and in which all the deities who move in circles take delight—[that is the sound of the lute].
There, that grape-wine instantly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

There, at every step, the earth is strewn with saffron flowers, whose petals are dark red and blooming like emerging pale sprouts, and which are variegated by rows of filaments shining with a deep, internal crimson luster.
It reveals the garden for the worship of the triad of the Samyag-devīs. || 37-45 ||
Where every person in the world is a poet, wise, brave, and eloquent; where the women of the city possess the radiance of the moon and graceful gait;
and where the path of the Suṣumṇā is infinite, blossoming and blazing with the fire of the vital breath (Aṅgāra).
The host of yoginīs, who have eclipsed the sun and moon and are as pure as the sky. || 37-46 ||
And there is the glorious city named Paravara, which the lord of the earth Pravarasena built;
he who, at the conclusion of the worship of Maheśvara installed by himself, [founded it].
As he was flying up into the sky, he reportedly cast down a bell for incense.
And she proclaimed his virtuous conduct through the charming and heroic shouts raised during the agitation;
for those whose forms possess the weight and splendor of the essence of noble conduct [speak out].
Even when abandoned, they resound all the more with the virtues of their master. || 37-48 ||
Possessing a splendor tawny with thick saffron from the dense body-unguents of the hero’s beloved, who has the stainless luster of the full moon,
he is fanned by the masses of white yak-tail whisks from the waving cane creepers.
Constantly bestowing the consecration of sovereignty upon Smara. || 37-49 ||
By means of the worship, anointing, perfumes, and flowers offered to the self-manifested *svāyambhuva* linga of Maheśvara established on the riverbank,
and by the flood of immersion in the waves that were being drawn toward [the shore], [the sins were washed away].
She is worshipped by sages, perfected beings, and humans whose sins have been destroyed.
A wish-fulfilling creeper that completely fulfills both worldly enjoyment and liberation, surpassing the ocean of gods and siddhas who delight solely in granting enjoyments—
she has descended as a digit of Hara’s Pināka bow.
That which the river Vitastā adorns incessantly.
In that place, on the bank of the Vitastā, he made his dwelling— a spot where a state of sanctity had arisen from the direct sight of the Moon-crested Lord as he traveled toward Kubera’s city.
The king bestowed abundant wealth upon the twice-born man.
In his great lineage there was one named Varāhagupta, who at the time of his end became the Blessed One himself,
his head embraced by the waves of the celestial river.
To whom he rendered supreme favor through his persistent insistence. || 37-53 ||
His son was Narasiṃhagupta, renowned among the people as Cukhalaka, whose intellect was as pure as the moon;
his mind was brightened by immersion in the essence of all the śāstras.
Devotion to Maheśvara adorned her most exquisitely.
Having cast aside the surging waves of the ocean of youth and firmly boarded the ship of dispassion by means of resolute effort,
he who reaches the mountain of devotion and contemplates Maheśa—
With jewels, he completely shattered those calamities of worldly existence.
His son was the renowned Abhinavagupta,
purified by the pollen of the lotus feet of the venerable Moon-crested Lord;
indeed, his mother separated him from him while he was still in infancy.
For destiny prepares one for future refinement.

"Bhoga" means the body. "Nimeṣiṇī" means that which perishes in an instant. Regarding its greatness, the reason is the possession of the eye of the scriptures. In the phrase "in the lineage (gotra) of the name," it means belonging to the lineage of Atri; thus, the name and the lineage are indicated through a pun. The word "karaiḥ" denotes both hands and rays.
"Supremely" (*param*) means "exceedingly. By these two verses, the suitability of this place as a dwelling has been shown.

"He unites [them] with their own splendors" (*svair vibhavaiḥ yunakti*)—by this, its status as the locus of all sciences (*sarvavidyākara*) is revealed. "The powers" (*śakti*) refers to the group of four Siddhas; for that indeed...

[The deity is] white, red, yellow, and black in color. Regarding "a multitude of arrows"—this refers to [the acts of] withering and so forth, for passion (*rāga*) and the like are its effects. Regarding "the wheels"—this refers to the forms of the primary wheel and the subordinate wheels. Regarding "dark-red"—this means blackish-brown. Regarding "the triad of goddesses"—this is stated because it is appropriate to the context and so forth. Regarding "eloquent" (*vāgmī*)—

—Also Bṛhaspati; and Śanaiścara, whose gait is smooth. By the term "Aṅgāraka," the fire of the *udāna* breath is also indicated. By the state of having swallowed the sun and moon, both types of eclipses are implied. That king Pravarasena built a city, and in that [city], this twice-born man [resided].
"King Lalitāditya made his residence"—this is the connection with what follows at a distance.

By the phrase "flying up into the sky," even here the suitability for spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) is revealed. "That" refers to the bell. "Made of fire" refers to iron. "Enjoyment and liberation" refers to those two [topics] indicated by the pair of verses.
"Pināka"—this refers to the weapon, namely the trident. "In the city of Kubera"—that is, in the northern direction.
"He separated"—he brought about a state of being naturally disjoined; that is to say, he became one whose mother was deceased. ||56||
He clarifies that very latent impression (saṃskāra):
"The mother is the supreme kinsman"—such is the popular saying;
for affection makes the bonds exceedingly tight.
When that root-bond has dissolved, I believe that liberation exists for him even while he is still alive. || 37-57 ||
Having been introduced by his father into the dense thicket of grammar,
his mind was purified by the stainless spray from the waves of the ocean of logic;
devoted to the enjoyment of the thick aesthetic flavor of literature, he was like Maheśvara himself.
He was seized by her, who was intoxicated with the madness of her own spontaneous devotion. || 37-58 ||
Having become one with that [state], he no longer regarded any worldly path whatsoever;
rather,
in the past, he had done so solely for the sake of increasing his enjoyment of it.
He himself performs service in the dwellings of his teachers. || 37-59 ||
Regarding the phrase "purā karoti": the use of the present tense (*laṭ*) is according to the rule *yāvatpurānipātayorlaṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.4).
Anticipating the question, "Who are those gurus?", he says: "Vāmanātha, the son of the excellent teacher Erakavara, who is the helmsman of the great ocean of the lineage of bliss (ānandasaṃtati)."
The son of the illustrious Bhūtirāja, who was graced by his own father, was like the sun in the great sky of the lineage of Śrīnātha. || 37-60 ||
The Lord Lakṣmaṇagupta— son of Utpala, who was the son of Somānanda, who rested upon the ocean that is the expansion of the Traiyambaka lineage,
and who is the full moon in the great ocean of the tradition known as the Fourth (Turya).
From Śrī Soma, it is said, Śambhunātha became the knower of all things. || 37-61 ||
Śrī Candraśarman, Bhavabhaktivilāsa,
Yogānanda, Abhinanda, Śivaśakti, Vicitranātha, as well as others— Dharmaśiva, Vāmanaka, Udbhaṭa, and Śrī...
The great ones, headed by Bhūteśa, Bhāskara, and others. || 37-62 ||

These [disciples], having bestowed upon him their own office— which was made gracious by the favor manifested through their devotion to service and which was made beautiful by mature instructions on the essence of the scriptures—
did so because they perceived that people were not yet fit vessels for it.
Thus, delighting in his own self, he became one who incessantly relishes the service of reality.

Then, as he was directing his mind toward [his brother] named Manoratha— who was devoted to Śiva, filled with the discernment of all the scriptures, and his own brother— in order to bestow grace upon him,
At that time, a few people approached him.

"Known as the lineage of Turya"—this refers to the one called Ardhatryambaka. "Those who were not [proper] fields"—the meaning is those who were for the most part unworthy recipients. "He attended upon them"—the meaning is that he experienced the state of being their disciple. || 64 ||
He points out those very few people: "There was indeed one named Karṇa, the son of the illustrious Śauri, who in his youth realized the essence of the truth of Śambhu."
By casting off his body, he demonstrated to the people the truth of the Great Sage Kṛṣṇa’s words concerning one who has fallen from yoga.
Then his childhood friend was the renowned son of a minister named Śrīmān Mandra, who was delightful with all essential virtues;
Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī together adorned him equally.
The power of good fortune eclipses the enmity of co-wives. || 37-66 ||
Other nephews of my paternal uncle— Śivaśakti, Śubhra, Kṣema, Utpala, Abhinavacakraka, Padmagupta, and others—
who regarded worldly prosperity as a mere blade of grass due to their service to Śambhu; |||
Meditating upon their own hearts as being completely filled within the heart.

Rāmagupta—who had mastered in its entirety the rituals concerning the maṇḍalas and other matters within the Trika scriptures (the *Ṣaḍardhaśāstras*), and whose entire path was devoted to the practice of serving his Guru and the weapons of Śambhu—[attained this]. (37.68)
Any other person as well, whose own collection of powers is rendered subservient by the impulsion of the descent of Śiva’s power (śivaśaktipāta),
[attains this] through a state of being untrained in the refusal of requests.
By him, too, this group was rendered worthy of favor. || 37-69 ||
He earnestly entreated the teacher for the complete and perfect mastery of the tantra, so that his intellect, blessed by destiny, might truly arise [in this realization].
Prosperity is indeed that which has the singular essence of a continuous flow of success.
He too accepted what was desired by him; for indeed, whatever comes forth from one's own instrument is already present for one who wishes to dance.
For the true gurus are indeed inclined toward bestowing grace.
By the power of my wisdom, through the great sprout of the birth of virtue. || 37-71 ||
Then, desiring to avoid the state of distraction,
he chose a residence for him in his own excellent city, where even down to the cowherds and children, Maheśvara was present.
People live in servitude in that which is like a seat (pīṭha).
It is said that his paternal aunt was created by the Creator as one whose thoughts of the variegated cycle of existence had dissolved—
she who was devoted solely to the pollen of the lotus feet of the Moon-crested Lord.
The rules for adornment, which describe what is appropriate for Vatsalikā, have been set forth. || 37-73 ||
She was like forgiveness incarnate, as if compassion had taken on a physical form,
like the very embodiment of auspicious character,
and like the full, matured state of the essence of dispassion.
The mountain Rohaṇa where the jewels of the meaning of reality are beautifully situated.
Even her brother Śauri, whose mental disposition was supremely purified by devotion to the moon-crested Lord,
having assumed the office of the Lord’s minister—
He who abandoned the position of minister to the king. || 37-75 ||
His daughter-in-law, the wife of Karṇa,
having shaken off the ways of worldly existence, gave birth to an only son named Yogeśvaridatta.
The reality of the object flashes forth in accordance with its name. || 37-76 ||
In her youth, when she was at the very height of her beauty, the Three-Eyed God himself, out of devotion, took pity upon her who was distressed by separation from her husband;
for misfortune befalls those who are destined to possess the splendor of future power.
Truth draws forth the succession of all goals.
Having attained the clear ornament for the body consisting of horripilation arising from devotion, the forehead-mark consisting solely of prostration to Śrī Śambhunātha,
and the ear-ornament consisting of the Śaiva scriptures;
She bore within herself an exceeding degree of good fortune.
Known by the name Ambā, she indeed beheld that teacher, her own brother, with the vision of Śambhu,
her noble intellect radiant with the power of what was yet to come.
Being mindful, one disregards them, not out of a sense of kinship. || 37-79 ||
His brother, Abhinava by name, was such not only by his name but also by his own virtuous deeds.
Regarding the words of Kṛṣṇa, it is sung as follows:
Even one who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous.
Or else, it arises in the family of wise yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in the world.
There he regains that same mental disposition belonging to his previous body;
from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more for complete purification.
By that very same prior practice, one is carried forward even against one's will;
even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Word-Brahman.
"But the yogin who strives through practice, having his impurities completely purified and perfected over many births, then attains the supreme goal" (6.47).
"In the heart"—that is to say, in the sphere of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). *Śakti* means capacity. This...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: that group (varga) requested the teacher for the sake of attaining the complete Tantra. "Of this" refers to the group. "Or else"—this is an indication of an alternative position intended to show the impossibility of their request. "Of him" refers to Mandra. "The minister" implies the practitioner (sādhaka) as well.
He demonstrates that novelty is produced solely by one's conduct:
"For him, thirst increased excessively for that very [state] through the juice of consciousness which he had drunk. (37.80)
And that other man, Lumpaka, whose radiant splendor was formed by the closing of the lotus of his heart as its contraction was destroyed by the multitude of rays from Śambhu,
attended upon him during his exertions.
Ah, the virtuous man indeed provides a hand to hold.
Thus, remaining in the house bestowed by Vatsalikā,
he concentrated his mind and reflected with his own intellect upon many things previously heard.
From them, he acquired the essence of the scriptures.
He composed that highly significant treatise, which sets forth the reality of the tantras as proclaimed by reasoning and scripture,
having obtained whose light he [has attained this].
The world proceeds happily in its ritual actions. || 37-83 ||
O virtuous ones, please favor this work of his; first accept it, for such is the rule.
Then, may that [work] also accept your mind.
And may he immediately favor [me] with the vision of reality. || 37-84 ||
And in order to reveal that this treatise possesses a name that is true to its meaning, he says: "He [composed] that compendium," and so forth.
Furthermore, the words "previously" and "that too" are stated in order to demonstrate the reversal of the sequence between "favoring" (*anugraha*) and "grasping" (*grahaṇa*). || 84 ||
Or rather, what need is there for the request of learned persons who possess only partial expertise? Śiva himself will be the listener here—thus he says:
"This essence of the scriptures, woven by Abhinavagupta..."
O Śiva, listen for a moment with your faculty of hearing directed everywhere;
this is indeed your praise, for it is a contemplation of your own nature. Thus, being newly gratified, make the world your own. (37.85)

O Supreme Lord Śiva! You, who are the listener, please hear from me this essence among all scriptures, which has been woven with excellence by Abhinavagupta—whose renown was attained through contemplation of Your feet and whose very self consists of the internalization of the true reality of all sciences; such is the meaning.

Since you possess the faculty of hearing everywhere—meaning, you are omniscient—the implication is that one who is not omniscient has no authority whatsoever to make such a definitive determination. Nor is this alone the reason here; thus he says: "This is indeed your praise. And its nature here is that of a hymn of praise.

"It is not to be doubted that it does not exist"—thus he says: "For that is the contemplation of Your form. That praise is indeed the contemplation of the form of You, the one to be praised; the meaning is that it is a repeated reflection upon Your essential nature.
And that very [contemplation] has been described here at every step as the non-dual consciousness of Śiva.
O Lord, being well-pleased with this new hymn of mine from all sides,
please make the entire world your own by means of its recognition as your very self, so that it becomes one in essence with your own nature.
May you accomplish this, so that everyone may possess the qualification for its realization; may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of What is to be Adopted," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
This thirty-seventh daily lesson has indeed been determined by Jayaratha;
may this [work] be entirely auspicious for the virtuous who contemplate it to its conclusion.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of What is to be Adopted," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the illustrious and great teacher of Maheśvara, the venerable Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by the illustrious Jayaratha. || 37 ||
This work is completed.
